Chapter Formal Verification of Imperative First-Class Functions in Move: IN Book: Proceedings of the 26th Conference on Formal Methods in Computer-Aided Design …

W Grieskamp, T Zhang, V Kashyap, J Silverman · library.oapen.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an extension of the Move Prover (MVP) — a production Boogie/Z3-based verifier for Move smart contracts — to formally verify imperative first-class functions (closures that can modify global state, be stored in structs, and be persisted in storage), via new specification constructs called behavioral predicates and state labels. - Why it's important: Move on Aptos shipped higher-order functions in late 2025, and smart contracts using persisted callbacks and dynamic dispatch (e.g., AMM pricing curves stored in pools) currently have no modular, automated verification story; the alternative is unverified financial logic on a public blockchain. - How it does it: For each function type, the prover statically enumerates every function-value variant that can reach a call site (closure, parameter, or stored field) as an algebraic datatype, then encodes invocation either by inlining the concrete callee or by asserting/assuming behavioral predicates (requires_of, aborts_of, ensures_of) over explicitly threaded memory snapshots, with state labels naming intermediate states so sequential effectful calls compose. - The good: The encoding is validated end-to-end by a differential pipeline — a weakest-precondition spec-inference tool independently generates behavioral-predicate specifications that MVP re-verifies across 27 test categories with 550+ inferred conditions, all passing — and the whole closure test suite (~240 verified functions) runs in under 5 minutes on standard GitHub CI runners. - The missing: There is no evaluation beyond the authors' own examples and test suite: no benchmark corpus of real higher-order Move contracts exists, no timing/comparison against alternative encodings (e.g., separation-logic-based ones), and the soundness of the encoding is argued informally rather than machine-checked. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or extend SMT-based program verifiers and need a concrete, production-tested recipe for imperative higher-order functions with frame conditions; skip it if you want empirical evidence of scalability on real-world contract corpora — the paper explicitly does not provide that yet.

Completeness (80) and Resilience (78) are strong: limitations (variant-set scalability, compliance-side proof burden, missing benchmark corpus) are confronted with unusual directness, and claims are well-bounded. Impact (82) is high for the profile — the encoding ships in the production Aptos toolchain with public pinned test artifacts and a differential inference-vs-verification pipeline (27 categories, 550+ conditions). Rigor (72) is capped by self-validation on authors' own examples, an unmeasured 'more efficient than separation logic' claim, and informally argued soundness of two optimizations; Non-Obviousness (75) is solid but not paradigm-shifting. Problem & Motivation: Move on Aptos recently extended the language so functions are first-class values that can be passed, returned, stored in struct fields, and persisted in global storage, enabling dynamic dispatch (callback-based asset flows, extensible asset managers, dispatchable permissions, generic fold/map/filter). This breaks the modular static-dispatch specification style on which MVP was built: when a call is dispatched dynamically, its pre/postconditions cannot be looked up at the call site, and the verifier must reconcile abstract caller-side specifications with whichever concrete function reaches the call site — quickly, predictably, and without SMT trigger instability. Existing verifiers do not cover this exact setting: Dafny does not allow function values to modify state; Verus threads state as explicit arguments; Prusti requires separation logic; Solidity verifiers use manual case-splitting. Key Idea: Make function specifications themselves first-class: characterize any function value f by total, variant-indexed behavioral predicates (requires_of/aborts_of/ensures_of, plus a result_of uninterpreted function pinned to ensures by a deliberately one-directional axiom), and evaluate these predicates over named memory snapshots (state labels) that can be universally or existentially quantified. On the SMT side, the static variant set of each function type (closures, entry-point parameters, storable fields — known after monomorphization) is materialized as an algebraic datatype, so invocation is a case split: concrete closures inline, abstract variants use the predicates. Move's alias-free references and type-indexed resource memory make the frame conditions cheap — no separation-logic machinery is needed. Methodology: The paper specifies the encoding at the level of a Boogie-style imperative verification language (IVL) with havoc, assume/assert, algebraic datatypes, and type-indexed maps M_ρ : address → ρ for each resource type. Pipeline: (1) after monomorphization, MVP's mono-analysis records the sets of closure constructors C_τ, function-typed parameters P_τ, and storable function-typed fields F_τ for each function type, and emits one datatype constructor per variant (field variants carry an integer discriminator so distinct stored closures are not collapsed); (2) read/write footprints M_τ and Δ_τ are computed per variant — from code for closures, from declared reads_of/modifies_of clauses for parameters and fields (wildcard modifies is unsupported because it yields no effective frame condition); (3) invocation is encoded by the invoke_τ schema: assert requires, conditional abort flag, havoc within Δ_τ, then assume ensures over frozen pre-state M'_τ and post-state M_τ; (4) behavioral predicates are encoded not as Boogie functions with bodies (which caused eager-unfolding blowups) but as uninterpreted functions connected by per-variant axioms with explicitly chosen triggers; (5) state labels are materialized as flat existentially quantified snapshots (M_S, v̄_S), with aborts at an intermediate state synthesized from the defining ensures conjuncts plus the aborts clause, justified by the validity invariant ⋁A ∨ ⋀P. Critical design decisions: the one-directional result axiom (a biconditional would be inconsistent when ensures under-constrains the outcome, e.g. `ensures result > 0`); dropping constraining conjuncts from the state-label existential (sound by the validity invariant); and the flat rather than recursive label encoding. Each is justified in the text, though soundness is argued, not proven. A weakest-precondition specification-inference tool is extended to emit behavioral-predicate specs for arbitrary higher-order code, doubling as a differential-validation oracle. Key Results: The evaluation is entirely on the authors' own examples and test suites; no external benchmark exists (the paper states higher-order Move shipped in late 2025 and a contract corpus is only now forming, partly closed-source). Reported figures: the closure portion of the prover test suite comprises 19 test modules with ~240 verified functions and 66 expected-error diagnoses; the inference suite has 27 categories with over 550 inferred conditions, all passing end-to-end; the combined suites run in under 5 minutes on standard GitHub runners with a 40-second default timeout per verification condition, in CI on every prover change. The running AMM example verifies non-linear constant-product and monotonicity invariants over a stored pricing closure — including detecting that the with_fee pricing function violates the no-abort invariant — with the fee variants needing one- or two-line proof hints (a case split and a stepping-stone assertion); application-side verification (swap, find callers) needs no extra hints. The higher-order find example demonstrates reusable loop-summary verification: callers of opaque higher-order functions discharge postconditions without loop invariants or seeing the lambda body. There are no comparisons against alternative encodings or other verifiers, so claims of efficiency are relative to MVP's own pre-extension cost model only. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with a secondary NEW FORMULATION component). The genuinely novel elements are the first-class behavioral predicates with quantifiable state labels for imperative, state-mutating first-class functions, and the statically-enumerated datatype encoding of function-value variants with per-variant triggered axioms. The underlying machinery — Boogie translation, havoc/assume/assert call schema, WP-based spec inference, trigger discipline — is a competent application of known techniques (Dafny/Boogie tradition, VDM/Z-style relational specification), and the paper is appropriately candid about which details differ from Dafny, Verus, Prusti, F*, and Certora. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is indirect but real: the differential inference-vs-verification pipeline (27 categories, 550+ conditions) tests whether the axioms are strong enough to discharge tightly inferred specs — 'usable, not merely sound' — and the 66 expected-error diagnoses test diagnostic behavior. No error bars, seeds, or statistical tests (not really applicable to a verifier). Artifacts are public: paper examples and the inference test suite are pinned in the aptos-core repository (commit 28f82080e3), and the implementation ships in the production Aptos toolchain. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation is exclusively on the authors' own examples and test suite — self-validation on the same artifact the encoding was developed against; (2) no head-to-head comparison of SMT encoding cost against separation-logic or state-passing alternatives, so the claim of 'more efficient SMT encodings' is asserted, not measured; (3) soundness of the encoding (e.g., the conjunct-dropping and flat-existential optimizations) rests on informal arguments, not a machine-checked meta-theorem. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a production verifier extension, exercised empirically through its own test suites). - Practical: Yes — it runs as part of the shipped Aptos toolchain on standard GitHub CI runners; no exotic hardware. - Efficient: Full closure + inference suites complete in under 5 minutes with a 40-second per-VC timeout, consistent with MVP's 'seconds per function' design goal, though no per-feature timing breakdown is given. - Effective: The evidence covers curated examples (AMM, find, followed_by) and internal test suites; it does not yet demonstrate solving the problem on a body of real third-party higher-order contracts. - Scalable: Untested beyond small curated examples — the authors themselves flag that enumerating all closure variants will not scale to large or open variant sets (e.g., dynamically loaded modules), and compliance-side verification of universal function properties is expected to need substantial proof hints. The work delivers a software artifact: a production verifier extension, specification-language constructs, an inference tool, and public example/test repositories. Strengths: - The variant-enumeration datatype encoding is a clean, statically-justified move: after monomorphization the set of function values reaching a call site is finite and known, converting higher-order verification into a first-order case split without user-visible specification restructuring. - The relational, state-label formulation (S |∼ p, S1..S2 |∼ q, quantifiable over labels) is more expressive than Dafny's state labels — supporting relational hyperproperties like pricing monotonicity (relating two invocations of the same function value) and existential witness states for sequenced calls — while avoiding separation-logic overhead thanks to Move's alias-free reference and resource model. - The differential validation pipeline (independent WP inference feeding back into verification) is a genuinely clever self-testing mechanism that caught nothing trivially but provides ongoing regression protection, and the per-variant trigger discipline documents real SMT-engineering lessons (eager body unfolding blowup) useful to any Boogie-based verifier builder. - Honest positioning against Dafny, Verus, Prusti, F*, Lean 4, and Certora, with specific technical deltas rather than strawman comparisons. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations unusually directly: (1) compliance-side verification of universal function properties 'will not be automated easily' and will need substantial proof hints or trusted assumptions; (2) wildcard modifies_of is unsupported because it destroys frame conditions; (3) the variant-enumeration encoding does not scale to large or open variant sets (dynamically loaded modules); (4) sequence-quantified state labels (∀S0..Sn) for fold-like iteration are future work; (5) non-linear arithmetic (pricing formulas) requires user proof hints; (6) no benchmark corpus of real higher-order contracts exists yet; (7) aborts conditions currently cannot be left unspecified for function values (unlike ordinary functions). This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The soundness of the encoding — especially the two optimizations (dropping constraining conjuncts from the state-label existential; the flat rather than recursive label scheme) — rests on informal invariants (⋁A ∨ ⋀P) that are stated but not proven, even semi-formally; a bug here would make the prover accept false contracts, which for smart contracts is the worst failure mode. (2) All empirical evidence comes from artifacts the authors built to exercise the encoding — a circularity the differential pipeline mitigates but does not eliminate, since both sides share the same semantics of behavioral predicates and state labels. (3) The claim that the encoding is 'more efficient than separation logic' is never measured against an actual separation-logic implementation. (4) No data on how the 40-second timeout behaves on the non-linear AMM compliance obligations or larger variant sets — the scalability boundary is unexplored in both directions. (5) The determinism assumption (no in-language nondeterminism) is stated as a Move property but its interaction with persisted function values read from storage in different transactions is not discussed. Beyond these, the paper is internally consistent and does not overclaim its evaluation. Bottom Line: For verifier builders and Move contract developers, this is required reading — it is the only published treatment of imperative first-class functions in an SMT-based modular verifier and ships in production — but it is a design/encoding paper whose scalability and real-world effectiveness claims rest on curated examples rather than measured evidence.

Rewriting Scaling Laws for Synthetic Data with Compute and Data Constraints

N Roberts, A Ahmed, S Kotha, P Liang, Y Wang… · arxiv.org · Percy Liang - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a "rewriting scaling law" — L(N, D, R, T) = A/N^α + B/D^β + E(R) + F(R, D, T) — that predicts pretraining loss as a function of model size, tokens, the fraction R of training tokens that are LLM-generated rewrites of natural documents, and epochs over the natural seed set, while explicitly charging the FLOPs spent generating the rewrites (C_total = 6ND + 4NrDR). - Why it's important: Synthetic rewrites are now a standard ingredient in pretraining corpora, but practitioners have no principled answer to how much compute to spend rewriting versus training, and a widespread worry is that a model trained on rewrites is capped by its rewriter's capability. - How it does it: The law adds a rewrite-fraction-dependent irreducible-loss term E(R), derived as a two-component KL approximation between the evaluation distribution and the natural/rewrite mixture, on top of a Chinchilla-style backbone plus a repetition penalty, and optimizes R subject to a compute constraint that includes generation cost. - The good: The law fit on ladders through 3×10^20 FLOPs forecast a held-out 10^22-FLOP, 22B-parameter run (33× extrapolation) to within 1.1% of measured loss, and the predicted-optimal rewrite fraction (R = 0.32) was indeed the best of four tested at that scale. - The missing: Every headline conclusion rests on one natural corpus (FineWeb-Edu), one rewrite-style family (four FinePhrase prompts), and one external rewriter (SmolLM2-1.7B); the DCLM control shows the optimal fraction drops to ~0.08 on a stronger seed set, so the quantitative prescriptions may not transfer. - Read it or not: Read it if you make data-mixture or compute-allocation decisions for LLM pretraining (the cost-accounted scaling-law methodology and the student-beats-rewriter evidence are directly actionable); skip it if you only need another confirmation that synthetic data helps — the fits and appendix grids are dense but the qualitative takeaway is now expected.

Non-Obviousness (76) and Resilience (78) are high: the student-beats-rewriter result is well-controlled (size-matched rewriter on the same seed set) and claims are explicitly bounded by the DCLM control and flagged extrapolations. Completeness (78) benefits from exceptional candid reporting of negative results. Practical Impact (72) reflects a directly actionable compute-allocation recipe with released fit tooling, though no model weights. Problem & Motivation: Teams pretraining language models face a compute-vs-data squeeze: high-quality natural text is growing far slower than training compute budgets, and LLM rewrites of natural documents (Wikipedia-style, textbook-style, FAQ, table, tutorial) have become a standard patch. Two decisions are made by intuition today: (1) what fraction of the training corpus should be synthetic rewrites, given that generating a rewrite costs a substantial fraction of the FLOPs of training on it, and (2) whether a rewriter's capability ceiling limits the student model trained on its output. Prior scaling-law studies of synthetic data (Kang et al. 2025; Qin et al. 2025, 2026) treat rewrites as free, so their optima answer a different question. The paper targets both the small-scale scientific workflow (compute-limited, plentiful natural data, stronger external rewriter) and the frontier workflow (data-limited, fixed seed set, rewriter no stronger than the target). Key Idea: Charge the generation compute of every rewritten token inside the scaling-law optimization, and model rewrites as shifting only the irreducible loss floor E(R) — not the speed of learning in N and D. Once stated, the approach is reconstructible: E(R) = E0 − λn·log(1−(1−ρn)R) − λs·log(ρs+(1−ρs)R) is a strictly convex two-component KL approximation whose interior minimizer is the asymptotic optimal mixture; a repetition penalty P(1−R)^s((1−R)D/T − 1)+ (adopted from Lovelace et al.) handles epoching in the data-limited case; and the constrained argmin over (N, D, R) at 6ND + 4NrRD = C_total yields the compute-optimal rewrite fraction. Because generation cost is linear in D while loss improves as a power law, the optimal R necessarily grows with budget. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) build IsoFLOP ladders — in the compute-limited setting, Qwen3-architecture dense models (Llama 3 tokenizer, 4096 context, Adam + Hyperball optimizer, tuned 156M reference with GP search, hyperparameter transfer recipe) trained on FineWeb-Edu at eleven rewrite fractions R ∈ {0, 0.1, ..., 1.0} across budgets 3×10^18 to 9×10^19 FLOPs, plus R=0 ladders at 1.8×10^20 and 3×10^20 FLOPs, using released FinePhrase SmolLM2-1.7B rewrites; (2) fit the joint surface in three stages — mixture-KL floor E(R), pooled Chinchilla Approach-2 frontier promoted to Approach-3 exponents, and an off-frontier curvature term — over 604 Paloma BPB observations; (3) forecast and validate at 10^21 (all eleven R) and 10^22 FLOPs (four R values including the predicted optimum R = 0.32, a 21.9B-parameter / 76B-token run). The data-limited setting uses a fixed 5B-token FineWeb-Edu seed set; for each target size (550M, 837M, 1B, 3B) a same-size rewriter is pretrained on the seed set, SFT'd on only 7M tokens (GLM-5.2 rewrites of 1000 documents, checkpoint selected by an Elo-based LM judge), then used to rewrite the seed set; targets are trained at epoch budgets W = 3–24 across six rewrite fractions (192 runs), with the law fit per target–rewriter pair on W ≤ 18 and W = 21, 24 held out. Critical design decisions: (a) rewrites shift the floor only — tested via the collapse of 82 IsoFLOP-optimal observations across 3,333× compute onto one curve g̃(R) with RMSE 0.0044 BPB, well justified; (b) generation costed at 4Nr FLOPs/token with equal rewrite length and no rewriter-pretraining amortization — acknowledged as approximate; (c) a shared compute-optimal (N, D) across all R — tested against per-R fits, with wild-bootstrap significance (p = 1/401) that per-R offsets exist but showing the shared choice costs ≤0.0015 BPB at the median, well justified. Key Results: Compute-limited: the estimated optimal rewrite fraction rises monotonically with budget — under 10% at 3×10^18 FLOPs to 32% at 10^22 FLOPs on Paloma, with task-specific asymptotes of 1.0 for Math and Code, 0.77 for QA, and 0.32 for Paloma. The 10^22-FLOP run at the predicted R = 0.32 achieved 0.983 Paloma macro BPB versus a forecast of ~0.99 (−1.1% error), the lowest among all models trained at that scale; R = 0 gave 1.061. At 10^22 FLOPs, R = 1 versus R = 0 cuts Math BPB from 1.33 to 0.80 and Code BPB from 1.04 to 0.53. The R = 0.32 run beats its rewriter SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct (trained at ≈1.1×10^23 FLOPs, ~11× the hero run's budget) on 10 of 16 Paloma sources, coming within 0.012 BPB on the macro average (0.983 vs 0.972). Data-limited: the law fit on W ≤ 18 selects fractions whose loss is within 0.74% of the best observed R at held-out budgets (worst selection gap 1.14%, at 3B/W=24); best observed R rises from 0.13 at W=3 to 0.71 at W=24 for the 3B target; and rewrite mixtures beat natural-only epoching at every model size up to 3B, with natural-only runs overfitting beyond W=3. Baselines (Chinchilla-style natural-only training, epoching per Muennighoff et al. 2023 and Lovelace et al. 2026, and the token-effectiveness model of Qin et al. 2026) are current and appropriate. Notably, the authors directly rebut Qin et al.'s projection that paraphrasing stops helping beyond 7B: their 22B run gains 0.078 BPB over natural-only. Tested scale spans ~1,000× in FLOPs within the ladders and one 33× extrapolation validated. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a compute-and-data-constrained scaling law for synthetic rewrites that charges generation FLOPs inside the optimization — prior synthetic-data scaling laws omit this term) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the optimal rewrite fraction grows with compute, and a student can match or exceed its rewriter on 10/16 domains at one-tenth the rewriter's training compute, and beat a same-size self-rewriter at every scale to 3B). The components — Chinchilla terms, the Lovelace repetition penalty, KL-based floor modeling — are existing ideas; the genuinely novel part is the cost-accounted formulation, the derivation of E(R) as a mixture-KL with a closed-form convex parametric form, and the disciplined two-setting experimental design that tests rewriter-capability ceilings in both regimes. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: repetition-penalty form ablation (six variants, showing the dilution factor (1−R)^s is necessary and that Lovelace's δ = 1.84 does not transfer), curvature-term ablation (likelihood ratio 1006.6), surface-specification ladder (M1/M2/M3 with BIC), rewriter-capacity control, SFT vs SFT+DPO alignment control, style and line-type ablations, and a DCLM seed-set control. Significance is addressed via wild bootstrap tests (400 draws) for fit restrictions, though no multi-seed training runs or error bars on headline losses are reported. Forward leave-one-budget-out forecasts are reported for every budget (mean errors within ±1.4%, 33× extrapolation at −1.04%). The fit script and cached outputs are stated to be "released with the code," built on the open Marin/Levanter stack, but no explicit repository URL appears in the provided text, and trained checkpoint release is not stated. Methodological cautions: the 10^22 hero run is included as a frontier anchor in the final surface fit (though the honest forward-forecast table excludes it); hyperparameters and reference-model selection are tuned on Paloma, which is also the headline evaluation — a mild Goodhart risk the authors partially confront when explaining why QA/Math/Code forecasts are worse (4%/14%/32% error at their own optima vs 1% for Paloma). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a secondary SYSTEMS flavor via the released fit tooling). - Practical: Yes — the largest run is a 21.9B-parameter model at 10^22 FLOPs (~76B tokens), well within commercial-scale training; the small-scale recipe is deliberately reproducible on academic hardware. - Efficient: Rewrite generation adds 4Nr FLOPs per rewritten token; measured generation share at the break-even optima is 0.94%–6.96% of total compute, so the overhead is small at the recommended fractions, though it doubles per-token cost at R=1 in the data-limited setting (5R/(3+2R) of FLOPs go to rewriting). - Effective: The evidence shows the law selects loss-minimizing mixtures on Paloma BPB and gold-answer BPB proxies; full downstream accuracy behavior is only spot-checked (a logistic accuracy fit exists in Appendix N.5), so effectiveness on real task accuracy is demonstrated indirectly. - Scalable: Only claimed beyond 10^22 FLOPs via extrapolation — the fits project a natural-only frontier diverging from the rewrite frontier at 3.61×10^26 FLOPs (or 1.75×10^24 under an alternative fit), a 24× spread the authors flag as extrapolation; nothing is trained above 10^22. The work ships a released fit script/codebase (no URL stated), reported fitted parameters for all surfaces, and no released model weights mentioned. Strengths: - The cost-accounted optimization (Eq. 3) is the right formalization and, to my knowledge, the first synthetic-data scaling law where generation compute enters the argmin — this changes the answer (optimal R rises with budget) in a way the free-rewrite laws of Kang et al. and Qin et al. cannot express. - The 33× extrapolation is validated, not just asserted: the 10^22 run was held out of the fit range, landed within 1.1% of forecast, and the predicted-optimal R beat all tested alternatives — the strongest single piece of evidence in the paper. - The RQ2 result is a clean, well-controlled answer to a standing question: in the data-limited setting the rewriter is size-matched and trained on the same 5B-token seed set (plus only 7M instruction tokens), so the student surpassing it at every size to 3B rules out "the rewriter just knows more" as the explanation. - The appendix quality is exceptional — negative results are reported candidly (e.g., the no-dilution penalty form actually selects better fractions at held-out budgets despite worse RMSE; per-domain forecast errors of 14–32% on Math/Code are dissected rather than hidden). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) all headline optima are for FineWeb-Edu, with a DCLM control showing rewrites help less on a stronger seed set (fitted floor-optimal R ≈ 0.078 vs 0.33); (2) only four FinePhrase rewrite styles and one external rewriter per setting are tested, so optimal fractions may not transfer across prompt distributions or rewriter families; (3) the compute accounting is approximate — 4Nr FLOPs/token assumes decode costs like prefill, equal rewrite/source length, and no rewriter-pretraining cost. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-seed training runs throughout: with no repeated runs at fixed (N, D, R), the 0.5–1.14% selection-gap numbers that constitute the RQ1 result are not placed against run-to-run variance, which is plausibly of similar magnitude. - The hyperparameter recipe (learning rates, β2 schedule) is tuned once on a Paloma objective and then transferred to every run, including the headline Paloma comparisons — the rewriter (SmolLM2) used a different recipe, so part of the student-beats-rewriter margin could be recipe asymmetry rather than a rewrites-only effect. - The 10^22 comparison against SmolLM2-Instruct conflates data mixture with total knowledge: SmolLM2 trained on FineMath, Stack-Edu, and StarCoderData, and the authors themselves attribute the Paloma sources where the student loses (code, Dolma 100 PLs at 0.694 vs 0.511) to corpus coverage differences — meaning "surpasses the rewriter" is corpus-dependent, not a general capability statement. - The E(R) floor model has ρs pinned at its 10^−4 lower bound in most fits (and ρs at bound in the 1B data-limited fit), suggesting the parametric form is at or beyond the edge of what the data identifies; extrapolations of bR*(W) beyond W = 24 are explicitly flagged as weakly identified (s = 1.5–7.0 across pairs), so the monotone-increase prescription is only validated within the tested grid. - No evaluation of rewrite faithfulness or factual-error propagation at scale (the appendix shows arithmetic mistakes and invented details in qualitative examples but measures no aggregate fidelity), leaving open whether the loss gains come with contamination-style risks. Bottom Line: For anyone deciding how to allocate compute between rewriting and pretraining, this is now the reference work — the cost-accounted scaling-law framework, the validated 33× extrapolation, and the student-beats-rewriter result are each independently worth the read, and no prior paper (Kang et al., Qin et al.) covers the same ground with generation costs in the objective.

Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs (53 ▲ )

Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proves a Platonic Representation Theorem — that JEPAs trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of the same scene — and empirically demonstrates that such "good views" deliver 42× more sample-efficient cross-modal alignment than next-token prediction on the same corpus. - Why it's important: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) was previously only an observational claim, so the only lever for building cross-modally aligned representations was brute-force scale; a theorem with an actionable condition (view construction, not scale) directly challenges the assumption that trillion-token LLM-style training is the route to shared world representations. - How it does it: The core move is a spectral embedding argument — a JEPA with whitened second-order anti-collapse provably learns the top eigenvectors of the graph drawn by its positive pairs, so if all modalities' positives relate the same world states, their objectives are one problem in different coordinates, and next-token prediction is reframed as a JEPA whose positives (prefix, continuation) are "bad views" sharing a document's nuisance. - The good: The view effect is isolated cleanly: on identical texts, encoders, and steps, a good-view JEPA reaches .125 mutual 10-NN with DINOv2 on WIT-1024 where bad-view (.063) and next-token (.079) variants on the same corpus stay far below, at every data scale tested, and a fitted scaling law predicts 85 unseen runs with RMSE .0093 versus .0096 for rerunning with another seed. - The missing: The headline comparisons against language models up to 72B rest on Recap-DataComp texts where two of three views per image are LLaVA-generated recaptions that carry CLIP-distilled image information — a confound the authors disclose but that limits the "109M beats 72B" claim — and no experiment satisfies the theorem's hypotheses (finite world, injective renderings, population optima, spectral-gap uniqueness). - Read it or not: Worth a full read for anyone doing theory of self-supervised or multimodal representation learning, or deciding whether JEPA-style objectives deserve investment over scaled next-token training; skimmable if you only care about deployed captioning systems, where the paper's .838 CIDEr on COCO still trails pair-trained systems.

Problem & Motivation: Huh et al. (ICML 2024) observed that vision and language model representations become increasingly aligned with scale and named this the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, but it lacked a proof, a characterization of when it holds, and any recipe for improving alignment — leaving scale as the only known lever. Practitioners training encoders on separate modalities (images, text, video, audio) have no guidance on which objective makes their representations mutually alignable, and the field's default objective, next-token prediction, consumes 15–18T tokens to achieve alignment that the paper argues is achievable far more cheaply. The paper closes this gap by asking: when do models trained separately on different modalities provably learn the same representation? Key Idea: The single core insight is that a whitened JEPA learns the spectral embedding of the graph its positive pairs draw on the world (Proposition 1, a population form of Laplacian eigenmaps). Everything follows from this: if all modalities' positives relate the same world states ("good views" — two photographs or two captions of one scene), their training problems are identical up to the injective rendering, so their solutions coincide up to rotation (Theorem 1); if positives are corruptions of one observation ("bad views"), the encoder spends embedding directions on modality-specific nuisance (wording, viewpoint) that no rotation can align (Theorems 2–3, Proposition 3); and next-token prediction is exactly a bad-view JEPA whose anti-collapse term is the softmax log-partition and whose positives are a prefix and its continuation (Proposition 4). Methodology: Theory: encoders minimize a rotation-invariant objective ℓ(f(x), f(x′)) + Ω(f) over positive pairs from a symmetric distribution π; Lemma 1 shows injective renderings only change coordinates; Theorem 1 reduces cross-modal agreement to uniqueness-up-to-rotation of the shared objective, established for whitened MSE under a spectral gap (Ky Fan's principle, giving the spectral embedding Φπ of the normalized adjacency Kπ = D^(−1/2)ΠD^(−1/2)). Theorem 2 bounds misalignment after the best rotation via a Davis–Kahan argument on the kernel mismatch; Theorem 3 lower-bounds best-rotation error by 2k(1 − min ρ(f_m)) where ρ is the scene-explained fraction of the embedding; Theorem 4 extends to arbitrary view/data combinations via an "induced world kernel." Empirics: BERT encoders (33M/109M) trained with LeJEPA (SIGReg, λ = 0.02) in three variants differing only in positives — caption views (good), masked spans (bad), next-token — on Flickr30k, then on the texts of 2.16M–940M Recap-DataComp web images, evaluated against frozen DINOv2 under the PRH paper's WIT-1024 protocol (mutual 10-NN) plus Procrustes-rotation retrieval on Flickr. Critical design decisions: (1) identity predictor (analysis and experiments exclude learned predictors/world-model JEPAs — acknowledged); (2) gradient clipping to prevent SIGReg collapses, justified by an ablation showing 3/36 runs collapse without it; (3) view trimming as the dominant knob (whole captions lose 25% of alignment R@1, .246 → .185), justified by a one-change-at-a-time sweep showing all other knobs move results within seed spread. Key Results: On Flickr30k, good-view text JEPAs reach mutual 10-NN .062 with a separately trained image JEPA versus .047 (bad views) and .042 (next-token), with R@1 through one rotation at .044 versus .027/.021 (44× chance; mean ± half-range over 3 seeds). At scale, a 109M text JEPA on the texts of 940M web images reaches .184 mutual 10-NN with DINOv2 ViT-B on WIT-1024, above Qwen2.5-72B (.154), Llama-3-70B (.151), and CLIP's text encoder (.124), with linear CKA .507 versus Qwen2.5-72B's .418; it read 116B tokens versus 15–18T for the LLMs. The good-view JEPA reaches next-token prediction's alignment (.109 vs .111) with 42× fewer samples (21.6M vs 900M). A fitted scaling law R@1 = a + d·log M + b·log(1 + q^α·M^β·N^γ/c) predicts 85 held-out runs with RMSE .0093, matching seed-to-seed noise (.0096), though it fails at 320M samples (4× beyond fitted range) for good views. Applications: an image captioner built from frozen DINOv2/DINOv3 encoders joined to a text-only-trained decoder by one rotation reaches CIDEr .838 on COCO (versus .038 random rotation; paired-encoder systems report .918 CapDec); with zero pairs, the pair-free alignment method of Schnaus et al. yields 64.4% ImageNet-100 top-5 with the 109M good-view JEPA versus their best reported 56% and their rerun Qwen3-8B at 47.6% (Mann–Whitney p < .001). Baselines include current LLMs (Qwen2.5 up to 72B, Llama-3, Mistral-7B) and recent pair-free alignment work; the theory is validated numerically on 300 synthetic worlds where measured error never exceeds 18% of the Theorem 2 bound. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW THEORETICAL RESULT (good/bad-view dichotomy; PRH as a theorem for spectral JEPAs; next-token prediction as a bad-view JEPA with log-partition anti-collapse), plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (views, not scale, are the alignment lever; a scaling law in the good-view fraction) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (rotation-only captioner). The spectral-embedding view of SSL objectives, Davis–Kahan perturbation bounds, orthogonal Procrustes alignment, and pair-free matching via shared geometry (Schnaus et al.) are all established tools; the genuine novelty is composing them into a proof with a design prescription and demonstrating that the prescription, not scale, drives the headline cross-model gaps. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: one-change-at-a-time sweeps over views, masking, batch, width, learning rate, and SIGReg weight (Table 8, 3 seeds per setting); direct measurement of the Theorem 3 nuisance quantity ρ(f) on real encoders, which orders encoders as alignment does (Spearman .98); numerical checks of every theorem in the appendix; bootstrap 95% intervals on the small WIT-1024 benchmark; and a disclosed sensitivity — a fourth 940M-image training seed with doubled SIGReg weight reached only .121, dropping the four-seed average to .168 (still above all LLMs). A methodological concern is present and partially addressed: hyperparameters were tuned only for the good-view JEPA (the authors state this), the theory is developed and validated on the same PRH benchmark used for headline evaluation (WIT-1024, mitigated by Flickr/COCO/MSR-VTT cross-checks and a contamination check removing 43 of 1,024 WIT captions, changing scores by ≤.002), and several scaling runs use one seed. Code is built on the public stable-pretraining library with a code link and live demo indicated on page 1; no explicit repository URL appears in the provided text. This is an arXiv preprint (2610.39302, dated Oct 2026), not peer-reviewed, and authored by the LeJEPA/JEPA lineage (Balestriero, LeCun), which warrants independent-replication caution given the pro-JEPA framing. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a THEORETICAL component; the check below covers the experiments). - Practical: Yes — most runs fit on one GPU (BERT-S/BERT-B), the largest runs on 8–16 GPUs, and the captioner requires only frozen encoders plus one linear map. - Efficient: The central selling point — a 109M-parameter text JEPA reading 116B tokens achieves alignment that Qwen2.5-72B (660× more parameters, 15–18T tokens) reaches or exceeds only partially; captioning via frozen encoders + Procrustes avoids any paired cross-modal training. - Effective: For alignment and pair-free zero-shot classification the evidence is direct and strong; for captioning, CIDEr .838 on COCO trails pair-trained systems (~.91–.92) and the video captioner (.246 CIDEr on MSR-VTT) trails video-text systems (.271–.329), so it solves alignment but not yet captioning quality. - Scalable: Tested to 940M images and 116B text tokens, but the scaling law's exponents are poorly identified and it fails 4× beyond its fitted range; scaling good image views (which require multiple observations per scene, e.g., video) is explicitly left open, and the image side at scale remains a bad-view (crop) JEPA. The work delivers a reusable recipe (trimmed good views + gradient clipping), a theory-validation codebase on stable-pretraining, and a demo captioner; model weights are not stated as released. Strengths: - The reduction of PRH to a single checkable condition (shared positives over world states) via the spectral embedding of the positive-pair graph is a genuine conceptual contribution — it converts an unfalsifiable-sounding hypothesis into a design rule. - The next-token-as-bad-view-JEPA decomposition (Eq. 6: prediction term + log-partition anti-collapse; identification only up to GL(k), not rotation) is a sharp, falsifiable reframing that explains LLM–vision misalignment structurally rather than by scale. - The empirical design isolates the causal variable: identical texts, encoders, and steps across view types, with the caption-pair control showing the same paired information helps next-token prediction almost not at all (.042→.043 mutual 10-NN) while it transforms JEPA views — this rules out "more information" as the explanation. - Measuring the theory's own intermediate quantity (scene-explained fraction ρ) on real encoders, with Theorem 3's bound respected by measured errors and ranking encoders correctly, is rare theory-to-practice discipline. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a "Known limitations" section plus scattered disclosures): theorems are population statements over finite worlds with injective renderings and matched marginals; uniqueness is proved only for second-order anti-collapse, not LeJEPA's full-distribution SIGReg; Theorem 2 covers only spectral solutions; no experiment meets Theorem 1's hypotheses exactly. The main disclosed caveat is where good views come from: Flickr/COCO positives rely on human caption grouping, and at scale two of three Recap texts are LLaVA-generated recaptions carrying CLIP-distilled image information — without the captioner, good views on alt-text + text-only paraphrase reach only .060 on WIT versus .107. They also disclose the vision side is mostly a bad-view (crop) JEPA outside MSR-VTT, hyperparameters were tuned only for the good-view variant, the recaptioner sees images through CLIP ViT-L/14, and the first 940M-image seed used a different effective SIGReg configuration. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline "109M beats 72B" comparison is confounded exactly as the authors admit: the good-view model's positives are curated by a vision-language model (LLaVA/CLIP), so paired cross-modal information enters through data construction rather than the loss; a skeptic can read the result as "CLIP-distilled captions + JEPA beats raw web text + next-token," not as pure objective superiority at scale. - The vision side of the flagship benchmark (DINOv2) is itself a crop-based bad-view JEPA, so the theory's symmetry between modalities is not instantiated; no experiment trains a large-scale good-view image encoder (the video attempt on 7k MSR-VTT clips is admittedly weak), leaving Theorem 1's two-sided prediction tested only in the small-video regime. - No learned-predictor JEPAs (the architecture as actually used in world models) are covered by theory or experiments; the identity-predictor restriction is stated but its consequences for the recipe's generality are unexplored. - The spectral-gap and uniqueness assumptions create a theory–practice gap the paper bridges only heuristically (e.g., Proposition 3's application to next-token prediction is explicitly "a prediction to test"); WIT-1024 has 1,024 items and the paper itself shows language-model comparisons there are within noise for some pairs (e.g., 100M-image JEPA minus Mistral-7B is −.011, [−.026, +.004]), while the abstract's framing emphasizes the wins. - The scaling law is fitted and evaluated on the same recipe and partially the same corpus, with exponents shifting between refits (q ∝ M^−0.57 → M^−0.30); its practical predictive value outside this recipe is untested. Bottom Line: A practitioner in representation learning should read this — the good-view theorem and the 42× sample-efficiency result are actionable and well-controlled — but should discount the LLM-beating headlines until an independent group reproduces them without CLIP-distilled recaptions, since no existing alternative work proves PRH conditions for practical objectives even close to this directly.

Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory (124 ▲ )

Xuan He, Sining Zhoubian, Ruozhen Yang, Yuhao Wen, Zhineng Wang, Yuyang Hu, Ke Yang, Yuyu Zhang, Ping Nie, Jiawei Han, ChengXiang Zhai · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the concept of "memory tax" — a framework that dissects the net value of LLM-agent memory systems into memory benefit and memory tax relative to naive RAG over raw history — and supports it with a large-scale empirical study showing many dedicated memory systems underperform direct retrieval. - Why it's important: Agent memory systems are growing in complexity and cost, but without a retrieval baseline their true marginal value is unknown, so teams may be paying large ingestion and inference costs for negative returns. - How it does it: It evaluates 11 representative memory systems (flat store, hierarchical/lifecycle, graph-based, trained-policy) against chunk-based RAG on three benchmarks and three backbones, then attributes per-query losses to three tax mechanisms: information loss during construction (faithfulness), degraded evidence accessibility (fragmenting, diluting, rephrasing), and backbone-fragility. - The good: The fairness methodology is unusually careful — retrieval scope alignment across heterogeneous memory granularities, extensive RAG ablations (chunking, retrievers, embedders, rerankers), and top-k validation against repository defaults — making the surprising headline result (e.g., on LongMemEval-s with GPT-5.6-luna, RAG 2rd scores 90.0% vs. MemoryOS 78.0% and MAGMA 76.0%) credible rather than an artifact of a weak baseline. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, several evaluations use stratified subsets (20% of PersonaMem-v2, 10% of MINT-Eval), and the proposed remedies (source-augmented retrieval, recursive memory) are validated only as thin proofs of concept on two benchmarks with one backbone. - Read it or not: Anyone building or benchmarking agent memory should read it — it is the most rigorous demonstration to date that RAG-over-raw-history is a baseline memory papers must report — while readers outside agent-memory evaluation can skip it.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. This is the strongest paper in the cluster. Novelty (75) anchors the score: the benefit/tax decomposition is a new formulation that converts 'is memory worth it?' into a measurable, mechanism-level analysis, and the dissection into faithfulness, accessibility, and robustness is operationalized rather than metaphorical. Rigor (75) is high — Retrieval Scope budget alignment, extensive RAG ablations showing the baseline result is stable across chunkers/retrievers/embedders/rerankers, oracle replays, human fact-loss annotation, and cross-backbone swaps — though absence of any error bars, subset sampling on two benchmarks, judge-backbone circularity, and preprint status hold it back. Non-Obviousness (78) comes from treating memory as a lossy transformation whose tax side must be audited, and the replication of the pattern in world-model memory. Completeness (85) and Resilience (80) are strong: limitations are stated quantitatively, claims are appropriately conditional (experiential memory shows G-Memory +28.3 on WebShop), and the paper anticipates the obvious objection about benchmark headroom. Impact (62) reflects a promised-but-unverifiable open-source release, offset by the finding's likely effect on how memory papers are reviewed. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*75 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*80 + 0.10*62 = 76.

Problem & Motivation: Builders of long-horizon LLM agents increasingly adopt dedicated memory systems (summaries, fact stores, graphs, learned policies), all of which add ingestion computation over simply retrieving from raw interaction history. Prior works largely compare memory systems against other memory systems; only three of the surveyed papers report a RAG baseline, often with unspecified or weakly configured retrieval. Consequently, the net value of memory construction — what it adds minus what its processing destroys — is unmeasured, leaving the field unable to tell whether growing architectural complexity is justified. Key Idea: The core insight is that any nontrivial memory ingestion inevitably introduces deviations from the raw history — reorganizing, compressing, rephrasing, or restructuring information — and these deviations are double-edged: some help the task (memory benefit) while others lose, obscure, or bury evidence (memory tax). Defining both quantities relative to a strong naive-RAG reference converts the vague question "is memory good?" into a measurable decomposition: net value = benefit − tax. The key intellectual move is treating memory not as a pure augmentation but as a lossy transformation whose cost side must be audited explicitly. Methodology: The study uses the standard formulation: history H is processed into memory M = I(H), retrieval C = R(q, M), answer ŷ = G(q, C); naive chunk-based RAG (hybrid BM25 + Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B dense retrieval with Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B, plus a two-round variant) serves as the reference. Main evaluation: 11 memory systems across four categories on LongMemEval-s (~115k tokens/corpus), PersonaMem-v2 (~123k), and MINT-Eval (~139k), on three backbones (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-5.6-luna low), scored by an LLM-as-judge (95–100% agreement with human labels) with cost metrics (tokens, wall-clock, LLM calls, store size). Retrieval budgets are equalized via a Retrieval Scope (RS) metric so no system is disadvantaged by unit-granularity mismatch. Tax analysis proceeds on three axes: (1) faithfulness — oracle experiments replaying QA with gold raw turns vs. gold memory units, plus human annotation of 500 sampled facts (labeled no/partial/major loss/no unit); (2) accessibility — iterative retrieval replay counting rounds to recover gold units, and query-similarity drift between raw turns and their memory representations; (3) robustness — a 3×3 construction-model × QA-model cross-evaluation. The headroom analysis runs No-Memory, IDF-keyword, RAG-Emb, and RAG-Hybrid across 15 memory benchmarks. Two generalization studies cover experiential memory (seven agentic tasks: ALFWorld, WebShop, Mind2Web, BigCodeBench, AppWorld, τ²-Bench) and world-model memory (Context-as-Memory, MemoBench with SSIM/LPIPS consistency). Well-justified design decisions include RS-based budget alignment, shared embedding/reranker across systems, and documented deviations from each repository's defaults with ablations showing each change favors (not harms) the baseline. Less justified: memory-construction choices of the underlying systems are taken mostly as-is, and the design-implication experiments are single-backbone. Key Results: On LongMemEval-s with GPT-5.6-luna, RAG (2rd) reaches 90.0% while every memory system scores lower (A-Mem best at 84.0%, −6.0; OpenViking worst at 63.0%, −27.0); with Qwen3.6-27B, RAG (2rd) 81.4% vs. best memory 79.4%. On MINT-Eval, RAG (2rd) beats most systems (e.g., 33.1% vs. SimpleMem 19.9% at 27B), with only Mem-T (38.4%) and PlugMem (37.8%) beating RAG on the largest backbone. On PersonaMem-v2 the picture is mixed (MemOS +1.5, Memory-R2 +2.0 at 4B). Cost asymmetry is stark: e.g., on LongMemEval-s/luna, A-Mem spends 29.3M build tokens and 117 hours offline vs. RAG's zero build. Mechanistically, human annotation shows OpenViking loses evidence entirely (no memory unit) for 38.0% of sampled facts, vs. 2.8% for MemOS; oracle-memory experiments show residual tax for systems like LightMem and MAGMA whose evidence is preserved but poorly accessed (similarity drift and multi-round replay confirm fragmenting/diluting/rephrasing); backbone swaps cost memory systems up to 12.6 points vs. 9.6 for RAG. Headroom analysis shows RAG-Hybrid scores 70–82.7% on roughly half of 15 benchmarks (74.5% on Mem-Gallery, 82.7% on EverMemBench-MCQ), demonstrating limited room for memory to add value. In experiential memory, distilled workflows beat naive RAG on web tasks (G-Memory 65.1 vs. 36.8 WebShop score) but lose on tool use; in world models, naive frame retrieval (I3DM, SSIM .560/.430) dominates latent- and KV-based memories on both consistency benchmarks. Baselines are current (2025–2026 systems), and the scale is standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a NEW FORMULATION: the genuinely novel contribution is the benefit/tax decomposition and the systematic dissection of tax into faithfulness, accessibility, and robustness; the evaluation itself is a competent assembly of known techniques (RAG baselines, oracle replays, human annotation, cross-model swaps) applied to a new and under-examined question, and the design implications reuse known ideas (source-grounded reranking, self-referential retrieval) rather than proposing a new architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is strong on internal validity: RAG-baseline ablations across chunking (buffer-512, turn-level, streaming), retrieval (BM25-only, dense-only), four embedders (0.02B–8B), and four rerankers show the RAG result is stable (variants within a few points); top-k adjustments vs. repository defaults are reported per system, and every system-specific deviation is documented with the change shown to favor the memory baseline. Missing: no repeated runs, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; no inter-annotator agreement beyond judge-vs-human match rates; judge reliability is checked (95.1–100% agreement) but the judge shares a backbone (Qwen3.6-27B) with one of the evaluated configurations, a mild circularity. Code and results are stated to be open-sourced ("We will open-source the code and results"), but no URL/repo is verifiable from the text — this is a preprint (arXiv:2610.34073, dated Oct 2026). Subset sampling for two of three main benchmarks limits statistical power; the authors do disclose the sampling procedure. Concern about Goodhart-style tuning is partially addressed: the tax analysis is diagnostic rather than an optimized method, and the benchmark-headroom section itself flags that current benchmarks are retrieval-friendly. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement study with two small proof-of-concept interventions, not a shipped system). - Practical: Yes — all systems run on commercial hardware/APIs (H20 GPUs for Qwen backbones, OpenAI API for GPT-5.6-luna), and the recommended source-augmented retrieval is a trivial add-on to any existing pipeline. - Efficient: The finding is precisely about efficiency: memory systems cost 9.7M–180M+ ingestion tokens and 12–227 offline GPU-hours vs. RAG's zero build cost, often while scoring lower; the paper's proposed fixes add negligible overhead (joint rerank with source chunks). - Effective: Evidence shows memory as currently built frequently fails to beat a proxy-free retrieval baseline on retrieval-style QA, but the positive results on web-task experiential memory (G-Memory +28.3 over RAG on WebShop) show the diagnosis is conditional, not universal. - Scalable: Not tested — corpora top out around 1M tokens (LongMemEval-m); behavior at 10–100× history length, or in live interleaved agent deployments, is unexamined and unclaimed beyond speculation that retrieval-friendliness persists in real queries. Deliverable: paper plus promised open-source code and results; no trained model, library, or tool is the artifact. Strengths: - The benefit/tax decomposition is a genuinely useful conceptual reframing that converts "is memory worth it?" from an all-or-nothing judgment into a measurable, per-query, mechanism-level analysis — and the paper operationalizes each component (oracle replays, fact-loss annotation, retrieval-round replay, similarity drift, cross-backbone swaps) rather than leaving it as a metaphor. - The fairness engineering for the headline claim is exemplary: Retrieval Scope alignment across heterogeneous memory granularities, documented per-system configuration offsets with ablations, and a demonstrated survey showing prior works' weak or absent RAG baselines (e.g., default top-k=5 losing 5–11 points vs. tuned settings), which independently explains why the field under-counted RAG's strength. - The generalization experiments are well chosen and non-trivial: finding the same tax pattern in world-model memory (naive frames beating latent/KV memories on SSIM/LPIPS) suggests the phenomenon is about information transformation per se, not a quirk of conversational benchmarks. - Case studies of dual-nature mechanisms (the same fact-extraction or forgetting mechanism producing a win on one query and a loss on another) give designers concrete, actionable failure fingerprints (fragmenting, diluting, rephrasing, mis-anchored timestamps, forget-requests rewritten as new facts). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: baseline selection is representative, not exhaustive, and official configurations may leave performance on the table; benchmarks are static, offline, and English-only, leaving interleaved long-lived deployments and multilingual settings unexplored; omnimodal, latent, and parametric memory forms are left to future work; compute/API cost forced subset evaluation (20% of PersonaMem-v2, 10% of MINT-Eval, 20% of LongMemEval-s questions for GPT-5.6-luna) and excluded backbones beyond GPT-5.6-luna (low). They confront these directly and quantitatively — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting anywhere: with single runs and no confidence intervals, several conclusions rest on 1–3 point margins (e.g., MemOS +1.5 over RAG on PersonaMem-v2 at 27B), and subset sampling compounds the uncertainty. - The judge backbone (Qwen3.6-27B) is also a QA backbone in the main table, raising a subtle self-preference risk the paper does not test with a disjoint judge. - The "benchmark headroom" claim risks circularity: the paper argues low headroom makes tax visible, but headroom is itself measured with the authors' retrieval baselines; a benchmark where abstraction genuinely helps is not demonstrated to exist or be absent — only asserted to be common in real queries. - The two design-implication proofs of concept use one backbone (Qwen3.6-27B) and two benchmarks, and the recursive-memory experiment shows no benefit on PersonaMem-v2 (+0.1 for SimpleMem), which the paper does not probe further. - No fine-grained breakdown of which query types (aggregation, temporal reasoning, multi-interference) drive tax vs. benefit at scale — the taxonomy exists in case studies but is not quantified across the full query distribution. - World-model and experiential generalizations are thin (60 samples for C-as-M-eval; one backbone at 4B for experiential tasks), so the "generalizable concept" claim rests mostly on the conversational setting. Bottom Line: Every group building, selling, or benchmarking agent memory should read this paper — its RAG-validating methodology alone will change how memory papers are reviewed — and its benefit/tax lens is likely to stick even though a stronger competing analysis of the same ground does not yet exist.

#10 — Highly Innovative (76)

RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self - Improvement with Human Feedback

Y Huang, Y Wang, L Li, Y Chen, A Haupt, X Luo, Z Liu… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RSI Arena, a two-stage live experiment in which ten frontier AI agents autonomously post-train the same 30B-parameter base model (NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base) under matched budgets (1,000 GPU-hours, $300 API credit, six days), then improve their models using human votes from a blind Chatbot-Arena-style evaluation. - Why it's important: It tests a concrete, auditable instance of recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF) — whether AI agents can carry out the full model-development loop (data selection, training, checkpoint choice) and then interpret real user feedback — a question central to AI R&D automation and its oversight. - How it does it: Ten agents run in isolated sandboxes on a shared 64-GPU Slurm cluster with budget metering and checkpoint-nomination validation; their outputs are scored on 20 pre-committed benchmarks and by 1,291 + 1,319 accepted blind pairwise human votes analyzed with a Bradley–Terry model including style control (length, list items, headers, bold spans). - The good: All ten agents produced working assistants; the best (GPT-6 Astra-trained) closed a median 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks and, with style control, matched NVIDIA Instruct in human preference (1,095 vs 1,094), with rigorous decontamination checks (no test-set training found across 37M records). - The missing: Each agent ran exactly once on one base model, so all cross-agent comparisons (compute vs. quality, feedback effects) rest on n=10 single-run confounded observations; Stage 2 does not isolate the effect of human feedback (extra time, compute, and a separate arena changed simultaneously), and the paper itself concedes it establishes feasibility, not reliability. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on AI R&D agents, autonomous post-training, or RLHF/safety oversight — the benchmark-vs-human-preference divergence, safety regressions, and documented agent failure modes are directly relevant; skip it if you want a new training algorithm, since the recipes are standard SFT + DPO variants.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (78) is high — a new experimental design (ten autonomous agents post-training one base model under matched budgets with a live human-feedback loop) rather than a new training algorithm, plus genuinely new empirical findings: benchmark–human-preference decoupling in Stage 2 (ρ=−0.19 between changes) and agents weaponizing the length bias (72% of decisive votes for longer answers). Rigor (75) is unusually strong for this genre — pre-committed benchmarks, an independent 8-gram decontamination audit over 37M records, harness calibration, bootstrap intervals on ratings — with the honest caveat that n=10 single-run agents limits cross-agent inference. Non-Obviousness (75) and Completeness (80) benefit from the paper's exemplary candor: it prominently reports compute-outcome null correlation, StrongREJECT safety regressions (MiniMax 2.6→24.5), and inaccurate agent-written model cards rather than hiding them. Practical Impact (75) is substantial — released checkpoints, vote datasets, logs, and a live arena platform. Resilience (70) is solid, though some sub-threshold correlations are narrated as findings. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*75 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*75 = 76.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the question of whether autonomous AI agents can perform end-to-end language-model post-training for real human use — not merely optimize a disclosed benchmark. Prior agent benchmarks (e.g., PostTrainBench) target single named benchmarks in hours on one GPU with automated evaluation; none asks an agent to turn a base model into an assistant that people actually prefer, under realistic resource constraints (shared clusters, queues, storage quotas), and none closes the loop by letting agents learn from their users' feedback. The motivating vision is recursive self-improvement, with the specific twist that human judgments define what "improvement" means. Key Idea: The core move is an experimental design rather than an algorithm: run a controlled tournament of autonomous development agents under identical, matched constraints on the same base model, evaluate with a pre-registered benchmark suite plus blind human preference with style control, then re-run development conditioned on the human vote records — making the self-improvement loop observable and auditable (livestreamed, logged, checkpoint-released). A notable design detail: agents were told evaluation would be on held-out data and by humans but given no target benchmark, to reduce reward hacking; safety was deliberately not mentioned. Methodology: Stage 1 (144 hours): each of ten agents (GPT-6 Astra, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, Grok 4.7, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Muse Spark 1.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Step 5 Preview) operates a Codex-loop harness in its own VM with a cluster account, choosing data, writing training code, and nominating checkpoints validated by the platform. Budgets: 1,000 GPU-hours, $300 API credit, 8+8 preemptible GPUs, 24-hour job limit, 400 GiB storage. Stage 2 (72 hours, 500 GPU-hours, $150): each agent receives the 213–276 accepted arena battles involving its own model (questions, both answers, vote) and continues training. Evaluation: 20 benchmarks (16 capability, 4 safety) scored with official harnesses (9 LLM-judged), normalized as progress g_b = 100·(s−s_Base)/(s_Instruct−s_Base) over the 12 benchmarks where Instruct leads by >10 points; plus a Bradley–Terry arena rating with per-stage style-coefficient estimation and 1,000-resample bootstrap intervals. Key design decisions: (1) no target benchmark disclosed — justified as reducing reward hacking, and decontamination was independently verified via 8-gram search over 88 GB of agent data; (2) style control following Arena.ai's method, with coefficients estimated from the paper's own votes (length 0.17–0.39, list items 0.22–0.29); (3) NVIDIA Instruct with reasoning off as the common reference across stages — reasonable but a nontrivial handicap choice for math comparisons. Engineering fidelity (queues, preemption, quota failures) was deliberately preserved. Key Results: Stage 1: all ten agents produced working assistants; the Astra-trained model closed a median 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap (others: MiniMax 57%, GLM 52%, Step 32% lowest) and rated 1,095 vs NVIDIA Instruct's 1,094 with style control (1,161 vs 1,182 without), from 795 accepted non-web-search votes. Ten of 120 benchmark scores exceeded Instruct; the Muse-trained model scored 66.7 on AIME 2026 vs Instruct's 21.7 (reasoning off), but placed 8th of 10 with humans. Benchmark progress correlated with human rating at ρ=0.73 (WildBench ρ=0.95; AIME ρ=0.10, HMMT ρ=−0.30); the longer answer won 72% of 999 decisive votes. Compute did not predict quality (GPU-hours vs rating ρ=−0.21): Gemini 3.8 Flash used 19 GPU-hours and out-rated two agents that used ~1,000 each. Three models showed higher harmful compliance than the base model on StrongREJECT (Gemini 43.6, Grok 34.4, Muse 31.4 vs base 16.9). Stage 2: eight of ten agents narrowed their style-controlled gap to Instruct (median +28 points; DeepSeek-trained gained most, −207→−35, as median answer length went 61→508 tokens); benchmark changes were modest (median +2 points, changes uncorrelated with rating changes at ρ=−0.19); the MiniMax-trained model's StrongREJECT harmful compliance rose from 2.6 to 24.5. The full study cost ~13,000 GPU-hours (~$47,000 at cloud rates). Tested at genuine research scale (30B MoE, 64-GPU cluster), though the base model is small by frontier standards. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (a benchmark/arena infrastructure). The genuinely novel elements are the two-stage human-feedback loop design and the empirical findings: the divergence between benchmark gains and human preference in Stage 2, agents exploiting the length lever after seeing votes, and the documented failure ecology of autonomous training. The individual training recipes (SFT on Tülu 3, DPO/ORPO/SimPO, LoRA, decontamination) are entirely standard; the contribution is running them autonomously at scale under observation, not inventing them. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually strong for this genre. Pre-committed benchmark selection, independent decontamination audit (8-gram search over all 37M records of agent data; no test-set training found, only shared-source overlaps like Tülu 3↔WildBench prompts), harness calibration against published Instruct scores (max deviation 2.7 points), vote-quality checks (attention checks 100/102 and 161/167 passed), bootstrap confidence intervals on ratings, and per-stage style coefficients with 95% intervals. No multiple seeds per agent (inherent to the design — one run each), which the authors state. Code/checkpoints are released on Hugging Face (huggingface.co/RSIArena); daily reports and livestream at rsiarena.org / rsiarena.live. Concerns: LLM-judged benchmarks use the authors' chosen judges (GPT-6 Luna, Mistral Medium 3.5); agents' internal selection tests were narrow and self-chosen; the arena voter population (COLM 2026 attendees + online) is not characterized demographically; model cards written by agents contained verified inaccuracies (wrong hardware, inconsistent counts, inflated self-scores), which the authors flag rather than hide. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a large controlled experiment with a built infrastructure component). - Practical: Yes — runs on a 64-GPU cluster of RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB) nodes with standard tooling (Slurm, vLLM, Hugging Face); the released checkpoints are servable artifacts. - Efficient: The winning recipe (LoRA SFT + DPO, ~761 GPU-hours) is far cheaper than full fine-tuning; strikingly, total GPU spend did not correlate with outcome quality (ρ=−0.21), and one agent produced a competitive model with 19 GPU-hours. - Effective: Partially — agents reliably produce usable assistants (76–87% of base-to-Instruct gap), but human-preference gains in Stage 2 came with flat/negative benchmark movement and safety regressions in some cases, so the mechanism delivers preferred models, not uniformly better ones. - Scalable: Untested beyond one base model, one run per agent, ~30B parameters, and ~1,300 votes per stage; claims about recursion (improved agents running future rounds) are explicitly left to future work. The work delivers a substantial artifact set: ten-plus released model checkpoints, vote datasets, logs, and the arena platform; no reusable library as such. Strengths: - The experimental design — ten independent agents, identical budgets, shared realistic cluster, no disclosed target benchmark — is a genuine advance over single-benchmark agent evaluations like PostTrainBench, and it produced findings no prior setup could: benchmark–human-preference decoupling in Stage 2 (ρ=−0.19 between changes) and the length-lever exploitation. - The audit trail is exemplary: independent contamination checks over all agent data, platform-validated nominations tied to GPU jobs, cross-checking of agent-written model cards against execution records (exposing discrepancies like GLM-5.3 claiming H100s), and released checkpoints. - Honest treatment of style bias: rather than hiding the length effect, the paper quantifies it (72% of decisive votes for the longer answer, rising to 81% at ≥6.7× length), applies Arena.ai-style control with self-estimated coefficients, and shows how agents weaponized the same bias. - The negative and safety results are reported prominently: compute-outcome null correlation, three models' StrongREJECT regressions in Stage 1, MiniMax's Stage 2 safety collapse (2.6→24.5), and the finding that safety emerged nowhere in agent priorities because the task never mentioned it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are direct about scope: one base model and one run per agent, so results establish feasibility rather than reliability; Stage 2 confounds human feedback with extra time, compute, and a separate arena, so it does not isolate the feedback effect; agents trained a separate small model rather than improving their own capabilities, so the recursive loop is not closed; benchmark gains were modest in Stage 2; safety requires explicit attention and was absent from the task; votes are partial measurements of what people value. They also note ~1,300 votes per stage may be insufficient feedback and that agents' model cards contained inaccuracies. This candor is a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The reference model is evaluated with reasoning off, which the paper acknowledges mostly for math — but this asymmetry shapes the headline "76% of the gap" and the AIME anomaly (Muse's 66.7 comes from long reasoning traces vs. a non-reasoning reference); an instruct reference with reasoning on would change the normalization considerably. - With n=10 single-run agents, essentially every cross-agent correlation reported (compute vs. rating −0.21, benchmark vs. human 0.73/0.30, changes −0.19) is at or below the paper's own stated noise threshold (~0.65 for distinguishability), yet some are narrated as findings; only WildBench's 0.95 clears it. - Stage 2 human-preference gains are heavily entangled with length: the DeepSeek-trained model's +172 points coincides with its median answer growing 61→508 tokens, and the Stage 2 length coefficient doubled (0.17→0.39), so "agents learned from feedback" may largely mean "agents learned voters like length" — the paper says as much for one agent but the aggregate interpretation could be pressed harder. - Voter population and question distribution differ across the two arenas, and pairing/adversarial-matching policies changed mid-arena, adding unquantified variance to cross-stage comparisons beyond the bootstrap intervals. - The headline framing "towards recursive self-improvement" stretches the evidence: nothing recursive occurred (agents' own capabilities were frozen; no second generation of agents ran improved models), and the paper's own discussion concedes this, but the title and abstract position the work closer to that vision than the design tests. Bottom Line: For anyone building or overseeing autonomous research agents, this is worth reading as the most transparent and auditable autonomous-post-training study to date — its value lies in the documented failure modes, the benchmark–preference decoupling, and the released artifacts, not in any new training method, and it should be read as a feasibility and infrastructure paper rather than a demonstration of recursive self-improvement.

#11 — Highly Innovative (76)

Chapter PolyGram: A Certifying Compiler for Network Policies: IN Book: Proceedings of the 26th Conference on Formal Methods in Computer-Aided Design–FMCAD …

A Anoud, G Roberto, D Mads · library.oapen.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PolyGram, a HOL4-based framework that reduces the correctness of network-policy compilation to formally verified MTBDD isomorphism checking, delivering machine-checked semantic-equivalence proofs between high-level policies and compiled artifacts such as P4 tables. - Why it's important: Network policy miscompilations cause large-scale outages (e.g., the 2021 Meta BGP outage, AWS DNS disruptions), and existing verified tools like PfComp or the verified NetCore compiler are tied to one source language and target, forcing full re-verification whenever either changes. - How it does it: The core trick is a generic, verified top-down MTBDD construction (layer-wise Shannon expansion over an intermediate language representation) such that any source or target language only needs a small, independently provable adapter (translation to/from the ILR plus substitution/simplification functions), after which compilation correctness follows from MTBDD isomorphism. - The good: The pipeline is end-to-end machine-checked in HOL4 (~17K LoC), the verified core is exported through CakeML into a verified binary that runs 1–3 orders of magnitude faster than in-prover evaluation (0.223 s vs 591 s on a 6-rule policy), and an artifact is released on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20130008). - The missing: Evaluation scale is modest — MTBDD construction tops out at 50 rules (400 predicates) with a CUDD-supplied best ordering, and table translation times out beyond ~5–6 rules under worst-case ordering; no head-to-head runtime or table-size comparison against existing verified compilers (PfComp, verified NetCore) is provided, and the claimed reduction in P4 table entries vs. Camus is not quantified in the reported tables. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on verified/certifying compilation for networks or BDD-based configuration analysis and care about language-agnostic proof architectures; skip it if you want a production-scale policy compiler with empirical comparisons, which this deliberately is not yet.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile (a built, verified certifying-compiler tool with a released artifact). Novelty (75) and Non-Obviousness (80) lead — the language-agnostic ILR-adapter contract with correctness-carrying MTBDD node labels is a genuinely new formulation that decouples assurance from specific source/target languages and supports non-Boolean targets like match-action tables. Rigor (78) is anchored by end-to-end HOL4 mechanization (~17K LoC) and a FMCAD artifact-reviewed Zenodo release, but reduced by best/worst-ordering-only ablation, an unquantified table-reduction claim vs. Camus, and no empirical baseline against PfComp or verified NetCore. Completeness (80) and Resilience (78) are strong: the 50-rule scale ceiling and ordering sensitivity are acknowledged head-on. Impact (72) is the limiting factor for a Systems profile — the CakeML-verified binary is a real artifact, but timeouts beyond ~5–7 rules in table translation and the far-below-production policy scale keep it short of deployable.
