Problem & Motivation: Network operators express firewall and forwarding policies in high-level languages, but these are transformed (optimized, prioritized, normalized) and compiled into low-level artifacts (OpenFlow rules, P4 match-action tables, FPGA circuits) before execution. Errors in this chain cause denial of service or outages, yet current practice relies on testing and simulation with weak guarantees. Existing formal tools (PfComp in Coq, verified NetCore-to-OpenFlow, verified iptables simplification) are each bound to a specific source language and target: any change forces re-verification of the whole toolchain, and the compilation algorithms themselves are typically unverified. The gap PolyGram targets is a reusable, language-agnostic assurance core where compilation correctness proofs survive changes to the source or target representation. Key Idea: Reduce translation correctness to isomorphism of reduced ordered MTBDDs. Each policy language is connected to an intermediate language representation (ILR) mapping Boolean variables (atomic packet predicates) to actions via two soundness-verified adapters (trans▶ into the ILR, trans◀ out). A generic, verified, breadth-first MTBDD construction (mk_mtbdd_opt) then converts ILR forwardings into canonical MTBDDs while carrying, inside each node label, the residual forwarding that witnesses semantic equivalence — so an untrusted compiler is validated by independently building MTBDDs for input and output and checking isomorphism, with canonicity (ordered + reduced form) making isomorphism equivalent to semantic equivalence. Critically, the untrusted parts (compilation heuristics, candidate isomorphism search, optimization strategy, variable ordering) require no proofs, so they can change freely. Methodology: The pipeline has two modes: translation validation (untrusted compiler maps forwarding to forwarding; both sides translated to MTBDDs and compared) and certified compilation (untrusted compiler consumes the input MTBDD and emits an ILR; a verified trans◀ produces the output forwarding). Technically: (1) each language gets an ILR plus four auxiliary functions (fv, simp, sub, final) and adapters proven to satisfy Definition 1's soundness conditions; (2) MTBDDs are built iteratively by mk_layer, which extracts non-terminal leaves, applies Shannon expansion sub(q,x,T/F), simplifies via simp, and relabels — with correctness (semantics of sub-MTBDD = semantics of its residual forwarding) preserved per layer and proven by bottom-up induction; (3) layer-wise merge/eliminate operations, proven to preserve well-formedness, ordering, and correctness, implement reduction, so any optimization heuristic composed from them is sound without further proof; (4) an untrusted SML procedure proposes an isomorphism via parallel depth-first traversal, checked in HOL4 against Theorem 4 in linear time. Two concrete instantiations are given: a first-match policy language (Theorem 1) and P4-style match-action tables whose semantics reuses HOL4P4 (Theorem 2). Design decisions worth noting: the top-down Shannon-expansion construction (vs. the bottom-up Boolean-composition BDD formalizations of Harrison/Verma et al.) is what enables non-Boolean targets like match-action tables — well justified; the untrusted MTBDD-to-table translation with shared-subgraph partitioning needs no proof — a clean exploitation of the validation architecture; delegating MTBDD construction to a CakeML-compiled binary with serialization/deserialization outside the TCB (in-prover mode) is a pragmatic trade-off explicitly flagged. Variable ordering is delegated to CUDD since correctness is order-independent — justified. Key Results: Evaluation uses the UCI Internet Firewall dataset (8 atomic predicates per rule). With the best CUDD ordering, verified CakeML MTBDD construction handles 50 rules (400 predicates) in 4.93 s. CakeML beats HOL4 EVAL by 1–3 orders of magnitude (e.g., 6-rule policy-to-MTBDD: 0.223 s vs 591.5 s). End-to-end policy-to-P4-table certification completes for up to 7 rules in seconds-to-tens-of-seconds with the best order, but times out (>1200 s) for 5+ rules under worst-case ordering in HOL4; table-side MTBDD construction is consistently slower than policy-side because variable substitution on tables removes only rows, not rules. Policy equivalence checking (via rule permutation) certifies up to 14 rules (96 predicates) end-to-end in 527 s. Certified minimization on 4 inputs reduces, e.g., 52 variables/147 predicates/35 rules to 24 predicates/4 rules. The new MTBDD-to-table translation algorithm provably reduces generated entries vs. Camus's path-per-row Algorithm 1 (e.g., avoiding 4× duplication of a fallback row in the running example), though no aggregate table-size numbers across the benchmark are reported. Baselines are conceptual (prior verified tools are tied to fixed languages), not empirical — no runtime comparison against PfComp or similar systems. Tested scale: standard academic benchmarks, well below production firewall sizes (hundreds-to-thousands of rules). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD: the genuinely novel elements are (a) the generic certifying-transformation contract (ILR adapters + correctness-preserving top-down MTBDD construction) that decouples compilation assurance from specific languages/targets, and (b) the reduction of trustworthy policy compilation to MTBDD isomorphism checking with an untrusted compiler on either side. The MTBDD-to-table translation is an incremental improvement over Camus (ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION), and CakeML export is a standard technique competently applied. The overall pattern (translation validation via canonical decision diagrams) is known; the novelty is in making the verified core representation-agnostic and in the top-down construction supporting match-action semantics. Rigor & Reproducibility: The formalization itself is the rigor guarantee: all verified components, theorems, and end-to-end compositions are machine-checked in HOL4 (~17K LoC, of which ~800 LoC serialization is TCB in the CakeML mode), and the artifact is peer-reviewed and released on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20130008, FMCAD artifact-reviewed badge). Ablation-style evidence exists in one dimension: best vs. worst variable orderings are systematically compared, isolating ordering impact. However: no error bars or multiple runs are reported; the claimed table-entry reduction vs. Camus is demonstrated only on the running example, not measured across the benchmark; there is no empirical baseline comparison with any prior verified tool; and the optimization/minimization evaluation covers only 4 inputs with no size thresholds. No Goodhart-style benchmark gaming is apparent since the tool proves properties rather than optimizing a metric, but the evaluation is exclusively on the authors' chosen dataset and configurations. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, verified tool evaluated on benchmarks). Practical: Yes — the CakeML binary runs as a standalone executable and the pipeline needs no user interaction with HOL4 (only deep-embedding of the input policy, automatable from JSON per the authors). Efficient: Seconds for tens of rules via CakeML, but in-prover certification costs grow steeply and table-side translation times out at ~5–6 rules under constrained orderings; MTBDD size is order-sensitive and can blow up exponentially. Effective: The evidence shows semantic-equivalence certification for the instantiated language pair (policy language → P4 tables) and for equivalence/minimization analyses — the core claim is demonstrated, though only at small policy scale. Scalable: Not demonstrated — 50 rules is far below production firewall sizes; the authors themselves flag ordering strategies, predicate-implication awareness, and efficient large-MTDD manipulation in HOL4/CakeML as open problems. Delivers a software artifact: HOL4 theories, CakeML binaries, and SML untrusted algorithms, released with the paper. Strengths: (1) The architectural insight of carrying residual forwardings inside MTBDD node labels makes the invariants (correctness, ordering) provable layer-by-layer during construction, giving a modular proof that accommodates non-Boolean targets like match-action tables — a real advance over bottom-up BDD formalizations. (2) The trust decomposition is clean and honest: compilers, heuristics, isomorphism search, and ordering all live outside the TCB, so adopters pay a small, bounded proof obligation (the four ILR functions plus adapters) per new language. (3) Verified CakeML export with a quantified 1–3 order-of-magnitude speedup bridges the usual ITP-usability gap without weakening guarantees in the in-prover mode. (4) Reuse of the same certified construction for duplicate-rule detection, equivalence checking, and minimization demonstrates the framework is not a one-shot design. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly acknowledge: (a) performance sensitivity to variable ordering, with deployment constraints (grouping variables per table) further restricting admissible orders and no tailored ordering strategy provided; (b) the construction ignores semantic relationships between predicates (e.g., ttl>10 ⇒ ttl>2), exploring impossible valuations and inflating MTBDDs; (c) scalability of verified large-MTDD manipulation in HOL4/CakeML, suggesting mutable arrays as future work; (d) in the CakeML mode, serialization/deserialization is unverified TCB (800 LoC). This is a candid, specific limitations discussion — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Scale: 50 rules is a small-policy regime; production firewall datasets often run to hundreds or thousands of rules, and the paper presents no extrapolation or argument beyond the ordering-sensitivity caveat. (2) The headline algorithmic contribution (reduced table entries vs. Camus) is never quantified across the benchmark — Tables I–IV report times only, not entry counts, leaving the claim anecdotal. (3) No empirical comparison with any prior verified compiler (PfComp, verified NetCore, iptables simplification) on shared inputs, so the practical cost of the generic approach versus specialized verified tools is unknown. (4) The P4 target covers only the specific table-emulation architecture of Fig. 2/Listing 1 (state-threaded table pipeline); the paper does not evaluate whether real P4 deployments, range-key widths, or memory/table-size limits of Tofino-class hardware are respected. (5) The ILR adapter obligations are called 'small,' but the tables instantiation costs 4.25K LoC versus 1.35K for policies — the per-language proof burden grows with target complexity and is not analyzed. (6) Equivalence-checking evaluation uses permuted policies of the same case study, which is a weak stress test for the isomorphism checker. Bottom Line: For researchers in verified compilation and network configuration assurance, this is a genuinely useful architectural contribution — a reusable, machine-checked MTBDD core with a well-designed trust decomposition — but practitioners seeking a deployable policy compiler today will find stronger, more specialized alternatives (e.g., PfComp) at the cost of the generality PolyGram is buying; its practical impact hinges on future scaling work the paper correctly identifies but does not deliver.

When AI Agrees Too Much: Manipulating Automated Code Review via Bias Injection

G Alexopoulos, N Alexopoulos, D Spinellis… · dimitro.gr · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper demonstrates that adversarially crafted pull-request metadata (descriptions, commit messages, comments) can manipulate LLM-based automated code review pipelines into approving PRs that reintroduce known CVEs, succeeding in 32/33 (97%) real-world cases via an iterative LLM-assisted refinement attack. - Why it's important: Organizations are increasingly deploying autonomous LLM review agents in CI/CD pipelines (1 in 7 PRs involve AI review as of late 2025), and a successful attack reintroduces known, exploit-ready vulnerabilities into widely used open-source packages — a cheap, automatable supply-chain attack vector. - How it does it: The attacker exploits the framing effect (presentation overriding code-level evidence) by generating persuasive PR metadata with an LLM against a local clone of the target's review pipeline, then iteratively refining the metadata using rejection feedback until the review approves — exploiting the asymmetry that attackers get unlimited tries while defenders get one shot. - The good: The end-to-end attack is validated against two real, popular ACR tools (Claude Code and CodeRabbit) on 33 CVEs across 20 real projects (314–71.1k GitHub stars, 9 languages, 24 CWE types), with a 100% success rate against Claude Code (17/17) and 94% against CodeRabbit (15/16), plus a simple metadata-redaction defense that recovers all bias-induced misses. - The missing: The defense evaluation is limited to metadata redaction — no prompt-hardening, diff-only review modes, provenance checks, or training-time debiasing are tested, and the attacker uses the same LLM as the defender pipeline in the Claude Code setting, leaving attacker-defender model asymmetry unexplored. - Read it or not: Worth reading for security engineers deploying LLM-based code review and for LLM-robustness researchers — it is the first systematic demonstration of framing-based manipulation as an exploitable ACR attack surface, and its counterintuitive finding that template attacks backfire while refined attacks succeed is directly actionable.

Problem & Motivation: LLM-based Automated Code Review (ACR) systems now sit in real CI/CD pipelines and issue accept/reject recommendations on pull requests, making their vulnerability-detection reliability a software-supply-chain security property. The authors target a specific, severe threat: vulnerability reintroduction — an adversary reverts a known CVE fix and frames the revert as benign, reusing existing exploits at near-zero cost. Prior work studied LLM bias in code evaluation (Moon et al.'s bias templates) and LLM vulnerability-detection effectiveness (CrossVul, Risse & Böhme), but nobody had examined whether framing susceptibility constitutes an exploitable attack surface in deployed ACR pipelines. The gap is real and timely: real incidents (XZ Utils, Minnesota hypocrite commits) show framing-as-trust-exploitation works on human reviewers, and ACR inherits this surface without human suspicion. Key Idea: The core insight is the attacker-defender asymmetry combined with framing susceptibility: because PR metadata is attacker-controlled 'presentation' while the diff is fixed 'substance', an adversary with access to a project's review process can clone the repository privately, run the same ACR pipeline locally, and iteratively LLM-refine the PR description/commit message using each rejection's feedback until the review approves — at ~$2 per iteration. A second, subtler insight is that naive template attacks (authority claims, self-declared correctness) backfire because they raise reviewer suspicion; successful attacks must instead generate diff-grounded, convention-following arguments, and even satisfy reviewer verification commands (e.g., planting grep-matchable strings in comments to defeat CodeRabbit's ripgrep checks). Methodology: Two phases. (1) Exploratory bias study: 250 CVE/patch pairs from CrossVul (stratified across 5 CWE–language combos, 247 vulnerable + 250 patched files) evaluated under five framing conditions (Neutral, Weak/Strong Bug, Weak/Strong Bug-free) across 6 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek V3, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5) — 14,910 queries with two-proportion z-tests (Bonferroni-corrected), plus two-author manual validation of justifications and root-cause categorization of 240 false positives. (2) Attack evaluation: an isolated testbed with real projects using Claude Code (emulated locally in containers, v2.1.15) or CodeRabbit (private repo clones); 33 CVEs across 20 projects constructed by reverting vulnerability-fixing commits. Two attack strategies: a template-based attack (adapted from Moon et al.'s authority/self-correctness/misleading bias types, 8 combinations × 33 CVEs = 264 tests) and the LLM-assisted refinement attack (seed prompt generating diff-grounded metadata; up to t=10 refinement rounds using rejection feedback; a CodeRabbit-specific enhancement that satisfies the reviewer's exposed verification commands). Outcomes manually classified (Approve/Unclear/Reject) by two authors with a conservative-label tiebreak; each passing PR re-reviewed 5 times for stochasticity. Defenses: metadata redaction (D-1: PR description; D-2: plus commit message/comments). Critical design decisions: restricting to single-file commits with clean ground truth (justified); conservative labeling of review outcomes (justified); using the same LLM family for attacker and defender in the Claude Code case (acknowledged but not justified — flagged as a limitation by the authors themselves). Key Results: Exploratory study: strong bug-free framing collapses detection dramatically — GPT-4o-mini drops from 97.2% to 3.6% detection on vulnerable code, DeepSeek V3 to 53.8%, Claude Sonnet 4.5 to 75.5%; Claude Opus 4.5 is the most resilient (only −6.9 points, non-significant). Bug-present framing effects are asymmetric and weaker. Under neutral conditions all models show ≥88% apparent false-positive rates on patched code, but manual analysis shows 75% of sampled alerts are genuine false positives, dominated by missing sanitization checks (40%) and factually incorrect behavior claims (39%); newer flagship models also find genuine unrelated bugs in 25% of 'fixed' files (up to 57.5% for Opus 4.5), suggesting improvement over pre-2024 models. Attack study: unbiased baseline rejects 94% (Claude Code) and 81% (CodeRabbit) of reverts. Template attacks flip essentially nothing (0/16 Claude rejections; 1/13 CodeRabbit, non-replicating across 5 reruns) and can backfire. LLM-assisted attacks: seed prompt alone succeeds 47%/44%; with refinement, 17/17 (100%) against Claude Code (76% converge within 2 iterations) and 15/16 (94%) against CodeRabbit (up to 10 iterations; the single failure is an eval() code injection CodeRabbit flags unconditionally). Passing PRs survive 76% (Claude) and 66% (CodeRabbit) of 5× reruns. Defense: D-1 redaction recovers 16/32 affected cases (50%); D-2 recovers 12/16 more, restoring baseline-level detection in all bias-induced cases. Cost per attack iteration: under $2. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (ACR manipulation as a supply-chain attack vector), NEW METHOD (LLM-assisted iterative contextual-bias injection against live review pipelines), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the framing effect in LLM vulnerability detection; the counterintuitive result that template bias attacks backfire while refined attacks succeed). The underlying ingredients — LLM framing susceptibility, prompt-driven adversarial metadata, iterative refinement loops — are individually known; the genuine novelty is the end-to-end demonstration against two deployed, real-world ACR tools on real CVEs, the identification of the attacker-defender iteration asymmetry, and the exploit of reviewer verification tooling (planted grep matches). The debiasing-by-redaction defense is a straightforward consequence of the diagnosis, not a novel technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for this venue tier. Ablations exist in the form of the staged attack comparison (baseline → template → seed → refinement rounds), the two defense variants (D-1/D-2 isolating which metadata elements matter — showing Claude Code is driven by PR descriptions while CodeRabbit is driven by commit messages/comments), and 5× re-review of passing PRs to account for LLM stochasticity. Significance testing (two-proportion z-tests, Bonferroni-corrected) is applied in the exploratory study but not in the attack study, where 5× reruns are reported as counts rather than confidence intervals. Manual labeling is dual-annotated with a conservative tiebreak. The paper claims a complete replication package and artifacts ('see supplementary material') but no concrete public URL appears in the provided text. Methodological concerns: (a) the attack dataset was constructed by the authors using their own selection pipeline on the same tools they then attack — inherent to the threat model but a single-testbed risk; (b) CodeRabbit results are self-run against a commercial black-box tool whose internals may change; (c) the attacker LLM equals the defender LLM in the Claude Code setting (authors acknowledge); (d) no evaluation against human reviewers or traditional static analysis in combination. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — an attack testbed). - Practical: Yes — the attack requires only LLM API access and a cloned repository; Claude Code runs locally in a container; total cost is under $2 per refinement iteration. - Efficient: The attack is cheap (sub-$2/iteration, ≤10 iterations); the defense (metadata redaction) is free and trivially deployable as a pipeline pre-processing step. - Effective: The evidence directly demonstrates the stated problem — 97% of reintroduced CVEs pass real ACR pipelines — though passing PRs are only robust (not certain) across reruns (66–76%), which the attacker's one-shot-need makes sufficient anyway. - Scalable: Not stress-tested; 33 CVEs across 20 projects is a moderate scale, and 100% success against a fixed Claude Code version may not transfer across tool/model updates — the paper claims generality of the mechanism but tests one configuration per tool. Deliverables: a full experimental testbed, attack prompts, and a claimed replication package (URL not stated in the provided text); no trained model or library. Strengths: - The backfire finding is genuinely non-obvious: template bias attacks (authority, self-correctness claims) actively trigger reviewer suspicion — 'security engineers would not need to assert their credentials in code comments' — which reverses the prior-work assumption that such templates transfer to security review and informs a better attack design. - The attack-defender asymmetry framing (unlimited local refinement vs. one defensive review) is an insightful abstraction that will likely generalize to other LLM-gatekeeper settings beyond code review. - The CodeRabbit verification-exploit (planting the exact string a ripgrep check matches inside a comment, two lines above the still-vulnerable sink) is a concrete, clever demonstration of how reviewer tooling itself becomes an attack surface. - Honest handling of false positives: rather than reporting the naive ≥88% FP rate, the authors manually show 25% of alerts on 'fixed' files are genuine unrelated bugs, and they report the debiasing defense that defeats their own attack — unusual candor for offensive work. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: results may not transfer to other ACR tools or model configurations; manual labeling is subject to observer bias (mitigated by best practices and released raw data); the attacker LLM in the Claude Code study is the same as the defender's (left to future work); no evaluation against human reviewers; ACR is only one check among several (human review, CI, static analysis) and the paper does not claim it is the only safeguard. This is a direct, thorough limitations discussion — a credibility positive. They also proactively disclosed to maintainers and CodeRabbit (strapi's security team responded; CodeRabbit acknowledged). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The defense space is explored only via metadata redaction. No prompt-hardening ('ignore claims in metadata'), diff-only review modes, metadata provenance/authorship analysis, or reviewer-side debiasing instructions are tested — redaction discards legitimate signal (real PR descriptions are useful for review), so a deployable defense trade-off analysis is missing. - The 100% success rate against Claude Code uses the same model family for attacker and defender; a weaker attacker model might fail, which would materially change the threat characterization (the authors note this but do not measure it). - CodeRabbit's verification-command leakage to the attacker (the review exposes the ripgrep/ast-grep commands) is a configuration-dependent assumption; the paper does not test whether hiding verification details degrades the attack. - The exploratory study's framing prompts are authored by the researchers, not derived from realistic attacker behavior — the mapping from 'Strong Bug-free framing' prompts to actual refined PR descriptions is qualitative, not measured. - Recall/robustness of passing PRs (66–76% across reruns) is reported but not analyzed: which metadata elements cause the variance, and whether attackers could select for more robust framings, is unexplored. - No dogs-not-barking check on why Claude Opus 4.5 resists framing (−6.9 points, non-significant) — understanding this outlier would inform model selection for ACR, but it is not investigated. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying or evaluating LLM-based code review should absolutely read this — it is the first rigorous, end-to-end demonstration that framing-based manipulation defeats real ACR pipelines at ~$2/attempt, and its metadata-redaction countermeasure plus the template-attacks-backfire finding are immediately actionable, outweighing the untested defense alternatives and single-configuration scope.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TenetBench, a 6,866-task corpus of 3,433 requests that conflict with clauses of fifteen Russian professional codes, each paired with a benign twin on the same scenario, plus an automated generation pipeline and a frozen LLM judge validated against human labels, used to evaluate fourteen model/reasoning combinations. - Why it's important: LLM assistants can help a notary, physician, or accountant breach a specific clause of their professional code while producing text that trips no generic safety classifier, and existing harm-taxonomy benchmarks cannot name the provision violated — the form a finding must take to be actionable by the body that wrote the code. - How it does it: A pipeline extracts deontic clauses from code texts, generates scenarios and conflicting/benign task pairs in one call (so the twin shares the scenario substrate and differs only in the legitimacy of what is asked), and a model judge frozen before any human labeling scores three independent axes (instrumental action, norm violation, refusal type) from which six outcome categories are computed deterministically. - The good: The pre-registration discipline is unusually strong — judge and thresholds were frozen before human labels existed, clause-substitution shows 0.913 of violation verdicts flip to non-violation under a foreign profession's clause, and the judge agrees with adjudicated human labels at Gwet's AC1 of 0.894–0.926 on 1,860 elements. - The missing: The judge, task generator, and the top conforming panel row all come from the same Qwen3.6 model family, and three of eight pre-declared instrument checks failed (verdict dependence on construction-side fields is 0.060 vs. a 0.020 bound; Problem & Motivation: Specialists bound by professional codes of ethics increasingly use LLM assistants that can produce text violating a named clause — a notary asking for deed wording, a psychologist asking for a letter to parents — without tripping any safety classifier, because the output looks like ordinary professional drafting. Existing evaluations answer neighboring questions: general harm taxonomies (HarmBench), refusal warrantedness (XSTest, OR-Bench), or legal reasoning (LegalBench). None returns a verdict tied to a specific provision of a code adopted outside the AI field, and none separates "the model breached a rule" from "the model refused too much" — a model refusing everything would score perfectly on any conflicting-request-only measure. The gap is a per-clause, per-profession diagnostic that also reports over-refusal, usable by auditors, regulators, and professional bodies deciding whether to admit an assistant into practice. Key Idea: The core move is pairing clause anchoring with a mirrored benign twin generated in a single call: every conflicting request and its benign counterpart share the scenario substrate (setting, actors, trigger, constraints, framing, request form) and differ only in the legitimacy of what is asked, so conformance and over-refusal can be measured on the same item, and a warning never softens a conflict verdict (the "safety theatre" category). A second key move is procedural: the judge (model + prompt + field list) and all eight validation thresholds were frozen before any human label existed and never revised afterward, closing the loop a developer could otherwise use to tune a judge until it passes agreement gates. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Intake: 53 codes collected, 44 pass a pre-fixed eligibility criterion (deontic clause structure, localizability of violation in answer text, legal status, non-duplication, licence); a hand reading of 745 clauses found only 0.208 localizable, with second-reader agreement at Cohen's κ 0.643 / AC1 0.811. (2) Generation: clause extraction from parse trees (1,898 extracted, 395 in scope after structural/ambiguity/concreteness filters), four scenarios per clause (1,579), then one generation call per pair producing the conflicting task and benign twin; seven validators across five classes (schema, referential integrity, pairing invariants, leak hygiene, style) accept 3,433 of 3,451 slots. Clause text is withheld under copyright; a hash-over-node-path identifier, locators, and SHA-256 digest with a published normalization rule replace it (mechanism from Amalvy et al.). (3) Evaluation: fourteen model/reasoning rows answer the same 675-task stratified set (279 conflicting, 279 twins, 117 orphans) at temperature 0; the frozen Qwen3.6-27B judge receives 17 fields (three partition-labels withheld) and returns three four-valued axis judgments plus an evidence span; a deterministic function maps the triple to six outcome categories. The ranking quantity is the non-conflict rate with three mandatory companions (invalid share, benign refusal rate, benign violation rate) that never affect ordering. Critical design decisions: single-call twin generation (makes the mirroring invariant checkable — well justified); withholding construction-side fields from the judge (partially failed — see gaps); anchoring identifiers over parse-tree paths rather than text (justified by the copyright-constrained release mode). Key Results: Eleven of fourteen rows produce clause-conflicting content on more than 0.6 of the 279 conflicting tasks; over the panel 2,622 of 3,906 conflicting-task answers (0.671) conflict with the clause, and 2,215 of those carry no refusal or warning. Claude Sonnet 5 leads at non-conflict rate 0.849 (95% CI 0.762–0.908), then Qwen3.6-27B at 0.717 and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 0.609; the bottom rows (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at 0.118, RuadaptQwen3-32B at 0.136) fail on most tasks. Non-conformance is almost entirely a refusal phenomenon: safe-refusal share spans 0.007–0.663 while compliant non-violation stays in 0.097–0.226. 0.726 of warned answers (400 of 551) still produce conflicting content. Conformance is highest on confidentiality clauses (0.611 vs. 0.279 on other domains) and lowest on procedural compliance (0.232) and conflicts of interest (0.252); weaker models conform to prohibitions twice as often as obligations (0.287 vs. 0.143, p=0.004). Enabling reasoning halved safe refusals in two Qwen3.6 models (e.g., 0.714→0.529, p=0.0023), and role-play framing raised violation share by 0.041 (p=0.0076). Model line and generation mattered more than size: Qwen3.6 rows beat Qwen3-generation rows by 0.434–0.563, while an 8B→235B size increase within Qwen3-VL moved the rate only 0.118→0.176 (not separated). Russian adaptation did not help (T-pro-it 2.1 +0.104 over its base, RuadaptQwen3-32B −0.018). Human validation: 0.995 of conflicting tasks rated fully plausible; judge-human AC1 0.894/0.915/0.926 on the three axes. Panel human-interpretable: models share one ordering of which breaches are recognizable (0.916 of refusals below the top three coincide with Claude Sonnet 5's refusals) and differ in how far along it they decline. This is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.29477), not stated as peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW METHOD (evaluation procedure). The genuinely novel elements are the assembly and the procedural discipline: clause anchoring and generation-from-norm-text exist (TRIDENT, MedSafetyBench, MedES), paired benign controls exist (SciIntBench, OpenSafeIntent, XSTest), and axis-independence judging has precedents (WildGuard) — but no prior resource combines a mirrored benign twin anchored to the same numbered provision, a prohibition on deriving one verdict axis from another, and a judge frozen before human validation with all thresholds pre-declared. The finding that reasoning mode reduces professional-code conformance is a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The pipeline itself is a competent combination of known techniques (clause extraction, scenario generation, validator acceptance) applied to a new language and legal system. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is among the most rigorously instrumented benchmark papers I have reviewed. Pre-registered elements: eligibility criterion, eight instrument checks with thresholds, panel manifest, agreement carrier (Gwet's AC1 fixed before annotation), sample sizes for target half-widths. The clause-substitution experiment (300 records, 1,500 verdicts, cut-point pre-fixed) shows verdicts follow the shown clause, with a control arm run three times bounding judge nondeterminism below 0.0126. Three of eight declared checks failed and are reported as failed: verdict dependence on construction-side fields (0.060 vs. 0.020 bound), evidence-span traceability (0.623 verbatim vs. 0.95 threshold, 0.937 under generous matching), and the ordering-by-refusal refutation arm (r²=0.984 exceeded the 0.90 threshold meant to refute). The authors withdraw the broad conformance claim and reframe the leaderboard as domain-scoped caution. Weaknesses: one response per task (intervals over items only, not response sampling); only 0.208 of clauses are localizable by a single reader's judgment; the judge, generator, and top panel row share the Qwen3.6 family (self-favor bias bounded at 0.068, which is narrower than the 0.434+ generation gaps but non-zero); a quarter of norm-violation labels passed through one adjudicator. Code (Apache-2.0) and data (CC BY 4.0, 2,235 pairs, ten of fifteen documents, 220 pairs held out by design) are on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22678484) with canary strings and a declared held-out subset against training-data contamination. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built resource and evaluation campaign; no formal results). Practical: Yes — evaluation runs at temperature 0 with a Q8_0-quantized 27B judge under llama.cpp on commodity hardware; the largest subject model (Qwen3-VL-235B) is servable locally, and the frontier row went through a provider. Efficient: One judge call and one subject call per task at 675 tasks per row; the cost profile is modest relative to alternatives requiring professional annotators per verdict, which is the paper's explicit design goal. Effective: The evidence shows the instrument measures what it claims after the authors' narrowing — discriminating caution (conflicting task vs. twin, positive in all fourteen rows, median paired difference 0.111, surviving length matching at +0.099) rather than broad code conformance; the broad claim is withdrawn, so the effective claim is the narrower one actually supported. Scalable: The pipeline regenerates tasks per run and processed two English codes (39 clauses, 78 records, judge-human AC1 0.823–0.958), demonstrating portability, but 10× scale would need more codes per profession and the route confound (provider vs. local serving, half-width 0.103) is not excluded at panel-reordering magnitude. Delivers a concrete software artifact: released dataset (partially withheld for copyright), generation/evaluation pipeline with twenty executable entry points, frozen judge, and 7,303 verdicts. Strengths: (1) The freeze-before-labels protocol — judge, thresholds, and panel manifest archived before any human annotation existed, with no correction loop afterward — is a genuine methodological contribution to LLM-judge validation, closing a documented loophole in agreement-gated judge tuning. (2) The clause-substitution experiment cleanly separates "the judge reads the clause" from "the judge reacts to the answer," with a dose-response result (0.687 flip for same-document clauses vs. 0.913 for foreign-profession clauses) that is more convincing than agreement statistics alone. (3) The paired twin design measures conformance and over-refusal on the same scenario, so the paper can show the most cautious models decline the conflicting request while still serving its legitimate twin (7 benign refusals out of 279 for the top row). (4) Uncommon honesty: three failed pre-declared checks are reported in full, the broad conformance claim is withdrawn, and the release documents exactly what is withheld and why. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. They state: the leaderboard orders domain-scoped caution, not broad conformance (the broad claim "is withdrawn"); the verdict depends in part on two construction-side fields (0.060 shift vs. 0.020 bound, 58 of 59 separated pairs preserved); evidence-span traceability misses the declared 0.95 threshold under the verbatim rule; the corpus covers one legal system in Russian, and duties violated only by subsequent specialist action fall outside the construct; the route (provider vs. local) effect is not excluded at panel-reordering magnitude; five documents are withheld and recomputing on the released ten shifts all rates upward by +0.0067 to +0.0521 without the ordering being claimed to survive; repetition of the campaign meets service nondeterminism (byte-identical reproduction in only 0.0071 of tasks); the local runtime version was not recorded, limiting replication; five codes are advisory, so verdicts against them report breach of a declaration, not an enforceable rule. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The judge, task generator, and the second-ranked panel row are the same model (Qwen3.6-27B), and the top three rows are all Qwen3.6-family — the family-leniency bound (0.068) is checked, but the annotators saw the same construction-side fields the judge saw, so the human-validation numbers cannot separate "the judge is right" from "judge and annotators share a cue," which the authors note but do not resolve. (2) The localizability rate (0.208) rests on one reader's judgment of 745 clauses; a second reader validated only a 180-clause subsample, so which professions' duties are representable is itself single-rater. (3) There is no empirical head-to-head with TRIDENT or AIReg-Bench on shared data — positioning is by feature table only, so claims of superiority over the nearest relatives are comparative descriptions, not measurements. (4) Tasks are self-generated and the authors concede "the target of inference is the dataset": no external validity check shows that models failing TenetBench also fail real professional interactions beyond the two codes of the English pilot. (5) The benign twins are never verified against their clause (0.251 draw at least one violation verdict), and whether that reflects twin construction failure or judge false positives is unresolved — the authors note the direction of the bias but not its magnitude. (6) One response per task means per-model variance from response sampling is unmeasured. Bottom Line: For anyone building or auditing LLM evaluations against external normative documents — especially with LLM judges — this paper is worth reading in full for its pre-registration and validation machinery, which is more rigorous than most published judge-validation work; its empirical findings (silent professional-code violation is the default behavior, reasoning reduces refusal) matter for deployment in regulated professions, but the resource itself is Russia- and Russian-specific, so practitioners outside that jurisdiction gain the methodology and the warnings rather than a directly usable benchmark.

Operability: On the Conditions for Epistemic Appropriation in LLMs

A Gasparro, P Ciancarini · neurosymbolic-ai-journal.com · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the "Operability" framework — three structural conditions (executability, semantic persistence, interpretable feedback) under which an LLM can repair its own erroneous output cumulatively rather than regenerate it — and delivers pre-registered experimental evidence for these conditions on job-shop scheduling and maze-solving tasks. - Why it's important: Verifier-in-the-loop systems are now common, but the field lacks an account of which structural properties of the model-verifier-domain configuration make iteration productive versus wasteful; this bears directly on the prerequisite for any system that improves on its own output. - How it does it: The core move is to hold the repair loop fixed and vary one factor at a time (feedback content, then solution medium), isolating that a persistent, externally-evaluated artifact — whose consequences the executor, not the model, propagates — is what turns errors into repairable building blocks. - The good: The pre-registered experiments are clean and honest: diagnostic feedback repaired 60% vs. 27% with pass/fail feedback at equal attempts (n=30, McNemar p=0.013), and an executable ASP encoding was solved 78% vs. 20% for prose under an identical loop (n=200 paired instances, p<0.0001), with the striking finding that models write correct BFS programs whose output they cannot mentally trace (path match: 2/65 attempts). - The missing: The media contrast (Experiment 2B) confounds semantic persistence with delegation of the search to Clingo by construction — the authors say so — and there is no resampling baseline, so the claim that repairing beats starting again is untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on verifier loops, LLM self-correction, and neurosymbolic architectures who want a falsifiable framing of when external verification grounds generation; practitioners seeking a better repair pipeline will find the techniques already known (it is the characterization that is new).
Why this rank

Rigor (80) is anchored by genuine pre-registration with committed git tags, exact McNemar and Wilcoxon tests with pre-registered thresholds, released raw responses, and factor-isolated experimental design — though a single confirmatory model and no resampling baseline hold it below the top band. Novelty (80) pairs a NEW FORMULATION (Operability conditions) with a striking NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (65/65 correct programs whose reported paths match their own output only 2/65). Non-Obviousness (80) is high: identifying that deterministic executor-propagated consequences — not feedback alone — turn errors into repairable building blocks was not predicted by prior work. Completeness (80) and Resilience (72) benefit from near-maximal limitation disclosure, including adversarial self-disclosure of harness confounds; Impact (50) reflects a released experiment repository rather than a deployable tool. Problem & Motivation: LLMs asked to perform tasks exceeding a single inference's computational budget (large-state-space search, constrained scheduling) still emit complete, often impossible answers rather than abstaining, and cannot reliably introspect or self-correct (Turpin et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2024). Prior verifier-loop systems (LLM-Modulo, PAL, CEGIS with SMT) show that loops help, but not which properties of the loop let a model build on its previous output rather than start over; existing work varies critics, prompts, and rounds rather than isolating structural factors. The motivating stake is the precondition for iterative self-improvement: a system must be able to take up and refine its own output. Key Idea: Epistemic appropriation through externalized semantics: when (i) a deterministic executor evaluates the artifact, (ii) the artifact re-enters context with meaning fixed by that executor, which propagates the consequences of local edits, and (iii) the feedback names what failed, then the model edits its artifact in place (keeping ~67% of ASP rules verbatim between attempts vs. 17% for independent encodings) instead of producing a new one. The theoretical hinge is Dherin et al. (2025)'s result that in-context content acts as a transient low-rank weight modification — so what re-enters the loop matters — plus the argument that only deterministic consequences of the model's own artifact constitute new information, unlike the model's narration of its own reasoning. Methodology: The paper contributes (a) a causal hallucination taxonomy (Structural / Epistemic / Training-induced) used explicitly as a conceptual frame only, not tested; and (b) the Operability framework formalized as a loop G→V→F→G over configurations, with four levels of external interaction (tool-use, execute-and-check, iterated pass/fail, Operability) distinguished by whether the three conditions hold jointly. Experiment 1 (maze with keys/doors, state space O(n²·2^k)) contrasts prose reasoning, mentally-traced code, and executed code on Claude Sonnet (45 mazes), Gemini 2.5 Flash (20), and Haiku 4.5 (20, hardened harness). Experiment 2 (job-shop scheduling, Clingo ASP + independent specification checker, Haiku 4.5 without extended thinking, chosen because stronger models sit at ceiling) is fully pre-registered: 2A branches 30 failed first attempts into pass/fail vs. diagnostic feedback arms (Wilcoxon on attempts-to-success, McNemar on 3-attempt success); 2B solves 200 paired instances in prose vs. ASP under an identical loop. Experiment 3 is an exploratory, non-statistical probe of Gemini 3 Flash and Claude Sonnet 4.6 using path-efficiency (reported path length / BFS-optimal) as a trace-fidelity metric. Critical design decisions: holding the loop constant while varying one factor (well justified, and the paper's differentiator); selecting a mid-capability model to study the repair regime (justified by a documented ceiling check on Sonnet 5, 43/46 first-attempt validity); the 2B media contrast (acknowledged confound with search delegation). Key Results: Experiment 2A: 42% single-shot validity; diagnostic feedback repaired 18/30 (60%, CI 42–75%) vs. 8/30 (27%) for pass/fail within three attempts, McNemar p=0.013, Hodges–Lehmann half-attempt threshold met (p=0.0016). Experiment 2B: ASP 157/200 (78%) vs. prose 39/200 (20%) within three attempts (+0.59, CI 0.52–0.67, p<0.0001); first-attempt 41% vs. 4%; among 113 instances failing in both media, 63% vs. 14% repaired. Exploratory: ASP steps remove 38% of reported violations with only 19% of steps introducing new violations; prose removes 90% but introduces new violations in 90% of steps (mean 2.86/step). Experiment 1: CODE executed solves 45/45 (Sonnet), 20/20 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 19/20 (Haiku, all optimal paths); non-executed conditions are not significantly better than prose and collapse as state space grows. The dissociation result — models' written programs are correct (65/65 Sonnet) but their reported paths match their own program's output only 2/65 — is the most striking finding. Experiment 3 (descriptive): Gemini 3 Flash saturates accuracy but with efficiency gradients (1.301 NL / 1.042 mental / 1.000 executed) and a documented case of CoT verbalizing BFS while reporting a heuristic's output; Sonnet 4.6 emitted ~127,000 tokens over 27 minutes without ever writing the declared BFS. Baselines correspond to published configurations (PAL, Stechly et al.'s binary feedback, LLM-Modulo-style critique) and are current. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (Operability as a characterized property of model–mechanism–domain configurations, with operational criteria per condition) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the factor-isolated feedback-content and medium contrasts; the write-code-but-can't-trace-it dissociation). The framework itself is a principled reframing of existing verifier-loop practice rather than a new integration technique — the authors say so directly, positioning within Kautz's Neural|Symbolic class — and the causal taxonomy is a conceptual contribution acknowledged as untested. The individual experimental ingredients (executor loops, diagnostic critique) are standard; the controlled isolation of which structural factor matters is the genuinely novel element. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for this venue: both parts of Experiment 2 and the Haiku maze run were pre-registered (designs, prompts, decision rules, analysis scripts committed via git tags before the governed calls); two departures from pre-registration are disclosed; raw responses are released at https://github.com/AndoSan84/operability. Statistical testing is appropriate (exact McNemar, Wilcoxon with pre-registered thresholds, Wilson intervals). Ablations exist at the condition level (2A isolates feedback content; 2B isolates medium), though not a full factorial of the three conditions. Concerns: confirmatory results rest on a single model (Haiku 4.5, thinking disabled) chosen because it fails; earlier maze runs used agentic CLI harnesses with unrecorded reasoning settings, 27 API-error attempts in one condition, and retries lacking the previous answer (persistence absent by construction); the exploratory repair analysis is post-hoc; Experiment 3 evidence is single-trial case study. No multiple-seed replication of the pre-registered arms is reported beyond the paired instance design. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent artifact in the released experiment code). Practical: Yes — all experiments run on commercial APIs and standard Python/Clingo tooling; the symbolic substrate is off-the-shelf. Efficient: The executor is cheap relative to model calls, but the symbolic bottleneck is real — 20/86 and 52/200 first-attempt ASP encodings did not run — and one thinking-model probe consumed $1.97 and 27 minutes for a single failed trial. Effective: The evidence shows repair in domains with decidable ground truth where the generator can produce valid formalism; it does not extend (and the authors do not claim) to open-ended or factual-hallucination settings. Scalable: Untested and largely orthogonal — the loop operates over a few attempts on one artifact; long-horizon self-improvement is explicitly deferred to future work. The work delivers a released experimental repository (pre-registrations, raw logs, analysis scripts) rather than a library or tool; the framework itself exists in paper form. Strengths: (1) The factor-isolation methodology — holding the loop fixed while varying feedback content and then medium — is exactly the experimental design the verifier-loop literature has lacked, and it yields two separable effects (2A vs. 2B contrast on edit locality). (2) The write-correct-code-but-report-something-else dissociation (65/65 correct programs, 2/65 matching outputs) is a crisp, quantified demonstration that formal syntax without execution does not ground generation. (3) The framework is falsifiable rather than tautological: the symbolic bottleneck is presented as a testable boundary (first-attempt validity as a generator–verifier alignment metric), and the internal-executor question is answered negatively for two specific models. (4) Unusually candid limitations section, including adversarial self-disclosure (harness confounds, unblinded interim look, non-pre-registered analyses). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: confirmatory results on one model in a regime where stronger models sit at ceiling; limited statistical power (2A detects only large differences); the 2B media contrast includes search delegation by construction and ran at a slightly easier difficulty via a floor rule; no resampling baseline, so repair-vs-restart is untested; persistence is last-step only and the context-removal experiment was pre-registered but not run; prompts gave no abstain option; earlier runs used agentic interfaces with unrecorded settings; Experiment 3 is case-study evidence; only reasoning hallucinations were tested, not factual confabulation; only one KR formalism (ASP) beyond Python was validated; and the conditional dependence of Conjecture 1 on generative capacity in the formalism. This is direct confrontation rather than minimization — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged issues: (1) the framework's three conditions are never tested as a full factorial — persistence is only ever varied jointly with the executor-propagation mechanism, so the claim that it is the binding condition rests partly on the exploratory Table 7 analysis; (2) both task domains are small-state, decidable, synthetic, and generated by the authors, so external validity of the 60/27 and 78/20 rates to realistic workloads is unknown; (3) the equivalence of the experimental feedback levels to published systems (e.g., "as in LLM-Modulo") is by analogy, not byte-identical replication of those systems' prompting; (4) Haiku 4.5's weakness is the enabling condition of the confirmatory experiments, so the framework is characterized precisely on the model where it pays off — a survivorship-of-regime issue the authors half-acknowledge but do not quantify across a model capability sweep; (5) the Dherin et al. low-rank weight-modification mechanism is invoked as theory but nothing in the experiments tests it, and it remains a conjecture doing explanatory work; (6) no comparison against simply sampling more independent attempts at matched token/compute cost, which the authors' own numbers (65% vs. 9% implied independent-recovery rates) suggest would be a fair and potentially competitive baseline. Bottom Line: A practitioner building verifier-in-the-loop or neurosymbolic systems gains a genuinely useful design vocabulary and two well-controlled factor-isolation results that justify investing in diagnostic feedback and executable media, though the headline loop techniques themselves are already standard — read it for the characterization and the honest experimental template, not for a new method.

#15 — Highly Innovative (75)

Every Weight Is a Path of Shared Discrete Decisions (19 ▲ )

Ammar Ali, Stamatis Lefkimmiatis · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TWIG, a tree-structured weight representation in which every weight is the product of shared discrete decisions along a tree path (shifts by powers of two, zero gates, signs, codebook indices), and shows that quantization, pruning, low-rank factorization, codebooks, and weight sharing are all edits of this one object. - Why it's important: Model compression methods today each carry their own format, solver, and kernel, fixed-weight hardware pays a constant multiplier per weight, and discrete optimizers (annealers, quantum devices) can only reach narrow rounding subproblems — a unified discrete weight format addresses all three frictions at once. - How it does it: The core move is factoring each weight into a product of decisions organized as a tree, so shared upper-path decisions are stored once, applied once, and (when values are powers of two) implemented in circuits as wire routing rather than multiplication. - The good: The framework is backed by explicit cost accounting (bits and additions), worst-case expressiveness guarantees, and concrete measurements — e.g., a bit-exact BF16 lossless format at 12.13 bits/weight (−24%) served 1.23× faster in vLLM at batch 1, and flat trees need 9–55% fewer adders than GPTQ-quantized weights at equal layer error on LLaMA-3-8B layers. - The missing: The quantitative evidence is deliberately narrow — five matrices for the circuit study, one model for compression, one single-run healing experiment — and key components (the edit menus, the whole-network circuit study) are deferred to follow-up papers, so no headline claim is validated at full breadth. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on weight compression formats, multiplierless inference hardware, or discrete optimization for neural networks — it is a framework-defining paper with real artifacts; skip it if you need production-ready compression numbers, since the strongest baselines (QTIP, QuIP#, AWQ, ShiftAddLLM head-to-head) are absent or deferred.

Problem & Motivation: Neural networks are trained over real-valued weights but deployed as finite bit patterns, and the conversion has fragmented into independent research families — pruning, quantization, low-rank factorization, codebook methods, weight sharing — each with its own storage format, solver, and kernel; combining them (e.g., 4-bit in one layer, pruned in another, low-rank in a third) is manual design with no common yardstick. Two further problems sit outside this picture: (a) on hardware with weights fixed at fabrication (printed classifiers, hardwired-LLM chips), every weight needs a dedicated constant multiplier, which is far larger and more energy-hungry than an adder; (b) choosing discrete weights is combinatorial, yet annealers and quantum optimizers have been applied only to narrow subproblems like adaptive rounding. The intended audience spans compression researchers, hardware designers, and the discrete-optimization community. Key Idea: Write every weight as the product of a path of small discrete decisions through a tree over the entries of the weight matrix, and let weights that belong together share the upper portion of their paths — a shared decision is stored once, applied once (in a circuit, a shared shift acts once on the subtree sum), and inherited by every weight below it. The key observation making this a framework rather than a format is that existing formats (group scales, block exponents, microexponents, ternary, codebooks, N:M sparsity) are already shallow special cases of this tree, so deepening the tree and mixing decision types unifies all compression methods as edits of one object, makes the application cost (adder count) explicit when states are powers of two, and turns state selection into the ground-state problem of a higher-order Boltzmann machine whose higher-order terms follow the tree paths. Methodology: A state tree assigns each internal node a state from a small alphabet (shift, gate/zero, transparent, sign, lookup index) and each leaf a private state; entry (i,j) equals a row scale ρ_i times a column base β_j times the product of path-node values (Equation 1), with row/column scales stored in FP16. Three composition operations — entrywise sum (residual precision), matrix product (low rank, rotations), and reference to a shared subtree (codebooks, cross-layer sharing, turning trees into DAGs) — make the representation universal. The theory (Section 3/Appendix A) proves: existing formats are ≤5-level state trees at no extra cost; counting/density lower bounds show no worst-case loss; a sum of t power-of-two trees achieves relative error 3^−t per entry, so precision and adder count become one quantity; shared shift bits realize exactly the magnitude patterns whose within-node exponent spread is bounded by subtree height; and a dynamic program over Pareto menus of per-matrix edits solves the budgeted network-wide compression problem exactly under additive costs. Empirically, the paper builds (1) a fixed-shape lossless BF16 format (shared exponent per 64 weights, 4-bit shift state, 8-bit leaf, escape side list) with a pointer-free CUDA decoder feeding tensor cores; (2) a GPTQ-style single-pass state selector minimizing layer error f_H = tr(EHEᵀ) plus a per-nonzero-digit price, used to compare adder counts against GPTQ at matched layer error; (3) an Ising/QUBO formulation of state selection (Kronecker-factored energy, pairwise with fixed node states, higher-order otherwise) attacked with simulated bifurcation and Gibbs sampling. Critical design decisions: leaf alphabet {0, ±1, ±½} with joint coding (~3.3 bits/weight, justified via Theorem A.10 encoding equivalence), fixed tree shape to preserve branch-free tensor-core addressing (explicitly traded against entropy coding and pointer sharing), and flat trees for the circuit study (justified by the observation that shared shifts save bits but not additions). Key Results: On five LLaMA-3-8B matrices (128 FineWeb calibration sequences), flat signed-power-of-two trees matched GPTQ layer error while using 9–15% fewer adders per weight at 3- and 4-bit accuracy on typical matrices, 20–55% on the two strong-outlier matrices (e.g., layer-1 down projection: 0.80→0.36 adders/weight at GPTQ-3 error, −55%), and 30–63% at 2-bit; counting digits only (excluding scales) still yields 6–53% savings at 3–4 bits. The lossless format stores whole models at 12.13 bits/weight (−24% vs BF16) bit-exactly, with the kernel at 97% of bandwidth floor: matrix-vector on A100 runs 1.03–1.27× faster than the authors' own BF16 kernel (the format effect, bounded by 1.32×) and 1.05–1.51× vs cuBLAS at batches 1–8; vLLM end-to-end generation is 1.23× faster at batch 1 on Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3.5-9B, ~1.17–1.21× at batch 8, parity at batch 32 (compute-bound). Whole-model dynamic-programming compression of LLaMA-3-8B to 3.25 bits/weight reaches WikiText-2/C4/FineWeb perplexity 6.95/10.93/9.76 vs 8.09/12.72/11.81 for the strongest GPTQ configuration, closing 58% of GPTQ's gap to FP16 (6.14) on WikiText-2. "Ising healing" of a 2.44-bit Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (46,239 codes changed, 0.004%) lowers validation KL 24%, WikiText-2 perplexity 13.74→12.85, and GSM8K accuracy 13.95→21.83 (single run, ±2 points at 95%); the paper honestly notes tuning only continuous scales helps more (GSM8K 27.5). A GPU lossless image codec reaches 9.47 bpp on Kodak (better than WebP 9.50, JPEG 2000 9.57, HTJ2K 10.53; worse than JPEG XL 8.66) at 2.9 Gpixel/s decode on A100 — 6× faster than HTJ2K, ~30× faster than JPEG 2000. Baselines are current for GPTQ (though run in plain form without clipping/grid search for the circuit study) but stronger modern quantizers are not compared. Scale: standard layer-level LLM experiments, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel pieces are the unified tree formulation in which every common weight format is a shallow special case, the explicit dual cost model (bits and adders read off the same tree), compression methods as edits of one object with a single exact budgeted optimizer across all method families, the higher-order Boltzmann-machine mapping of tree state selection, and the bit-exact 12.13-bit BF16 format with a working serving kernel. The ingredients — shared scales, signed-digit weights, QUBO formulations, knapsack bit allocation, path-structured decision diagrams — are all classical; the paper says so and restates several known theorems with attribution, which is honest but caps the theoretical novelty. Rigor & Reproducibility: The appendix contains full definitions and short, mostly correct-looking proofs, including several explicitly flagged as restatements of classical results (reduced-rank regression, counting bounds, multiple-choice knapsack, Reitwiesner's non-adjacent form). Ablations of a kind exist: solver ablation for healing (greedy 20.32 / bifurcation 21.00 / combined 21.83 GSM8K), edge-bit vs node-bit encoding consistency check, and a careful format-vs-kernel decomposition of speedups via their own BF16 kernel — unusually rigorous attribution. No error bars or multi-seed repeats for the LLM experiments; the GSM8K gain is a single run (the authors state the ±2-point binomial interval themselves). Code and a vLLM plugin are public (github.com/ammarali32/StateTree-Representation), but the compression edit menus and several results are deferred to follow-up papers, so the compression and healing numbers are not yet reproducible. Concerns: the compression comparison is against GPTQ only, in the authors' own pipeline, on one model (LLaMA-3-8B) — no QTIP, QuIP#, AWQ, or AQLM despite citing them; the circuit study counts additions as a first-order proxy without area/energy measurement and compares against GPTQ rather than addition-targeting quantizers (APoT, ShiftAddLLM), which the authors acknowledge; and the 2.44-bit healing model's perplexity (~13.7) is far from any useful operating point, making the +7.9 GSM8K gain a proof of concept rather than a practical result. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a substantial theoretical component). Practical: Yes — the lossless format and CUDA/vLLM kernel run on commodity A100 hardware today with a public artifact. Efficient: The format reduces weight memory 24% with bit-exact values and no calibration; kernel engineering contributes up to 1.27× beyond the format, though the tree is up to 15% slower than its own BF16 kernel in compute-bound (batch 32) regimes. Effective: The storage/serving result is genuine end-to-end evidence; the circuit result solves only a proxy (adder count at matched layer error, not measured area/energy or end-to-end model quality), and the compression result uses GPTQ as the sole comparator. Scalable: Not tested beyond 8–9B models; the adder-count story extrapolates to hardwired chips but no silicon is built, and whether quantum solvers beat classical ones on the induced Ising problems is acknowledged as open. Deliverable: a real software artifact (format, kernel, vLLM plugin) plus a reusable formulation; the tree-compilation flow and edit menus stop at paper form. Strengths: - The unifying observation that FP formats, group scales, microscaling, ternary, codebooks, and N:M sparsity are all shallow state trees is verifiably true (Prop A.4 gives the constructions) and reframes the compression landscape in a way that is immediately useful for comparing and combining methods. - The dual cost model (bits vs additions) with the proof that shared shifts save only bits while nonzero leaf terms save only additions is a genuinely non-obvious insight, and the experiments confirm it (deepest trees won on bits, flattest on adders). - Exceptional cost attribution in the serving experiments: timing their own BF16 kernel to separate kernel-engineering gains (≤1.27×) from format gains (≤1.32×) against a stated theoretical bound is more honest than typical kernel papers. - Breadth of validation across four unrelated domains (LLM serving, LLM compression, discrete post-hoc repair, lossless image coding) demonstrates the representation is a property of numbers, not of one model family. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually direct: the circuit measurements are "first evidence on selected models and layers," adder counts are a "first-order proxy for circuit size, not a measurement of area," the healing GSM8K gain comes from a single run with a stated ±2-point interval, continuous-scale tuning outperforms discrete healing on the same token budget, GPTQ was run in plain form, and the whole-network circuit study and the compression edit menus are deferred to separate papers. They also state that shared subtrees/entropy coding were deliberately dropped to preserve fixed addressing, and that quantum advantage is an open question. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Missing strong baselines throughout: the compression headline (6.95 WikiText-2 at 3.25 bits) is compared only against GPTQ in the authors' pipeline, while cited stronger quantizers (QTIP, QuIP#, AQLM, trellis methods) are absent — the true state of the art at 3 bits is materially better than GPTQ, so the 58%-of-gap claim is against a soft baseline. - The circuit comparison excludes the methods designed for exactly this target (APoT, ShiftAddLLM, AddNet) despite the related-work section discussing them in detail. - Additivity of edit costs across matrices is an assumption; the iterate-until-fixed-point procedure mitigates but does not eliminate the Goodhart risk of a knapsack optimized on its own calibration cost model. - All LLM evidence is on LLaMA/Qwen-family models at ≤9B with a single seed; nothing establishes behavior on other architectures, scales, or training runs. - The Boltzmann/quantum connection is a reduction, not a result: no evidence that any annealer or quantum device outperforms the greedy baseline on the induced machines (the paper's own ablation shows simulated bifurcation adds ~1.5 GSM8K points over greedy, and the combined run is dominated by the accept/reject loop). - The fixed tree shape forfeits the entropy-coding and pointer-sharing savings the authors themselves enumerate, so the 12.13-bit figure is not the best achievable and the trade-off against the added decoder complexity is asserted rather than measured. Bottom Line: A practitioner in compression formats, multiplierless hardware, or discrete optimization of weights should read this — it is the clearest unified account of where weight formats are converging, backed by one genuinely working artifact (the bit-exact 12.13-bit serving format) — but treat the compression and circuit numbers as directional evidence against soft baselines rather than results that establish superiority, and expect the substantive follow-up papers to carry the real load.

VibeVideoBench: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation (172 ▲ )

Muxi Diao, Wenbin Xu, Lele Yang, Xuyang Ma, Yuzhe Chen, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Changyi Liu, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Han Li, Wentao Zhang, Weiran Xu, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VibeVideoBench, a 239-task benchmark that scores multimodal agents on producing complete, sound-tracked MP4 videos entirely via code (no image/video generative models) within a one-hour sandbox, using a three-level evaluation of program checks, ~13k task-specific rubric checks, and five per-task-anchored quality dimensions. - Why it's important: Diffusion video models cannot reliably render exact numbers, rule-consistent state, or narration synced to on-screen events — properties real videos (lessons, explainers, data stories) demand — and no existing benchmark measures whether general agents can deliver such videos end to end. - How it does it: Tasks are rewritten from four real-world sources into self-contained specifications whose every requirement is traceable to checkable rubric items, judged by three independent VLM panels with modality routing so audio checks only reach audio-capable judges, validated against blind human pairwise preference on all 239 tasks. - The good: Across 2,151 rollouts of nine frontier agent systems, the three-panel judge mean ranks systems almost exactly as blind humans do (Spearman ρ=0.98), while honest reporting of judge weakness (73.3% pair-level agreement, κ=0.42–0.54, injected audio offsets undetected) makes the reliability claims unusually well-characterized. - The missing: Each (system, task) pair gets exactly one scored run with no seed variance at the rollout level, all judges and evaluated systems are proprietary vendor models (three judges double as evaluated agents), and the benchmark is mostly English (209/239) and 1080p-class. - Read it or not: Anyone building or evaluating agentic coding systems, or studying VLM-as-judge reliability on perceptual/temporal outputs, should read it; researchers in diffusion-video generation can safely skip it.
