Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) and their users increasingly ask agents for finished videos — classroom lessons, paper explainers, data stories, product demos — where the deliverable requires exact text and numbers, rule-consistent state changes, multi-minute structure, and sound aligned to events. Pixel-generating diffusion models do not guarantee these; programs do. Prior evaluation is blind to this: video benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter) score short silent diffusion clips; code-to-visual benchmarks score static artifacts; code-video pipelines (TheoremExplainAgent, Code2Video, Paper2Video) are hand-built single-renderer pipelines, not general agents; and agentic benchmarks (SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, OSWorld) verify textual or unit-testable outcomes, whereas a video is a perceptual, temporal, audio-visual artifact with no unit test. The gap: no benchmark measures whether general multimodal agents can plan, render, inspect, and deliver a complete audio-visual video built with code. Key Idea: Treat video delivery as an agentic task with a hierarchical, evidence-based rubric rather than a holistic score: (1) tasks are rewritten into self-contained specification contracts that fix exactly what must be checkable while leaving creative freedom explicit; (2) every check traces to a prompt requirement, demands visible process rather than claimed results, and carries a modality tag so judges that cannot hear never decide audio questions; (3) missing videos are handled as a first-class second axis (delivered-only vs. no-video-as-zero) instead of being silently ignored. The one-hour sandbox with no image/video generative model — only TTS — forces the "program paradigm" where every frame is rendered by code. Methodology: Task construction (Fig. 2a): four source streams — web prompts written for code-video tools, dense captions of real videos, real asset packs (3D scans, game sprites), and lecture notes/classic papers — are expanded by LLM drafters with cross-review under a specification contract (facts, stages with dwell times, four-channel audio policy, creative-freedom statement), then human-curated, fact-checked, and de-duplicated to 239 tasks (12 categories, 43 subcategories, 8 s–15 min targets, 201 tasks shipping assets totaling 2.69 GB). Rubric construction: each task gets 1,449 L1 program checks in total (delivery spec verified by ffprobe, decode, audio-level, VAD, and Whisper-LID code), 12,985 L2 atomic pass/fail checks (~54/task, each quoting the requirement it enforces, core/detail tagged, modality-tagged), and 1,195 L3 dimension scores (five 1–5 dimensions with per-task anchors at 1/3/5), refined in model-review/human-review loops. Rollout: nine agent systems (six labs) in native vendor harnesses at highest accepted effort, one fixed instruction, fresh Docker container (8 CPU, 32 GB, no GPU, ffmpeg/three.js/TTS toolchain), 3,600 s wall clock, all traffic logged; infra-fault runs re-run. Judging: three system-blind panels (J1 Gemini 4 Argon, J2 Gemini 3.8 Flash watching full video; J3 routing visual checks to GPT-5.6 Sol on sampled frames and audio checks to Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash), computed per panel and averaged, never mixed. Human validation: blind pairwise preference on all 239 tasks with Bradley–Terry Elo and 2,000-sample bootstrap CIs. Critical design decisions: modality routing (justified by documented omni-model audio weakness and the stress test showing judges miss 0.5 s/1.5 s audio offsets); process-over-claims checks (well justified — final reports claim verifications that fail program checks); evaluating model+harness as one unit (justified as deployment-realistic, though it confounds model and harness effects). Key Results: Nine systems, 2,151 scored rollouts, 6.5k video judgments. GPT-6 Astra (Codex CLI) and Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code) lead: human Elo 1242 and 1203; delivered-only L3 overall 4.13 and 4.07 (1–5); L2 strict success 74.5% and 76.3% — i.e., even the best system fails a core requirement on ~24% of tasks. Opus is the only system to deliver all 239 videos (99.6% spec compliance); Gemini 4 Argon delivers 77% and falls from 4th to 7th when missing videos count as zero. Of 224 failed deliveries, 169 (75%) are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly, or never started; 45 are stalled renders (33 ffmpeg stderr-pipe deadlocks, exclusive to the two Gemini systems); 7 are self-destroyed outputs (e.g., DeepSeek re-encoding over a verified video one minute before deadline). Opus finishes a median 24 minutes early vs. 10–11 for Sol and GLM. 95% of runs inspect their own frames, but cross-system self-inspection volume does not predict quality (ρ=−0.07, n=9). Judge-human agreement: system-level ρ=0.98, pair-level 73.3% (63% when panel score gap <0.2, 86% when ≥0.5); per-video κ=0.42–0.54; on human-labeled "both bad" pairs, judges score videos identically to other pairs (3.81 vs. 3.83), so scores order but do not certify. Cost spans $0.32–$15.38/task (49×), with a Pareto frontier of GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and GPT-6 Astra. Ablations: injected-defect stress test shows judges catch all picture defects but zero audio offsets; a grounded 404-question quiz correlates with judge scores at ρ=0.93; longer budgets increase delivery but not delivered quality; CPU cores (2 vs. 8 vs. 16) have no significant effect. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW METHOD (evaluation protocol). Genuinely novel: the first benchmark of general-purpose agents building complete audio-visual videos with code across open domains, the traceable three-level rubric with modality-routed judging, and the finding that delivery reliability (time management, not quality) is a distinct failure axis. The components are standard combinations — rubric-based LLM judging, pairwise human validation with Bradley–Terry, sandboxed agent evaluation — applied to a new, well-chosen setting; the trajectory-level behavioral analysis (renderer house styles, self-inspection ineffectiveness) is a competent empirical study rather than a new technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a benchmark paper. Ablations are present and targeted: judge stress test with 10 injected defect types (180 judgments), time-budget (15/30/60/120 min × 3 systems × 20 tasks) and CPU-budget (2/8/16 cores × 6 systems × 20 tasks) sweeps, and a grounded quiz cross-check. Bootstrap CIs, per-pair win probabilities, per-panel leaderboards, self-preference analysis with CIs, and a pre-registered core/detail distinction fixed before outputs were seen. Concerns: one scored run per (system, task) with no seed replication at the rollout level, so per-task variance is unmeasured; the three judges include three of the evaluated models (self-preference is measured — two panels favor their own model by ~+0.16–0.20 — and the ranking is shown robust to dropping them, which is good practice, but circularity remains structural); all evaluated systems and all judges are proprietary and vendor-provided, making the numbers impossible to independently re-verify at full scale; tasks were LLM-drafted from public web prompts, creating contamination and provenance risk (partially mitigated by the contract/rewrite pipeline). No public code/data URL is printed in the provided text beyond a project page (vibevideobench.github.io); release of rubrics, trajectories, and 2,151 runs is described but not verifiable from the paper alone. This is a preprint (arXiv 2610.35864v2). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a benchmark and measurement study; the artifact is the dataset, rubrics, and evaluation pipeline). - Practical: Yes — rollouts run on CPU-only containers (8 cores, 32 GB, no GPU) with open toolchains (ffmpeg, three.js, cairo), though it requires paid access to frontier proprietary agents and VLM judges. - Efficient: Carefully quantified — $0.32–$15.38 mean list-price API cost per task (49× spread, ~$12.8k total), 61k–289k output tokens per task; judging cost roughly 3 panels × 2,151 runs. - Effective: The evidence supports the stated problem for system-level ranking (human-validated, ρ=0.98), but the protocol itself documents that per-video scores do not certify acceptability — a self-known limitation of the tool it ships. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 239 tasks; judge cost grows linearly with tasks × panels, and panel disagreement at the video level (κ≈0.5) would grow with task diversity; claims about longer/harder videos are extrapolation from a 15-min cap and few long tasks. The work delivers a benchmark artifact (tasks, ~13k rubric checks, rollouts, sandbox spec); no trained model or reusable software library beyond the evaluation harness is claimed. Strengths: - The evidence-traceable rubric design (each L2 check quotes the prompt requirement it enforces, requires visible process over claimed results, and carries a modality tag) is a real methodological contribution to evaluating non-unit-testable artifacts, directly addressing the "agent claims verification that doesn't hold" failure mode it documents. - The delivery-reliability finding is genuinely useful and non-obvious: 75% of 224 failures are time-management failures (late/slow/never-started final renders), a diagnosis with actionable implications for agent design that no quality metric would have surfaced. - Unusually honest judge evaluation: the paper measures its own judges' failure modes (undetected audio offsets, leniency differences, self-preference, inability to flag "both bad") and derives a precise scope claim — judges certify system rankings, not single videos — instead of overselling VLM judging. - Breadth and realism of the study: nine systems from six labs in native harnesses at 2,151 rollouts with per-run trajectory analysis, a human preference study covering all 239 tasks, and per-run cause assignment for every failure. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (App. J): fixed one-hour budget (longer budgets left to future work, though they ablate this in App. I.3); rubrics measure specification adherence, not creativity (creativity enters only through the aesthetics dimension); all judge panels are proprietary models, and the judges are insensitive to audio-visual timing offsets; coverage is mostly English (209/239) and limited to 1080p-class outputs with few very long tasks. They confront limitations directly — the judge-dependence discussion (App. D, App. I.1) is more thorough than typical — which is a credibility positive. The broader-impact section acknowledges the persuasive-misinformation risk of precision-looking generated video. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Confounding of model and harness: evaluating "model + native harness" as one unit means observed differences (e.g., Gemini systems' ffmpeg deadlocks in Antigravity) cannot be attributed to the model, the harness, or the provider's scaffolding choices — the paper's framing acknowledges this as a fairness trade-off but never attempts a cross-harness control. - Single TTS vendor (Qwen3-TTS-Flash) for all systems: audio-quality dimension (AQ) partially measures the shared TTS, not the agent; GPT-5.6 Sol's 48 silent videos are the exception that shows the tool's presence matters, but no ablation varies the TTS provider. - No open-weight agent system is evaluated, so the leaderboard covers only six proprietary labs and the cost–quality Pareto frontier says nothing about what a locally-hosted agent could do. - The human preference study measures quality of delivered videos only, so the validated headline claim is narrower than the leaderboard presentation implies (the authors note humans never see missing videos and that human Elo correlates at only ρ=0.77 with the no-video-as-zero headline score — a gap they surface but do not resolve). - Rubric ground truth for lessons and papers rests on 330 checks rewritten to be self-contained and "six audit agents re-derived every number" — this verification chain is LLM-heavy, and no inter-annotator agreement statistic for the human rubric-review loop is reported. - Task funnel attrition is heavily toward checkable content (selectors kept 17% of story/comedy and 15% of game drafts), so the benchmark systematically under-represents open-ended creative requests, which the authors frame as design intent rather than a coverage bias. Bottom Line: For anyone building agentic coding systems or multi-modal evaluation pipelines, this is the reference benchmark and the most instructive VLM-judge reliability study currently available in the code-video space — read it; no prior work (Code2Video-Compass, ArtifactsBench, AgenticVBench) covers general agents, open domains, audio, and delivery reliability in one protocol, though its vendor-only leaderboard and 239-task scale mean conclusions should be treated as system-level, not per-video, truth.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ChronoReplay, a post-training data recipe (chronologically ordered replay episodes, native-format targets, and family-balanced loss weighting) that lets a single Qwen3-VL-8B checkpoint serve categorical, metric, and timestamp spatial queries over one causal video history, gaining +13.41 OST-Bench, +7.44 UCS-Bench, and +4.91 OVO-S-Bench points under matched observation access. - Why it's important: Existing streaming-spatial post-training is single-interface — a recipe supervises one answer format and reports the benchmark sharing it — so practitioners cannot know whether one model can serve all three readouts without building a new memory architecture or new annotation; Problem & Motivation: A VLM watching a causal video stream must answer heterogeneous spatial questions — categorical ("is the mirror left or right?"), metric ("how far is the sofa?"), and temporal ("when did we pass the plant?") — using only observations available before the question. Current post-training recipes supervise one answer format and report the benchmark sharing it; recipes mixing qualitative and metric questions operate on single images. The authors name the resulting empirical pattern "interface lock-in": single-family training improves its dominant readout while transferring unevenly or degrading others (in their diagnostic, categorical-only training raises OVO-S to 58.03 but drops OST from 50.52 to 47.48). A second, subtler problem: a metric or temporal target is only meaningful under the history that produced it, so supervision detached from its valid causal prefix is ambiguous. The audience is VLM post-training and embodied/streaming-perception researchers. Key Idea: The core trick is chronological replay with explicit family mass control: convert all heterogeneous spatial supervision into ordered episodes where every target is conditioned on its legal causal prefix (so the model learns accumulation, not isolated snapshots), and normalize each supervision family's risk before combining them — L_replay = (1−λ)L_P + λL_T with λ = α/(1+α) — so relative family influence is set by one scalar rather than by row counts. Keeping targets in native formats (options, units, timestamps) is the second half, defended by an information-theoretic argument (Proposition 1: minimal risk equals H(Y|Z,Q)) and tested with a lossless re-serialization control rather than asserted. Methodology: Two stages. Stage I (Causal Replay construction) builds a preservation family D_P of 33,180 single-turn examples (30,635 categorical, 2,545 numerical from ARKitScenes geometry) and a trajectory family D_T of 6,381 ordered episodes with 45,006 supervised metric/counting/judgement/temporal turns, each turn conditioned on nested causal prefixes (Eq. 3, Algorithm 1). Stage II (family-balanced learning) fine-tunes the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct language model and visual merger (visual encoder frozen) for one epoch, minimizing answer-length-normalized, weighted family risks with α = 0.5 (trajectory gets 1/3 of loss mass). Critical design decisions: (1) native vs. canonical answer serialization — honestly tested and found to redistribute gains (native +2.92 UCS, canonical +1.48 OST), not universally better; (2) chronological ordering — tested against a cyclic-shift control that preserves all turn content and weights; (3) family mass ratio — swept (α ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1.0}), with 0.5 best on the OVO-S/OST mean (61.20 vs 60.92). Justification quality is above average because each decision has a matched control, and Appendix A's propositions (population-level entropy identities and objective invariances) are explicitly framed as motivation, not proof of optimization behavior. An inference-time adaptive frame-selection policy (local/multiscale/global coverage by query scope) is evaluated separately as an access effect, not a training effect. Key Results: Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct under Uniform-128 causal access: OVO-S-Bench 48.98→53.89 (+4.91, positive in all 12 task families), scene-disjoint OST-Bench 50.52→63.93 (+13.41, positive in all 15 subtypes, largest: Direction Estimation +26.86, Order Judgement +20.57), UCS-Bench (8,114 questions) 45.33→52.77 (+7.44, positive in all 8 subcategories). Three-benchmark mean 56.86 vs 50.74/50.76 for single-family variants. OVO-S 53.89 is numerically comparable to the published Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B reference (53.64) but below Gemini-3.1-Pro (59.19). Adaptive access adds +4.09 to 57.98 using 80.5 frames average; at matched ~81-frame cost, adaptive beats uniform 57.98 vs 52.40. Paired-seed objective comparison: full objective over natural turn weighting by 0.92±0.27 (OVO-S), 1.43±0.19 (OST), 1.17±0.25 (UCS) across three seeds. Published baselines in the tables (GPT-4o/4.1, Gemini-2.0, InternVL-2.5, etc.) are reference points under their own protocols, not matched comparisons; matched attribution is confined to Qwen3-VL-8B variants. Tested scale: one 8B model, ~39.5K training rows, three benchmarks, indoor scenes only. Notably, the paper's own error analysis (Appendix F.5) documents a global-layout regression on an OVO-S L4.3 item where the untrained base is correct and ChronoReplay is wrong. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the "interface lock-in" specialization pattern and the crossed native/canonical format transfer effect) plus a NEW METHOD in the weak sense of a data-construction recipe; the ingredients — multi-task loss balancing (GradNorm/Uncertainty-Weighting lineage), instruction-mixture balancing, ordering-aware state-tracking supervision (cf. PAR from the same group), and standard SFT — are existing ideas recombined and carefully ablated for streaming spatial VLMs. No new architecture, memory mechanism, or annotation is introduced. The theoretical appendix contains standard conditional-entropy identities, not new theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: scene-disjoint train/test separation with 243 overlapping ScanNet scenes withheld; matched controls (origin-shift, lossless re-serialization, family mass, topology) all sharing initialization and optimization settings; paired-seed replication for the objective and order comparisons with reported sample standard deviations; a four-GPU replication within 0.34 points; benchmark scorers left frozen with documented extraction contracts; code (github.com/yihaohu0118/ChronoReplay), frozen training manifests, model weights, and converted annotations released via a Hugging Face collection. Weaknesses: the headline checkpoint is a single seed; the single-family diagnostic conflates data source and task coverage with answer interface (the authors admit this in Appendix D.7); the trajectory family is literally OST's released training split, so the largest headline number (+13.41 OST) cannot be attributed to the chronological mechanism — the order control isolates only 2.41 points of it; published external baselines are quoted under incompatible protocols. This is a preprint (arXiv, 2026-dated) and has not, to knowledge, undergone peer review. The paper is unusually disciplined about separating claims from evidence — e.g., explicitly decomposing the 13.41-point recipe gain from the 2.41-point order contribution — which raises confidence in what it does claim. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent inference-time component). - Practical: Yes — post-training an 8B model (LM + merger only, visual encoder frozen, bf16, 32K-token sequences) is routine on commodity multi-GPU setups; a four-GPU run is demonstrated. - Efficient: Training is one epoch over ~39.5K rows; adaptive access reduces inference cost (80.5 vs 128 frames) while improving accuracy. - Effective: The evidence supports cross-benchmark transfer under matched access on three indoor-scene benchmarks, but OST gains are partly in-domain data exposure; no evidence outdoors or on other embodiments. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B parameters, one seed for the headline, and ~45K supervised turns; behavior at 10× data or larger base models is claimed only implicitly. Deliverables: code, scoring scripts, frozen manifests, model weights, and converted training annotations (media not redistributed); a reusable data-construction recipe rather than a software library. Strengths: - Rarely seen attribution discipline: every mechanism claim is backed by a matched intervention (cyclic shift, lossless serialization wrapper, family-mass sweep, paired seeds), and the paper explicitly refuses to assign the full recipe gain to any single component. - The native/canonical crossed result (native better on UCS by 2.92, canonical better on OST by 1.48) is a genuinely informative finding about answer-format-dependent transfer, backed by a lossless-encoding argument that rules out information loss as the explanation. - Honest negative results: Appendix H reports that auxiliary relation-supervision diagnostics (including a state-path firewall) improve a withheld readout without improving native transfer, and Appendix F.5 documents a concrete regression against the base model. - Reproducibility infrastructure (pinned model revision, versioned result records, macro-bound reported values, audited scene identities) is well beyond typical practice for a data-recipe paper. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the recipe adds no memory mechanism, that evaluation covers only indoor scenes, that the single-family comparison "does not assign the full joint gain to one isolated mechanism" (source and task coverage differ), that the shift control tests chronological alignment as a whole rather than a latent origin representation, that native format is not universally superior, that the topology replication is not an independent-seed variance estimate, that L4 remains hardest with a documented layout regression, and that surveillance/safety-critical uses are unaudited. They confront limitations directly and repeatedly — a strong credibility signal; the limitations section reads as an honest attribution boundary rather than minimization. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The trajectory family is drawn from OST's own released training data, so the +13.41 OST headline is confounded by in-domain exposure to a degree the framing does not fully foreground; a control training on the same OST episodes shuffled within turns but with flattened/canonical objectives partially addresses this (ordinary token SFT: 60.7 OST), but the reader must reconstruct the decomposition. - Only one base model (Qwen3-VL-8B) is tested; "interface lock-in" and the recipe's benefit on other VLM families or scales is unverified. - OVO-S and UCS training data come from ScanNet/Matterport3D/ARKitScenes-style sources; whether the categorical/numerical pools themselves overlap distributionally with the test benchmarks (beyond scene identity) is addressed only by scene-ID isolation, not by source-dataset isolation for OVO-S/UCS-style queries. - Adaptive frame selection is evaluated only on OVO-S; its generalization to the other two benchmarks is claimed by design, not measured. - The three benchmarks are recent and niche; no standard general-video or general-VQA regression check is reported to confirm the recipe does not damage non-spatial capabilities. - No comparison against any published competing spatial post-training recipe (e.g., Spatial-MLLM, Cambrian-S style mixtures) under the matched protocol — the only matched baselines are the authors' own ablations. Bottom Line: A practitioner post-training VLMs for streaming spatial understanding gains concrete, well-controlled, reusable guidance (chronological episode construction, family-mass normalization, native-format effects) from this unusually honest recipe paper, but should discount the headline OST number as partly in-domain and verify the transfer claims on their own base model and domain, since no external recipe baseline or second model family is tested.

HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory (79 ▲ )

Junming Zhang, Rubin Wei, Xu Cheng, Hao Sun, Jiarui Wang, Ruoxi Cheng, Xiquan Wang, Peisong Wu, Mingsong Chen, Zhouhan Lin · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HABIT-Bench, a 4-domain, 3,328-probe benchmark that evaluates whether LLM-agent memory systems can infer user behavioral defaults from weak, distributed evidence across hundreds of synthetic sessions and then apply them with the correct scope, exceptions, temporal validity, and user endorsement. - Why it's important: Long-term personalization agents must decide when history actually justifies acting on a user habit, and current memory systems are marketed on exactly this capability despite no benchmark isolating habit induction from plain retrieval. - How it does it: The authors synthesize user lifelines from task-oriented dialogue seeds (CookDial, MultiDoGO, Taskmaster-2) controlled by latent habit graphs with private annotations of habit states and supporting sessions, then score four-choice action selection by exact match under a shared answerer LLM. - The good: The headline result is clean and damning — eight memory methods reach only 27.01–33.61% macro accuracy (25% is random), fail to beat BM25/dense retrieval, and are beaten by the compressed-history control at 41.98% (GLM-5.3-Flash), while Oracle Habit State hits 98.41–99.26%, proving the answerer can solve the task when given the right state. - The missing: The best methods recover only 11.17–13.89% of annotated evidence, so the paper cannot cleanly separate retrieval failure from decision failure at the performance frontier, and all histories are synthetic rather than longitudinal records of real users. - Read it or not: Anyone building or evaluating agent memory systems should read this — it is a direct negative result against elaborate memory pipelines — but general LLM researchers can safely skim the main tables.

Completeness (85) is exceptional: the limitations section confronts the retrieval-protocol confound, the synthetic-only population, and the non-causal nature of the evidence metrics with unusual precision. Problem & Motivation: LLM agents in long-term user relationships must infer habits — behavioral defaults like preferred workflows or cooking styles — from incomplete observations scattered across sessions, and then decide when those defaults apply. A repeated choice may hold only in one context, an assistant's suggestion does not become a user preference, and habits change over time. Existing benchmarks cover adjacent territory (LoCoMo and LongMemEval for recall, PrefEval for explicit preferences, PERMA/DynamicMem for evolving preferences, OP-Bench/BenchPreS for withholding personalization) but none jointly test weak-evidence induction, contextual gating, exceptions, temporal drift, and withholding unsupported personalization (Table 1). Practitioners deploying memory systems currently have no instrument that distinguishes "retained the history" from "inferred and correctly gated the habit." Key Idea: Factor habit memory into two separable failures — reconstructing the behavioral default from distributed evidence, and deciding when the evidence justifies applying it — and measure both with a four-choice action-selection interface where distractors are designed to be plausible violations of a specific habit dimension (outdated choice, over-extended scope, unaccepted suggestion treated as ratified). The construction trick is combining real dialogue seeds (which provide natural task surface) with synthetic, graph-controlled habit states and privately annotated evidence topology, so gold labels are deterministic and attributable to specific sessions while the evaluated method's memory representation stays unrestricted. Methodology: Construction proceeds per domain: source dialogues supply task seeds and interaction patterns; templates or motifs define habit candidates (e.g., 20 Food habit templates, 8 Finance workflow variants); each user's history interleaves scheduled signal sessions (shortlists, distant ordinal resolutions, ratified reuses, boundary contrasts, one-case exceptions, rejected suggestions) with ordinary sessions; a naturalization pass rewrites sessions into natural conversation. Histories are then frozen before blind recoverability checks (authoring-before-annotation for Travel). The evaluator defines the gold action as Resolve(x_p, A_p, Z_u(τ_p)) over annotated habit states at a target time. Evaluation feeds sessions chronologically into user-isolated memory, retrieves context under per-method token budgets, and has a shared frozen-temperature answerer select one of four choices by exact-match JSON parsing. Eight memory methods (A-MEM, Mem0, MemOS, MemRL, LightMem, SeCom; Letta and MIRIX as multi-store) are compared against five retrieval baselines, No Memory/Full Memory controls, and two private oracles, totaling 308 configurations. Critical design decisions: (1) exact-match scoring without an LLM judge — well-justified, removes judge variance; (2) retrieval baselines select sessions using only the request, not the alternatives — stated but not defended, and it disadvantages baselines that cannot rank by action fit; (3) adapter-based evaluation of memory methods through MedMemoryBench adapters rather than upstream-native end-to-end runs — disclosed, but it means the tested pipelines may not reflect each method's intended retrieval behavior. Key Results: Best memory-method macro accuracy is 33.06% (A-MEM, Qwen3-235B-A22B) and 33.61% (A-MEM, GLM-5.3-Flash), versus 25% random and 32.50% (BM25) / 33.21% (Dense RAG) for retrieval baselines; the Full Memory compressed-history control reaches 41.98% with GLM, exceeding all eight methods. Domain asymmetry is large: best memory-method accuracy on Travel is 54.62% (Letta, GLM) versus 28.29% on Finance and 25.44% on Software, where all eight Qwen methods fall below the 23.54% No Memory point estimate. Oracle Evidence yields 39.26–58.25% (Qwen-235B), showing annotated evidence alone leaves large decision errors; Oracle Habit State yields 98.41–99.26%. Evidence diagnostics (Qwen3-32B): Hit@5 37.77–41.44% but evidence recall only 11.17–13.89%; Joint A+E 12.92–16.20%; Clean Grounded@5 5.49–8.20%. Model-size sweep (Qwen3-4B→235B) is modest and non-monotonic (e.g., LightMem drops from 28.14% at 14B to 25.04% at 32B). Sensitivity study on 32 users/954 probes: accuracy 24.83–31.71% across retrieval top-k of 2–20 and ingestion chunks of 128–4096 tokens. Cost: A-MEM build took 54.59 hours and 107.80M LLM tokens for the cohort, against 13.24 minutes and 3.39M tokens for queries. Human validation on 1,469 probes shows reviewer A/B answer agreement of 99.50% (Food), 100.00% (Finance), 99.68% (Software), 92.84% (Travel), with Cohen's κ up to 1.0000. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the benchmark axis itself — jointly requiring weak-evidence habit induction, contextual gating, exceptions, temporal validity, and user-endorsement discrimination, which the paper's Table 1 coverage matrix shows no prior benchmark fully combines — plus the finding that memory pipelines do not beat retrieval or history compression on it. The underlying mechanics (synthetic lifelines from dialogue seeds, four-choice probing, oracle controls) are competent combinations of standard benchmark-construction ideas; the method roster (A-MEM, Mem0, MemOS, etc.) is entirely off-the-shelf. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: retrieval top-k, ingestion granularity, evidence-access oracles, capability slices (temporal, provenance, reference reconstruction, induction, exception handling), and a five-model size sweep. Uncertainty is partially handled — 95% user-cluster bootstrap intervals appear in supplementary Qwen3-8B tables and sensitivity plots, but the main Qwen-235B and GLM tables report point estimates without intervals or seed variation (temperature is zero, which mitigates but does not eliminate variance). Human validation is unusually rigorous: three-reviewer gold-blind protocol, frozen records, stratified sampling, and κ reported per domain. Code and data are released (GitHub: github.com/LUMIA-Group/habit-bench; HuggingFace: hollyming/HABIT-Bench). Methodological concerns the authors themselves flag: memory methods are evaluated through shared adapters, not upstream-native end-to-end runs; the model-size comparison changes both memory-stage and answer models and uses a revised reader protocol at 235B, so it is not a scale-only ablation; the sensitivity cohort is small (32 users, 954 probes). A further concern they only partially address: retrieval baselines cannot condition on the answer alternatives, a structural disadvantage not ablated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built benchmark plus a large evaluation campaign; no deployed tool). Practical: Yes — everything runs on accessible API/served open-weight models (Qwen3 served in BF16 with 8-way tensor parallelism, GLM via API), so any group with inference access can run it. Efficient: Unfavorable for the tested memory methods — A-MEM build cost 54.59 hours and 107.8M tokens on a 32-user cohort, and since it fails to outperform BM25, the cost buys nothing here; the benchmark itself is cheap to score. Effective: As a diagnostic, yes — the oracle gap (33% vs. 98%+) cleanly demonstrates the capability deficit; as a deployment signal, the domain variance means Food/Travel results may not transfer to Finance/Software workloads. Scalable: Untested — the sensitivity study is 32 users, and the authors explicitly refuse to extrapolate cost measurements to the full dataset; at 100× history length the Full Memory compression baseline may degrade unpredictably. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: benchmark dataset, evaluation harness, and adapters. Strengths: - The Oracle Evidence / Oracle Habit State ladder is the paper's best contribution: it decomposes the 65-point gap between best system and ceiling into evidence-reconstruction error versus decision error, showing that even perfect evidence retrieval leaves 40%+ of probes unsolved — a diagnostic structure most memory benchmarks lack. - The distractor design targets specific failure semantics (unaccepted suggestions, expired defaults, out-of-scope extensions) rather than surface plausibility, and the appendix case studies (Figures 6–9) make the intended reasoning chain auditable. - The three-reviewer gold-blind validation protocol with frozen records, adjudication, and retained audit flags (including the four Finance Modify decisions) exceeds the validation standard of most benchmark papers. - The negative result on memory methods versus BM25/compression is reported with unusual candor about its own confounds (per-pipeline budgets differ, adapters are not end-to-end), which strengthens rather than weakens the finding. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that: memory methods were evaluated through benchmark adapters, not upstream-native end-to-end runs; the model-size comparison does not isolate parameter scale; the sensitivity/cost analysis covers one 32-user cohort and does not extrapolate; Travel is "a controlled diagnostic set, not an independently sequestered generalization test"; evidence metrics have differing denominators and cannot be read as a causal error decomposition; and boundary diagnostics do not constitute a global false-personalization rate. This is a paper that confronts its limitations directly — the limitations sections are unusually precise — which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The retrieval-baseline protocol (retrieval uses the request only, never the four alternatives) is a confound the authors note but never ablate; BM25 matching the best memory method despite this handicap makes the "memory pipelines don't beat retrieval" claim potentially conservative — or, alternatively, the memory adapters' retrieval-only interface could be handicapping them. Neither direction is isolated. - With evidence recall at ~12%, most evaluated failures are plausibly retrieval failures, yet the paper's central framing targets habit induction; no experiment provides a memory-system-controlled comparison (e.g., all methods given the same retrieved candidates) to separate representation quality from retrieval quality at the frontier. - All 114 users are synthetic and their habits are template/graph-inserted; whether real human habit evidence has the same temporal topology (clean shortlist→distant-resolution chains) is unverified, and the authors' claim that synthetic construction is source-grounded does not close this gap. - Human validation tested decision recoverability from oracle evidence packets, never human performance on the actual task (finding evidence in a full 540-session history), so "human-solvable" is established only under the most favorable condition. - Only two primary LLMs, both from a single lineage of Chinese-lab models (Qwen, GLM); no Western frontier model (e.g., GPT, Claude, Gemini class) appears in any table, limiting external validity of the "33% is the frontier" claim. Bottom Line: For anyone building memory or personalization layers for LLM agents, this is the most pointed available instrument for testing whether a system actually infers and gates user habits rather than just retrieving text, and its negative result against elaborate memory pipelines justifies the read; researchers outside agent-memory will find the headline finding interesting but the paper skippable.

AV-FABLE: Audio-Visual Manipulation Forensics in Long-Form Videos (37 ▲ )

Yuesheng Huang, Hoi Fan Au, Jiaqi Hou, Ruicheng Zhang, Jiarui He, Haocheng Yang, Bin Hu, Kewei Zhang, Weijian Deng, Jun Zhou, Xiu Li · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AV-FABLE, a 998-hour dual-timeline benchmark of 16,650 pristine–manipulated twin video pairs with 27 editing configurations for localizing sparse audio and visual manipulations in open-scene long-form videos, plus NFSR, a detector that reads frozen Qwen3-Omni perception features with modality-separated temporal decoders. - Why it's important: Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks focus on short talking-head clips, while real-world disinformation attacks brief events inside otherwise authentic long videos on either modality — a setting video-level classification and joint-timeline evaluation cannot measure correctly. - How it does it: An event-driven generation pipeline (SEE-Forge) executes and timestamp-grounds edits on separate audio and visual timelines with matched pristine twins, and NFSR fuses intermediate-layer and interface features from a frozen AV-LLM with host-conditioned FiLM into independent per-modality interval decoders. - The good: The paper shows a striking, well-controlled dissociation — zero-shot Qwen2.5/Qwen3-Omni prompting is near chance (51–52 detection AUROC, ≤0.30 mAP), yet linear probes on the same frozen features reach 90.8 (audio) and 80.8 (visual) AUROC — and NFSR converts this into the best AV-mAP in-domain (91.30 vs. 84.76 for matched-feature UMMAFormer) and in all three OOD settings. - The missing: Ground truth is the executed edit interval, not the perceptually manipulated region, and generator holdout experiments (mAP drops of 16.6–32.8 points) suggest models partially key on generator-specific synthesis artifacts rather than manipulation semantics — a confound the authors partially but not fully exclude. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on deepfake detection/temporal localization or multimodal benchmarks — the dual-timeline evaluation protocol and the representations-vs-language-interface gap are broadly instructive; skip it if you need a deployable forensic system, since explanation quality and OOD visual coverage remain far from practical.

Problem & Motivation: A few manipulated seconds can change the meaning of a long, otherwise authentic video: a replaced utterance, an inserted sound, or a modified action may affect audio, visual, or both, with different temporal boundaries. Video-level authenticity labels and joint-timeline localization (which merges modalities) reward finding the right moment while ignoring which stream was altered. Prior benchmarks cover parts of the setting — LAV-DF and AV-Deepfake1M/++ (speaker-centered clips), TASLE and ActivityForensics (long-form, visual-only edits), AVID (long-form AV inconsistency) — but none combines open-scene long-form video with independent audio and visual timelines, pristine twins, and modality-aware evaluation. The beneficiaries are forensics/disinformation researchers and, ultimately, platform trust-and-safety teams evaluating AV-LLMs as detectors. Key Idea: The core insight is twofold. (1) Evaluation design: preserving modality identity via separate per-track timelines and a native-track metric exposes forensic failures (e.g., a model with a complete audio blind spot can still post the best Joint-mAP) that joint-timeline evaluation structurally hides. (2) Method: AV-LLMs encode strong forensic evidence in frozen perception representations that their language interfaces fail to expose zero-shot, so a lightweight supervised readout — combining intermediate-layer and interface features, modulated by host-video statistics (FiLM), and decoded by independent audio/visual temporal pyramids — recovers that signal for modality-specific interval prediction. Methodology: SEE-Forge constructs the benchmark: (i) build an event catalog per host video (ActivityNet, EPIC-KITCHENS-100, HDTF) from captions, ASR, acoustic onsets, motion, and object interactions; (ii) Gemini 3.7 Flash plans a single-event edit (track, interval, operation, target), verified for observability and generator compatibility; (iii) one of 27 generator/route configurations executes the edit (masked V2V with SAM 2 masks, frame-conditioned generation, joint AV generation, Foley/text-to-audio, TTS speech replacement) with 2–5 s context and seam checks; (iv) reinsertion plus a matched export pipeline produces a pristine twin, controlling content and processing shortcuts (metadata-only probes reach at most 54.6 AUROC); (v) two human reviewers verify all 22,153 events (Cohen's κ = 0.84 retention, 0.82 explanation eligibility, 7.7% third-reviewer adjudication). NFSR extracts frozen Qwen3-Omni intermediate-layer (layer 16) and interface features at 0.25 s resolution, fuses them via modality-specific gated projections (D = 256), applies host-conditioned FiLM using per-video channel statistics, and feeds each modality to an independent Mamba-backed temporal pyramid (ActionFormer-style) predicting per-point classification logits and left/right boundary distances, trained with sigmoid focal loss plus 1D DIoU loss (λ = 1). Video-level detection and four-way attribution (clean/audio-only/visual-only/both) use track scores converted to upper-tail probabilities against 256 pristine calibration videos, with thresholds calibrated once at a 5% FAR budget. Key design decisions: dual-depth feature reading (justified by layer-sweep CV and ablation: removing intermediate features costs 6.55 ID / 8.72 OOD AV-mAP), host conditioning (justified: −4.73 OOD AV-mAP when removed), and modality separation (justified by a cross-track false-alarm control where a cross-modal readout's visual head fires on 11.8–15.1% of audio-only edits vs. 2.9% for the separated readout). Key Results: In-domain on AV-FABLE (2,347 ID test pairs), NFSR reaches 96.04 detection AUROC, 91.30 AV-mAP (92.24 A-mAP, 90.36 V-mAP), 83.61 attribution F1, versus 84.76 AV-mAP for UMMAFormer trained on the identical frozen features and budget; the best zero-shot AV-LLM (Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B) achieves 52.28 AUROC and ≤0.30 mAP per track, and timestamp SFT via the language interface reaches only 57.30 A-mAP / 18.30 V-mAP. Across the three OOD settings — source transfer (HDTF + source-disjoint TASLE subset), held-out generators on seen routes, and held-out TI2V route+generator — NFSR posts the highest AV-mAP (70.15, 49.12, 68.07 respectively) without threshold recalibration, holding realized FAR within 2.97–4.67%. Cross-dataset transfer to TASLE's official protocol yields 51.01 F1Det vs. 67.24 for TASLE-trained MSLoc-PG, though NFSR leads on the pure Kling/Jimeng subset (48.02 vs. 42.26) and TVSum localization. Notable negative results: zero-shot prompting is near chance despite informative internal features; held-out-generator drops of 16.6–32.8 mAP despite route coverage; OOD visual Event-IoU stays at 26.42–41.21, which the authors flag as the main open problem; and better language-based candidate verification (SFT/GRPO raising OOD candidate AP from 39.1 to 53.4) does not improve end-to-end localization. Scale: 16,650 pairs, 998 hours total, minute-scale videos (median 88 s), median event ~9 s; baselines span official-weight, adapted, and matched-feature configurations, with three seeds for NFSR, UMMAFormer, and TASLE-trained ActionFormer (± std ≤1.5 points) but single runs for many others. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the dual-timeline, native-track evaluation protocol and twin-pair construction for open-scene long-form AV forensics are genuinely new), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the dissociation between frozen-representation probe performance and near-chance zero-shot language output in AV-LLMs), and NEW METHOD (NFSR). The method itself is a competent composition of known ingredients — frozen-encoder probing, FiLM conditioning, ActionFormer-style temporal decoding, Mamba backbones — applied to a new setting; the benchmark design and the representations-vs-interface finding are the substantive novelty, not the architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed (per-component removal under matched budgets, three seeds with sample standard deviations, encoder-replacement sweep across Whisper/BEATs+CLIP/Qwen2.5/Qwen3, training-fraction sweep, corruption robustness, cross-track false-alarm controls, feature decomposition into predicted/residual components). Thresholds are calibrated on source-validation data only, and the authors state all architecture/hyperparameter choices were fixed without OOD test access. Construction quality controls are unusually strong for a generated dataset: matched export pipelines, metadata-only shortcut probes, human review with reported inter-rater agreement. The paper candidly reports unfavorable comparisons (MSLoc-PG wins on the full TASLE test; TASLE-trained models win their own benchmark; corruption degrades visual recall). Concerns: ground-truth intervals are execution coordinates rather than perceptual boundaries (systematic label definition); the authors acknowledge that generator-specific synthesis traces inside edited intervals cannot be fully separated from legitimate forensic evidence, and the generator-holdout sensitivity supports this worry; the headline "gap" finding rests on two Qwen-Omni model families plus video-SALMONN; code, dataset manifest, evaluator, and weights are promised for public release but no URL is yet given. This is a preprint (arXiv 2610.33413), not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark plus a trained detection system with experiments). Practical: Yes — NFSR trains only small 256-d readouts on cached frozen encoder features, though feature extraction requires the Qwen3-Omni-30B (A3B) encoder, which is publicly available. Efficient: Competitive — the heavy encoder is frozen and features cached at 0.25 s resolution; readout training is 12 epochs of a lightweight decoder, far cheaper than fine-tuning a video model. Effective: Strongly supported in-domain and under the tested OOD shifts for detection/attribution/localization ranking, but Event-IoU under shift (26–41 V-IoU) and the explanation dimension (baselines misidentify operations/targets) show the practical forensic problem is only partially solved. Scalable: Not stress-tested — videos are minute-scale (median 88 s) and the Mamba backbone is chosen for linear-time scaling, but 10–100× longer videos or higher frame-rate grids are claimed, not measured. Deliverable: dataset (annotations, generated assets, reconstruction utilities), code, evaluator with unit tests, and model weights promised for release; not yet available. Strengths: - The dual-timeline/native-track evaluation protocol is a genuine conceptual contribution: the demonstration that a visual-only model can top Joint-mAP while missing every audio event (Table 11) is a concrete, quantified critique of prior evaluation practice. - The representations-vs-language-interface finding is cleanly isolated: zero-shot, SFT-through-language, linear probes, and full readouts are compared on the same frozen features, making the conclusion hard to dismiss as a prompting artifact. - Benchmark construction discipline exceeds field norms: pristine twins under matched export, metadata-shortcut probes (≤54.6 AUROC), executed-edit ground truth, two-reviewer human verification with reported κ, and source-disjoint splits with three distinct, well-defined OOD settings. - Honest self-reporting of failure modes: low FAR is explicitly decoupled from coverage, the TASLE head-to-head loss is printed, and the generator-artifact confound is discussed rather than buried. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (i) intervals mark where edits were applied, not perceptual boundaries, and reviewers do not re-draw them; (ii) generator-specific synthesis traces (local resampling, texture, acoustic residue) inside edited intervals are legitimate or spurious evidence that the held-out-generator setting cannot disentangle, so pipeline-specific cues cannot be fully excluded; (iii) visual coverage under distribution shift is "the main open problem"; (iv) explanation quality is weak — current baselines produce well-formed but often semantically wrong outputs; (v) future work includes broader real-world editing processes and corruption robustness. The limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central confound the paper flags but does not resolve: if NFSR partly detects generator fingerprints rather than manipulation semantics, the strong ID numbers overstate forensic capability, and the 16.6–32.8 mAP generator-holdout drops are consistent with substantial artifact reliance. A same-generator-perception control (e.g., can the model detect real post-production edits?) is absent. - Ground truth by execution rather than perception means the benchmark cannot distinguish a model that localizes the manipulated content from one that localizes generator processing spans; no human-perception-anchored evaluation subset is provided. - The headline AV-LLM gap claim generalizes from two Qwen-Omni generations and one video-SALMONN model; other AV-LLM families, fine-tuned forensic LLMs, or prompted chain-of-thought variants are not tested zero-shot. - Many baselines (Xception, DeMamba, BA-TFD+, AASIST, DAV-Det, AuViRe, ICS-Sync) are single-run adaptations and perform near chance on localization, so the baseline field is thin at the top; the only strong comparator is UMMAFormer on shared features. - Benchmark dependence is demonstrated by the authors' own F.2 analysis (TASLE-trained readout reaches 25.2 V-mAP on AV-FABLE; AV-FABLE readout 59.0 on TASLE), yet the headline results are predominantly on the authors' own benchmark, whose edit distribution NFSR's design choices implicitly co-adapt to. - Construction relies on a proprietary planner (Gemini 3.7 Flash), limiting reproducibility of the data pipeline even if annotations are released. Bottom Line: A practitioner in multimodal forensics should read this paper for its dual-timeline evaluation protocol and the compelling frozen-features-vs-language-interface finding, but should treat the headline localization numbers as partly artifact-driven until independent perceptual-boundary and real-edit validation exists.

Pipelining vs. Combining in Aggregation Tasks

GM Domingues, C Mathieu, B Patt-Shamir · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proves general lower bounds and gives asymptotically optimal distributed algorithms for the aggregation (convergecast) task when each node's input value of s bits exceeds one packet, so pipelined multi-message transfers must be interleaved with combine operations. - Why it's important: Aggregation (the "reduce" collective) is a core bottleneck in datacenter collectives and GPU communication libraries, and every existing implementation uses naive combine-in-each-step schedules that break pipelining; this work gives the first formal treatment of the pipelining-vs-combining tradeoff with matching bounds on standard topologies. - How it does it: The core move is a non-standard recursive construction of Hamming codes whose codewords are 3-separated, which lets the algorithm build a computation tree over the hypercube where all distance-3 pairwise transfers at each level are node-disjoint and can be routed concurrently. - The good: The hypercube results are the strongest: O(s + d) rounds with splittable flows and O(sd/log d + d) with unsplittable flows on Q_d, and the splittable bound matches the paper's general lower bound; complete bipartite schedules are proven optimal up to constants against the stated lower bound. - The missing: There is no splittable-flows algorithm or approximation for general graphs (explicitly left open), no constant-factor algorithm for trees, and no empirical evaluation of how the theoretical schedules compare to deployed libraries like NCCL under realistic bandwidths and latencies. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on distributed graph algorithms, CONGEST-style theory, or collective-communication scheduling; skip it if you need deployable systems results, since the paper stops at asymptotic schedules with no implementation.

Problem & Motivation: The convergence of pipelining (streaming a large value through a path as a train of packets) and combining (fusing two complete values en route to cut traffic) creates a serialization-parallelization dilemma in convergecast: pipelining wants values to flow unbroken, but combining requires both operands fully present, forcing the pipeline to stall and restart. Practitioners designing collective-communication libraries (e.g., for GPU clusters doing ML training, where in-network aggregation and reduce operations are hot spots) currently use combine-in-each-step schedules; prior theory on convergecast, broadcast, and LogP/postal-model aggregation assumed values fit in a single message, so this regime was unanalyzed. The paper asks: what is the optimal makespan when each of n nodes holds an s-bit value, under a length-preserving commutative associative black-box operator (e.g., multiplication modulo a prime, convolution, sketch merging — operators that forbid combining partial values)? Key Idea: Treat a schedule as a binary computation tree whose internal nodes are combine events, and characterize the makespan through a relaxed "fluid model" (tokens with influx rate r and latency ℓ, annihilating pairwise) that yields a weight-growth lower bound of ℓ·log_{rℓ+1} n on any aggregation; for the hypercube upper bound, exploit the recursive structure of Hamming codes C_r = {(x, x⊕c, π(x))} so that each combine step moves values between codewords at Hamming distance exactly 3, and 3-separation guarantees all such transfers in a level are concurrently routable over three disjoint dimension-hops. Methodology: The model is synchronous networks of unit-bandwidth half-duplex links, instantaneous combines, free control messages, and no network coding; two transfer regimes are studied — unsplittable flows (all packets of a value follow one path, motivated by TCP) and splittable flows. Lower bounds decompose into three terms proved separately: diameter/2 (indistinguishability argument with two executions differing at one input), ⌈s/δ⌉ (cut at the min-degree node), and the fluid-model term ℓ·log_{rℓ+1} n instantiated with rate Δ/s and latency s (unsplittable) or max{1, s/Δ} (splittable). Upper bounds: complete bipartite graphs and cliques use degree-parallel piece routing and (⌈n₁/s⌉+1)-ary combine trees (Lemma 15, Theorem 16, Corollary 18); the hypercube algorithm (a) routes all values to nearest Hamming codeword nodes in O(s) rounds, (b) builds computation tree T_r bottom-up via the generator G_r, zeroing coordinates in blocks (levels i = 1..2^{r−1}−1 via G_r(e_i, 0), then recursing on C_{r−1}), and (c) realizes each level's distance-3 transfers concurrently in O(⌈s/d⌉) rounds by splitting each s-bit message into d parts routed through u → u⊕e_i → v⊕e_i → v 3-hop paths (Lemma 28); for unsplittable flows the tree is compressed by coalescing b = r − ⌊log r⌋ levels so that top-level paths (canonical paths offset by e_j per child) remain disjoint, giving O(sd/log d + d). General graphs reduce to trees via a BFS spanning tree plus a separator hierarchy (Jordan-type 1869 separator theorem) whose O(log n) levels each cost O(s + diam(G)). Critical design decisions: black-box operator (no piecemeal combining) — cleanly justifies the dilemma but excludes XOR-style operators; root-agnostic analysis (arbitrary-root costs at most 2× more) — reasonable; fluid relaxation for lower bounds — standard and well-argued. Key Results: All results are asymptotic worst-case bounds; no experiments were run (none are claimed). Splittable lower bound (Thm 1): Ω(⌈s/Δ⌉·log n/log(⌈Δ/s⌉+1) + diam(G) + s/δ) for any graph; unsplittable lower bound (Thm 2): Ω(s·log n/log(Δ+1) + diam(G)) — note the degree dependence drops from linear (Δ) to logarithmic (log Δ) between the regimes when s ≥ Δ. Complete bipartite K_{n1,n2} (Thm 3/16): O(⌈s/n₁⌉·log n₂/log(⌈n₁/s⌉+1) + ⌈s/n₂⌉) splittable — proven to match the lower bound up to constants (Remark 17) — and O(s) unsplittable. Clique K_n (Thm 4/18): O(⌈s/n⌉·log n/log(⌈n/s⌉+1)) splittable, O(s) unsplittable; holds for any graph containing a balanced biclique. Hypercube Q_d, n = 2^d (Thm 5): O(s + d) splittable and O(sd/log d + d) unsplittable — at s = Θ(log n) this is Θ(log n) and Θ(log² n/log log n) respectively; the authors state these are optimal up to constants. General graphs, unsplittable (Thm 6): O((s + diam(G))·log n), an O(log n)-approximation since unsplittable aggregation needs ≥ s rounds. Line graph (Cor. 38): exact count n + (s−1)(⌈log₃ n⌉+1) rounds, e.g., a 9-node line with s = 4 finishes in 10 steps, versus ns for either extreme strategy. Baselines here are the paper's own lower bounds (the only available yardstick); tightness is shown for some topologies, not all. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with NEW EMPIRICAL-FINDING-style tight bounds: the abstract problem (length-preserving black-box aggregation with pipelined transfers under splittable/unsplittable flow constraints) is a genuinely new formulation in the convergecast literature, and the recursive-Hamming-code computation tree is a genuinely new algorithmic technique (the authors flag it as their main methodological contribution, building on a little-known recursive description of Hamming codes from 1972/2004). The general-graph result (BFS tree + separator hierarchy) is a standard combination of known ideas applied to the new setting, and the clique/biclique algorithms are competent degree-parallel scheduling of known techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is a theory paper: correctness rests on complete proofs, which are included (most deferred to Appendix A), and the constructions are explicit and checkable (Algorithm 1 for tree construction, explicit routing in Lemma 28 and Lemma 34). The key optimality claims are supported: Remark 17 proves the biclique upper bound matches Thm 1 up to constants, and Corollary 38 gives an exact step count for lines. There are no ablations, seeds, or error bars — not applicable to this genre. No code, data, or artifact is released (none expected; the value is the technique, and the Hamming-code construction is fully specified so reimplementation is feasible). Methodological cautions: the hypercube upper bound is claimed "optimal" but tightness is asserted against the general lower bound rather than a hypercube-specific matching lower bound in all parameter regimes (e.g., the additive +d and the unsplittable +d term's tightness are not separately proven); the fluid-model lower bound is a relaxation, so matching upper bounds are required to certify tightness, which is done only for bicliques. The result is a LIPIcs-formatted preprint (arXiv:2610.31383v1, dated Oct 2026), not yet peer-reviewed-published as far as the document shows, though the acknowledgment thanks a referee, suggesting a prior version was reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL — proofs and asymptotic schedules, no primary experiments. - Sound: Assumptions are explicit and unusual ones are defended (instantaneous combine, free control messages, half-duplex links, no network coding); proofs in the appendix appear complete, with the fluid relaxation clearly stated as a relaxation. - General: Results hold for all graphs (lower bounds) and specific common topologies (upper bounds), but under restrictive modeling: uniform unit bandwidth, black-box length-preserving operator, and the no-partial-combining assumption excludes common operators like bitwise XOR, which the authors note as a limitation of scope. - Tight: Bounds are tight up to constants for cliques and complete bipartite graphs (proven) and claimed for hypercubes; for general graphs the O(log n) gap to the lower bound is provably loose-ish but no constant approximation is known — the splittable general-graph case has no upper bound at all. - Implementable: Yes — the schedules are fully constructive (explicit trees, paths, and round counts), though nothing has been operationalized or benchmarked in this paper. The paper delivers no software artifact; it stops at paper form with reusable proof and scheduling techniques. Strengths: - Genuinely new technique: the recursive construction of Hamming codes as nested 3-separated sets (Definition 21, Algorithm 1) that yields level-wise concurrent distance-3 routings is an original non-standard use of coding theory, and it cleanly separates the splittable (O(s+d)) from the unsplittable (O(sd/log d + d)) regimes by coalescing tree levels. - Clean problem formulation: the length-preserving black-box operator plus the splittable/unsplittable dichotomy isolates exactly the pipelining-vs-combining tension, and the two lower-bound theorems quantify precisely how the unsplittable constraint worsens degree dependence from Δ to log(Δ+1). - The fluid-model lower-bound machinery (Lemma 12, weight-growth induction) is a simple, reusable device for aggregation-style annihilation dynamics and is likely applicable to related scheduling problems. - Honest optimality accounting: the paper distinguishes which upper bounds are matched (bicliques, cliques) from which are merely logarithmic approximations (general graphs), and states open problems explicitly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion openly lists three open problems that bound the paper's scope: (1) no approximation algorithm or hardness for general graphs under splittable flows, (2) no constant approximation for trees, (3) no theory for non-uniform link bandwidths. Footnote 1 also concedes the model excludes operators permitting partial-value combining (e.g., XOR), which limits direct applicability to some practical reductions. The authors confront these boundaries directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. They do not, however, discuss the gap between their abstract unit-bandwidth synchronous model and real datacenter conditions (latency, jitter, full-duplex links, control-message overhead they assume away). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No empirical or simulation validation whatsoever: even a small-scale simulation comparing the Hamming-code hypercube schedule against the combine-in-each-step baseline (the strategy used by NCCL-style libraries) would materially strengthen the practical-relevance claim, which currently rests only on asymptotics. - The claim that these techniques "may be useful in other contexts" and the motivation from datacenter reduce/GPU collectives are extrapolations: the model's instantaneous-combine, free-control-message, and no-network-coding assumptions, plus half-duplex unit links, all deviate from real ML-cluster settings in directions that could change the optimum. - Tightness of the hypercube bounds is asserted but not proven against a hypercube-specific lower bound; the general lower bound may not be simultaneously achievable in all three terms for Q_d, and the additive +d terms are not separately certified as necessary. - The splittable-flows general-graph case is entirely open — the paper has lower bounds but no algorithm, a conspicuous asymmetry the authors acknowledge only as an open question rather than flagging as the biggest hole in the theory. - Dogs-not-barking: no comparison table against prior convergecast/LogP/postal-model results quantifying improvement on overlapping special cases (e.g., single-message values, s ≤ message size), making it hard to see how much is genuinely new versus re-derivable from Karp et al. 1993-style analyses. Bottom Line: For a distributed-algorithms theorist, this is a clearly worthwhile read — the recursive-Hamming-code scheduling technique and the sharp splittable-vs-unsplittable lower-bound separation are new tools likely to transfer — but a systems practitioner seeking better reduce schedules will find no implementation, no simulations, and no concrete guidance beyond asymptotics, so the practical payoff remains speculative.

Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty (140 ▲ )

Yifan Sun, Naicheng Yu, Jiawen Gong, Jingyan Shen, Huan Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a measure-theoretic view of LLM benchmarks — treating a benchmark as an empirical probability measure over a difficulty axis — and derives from it two diagnostic metrics (a 1-Wasserstein Difficulty Distribution Mismatch, DDM, and a maximum-gap statistic), a three-item-per-benchmark LLM gap-filling algorithm (BENCHFILL), and four gap-filled public benchmark variants. - Why it's important: Leaderboard rankings and RL/finetuning progress monitoring can be distorted or blinded when a benchmark's items are unevenly spread or locally absent along the difficulty axis, so practitioners may mis-rank models or prematurely discard training runs that made real, localized progress. - How it does it: The core move is re-casting the benchmark score as an integral with respect to the empirical measure induced by IRT-estimated item difficulties, which turns score distortion into a Wasserstein-distance bound and undetectable localized improvement into a minimax hypothesis-testing phase transition at the maximum gap. - The good: The theory is matched by careful practice: item difficulties come from a diagnosed 1PL IRT fit (MCMC diagnostics, leave-one-out stability with mean Pearson/Spearman ≥ 0.9723/0.9704, posterior uncertainty on the metrics themselves), and BENCHFILL is validated behaviorally — a 1-item insertion flips post-SFT gain detection from 0/3 to 3/3 on AIME variants with p < 0.05. - The missing: The paper never demonstrates a concrete real-world rank flip or mis-computed leaderboard conclusion caused by DDM on actual model pairs — Theorem 2.1 is worst-case with an unspecified Lipschitz constant L, so the practical magnitude of measure mismatch on published leaderboards remains unevidenced. - Read it or not: Read it if you build, audit, or select benchmarks or use them as RL progress monitors; skip it if you only consume existing leaderboard numbers and already accept that small benchmarks like AIME are noisy.

Rigor (78) is a standout: psychometric-standard 1PL IRT fitting with MCMC diagnostics and LOO stability, permutation testing with 100,000 draws, posterior uncertainty propagated into the metrics themselves, and released code, difficulty annotations, and gap-filled datasets — docked modestly for the preprint status and third-party agentic difficulty estimates. Novelty (78) reflects a credible NEW FORMULATION (benchmarks as empirical measures over difficulty) whose components are standard but whose formalization is genuinely first. Non-Obviousness (75) is high — the minimax detection-boundary characterization gives Max Gap sharp operational meaning. Completeness (68) and Resilience (70) are reduced by the absence of any demonstrated real-world leaderboard mis-ranking and the unexamined unidimensionality assumption.
