Problem & Motivation: Benchmark scores are used in two ways — ranking models on leaderboards and monitoring training progress — and in both cases conclusions depend on how benchmark questions are distributed over difficulty, not just on model ability. A benchmark that over-weights easy items can make two models look tied when the evaluation-relevant difficulty regions separate them (measure mismatch), and a benchmark with no items in a difficulty band cannot register a model's localized improvement there, however many rollouts are run (coverage gap). The authors argue this affects essentially everyone who publishes or consumes LLM evaluations, and that prior benchmark-reliability work (contamination, prompt sensitivity, signal-and-noise) has not formalized these two distributional failure modes. Key Idea: Represent a benchmark as the empirical measure ν_B = (1/n)Σδ_{z_i} over a continuous difficulty axis z ∈ [0,1], with item difficulties estimated by 1PL Item Response Theory; then benchmark-score distortion versus any target distribution µ is controlled by W₁(ν_B, µ), and a benchmark's inability to detect localized improvement is exactly characterized by its maximum adjacent spacing G(B). A maximin argument (Theorem 2.2) justifies the uniform distribution as the neutral default target when no application-specific difficulty prior exists. Methodology: Difficulty estimation: run 12 capability-stratified LLMs (1.7B–397B for non-agentic; HAL-reported frontier models for agentic) for up to 32 rollouts per item on 25 benchmarks across 7 domains, form the response matrix, fit a 1PL IRT model P(Y=1)=σ(θ_j−b_i) (with a guessing parameter for multiple choice) via NUTS MCMC, and pass 7 pre/post-fit diagnostics (informativeness, monotonicity inversion rates, R̂, ESS, divergences, LOO stability); BIC selects 1PL over 2PL on 21/25 benchmarks and MIRT fits fail convergence. Metrics: min-max normalize difficulties, compute DDM as the L₁ distance between the benchmark ECDF and a same-size empirical uniform reference, and compute Max Gap and Top-5 gap sum. Theory: (i) a Lipschitz coupling argument giving |D_B−D_µ| ≤ L·W₁(ν_B, µ) plus a finite-sample Hoeffding extension; (ii) a bathtub-principle proof that uniform is the unique maximin target; (iii) a minimax testing proof that G(B) is the exact asymptotic detection boundary for interval-localized improvements of width w. Intervention: BENCHFILL, an evolutionary rewrite-and-annotate loop — retrieve parent items nearest the target difficulty, LLM-rewrite into children, validity-check answers with GPT-5.4, annotate child difficulty by online calibration against frozen model abilities, update a memory of item–difficulty pairs, and pick the child closest to the gap midpoint, with human review before insertion. A calibration appendix adds greedy quantile-matching pruning toward a target measure. Critical design choices: 1PL (justified by BIC and diagnostics), uniform default target (justified by the maximin theorem, explicitly framed as a neutrality default not universal optimality), and rewriting rather than authoring items (justified by cost and style preservation, though human review remains in the loop). Key Results: Across 25 benchmarks (30–4241 items): 10/25 have DDM ≥ 0.10 (e.g., ScienceQA 0.178, MATH-500 0.164, MBPP+ 0.163, HumanEval 0.148, MedQA 0.157); 8/25 have Max Gap ≥ 0.10 (AMC23 0.217, HumanEval 0.165, AIME24 0.179, SWE-bench-Mini 0.149, BBH-5 objects 0.128); 9/25 have Top-5 gap sum ≥ 0.30, with AIME24/25 near 0.50 despite heavy use for monitoring RLVR training. Posterior uncertainty is small for DDM (SD ≈ 0.011) and, for Max Gap, the observed gaps exceed a same-size uniform-sampling baseline with median posterior probability 0.999 (median ratio 3.85×; 18.8× on ScienceQA). BENCHFILL, inserting only 3 items per benchmark, reduces the top-3 gap sum by 21.09%–38.88% (average 32.67% vs. 35.06% oracle and 17.52% for a budget-matched best-of-N uniform-parent baseline), with mean target difficulty deviation < 0.01 on 7 of 8 benchmarks. Quantile-matching calibration on 8 math benchmarks improves average Spearman agreement with a leave-one-out cross-benchmark reference ranking from 0.890 to 0.930 (Kendall 0.802→0.848), versus 0.895/0.801 for random pruning. Behaviorally, on AIME24/25/26 with one inserted item and mild SFT, the BenchFill-augmented benchmarks detect the localized gain at p < 0.05 in 3/3 cases while original and baseline-augmented variants detect 0/3. Baselines are appropriate for what is tested (uniform-parent rewriting, random pruning, oracle insertion), though there is no comparison against other difficulty-targeted data augmentation methods. Scale is standard benchmark-audit scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, plus a modest NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (BENCHFILL and the BenchFill datasets). The genuinely novel elements are the measure-theoretic formalization of benchmarks over difficulty and the exact minimax detection-boundary characterization of maximum gap — the claim that this is the first formalization of measure mismatch and coverage gaps as benchmark failure modes appears credible against the cited related work. The components themselves are standard: 1PL IRT is established psychometrics widely used in LLM evaluation (Easy2Hard-Bench, tinyBenchmarks, etc.), Wasserstein distance and hypothesis testing are off-the-shelf, and BENCHFILL is a competent combination of LLM rewriting, IRT calibration, and evolutionary search applied to a new objective. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and meaningful: 1PL vs. 2PL vs. MIRT model comparison via BIC plus convergence diagnostics, LOO robustness over the 12-model panel, prior-structure sensitivity checks, posterior uncertainty on both metrics, and a budget-matched baseline plus oracle for BENCHFILL. Statistical testing appears where it matters most (stratified randomization test with 100,000 permutations for gain detection; posterior probabilities for gap-vs-uniform comparisons). Code (GitHub: ASTRAL-Group/benchmark-difficulty-measure), difficulty estimates for all 25 benchmarks, and four BenchFill datasets (HuggingFace: Yifan99/BenchFill) are publicly released. Concerns: (1) difficulty is estimated from the same population of models that defines the framework's motivating examples, and difficulty under a 1PL model conflates discrimination; (2) the claim that measure mismatch "distorts leaderboard conclusions" is supported only indirectly via the calibration-to-reference-ranking experiment, not by showing an actual published ranking flip; (3) agentic-benchmark difficulties rest on third-party HAL results with 1 rollout per item, a weaker data basis; (4) the localized-improvement detection experiment uses 3 AIME cases with specific SFT setups — encouraging but small. The paper is a NeurIPS 2026 submission/preprint (arXiv:2610.29927), so results have not yet cleared peer review. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a small theoretical core). Practical: Yes — all evaluation and IRT fitting ran on single 48GB/96GB GPUs (L40S, RTX PRO 6000); the main cost, 12 models × up to 32 rollouts × 25 benchmarks, is a one-time amortizable audit. Efficient: Difficulty estimation and metric computation are cheap once the response matrix exists; BENCHFILL adds LLM rewriting plus calibration rollouts but inserts only 3 items per benchmark, far cheaper than building new benchmarks. Effective: The evidence shows the metrics diagnose real maldistribution and that filled items land on target and enable detection of localized gains in 3 tested cases — whether filling ~3 gaps materially changes training-monitor decisions at scale is shown only in that limited setting. Scalable: Scaling to benchmarks 10× larger should be straightforward for the metrics (difficulty estimation cost grows with items × models), but the paper does not test gap-filling beyond 8 benchmarks × 3 gaps, and large benchmarks with correlated difficulty clustering (e.g., ScienceQA at 4241 items, 18.8× the uniform gap baseline) suggest gaps are structural, not merely a small-n artifact — the paper asserts but does not demonstrate that BENCHFILL closes gaps at that scale. Deliverables: a real software artifact (pipeline code), released difficulty annotations, four gap-filled benchmark datasets, and a reusable diagnostic recipe; the calibration algorithm is paper-form (appendix only). Strengths: - Theorems that actually bind to practice: Theorem 2.3's minimax detection boundary gives Max Gap a sharp operational meaning (power = α below the boundary regardless of rollout count, power → 1 above it), elevating a heuristic coverage statistic to a precise monitor-resolution limit. - Difficulty estimation done to psychometric standard: stratified 12-model panel, guessing parameters, 7 diagnostic checks, LOO stability (worst-case Pearson 0.9137), and posterior uncertainty propagated into the reported metrics — most LLM benchmark-analysis papers do far less. - The detection experiment (Table 12) is the paper's best evidence: it demonstrates the failure mode end-to-end and shows the intervention fixes it, rather than only optimizing the metric it defines. - Honest framing of the uniform target as a maximin default rather than a claim that uniform is universally correct, and release of curated artifacts that others can immediately use. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the framework is primarily post-hoc (diagnose and patch existing benchmarks rather than design difficulty structure at construction time), position the perspective as opening a research direction rather than exhausting consequences of the measure view, note that non-uniformity is not inherently bad when it matches an intended objective, and acknowledge that Max Gap's magnitude depends on benchmark size (while arguing this is a real coverage limitation, not a nuisance). They do not confront the model-dependence of IRT difficulty, the single-difficulty-axis assumption, or the limited scale of the detection experiments — limitations are acknowledged politely but not deeply. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No demonstrated real-world instance of measure mismatch changing a leaderboard conclusion: Theorem 2.1's bound involves an unspecified L, and the calibration study measures correlation with other math benchmarks (itself a proxy), not agreement with a deployment-relevant difficulty distribution. - Difficulty is treated as a scalar on [0,1]; benchmarks differ along topic, format, and modality axes where analogous mismatch/coverage failures presumably exist, and the paper's own MIRT fits failed to converge — leaving the unidimensionality assumption unexamined rather than validated. - IRT difficulty is relative to the 2025–2026 model population; as frontier models saturate items, the entire difficulty distribution and all gap statistics shift, and the paper does not address temporal validity of the released annotations. - The gain-detection experiment couples BenchFill items with a targeted SFT run; it does not establish that the filled items preserve benchmark construct validity or contamination resistance for general use, and human review passed all 24 items "without modification," which invites scrutiny of reviewer independence. - The rewriter's validity judge is GPT-5.4, itself a frontier LLM; a circle-of-trust concern for generated item correctness that human review only partially mitigates. Bottom Line: Practitioners who build or maintain LLM benchmarks — or who use AIME-style small sets as RL reward proxies — should read this paper for its metrics, released difficulty annotations, and the detection-boundary insight; anyone only comparing leaderboard numbers will find the diagnosis useful but the paper stops short of proving how often their conclusions are actually wrong.

Haoyu Zhao, Sitian Tu, Yuxuan Huang, Huichi Zhou, Zhangyue Yin, Jiahao Huang, Jingyuan Xu, Tianmiao Shi, Jin Shi, Nianxi Zhang, Yangmiao Zhang, Zhuolang Chan, Huiyan Hu, Chenchao Sheng, Yaqing Luo, Yue Chen, Huaxiu Yao, Meng Fang, Jun Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a benchmark of 120 human-authored professional tasks organized as five-level gated ladders (600 levels, 89 roles, 12 domains) designed to measure whether LLM agents improve through accumulated experience rather than one-shot task solving. - Why it's important: Existing agent benchmarks score isolated tasks, so the field cannot measure whether agents retain, refine, and reuse knowledge across successive assignments — the capability needed for sustained real-world deployment and for recursive self-improvement (RSI). - How it does it: Later levels of each ladder require artefacts, procedures, preferences, and lessons established in earlier levels, agents must pass each level to unlock the next, and a tool-using evaluation agent grades submissions against 16,125 human-authored rubric criteria, with configurable diagnostic feedback (K=1 vs K=2 submission budgets). - The good: Across 17 harness–model configurations, no system exceeds 47.67% level completion or 23.3% full-ladder completion even with feedback and revision, and the evaluation agent shows 96.86% agreement with human rubric labels — evidence the benchmark is both hard and reliably graded. - The missing: The paper never runs the controlled experiment that would isolate actual cross-task learning — resetting harness state between tasks to compare against the persistent-state condition — so the headline numbers conflate single-task capability with experiential learning. - Read it or not: Read it if you build agent memory, skill-learning, or RSI systems and need a credible evaluation target; skip it if you want a demonstrated continual-learning method, since the paper contributes the exam, not a passing grade.

Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying LLM agents in professional workflows need systems that improve over time — learning a tool procedure once, avoiding a repeated mistake, remembering a user's preference. But current evaluation infrastructure cannot detect this. General capability benchmarks (GAIA, SWE-bench) score tasks independently; memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval) test retrieval over histories via question answering rather than whether retained knowledge improves task execution; workflow benchmarks with persistent state (ClawMark, WildClawBench) benefit from continuity but do not require that experience transfer into later performance. There is no standard instrument that measures improvement through accumulated experience under controlled feedback conditions. Key Idea: Structure professional work as gated task ladders whose later levels are functionally unsolvable without knowledge from earlier levels — five explicit transfer types (Tools and Skills, Data Dependency, Strategy, User Context, Domain Knowledge) connect the five levels of each ladder — and let the agent's harness decide what to retain (model parameters stay frozen; learning lives in persistent harness state). Cross-level file references appear in 88 of the 120 ladders, rising from 73 ladders at L2 to 84 at L5, so experience reuse is a structural requirement, not a bonus. Methodology: CLE's construction pipeline: 50+ domain professionals author tasks grounded in real files from their own occupations (23,981 input files, 77 extensions, deliberately retaining noise like duplicates and conflicts); 19 stateful mock applications expose 1,024 APIs with per-run databases that carry each ladder's effects across levels; an agent-driven auto-review (using a human-refined review skill, including an end-to-end test run) gates drafts, then two independent human reviewers must both accept a task for admission. Evaluation is framed as a POMDP ⟨X, A, O, P, Ω, R⟩ where reward equals the evaluator's binary verdict on submission actions, and the objective is expected number of levels passed over a serial stream of all 120 ladders. The evaluator agent (DeepSeek V4 Flash) verifies each submission against human-authored rubrics (16,125 checklist items, mean 26.9/level, rising from 18.74 at L1 to 36.83 at L5) in an isolated Docker-isolated grading environment with audit logs. Two protocol settings are compared: K=1 (one submission, no feedback) and K=2 (diagnostic feedback naming the failing rubric category after first failure, then one revision). The paper also contributes a formal framework: (θ, s) update operator U_n covering parametric and non-parametric learning, a five-tier capability hierarchy (T1 guided learning to T5 self-driven problem selection), and a taxonomy distinguishing CL from online learning, test-time training, case-based reasoning, and RSI. Critical design decisions: (1) gating levels on pass/fail — justified as forcing genuine progression; (2) hiding rubric detail while exposing category-level diagnostic feedback — justified as a realistic partial learning signal; (3) frozen models with harness-only state — justified as the current dominant deployment mode, though it means CLE as-run measures harness-based learning only. Key Results: Best system: Claude Code with Opus 5 at 42.17% completion (Trial 1) and 47.67% (Trial 2), completing all five levels in 23.33% of tasks (28/120). GPT-5.6-Sol and GPT-5.6-Terra under Codex reach 33.17% at roughly 2.5× lower cost ($210.83 and $83.16 vs $720.56). Median Trial 2 gain from feedback and revision is +5.33 pp (16 of 17 configurations improve; OpenClaw/DeepSeek V4 Pro declines −1.33 pp); Sonnet 5 gains most (+13.17 pp). Median cumulative pass rates in Trial 2 fall from 62.50% at L1 to 8.33% at L5. Harness matters: Hermes-Agent beats OpenClaw on all six shared backbones (mean advantage 11.42 pp in Trial 2). Costs span $8.26 (Hermes/Hy3, Trial 2) to $720.56, with completion-vs-cost and completion-vs-runtime Pareto frontiers reported. Counter-intuitive finding: model generation does not monotonically improve performance — Gemini 3.8 Flash (30.67%) trails Gemini 3.7 Flash (33.67%) while consuming 1.8× the tokens. Level-1 performance correlates with overall completion (Spearman ρ=0.75) but only weakly with full-ladder completion (ρ=0.42 vs L5). Benchmark scale: 600 levels per run × 17 configurations × 2 trials, i.e., stress-scale for evaluation, though all at frontier-model API scale. Baselines are the strongest available frontier systems in their own production harnesses — current and strong, not outdated. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely novel contribution is the gated-ladder design in which later levels require artefacts, procedures, and lessons from earlier ones, combined with a configurable feedback protocol and audited agentic grading — the paper's Table 2 comparison shows no prior benchmark combines tiered tasks, cross-level reuse, configurable attempts, milestone feedback, and audit trails. The POMDP formulation and U_n notation are competent packaging of standard ideas; the data-construction pipeline (expert authoring plus agent pre-review plus dual human review) applies known quality-control patterns at new scale. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluator is validated against adjudicated human labels on 12 tasks (732 rubric items) at 96.86% item-level agreement and 99.46% self-consistency across three repeated grading runs — a strong, unusual step for agentic-judge benchmarks. However, the main actor results come from single runs per configuration: no seeds, no error bars, no significance tests on the +5.3 pp median gain or harness comparisons. No ablations decompose which benchmark components drive difficulty. Code, data, and a Hugging Face release are provided (https://github.com/haoyu-zhao/Continual-Learning-Exam). Methodological concerns: (1) the paper explicitly concedes that Trial 1 vs Trial 2 compares feedback-plus-revision jointly, and that a matched comparison resetting harness state between tasks — the experiment that would actually isolate knowledge retention — was not run; (2) a single fixed task order for all configurations means content effects and order-specific state contamination are unmeasured; (3) Gemini-generation comparisons (Table 7) rest on single runs with cost differences that partly reflect workload, which the authors do flag. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS — a built benchmark, environment, and evaluation service, evaluated by running frontier agents through it. - Practical: Yes — runs against commercial model APIs and four public harnesses; grading is Docker-isolated and can run on separate machines. - Efficient: Full runs cost $8–$721 and 14–143 hours of active runtime per configuration, so a complete evaluation is comparable to a mid-size agent benchmark, not cheap at the frontier end. - Effective: It reliably measures gated multi-assignment professional task completion, but whether it measures experiential learning specifically is unproven without the harness-reset ablation — the headline numbers also reflect raw task capability. - Scalable: Untested beyond 120 ladders; the authors state the block formulation supports starting mid-ladder with prepared artefacts, and post-training use of the dataset is claimed but not demonstrated. Deliverables: public dataset (600 levels, 23,981 files), 19 stateful mock applications with 1,024 APIs, evaluation-agent grading service, and leaderboard infrastructure — a substantial reusable artifact. Strengths: - Structural forcing of experience reuse: 88/120 ladders contain explicit cross-level file references, making continual learning a pass/fail requirement rather than a soft advantage — a design no prior agent benchmark enforces this consistently. - Validator transparency unusual for agentic-judge benchmarks: 96.86% human agreement at rubric-item level and 99.46% grading stability are reported and appendix-documented, directly addressing the biggest weakness of LLM-graded evaluations. - Honest difficulty calibration: the paper leads with the finding that the best frontier system fails over half the levels, and reports cost/runtime Pareto trade-offs rather than only accuracy — useful for practitioners choosing agents. - The conceptual framework (U_n update operator, T1–T5 capability tiers, disambiguation of CL vs RSI vs TTT vs CBR) gives the field shared vocabulary and a measurable roadmap, which is a real intellectual contribution beyond the dataset itself. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that (1) Trial 1 vs Trial 2 conflates feedback and revision opportunity, and a matched harness-reset comparison would be needed to isolate retained knowledge; (2) Trial 2 gains do not consistently extend to later ladder levels (Qwen3.8-Max configurations improve at L1–L3 but not L4–L5); (3) resource totals cover runs with different workloads and do not establish efficiency on matched workloads; (4) conditional pass-rate increases at later levels reflect survivorship and accumulated experience, not easier assignments. This direct confrontation of limitations is a credibility positive. They do not discuss single-run variance, task-order effects, or evaluator coverage limits in the main text. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No memory-off / state-reset control condition: without comparing persistent-state harnesses to themselves with experience wiped between ladders, the benchmark's namesake capability — continual learning — is inferred, not measured; a strong single-task agent could score highly here. - Single run per configuration with a single fixed task order; given that harness state persists across all 120 ladders in one serial stream, run-to-run variance and order sensitivity could be material, and no repeat runs or random orders are reported. - Evaluator agreement validated on only 12 tasks (60 submissions, 732 items) out of 120 tasks — roughly 4.5% of rubric items — leaving open whether agreement holds for the harder, longer L4–L5 rubrics. - The claimed post-training use of CLE for continual learning is asserted in the abstract but never demonstrated; no fine-tuning experiment is run. - Harness confound: performance differences (e.g., Hermes vs OpenClaw's 11.42 pp gap) mix memory management, prompting, and tooling; no ablation identifies which harness component drives the advantage. - K=2 diagnostic feedback discloses only the failing rubric category while rubric granularity grows from ~19 items at L1 to ~37 at L5, so feedback informativeness varies systematically with level — an unexamined interaction with the measured feedback gains. Bottom Line: This is the most carefully constructed and honestly evaluated attempt yet to make LLM-agent experiential learning a measured quantity rather than a claimed one, and anyone building memory or self-improving agent systems should adopt or at least run against it — but its headline scores measure task capability and harness quality as much as continual learning, until the authors (or someone else) run the harness-reset control the paper itself says is needed.

BehaVerify: A Formal Verification Tool for Behavior Trees

SSSBW Diego, MLL Nam, AMTNK Potteiger… · woodingben.com · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BehaVerify, a distribution-ready open-source toolbox that verifies Behavior Trees (BTs) and Neuro-Symbolic BTs against LTL/CTL/invariant specifications via an SSA-style "fastforwarding" encoding into nuXmv, and generates executable Python (PyTrees/ROS) and Haskell implementations from the same DSL. - Why it's important: BTs increasingly control safety-critical robots (drones, underwater vehicles, mining, medical devices), but no prior BT verification tool supported CTL, non-Boolean variables, neural-network leaves, runtime monitors, and code generation in one pipeline, leaving practitioners to assemble incompatible toolchains. - How it does it: A tick of a BT is a loop-free computation, so the entire tick is compiled into a single nuXmv transition using static single assignment (SSA) form — intermediate variable versions become DEFINEs, collapsing per-node traversal states and making reachable state count independent of node count. - The good: The first controlled ablation isolates the encoding itself: on a binary-tree benchmark scaled to 2,055 nodes, the naive encoding times out at N≥8 while fastforwarding verifies CTL in 2.24s at N=10, with reachable states growing linearly (FF log2 ≈ 12.6) versus roughly quadratically (naive). - The missing: Cross-tool comparisons are on each tool's own examples with acknowledged semantic mismatches (PyTrees vs. BehaviorTree.cpp node semantics), and the flagship neuro-symbolic experiment uses only table-mode enumeration of a 10^4-entry input domain — no evaluation of the symbolic (piecewise-linear) network encoding is reported. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or verify BT-based robot controllers and want a working verification pipeline (pip/Docker installable with a reproducibility package); skip it if you seek new verification theory, since the authors themselves frame this as engineering consolidation of four prior theory papers.

Problem & Motivation: Behavior Trees are hierarchical controllers, re-evaluated from the root on each "tick," that have displaced hand-written state machines in robotics and safety-critical autonomy (drone inspection, underwater vehicles, network defense, surgical insertion). Because these are safety-critical deployments, designers need to prove that temporal properties hold — e.g., a drone always can reach its goal, a battery-critical landing takes priority. Existing BT verification tools each cover only part of this need: MoVe4BT lacks CTL, invariants, and variables in specifications; BT2Fiacre and BT2BIP do not support neural-network leaves or code generation for deployment; and prior BehaVerify publications established theory (Stateful BT semantics, neuro-symbolic extension, runtime monitors) in three separate research prototypes that were never released as a usable tool. The gap this paper closes is consolidation and distribution: one DSL, one CLI, one verified model feeding verification and deployment backends. Key Idea: Fastforwarding — compile one whole BT tick into a single model-checker transition by treating the depth-first intra-tick traversal as a loop-free SSA computation: each variable update introduces a fresh "stage" version, deterministic updates become DEFINEs (costing no state), nondeterministic intra-tick choices become branching of that single transition, and stages remain queryable in specifications via an `at n` operator. The authors are candid that SSA-style encodings are standard in software model checking (large-block encoding, bounded model checking of C); what is BT-specific is how guards arise from node return statuses and how stages are exposed to LTL/CTL. A secondary mechanism for the neuro-symbolic extension is "table mode": because network inputs have bounded integer domains, the network is exhaustively evaluated with ONNX Runtime over all input combinations and emitted as a finite case expression, keeping the model exact and finite-state. Methodology: The pipeline (Figure 2) is: user writes a `.tree` DSL file (textX grammar) containing the BT, variable declarations (blackboard vs. environment), Lisp-style update functions, and LTL/CTL/invariant specifications; a parser with type/scope checking builds one internal Stateful BT model; backends then read that model — (1) a nuXmv encoder emitting either the fastforwarded or naive `.smv` model, (2) Python code generation built on PyTrees for deployment through ROS, (3) Haskell code generation as a pure executable reference semantics used for differential testing, and (4) LaTeX/GUI renderers for trees and counterexample traces. Neural-network leaves enter through ONNX declarations (table mode used in experiments; symbolic piecewise-linear modes over reals or bit-vectors available but untested here). Fastforwarding's soundness is argued as bisimilarity to the tick-level SBT semantics of [29] — the constructed Kripke structure matches tick-boundary semantics up to auxiliary variables, preserving full CTL*, with both encodings returning identical verdicts on every instance where the naive encoding completed. Critical design decisions: (a) adopting PyTrees semantics (no true parallel nodes) — justified as deliberate alignment with the deployment library; (b) stage-collapsing of deterministic updates into DEFINEs — well-justified, this is what makes state count node-independent; (c) table-mode neural encoding — sound and exact but its cost scales with input-domain size, not network size, a limitation the authors state. CI/CD runs 406 pytest tests across Python 3.10–3.12 with nuXmv download-and-verify checks. Key Results: All experiments ran on an i7-10750H (6-core/12-thread) with 16GB RAM, 5-minute per-instance timeout, timings averaged over three runs. (1) Encoding ablation on a binary-tree benchmark scaled to N=10 (2,055 nodes): fastforwarding verifies CTL in 2.24s and LTL in 153.65s, with reachable states growing linearly (log2 ≈ 12.6/13.0 total), while the naive encoding inside the same tool times out at N≥8 (CTL) and N≥7 (LTL), with naive total state space 2^226.86 at N=7 vs. FF's 2^10.01. (2) Versus MoVe4BT (same benchmark), MoVe4BT crashed at 2,055 nodes ("QProcess: Destroyed while process (mono) is still running"); BehaVerify's naive-vs-FF gap is of the same order as the BehaVerify-vs-MoVe4BT gap. (3) Versus BT2Fiacre on a recreated UAV drone (x,y ∈ [-30,30], height ∈ [0,80]): BehaVerify checks the height invariant in 86.87s (drone3) / 0.48s (reactive rewrite droneNew) while BT2Fiacre times out; the rewrite shrinks reachable states from log2 22.83 to 16.53. BehaVerify also falsifies a previously unreported battery-priority violation in the BT2Fiacre drone tree. (4) BT2BIP recreations (Mars Rover, Train Control): verdicts agree; BT2BIP times out on LTL for larger trees. (5) Neuro-symbolic drone (10×10 grid, 22 obstacles, one 1,000-neuron ReLU network per configuration, table mode over 10^4 inputs): translation 0.54–0.55s, invariant verified in 0.87–0.95s, CTL verified in 9.24s (1.0-accuracy network) but falsified for the 0.9995-accuracy network — the imperfect network emits non-progressing actions and the drone never reaches the goal, a closed-loop failure invisible to open-loop network verification. Baselines are the current published BT verification tools, though tested on their own examples rather than a shared benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. Genuinely novel: the first distribution-ready consolidation of SBT verification, neuro-symbolic BT verification, and verified runtime monitors behind one DSL/CLI; the first controlled ablation isolating the fastforwarding encoding; the first BT tool supporting neural-network leaves; the newly discovered battery-priority bug. Explicitly not novel: fastforwarding itself, which the authors identify as SSA form / large-block encoding applied to BT tick semantics — a known technique in a new setting. The neuro-symbolic extension (replacing a leaf with an exhaustively enumerated bounded-domain network) is a straightforward combination of prior NSBT theory [27] with standard finite-state model checking. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a tool paper. The fastforwarding-vs-naive ablation is precisely the experiment missing from prior work (the earlier comparison against MoVe4BT could not separate encoding from tool effects). A reproducibility package (Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20280547) contains one Docker image with pinned versions regenerating Tables 4–5; code is open source at https://github.com/verivital/behaverify with PyPI release (v1.0.0), documentation, tutorial examples, and 406 CI tests. Timings are three-run averages. Weaknesses: no error bars, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported; the neural-network experiment reports single timings; counterexample claims rest on the authors' own encodings. Cross-tool comparisons inherit acknowledged semantic mismatches (each tool tested on its own examples), the BT2BIP toolchain would not run in the authors' containers (only the BehaVerify side is reproduced), and BT2BIP examples are small enough that "timing comparisons against them carry little information" by the authors' own admission. The soundness argument for fastforwarding is a bisimilarity claim referencing [29], not restated or machine-checked in this paper. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, distributed tool evaluated by benchmarks and real-robot deployment). - Practical: Yes — cross-platform (Linux/macOS/Windows), installs via pip or Docker, runs on a 16GB-RAM laptop, with GUI and ROS/PyTrees integration; deployed on real underwater vehicles and quadcopters in prior work. - Efficient: Verification is fast (sub-second to ~154s) versus timeouts for competing tools; translation time is under 1s except 3s at the largest benchmark; table-mode NSBT cost scales with input-domain size (10^4 rows), which will not generalize to larger or continuous domains. - Effective: The evidence shows the tool verifies real trees and found a real (previously unreported) battery-priority bug plus a genuine closed-loop failure of a 99.95%-accuracy network — beyond proxy claims; but effectiveness at scale on a full robotic application versus BT2Fiacre is listed as future work. - Scalable: Tested to 2,055 nodes with linear reachable-state growth under fastforwarding; 10–100× further scaling is projected by the linear growth but not tested, and BDD-based verification of larger neural-network tables or continuous domains would require the untested symbolic modes. The work delivers a substantial software artifact: a PyPI/Docker-distributed toolbox with CLI, GUI, code generators, and a reproducibility package. Strengths: - Honest positioning: the authors explicitly disclaim the theory as new, classify fastforwarding as an application of SSA, and clearly separate what is consolidated from what is new (distribution release, ablation, new comparisons) — rare clarity in tool papers. - The within-tool naive-vs-fastforwarding ablation is methodologically the right experiment and decisively attributes the scalability advantage to the encoding (naive total states 2^226.86 vs. FF 2^10.01 at N=7; naive CTL timeout at N≥8 vs. 2.24s FF at N=10). - The neuro-symbolic result is the most interesting finding: a 0.05% input-error rate network passes open-loop checks but provably fails the closed-loop AG(AF reach) property, with nuXmv producing a multi-tick non-progressing counterexample — a concrete demonstration that open-loop network verification is insufficient for closed-loop autonomy. - Verification utility beyond confirming properties: cheap specifications plus fast checking surfaced a real battery-priority bug in a published BT2Fiacre example that the original tool's specification set never checked. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly state: no all-tools-on-all-benchmarks comparison is possible due to semantic mismatches (PyTrees vs. BehaviorTree.cpp, e.g., sequence-with-memory has no PyTrees counterpart); no true parallel node execution (deliberate PyTrees alignment, not an implementation gap); no native per-node duration primitive (recoverable via tick counters); BT2BIP examples too small for meaningful timing; the BT2BIP toolchain would not run in their containers; the DSL is verbose for end users; and table-mode NSBT cost grows with input-domain size, requiring symbolic modes for larger/continuous domains. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evaluation of the symbolic network-encoding modes (piecewise-linear over reals or bit-vectors) — only table mode on a 10^4-entry domain is tested, so the neuro-symbolic story is untested exactly where it would matter (larger or continuous inputs). - Single-run neural timings with no variance, and only two networks of one architecture (one 1,000-neuron layer); no sensitivity to network size despite the claim that table mode is input-domain-bounded. - The bisimilarity soundness argument for fastforwarding is cited to prior work rather than proven or mechanically checked here; empirical agreement of encodings is supportive but not a proof. - The BT2Fiacre speedup is measured on a recreated, semantically-approximate tree ("closest possible"), so cross-tool speedup magnitudes carry uncertainty the paper cannot quantify. - No comparison against ArcadeBT (CHC-based) or BTCompiler; the tool landscape comparison relies on a feature table plus two timing baselines. - LTL results are given only for the synthetic binary-tree benchmark; the realistic examples use CTL/invariants, so LTL scalability on domain models is not characterized. Bottom Line: For anyone verifying BT controllers — especially with neural-network leaves — BehaVerify is now the most capable and only installable tool in this space, and the paper's honest ablation makes the fastforwarding advantage credible; read it, but treat the cross-tool speedups as indicative rather than exact, and note that neuro-symbolic scalability beyond small enumerated input domains remains unproven.

Zixian Gao, Lixin Xiu, Penghao Luo, Xiangcheng Cao, Ziqi Cai, Zhen Li, Erwin Wu, Kaipeng Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DirCast, a single streaming video-language model that simultaneously directs (chooses which of ten player camera feeds goes on air each second) and commentates (generates live speech over its own shot choices) for Dota 2 broadcasts, plus a 27-match multi-camera dataset with human directing labels and caster transcripts. - Why it's important: The long tail of esports and sports matches is streamed with a fixed camera and no commentary because trained director/caster crews are expensive; a model that produces a complete broadcast from raw feeds removes that bottleneck. - How it does it: A causal video LM processes all ten feeds per second at low resolution with game-state tokens, applies a hold-or-switch cut gate plus pointer to select one feed, reads that feed at high resolution before speaking, and keeps only the produced program (aired shots + spoken words) in context so cost per second is bounded. - The good: DirCast beats eleven streaming commentators (29.21% win rate vs GPT-4o under the Proact-VL protocol vs 19.38% for the strongest baseline) while producing its own broadcast, and directs with Top-1 agreement of 27.0 vs 25.4 for the best rule baseline and 13.5 for GPT-5, with ablations isolating each component across three seeds. - The missing: Commentary quality is judged only by LLM judges (GPT-5, since the official GPT-5.1 judge was unavailable), with no human evaluation, and directing agreement is evaluated on only 4 test matches with modest absolute Top-1 (27%) on a task where trivial persistence is reported to reach ~80% per-second accuracy under a different accounting. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on streaming video LLMs, proactive commentary, or multi-camera view selection — it defines and operationalizes a new coupled task with a dataset and strong baselines; skip it if you need general-domain (non-Dota 2, non-esports) results, which the paper does not provide.

Problem & Motivation: Live broadcasts need a director choosing the on-air camera every second and a caster narrating that choice, both causally (past only). Existing streaming commentators (LiveCC, StreamingVLM, Proact-VL, MMDuet, etc.) assume a finished, human-directed program as input, so the hardest part of live production — deciding what the audience sees — is never modeled. Practitioners streaming lower-tier matches without crews get no help from these models, because the models cannot ingest raw multi-camera feeds. Prior work studies view selection and commentary generation separately; the paper argues the two are coupled: a director's mistake determines what the commentator sees, and errors compound over the stream (exposure bias), while ten simultaneous feeds at full resolution blow past any streaming model's context budget. Key Idea: Treat the produced broadcast itself as the model's memory: one causal video LM processes each second as a chunk containing ten low-resolution feed views paired with game-state tokens, makes a factored hold-or-switch directing decision (a cut gate on the current shot times a pointer over the other nine cameras), then appends the chosen camera at high resolution followed by the commentary token and words — so commentary is generated conditioned on the directing choice, low-resolution views expire after W=8 seconds, and only the aired program and spoken words persist. A hold-or-switch factorization (rather than a 10-way classifier per second) makes holding the default and eliminates flickering cuts. Methodology: The pipeline per second t: (1) chunk construction — game clock, event text, ten low-res views (128 px) each with a state token encoding hero health/nearby enemies/recent damage; (2) directing — a sigmoid cut gate g_t over director and current-shot hidden states, and a pointer π_t(k) comparing the director state to each camera's content/state via dot products plus a learned player-slot embedding; P(c_t=k) = (1−g_t)·1[k=current] + g_t·π_t(k); (3) append chosen feed at 288 px, then a commentary token whose probability gates speaking, then the words. Training on Qwen3-VL-8B with LoRA (3 epochs, 8×H100) uses three losses (language modeling, binary speak/silence, gate+pointer directing) plus two fixes for imitation gaps: perturbed program rollouts (the on-air feed in the input drifts from the human choice while targets stay human, addressing exposure bias à la scheduled sampling/DAgger) and event-anchored targets (cuts to killer/victim cameras around kills count as correct). At inference, cut and speak thresholds adaptively track the model's own running decision rates toward human rates (cut 7.9/min, speech ~74% of seconds), without test-time tuning. Dataset: 27 professional Dota 2 matches rendered as ten hero-chase cameras from replay files, aligned to broadcasts via HUD-clock OCR (~0.3 s residual), labeled per second via HUD name-tag OCR, with broadcast-state filtering, VLM verification of carried-over labels, and GPT-5-mini polishing of Whisper transcripts under a word-count/content guard. Design decisions (hold-or-switch factorization, state tokens, program memory) are each ablated; the event-anchored target involves an acknowledged trade-off (Top-1 vs Any-visible). Key Results: On 4 unseen test matches (496 clips, 11,283 strict live seconds): Directing — DirCast Top-1 26.95, Tol-top1 32.0, Any-visible 41.81, cut precision 15.8, cut F1 14.1, cuts/min 6.7 (human 7.9), kill coverage 89.1% (human 50.3%), fight coverage 41.1% (human 37.4%); best baselines are the game-state action rule (Top-1 25.4, Any-vis 36.1, kill coverage 78.5) and, among eight zero-shot VLMs, InternVL3.5-8B (Top-1 19.1); GPT-5 reaches only Top-1 13.5 and most zero-shot VLMs cut 20–56 times/min vs the human 7.9. Commentary (Proact-VL protocol, GPT-5 as judge replacing the unavailable official GPT-5.1): CC win rate vs GPT-4o 29.21% vs 19.38% for the best of eleven streaming commentators (LiveCC-7B-Base) and 18.25% for Proact-VL fine-tuned on the authors' data; TimeDiff 0.30 s behind human casters; PAUC 0.024 vs 0.015 best baseline; all seeds beat LiveCC-7B-Base and Proact-VL at p<0.001 (paired bootstrap). F1 (78.22) and fidelity are confounded by speaking rate, which the paper analyzes honestly (always speaking yields F1 84.8; speaking 10% of the time inflates fidelity). Ablations: removing hold-or-switch drops Top-1 from 27.00 to 21.65; state tokens and program rollouts each cost ~4 points; the joint model beats separate director+commentator models (Top-1 27.00 vs 25.17; CC 29.21 vs 24.36) at half the memory (18.9 GB vs 37.8 GB). Streaming eight 288-second windows on one GPU: 36-second token horizon holds the cache at 6.9k tokens, 0.29 s compute per video second, and slightly improves Top-1 (25.1) and late-stream speech rate (76.7) versus keeping everything. Training-data scaling from 5→20 matches shows an accelerating curve (Top-1 20.08→26.56) with no saturation. Baselines are current (2025–2026 venues); the strongest commentary baselines are also fine-tuned on the authors' training split. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (live broadcast production: joint causal directing + commentary from raw multi-camera feeds), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (27-match multi-camera Dota 2 corpus with per-second directing labels, game state, and polished commentary), and NEW METHOD (program-as-memory streaming + hold-or-switch directing with perturbed rollouts). The genuinely novel part is the coupling of directing and commentary in one causal model where the model's own program is its context; individual ingredients — low-res/high-res coarse-to-fine processing, KV-cache eviction, scheduled-sampling-style rollouts, pointer networks — are known techniques recombined for a new task, which the paper itself acknowledges via its related-work positioning. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover the main architectural and training components (hold-or-switch, state tokens, program rollouts, event-anchored targets) and the joint-vs-separate question, with the commentator-on-human-program control correctly isolating that directing skill improves commentary. DirCast is averaged over three seeds and the seed-level bootstrap significance is reported for the headline commentary comparison; baseline VLM direction is not multi-seeded. Code and project page are linked (github.com/ZixianGao/DirCast-code); dataset release is implied via the project page but no explicit dataset URL or license is stated in the text. Concerns: (1) evaluation on only 4 test matches; (2) commentary is judged by GPT-5 while references were polished by GPT-5-mini and the comparison opponent is GPT-4o — same-family judge effects are plausible and the official GPT-5.1 judge was unavailable, so all CC numbers are relative, not absolute; (3) no human subjective evaluation of broadcast quality; (4) Top-1 agreement of 27% is low in absolute terms, and the appendix's admission that a persistence baseline reaches ~80% per-second accuracy under a different accounting makes the headline agreement numbers hard to interpret without the switch-second breakdown the text promises but does not show in Table 1; (5) directing labels are derived from OCR of HUD name tags with model-verified carry-overs, an automated pipeline with residual label noise (strict mask keeps 69% of live test seconds). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with runtime measurements; closest to SYSTEMS but evaluated on benchmarks rather than deployment). - Practical: Yes — inference runs on a single GPU (18.9 GB, presumably an H100-class card); the game-state inputs require Dota 2 replay/spectator data, which is available for this game but not for arbitrary video. - Efficient: 0.29 s compute per video-second and a 6.9k-token cache at the 36 s horizon versus 92.6k tokens and P95 >1 s/video-second if all views are kept — a large, measured efficiency win, though the 36 s horizon means the model sees at most ~36 seconds of history. - Effective: Evidence supports the claim on its own benchmark (best directing agreement and commentary win rates among tested systems, more kills on air than human crews), but commentary superiority is only demonstrated under LLM-judge metrics; effectiveness with human viewers is unevaluated. - Scalable: Only tested on 288-second windows (8× the training clip); full-match (40+ minute) behavior, multi-match concurrent streaming, and the unsaturated data-scaling curve beyond 20 matches are claimed as future work, not measured. The work delivers code, a project page, and presumably the dataset and LoRA-tuned model; it stops at paper form as a deployed tool. Strengths: - Genuinely new task formulation: the paper identifies that streaming commentary models inherit a human director for free, and defines and measures the coupled problem rather than the easier halves separately. - The program-as-memory design is a clean, well-motivated solution to bounded-cost streaming that is validated quantitatively (Table 5: 13× cache reduction with accuracy unchanged or improved), not just asserted. - The training-side fixes for imitation gaps — perturbed program rollouts against exposure bias and event-anchored targets against inconsistent human labels — are targeted, well-argued, and each ablated with sensible signs. - Unusually honest metric analysis: the paper explicitly explains why F1 and fidelity favor degenerate speaking rates, reports that its own model loses those two metrics, and quantifies how the human director covers fewer kills (50.3%) than DirCast (89.1%) — a finding that cuts against pure human-imitation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge the event-anchored target trade-off (matching the human director vs covering events, with Any-visible rising to 43.06 when removed); that GPT-5.1, the official judge, was unavailable so GPT-5 judged all models; that F1 and fidelity metrics reward extreme speaking rates rather than quality; that the data-scaling curve is unsaturated and scaling to hundreds of matches is future work; and that the action rule beats them on fight coverage by construction. They confront limitations directly and with numbers, which is a credibility positive. Not stated: any discussion of single-game (Dota 2-only) generality, LLM-judge bias, or human perceptual evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Absolute directing performance is weak: Top-1 of 27% against a human director, on a task where the appendix reports persistence reaches ~80% per-second accuracy under a different accounting — the paper promises switch-second accuracy "separately" but Table 1 does not report it, leaving the headline number hard to contextualize. - All evaluation is LLM-judged (GPT-5) with references polished by GPT-5-mini and the opponent being GPT-4o; no human study of whether DirCast's broadcasts are actually preferable to watch. - Four test matches is a very small evaluation set for a task with high match-to-match variance (the scaling figure itself shows large gains from added matches); no per-match error bars. - The method depends on structured game state and event streams from the replay file, so the approach does not transfer to sports or games without such telemetry; the paper frames the contribution as general broadcast production but the mechanism is Dota 2-specific in its grounding. - Baseline directors are zero-shot VLMs and rules; no fine-tuned directing baseline (e.g., the same backbone trained only on the directing loss with a simple classifier head, without the full DirCast machinery) isolates how much comes from data vs architecture. - The kill-coverage comparison against the human director (89.1% vs 50.3%) conflates a virtue with a difference in objective — human crews deliberately stay with narrative threads — and the paper's own framing accepts human imitation as the training target while marketing coverage as a win. Bottom Line: A practitioner in streaming video models, esports production, or proactive commentary gains real, reusable machinery — a new task, dataset, and a measured recipe for coupling action selection with narration — and should read this despite the LLM-judge-only commentary evaluation and single-game scope, which a human study and a second game would need to settle.

Foresight-on-Graph: Vision-Guided Knowledge Graph Reasoning with Large Language Models

Y Hu, R Lei, Z Wei, Y Liu, C Hong, J Zheng, J Zhang · aclanthology.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FoG, a training-free framework in which a vision-language model plans multi-hop paths over a visually rendered, coarsened relation graph extracted from a knowledge graph, rather than traversing the KG hop-by-hop through text. - Why it's important: Interactive KGQA methods like ToG and PoG waste LLM calls on myopic one-hop exploration of large graphs, which is slow, expensive, and error-prone on multi-entity questions; FoG targets both the accuracy and the per-question API cost of this paradigm. - How it does it: An LLM first predicts the implicit relation path for the question; Sentence-BERT fuzzy matching filters irrelevant relations; a relation-based union-find coarsens subgraphs of ~10^5–10^6 entities into tens of equivalence-class nodes, which are rendered as an image for VLM path selection and instantiated via SPARQL, with iterative re-centering when evidence is insufficient. - The good: The controlled evidence chain is credible — a modality study on ExplaGraphs (GPT-4o: 97.1% vision vs 89.7% text), three textual serializations of the same graph performing within ~1 point of each other (ruling out format artifacts), and a 3-run evaluation showing FoG beats GPT-4o re-runs of PoG by 4.9/5.2/6.4 Hit points on CWQ/WebQSP/GrailQA while using ~2.5× fewer LLM calls than ToG. - The missing: The headline framing is vision, but the FoG-T ablation shows the relation-graph coarsening alone (text modality) already delivers most of the gain over PoG (e.g., 67.2 vs 63.2 on CWQ at GPT-3.5); the vision contribution is 2.5–5.1 points, and no open-weight-VLM deployment or dense-graph stress test establishes where visual reasoning breaks (authors concede VLMs misread dense graphs; 52% of WebQSP failures are the VLM missing the correct path). - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building LLM×KG agentic systems who want a concrete, well-ablated demonstration that graph coarsening plus visual serialization beats hop-by-hop traversal; skippable if you only care about the vision claim itself, which is real but secondary to the coarsening trick.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building LLM-based knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) face two failure modes in existing synergy-augmented methods (ToG, PoG): myopic exploration, where the LLM sees only 1-hop neighbors and wastes exploration width on irrelevant branches (e.g., "Composer" or "In Album" edges when the answer requires reaching an "Award" node), and fragmented reasoning, where multiple topic entities are explored independently without seeing their interconnections. Single-pass retrieval-augmented methods (G-Retriever, GNN-RAG) avoid this but are hard to interpret and cannot correct retrieval errors mid-reasoning. The gap FoG closes: no prior method gives the reasoning LLM a multi-hop, multi-entity view of the local KG neighborhood at each decision step, despite subgraphs growing exponentially with hops. Key Idea: The core trick is relation-based graph coarsening: collapse all non-topic entities that share the same (head-entity, relation) or (relation, tail-entity) pattern into equivalence classes via union-find, so a subgraph with hundreds of thousands of entities becomes a relation graph of tens of nodes that fits in one rendered image a VLM can inspect for multi-hop paths at once. The insight is that for path planning, the relation skeleton matters more than individual entity identities — entity names are suppressed (rendered as anonymous "Node k" circles) except for topic entities, and unresolved nodes become SPARQL variables. Methodology: FoG is a four-stage, training-free pipeline (GPT-4o as VLM, GPT-3.5-turbo or GPT-4o as text LLM, Sentence-BERT/msmarco-distilbert as encoder, local Virtuoso SPARQL endpoint over the final Freebase dump). (1) Relation Path Prediction: an LLM infers the relation chain z = {r1...rl} implied by the question and topic entities Tq. (2) Relation Graph Construction: candidate relations from the k-hop neighborhood (k=2) are scored by cosine similarity to the whole predicted path and to each relation in it (Top-kpath=20, Top-krel=10 per relation, merged); the filtered subgraph is then coarsened by union-find with path compression, merging non-topic entities sharing a head-relation or tail-relation pattern; topic entities are kept as anchors. The paper reports ~99.9% size reduction (e.g., 29 relation types / ~300K entities / ~580K edges → 14 nodes / 23 edges). (3) Visual Graph Analysis: the coarsened graph is rendered via Graphviz dot (hierarchical layout, color-coded node types, image cropped if aspect ratio >1.8); the VLM selects up to 3 relation paths from the image, which are converted to SPARQL queries to retrieve instantiated paths. (4) Dynamic Visual Exploration: an LLM judges evidence sufficiency; if insufficient, the VLM picks exploration entities, the view recenters, one-hop relations are added, and the loop repeats (max 3 rounds). This is prompted LLM/VLM orchestration over symbolic graph access — no learned parameters, no explicit objective function. Critical design decisions: (a) suppressing entity names in non-topic nodes to emphasize relations (justified via the merging procedure and examples, though it discards information the VLM could otherwise use); (b) hybrid image + authoritative text description in the path-selection prompt (the prompt tells the VLM to verify edges against the text description — a sensible hedge that slightly undercuts a pure-vision claim); (c) fixed budget k=2 hops, kpath=20, krel=10, validated by sensitivity studies. Key Results: On full test splits of CWQ (3,531 questions) and WebQSP (1,639) and the ToG-subset of GrailQA (1,000), with Hit (exact-match) over 3 independent runs: FoG with GPT-4o reaches 79.1 on CWQ, 91.5 on WebQSP, and 90.6 on GrailQA, versus re-run PoG+GPT-4o at 74.2/86.3/84.2 and ToG+GPT-4o at 70.8/83.3/82.1. With GPT-3.5-turbo, FoG hits 72.3/88.7/83.6, surpassing the fine-tuned GNN-RAG+RA on CWQ (68.7) but not on WebQSP (90.7). The largest gain is GrailQA compositional questions: 92.0 vs 69.1 for PoG+GPT-4o (+22.9). The text-only variant FoG-T still beats PoG (67.2/86.0/80.7 with GPT-3.5). Efficiency: on CWQ, FoG uses 8.6 LLM calls and ~7,760 tokens per question at 21.2s, versus ToG's 22.6 calls / 8,183 tokens / 96.5s and PoG's 13.3 calls / 7,803 tokens / 23.3s. Baselines are current (GNN-RAG is ACL 2025 Findings; PoG is NeurIPS 2024) and the authors re-ran ToG/PoG with GPT-4o to control for backbone — a strength. Intermediate-preservation analysis shows the pipeline retains at least one gold path in only 82.63% (WebQSP), 70.25% (GrailQA), and 24.23% (CWQ) of cases, with CWQ's low number attributed to many gold chains exceeding the 2-hop limit. A VLM-swap check (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) shows near-parity (−0.9 WebQSP, −2.4 CWQ). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (vision-guided planning over coarsened KG relation graphs for interactive KGQA) plus an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (the fuzzy-selection + relation-based union-find coarsening enabling VLM-scale graphs). The genuinely novel element is the combination of relation-level graph coarsening with visual rendering as the planning substrate for a VLM; the ingredients are standard — LLM relation-path prediction, Sentence-BERT semantic matching, union-find coarsening, SPARQL templating, iterative agentic exploration — applied to a new setting (visual KG reasoning rather than abstract graph tasks, distinguishing from GITA and visual-graph benchmarks). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (Table 4): removing relation path prediction drops CWQ from 72.3 to 47.7 (random relations) or 47.7→23.3; removing dynamic exploration drops to 61.1; removing vision (FoG-T) drops to 67.2; removing coarsening is OOC (pipeline aborts), which doubles as evidence the coarsening is load-bearing. Three repeated runs are averaged, but no error bars, seeds-per-variant analysis, or significance tests are reported. Hyperparameter sensitivity (hop order, selection budget) and information-preservation diagnostics are included, plus an appendix error analysis (52% VLM-missed-path, 25% reasoning errors, 19% answer not in subgraph, 4% answer not in Freebase). Code is released at https://github.com/hyworrywart/FoG. Methodological concerns: (1) some baseline numbers are copied from original papers computed under different backbones/protocols, though the GPT-4o re-runs mitigate this; (2) GrailQA uses only ToG's 1,000-question subset; (3) FoG assumes gold topic entities provided by the benchmark with no entity-linking component, which flatters end-to-end applicability; (4) evaluation is only on Freebase-backed benchmarks, so generalization to other KGs is untested; (5) the modality study uses ExplaGraphs, a different task, as a proxy for the vision claim. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a prompted agentic pipeline, actually run end-to-end at benchmark scale). - Practical: Runs on any GPT-4o-class VLM plus a local Virtuoso SPARQL endpoint over the public Freebase dump; no training, but it requires a closed-source VLM for best results (open Qwen2.5-VL-72B costs 0.9–2.4 points). - Efficient: Cheaper than ToG/PoG per question (8.6 vs 22.6 calls on CWQ, 21.2s vs 96.5s), with token counts comparable (~7.8K); visual tokens (~1.4–1.6K) are itemized in the appendix. - Effective: Strong Hit-accuracy evidence on three standard benchmarks, but Hit is a lenient metric (any one predicted answer matching counts), and the 24.23% gold-path preservation on CWQ shows the 2-hop construction loses the true reasoning chain for many hard questions — accuracy is achieved partly despite, not because of, faithful path recovery there. - Scalable: Coarsening demonstrably handles subgraphs with ~10^5–10^6 entities, but the authors admit VLMs misread large or dense visual graphs and offer no experiments beyond these benchmarks; behavior on denser real-world KGs is claimed, not tested. The work delivers a released code artifact with prompts, SPARQL templates, and rendering configuration; no trained model weights (none are needed). Strengths: - The relation-based union-find coarsening is a genuinely useful, reusable primitive: it collapses million-entity subgraphs to tens of nodes while provably preserving edge directionality and topic-entity anchors, and the OOC ablation shows it is indispensable rather than decorative. - The evaluation anticipates and defuses the obvious confound: three structure-preserving textual serializations of the same graph score within ~1 point of each other, so the 2.5–5.1-point vision gain is not a serialization artifact, and the ExplaGraphs modality study (97.1 vs 89.7 for GPT-4o) independently supports VLMs reading graphs better as images. - Honest intermediate diagnostics: the paper measures what fraction of gold relations/answers/paths survive its own pipeline per dataset, and the appendix failure breakdown quantifies where reasoning fails — unusual transparency for this literature. - Backbone-controlled baseline re-runs (ToG/PoG with GPT-4o under identical splits and protocol) prevent the common trap of crediting prompt engineering for model-progress gains. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section states FoG depends on current VLM visual reasoning: when relation graphs become large or visually dense, models may miss valid paths or misread topology, motivating stronger graph-aware VLMs and more scalable visualization. The appendix error analysis (52% of WebQSP failures from the VLM missing the correct path) substantiates this. The authors confront the limitation directly rather than minimizing it, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The framing overweights vision relative to the evidence: the coarsened relation graph plus relation-path prediction (FoG-T) delivers most of the improvement over PoG, yet the title, motivation, and headline claims foreground the visual modality, whose marginal contribution is the smallest ablated component on WebQSP (86.0 → 88.7). - The path-selection prompt includes the full textual graph description and instructs the VLM to verify every edge against it, so "vision-guided" reasoning is partially text-assisted; no vision-only (no text description) condition isolates how much the image alone contributes. - Gold topic entities are assumed; no entity-linking evaluation or error budget for imperfect linking is provided, which matters for real deployments. - Evaluation is confined to Freebase; no Wikidata or domain KG experiment tests whether Freebase's clean relation-schema structure is a precondition for fuzzy matching and union-find to work. - No statistical significance testing despite 3-run averaging, and the Hit metric can credit spurious paths; no faithfulness metric on the produced reasoning paths. - The 24.23% gold-path preservation on CWQ is explained away by the 2-hop limit rather than treated as an accuracy-robustness tension worth quantifying. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agentic KGQA systems should read this: the relation-coarsening mechanism and the honest ablation/preservation diagnostics are immediately reusable and the efficiency gains are real, but read it for the graph-condensation recipe rather than as proof that VLMs should reason over graph images — the data supports the former more than the latter.

Problem & Motivation: Time-series foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM, Moirai) overwhelmingly decode with a fixed strategy: direct one-shot prediction of the horizon, rolling out autoregressively only when the horizon exceeds the native output length. The classical direct-vs-iterated trade-off (error compounding vs. loss of sequential conditioning) is well known, but prior work treats the decoding granularity as a global hyperparameter, not a per-instance choice. The authors argue the optimal rollout schedule varies with the input window and the backbone, and that this variability can be exploited for frozen, patch-based pretrained backbones without touching their weights. The intended users are practitioners running frozen foundation models on tasks whose historical windows are available for selector training; the scope explicitly excludes transfer to unseen tasks. Key Idea: Reformulate the choice of rollout schedule as a per-window inference-time decision problem, and make it tractable with a prefix-retaining dynamic program: at each prefix length K, retain exactly one prediction prefix (beam width one per length), generating K candidates per row by extending each retained prefix with a single model call — reducing the exponential rollout space to H(H+1)/2 evaluations while empirically capturing 96.7% of the MASE reduction that exhaustive search achieves over one-shot decoding. The second key move is replacing the unavailable ground-truth selection at inference with a learned scorer that reads cached backbone hidden states (not just predicted values) for each candidate prefix, and deploying it conservatively through a 5-scorer agreement gate whose abstention falls back to the backbone's own one-shot forecast. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) DP surrogate search (Algorithm 1): for K = 1..H, form candidates P(i)_K = [Pred_i, g([X, Pred_i], K−i)] for each predecessor i < K, score each by prefix error ℓ against the ground-truth prefix Y_1:K (MASE in practice), and retain the argmin along with a feature prefix built from channel-averaged encoder hidden states. The surrogate is a heuristic — retaining one prefix per length can discard histories that are suboptimal mid-horizon but optimal at the end — and the authors quantify this loss (the surrogate retains 66 of 1024 rollouts at H=11 but captures 96.7% of exhaustive-search gain on 58 tasks with 2≤H≤11). (2) Learned scorer S_ψ: a two-stage transformer (per-candidate encoding with [CLS], then cross-candidate attention with candidate-index and prefix-length embeddings) trained with cross-entropy against a softmax over negated, temperature-sharpened prefix errors, on historical windows strictly preceding the official evaluation windows (~1.7M training rows over 66 tasks for Chronos-2). (3) Agreement-gated deployment: five seed-replica scorers vote; deviation requires 4-of-5 consensus on a non-one-shot candidate. Critical design decisions: the prefix-retaining surrogate (justified by the 96.7% capture measurement), hidden-state features over values alone (justified by ablations showing pointwise-MLP and context-only scorers are significantly worse), and the pre-fixed 4/5 threshold (chosen before evaluation, with a post-hoc ablation showing insensitivity among gates allowing one dissent). A DAgger round on the policy's own states was tried and did not improve skill — honestly reported. Key Results: On fev-bench (100 tasks, 7 domains) with frozen Chronos-2, the deployed policy achieves +0.20% point-forecast skill (MASE) over one-shot decoding on the full benchmark [95% CI +0.06, +0.37], rising monotonically to +0.68% [+0.17, +1.25] on the 19 tasks with H≥9 (12 wins, 3 ties, 4 losses); win rate 54.5% → 71.1%. The DP oracle with ground-truth selection attains +3.25% and +9.13% on these subsets, so the selector recovers ~6–8% of headroom. With frozen Moirai-1.1-R-small: +0.23% [+0.07, +0.40] full benchmark, +0.28% at H≥9. Fixed baselines are current and properly controlled: no constant-chunk schedule beats one-shot (full autoregression is −3.11% full, −10.73% at H≥9, losing all 19 deep tasks), per-task and per-horizon fixed schedule selection fails (−0.25% and 0.00%), and pointwise ensembles of schedules are significantly worse. Gains concentrate in the energy domain (+0.97% on 21 tasks) and deeper horizons; the policy deviates on only 5–12% of forecasts per median task. Latency on one RTX 3090: 13.7× slowdown at H≥2 (0.25s → 5.08s median), 103.6× at H≥9 (18.14s), tracking H(H+1)/2 backbone calls; probabilistic metrics (SQL/WQL) are flat to slightly worse, and the authors claim point accuracy only. Tested scale is a standard public benchmark (100 tasks), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM and NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel elements are (i) framing per-window rollout-schedule selection of a single frozen pretrained forecaster as an inference-time decision problem — distinct from DyStrat/Stratify, which train separate forecasters per strategy, and from MoE routing, which selects experts rather than decoding schedules — and (ii) the prefix-retaining DP that makes the exponential partition space quadratic. The scorer architecture, seed-replica ensembles, and selective prediction are standard tools competently combined; the DP surrogate itself is a beam-search variant (beam width one per prefix length), so the novelty lies in the problem framing and the empirical validation of the surrogate, not in algorithmic machinery. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is a standout. Ablations isolate which components matter: the cross-candidate scorer beats a pointwise MLP (+0.27% paired, CI excludes zero on H≥2) and a context-only scorer; ensemble-size/threshold ablations across seed subsets show the gate (not the seed draw) drives reliability; DAgger and transfer folds test the training-distribution assumptions. Statistical reporting is exemplary: task-level bootstrap with 20,000 resamples, paired comparisons, pre-fixed thresholds, pipeline validated against published per-task Chronos-2 MASE to 1.5×10⁻⁷ relative difference. Concerns: (1) the selector is trained on historical windows of the very tasks it is evaluated on — the authors are transparent about this (strictly preceding windows, chronological validation split) and their own 5-fold experiment shows no significant gain on unseen tasks, but this means the method's scope is narrow and Goodhart-style overfitting to task idiosyncrasies cannot be excluded; (2) no code or weights release is mentioned (Not stated); (3) only two backbones, both patch-size-16-compatible; (4) hyperparameters for Moirai were selected from 72 configurations ranked on validation, a modest search with limited data (~123K examples). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Yes — runs on a single RTX 3090 with the frozen backbone and 3.4M-parameter scorers, no backbone fine-tuning. - Efficient: No — 13.7× to 103.6× latency slowdown growing quadratically in H (the authors note intra-row batching could cut sequential calls to H, but did not implement it). - Effective: Only for point MASE on tasks with history and deep horizons; the effect is +0.20–0.68% skill, concentrated in the energy domain, with probabilistic metrics flat-to-negative. - Scalable: Untested beyond H=18 (exhaustive oracle infeasible there); the quadratic candidate count and per-task training requirement both scale poorly to many tasks or much deeper horizons, and the paper does not claim otherwise. The work delivers a method and protocol but no stated software artifact (no code, CLI, or dataset release mentioned); it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The DP surrogate is a clean, verifiable reduction with a quantified approximation gap (96.7% oracle capture), rather than an unexamined heuristic — rare discipline in this genre. - The evaluation is among the most self-critical this reviewer has seen: the paper volunteers that its selector recovers only 6–8% of oracle headroom, that the oracle is structurally guaranteed to never lose (one-shot is always a candidate), that gains vanish on unseen tasks, that DAgger fails, and that probabilistic metrics do not improve. - The negative results on fixed baselines (per-task schedule choice, per-horizon choice, schedule ensembles, full autoregression) are themselves a useful empirical finding, establishing that no cheaper alternative captures the per-window gain. - The agreement gate is a principled instantiation of deep-ensemble uncertainty plus selective prediction with a cost-free abstention target (one-shot decoding), and its behavior is characterized across ensemble sizes and seed subsets. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: no transfer to unseen tasks (the gain depends on the evaluated task's history); point-accuracy claims only, with probabilistic metrics flat or slightly worse; the effect size is small and diluted on the full benchmark; the oracle headroom is an optimistic upper bound exploiting realized noise; the gain concentrates in the energy domain; inference cost grows quadratically with horizon depth, suiting only accuracy-over-latency settings; and the agreement gate does not restore the ground-truth guarantee. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The cost-benefit case is left to the reader: a ~100× slowdown for +0.68% MASE on 19 deep tasks is hard to justify in any but the most latency-insensitive, accuracy-critical settings, and the paper offers no analysis of when that trade is worth it beyond the qualitative "accuracy matters more than latency." - Only two backbones are tested, both sharing patch size 16; whether the DP surrogate's high oracle-capture rate or the scorer's signal generalizes to backbones with different patch granularities or decoder architectures (e.g., Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM) is unexamined. - The energy-domain concentration is observed but unexplained; no mechanism is proposed for why energy series benefit from schedule fragmentation while equally deep mobility tasks do not. - The proposed intra-row batching that would reduce sequential depth from H(H+1)/2 to H backbone calls is mentioned but not implemented or measured, so the reported 103.6× slowdown may overstate the achievable cost. - Selector training requires running the full DP with ground truth over up to 10,000 historical windows per task; the data-generation cost and its scaling with the number of tasks a deployment serves are not accounted. - No significance analysis of the interaction between the agreement gate's low deviation rate (5–12%) and the win/loss counts — with so few deviations per task, per-task win rates on small subsets rest on few effective decisions, though the bootstrap on skill partially mitigates this. Bottom Line: A rigorously executed, unusually honest paper that opens a genuinely new problem — per-instance decoding-schedule selection for frozen forecasting backbones — but whose tiny measured gains (+0.20–0.68% MASE) at quadratically growing latency and with no cross-task transfer mean most practitioners gain more from the paper's negative results and evaluation template than from deploying the method itself.
