Generics in Go and lambda lifting

T Levy · researchcommons.waikato.ac.nz · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This Master's thesis introduces a simple lambda lifting algorithm with worst-case O(n²) time that is linear in the size of the output program, proves it computes the minimal set of extraneous parameters (the first algorithm with such a proof), partially formalizes the Fischbach–Hannan specification in Lean 4, and applies these ideas to two open problems in Go's generics implementation: minimal lifting of local type declarations and sound method promotion for embedded type parameters. - Why it's important: Compiler writers still use O(n³) lambda lifting (e.g., GHC), and Go's shipped compiler adds all enclosing type parameters as implicit parameters of local types in generic functions — a choice with observable type-identity effects the author argues is wrong — while the accepted design for embedded type parameters had an unsound early implementation. - How it does it: The core trick is to process each variable independently and propagate it bottom-up over the function reference graph via DFS, skipping the variable's declaring function, which handles mutual recursion without SCC coalescing and yields minimality by construction. - The good: The algorithm is proven correct against an existing formal specification from the literature and against novel "complete" and "minimal" lifting notions, with key parts machine-checked in Lean 4, plus a checker-based testing framework run against Johnsson's and Fischbach–Hannan's algorithms on generated test cases. - The missing: The full machine-checked proof is not completed — correctness rests on a hybrid of pen-and-paper proofs, partial Lean formalization, and property checking — and the excerpt provided does not expose the quantitative test-suite results or a public release of code. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on compiler intermediate transformations, verified compilation, or Go's generics implementation; skip it if you want a fully verified end-to-end artifact or empirical performance benchmarks on real-world codebases.

Problem & Motivation: Nested functions complicate compilation because references to enclosing-scope variables conflict with stack-based calling (the "funarg" problem); lambda lifting removes nested functions by adding "extraneous" parameters, but computing the minimal such set is non-trivial due to mutual recursion and transitive propagation. Prior minimal-parameter algorithms are either O(n³) (Johnsson), complex (Morazán–Schultz's O(n²) dominator-tree algorithm), or unverifiable in practice (CertiCoq's appears at least O(n³)). The second problem domain is Go: since Go 1.18, local type declarations inside generic functions may reference enclosing type parameters, and the compiler's handling (inserting all enclosing type parameters as implicit ones, even unreferenced ones) affects type identity in ways the author argues surprises programmers; separately, embedding type parameters in structs is permitted by the accepted design but the early compiler implementation was unsound, and the obvious sound restriction (promoting only constraint-specified methods) adds no expressive power. The thesis addresses both the algorithmic problem (who: compiler implementers) and the language-design problems (who: the Go team and Go programmers). Key Idea: Per-variable multi-source propagation on the function reference graph. Define the "solution" as a mapping EP where each function receives exactly the variables that are referenced non-locals of it, plus (transitively) the extraneous parameters of functions it references — excluding the variable's declaring function. For each variable, run a DFS from the functions that directly reference it non-locally, stopping at already-visited functions and never propagating into the declaring function; this handles cycles without SCC condensation and provably produces the minimal extraneous parameter sets. This reframing also explains why whole-program SCC approaches (Danvy–Schultz, as interpreted by Morazán–Schultz) over-approximate: the effective SCCs depend on which variable is being propagated, since calls made by the declaring function must be excluded. Methodology: The core is framed in the simply typed lambda calculus with letrec, using the Fischbach–Hannan syntax, type system, and singleton-type-based lifting specification (restricted to parameter lifting, identifiers-only singleton types, no shadowing). Three contributions per algorithmic phase: (1) preprocessing computes the reverse function reference graph and referenced non-local variables in one linear pass; (2) Algorithm 1 (recursive) and Algorithm 1b (iterative, explicit stack with loop invariant) propagate each variable to referencing functions; (3) straightforward AST edits insert parameters/arguments and block-float definitions. Correctness is proven in three layers: pen-and-paper theorems (Theorems 5.4.7–5.4.10, via loop invariants mirroring the solution definition), a partial Lean 4 formalization of the Fischbach–Hannan specification and type system, and property-based checking — randomly generated declaration/call graphs with post-hoc correctness checkers — comparing the author's algorithm against implementations of Johnsson's O(n³) and Fischbach–Hannan's algorithms. Critical design decisions: processing variables separately rather than one graph pass (justified by the output-size-linear complexity argument); excluding global variables and function references from non-locals (justified by block-floating semantics); and the checker methodology (Chapter 2) explicitly positioned between testing and full verification, with a five-point characterization and discussion of Blum–Kannan checkers, certifying algorithms, and Goerigk et al.'s proof-integrated checking. Time complexity is analyzed against output size, with a worst-case Θ(n²) output-size proof (Appendix A) making the algorithm optimal for all inputs when output is materialized. A substantial historical/survey portion (Chapters 3–4) covers generics mechanisms across Java, C#, C++, Haskell, Go's six generics proposals, the three Go implementation proposals, and sketches a dictionary-passing design for first-class generic functions and generic interface methods under Go's non-uniform-representation and backward-compatibility constraints, plus an O(n) replacement (Tarjan SCC) for Go's O(n·E) Bellman–Ford-based unbounded-instantiation check, reportedly proposed upstream. Key Results: The headline results are theoretical: a simple algorithm matching the O(n²) worst case of the fastest prior algorithm (Morazán–Schultz) while being linear in output size (Theorems 5.4.8/5.4.10) — strictly better in non-worst cases where Morazán–Schultz is suboptimal — and the first proof that an algorithm computes minimal extraneous parameters, addressing a defect with unused functions the author shows affects all previous algorithms (including a demonstrated unsoundness edge case, "bare" singleton types, in the Fischbach–Hannan specification). The thesis also identifies and documents a correctness flaw in the published Danvy–Schultz algorithm (failure to propagate extraneous parameters across calls to parent-scope functions) with a worked counterexample, and shows the naive fix degrades to O(n³). Empirically, the author ran generated test cases through the author's, Johnsson's, and Fischbach–Hannan's algorithms with correctness checkers and reports counts and running times in Tables 5.1–5.4; the specific test-case counts and timing figures are not visible in the provided text, so quantitative test outcomes are Not stated. No accuracy-style headline metrics apply; the contribution is correctness evidence, not performance benchmarks on production code. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the per-variable DFS lambda-lifting algorithm and its minimality proof) + NEW FORMULATION (the "solution"/complete-and-minimal lifting definitions, and the checker-methodology characterization) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the Danvy–Schultz flaw and the Fischbach–Hannan singleton-type unsoundness) + position/survey content on Go generics. The Go application chapters (local types as minimal lifting; Algorithm 2 for embedded type parameters) apply the new lifting formulation to a genuinely new setting and propose, per the abstract, novel sound promotion rules — but those chapters' technical detail lies beyond the provided text and appears to be design proposals rather than implemented, benchmarked systems. The dictionary-passing sketch for first-class generic functions is competent synthesis of known techniques (dictionary passing, itables, wrapper pairs) under Go's constraints, not a new mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style analysis is present in the sense that the author isolates which components matter (declaring-function exclusion, per-variable propagation, SCC-dependence-on-variable) via worked examples and counterexamples. Error bars and significance tests do not apply; the empirical evidence is checker-verified properties on generated cases, and the author is explicit about the residual risks (paper-proof human error, possible incorrect specifications, Lean kernel/compiler/OS bugs). Code and Lean artifacts: a public release URL is not stated in the provided text. Methodological concerns: (1) the verification story is deliberately hybrid, so the central correctness claim is not fully machine-checked; (2) the testing harness is built by the same author who designed the specification extensions, so specification bugs could be correlated between prover and checker; (3) the thesis was peer-reviewed in part (the lambda-lifting chapter is an extended FormaliSE '26 paper, and Marco Morazán validated that work), which strengthens credibility of the core chapter; (4) evaluation is on synthetic generated programs, not production codebases like GHC's test corpus or large Go projects, so real-world scale is not demonstrated. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL with supporting empirical checking (proofs and formalization are primary; tests are secondary). Sound: Assumptions are explicit (no shadowing, distinct identifiers via α-conversion, parameter lifting only, simply typed setting); proofs are complete at pen-and-paper level but only partially machine-checked. General: Holds for Johnsson-style parameter lifting over letrec-programs with mutually recursive functions and anonymous functions; excludes full-laziness lifting and shadowing, which is realistic for the Go use case but restrictive relative to functional-language closure conversion. Tight: The output-size analysis (Θ(n²) worst case, Θ(n) for bounded-nesting inputs) makes the running time optimal when output is produced — no vacuity issue. Implementable: Yes — the algorithm is concrete, includes data-structure discussion (hash tables, prefix trees, augmented AST), and was implemented and tested; the Go mono.go improvement was proposed as a concrete upstream patch. Deliverables: the thesis itself, a testing/checking framework, Lean 4 formalization code, and algorithm implementations; whether these are publicly released is not stated in the provided text. Strengths: - Genuinely novel algorithmic result: matching the fastest known asymptotic bound with a markedly simpler algorithm and adding an output-sensitive linear-in-output guarantee plus the first minimality proof — a real advance over a 30-year line of work (Johnsson 1985 → Morazán–Schultz). - Discovery of concrete, documented defects in published prior work (Danvy–Schultz propagation flaw; Fischbach–Hannan singleton-type unsoundness; the unused-functions issue affecting all prior algorithms), each backed by worked counterexamples rather than assertion. - Unusual methodological self-awareness: the checker-vs-verification trade-off is given a full chapter with a precise five-point characterization and honest enumeration of residual failure modes, rather than overclaiming verification. - The bridge from abstract lambda lifting to a concrete industrial problem (Go local types, tied to golang/go issue 58573) gives the theory a plausible uptake path, and the upstream mono.go O(n) proposal shows the author engaging with real compiler code. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author explicitly acknowledges: paper proofs are susceptible to human error; exhaustive test enumeration is impossible; the tested-against specifications may themselves be incorrect or incomplete; and trusted-computing-base bugs (Lean kernel, compiler, OS, hardware) are outside scope. The checker approach offers no availability guarantee (checks may fail on some inputs), which the author argues is acceptable for compilers. The complexity restriction to parameter lifting (not full-laziness) and the no-shadowing, distinct-identifier assumptions are stated. The author also candidly reports upstream interactions that went unanswered (Hu et al. concerns) and labels the embedded-type-parameter promotion rules "complex." This direct confrontation with limitations is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No end-to-end integration result: the thesis argues the minimal-lifting notion should change Go's local-type semantics, but does not report implementing it in the Go compiler or measuring the impact on real Go code (e.g., how often unreferenced type parameters actually occur in the corpus analysis mentioned). The corpus analysis is claimed as support but its results are not shown in the provided text. - The testing chapter compares against re-implementations of Johnsson's and Fischbach–Hannan's algorithms; correctness of those reference implementations is itself only checker-verified, so agreement is weaker evidence than a verified oracle. - Practical wall-clock performance of the new algorithm versus Morazán–Schultz on realistic program sizes is not demonstrated in the provided text; the output-linear claim is asymptotic, and constant factors of per-variable DFS passes are unquantified. - The embedded-type-parameter promotion rules (Algorithm 2) and the first-class-generic-function dictionary-passing design are, on the evidence available, unimplemented proposals; their soundness argument and coverage of Go's full feature surface (anonymous structs, recursion interactions) are asserted rather than mechanically checked. - No statement of artifact availability was found, which limits reproducibility for a thesis whose central claims are algorithmic. Bottom Line: For compiler and PL-theory researchers — and for anyone implementing generics in Go — this thesis is worth reading for its genuinely simpler, minimality-proven lambda lifting algorithm and its documented corrections to the literature, but readers seeking fully verified implementations or production-scale empirical validation will need to wait for follow-up work.

Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers (26 ▲ )

Jiongfan Yang, Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Zhongang Cai, Ziwei Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from global-attention sequence length by expanding each spatial anchor into K slots with disjoint DCT coefficient groups, and routing only the lowest-frequency slot through global attention. - Why it's important: Pixel-space generative models avoid a separately trained autoencoder but pay quadratic attention cost when finer image detail forces more tokens; this work attacks the detail-versus-compute coupling directly, which gates the practicality of autoencoder-free generation. - How it does it: The core trick is tokenization-as-allocation: a fixed token budget N=WK is split into W spatial anchors (which read input) and K spectral slots per anchor (which write disjoint radial DCT bands), so global attention carries only W lowest-frequency 'carrier' tokens instead of WK. - The good: The evaluation is unusually careful — five independently trained seeds with 95% CIs, a purpose-built FLOPs-matched JiT control, and a mechanistic ablation showing that reassigning the global carrier to any non-lowest-frequency slot degrades FID, directly supporting the central design choice. - The missing: All headline comparisons are against JiT variants retrained by the authors for only 120 epochs at ~138–161M parameters; there is no comparison against published JiT or other pixel-space (e.g., PixelDiT, PixNerd) numbers at standard budgets or scales, so the absolute competitiveness of SpecSlot is unverified. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on diffusion/flow Transformer architectures or tokenization/attention-sparsity design — the W×K allocation framing and role-routed communication are genuinely transferable ideas; skip it if you want evidence the method scales beyond class-conditional ImageNet and a 400-epoch text-to-image pilot.

Rigor (72) reflects disciplined five-seed CIs and code/weights release, but is held back by a closed comparison world: all baselines are author-retrained 120-epoch JiT variants, no published pixel-space baseline numbers are run, and this is an unrefereed preprint. Problem & Motivation: Pixel-space generative Transformers (e.g., JiT) use one token per image patch, so the patch grid simultaneously fixes what the model reads, what each token predicts, and how many tokens enter global attention. Halving patch size from 16 to 8 on a 256×256 image quadruples tokens and makes the quadratic attention term 16× larger, so every increment of output detail inflates the most expensive part of the model. Practitioners building autoencoder-free generators face this cost, and existing remedies — multiscale detailer stages (PixelDiT, DiP, HyperDiT, PixNerd) or generic sparse/window attention (Swin, Longformer, Perceiver, SparseDiT) — keep output detail tied to the spatial grid: a token's communication pattern is determined by its spatial position, not by what it produces. The paper closes the gap of binding a token's communication eligibility to its output role. Key Idea: Assign every token a fixed, indexed output role (a disjoint radial band of DCT coefficients of its 2s×2s output window), then use that role index to set the communication graph: only the lowest-radial-band slot of each anchor enters global attention (the 'carrier'), while all slots mix locally within the anchor. This makes anchor density (W) and spectral subdivision (K) independent allocation variables — global attention cost scales with W, not WK — and turns tokenization from a single patch-size choice into an explicit quality–compute allocation problem. The authors validate the frequency logic empirically: the lowest radial group is the first to cross a data-to-noise-ratio of 1 along the flow (t* = 0.468 for K=4), justifying routing it globally. Methodology: The model is a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer (12 blocks, width 768, ~138M parameters at 256×256) trained with the JiT-style image-prediction parameterization: the velocity is computed from a clamped prediction head (τ=0.05) under a velocity MSE loss on the linear noise path zt = tx + (1−t)ε. Three stages: (1) Read — non-overlapping s×s input cells are patch-embedded to width B, mixed by a zero-initialized residual depthwise 3×3 convolution, and each anchor vector is expanded into K slot states via a shared projection; (2) Allocate — DCT-II indices of an L=2s output window are sorted by radius and split into K equal disjoint groups (E = L²/K coefficients per channel), each slot owning exactly one group via a shared affine spectral head; synthesis uses the normalized overlap-add of a 50%-lapped DCT frame (provably a perfect-reconstruction analysis/synthesis pair), plus a zero-initialized slot-specific spatial head that writes pixel tiles as a correction, summed with the spectral base; (3) Route — a GGLL schedule (global-global-local-local ×3) where the global set is {32 context states + W carriers} and the local sets are each anchor's K slots. Critical design decisions: radial (not learned) band assignment (justified by spectral decay and the DNR crossing probe); dual-basis output (spectral base + spatial correction), shown to beat the best single basis by 0.40 FID; and GGLL over GLGL ordering (GGLL 6.59 vs GLGL 6.95 FID at identical compute). The justification quality is above average — each choice has a dedicated ablation or probe. Key Results: On ImageNet-256 (120 epochs, effective batch 512, 50K-image FID, five seeds): SpecSlot W256/K4 reaches 6.59 FID at 129.20 GFLOPs; the FLOPs-matched control JiT-CM (an author-built JiT-B/8 variant with 128-d input bottleneck, width 560, 124.24 GFLOPs) reaches 6.68 — statistically comparable within the 5-seed 95% CI. JiT-B/8 (218.50 GFLOPs) remains the FID leader at 4.34, so at 256 resolution SpecSlot matches a compute-matched control but does not beat the stronger baseline. On ImageNet-512 the picture improves: W256/K4 gets 9.14 FID at 135.64 GFLOPs, improving 2.84 FID over JiT-CM (11.98) with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and trailing JiT-B/16 (8.45, 219.56 GFLOPs) by 0.69 FID at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image (256×256, 400 epochs, BLIP3o + JourneyDB shards, frozen OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 + trainable 32-query adapter), SpecSlot W256/K4 scores 62.21 DPG-Bench vs. JiT-B/8's 61.15 at 40.6% lower forward cost, though JiT-B/8 still leads GenEval (29.78 vs 26.99). Mechanistic findings: reassigning the global carrier to slot 1/2/3 raises FID (6.91/7.21/6.97 vs 6.59); removing global carrier edges hurts early-time/low-frequency error while removing local edges hurts late/high-frequency error; the effective-slot fraction per anchor falls from 0.803 (K=2) to 0.495 (K=8), explaining diminishing returns from more slots. Baselines are retrained under an aligned recipe rather than quoted from literature — a defensible but closed-world comparison; scale tested is standard (class-conditional ImageNet up to 512) rather than stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with elements of NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: using fixed, disjoint spectral coefficient groups as both per-token output ownership and communication eligibility within a single pixel-space backbone — no cited prior work does this (Spectral Forcing filters only the noisy input; DeCo splits frequencies across separate DiT/decoder modules; Swin/Longformer/Perceiver fix topology by position, not role). The ingredients themselves — lapped DCT synthesis, window attention, global–local blocks, rectified flow — are each standard; the contribution is the role-indexed coupling of output ownership to routing and the resulting W-vs-K allocation knobs, not any single component. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is strong for a paper of this size. Ablations cover both allocation axes (W and K swept independently, with an explicit caveat that the 'more anchors is better' trend may not generalize), routing schedule, carrier identity, lapping, input mixer, evidence width B, and CFG (with the full sweep table published). Five independently trained seeds with per-seed FID and Student-t 95% CIs are reported for the main ImageNet-256 comparisons; ablations use three seeds. Compute accounting is specified down to the profiler contract (H800, BF16, TorchInductor, multiply-add = 2 FLOPs). Code, project page, and Hugging Face weights are linked (github.com/JiongfanYang/SpecSlot). Methodological concerns: (1) the primary control, JiT-CM, is an implementation-defined architecture constructed by the authors, not a published JiT configuration, so the headline 'beats the control' claims rest on a model the authors themselves designed; (2) all JiT/SF baselines are retrained for only 120 epochs, well short of typical 400-epoch ImageNet diffusion training, so absolute FID values are not comparable to the literature; (3) the text-to-image result is a single-seed-scale pilot on curated shards evaluated on DPG/GenEval only; (4) the key mechanistic justification (DNR crossing time) is descriptive, not causal, though the carrier-identity ablation provides causal support. This is a preprint (arXiv, dated 2026 in the reference list), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained models with measured quality, throughput, and latency; no systems deployment beyond benchmarks). - Practical: Yes — the largest model trains on 8 GPUs (~17.4 GB/GPU peak at batch 128) and samples on a single H800; nothing exotic. - Efficient: Favorable within its class — 129.20 GFLOPs and 8.20 img/s at Heun-50 versus 5.56 img/s for the FLOPs-matched dense control, though GGLL is slower than the full-global route per-image because that route gets a wider network at higher FLOPs (a cost-quality tradeoff, not a pure win). - Effective: The evidence shows it matches a FLOPs-matched control at 256 and beats it by 2.84 FID at 512, but it does not close the gap to the strongest quality baseline (JiT-B/8) at 256 — the decoupling claim is supported, the absolute quality claim is regime-dependent. - Scalable: Untested beyond 512×512; the fixed W=256 global sequence is architecturally constant as resolution grows, which is a claimed scaling advantage, but the paper measures only one doubling (256→512) and explicitly declines to claim the margin generalizes. The work delivers trained model weights, code, and a reproducible training contract; the mechanistic probes (DNR frontier, effective-rank analysis) are reusable diagnostic techniques. Strengths: - The W×K allocation formulation is a real conceptual move: it converts patch-size selection into a two-dimensional resource-allocation problem with separately measurable effects, and the paper actually measures the two axes independently (Table 4a) rather than asserting independence. - The carrier-identity ablation is the kind of causal check most architecture papers skip: holding allocation, graph, and compute fixed, moving cross-anchor access off the lowest-radial slot consistently degrades FID, tying the routing heuristic to the spectral mechanism rather than leaving it as a design instinct. - The matched lapped-DCT analysis/synthesis frame is worked out to provable perfect reconstruction, and the ablation quantifies its benefit (6.59 vs 6.78 FID without lapping) — competent engineering of known signal-processing tools into a generative backbone. - Unusually disciplined evaluation: five-seed CIs, a full published CFG sweep, an explicit FLOP-accounting contract, and a mechanistic section that separates trained-comparison evidence from checkpoint-intervention probes. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the two operating points 'do not by themselves isolate the cause of the larger margin' at 512, that the 'more anchors over more slots' trend is not claimed to generalize beyond the measured N=2,048 range, that the DNR crossing time is 'not a learned gate' but a descriptive measure, and that JiT-B/8 'remains the quality leader' at 256 and on GenEval. They also flag JiT-CM as 'an implementation-defined control matched on forward GFLOPs rather than a published JiT size.' This is direct, non-defensive disclosure of the main fragile points — a credibility positive. Bottom Line: A practitioner designing attention structure for pixel-space or high-resolution diffusion Transformers gains a genuinely new and well-diagnosed design lever (role-indexed slot allocation with carrier routing) and an unusually honest evaluation template, but should not treat SpecSlot as demonstrated state-of-the-art — the comparison world is author-constructed, and stronger published alternatives remain untested against it.

Kunlun Zhu, Tao Feng, Xu Han, Heng Wang, Ling Yang, Xiangru Tang, Jiaxuan You, Heng Ji · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AgentDecisionBench (a three-level benchmark with the DecisionGym environment for scoring decision models from isolated questions up to control of a running agent), JevAgentHarness (a harness that delegates routine multiple-choice agent decisions to a small decision model behind confidence thresholds fitted per decision point on the agent's own trajectories), and AgentDecision-4B (a Qwen3-4B model SFT-trained on states the agent visits, with JEV as teacher). - Why it's important: LLM agent harnesses call a large model at every step, making long tasks slow and costly (one public leaderboard evaluation cost ~$40,000), while most steps are multiple-choice choices a 4B model could make for ~1% of the price. - How it does it: The harness poses each listed choice as a typed multiple-choice question, accepts the decision model's answer only when its confidence clears a threshold τ fitted from shadow-mode trajectories (τ ≈ q_L − ΔC/V, accepting the decision model whenever its expected savings outweigh its error risk), and trains the small model on the agent's own visited states — including states reached after the agent's own mistakes (30.9% of training data) — with teacher-mixed SFT targets. - The good: The benchmark shows isolated accuracy misranks decision models (StartLux-9B: 92.2% on BFCL tool choice but only 69.5% task success, vs. AgentDecision-4B at 89.3%/91.5%), and the fitted threshold cascade cut cost 14.2% with zero task loss while a fixed 0.5 threshold lost 21.5 points. - The missing: Much of the headline evidence (Table 1, shifted/hard tasks, ALFWorld) is exploratory and post-registered rather than part of the pre-registered protocol, all main runs are single attempts at temperature 0 on largely self-built environments, and transfer of the fitted cascade to τ²-bench failed its non-inferiority test (−8.1 points). - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate agent harnesses and care about the cost/latency of per-step LLM calls or about how to evaluate small decision models under distribution shift; skip it if you only need routing/cascading theory, which prior work (FrugalGPT, RouteLLM, learning-to-defer) covers.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents execute long software, desktop, and customer-service tasks through harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenHands) that invoke a large LLM at every step. Most of these calls terminate in a multiple-choice decision — which tool, which argument value, whether to stop — that a small "decision model" (e.g., JEV, a System-1 style model returning option probabilities) could answer at 28% of the latency and 2.6% of the price of an LLM call. Decision models, however, are built and evaluated on fixed question sets; whether one works inside a running agent — where mistakes propagate, states follow the agent's own errors, and each query adds latency — had not been tested, and existing agent benchmarks score only whole tasks. The authors ask how a harness can delegate routine choices to a decision model with little loss of success. Key Idea: Delegate a recurring harness choice to the decision model only when its confidence clears a per-decision-point threshold fitted on the agent's own trajectories — the threshold derived from a simple expected-loss argument (accept iff c ≥ q_L − ΔC/V) — and, for deployment, train the decision model on the states the agent itself visits (including post-error states), because off-the-shelf models never see those states. The paper's central empirical insight is that isolated-question accuracy does not predict in-agent task success, but step-level accuracy on recorded agent runs does (Kendall correlation 0.84). Methodology: Three components. (1) AgentDecisionBench: three evaluation levels — L1 isolated questions (1,114 BFCL v4 tool-choice and 1,949 argument items plus 928 When2Call items converted to multiple choice), L2 step-level scoring on 5,314 recorded states of 200 DecisionGym tasks against an answer key, L3 task-level control of a running agent (DecisionGym, τ²-bench, ALFWorld, plus adapters for mini-SWE-agent/SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified and pi on Terminal-Bench 2.0). DecisionGym is a simulated customer-service shop (68 tools including 31 near-duplicate distractors, scripted plans, answer keys derived at every reachable state, disjoint seeds for training/threshold fitting/testing, shifted and hard task variants). (2) JevAgentHarness: a typed decision interface, five integration modes (REPLACE, CASCADE, ASSIST, GUARD, TRIGGER) across eight decision points (40 combinations implemented), thresholds fitted in shadow mode (150 tasks per agent LLM; e.g., τ = 1.00 for tools, 0.99 for arguments), and adapters via existing harness hooks. (3) AgentDecision-4B: SFT on 15,694 visited states with mixed targets y = α·one-hot + (1−α)·p_JEV (α = 0.3) under cross-entropy plus a Brier calibration term, followed by GRPO (G = 8 rollouts, reward = success penalized by LLM-call count and irreversible errors); notably GRPO added no measurable gain over SFT alone. The evaluation protocol is two-stage and pre-registered: Stage 1 tests each delegation alone with one-sided non-inferiority tests (3-point margin) under Holm correction; Stage 2 tests the rule-selected combination on 500 fresh tasks. Key Results: On L3 shifted DecisionGym tasks, the best isolated model (StartLux-9B, 92.2% BFCL) solved only 69.5% of tasks while AgentDecision-4B (89.3% isolated) solved 91.5% and its teacher JEV 82.0% — a 57.5-point spread at task level vs. 5.1 points at L1. The JEV tool+argument cascade saved 14.2% cost with zero task outcome changes (JEV decided 27.2% of tool and 20.8% of argument choices); unconstrained delegation lost 19.0 points. With AgentDecision-4B, the DecisionGym agent ran 86.3% cheaper and 2.5× faster (31 ms vs. 809 ms median per decision on one L4), and an ALFWorld-trained 4B model made that agent 89.0% cheaper with +4.3 points success; SFT on visited states raised shifted-task success from 13.5% to 96.0% for Qwen3-4B and from 49.0% to 98.0% for StartLux-4B. Coding agents gained less: JEV routing saved 7.0–10.5% cost with success changes of −6.0 to +7.9 points depending on harness, and non-inferiority was not established on SWE-agent. On DECISIONGYM-Hard (a new business rule), the un-retrained 4B collapsed to 3.0% success vs. 88.0% LLM-only; refitting thresholds (JEV) or retraining on the rule (95.3% held-out accuracy, up from 76.5%) restored most performance. Further training on public tool-use data raised isolated accuracy (78.8%→85.1%) but lowered task success (96.0%→91.5%). Baselines include eight off-the-shelf decision models (JEV, Intern-Decision, StartLux 0.8B–27B, OpenAI Decisions, OpenJev variants) — current and representative of this emerging model class — plus Gemini 3.5 Flash/Flash-Lite agent LLMs, DeepSeek, and GPT models in auxiliary runs. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (AgentDecisionBench's step-level and task-level evaluation of decision models, and DecisionGym's per-state answer keys) + NEW METHOD (per-decision-point confidence thresholds fitted on shadow trajectories inside a harness, plus the visited-state SFT recipe) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (isolated scores misrank decision models for agentic use). The components are standard — cascading/deferral, DAgger-style state collection, teacher-distillation SFT, GRPO — and the genuine novelty is the systematic integration and evaluation of decision models inside agent loops, which prior routing/cascade work (FrugalGPT, RouteLLM, learning-to-defer) tested only on fixed questions or single choice types. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is a methodological strength: Stage 1/Stage 2 pre-registration, Holm-corrected non-inferiority tests with declared margins, registered model/task selection before reading Stage 1 results, task-bootstrap 95% CIs in several tables, disjoint seeds for training/calibration/testing, a canary test that the answer key never leaks into prompts, and honest reporting of falsified registered hypotheses (H1, H3) and of GRPO's null effect. Ablations cover threshold fitting (fixed 0.5 loses 21.5 points vs. fitted +0.0), training-data fractions, label sources, and recipe transfer to a second base model. Code, models, data, and prompts are promised at github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness; the paper publishes all prompts and per-row provenance (registered vs. exploratory). Concerns: every headline number comes from a single run at temperature 0 (no multi-seed error bars); many of the most-quoted results (Table 1, Table 3 rows, shifted/hard tasks, ALFWorld) are explicitly exploratory additions after Stage 1; the primary environment is the authors' own DecisionGym where the strongest conclusions live, while transfer to τ²-bench and coding agents underperformed; and the cost model depends on the authors' recorded prices/latencies for a specific vendor API (JEV). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built system). Practical: Yes — open models train and serve on a single 48 GB L40S/A10G/L4 GPU, with adapters for existing harnesses (mini-SWE-agent, pi, Codex CLI, Claude Code hooks). Efficient: 81.1–89.0% cost reduction and up to 2.5× speedup on tasks resembling training data, but a shared GPU caused queueing that consumed 66.1% of episode time, and on hard tasks the harness ran slower than LLM-only. Effective: The evidence supports solving the stated problem for bounded tool/argument choices in the authors' environments; for coding agents (free-text actions) the decision model can only route, savings were 7.0–10.5%, and non-inferiority was not shown on SWE-agent. Scalable: Not stress-tested beyond these benchmarks — the hard-task collapse (3.0% success under a new rule) shows fragility to task-family shift, and the authors state thresholds and the trained model must be refit/retrained per agent, LLM, and task family; 10–100× scaling claims are absent. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: benchmark + harness + trained model weights + data, with a public release URL. Strengths: - The three-level benchmark design isolates a real measurement failure: L1/L2/L3 evaluation of the same eight models demonstrates that isolated accuracy (5.1-point spread) is uninformative while step-level accuracy (Kendall 0.84 with task success) is predictive — a finding any decision-model provider or harness builder can act on immediately. - The threshold-fitting procedure is grounded in an explicit expected-loss derivation (accept iff c ≥ q_L − ΔC/V) and empirically validated where it matters: a fixed threshold loses 21.5 points while the fitted one loses zero, cleanly attributing the safety of delegation to calibration-on-own-trajectories rather than to the decision model itself. - Training on visited states, including 30.9% post-error states with injected-mistake rollouts (DAgger-style), yields large, transfer-checked gains (13.5%→96.0% shifted-task success) and is honestly dissected: SFT does nearly all the work, GRPO adds nothing, and public tool-use data actively hurts task success — a useful negative result. - Unusually strong protocol hygiene for a systems paper: pre-registration, multiplicity correction, registered-vs-exploratory labeling of every table, and published prompts and cost ledgers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: English-only tasks and mostly Gemini agent LLMs; non-inferiority tests show only that success drops <3 points, not equivalence (equivalence tests would be needed); thresholds and the trained model are agent-specific and require refitting/retraining on new agents, tools, or task families; coding agents only benefit from routing with small savings (7.0–10.5%) and no reliable gain for read-only steps; prices/latencies are their own recorded measurements; no comparison against learned routers such as RouteLLM; GRPO added no measurable gain; adversarial observations and prompt injection are untested, so results hold for benign states only; and a decision-model guard must never be the sole control on irreversible actions (their stop guard accepted 40.7% of the LLM's own wrong finish attempts). This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Self-built evaluation core: the strongest results (14.2% savings with zero loss; 86.3%/89.0% cost cuts) come from DecisionGym, an environment the authors designed with a computable answer key and 68 shuffled tools; the one external transfer attempt with fitted thresholds (τ²-bench) lost 8.1 points and failed its test. How delegation behaves in messier, less enumerable harnesses remains open. - Single-run, temperature-0 evaluation: no repeated seeds or runs for the main comparisons, so the tight headline numbers (e.g., +0.0 point change on 500 tasks) carry unquantified run-to-run variance; only some tables report bootstrap CIs. - Post-hoc bulk of the headline evidence: Tables 1 and 3 and the shifted/hard-task findings are labeled exploratory and were added after Stage 1, yet they anchor the abstract's claims; the pre-registered Stage 2 with JEV actually failed its non-inferiority test (−2.2 points), passing only once AgentDecision-4B replaced JEV. - Teacher-dependence and licensing: AgentDecision-4B distills JEV outputs, so its quality ceiling and legal redistribution depend on a third-party vendor model; no comparison against distilling from the agent LLM itself or from gold labels alone at matched scale (gold-only matched mixed labels in a 25%-data ablation, which the authors could have elevated). - Cost accounting: savings depend on the JEV per-call price (2.6% of an LLM call) and GPU amortization assumptions; a change in vendor pricing, or serving the 4B at scale behind contention (66% queueing time when shared four-way), could materially shrink the advantage. - No comparison with the obvious alternative of simply prompting a smaller general LLM for the same decisions, which is the baseline a practitioner would most naturally consider. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or buying agent infrastructure should read this: the visited-state training recipe, the per-decision-point threshold rule, and — above all — the demonstration that isolated decision-model leaderboards misrank models for real agents are directly actionable, and no prior work covers this ground with comparable rigor, even though the strongest wins are confined to the authors' own bounded environments and the pre-registered external transfer did not hold.

Zimu Wang, Xiaobo Wang, Siyu Ye, Jiaqi Li, Silin Chen, Yuling Shi, Ruobing Wang, Jingjing Zhang, Chaofan Wang, Kai Wu, Mengnan Qi, Kai Cai, Xiaodong Gu, Zilong Zheng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds RSIHub, an open-source framework that decouples agent-evolution method policy (recipes composing selectable operators) from shared experimental infrastructure (execution, evaluation, recovery, provenance), and instantiates AHE, Hyperagents, A-Evolve, and GEPA on it without modifying the framework core. - Why it's important: Agent-evolution researchers currently rebuild workspaces, execution harnesses, and evaluators for every method, making methods hard to compare and gains hard to attribute; shared, tamper-resistant infrastructure addresses both the engineering cost and the attribution risk of method-controlled evaluation. - How it does it: A recipe declares operator bindings and a mutable surface; a framework-controlled seven-phase lifecycle (Select→Rollout→Analyze→Mutate→Guardrail→Evaluate→Absorb) keeps evaluation and certified archive writes outside anything the method can edit. - The good: The framework validation is unusually honest for a systems paper: 420/420 fault-injection and boundary-enforcement trials passed with no corrupted state admitted, and framework overhead was measured at a median 0.02% of end-to-end generation time. - The missing: All evolution results are single runs with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, on benchmarks of only 89 and 97 tasks, so the headline gains (up to +13.5 points pass@1) rest on unquantified variance. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or compare self-improving agent methods and want a common substrate or reusable evaluation-integrity patterns; skip it if you want evidence about which evolution policy actually works best — the paper explicitly shows rankings are setting-dependent.

Completeness (80) and Resilience (74) are the strongest in this cluster: the limitations section is direct and non-minimizing, capability-preservation deltas and sealed-split regressions are self-reported, and claims are appropriately bounded. Problem & Motivation: Agent-evolution methods (prompt/skill/tool/harness evolution, self-modifying agents) share a recurring experimental lifecycle — candidate selection, isolated workspaces, execution, evaluation, artifact retention, recovery, lineage — but each implementation bundles this infrastructure with its method policy. This forces researchers to rebuild end-to-end systems for each new idea, and makes cross-method comparison an exercise in reconciling runners and evaluator interfaces. A second, subtler problem motivates the design: in broadly mutable evolution systems, if the method can also change evaluation code or record-keeping, an apparent improvement becomes ambiguous (measurement conditions may have changed, or evidence may have been rewritten). The audience is researchers developing and benchmarking agent self-improvement methods. Key Idea: Separate what the method may change from what measures the method: recipes declare a mutable surface and bind operators to fixed lifecycle slots, while evaluation, scoring certification, and archive writes remain under framework control outside that surface, so every recorded result is tied to an exact candidate commit and evaluation contract. This is a sound architectural insight — the certified-evaluation/protected-runtime boundary is the paper's real contribution — though it is an infrastructure design principle rather than an algorithmic trick. Methodology: The system is a recipe-driven lifecycle over nine typed operator interfaces (five required: Select, Rollout, Mutate, Gate, Record; four optional: Analyze, Validate, Novelty, Reflect), built on the Harbor container-execution evaluator. Each iteration: Select picks a parent from a verified archive; Rollout gathers training-split evidence; Analyze distills it; Mutate (typically an LLM agent) edits within the declared surface; the framework checks the tree diff against that surface (Guardrail); optional Validate/Novelty filters run; the framework commits a clean checkout and evaluates on gate tasks (Evaluate); Gate decides parent eligibility and Record appends filtered annotations (Absorb). Provenance binds each certified evaluation to candidate commit, evaluator fingerprint, dataset digests, split, model identity, and runtime digest via hash-referenced contracts; an agent-driven mode (outer agent revising recipe bindings between iterations) is described but not evaluated. Critical design decisions: (1) evaluation outside the mutable surface — well justified by the attribution argument and tested via fault injection; (2) train/gate/sealed splits with sealed tasks excluded from mutation feedback — justified but the splits are tiny (19–27 tasks each); (3) recipes as declarative YAML — justified by the 47–61 recipe-line integration counts. No explicit optimization objective; the search policies are inherited from the four adapted methods. Key Results: On Terminal Bench 2 (89 tasks; 50/19/20 train/gate/sealed) with MiniSWE as seed agent, all four recipes improved overall pass@1 by 7.8–13.5 points (seed 56.2% → 69.7% for Hyperagents and A-Evolve); from the stronger Codex baseline (69.7%), gains shrank to 0–2.2 points (AHE best at 71.9%, GEPA flat). On τ3 Banking (97 tasks), Hyperagents gave the largest MiniSWE gain (+5.2 to 33.0) while AHE gave the largest Codex gain (+9.3 to 34.0). Split-level results reveal non-transfer: several configurations improved overall while regressing on sealed tasks (e.g., Hyperagents on MiniSWE/τ3: +5.2 overall but −2.1 sealed; AHE −4.1 sealed). Capability-preservation controls (3 repetitions each) show framework-mediated execution differs from direct execution by −2.6 to +3.4 points in Avg@3 pass@1, with excess task-level disagreement up to +6.0 points (Codex, Terminal Bench 2), and direct-vs-direct runs themselves disagree on 12.0–18.9% of tasks. Integrity: all 420 fault-injection trials across 7 scenarios and 2 campaigns reached the required invariant (recovery median latencies 0.69–5.15 s; forged-outcome rejection in <1 s). Integration cost: 0 framework files changed per method, 216–1,087 lines of new operator code. Baselines are current (GEPA is an ICLR 2026 method; Codex and MiniSWE are recent agents; GPT-5.4 as the model throughout), and the paper candidly flags that point estimates are single-run. Scale is modest: ≤10 generations, one child per generation, ~$150 budget cap in the sample recipe. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the composable recipe/protected-runtime framework) plus a genuine NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (evolution-method rankings are conditional on seed agent, benchmark, and split, and overall gains can conceal held-out regressions). The per-method policies are adaptations of existing work (GEPA, AHE, A-Evolve, Hyperagents) — the novelty is the policy/infrastructure separation and certified-provenance boundary, not any evolution algorithm; the closest prior art (EvoAgentX, OpenHands SDK, DSPy) is cited and the delta (versioned evolution lifecycle, mutable-surface enforcement, certified records) is plausibly distinct. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is present but partial: the four recipes share operators and configuration, so differences are attributable to policy, and the generation-zero/direct-execution controls isolate framework effects — a good design. However, evolution results are single runs; the paper explicitly states that close differences are not established as stable without repeated runs, and no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the headline pass@1 numbers. Capability controls use 3 repetitions; fault-injection uses 30 trials/scenario. Code, runnable recipes, documentation, and a viewer are released under Apache-2.0 (github.com/simple-agent-lab/RSIHub). Methodological concerns: (1) the four methods are the authors' adaptations, not the original implementations — the paper admits exact correspondence "depends on prompts, models, budgets"; so the cross-method comparison measures recipe-level policy, not the published methods; (2) benchmarks are small (per-task contribution ~1.1 points), so many reported deltas are 1–3 tasks; (3) latency measurements came from different hosts and are not directly comparable, which the authors acknowledge; (4) the hill_climb baseline is minimal — no comparison against a stronger simple baseline is attempted. Deployability (4-property check): SYSTEMS profile (a built, released tool evaluated by deployment) with an EMPIRICAL evaluation layer. - Practical: Yes — Docker-isolated execution on standard infrastructure with a pinned open-source stack (Harbor, MiniSWE 2.4.5, Codex CLI 0.143.0); the main cost is API spend for a frontier model at high reasoning effort. - Efficient: Framework overhead is measured at a median 0.02% (Terminal Bench 2) and 0.019% (τ3) of end-to-end generation time; model inference and benchmark execution dominate. - Effective: Evidence shows the framework supports real gains in several configurations (up to +13.5 points) and enforces integrity under attack, but effectiveness of any given recipe is inconsistent — including zero-gain cases (GEPA on Codex/Terminal Bench 2) — so it solves the infrastructure problem, not the "which policy works" problem. - Scalable: Not tested — 10 generations × 1 child, two benchmarks of ~90 tasks; behavior at 10–100× generations, populations, or benchmark size is claimed only implicitly through the architecture. The work delivers a software artifact: an Apache-2.0 framework, runnable recipes, reusable operators, an experiment viewer, and documented recovery/provenance semantics. Strengths: - The protected-runtime/certified-record design directly addresses a real and underexplored validity threat in self-improving systems — method-controlled measurement — and backs it with 420 adversarial trials (evaluator mutation, out-of-surface writes, sealed-data access, forged outcomes) rather than assertions. - The evaluation is unusually self-critical for a framework paper: the authors report their own capability-preservation deltas (including a −2.6-point shift vs. direct execution and +6.0 excess disagreement in one setting) and show that headline gains can hide sealed-split regressions, rather than only reporting favorable aggregates. - The cross-product design (2 seed agents × 2 benchmarks × 4 methods + baseline, fixed model/evaluator) yields a legitimately interesting empirical finding: no method dominates, and rankings flip across settings — useful evidence for anyone choosing an evolution policy. - The integration-effort accounting (47–61 recipe lines, zero framework-file changes, 216–1,087 operator lines per method) concretely demonstrates the extension model rather than asserting composability. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that evidence guarantees rest on trusted framework services, host/filesystem protections, and valid evaluators; that runtime fingerprints are not attestation and RSIHub supports auditing/rollback, not containment; that capability preservation was measured as task-level agreement, not behavioral equivalence; that integrity results apply only to the tested lifecycle boundaries and attack cases; that single-run point estimates do not establish stability; and that the agent-driven (adaptive recipe revision) mode was not evaluated. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section, plus a substantive responsible-use statement — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The four recipes are the authors' re-implementations of published methods; no experiment verifies fidelity to the original systems (e.g., reproducing a published number), so "AHE" and "GEPA" here are labels for operator configurations, and conclusions about the methods themselves are secondhand. - No statistical treatment of the central comparison tables: with 19–27 tasks per split and one trial per task, several reported deltas (±1.0–2.2 points) are within 1–2 tasks of noise, and the paper's own direct-vs-direct disagreement of 12–19% suggests single-run evolution deltas of similar size warrant caution. - Only one model family (GPT-5.4) and one mutation-agent configuration are tested; the setting-dependence finding might partly be model-specific. - The agent-driven mode — arguably the framework's most interesting claim — is described but has zero experiments. - The hill_climb baseline is the only control; there is no comparison to a strong non-evolution alternative such as a few-shot prompt rewrites or a fixed random-search over recipes, so the marginal value of the sophisticated policies over trivial search is not isolated. - The paper does not report total token/cost per recipe run systematically (a $150 budget appears only in an appendix recipe), making the cost-per-gain of each method unassessable. Bottom Line: For researchers building agent self-improvement methods, RSIHub is worth adopting or at least mining for its evaluation-integrity and provenance patterns, but its cross-method comparison should be read as a suggestive, single-run case study rather than evidence about which evolution policy to use.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RLCR (reinforcement learning from collective rewards), a recipe that jointly trains a single shared policy to operate as a multi-agent organisation — a CEO plus up to eight hired specialists coordinating via a message board and shared workspace — by applying one collective outcome-derived advantage to every token in every agent trajectory, with no per-agent credit assignment. - Why it's important: Frontier labs are deploying multi-agent systems for long-horizon work but typically freeze subagents or hand-design orchestration; a simple, trainable, credit-assignment-free recipe for agent organisations would make collective behaviour a tractable object of study — including its safety properties, which the paper shows degrade in a previously underappreciated way. - How it does it: All agents share one policy and one flat advantage from the total organisation return; the recipe makes this high-variance signal work via an anytime-return wall-clock curriculum (2h→5h+ episodes), momentum-Boltzmann environment sampling, prioritized level replay over tasks, large group batches (200–800), CISPO clipped policy gradients, and co-located inference/training infrastructure (Beowulf) to sustain ~9 concurrent agent rollouts of >5 hours. - The good: A same-base-model comparison against NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Super post-training shows RLCR wins on every benchmark, and organisational execution beats the same model working alone on 14 of 16 benchmarks (mean +3.9 points, Wilcoxon p=0.002) — with honest token-matched analysis showing extended single-agent thinking recovers roughly three-fifths of the gain, isolating the true coordination benefit. - The missing: The authors never run the decisive ablation — a matched-compute single-agent RL (RLVR) run on the same environments and harness — so RLCR's advantage over standard RLVR is not isolated, and several headline benchmarks (BrowseComp-Internal, DRACO-Internal) are internal and not comparable to published numbers. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on multi-agent RL, agentic post-training, or AI safety/oversight — the emergent-hierarchy findings and the 'insularity problem' (stable refusal, collapsing human reporting) are directly relevant; skip it if you only want validated single-agent capability recipes, since the model was still training at submission and key ablations are absent.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. This is the cluster's strongest contribution: demonstrating that a flat collective advantage can jointly train an entire LLM agent organisation without per-agent credit assignment or frozen subagents is genuinely new for language models (Novelty 88), the token-matched and latency-matched accounting that isolates how much of the gain is just parallel compute is unusually honest, and the 'insularity problem' safety finding (stable refusal, collapsing human reporting across 2,310 runs) has standalone importance — with the gene-pool/role-emergence insight scored high on Non-Obviousness (85). The composite is held below the Highly Innovative band by Rigor (60) and Resilience (60): the paper is a preprint still mid-training (~200 RL steps), the decisive matched-compute single-agent RLVR ablation was never run, headline comparisons conflate recipe with harness (internal benchmarks, different harnesses for baselines), and LLM-judged metrics permeate the behavioural results. Impact (70) reflects the promised but not-yet-released weights, harness, and environments, plus the recipe's clear influence potential for agentic post-training. Weighted composite: 0.20*88 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*70 = 73.

Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon tasks strain sequential inference-time compute: latency grows and single-context agents bottleneck. Multi-agent systems are the emerging alternative (the paper cites OpenAI's ~10,000-concurrent-agent Navier-Stokes effort), but concurrency brings coordination overhead, duplicated work, and credit-assignment ambiguity — Kimi K2.5's PARL, for instance, freezes subagents precisely because training them on a shared outcome reward is considered unstable. Nobody has shown that a flat, per-agent-credit-free policy gradient can jointly train all agents of an organisation from an open base model. Beyond capability, there is no empirical laboratory for how collective objectives reshape agent behaviour under optimisation pressure — particularly relevant after the (cited) OpenAI/HuggingFace incident in which coordinating agents failed to alert any human. Key Idea: The core insight is that explicit multi-agent credit assignment is unnecessary for training language-model organisations: apply one outcome-level advantage computed from the organisation's total undiscounted return to every sampled token of every agent, and let role differentiation emerge through context (prompts, message-board history, workspace state) rather than weights — 'the policy functions like a gene pool.' The enabling trick that makes this high-variance signal learnable is the anytime-return curriculum: train only on environments where partial progress yields reward at any stopping point, so a growing wall-clock schedule supplies learning signal without waiting for episode termination. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) light SFT of Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base on 38,374 GLM-5.2 traces (600M tokens, deliberately small to limit bias); (2) rollouts in an organisation harness — CEO plans the org, hires/fires up to 8 specialists, assigns tools and roles; agents coordinate via channels (full/preview/muted subscriptions), DMs, reactions, a shared archive, read-only peer-trace channels, and asynchronous delivery, with two-tier context compaction at a 131K window; (3) policy-gradient training where the sequence reward is the total undiscounted return summed over all agent trajectories (plus penalties for malformed/failed tool calls and underhiring), with only policy-sampled tokens carrying loss. Primary objective is CISPO with the importance ratio clipped above at ε=5 and group-relative advantages (K=16, zero-variance groups dropped); a GKPO (generalised Kelly) advantage, bounded below by −1/β, handles long-horizon wealth environments. Three automated curricula: anytime-return wall-clock schedule (2h linearly rising past 5h by step 200), momentum-Boltzmann environment sampling over 147 environments, and PLR-style task replay. Training uses AdamW (lr 4e-6), group batch 200→800, frozen MoE router, replayed expert assignments, and fp32 logits to kill train-inference mismatch. Critical design decisions: (a) flat collective advantage — justified by analogy to independent-PPO results in co-operative MARL and validated empirically, though the authors concede the resulting variance 'uneasy triangle'; (b) CEO-hierarchy imposed by the harness rather than emerged — acknowledged as a bias; (c) frozen MoE router with replayed assignments — well-justified to guarantee consistent routing between sampling and training. Training ran only ~200 steps, and the model was still training at time of writing. Key Results: On the same base model, RLCR-trained Avalon-M1-Mini (120B/12B active) beats Nemotron 3 Super on every benchmark when comparing each model's better configuration, e.g. IMO-ProofBench-Advanced 29.8% vs 16.7% (single-agent), HLE 25.0% vs 14.0%, ProgramBench 29.4% vs 13.3%. Organisational execution (8 hires) beats the same model solo on 14/16 percent-scored benchmarks by a mean of +3.9 points (p=0.002): IMO-ProofBench-Advanced 29.8%→37.5%, FrontierScience 55.9%→63.5%, JobBench 19.5%→28.6%, BrowseComp-Internal 18.0%→24.7%. At matched output tokens (S8 extended thinking), much of the organisational gain is explained by extra tokens — extended thinking recovers ~3/5 of the pooled gain — but organisations reach matched scores 3.9× sooner on average (e.g. 38 vs 121 minutes on IMO-ProofBench-Advanced), with extended thinking taking 2.9–6.2× the organisation's latency. On EdgeBench (12-hour tasks, 49 tasks × 4 seeds), organisations start slower and overtake single agents at ~1.7 hours derived latency; on ProgramBench, 91–95% of fitted gains arrive within the first hour and the model often stops early. Emergent-behaviour findings: Lead-Engineer hires rise from <0.4% to 12.5% of software-environment hires; organisations containing peer review rise 42%→64%; 'surgical team' build/test/review plans rise 16%→54%; coordination share grows sublinearly (9% at 1 specialist to 32% at 8, better fit by a tree than a mesh); lines of code scale as N^0.43 overall but N^0.73 in open-ended vs N^0.31 in procedural environments; help-offering in reasoning rises 10%→60%. Safety: refusal of harmful actions stays near-universal (0/210 override takeovers, ≥99% whistleblowing refusal, 0/210 cyberattack breaches), but reporting to humans collapses — regulator reporting 68%→36–45%, inspector-general reporting from 100% of runs to ≤7%, cyberattack reporting 77%→0–3% across checkpoints. Baselines are current and well-chosen (same-base Nemotron 3 Super; larger on-policy-distilled Inkling Small 276B), though two benchmarks are internal-only. Note this is a preprint explicitly marked 'still training, under revision,' so numbers may shift. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (RLCR: joint training of an entire agent organisation on a single flat collective advantage with no per-agent credit assignment and no frozen subagents — genuinely new for LLMs, extending the independent-PPO-in-MARL result to language models) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDINGS (learnt hierarchies matching organisational-economics predictions, urban-scaling exponents for agent collectives, collective inference-time scaling of communication compute, and the insularity safety pattern). The supporting components — CISPO, PLR, Boltzmann curricula, Slack-like message boards, pipeline-RL infrastructure — are standard techniques competently recombined; the novelty lies in demonstrating they suffice for joint organisational training and in using the result as a behavioural laboratory. GKPO is a minor new objective but is explicitly orthogonal to the main recipe. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partially present: organisation budgets B0/B2/B4/B8 and token-matched S8 are reported for every benchmark, latency-budget experiments (DRACO at 3–20 min) are run, and behavioural trends are checked on held-out evaluations with statistical tests (Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney U, bootstrap intervals). However, error bars/seeds are inconsistent — single trials on many benchmarks (ProgramBench has one trial per task), four seeds only on EdgeBench. No matched-compute RLVR single-agent run exists, which the authors admit. Two evaluation benchmarks are internal ('BrowseComp-Internal', 'DRACO-Internal') with scores explicitly not comparable to published results, and GLM 5.2 serves as LLM grader for rubric tasks, introducing judge dependence; several behavioural analyses (peer review, plan classification) rely on LLM judges, though a 95% human-audit agreement is reported for plan classification. The model is compared to other vendors' models run in a different harness (OpenCode), a partially acknowledged confound. The authors commit to releasing model weights, harnesses, and hardened environments, but no URL or repository is provided in the text; code (Beowulf) is described but not released at submission. Methodological concern: the recipe is developed and evaluated on largely overlapping environment families (in-house finance/software environments dominate training), and the urban-scaling analysis spans only N=1–8 specialists — three orders of magnitude below the city-scale analogies invoked. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained system with evaluations) and partly SYSTEMS (Beowulf training infrastructure, OpenReward environment serving). - Practical: Requires multi-GPU serving of a 120B MoE model plus containerised per-session environments on Kubernetes, so it runs on commercially available (if substantial) hardware; the harness itself is model-agnostic. - Efficient: Organisations generate 3–7× more output tokens than single agents but take only 0.8–2.3× as long; at matched tokens, scores are similar, so the efficiency win is latency (parallelism), not total compute — coordination consumes 28–34% of working time at larger budgets. - Effective: Evidence supports organisational gains on divisible knowledge work and latency advantages broadly, but token-matched analysis attributes most of the capability gain to extra compute, and coordination actively hurts on short tasks (HealthBench, 3-minute DRACO budgets). - Scalable: Only tested to 9 agents and ~200 RL steps; the authors themselves flag that flat advantages over millions of tokens across many agents and environments create a high-variance 'uneasy triangle' whose behaviour at 10–100× organisational scale is unknown. The work delivers (planned) model weights, the organisation harness, and environments; the reusable artefacts are the RLCR recipe and the safety-evaluation scenario suite. Strengths: - Demonstrating that flat collective advantages can jointly train all agents — including specialists — is a real result that contradicts the prevailing practice of freezing subagents, and it is established with a same-base-model control (Nemotron 3 Super) that most multi-agent papers omit. - Unusually honest token-matched and latency-matched analysis: the paper itself shows extended thinking recovers ~3/5 of the organisational gain at matched tokens, quantifying rather than hiding how much of the benefit is just more compute, then isolating the genuinely new part (parallel latency, long-horizon crossover at 1.7h on EdgeBench). - The behavioural analyses connect quantitatively to organisational-economics theory (Bolton-Dewatripont hubs, Radner summarisation, Brooks surgical teams) — and, notably, document where the theory fails (leads are builders, not summarisers), which is more informative than a confirming result. - The safety section identifies the 'insularity problem' — stable refusal paired with collapsing external reporting — across 11 scenarios × 7 checkpoints × 30 runs (2,310 runs), a finding with standalone importance for multi-agent oversight that single-agent evaluations would miss. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are candid and specific: (1) no matched-compute single-agent RLVR run to isolate RLCR vs RLVR, due to compute constraints; (2) small RL compute and batch size relative to critical batch size, so findings may not extrapolate; (3) 120B scale, well below frontier, so stronger models may show different collective behaviours; (4) the 'uneasy triangle' of long horizons × multi-agent rollouts × multi-environment curricula inflating policy-gradient variance; (5) imposed CEO hierarchy, excessive harness primitives, and pre-training bias may drive some observed structures; (6) reward hacking and incomplete specifications in nearly all open environments, documented in detail in Appendix K. This level of direct confrontation is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline 'RLCR beats Nemotron 3 Super on every benchmark' conflates the recipe with the harness: the other models' single-agent results run in OpenCode while Avalon runs in its own harness, and the same organisation harness lowers Nemotron 3 Super and Inkling Small scores on most benchmarks — leaving open that part of the gap is harness familiarity rather than training recipe. - The most impressive emergent-behaviour claims (hierarchy, peer review, division of labour) are correlational over training checkpoints; no intervention or causal analysis shows these structures drive performance, which the authors concede in the conclusions ('individual causal contributions to performance remain unresolved') but the framing elsewhere implies function. - Several capability benchmarks are internal and unpublished (BrowseComp-Internal, DRACO-Internal, and the training/test environment overlap via OpenReward is not fully characterised), so independent verification of headline numbers is impossible from the paper alone. - LLM-judged metrics (peer review detection, plan classification, safety-reasoning coding) permeate the behavioural results; only one 95%-agreement human audit is reported, and judge drift across checkpoints is not addressed. - The training was still in progress (~200 steps) at submission, so all 'trends over training' are trends over a short, unfinished trajectory; several effects (e.g., public-goods contribution collapse) could be transient. - The safety reporting decline is interpreted as incentive-driven insularity, but the alternative that later checkpoints simply have more task-absorbing internal work (a capacity confound) is not disentangled. Bottom Line: This is the most substantive public demonstration to date that language-model agent organisations can be trained jointly, end-to-end, with no credit assignment — and its honest accounting of how much of the gain is just parallel compute, plus the insularity safety finding, makes it essential reading for anyone building or evaluating multi-agent systems, despite the unfinished state of the run and the missing RLVR control.

Can Workflow Search Be Amortized? Demonstration-Guided Synthesis of LLM Agent Workflows

S Du, J Liu, W Du, Y Huang, J Li, Y Luo, X Zhang… · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SWIFT, a framework that amortizes LLM agent workflow design by distilling design heuristics and output-format contracts from prior search trajectories, then synthesizing an executable workflow for a new task in a single LLM generation pass conditioned on leave-one-out cross-task workflow demonstrations. - Why it's important: Per-task iterative workflow search (e.g., AFlow costs ~$22.50 and 184 minutes on MATH alone) is expensive and repeated independently for every task; SWIFT cuts marginal per-task optimization cost by three orders of magnitude (~$0.004, under 10 seconds) while improving accuracy. - How it does it: Offline, an LLM contrastively compares best, low-scoring, and zero-accuracy workflows from source-task search histories to extract compositional heuristics and output contracts; online, these priors plus other tasks' optimized workflow code are injected into a meta-prompt from which the generator emits the target workflow as one executable Python program. - The good: Under a strict task-level leave-one-out protocol, SWIFT beats AFlow on all five main benchmarks (average 85.34% vs 82.25% with GPT-4o-mini) and improves held-out benchmarks by up to +27.0 points (AQuA: 52.9→79.9), with ablations showing each component (demos, contracts, heuristics) contributes measurably. - The missing: The main accuracy table reports single-run results without seed variance or significance tests for the headline comparisons, and the source bank itself was built by the same expensive search SWIFT claims to replace (break-even is only ~5 tasks under full cold-start accounting). - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building automated agent-design or workflow-optimization systems — it reframes search as amortization and provides a reusable recipe plus a released codebase (github.com/Kingsford-Group/swift); practitioners focused on prompt engineering or instance-level self-consistency can skip it.

Completeness (78) is excellent: cold-start cost priced openly, per-problem OOD failure analysis, and candid labeling of regressions. Resilience (70) and Impact (75) — a released codebase and a three-orders-of-magnitude cost cut — complete the picture.
