Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying LLM agents need structured programs that orchestrate LLM calls, tools, and control flow; hand-designing them is labor-intensive, so methods like AFlow, ADAS, GPTSwarm, and MaAS automate workflow design via iterative search. These methods optimize each new task independently, paying the full discrete, non-differentiable search cost (N candidates × cost C per evaluation) every time, with limited explicit reuse of structure across tasks and a risk of over-specializing to small validation sets. The paper observes that optimized workflows across math and code benchmarks converge to a small family of templates (multi-path reasoning with verification for math; execution-feedback repair loops for code), suggesting the effective workflow space is far smaller than the naive combinatorial view — and that this regularity can be exploited to amortize discovery cost across tasks. Key Idea: Replace per-task iterative search with demonstration-conditioned one-shot synthesis: treat other tasks' optimized workflows as in-context demonstrations (analogous to few-shot prompting, but at the program level), and inject two distilled priors — compositional heuristics (contrastively extracted from high- vs low-performing trajectories) and output contracts (interface/format constraints mined from workflows that failed only due to parser mismatches) — so a frozen LLM emits a complete executable workflow in one call. The output-contract idea targets what the authors call the "structural-functional gap": a topologically sound workflow can fail because intermediate nodes emit unparseable formats, and without contracts the synthesizer hedges by generating bloated topologies (3–4× more nodes at −4.4 to −4.6 accuracy). Methodology: Workflows are operator compositional graphs realized as executable Python programs over AFlow's six-operator library (Custom, AnswerGenerate, Programmer, CustomCodeGenerate, ScEnsemble, Test). The formal objective is the standard argmax of expected accuracy over a discrete workflow space; SWIFT instantiates an amortized map w_target ← f_φ(O, H, C, D_demo, T_target) with a frozen LLM. Phase 1 (offline): for each source task, select the best-validation workflow, hard negatives (lowest-scoring workflow with accuracy between 0 and γ·best, γ=0.6, plus one zero-accuracy workflow), extract their execution traces and parser error logs, and have a reflection LLM distill per-task heuristics H and contracts C. Phase 2 (online): construct a meta-prompt containing operator definitions, H∪C, leave-one-out demonstrations (target-task data, traces, and workflows fully excluded), and the target task description; a single temperature-0 generation produces the executable workflow, which is run directly on test instances. Critical design decisions: (1) mining contracts specifically from format-failed intermediate workflows — well-justified by the topology ablation (Appendix H); (2) strict leave-one-out at the task level — clear and honest about what it does and does not rule out (domain-level regularity transfer is counted as part of the signal); (3) no target-task refinement or validation loop — a deliberate bet that pays off on accuracy but means synthesis quality rests entirely on the meta-generator. Key Results: With GPT-4o-mini, SWIFT averages 85.34% over GSM8K (94.31), MATH (55.14), HumanEval (95.42), MBPP (83.28), and MultiArith (98.54, not in the demo pool), versus 83.59 for MaAS and 82.25 for AFlow — improving over AFlow on all five benchmarks (baseline numbers taken from the MaAS paper, so comparisons inherit that paper's setup). On four fully held-out benchmarks: SVAMP 81.0→95.8 (+14.8), AQuA 52.9→79.9 (+27.0), AIME 24–25 8.3→14.6 (+6.3, dominated by base-model reasoning failures), BigCodeBench 31.6→34.3 (+2.7; failure analysis attributes most errors to missing sandbox dependencies, with an environment-normalized score of 55.04%). Efficiency on MATH: $0.004 and 0.13 min optimization vs AFlow's $22.50 and 184 min; total pipeline 14× cheaper and 29× faster than AFlow and 2× cheaper/10× faster than MaAS, at the highest accuracy; break-even under full cold-start accounting is ~5 downstream tasks (C_source ≈ $112.50). Ablations: removing demonstrations collapses MATH to 2.47% (from 55.14) while costing GSM8K only 3.1; shuffled demo code lines give 0.00 on MATH; cross-domain demos cost −8.4 average; randomized operator names cost only −4.9 average, showing transfer rides on topology/interfaces rather than human-readable names. Cross-backbone portability: 16 of 18 benchmark–model pairs improve (e.g., MBPP +21.01 with Grok-4.1-fast), but Gemma-3-12B-IT loses 9.88 points on MATH, and Qwen→GPT generator-swap analysis shows synthesis quality is task- and generator-dependent. Matched controls (Direct-Reuse and Explicit-Adapt retrieval baselines, Appendix I.6) trail SWIFT by 6.05 and 3.48 macro-average points. Baselines are current (AFlow ICLR 2025, MaAS ICML 2025) and reasonably strong. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (amortized, demonstration-conditioned single-pass workflow synthesis) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (workflow search converges to a small reusable template family; interface contracts, not operator names, carry much of the transfer signal). The individual mechanisms — operator libraries and executable graphs (AFlow), few-shot demonstration conditioning (standard), trajectory analysis (related to Agent Workflow Memory) — are known; the genuinely new move is operating at the program level with leave-one-out cross-task workflow demonstrations plus contrastively distilled heuristics and contracts, extending the amortized-optimization principle (cf. amortized variational inference, neural program synthesis) to agent workflow design. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: component removal (heuristics, contracts, demos), demo corruption (shuffled code, cross-domain, random operator names), demo count sweeps, topology comparison with/without contracts, generator–executor coupling (Qwen→GPT), three-seed synthesis variability (AQuA 79.74 ± 3.68, BigCodeBench 34.17 ± 0.25), semantic-retrieval variants, workflow-reuse controls, and per-problem OOD failure analysis. The leave-one-out protocol is explicitly constructed to prevent leakage, and the authors candidly flag where it does and does not rule out transfer. Concerns: (1) headline Table 1 results are single runs — the authors acknowledge this and interpret small differences cautiously, but the SWIFT-vs-MaAS margin (85.34 vs 83.59) is within plausible run-to-run noise given the ±3.68 SD observed on AQuA; (2) baseline numbers for Table 1 are imported from Zhang et al. (MaAS) rather than re-run; (3) all main results use GPT-4o-mini only as generator and executor, with the same benchmark family (math/code with deterministic correctness) serving both as source bank and evaluation domain; (4) MATH evaluation uses only the Level-5 subset (486 problems), limiting comparability to papers using the full MATH set. Code is released at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/swift. This is a peer-reviewed EMNLP 2026 proceedings paper. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method with executed experiments and a released system). Practical: Yes — everything runs through a single commercial API (GPT-4o-mini), with total execution cost of $6.08 across all nine benchmarks. Efficient: Marginal per-task optimization is ~$0.004 and <11 s vs $22.50/184 min for AFlow; even full-pipeline cost is 14× cheaper than AFlow, though cold-start users pay a one-time ~$112.50 source-bank cost. Effective: Evidence supports solving the stated problem on static benchmarks with automatic correctness signals, but the authors themselves note this does not establish effectiveness in stochastic, interactive, or irreversible environments (InterCode-Python gains are marginal: 0.43 vs 0.40 first-turn success). Scalable: Only claimed implicitly via the cost model (n·C_synth vs n·C_search); no experiment tests whether the demonstration pool or contract set remains useful at 10–100× more diverse task families — transfer already degrades sharply on domain-mismatched tasks. The work delivers a software artifact (open-source codebase) and reusable distilled priors, not just a paper. Strengths: - The reframing of workflow design as amortized optimization with a rigorous task-level leave-one-out protocol is a genuine conceptual contribution, and the break-even analysis (Appendix G) honestly prices the cold-start case rather than hiding the source-bank cost. - The output-contract mechanism is a non-obvious, empirically grounded insight: formatting failures at node interfaces cause the synthesizer to hedge with bloated topologies (5 nodes vs 2 on GSM8K at −4.4 accuracy), and contracts mined specifically from format-failed workflows fix both. - The ablation that randomizes operator names is a clever mechanism study — it shows transfer rides on topology, interfaces, and code context rather than readable labels, which is a finding relevant to the whole automated-agent-design subfield. - Exceptional failure analysis: per-problem OOD breakdowns attribute AIME failures to the base model's reasoning ceiling and BigCodeBench failures to sandbox dependencies (with an environment-normalized 55.04% supplementary score), plus a generalizable observation that text-based ScEnsemble voting is unsuitable as the terminal check for code tasks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that evaluation is limited to static benchmarks with automatic correctness signals and does not establish effectiveness in stochastic, interactive, or irreversible environments, and that the method assumes access to source workflows — under cold-start deployment the upstream source-bank cost must be accounted for (with the ~5-task break-even given in Appendix G). They also note in the text that small accuracy differences should be interpreted cautiously under the shared baseline evaluation protocol. They confront limitations directly, including a dedicated appendix on the ScEnsemble code-voting failure mode and honest labeling of preliminary results (InterCode, Gemma regressions) — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No error bars or significance tests on the main Table 1 comparison against MaAS and AFlow; the 1.75-point average margin over MaAS, with per-benchmark gaps of ~0.5–2 points on MBPP, is not clearly outside the observed synthesis variability (SD up to 3.68). - The source bank is restricted to four math/code benchmarks; whether amortized synthesis works over a heterogeneous task bank (e.g., including QA or agentic-tool tasks in the pool) is untested in the main results, so the "three orders of magnitude" claim is conditioned on a narrow, template-rich domain mix the authors themselves show favors math transfer. - Evaluation on MATH uses only Level 5 (486 problems), which departs from standard full-MATH protocol and complicates direct comparability beyond the imported baseline numbers. - The offline distillation and online synthesis use the same model family (GPT-4o-mini) for generator and executor in primary results; generator-side portability is only partially explored (Qwen→GPT degrades MATH by ~10 points vs GPT→GPT), leaving generator–executor coupling as an open dependence. - The demonstration pool and heuristics are distilled from AFlow's own search outputs, so SWIFT's advantage over search could partly reflect that the search baseline overfits small validation sets — a confound acknowledged qualitatively but not disentangled experimentally. Bottom Line: For anyone building automated agent/workflow-optimization pipelines, this is one of the more credible and complete papers in the 2025–2026 wave — the amortization framing, leave-one-out protocol, and contract insight are genuinely useful and the code is available — but read the headline accuracy margins with skepticism given single-run results, and look elsewhere if your target tasks are interactive or far from math/code template families.

DBCM: Dual-Branch Calibration Module for Test-Time Adaptation in Time Series Forecasting

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DBCM, a dual-branch calibration module for test-time adaptation (TTA) in time series forecasting (TSF) that decomposes residual correction into a channel-shared adapter plus a channel-wise low-rank (LoRA) adapter, applied to both the input and output sides of a frozen forecaster. - Why it's important: Existing TSF-TTA methods spend limited online supervision on fully independent per-channel adapters, which the authors show is redundant; a more parameter-efficient correction structure directly improves forecasting accuracy under deployment-time non-stationarity at no extra backbone cost. - How it does it: The core move is an empirical observation that forecast residuals are concentrated in a low-dimensional shared channel subspace (EVR@30% ≈ 93%, Rank@90/C ≈ 42% across backbones), motivating a shared temporal adapter (one L×L matrix applied to all channels) complemented by a per-channel rank-8 LoRA branch, a linear channel mixer, and two-level nonlinear gating. - The good: The claim is supported by a coherent chain of evidence — residual spectrum analysis, a subspace-alignment metric (DBCM 0.774 vs TAFAS 0.671), and a component ablation showing that replacing TAFAS's channel-wise adapter with a shared one matches performance with 10× fewer parameters (0.18M vs 1.70M). - The missing: No public code or data release is stated (only a promise of hyperparameter configs with an 'official implementation'), and the headline Exchange-rate gains carry very large seed variance (e.g., ±0.0837 for DBCM on PatchTST/H=720), weakening the strongest headline numbers. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on test-time adaptation, forecasting calibration, or parameter-efficient fine-tuning — the residual-spectrum analysis and shared-vs-specific adapter decomposition are directly transferable ideas; skip it if you only need a new forecasting backbone.

Problem & Motivation: Multivariate time series forecasters are trained offline assuming stationarity, but deployed on non-stationary streams (energy, finance, weather), so pre-trained models degrade at test time. TSF-TTA addresses this by adapting lightweight calibration modules around a frozen forecaster, supervised by forecast residuals (the gap between prediction and ground truth) that become available incrementally as test time steps are revealed. All prior TSF-TTA methods (TAFAS, PETSA, DynaTTA, COSA) use channel-wise adapters, implicitly assuming residuals are fully channel-specific; the paper argues this wastes limited online supervision re-fitting correction patterns that are actually shared across channels. The gap addressed is the missing empirical characterization of residual channel-space structure and the corresponding over-parameterization of existing adapters. Key Idea: The single core insight is that forecast residuals — the direct supervision signal for TSF-TTA — exhibit strong shared structure across channels (concentrated eigen-spectrum of the centered channel-space Gram matrix), so corrections should be decomposed into (1) a single shared temporal adapter applied to all channels and (2) a channel-wise LoRA branch with rank r≪L that captures only the limited residual channel-specific variation, wrapped in channel mixing (which 'preconditions' residuals into a more concentrated subspace) and input-dependent nonlinear gating. This is a genuine, testable hypothesis-backed design principle, not just an architectural tweak. Methodology: The pipeline is standard TSF-TTA: X→C_in(X)→frozen forecaster f_θ→C_out(ŷ), where both C_in and C_out share the same DBCM architecture. Each DBCM is: (i) linear channel mixing X + XW_mix (residual form, W_mix ∈ R^{C×C}); (ii) a shared adapter — one learnable L×L temporal matrix applied uniformly to all channels; (iii) a channel-wise LoRA adapter — per-channel U_c V_c with rank r=8, concatenated across channels; (iv) a learnable channel bias; (v) an inner sigmoid gate G = σ(W_gate X_mix + b_gate) modulating the correction values (GLU-style: C_base + C_base⊙G), followed by an outer channel-wise tanh(g) gate on the residual path. Optimization follows the TAFAS protocol: Adam on a partial-observation MSE loss using revealed ground-truth steps, updates triggered by periodicity analysis (PAAS), with the source forecaster frozen. Critical design decisions: (a) shared vs. channel-wise decomposition — well-justified by the Section 4 spectrum analysis and the TAFAS-Shared ablation; (b) rank r=8 — justified by a rank sweep showing no gain beyond 8 and degradation at 64/full rank; (c) linear channel mixer over MLP/attention/uniform alternatives — justified by an ablation (Table C.11) showing marginal differences, favoring the simplest option. The loss is plain squared error on revealed targets; no auxiliary objectives. Key Results: Across 144 settings (6 datasets — ETTh1/h2, ETTm1/m2, Exchange, Weather — × 4 horizons {96,192,336,720} × 6 backbones — iTransformer, DLinear, FreTS, PatchTST, OLS, MICN), DBCM reduces MSE by 6.20% over the frozen baseline versus 4.07% for TAFAS and 2.61% for PETSA (Avg. Rank 1.00–1.10 for DBCM across all backbones). Gains widen at long horizons (8.87% vs 5.46% for TAFAS at H=720). The most dramatic gains are on Exchange (strongest non-stationarity by ADF statistic −1.90): DLinear H=720 improves 15.7% (0.8383→0.7066) vs 0.9% for TAFAS; PatchTST H=720 improves 25.0% (0.8814→0.6609). Scalability checks: on Electricity (321 channels), DBCM wins at all horizons (e.g., 5.45% improvement for iTransformer H=720 vs 2.33% TAFAS); on time series foundation models (Moirai, Chronos, Chronos-2), DBCM is best on all four ETT datasets, e.g., reducing Chronos ETTm1 MSE from 1.5167 to 0.3862. It also beats DynaTTA (which often degrades the baseline), outperforms COSA and DynaME under matched protocols, is complementary to RevIN/DDN normalization, and holds on synthetic-shift TTFBench. Efficiency: 5.63% adapter parameter ratio vs TAFAS's 16.00% and PETSA's 1.14%, with comparable latency/memory and the highest throughput (12,340 samples/sec vs 12,023/11,815). Baselines are current and strong (TAFAS/PETSA are the SOTA TSF-TTA methods; COSA, DynaTTA, DynaME covered in appendices). Testing scale is standard benchmark, not stress-scale, except the 321-channel Electricity test. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the channel-space concentration of forecast residuals and the subspace-alignment analysis of adapter corrections) plus NEW METHOD (the dual-branch shared/low-rank calibration module). The ingredients are individually standard — LoRA adapters, channel mixing (TSMixer-style), gated linear units, TAFAS's input/output-side calibration framework — but the combination is genuinely motivated by a new diagnostic analysis, and the finding that a purely shared adapter matches fully channel-wise TAFAS is a non-obvious empirical result for this subfield. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: component-wise incremental ablation (Figure 3a) with parameter counts, LoRA rank sweep, channel-mixing strategy, gating function, bias parameterization, and input/output-side decomposition. Results are averaged over 3 seeds with standard deviations reported in Table C.14, and baselines are tuned with an identical search budget following TAFAS's procedure. No significance tests are reported. Code is not yet released — the paper only promises that selected hyperparameters 'will be provided in our official implementation' (no URL given), which is a reproducibility concern. Methodological flags: (a) the method is developed and evaluated on the same standard benchmarks it motivates its design from (the channel-space analysis and experiments both use ETT/Weather/Exchange), though the TTFBench synthetic-shift evaluation mitigates this partially; (b) the authors correctly identify and handle a label-leakage issue in COSA's protocol and re-run comparisons under both protocols — a credibility positive; (c) Exchange-rate results for DBCM show seed standard deviations up to 0.146, larger than the margin over baselines in some cells, though average rank still favors DBCM. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a lightweight SYSTEMS artifact). Practical: Runs on a single RTX 4090 (RTX 6000 ADA for foundation models) — commodity hardware. Efficient: 5.63% adapter parameter ratio (vs 16.00% for TAFAS), ~0.03% for Chronos; DBCM has the highest throughput (12,340 samples/sec) and comparable peak memory (~493 MB) to alternatives, with millisecond-level adaptation overhead offset by periodic (PAAS-triggered) updates. Effective: The evidence shows it improves forecast MSE across all 144 tested settings and 321-channel data, i.e., it works on the proxy (benchmark MSE under chronological splits) rather than on documented real-world deployments. Scalable: Parameter count scales as O(L² + H² + Cr(L+H) + C²) — the C² channel mixer is the weakest link and is only tested at C=321; behavior at 10× channels (thousands of sensors) is extrapolated from latency results, not tested. The work delivers a method specification with PyTorch-style pseudocode (Algorithm 1); no released library or trained weights at submission time. Strengths: - The residual-spectrum analysis (Table 1, EVR@30% ≈ 93% vs 33–43% for isotropic residuals) is a genuinely new diagnostic that converts an architectural intuition into measurable evidence, and it predicts an actionable result: a shared-only variant of TAFAS matches full TAFAS with ~10× fewer parameters. - The evidence chain is internally coherent: spectrum analysis → subspace alignment (DBCM 0.774 vs TAFAS 0.671 vs random 0.246) → incremental ablation, so each design decision traces back to a measurement rather than a hunch. - Honest protocol handling: the authors flag COSA's label-leakage issue, re-run the comparison under COSA's own protocol and still win, and report the DynaTTA baseline's instability rather than cherry-picking. - Breadth of validation — 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons, plus 321-channel data, three foundation models, a synthetic-shift benchmark, normalization-stack compatibility (RevIN/DDN), and efficiency tables — is above the norm for this subfield. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that their analysis covers only the output space (residuals, output-side corrections) and does not characterize input-side adaptation dynamics, a limitation shared with prior TSF-TTA work; input-side DBCM is trained only via the final prediction loss. They also note (in the conclusion and Appendix G) that residual low-rankness is an empirical hypothesis whose strength varies by dataset and forecaster — not a universal property — and that adaptively determining channel-wise branch capacity per dataset is future work. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No public code, data splits, or trained checkpoints are released at submission; reproducibility currently rests on pseudocode and a promise of future artifact release. - Seed variance on Exchange (up to ±0.146 for DBCM at PatchTST H=720, versus a baseline MSE of 0.8814) is large enough that the biggest headline improvements overlap with baseline uncertainty in some cells; no significance testing is provided. - The evaluation uses only standard long-term-forecasting benchmarks whose test shifts are mild (the authors admit this themselves when introducing TTFBench); real deployment evidence (concept drift in production systems) is absent. - The channel mixer's O(C²) parameters are only stress-tested at C=321; high-channel-count regimes (e.g., M4-scale or thousands-of-sensor IoT) are untested despite the shared-adapter motivation being strongest there. - Hyperparameters for DBCM (LoRA rank 8, gating initial values) are tuned per the TAFAS procedure but the paper does not report sensitivity of the main comparison to the shared tuning budget for the baselines, and the appendix comparison with DynaTTA relies on a configuration inherited from COSA due to stated reproducibility issues in the official code — reasonable, but the DynaTTA numbers may under- or over-represent that method. Bottom Line: For anyone building or deploying TSF-TTA calibration, this paper is worth reading for the residual-structure analysis and the demonstration that shared-plus-low-rank adapters beat fully channel-wise ones at lower cost; it is the strongest entry in this specific subfield, and no published alternative covers the same ground more convincingly.

Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs (91 ▲ )

Donghyeon Cho, Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Eunho Yang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LOWN, a training-free, threshold-free decoding method for diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) that decides at every denoising step whether to process the visual tokens and how many tokens to unmask, retaining 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score across ten benchmarks at 0.353× the decoding FLOPs. - Why it's important: DVLMs recompute the entire multimodal input (89–97% of which is visual tokens) at every denoising step because bidirectional attention blocks exact KV caching, so image-access redundancy is a large, previously unaddressed source of decoding waste. - How it does it: LOWN caches the top-1 predictions and confidences from the last image-conditioned (FULL) forward as an "anchor," runs a cheap TEXT-ONLY forward each step, and treats agreement between the two as a certificate: a certified confidence-ordered prefix longer than the per-step budget k is unmasked without the image; otherwise a FULL forward refreshes the anchor. - The good: The measurement is convincing and self-critical — a fresh FULL forward overturns only 2.2–4.7% of tokens LOWN actually accepts on TEXT-ONLY steps, and LOWN (0.35× FLOPs) sits within 0.02× of an oracle image-access schedule (0.33×), leaving almost no headroom for a better router. - The missing: Evaluation is confined to LLaDA-family backbones, greedy batch-size-1 decoding with temperature and classifier-free guidance fixed at zero — no results under sampling, batching, or on non-diffusion VLM families, and no test of whether the agreement-based certificate degrades for tasks requiring longer, more visual generations. - Read it or not: Read it if you build inference-time accelerators for diffusion LMs/VLMs or deploy DVLMs where latency matters; skip it if you work on autoregressive VLMs, where the bidirectional-attention bottleneck it exploits does not exist.

Completeness (78) is excellent, including a worked worst-case example and honest reporting that the composed configuration loses to Fast-dLLM alone. Resilience (70) is high because the near-oracle result and orthogonality demonstrations are hard to dispute, though single-seed greedy-only evaluation and same-benchmark development temper it. Impact (68) reflects linked code/project page and substantial measured wall-clock savings, but no confirmed verified artifact at scale. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*68 = 72.

Problem & Motivation: Discrete diffusion VLMs (LLaDA-V, LaViDa, VidLaDA) generate responses by iteratively unmasking tokens over T denoising steps, and their bidirectional attention forces a full forward pass over visual tokens, prompt, and partial response at every step. Visual tokens constitute 89–97% of the input on the studied benchmarks, yet a forward without them costs only 3–10% as much — so most decoding compute reprocesses an unchanged image. Existing accelerators either prune visual tokens (losing information permanently), cache intermediate states, or unmask more tokens per step; none asks whether the current step needs the image at all. The paper measures this directly: along LLaDA-V's baseline trajectories, removing the image changes an unmasked token at only 22.8% of steps on average (7.9% on MMBench to 43.8% on DocVQA), and image-dependent steps cluster early and vary by task, so a fixed schedule cannot capture them. Key Idea: Turn prediction agreement between the last image-conditioned forward (the "anchor") and a cheap TEXT-ONLY forward into a certificate of visual redundancy — agreement simultaneously certifies that the image is not needed for that token and that the stale anchor remains valid after the response state changed — and use the length of the certified prefix to decide both whether to run a FULL forward and how far to advance unmasking, all without training or a tuned threshold. Methodology: LOWN keeps the anchor (top-1 predictions and softmax confidences on still-masked positions from the most recent FULL forward). Each step runs a TEXT-ONLY forward (visual tokens removed, position IDs preserved), orders masked positions by decreasing anchor confidence, and takes the longest prefix whose TEXT-ONLY prediction agrees with the anchor (with a repetition guard against adjacent identical tokens). If this certified prefix contains at least k tokens (the baseline's per-step unmasking count), the step skips the image and unmasks the whole prefix to anchor predictions; otherwise it runs a FULL forward, replaces the anchor, and unmasks k positions in disagreement-first order (positions where the two forwards differ first, then by FULL confidence). The state update is a two-branch rule (Equation 2); cost analysis gives relative FLOPs R = f + σρ, where f is the FULL-forward frequency, σ the relative step count, and ρ the TEXT-ONLY/FULL cost ratio. Critical design decisions: (1) agreement as a joint test of image-necessity and anchor validity, justified by measured 4.1–11.0% overturn rates for one-step-old anchors; (2) whole-prefix acceptance to unmask more than k tokens on image-free steps, justified against a uniform step-reduction ablation (Table 12) showing fewer steps degrades quality; (3) disagreement-first ordering on FULL steps, which lifts ChartQA and DeCapBench scores. All three are empirically ablated rather than merely asserted. Key Results: On LLaDA-V over ten benchmarks (MathVista, ScienceQA, ChartQA, MME, MMBench, DocVQA, CapArena, LLaVA-Bench, GQA, DeCapBench), LOWN retains 99.6% of the baseline score at 0.353× decoding FLOPs (98.6% when per-benchmark gains are capped at 100%). At matched FLOPs, it outscores RedVTP (93.0% normalized avg), ZOO-Prune (94.2%), and KLASS (91.9%) on eight of ten benchmarks. Composed with RedVTP at 50% retention, it scores 98.3 normalized at 0.223× FLOPs, beating all comparators on all ten benchmarks; it cuts partner pruner FLOPs by a further 57.6–60.6% and Fast-dLLM KV-cache time by 38.1–50.1% (combined 5.6–7.0× wall-clock speedup over the uncached baseline, at a 2.0-point quality cost vs. LLaDA-V and 5.0 points below Fast-dLLM on LLaVA-Bench). It transfers unchanged to LaViDa (99.7% at 0.174× FLOPs) and to VidLaDA-8B on video (EgoSchema 60.2 vs. 60.6 at 0.255× FLOPs; MLVU 43.3 vs. 41.8 at 0.272×). Wall-clock generation time falls 57.4% on average (up to 73.2%) across the ten LLaDA-V benchmarks on H200 GPUs. Baselines are current (CVPR/ICLR 2026 methods) and the matched-budget protocol gives every competitor at least LOWN's compute, which strengthens the comparison. Against a matched random image-access schedule, LOWN gains 4.9–13.0% in task-normalized quality. An oracle schedule that reads the image only when needed costs 0.33× vs. LOWN's 0.35×, indicating the adaptive rule is near-optimal for this family of heuristics. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (most DVLM decoding steps do not require image access, and image-dependent steps are input- and step-dependent) plus NEW METHOD (a training-free, threshold-free certificate-guided router that jointly decides image access and unmasking count). The certificate mechanism is a genuinely new control signal — agreement between a stale image-conditioned prediction and a text-only prediction — rather than a standard confidence threshold; it composes orthogonally with existing pruning and caching rather than replacing them. The overall framework (accelerated DVLM decoding via confidence-ordered unmasking, token pruning, approximate KV caching) is a known landscape; the routing axis is the new element. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: fixed-period and random image-access schedules (Table 4), decomposition into visual routing vs. disagreement-first ordering vs. whole-prefix acceptance (Tables 5, 14), certificate reliability by anchor age with per-benchmark overturn rates (Table 15), anchor-age distributions (Table 16), and an oracle-cost comparison. 95% confidence intervals accompany the trajectory measurements. Both FLOPs-matched and wall-clock-matched comparisons are reported, with competitor settings selected by compute, not by score — a protocol detail many papers omit. The paper honestly reports that the 99.6% average includes four benchmarks where LOWN beats the baseline (98.6% when capped) and that combined-with-cache scores fall below Fast-dLLM alone. Code and a project page are linked (https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/), though the repository itself was not verifiable from the text. Concerns: judging uses GPT-4o/GPT-3.5/Qwen3.5 for open-ended benchmarks (same judge for all methods, but LLM-judge noise is unquantified); the motivating measurement and the method's development use the same ten benchmarks it is evaluated on, so the adaptive rule could partially fit benchmark idiosyncrasies; single-seed greedy decoding with no variance estimates for task scores. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a decoding procedure run and measured on real models). Practical: Yes — runs on a single H200 GPU at batch size 1 with no model changes, using the released LLaDA-V/LaViDa/VidLaDA checkpoints. Efficient: 0.353× decoding FLOPs and 0.426× wall-clock standalone; the overhead is one TEXT-ONLY forward per step at 3–10% of a FULL forward. Effective: Evidence covers benchmark scores (multiple-choice, document/chart QA, captioning) plus qualitative examples, but not long-form generation quality under human evaluation or sampling-based decoding. Scalable: Untested beyond these backbones and task mix; cost is not knowable before decoding (acknowledged), and gains shrink on visually dense tasks (DocVQA worst case 0.90× on one sample), so workloads dominated by such tasks would see far less benefit. The work delivers a method with a linked project page and code claim; no trained model or dataset artifact is produced. Strengths: - The diagnostic measurement (paired FULL/TEXT-ONLY logging along baseline trajectories, per-benchmark with confidence intervals, replicated on LaViDa) is a genuine contribution in itself and directly motivates the design rather than decorating it. - The certificate is a clean, parameter-free control signal: it requires no training, no threshold tuning, and no benchmark-specific hyperparameters, in contrast to KLASS which uses per-benchmark thresholds — a real robustness advantage, not just convenience. - The matched-budget evaluation discipline (competitors get at least LOWN's FLOPs and wall-clock, selected by compute not score) and the oracle-cost comparison (0.33× vs. 0.35×) make the efficiency claim unusually hard to dispute. - Orthogonality is demonstrated, not claimed: composition with two pruners and a KV cache is measured, and the finding that mild pruning + routing beats aggressive pruning (MathVista 54.9 @ 0.195× vs. 51.7 @ 0.354×) is an actionable insight for practitioners. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) reused anchor tokens can differ from a fresh FULL prediction, with error growing with anchor age; (2) savings shrink on chart/document tasks where visual dependence persists; and (3) LOWN's cost cannot be predicted before decoding since the same agreement rule determines how many FULL forwards a response needs, partially mitigated by pairing with pruning for budget control. They confront limitations directly, including a worked worst-case example (a DocVQA sample at 0.90× baseline FLOPs) — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Evaluation covers only the LLaDA family (LLaDA-V, LaViDa, VidLaDA); whether the agreement statistics hold for MMaDA, Dimple, or future DVLM architectures with different vision encoders or token budgets is untested, and the 3–10% TEXT-ONLY cost ratio is specific to inputs where visual tokens dominate — models with smaller visual fractions would see the advantage shrink. - All quality results use greedy decoding at temperature zero and batch size 1; sampled decoding, classifier-free guidance > 0, and batched serving (where the extra TEXT-ONLY forward interacts differently with memory bandwidth) are unexamined, so the wall-clock claims may not transfer to production serving. - The router is developed and evaluated on the same ten benchmarks used to characterize image dependence — there is no held-out benchmark to rule out implicit fitting of the acceptance rule (prefix length, disagreement-first order) to these tasks' statistics. - The combined-with-cache configuration loses to Fast-dLLM alone on all three reported tasks (by 5.0 points on LLaVA-Bench); the paper reports this but does not analyze when the composition is preferable, leaving the practical recommendation ambiguous. - The certificate's top-1 agreement gives no formal or probabilistic guarantee on accepted tokens; a calibration analysis (e.g., bounding accepted-token error as a function of prefix length or confidence margin) is absent, and the repetition guard is a patch whose effect on quality is not isolated. - LLM-judged open-ended benchmarks (LLaVA-Bench, CapArena, DeCapBench with GPT-4o/Qwen3.5) carry judge variance that is not quantified with repeated judging or agreement statistics. Bottom Line: For anyone accelerating DVLM inference, this paper is worth reading: the empirical finding that most denoising steps need not see the image, plus a near-oracle-optimal training-free router validated with unusually fair matched-budget comparisons, makes it the current reference point for image-access scheduling in diffusion VLMs — though its confinement to the LLaDA family and greedy batch-size-1 decoding means autoregressive-VLM practitioners and production-serving teams should treat the numbers as promising rather than settled.

A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement (150 ▲ )

Yu Liu, Youxing Li, Yuedong Tan, Zhiwei Yang, Zihan Su, Hanqi Feng, Shaojie Zhang, Libin Liao, Zihao Wan, Chenxu Wu, Cong Cao, Fangfang Yuan, Yanbing Liu, Ziheng Chen, Pei Fu, Radu Timofte, Zongwei Wu, Nicu Sebe, Barnabas Poczos, Jian Luan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces A-RSI, a zero-data multimodal self-improvement loop in which a training-log-triggered detector decides when the current RL task pool is exhausted and replaces it with 400 fresh program-generated tasks whose reference answers are computed, not voted on. - Why it's important: Recursive self-improvement loops stall when they keep spending updates on spent data, and many reported gains partly reflect shorter completions rather than better reasoning — a failure mode this paper measures and exposes in a released baseline (MM-Zero v5). - How it does it: The controller counts prompts with nonzero within-group GRPO advantages (U_w) and logged training accuracy; when U_w drops below 85% of its value two windows earlier, or accuracy rises ≥10 points, the whole pool is swapped while model weights continue, with no access to validation or test scores. - The good: The evidence discipline is unusually strong: 1,000/1,000 independent answer recomputation agreement, Z3-checked specification properties, controlled reward stress tests, and a length-budget audit showing A-RSI retains 80% of its gain at doubled output budget versus 59% for MM-Zero v5. - The missing: Every policy arm was trained exactly once with no seed replication, and the detector-triggered timing was never shown better than a fixed three-window schedule — the paper itself concedes this. - Read it or not: Read it if you build self-improvement or RLVR training loops and need a principled, testable answer to "when is my training data spent?"; skip it if you want a new capability jump, since the net gain is +3.27 Macro11 points on an 8B model.

Problem & Motivation: Zero-data (RSI) self-improvement systems must generate their own training experience, and prior work (Absolute Zero, R-Zero, MM-Zero, Vision-Zero) concentrates on what experience to generate next — harder problems, competence-matched tasks, self-play. Two gaps remain. First, these systems lack a signal for when the current task pool has ceased to provide learning signal, so they either reuse a stalling pool or refresh blindly every step. Second, supervision is commonly derived from self-consistency or majority voting, so the model's own uncertain predictions become labels for its next update. The practitioners affected are anyone running RLVR-style post-training loops for multimodal reasoning models without external labeled data. Key Idea: Decouple the refresh decision from the label source: pool exhaustion is a training-dynamics question, answer correctness is a program-execution question. The core trick is to repurpose a batch-level GRPO detail — prompts whose sampled responses all receive equal rewards contribute zero advantage and no gradient — as a pool-level saturation statistic (U_w, the count of distinct prompts with nonzero advantage within a window), lagged two windows, as the sole trigger for wholesale pool replacement. Training never consults evaluation scores; answers come from the same sampled configuration used to render the image and compose the question. Methodology: Three phases. (1) Before training, the base model writes a fixed library of parameterized programs across four families (geometry, charts, tables, counting); each program samples parameters, renders an image, composes a question, and computes the reference answer from one shared configuration (Eq. 7), passing construction, freshness, and contamination checks into a 16,000-task reservoir; disjoint 400-task pools are pre-drawn under fixed family quotas (194/131/54/21). (2) During training, only a Solver policy is optimized with GRPO on reward r = r_ans + 0.1·r_fmt + 0.3·r_stop, where the stopping term penalizes truncation by −1; each window is 100 GRPO updates with 8 rollouts per prompt, 4,096-token rollout limit. (3) After each accepted window, the controller computes U_w and accuracy a_w from logs and fires a refresh when U_w ≤ 0.85·U_{w−2} or a_w − a_{w−2} ≥ 0.10, after a minimum of three within-pool windows (Eq. 4); the pool is swapped, weights carry forward, optimizer resets. Critical design decisions: (a) including auxiliary-reward variation in U_w — the second refresh in the recorded run would not fire on correctness-only variation, a dependency the authors disclose via reward-component replay but do not justify as necessary; (b) random replacement selection — well-justified empirically (all tested difficulty/rollout-based selectors lose to random by 0.05–2.63 points); (c) a health gate accepting only windows with ≥97/100 normal gradient steps — pre-registered and demonstrably binding (No-Refresh halts at window 7). Key Results: On an eleven-benchmark suite (22,042 questions: MMSI, MathVerse, MathVision, MMMU-Pro variants, MMMU, ChartQA, VisNumBench, PhyX-MC, SCEMQA-MC) at an 8,192-token limit: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct improves from 57.77 (St) to 61.05 Macro11 after eight continuation windows using 800 fresh tasks; MiMo-VL-7B-SFT improves 59.08 → 60.71. Matched-update comparisons at window 6: A-RSI 60.40 vs 58.35 for continued reuse (+2.05). At window 8, Continuous (refresh every window, 3,200 tasks) scores 60.64, Periodic 59.89, Frontier 59.59; No-Refresh halts at S31 after failing its health gate. All difficulty-aware selection variants trail random controls (−0.48 to −2.63). Baselines include released MM-Zero v5 weights (57.37 at 8,192 tokens), which the authors reproduce and show lose 41% of their gain when the output budget doubles, versus 19% for A-RSI. The detector fires consistently at three windows on both models (retention ratios .62–.84). Scale is standard (7–8B models, ~1,600 training tasks consumed) — toy-to-standard, not stress-scale. Notably, an adversarial check found the production answer checker fails 220/16,000 adversarial variants (ambiguous gold-prefixed answers), though only one logged response was affected. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (training-log-triggered pool refresh, repurposing GRPO zero-advantage groups as a saturation diagnostic) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (random task replacement beats difficulty-frontier, bandit, and rollout-based selection in this setting; many zero-data gains are substantially termination effects). The underlying components — GRPO, programmatic task generation, verifiable rewards — are standard; the genuinely novel element is the WHEN question (pool-refresh timing from logs alone) as an explicitly isolated control problem, and the machine-checked refresh specification. The finding that self-assessed difficulty has AUC ≈ 0.50 (models are blind to their own state) is a useful supporting observation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Exceptional verification depth for the data pipeline: 1,000/1,000 independent answer recomputation agreement on audited tasks, byte-for-byte image reproduction for 800/1,000 tasks (200 referring-chart images unresolved due to font differences), 4,000/4,000 injected-defect detection, Z3 proofs of four specification properties, 321,605 threshold conformance cases for the detector, and access guards with logged zero test-set access. However, rigor has a soft spot the authors name plainly: every policy arm is a single training run, no seeds are replicated, and the paper reports observed run-to-run spread (1.25-point range across identical-data runs at 4,096 tokens) without confidence intervals on headline differences — several margins (+0.40, +0.70) are within this noise. Component ablations for the detector itself (e.g., accuracy condition vs U_w condition) are log-replays, not trained ablations; the accuracy condition never fires alone in the recorded runs. Code, data, or model weights release is not stated in the provided text. The most serious methodological concern: task-family quotas and chart/table vocabulary were fixed using evaluation-benchmark metadata (disclosed in Appendix Q.2), a benchmark-informed design leak the controller itself does not commit; and two initial-pool questions were found to be isomorphs of MathVerse items. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs the full training loop and evaluates it). - Practical: Yes — 7–8B open-weight VLMs (Qwen3-VL-8B, MiMo-VL-7B) trained with FSDP2 and colocated vLLM, feasible on standard multi-GPU setups; no frontier-model dependence. - Efficient: Attractive on data — 800 fresh tasks for the full gain (4.09 points per 1,000 tasks vs 0.90 for every-window refresh), though total RL compute is unchanged (all arms use matched updates). - Effective: Partially — the +2.05 gain over continued reuse at matched updates is real in-run and survives format-corrected scoring (+3.27 vs +3.33), and 80% of gain persists at doubled output budget; but the completion-stratum decomposition shows Qwen's aggregate both-finished contribution is negative (−0.71), so much of the measured gain sits outside verified non-truncated correction. - Scalable: Untested beyond 8 windows, a 16,000-task reservoir, and 4 task families; the reservoir budget (800 of 14,482 eligible tasks consumed) and the halt-on-exhaustion rule both imply the loop as specified will terminate, and the authors flag that no refresh policy exists for low-entropy models. Deliverable: currently paper form — no released library, weights, or dataset is stated. Strengths: - Genuinely reframes a neglected control variable: refresh timing as a separate decision from task selection, with a concrete, implementable, log-only trigger — the SMT-checked specification makes the controller reproducible and auditable in a way almost no RL training loop paper attempts. - The length-budget audit is a substantive negative result for the field: a four-route demonstration that a published MM-Zero gain is largely termination behavior (untrained base at 16,384 tokens ≈ trained MM-Zero at 4,096; paired test finds no training contribution beyond budget, p = 0.138/0.434), plus a practical reporting recommendation (base model at relaxed limit, truncation rates, gains at ≥2 budgets). - Honest negative results on its own design choices: all difficulty-aware selection rules lose to random, the detector's timing shows no advantage over a fixed schedule, and the paper's Appendix M table explicitly separates supported from unsupported claims. - The saturation signal is validated across two backbones with model-divergent behavior (MiMo keeps its third pool while Qwen refreshes), demonstrating the controller adapts through observed state rather than schedule. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually direct (Appendix U, Section 9, Appendix M): single training run per arm with no replicated uncertainty; the detector's timing advantage is unestablished because realized refreshes coincide with a three-window schedule and no fixed-schedule random control was trained; the second refresh depends on including auxiliary-reward variation in the signal; "saturation" is operational, not proof of mastery (a zero-accuracy zero-signal model also fires); the pre-registered primary endpoint (Frontier − No-Refresh) became unreadable when No-Refresh halted; A-RSI's +0.79 margin over MM-Zero is within training noise; task mix and vocabulary were informed by benchmark metadata; 16k evaluation of the main run is pending. This level of self-confrontation is a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The refresh rule itself is never ablated in training: the comparison confounds timing, selection, and pool size (500 → 400 tasks) simultaneously, and with detector-triggered timing held fixed, periodic refresh beats it by 0.30 — so the headline A-RSI number could be driven by random selection alone with any reasonable schedule. - The accuracy-increase condition (η = 0.10) is carried through every experiment but demonstrably never fires alone in any recorded run; it is dead specification weight presented as a co-equal trigger, and its interaction with dynamic resampling is unexamined. - External validity is narrow: four task families with quotas tuned to the evaluation suite's visual-type distribution, and gains concentrate in geometry/counting/truncation-heavy benchmarks (PhyX +8.33) — transfer to non-templated visual reasoning is untested. - The zero-data claim has soft edges: 342 of 500 initial-pool questions use model-rewritten wording via an API-served model, and the family mix follows benchmark statistics — a strict reading makes this "no external labeled data," not "no benchmark-informed design." - Missing standard baseline: a simple fixed three-window random-refresh arm was never trained, despite the authors identifying it as the decisive control. - Reward-removal ablations for the termination term (which demonstrably drives early-window gains of +1.22) are pending, not completed. Bottom Line: A practitioner running zero-data RL loops gains real, actionable machinery here — a log-only saturation trigger, a template for verifying self-generated supervision, and a sobering audit method for termination-inflated gains — and should read it despite the modest +3.27 headline, because the methodological contributions outvalue the result and no alternative paper covers the timing question with this rigor.

Connecting Quantum Proof Systems and Hoare Logic

L Li, ZD Tagba, A Potanin · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an intermediate Hoare-logic language with array theory (HLIR) and proves that the Qafny quantum proof system translates into classical Hoare logic completely (every Qafny proof becomes a valid Hoare triple) and soundly (a valid translated triple certifies only true quantum specifications), with the completeness direction mechanized in Rocq. - Why it's important: Quantum programs cannot be validated by runtime testing, yet verifying them today requires bespoke proof systems on interactive theorem provers at substantial human cost; this result means classical automated verifiers (Dafny, SMT-based separation logic) can in principle discharge quantum proof obligations, and it supplies the correctness argument that the existing Qafny-to-Dafny compilation (Qafnyc, 37 verified programs) has lacked. - How it does it: It represents an EN(n)-typed quantum state (a linear sum of basis-kets) as an n-dimensional array of records (amplitude, bit-vector), factors every quantum operation (oracles, H/QFT, quantum conditionals, measurement) into a fixed set of classical array-aggregate primitives (mapN, filterN, locateN, assignN, copyN, enumN, ampN, sqrtSum, upDim, concat), and proves that Qafny's tensor-based separation conjunctions are pure, i.e., replaceable by ordinary conjunction once locus disjointness is type-tracked. - The good: Translation completeness is mechanized in Rocq, and a translation-size theorem bounds the output to at most eleven HLIR statements per Qafny statement with polynomial-size conditions in the symbolic array representation, showing the compilation is effective rather than merely existential. - The missing: Translation soundness (the direction that makes a classical verdict trustworthy) is proved only on paper, the Quantum Hoare Logic translation is illustrated by examples only, and no end-to-end artifact connects HLIR to a concrete verifier or measures how real SMT solvers handle the generated conditions. - Read it or not: Worth reading for programming-languages and formal-verification researchers working on quantum proof systems or proof-system embeddings; skippable for practitioners who need a working automated quantum verifier today, since the pipeline stops at the idealized IR.

Problem & Motivation: Verifying quantum programs is currently expensive: existing frameworks (Qafny, QBricks, Quantum Hoare Logic, quantum separation logic) are specialized proof systems built on interactive theorem provers such as Rocq, Lean, Isabelle, or Why3, and even modest quantum algorithms demand substantial manual proof effort. Because exponential state spaces and probabilistic measurement make runtime testing essentially useless for quantum software, formal verification is the only viable correctness path, so the cost of bespoke proof infrastructure is the chief barrier to scalable quantum software assurance. Prior classical tools (Dafny, SMT-based separation logic) have mature automation, and Qafnyc already compiles Qafny verification conditions into Dafny, but that compilation ships with no correctness argument — nothing guarantees a Dafny verdict says anything true about the quantum program. The paper closes this gap by showing that quantum verification reduces, with provable guarantees in both directions, to classical Hoare-logic verification of array programs. Key Idea: The core insight is a state-encoding trick plus a purity observation: (1) an EN(n)-typed quantum state — a syntactic linear sum with n summation operators over basis-kets — is faithfully representable as an n-dimensional classical array whose elements are records {amplitude, bit-vector}, with an index map ind_φ locating each qubit range's bits inside each basis vector; (2) under this encoding, each quantum operation's semantics factors into compositions of classical higher-order array operations (map, filter, zip-assign, enumerate, concatenate), so each Qafny proof rule becomes an explicit Hoare-logic proof-tree skeleton; and (3) tensor-based separation conjunctions in Qafny/QHL-style systems are "pure" — equivalent to ordinary conjunction — because loci of a state are disjoint by construction and there are no qubit reference types to alias, eliminating the need for separation logic on the classical side. Together these make quantum proof obligations deterministic and dischargeable by off-the-shelf classical verifiers. Methodology: The paper defines HLIR, an imperative language whose statements are array-aggregate operations, each proved valid against Hoare logic with array theory via nested while-loop proof trees (Lemma 2.1, the pointwise-update lemma, reduces each aggregate to a single substitution). The translation has two judgments: program translation σ ⊢ μ ⊲ σ′ ≫ e (guided by Qafny's type system, which tracks the EN(k) rank of each locus) and assertion translation σ ⊢ φ ≫ P. Operation classes: (1) superposition-creating gates (H, QFT) translate to copyN/enumN/ampN, adding one array dimension; (2) basis-mapping operations (X, RZ, oracles ι) translate to locateN/mapN/assignN; (3) quantum conditionals split the array with filterN, translate the body, and reassemble with upDim/concat; (4) measurement filters matching basis-kets and renormalizes amplitudes by sqrtSum, binding outcome and probability as ordinary classical variables so feed-forward control translates to classical control. The main theorems are translation completeness (Thm 7.13: every derivable Qafny triple yields a valid Hoare triple; mechanized in Rocq), translation soundness (Thm 7.14: a valid translated triple yields a Qafny derivation with semantically equivalent conditions, proved by induction on Qafny typing on paper), and translation size (Thm 7.15: ≤11 HLIR statements per Qafny statement, polynomial-size conditions). Critical design decisions: the pureness theorem (justified by Qafny's type-enforced locus disjointness and absence of aliasing — reasonable but a genuine restriction relative to reference-semantics languages); the symbolic array representation, which bounds translation size but pushes the exponential state space into assertion complexity rather than eliminating it (the authors are explicit that the bound concerns condition size, not solver time); and the choice to prove soundness only on paper, which is the weaker link. Key Results: The results are theorems, not benchmarks. Translation completeness is mechanized in Rocq for all covered Qafny operations (oracle, H/QFT, quantum conditional, measurement, sequencing, for-loops). The size bound is concrete: at most 11 HLIR statements per Qafny statement (4 for an oracle or H application, 11 for a conditional, 7 for measurement), with polynomial-size assertions in |φ| + n where n is the maximum EN(k) rank. The pureness theorem (Thms 5.2, 5.3) is stated and proved for both QHL and Qafny and claimed general for tensor-based separation conjunctions in other systems (Le et al. 2022; Zhou et al. 2021). The approach is illustrated on the Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm and GHZ/Bell-pair state preparation. There is no empirical evaluation: no end-to-end verified program, no solver timing, no comparison of proof effort against the original Qafny system. The QHL (CQHL) translation is by example only, routed through Qafny, with the full QHL translation explicitly deferred to future work. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (meta-theoretic): the genuinely novel contributions are the translation-completeness/soundness pair for a quantum-to-classical proof-system embedding (distinct from compiler correctness of proof-system-to-semantics arrows) and the purity result for tensor-based quantum separation conjunctions. The array encoding of basis-ket sums and the individual HLIR primitives (map, filter, concat) are standard functional/aggregation constructs applied in a new setting; the reduction to classical automation is enabled by the purity observation and the index-map treatment of locus reordering, which is the non-obvious step. This sits on top of the authors' own prior Qafny (ECOOP 2024) and Qafnyc (OOPSLA2 2025) work, supplying that pipeline's missing foundation rather than a new verifier. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations in the empirical sense do not apply; structurally, each translation component (oracle, H/QFT, conditional, measurement) has a standalone validity lemma, and the completeness proof is mechanized in Rocq, which is the strongest rigor signal. Translation soundness is not mechanized — proved only on paper by a comparatively short induction — so the trust-critical direction rests on unaudited prose. The paper is explicit about the scope of its size theorem (condition size, not solver time), which is honest but also where the practical question lives. No code repository, artifact, or mechanization URL is mentioned. A hidden assumption is flagged by the authors themselves: Lemma 6.1 requires a finite global universe of qubits (Disjointness Preservation / Quantum State Shrinking), valid in Qafny's no-reference-type setting but a real restriction elsewhere. Evaluation-on-own-benchmark concerns do not arise since there is no benchmark; the main methodological concern is that the practical payoff (automated discharge of generated conditions) is asserted, not demonstrated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (theorems with partial Rocq mechanization; no primary experimental claim and no built tool evaluated by deployment). - Sound: Translation completeness is mechanized in Rocq for the covered fragment; translation soundness is paper-only, and both rely on the prior, separately claimed semantic soundness of Qafny, so the end-to-end soundness story chains one unmechanized link. - General: The result holds for Qafny's fragment (H, QFT, oracles, quantum conditionals, measurement, loops) under type-tracked locus disjointness, no qubit references, and a finite global qubit universe; the QHL extension is illustrative, and richer types (oracle/Hadamard variants) are explicitly future work. - Tight: Not a bounds paper in the approximation sense; the size theorem (≤11 statements per statement, polynomial conditions) is a concrete, arguably near-minimal constant per operation class, though it is silent on solver-time blowup, where vacuity could still bite. - Implementable: The embedding is constructive — every rule maps to an explicit HLIR derivation and proof-tree skeleton — and Qafnyc demonstrates the Dafny-side viability empirically, but this paper itself releases no artifact and connects to no concrete back-end. The work delivers a reusable proof technique and (partially) a mechanized theory; it stops at paper-plus-mechanization form, with no library, CLI, dataset, or trained artifact. Strengths: - The translation-completeness/soundness framing as properties of the translation itself (compiler-correctness style, left of their Figure 1) is a genuine methodological contribution: it sidesteps the failure mode the authors identify, where relative completeness of Hoare logic cannot be pushed backward through predicate transformation without exponential state listing. - The pureness theorem is a crisp, transferable insight: once qubit disjointness is tracked typewise (as Qafny does), tensor separation conjunctions in quantum proof systems collapse to ordinary conjunctions — this is what makes a separation-logic-free classical target possible, and it applies beyond Qafny. - The completeness direction is mechanized in Rocq, and the size theorem quantifies the compilation (≤11 statements per statement, polynomial conditions), so the reduction is effective and auditable rather than merely existential. - The measurement translation (filter-and-renormalize, with outcome and probability bound as ordinary classical variables so feed-forward/teleportation-style control becomes classical control) is a clean solution to what is usually the awkward case in embedding quantum logic classically. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state clearly that the result shows quantum verification is no harder than classical verification, not that it is easy — statistically driven programs such as quantum machine learning remain hard, though they note classical ML verification is comparably hard. They confine the full QHL translation to future work (only examples and an appendix sketch are given), list richer quantum types (oracle and Hadamard variants) and connection to a concrete automated back-end as future work, and explicitly scope the size theorem to symbolic condition size rather than verifier time. They also flag the finite-global-qubit-universe assumption behind the disjointness lemma and note that in a reference-semantics language the disjointness would need separate discharge. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' stated limitations, a reviewer would flag: (1) no measurement of whether real SMT/Dafny solvers can actually discharge the generated verification conditions — the symbolic representation hides but does not remove exponential-size quantified assertions, and the entire practical motivation ("no quantum-specific infrastructure needed") rests on this untested step; (2) translation soundness, the direction that makes classical verdicts trustworthy, is the unmechanized one, which inverts the ideal prioritization; (3) the proof that Qafny's semantic soundness composes with the translation to give end-to-end program correctness is asserted via Proposition 3.2's narrative rather than stated as a single end-to-end theorem with a machine-checked chain; (4) no data on whether the embedding actually reduces human proof effort relative to native Qafny — the motivating pain point — since the translated proof skeletons are fixed but the remaining SMT obligations' difficulty is unknown; (5) the generality claim over other tensor-based systems (QSL, Le et al.) is stated as a remark with proofs given only for QHL and Qafny. None of these undermine the core theorems, but they leave the practical claim at the level of a plausible research program. Bottom Line: For verification researchers, this is a solid and genuinely useful meta-theorem that finally gives the Qafny-to-Dafny pipeline a correctness foundation and a transferable purity insight, but practitioners seeking an actual automated quantum verifier will not find one here — the hard last mile (solver behavior on the generated conditions, soundness mechanization, full QHL coverage) is exactly what remains open.

InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants (113 ▲ )

Qinsi Wang, Wei Wen, Chong Zhou, Saksham Suri, Zechun Liu, Lemeng Wu, Hai Helen Li, Yiran Chen, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi, Qi Qian · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds InteractiveWorld, a human-centric simulation environment on Isaac Sim (8,000+ objects, 50+ scenes) in which an evaluated MLLM assistant guides an autonomous, LLM-driven human agent through natural language, and introduces InteractiveBench, a 120-task closed-loop benchmark with state-verifiable scoring for egocentric assistants. - Why it's important: Existing egocentric assistant benchmarks are open-loop (the model's output never changes the video), so nobody can measure whether an assistant's advice actually helps a person complete a physical task — the core question for wearable AI assistants. - How it does it: The key move is role inversion: unlike robot-centric simulators where the AI is the actor, here the AI only speaks while an MLLM-driven human grounds free-form guidance into 36 executable action primitives, and success is checked against final simulator object states (with pre-satisfied predicates baseline-excluded). - The good: The validation pipeline is unusually rigorous — an Oracle Assistant scores 100% pass and zero assistance scores 0% with the same human agent, and each task passes silent/wrong/early-responder causal controls before models are run. - The missing: All evaluation uses an LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro) as the simulated human, so results conflate assistant quality with human-executor quirks; no real-user validation details are in the provided text, no error bars or significance tests are reported, and there is no evidence yet that the environment improves models (only a mixed-result memory-augmentation probe). - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate egocentric/wearable AI assistants and need a closed-loop, verifiable testbed; skip it if you only need another static egocentric video-QA benchmark, of which there are already many.
