Problem & Motivation: Teams running ML workloads face rising GPU costs, constrained accelerator capacity, and vendor dependence, making migration to TPUs attractive — but the dominant cost of such moves is engineering effort (patching, tuning, operating), not hardware. Coding agents promise to cut that effort, yet prior repository-level migration work validates success via compilation and test suites, which rarely exist for ML research code (only 7 of the 148 collected repositories had author-written tests). Worse, agent-reported success is documented to be unreliable, and legitimate cross-accelerator floating-point differences make numerical comparison non-trivial. The open question the paper targets: what evidence is sufficient to accept an agent-generated hardware migration, and at what total cost? Key Idea: The key insight is that accelerator migration correctness is a multi-dimensional property that successful execution cannot establish — so the paper operationalizes it as an ordered L0–L4 assessment hierarchy, separates agent predictions (before attempts) from agent claims (after runs) from independently measured levels, and anchors every judgment to a GPU reference run rather than a fixed numerical tolerance, since no universal threshold separates floating-point noise from defects. Methodology: The study has four phases. (1) Project selection: LLM-assisted search collected 148 PyTorch repositories (peer-reviewed 2022–2026 papers modifying/fine-tuning foundation models, single-16-GB-chip experiments), screened by a regex-based challenge label and feasibility penalty, from which ten were sampled stratified by area/challenge with a fixed seed and manually verified. (2) Agent setup: each migration uses a fresh Claude Code session given the paper, repo, and protocol; the agent selects one sub-experiment tied to the paper's key claim, runs GPU reference executions (200-step smoke test + full run, fixed seed), then iterates TPU attempts (attempt 0 = unmodified code) recorded as pull requests and failure issues, with fail-fast gates (10 attempts / 3 hours; smoke-test thresholds of 5% loss / 1% metric divergence; 5-hour runtime estimate). (3) Level checks: L0–L2/L4 are categorical; L1 is reported as a measurement, not a verdict; L3 compares against the paper's claim or, if the GPU run itself misses the claim, against the GPU run. (4) Manual analysis: the first author assigns failure root causes (seven non-exclusive categories, C1–C7) from errors, agent diagnoses, and fixes; costs use on-demand list prices. Two case studies extend the main protocol: single- vs. four-chip TPU LoRA+ migration, and PyTorch/XLA vs. TorchTPU backends on the same v5e-1 chip. Critical design decisions: independent verification rather than agent self-report (well justified by prior false-success literature), L1 as measurement rather than verdict (well justified given no universal tolerance exists), and single-seed full runs (acknowledged but a real weakness). Key Results: Of ten projects, 8 reach L3 (goal preservation), 3 of those also L4 (faster and cheaper than GPU), 1 stops at L2 (CoFi: TPU run selected a smaller pruned model), and 1 fails L0 within the attempt budget (BiLLM). Migrations needed a median 6.5 attempts (range 3–11) and 2.4 human interventions on average; median code churn was 7.5 files, +131.5/−18.5 lines. Of 70 execution attempts, 53 (76%) failed, and 26 of those (49%) raised no error; lazy-tensor execution (repeated recompilation, host synchronization) was the top cause (13 failures across 7 projects, all silent). Median GPU–TPU metric difference was 0.43% (range 0.01%–3.43%). Agent token costs were $2.00–$22.55 (median $9.74), but per-run TPU costs ranged 0.47–3.6× GPU, and 5 of 9 completed TPU runs cost more than GPU. Case studies: on four chips, LoRA+ silently lost 1.64 points (86.53%→84.89%, below the published plain-LoRA baseline of 85.6%) because accelerate 0.27.2 clips gradients per-chip before averaging, while the single-chip run matched the GPU (86.54%); with TorchTPU, GPT-2 LoRA+ trained 1.86× faster (1.98 h vs. 3.68 h GPU) and 25% cheaper ($2.37 vs. $3.14) with 88% vs. 11% chip duty cycle, though MNLI-matched accuracy came in 0.16 points below the GPU and narrowly missed L3. The agent over-predicted 40/57 attempts (70%) but its final claims never exceeded measured levels in the nine completed main-protocol projects; the only false success came in the four-chip case study, which omitted the pre-run smoke-test gate. Six of seven smoke-test stops were false alarms. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with a reusable NEW FORMULATION (the L0–L4 consistency hierarchy for hardware migration). The genuinely novel parts are the documented silent-failure taxonomy for cross-hardware ML migration (especially the per-chip gradient-clipping distributed-semantics failure and the 49% silent-failure rate) and the systematic separation of agent-claimed from independently verified outcomes in this setting. The individual techniques — Claude Code, PyTorch/XLA, smoke-test gates — are standard tools applied to a setting (agent-driven GPU-to-TPU repository migration with behavioral verification) that has not previously been studied at this level. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations in the classic sense are absent, but the design contains a meaningful internal contrast: the four-chip case study dropped the smoke-test gate and produced the study's only false success, isolating that gate's value. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported — single-seed full runs throughout, which the authors explicitly flag by demoting L1 to a measurement. Baselines are appropriate (original code on NVIDIA L4 GPU, published paper values as references); there is no competing agent, so no cross-agent comparison. A Zenodo replication package (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23599327) releases the 148-project screening data, prompts, all migration repositories, agent trajectories, and per-judgment evidence — unusually strong for reproducibility. Methodological concerns: n=10 makes results descriptive only; the regex challenge labels matched observed failure causes in only 3/8 projects, so the stratification variable has weak predictive validity; the agent reads the level definitions before migrating, which may inflate its diligence; and cost comparisons use list prices with one run each. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (an empirical study, not a shipped system). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on commodity cloud hardware (one NVIDIA L4, TPU v5e chips) and off-the-shelf Claude Code at list-price token costs of $2–$23 per migration. - Efficient: Agent token cost is modest, but the total cost picture is mixed: median migration time 1.88 hours, 2.4 human interventions, and TPU per-run costs of 0.47–3.6× GPU mean the economics are workload-specific, which is precisely the paper's point. - Effective: The evidence shows execution-based verification catches silent behavioral drift that agent self-reports miss, but with single runs per configuration the effectiveness of the acceptance criteria themselves (e.g., L3 thresholds) is demonstrated only on these ten workloads. - Scalable: Not tested — all workloads fit one 16 GB chip; larger models, multi-chip production targets, and other accelerators are explicitly left open, so the 7/9 sub-25%-utilization finding may not transfer. The paper delivers a paper plus a substantial reusable artifact: the Zenodo replication package with screening data, protocols, and full migration traces; it stops short of a migration/verification tool, which the authors list as future work. Strengths: - The four-chip gradient-clipping case study is a genuinely valuable finding: it identifies a concrete, plausible, and previously under-appreciated failure class (distributed training semantics changed by pinned dependency versions) that survives exit-code-0 execution and fools the agent's own diagnosis. - The three-way separation of predicted level, claimed level, and measured level is a clean methodological device that turns vague "agents overclaim" folklore into quantified evidence (70% prediction optimism vs. accurate final claims in-gate, one false success out-of-gate). - Honest cost accounting: the paper refuses to declare TPU migration economically favorable, reporting that TPU/GPU per-run costs span 0.47–3.6× and that six of seven automated smoke-test stops were false alarms — a nuanced result rather than a sales pitch. - The 49% silent-failure rate, with lazy-tensor recompilation as the leading error-free cause, is actionable for tool builders in a way that typical agent benchmarks (pass/fail on tests) are not. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The threats-to-validity section is direct and thorough: single agent (Claude Code / Opus 5.5), single target (one TPU v5e chip, mostly PyTorch/XLA), PyTorch only, ten research projects fitting one chip, single seed per run, no statistical generalization, nondeterministic agent behavior, the agent reading level definitions (potential diligence inflation), experimenter decisions influencing outcomes, dependency upgrades conflated with migration effects, LLM-assisted search possibly missing eligible projects, exclusion of widely-adopted projects possibly biasing difficulty, and a fast-moving software stack (TorchTPU released after study design was fixed) that may already invalidate some observed failures. The authors confront limitations squarely rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No comparison agent or model is run, so none of the findings (false-success rate, diagnosis quality, stopping behavior) can be attributed to coding agents generally versus Claude Code specifically — a single-agent n=1 study of agent behavior is itself a small sample. - All full runs are single-seed, yet several headline judgments (the TorchTPU 0.16-point L3 miss, L1 differences below 1%, the CoFi borderline outcome) sit within or near plausible run-to-run variation; the authors note this for L1 but still make categorical L3/L4 verdicts on single runs. - The L3 relaxation (judging against the GPU run when the original code misses the paper) lets three projects count as successes despite failing to reproduce published claims — a defensible design but one that inflates the "8/10 reach L3" headline; a stricter reading yields 5/10 reproducing published claims. - The four-chip case study's omission of the smoke-test gate is presented as revealing the gate's value, but it also means the study's most dramatic finding (the false success) comes from a protocol variant the authors themselves weakened, and it is generalizable only as an illustration, not a rate. - Root-cause labels come from a single analyst (the first author) without inter-rater agreement checks, and the paper's own threat section concedes another analyst might classify some failures differently. - Human interventions are counted and averaged but not decomposed in cost terms, so the true marginal cost of oversight versus a (hypothetical) non-agentic manual migration baseline is never established — there is no manual-migration control. Bottom Line: For ML-platform engineers and agent-tool builders, this is the most concrete published evidence I know of that agent-driven accelerator migration requires execution-grounded, configuration-specific verification — the silent distributed-gradient-clipping failure and the 49% silent-failure rate alone justify the read — despite the single-agent, single-seed, ten-project scope limiting its conclusions to descriptive, illustrative findings rather than generalizable rates.

BELIEFMEM: Belief-Revising Memory for Conversational LLM Agents

F Meng, J Wu, J McAuley · aclanthology.org · Julian McAuley - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BELIEFMEM, a conversational memory system that operationalizes AGM belief revision (in Hansson's belief-base form) as the write semantics of a history-preserving fact store, replacing append-or-replace heuristics with four LLM-classified actions (EXP/REV/DUP/CON). - Why it's important: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate contradictory, retracted, and stale user beliefs under additive memory designs, degrading answer quality over time; a principled revision discipline directly targets this compounding failure mode. - How it does it: A single LLM call jointly extracts claims and classifies each into EXP/REV/DUP/CON against an active-memory window, with a second similarity-graph resolver across sessions; superseded/retracted facts are never deleted but get predecessor pointers, and a query-time selector chooses between surfacing the belief head, the full lineage chain, or nothing. - The good: The contradiction-resolution gain on BEAM–100K is decisive — 56.2% vs. LIGHT's published 1.8–3.7% across four backbones — and the paper is unusually candid about variance (five-run distributions), cross-backbone caveats, and ablations showing inline revision alone carries the gains. - The missing: The headline BEAM number (54.5%) is the maximum of five runs (mean 52.94 ± 0.65), BEAM baselines are quoted from other papers using different LLM backbones, and answer prompts are tuned per benchmark, leaving backbone-matched same-prompt comparisons incomplete. - Read it or not: Read it if you build persistent-memory or agent-memory systems and want a principled write-time semantics plus an honest ablation story; skip it if you only want AGM theory — the formalism is borrowed, lightly violated, and not proven (Appendix B explicitly documents which postulates are approximated or broken).
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is the strength — mapping AGM/Hansson belief revision onto write-time memory semantics is a genuine new formulation with no precedent per the paper's own survey, and the reframing of the binary supersede-or-keep decision as the root failure mode is non-obvious (72). Completeness (80) is high: the per-postulate fidelity table, per-component ablations showing secondary components add ~nothing, and categorized failure analysis are unusually candid. Rigor (68) is pulled down by max-of-five-runs headline reporting on BEAM, cross-backbone quoted baselines, and per-benchmark tuned answer prompts absent from baselines. Resilience (68) suffers because the +21.8 BEAM margin leans on non-causal cross-backbone comparisons, and no verifiable artifact is provided (Impact 60). Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*60 = 71.

Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon conversational LLM agents (assistants, copilots, support bots) persist user state across sessions. Existing structured memory systems (Mem0, MemGPT, Zep, A-MEM) reduce every fact relationship to a binary write-time decision — supersede or keep both — producing three compounding failures: contradictions coexist with equal status, scope-narrowing updates destroy information, and retractions never propagate. The authors reframe this as a belief-revision problem: conversation is a stream of corrections, retractions, and refinements, not an append-only log. The intended audience is memory-system designers and, aspirationally, the formal belief-revision community, which has not previously intersected LLM conversational memory. Key Idea: Map AGM's three operators (expansion, revision, contraction) plus a duplicate/no-op case onto write-time classification of atomic claims over a Hansson belief base — an explicit fact list (no deductive closure, Recovery postulate rejected) where revision and contraction are realized as status transitions (ACTIVE/SUPERSEDED/RETRACTED) and immutable predecessor pointers rather than deletion, so the full revision lineage stays queryable. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Per-round resolver R_inline: a single LLM call jointly extracts atomic claims from a dialogue batch and classifies each against a window of active beliefs, emitting actions plus contraction targets; contractions are processed before revisions to enforce a single-target invariant (each belief is targeted at most once per round), keeping the lineage a forest (Algorithm 3). Three semantic disciplines govern it: atomic-claim decomposition with a fixed precedence (enrichment→EXP, entailment→DUP, strict subsumption→REV, scope-narrowing→EXP), an event–state distinction (past events are never contracted by present-tense state changes), and the single-target invariant. (2) Cross-session resolver R_cluster: at session close, a bidirectional-max cosine similarity graph (mxbai-embed-large-v1, τ = 0.6–0.7) over new facts plus top-k neighbors is partitioned into connected components; an LLM labels groups REV/DUP/KEEP using episode, event-date, and recording-time metadata, and REV groups emit time-ordered revision chains (Algorithm 4). (3) Query-time retrieval: vector search over the ACTIVE subset, cross-encoder reranking, lineage attachment (depth cap 5), then a context-selection LLM S emits per-fact {head, chain, drop} decisions. Storage is PostgreSQL + pgvector. The framework is explicitly AGM/Hansson rather than a formal guarantee: Appendix B honestly labels Closure and Consistency as approximated, Inclusion as principally violated (deliberately, for lineage preservation), and Recovery as unimplemented. Critical design decisions: folding revision into the extraction call (makes revision nearly free in LLM calls — well-justified by the ablation showing R_inline is the dominant contributor); never-delete lineage (justified by auditability, but ablations show chain rendering hurts several axes); and a chain-forward default selector policy the authors themselves flag as suboptimal. Key Results: On LoCoMo (1,540 questions, 10 conversations, LLM-judge protocol), BELIEFMEM scores 85.5% with gpt-4o-mini (+17.1 over Mem0-graph's 68.4%, backbone-matched) and 92.3% with gpt-5.4-mini; a backbone-matched turn-chunked Raw-RAG control scores 74.5%, so the mechanism gain is +17.8. Per-category, the largest gain is multi-hop (+33.8 over Mem0-graph, 81.0%). On BEAM–100K (400 questions, 20 conversations), BELIEFMEM scores 54.5% with gpt-5.4-mini vs. LIGHT's four-LLM mean of 32.7% (+21.8; +18.7 over LIGHT's best single cell of 35.8%), with contradiction-resolution at 56.2% vs. LIGHT's 1.8–3.7%. Knowledge-update (38.8%) is only within LIGHT's 30.0–45.0% range. Ablations on BEAM at gpt-4o-mini show R_inline alone scores 49.9% (vs. 50.3% for the full gpt-4o-mini system): cluster consolidation adds +9.6 on information extraction but −3.4 on preference-following, and lineage rendering adds +4.4 on contradiction-resolution but −10.3 on multi-session reasoning. Five-run variance: 91.91 ± 0.21 (LoCoMo), 52.94 ± 0.65 (BEAM), with the BEAM headline being the maximum run. Baselines on LoCoMo are quoted from the Mem0 paper (7 systems, GPT-4o-mini); BEAM baselines are quoted from the BEAM paper — different backbones in both cases. Notably, BELIEFMEM beats the full-context upper bound (72.9% on LoCoMo), which is a strong but surprising result given memory compression usually loses to full context. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW FORMULATION — applying AGM belief revision to LLM conversational memory write semantics is, per the paper's own related-work survey, without precedent (a concurrent independent work, Park 2026 "Kumiho," proves postulate compliance for a property-graph architecture but requires structured input and asynchronous consolidation). The execution is a competent combination of known components (LLM claim extraction, vector retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, pgvector); the genuine novelty is the operator mapping, the history-preserving pointer/status encoding, and the empirical demonstration that write-time revision specifically drives contradiction-resolution accuracy. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and genuinely informative — they isolate R_inline as the dominant driver and quantify per-axis costs of cluster and lineage components, which is more honest than typical system papers. Five-run distributions with standard errors are reported (temperature 0 everywhere, so variance comes from judging and API sampling). Failure analysis categorizes all 181 wrong BEAM answers by response shape. However: (a) the headline BEAM figure is the max of five runs while the LoCoMo headline is a representative run — inconsistent and slightly favorable reporting; (b) BEAM baselines are cross-backbone quoted numbers, which the authors correctly flag as "a reference point, not a causal estimate," but the +21.8 headline leans on it anyway; (c) answer prompts are tuned per benchmark ("a BEAM-tuned answer prompt ... and a LoCoMo-tuned variant"), a form of benchmark-specific engineering not matched in baselines; (d) retrieval top-k is set to each originating study's own value rather than swept — a reasonable anti-overfitting choice but one that couples baseline strength to baseline authors' choices. No public code or data URL is stated in the provided text (prompts are described as "released with the code" without a link). The τ thresholds differ per benchmark (0.6 vs. 0.7) without a sensitivity sweep. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system, run end-to-end on benchmarks). Practical: Yes — single host, no GPU, CPU-only reranker, ~$3–5 and ~30–45 minutes per benchmark run on commodity API models plus Postgres/pgvector. Efficient: Revision is folded into the unavoidable extraction call (no extra write-time LLM calls), but retrieval adds one selection LLM call per query and cross-session clustering adds session-boundary LLM calls; cost relative to plain RAG is higher but modest. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem on the axes that probe belief revision (contradiction-resolution 56.2% vs. 1.8–3.7%), while remaining ordinary on temporal reasoning (35.0%) and summarization — the mechanism is real but narrow. Scalable: Not tested beyond 128K-token conversations and 20-conversation splits; the 10- and 20-conversation evaluation sets are small for the field, and the similarity-graph clustering cost at 10–100× more sessions/sessions-per-user is unexamined. The work delivers a described software system (Python, pluggable backends, YAML prompts) but no verifiable artifact URL in the text provided. Strengths: - The core reframing is intellectually substantive: identifying the binary supersede-or-keep decision as the structural root cause of memory inconsistency, and importing a 40-year-old formalism that fits with surprising precision (Hansson bases ≈ explicit fact lists; rejecting Recovery ≈ avoiding resurrection of retracted consequences). - The ablation section does the rare thing of showing the paper's own secondary components (cluster, lineage) add almost nothing to headline accuracy (+0.4) and sometimes hurt, then quantifying per-axis tradeoffs — this is self-critical empirical work. - The failure analysis is diagnostic rather than decorative: localizing contradiction-resolution failures to the answer prompt (14/24 confident assertions where the lineage was present) cleanly separates memory failure from answer failure. - Backbone-matched controls (Raw RAG at 74.5% under BELIEFMEM's own answer model and embedder) partially isolate mechanism from backbone effects. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: evaluation is English-only on Anglophone data; single-writer assumption (no concurrent multi-agent writes); no primitives yet for entailment suppression, temporal expiration, or unresolved tension; the cross-backbone BEAM comparison is not a causal estimate; the current context-selection policy is chain-forward by default and the dynamic selector is unvalidated ("left to future work"); knowledge-update is "competitive but not dominant"; temporal reasoning is weak. They confront limitations directly — notably the per-postulate fidelity table that admits Inclusion is principally violated — which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline BEAM number is the maximum of five runs while the LoCoMo headline is a standard run; reporting the max in the abstract/conclusion without that qualifier in the same breath inflates the result by ~1.6 points over the mean. - Per-benchmark tuned answer prompts (BEAM-tuned vs. LoCoMo-tuned variants) are an uncontrolled degree of freedom absent from all baselines; the authors' own failure analysis says tighter contradiction-surfacing prompts "should recover most" of the biggest failure cell — meaning part of the headline gap may be prompt engineering, not the belief-revision store. - No baseline reimplemented under BELIEFMEM's prompts/backbone on BEAM; the 1.8–3.7% LIGHT contradiction-resolution figures are other papers' numbers on other backbones, so the ∼52-point margin is directionally credible but its magnitude is not apples-to-apples. - Evaluation sets are small (10 conversations for LoCoMo, 20 for BEAM), and both benchmarks are known to the memory community, creating mild benchmark-familiarity risk; no held-out or synthetic-probe validation. - Cost of R_cluster's connected-component LLM resolution is not reported (how many clusters × how large per session flush), so end-to-end write-time cost at scale is unquantified. - Whether beating full-context (72.9%) on LoCoMo is a memory win or a judging artifact (LLM-judge scoring of concise grounded answers vs. long-context outputs) is not analyzed. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent memory should read this — the AGM-as-write-semantics framing and the inline-revision ablation give a genuinely better design target than Mem0-style add/update/delete, but the 92.3%/54.5% headlines should be discounted for cross-backbone baselines, per-benchmark prompt tuning, and max-of-runs reporting before believing the margins.

PathSoft: Hybrid Soft Prompting with Ranked Reasoning Paths for Knowledge Graph Question Answering

Y Teng, X Zhou, J Zhang, Y Lian, G Chen, H Guan… · aclanthology.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PathSoft, a hybrid soft-prompting framework for KGQA that ranks candidate reasoning paths with a lightweight MLP and encodes the ordered entity–relation structure of the top-k paths into 16 continuous soft prompt tokens prepended to the embeddings of a frozen LLM alongside the textual paths. - Why it's important: KG-augmented LLM methods typically linearize noisy path/subgraph evidence as plain text, which both wastes context length and discards the ordered structure that indicates how evidence relations connect to the question — PathSoft targets answer quality and inference cost simultaneously on standard KGQA benchmarks. - How it does it: A two-stage pipeline: PathMLP (a 1.07M-parameter binary classifier over question–path interaction features [q; p; q−p; q⊙p] from frozen GTE-Large embeddings, trained with BCE) selects top-20 answer-reaching paths, then PathSoftAdapter (frozen BERT element embeddings → Bi-GRU path encoder → question-aware multi-head attention → projector) produces soft prompts injected at the embedding layer of a frozen Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B backbone. - The good: The most credible evidence is the controlled comparison (Appendix C.3) where all baselines (GCR, SubgraphRAG, LightPROF, FiDeLiS) receive the identical PathMLP-selected top-20 paths and matched backbones, yet PathSoft still wins (e.g., 73.21% vs. 57.07% Hit on CWQ with Llama-3.1-8B), isolating the hybrid representation as the source of gains. - The missing: The largest error source on CWQ is the candidate-path pool itself — ~19% of questions lack any answer-reaching path in the enumerated pool and ~17% more are lost to top-20 ranking — so the path-enumeration bottleneck is analyzed but not addressed; no statistical significance tests or multiple-seed variance are reported. - Read it or not: Read it if you build KGQA or KG-augmented RAG systems and want a concrete, well-ablated recipe for injecting structured path evidence into frozen LLMs cheaply; skip it if you are looking for advances in path retrieval itself, since that component is deliberately simple and the paper identifies it as the bottleneck.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (76) is the top contributor — the matched-evidence/matched-backbone controlled comparison (Appendix C.3) cleanly attributes gains to the hybrid representation, and structure-sensitivity ablations directly substantiate the central claim, offset by zero variance reporting. Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building KGQA systems face a reliability problem: LLMs hallucinate and produce unverifiable reasoning, and entity–relation paths from a KG provide verifiable evidence — but a question yields thousands of candidate paths (WebQSP test average: 3,380 paths/question) of which only a few reach correct answers. Existing KG-augmented LLM approaches linearize all retrieved evidence into textual prompts, (a) introducing noise that distracts generation, and (b) flattening the ordered entity–relation sequence of each path into plain text, underexploiting the sequential structure. The gap closed is the combination of reliable path selection with structure-preserving, parameter-efficient injection into a frozen LLM. Key Idea: The core trick is a hybrid representation: the same selected paths are delivered to the LLM twice in complementary form — as readable textualized paths (discrete, interpretable evidence) and as a question-aware, order-preserving continuous soft prompt (16 embedding tokens produced by Bi-GRU encoding of entity–relation sequences with question-conditioned attention) — prepended at the frozen LLM's embedding layer. The soft prompts carry relational-order signal that text alone loses, letting the LLM down-weight high-ranked but relation-mismatched distractor paths. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Candidate path ranking (PathMLP): candidate paths are enumerated from topic entities (2-hop for WebQSP, 3-hop for CWQ) in pre-constructed local graphs; a frozen GTE-Large encoder produces question and textualized-path vectors; interaction features [q; p; q−p; q⊙p] feed a two-hidden-layer MLP with sigmoid output, trained with binary cross-entropy where labels come free from terminal-entity/gold-answer overlap (no annotated reasoning chains). Top-20 paths retained. (2) PathSoftAdapter: frozen BERT encodes each path element (entity/relation) separately; a bidirectional GRU encodes each path's ordered element sequence; multi-head scaled dot-product attention with the projected question as query aggregates the k path vectors; a projector maps the aggregate z to a S ∈ R^{n×d_LLM} soft prompt (n=16). (3) Hybrid prompting and training: soft prompts are prepended to token embeddings of a textual prompt (instruction + paths + question + answer format); the LLM is frozen and only the adapter is trained with a teacher-forcing generation loss on answer-token positions only (L_gen = −Σ log p(a_t | a_<t, S, T)). Critical design decisions: (i) path ranking formulated as reachability classification with self-supervised labels — well-justified, avoids annotation cost; (ii) Bi-GRU over element order rather than pooled path vectors — justified by ablation (mean-pooling drops CWQ Hit from 72.56 to 65.07 with Qwen); (iii) hybrid text+soft input rather than soft-only — justified by controlled ablation showing complementarity. Training of PathMLP and the adapter is fully decoupled, which is simple but means the ranker never sees downstream generation feedback. Key Results: On WebQSP (1,628 test questions) and CWQ (3,531 test questions), Freebase-grounded, following RoG's splits and local graphs: PathSoft with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct achieves 88.81% Hit / 78.27% F1 on WebQSP and 73.21% Hit / 62.07% F1 on CWQ — the best overall across a 16-method comparison spanning pure LLMs, graph-reasoning models (ReaRev: 76.40% Hit WebQSP), tuned KG+LLM methods (GNN-RAG: 85.70/66.80 Hit), and frozen/prompting methods (SubgraphRAG Llama: 85.57/57.07 Hit). Gains over the strongest same-backbone baseline (SubgraphRAG) are largest on CWQ (+16.14 Hit with Qwen, +16.14 with Llama). Ablations: Text-only (ranked paths, no soft prompts) gets 80.52/45.57 Hit (WebQSP/CWQ, Qwen); Soft-only (no ranking, random 20 paths) 71.24/56.56; full PathSoft 86.17/72.56 — the combination is best everywhere, with the soft-prompt contribution largest on CWQ (+27 Hit over Text-only with Qwen). PathMLP ranking quality: C@20 coverage of 85.99 on WebQSP (oracle pool 95.70) vs. 63.55 on CWQ (oracle 80.91). Efficiency: one LLM call per question, ~642–661 input tokens and 1.26–1.38 sec/question on CWQ, versus FiDeLiS's 45,926 tokens and 180.96 sec/Q at 63.50% Hit, and SubgraphRAG's 2,543 tokens and 6.48 sec/Q at 57.07% (matched Llama). Additional: 90.89% Hit on WebQSP with Qwen2.5-14B; 78.80% on 500 sampled GrailQA questions; 40.75% on 2,000 sampled BioGraphletQA questions. Structure-sensitivity: shuffling within-path element order drops CWQ Hit from 72.56 to 63.40 (Qwen). Baselines are current (2024–2025 methods including GCR, SubgraphRAG, LightPROF, EffiQA), and the matched-backbone/matched-evidence comparisons in Appendix C.2–C.3 are unusually careful for this literature. Tested at standard benchmark scale, not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component). The genuinely novel piece is the hybrid delivery of ranked paths as both textual evidence and order-preserving question-aware soft prompts for generative KGQA — prior soft-prompting work (LightPROF, QAP, OntoSCPrompt) encodes reasoning graphs, general KG representations, or ontology information, not ranked ordered paths, and prior path-based methods (RoG, ToG, FiDeLiS) use text only. The individual components — MLP binary ranker, Bi-GRU sequence encoder, cross-attention aggregation, soft-prompt injection into a frozen LLM — are all standard; the contribution is their specific composition and the demonstrated complementarity of dual textual+continuous representations of the same evidence. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: component ablation (ranking vs. soft prompts), controlled hybrid ablation with identical evidence across variants, structure-sensitivity tests (shuffled path order, shuffled path elements, entity-only, mean-pooling), soft-token-count sensitivity (n ∈ {8,16,32}; 16 best), top-k sensitivity (k=20 default), matched-backbone and matched-evidence baseline comparisons, path-rank distribution analysis, error decomposition, and qualitative case studies including a failure case. However: no error bars, no multiple seeds, and no significance testing are reported anywhere, despite small margins in some comparisons (e.g., WebQSP shuffled-order variant 85.80 vs. 86.17). Code is released at https://github.com/tengyan1786-blip/PathSoft; no model weights or precomputed path pools are mentioned as released. Methodological concern: the ranker's labels derive from gold answers on the same benchmark splits used for evaluation (standard practice in KGQA, but the reachability supervision directly leaks answer-set membership signal). Baselines in the main table mix backbones (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5, Llama-2-7B), which the authors themselves flag and correct in Appendix C.2. Efficiency numbers are self-measured; baseline efficiency figures are carried from a common setup whose comparability across hardware/APIs is unclear. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained framework evaluated on benchmarks; also ships a system-like artifact). - Practical: Yes — runs on a frozen 7B–8B open-weights LLM plus a 1.07M-param ranker and a ~63–72M-param adapter, all commodity-hardware scale, with no API dependence. - Efficient: Strong — one LLM call, ~620–660 input tokens, 1.2–1.5 sec/question, an order of magnitude cheaper in tokens and latency than iterative methods (FiDeLiS: 35k–46k tokens, 104–181 sec/Q), and cheaper than SubgraphRAG at equal or better accuracy. - Effective: The evidence covers the stated problem on WebQSP/CWQ (and sampled GrailQA/BioGraphletQA), but ~36% of CWQ errors stem from candidate-path construction and ranking rather than generation, so effectiveness is capped by upstream retrieval coverage the method does not solve. - Scalable: Not stress-tested — only 7B/8B and one 14B backbone are tried; behavior at much larger candidate pools, deeper multi-hop questions, or larger KGs is claimed only via the CWQ-vs-WebQSP trend, not measured. The work delivers a code artifact (GitHub repository) plus trained-module recipes; no released model weights or datasets. Strengths: - The controlled-evidence experiment (Appendix C.3) is the paper's best methodological move: giving every baseline the same PathMLP-selected top-20 paths and matched backbones cleanly attributes gains to the hybrid representation rather than to retrieval quality or backbone choice — a comparison most KG-augmented LLM papers omit. - The error decomposition (Table 13) honestly locates the main remaining failure (49% of CWQ errors from top-20 ranking misses, 32% from candidate-pool misses) rather than burying it, and the failure-case appendix (Table 19) demonstrates the coverage limitation concretely. - The structure-sensitivity ablations (shuffling within-path element order costs 9 Hit points on CWQ; replacing Bi-GRU with mean pooling costs 7.5) directly substantiate the central claim that ordered path structure — not just extra evidence — drives gains. - The self-supervised reachability label for path ranking (terminal entity overlaps gold answer set) removes the need for annotated reasoning chains, making the ranker cheap to train on any KGQA dataset. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state three: (1) dependence on candidate-path quality/coverage — if no answer-reaching path is enumerated, PathSoft cannot recover the evidence; (2) generalization evaluations on GrailQA and BioGraphletQA use only randomly sampled subsets (500 and 2,000 questions), so full-scale cross-domain/cross-KG generality is unproven; (3) added trainable modules and path enumeration bring preprocessing and training costs despite avoiding full LLM fine-tuning. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, so small wins (e.g., +0.60 Hit over SubgraphRAG on WebQSP with Llama in the main table's closest margin context) cannot be assessed; the matched-evidence margins are large enough that this matters mainly for WebQSP Text-only comparisons. - The reachability label is derived from gold answers on the same datasets used for final evaluation, so the ranker is trained on the evaluation distribution — standard in KGQA but worth flagging as a Goodhart risk for out-of-distribution claims. - Candidate path enumeration (top-100 saved pools, oracle coverage 80.91% on CWQ) is a fixed upstream component adopted from the RoG setup; the paper analyzes but does not vary its construction, leaving the identified 19% coverage ceiling unaddressed. - Soft prompts are per-question aggregates collapsed to 16 tokens after attention pooling over 20 paths; no analysis of information loss versus per-path soft prompts (e.g., 20 × n tokens), which would test whether the bottleneck is capacity or representation. - Comparison baselines with tuned LLMs (GCR tunes 8.03B params) are arguably a different cost class; conversely, no comparison against simple LoRA fine-tuning of the same backbones on the same path evidence, which would establish whether the frozen-LLM constraint is actually necessary. - Sub-path supervision is absent: PathMLP labels only terminal entities, so a path reaching a wrong entity through a correct intermediate step is penalized identically to a fully wrong path; no analysis of whether step-level supervision would close the 17% top-20 miss rate. Bottom Line: A practitioner building KGQA or KG-grounded RAG pipelines gains a concrete, cheap, well-controlled recipe — ranked paths plus order-preserving soft prompts into a frozen 7–8B LLM — that beats current frozen-LM baselines at a fraction of their latency, but the method's ceiling is set by path enumeration, so anyone whose bottleneck is retrieval coverage rather than evidence consumption should look to path-construction work instead.

The Cost of Sounding Different: Accent Bias in Audio Language Models

A Srivastava, O Ahia, L Lucy, A Christendat… · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an audit framework showing that audio language models systematically assign lower "delivery" scores to Chinese- and Nigerian-accented English speakers than to American- and British-accented speakers, even when the spoken content is held identical, and that these penalties correlate with acoustic distance from American English (Spearman ρ = −0.35 to −0.66, all p < .05). - Why it's important: Audio LMs are being deployed in hiring pipelines, oral assessments, and English proficiency tests that gate employment, education, and immigration, so accent-linked scoring disparities translate directly into allocational harm for non-Anglosphere speakers. - How it does it: The authors hold scripts constant across speakers (synthetic ElevenLabs voices for scale plus a newly collected 52-speaker human corpus), prompt six audio LMs for 1–7 delivery/content ratings under three evaluative framings, and correlate scores with XLS-R-based duration-normalized DTW acoustic distance while ruling out transcription failure via WER. - The good: The dual evidence design—synthetic speech for controlled scale, human recordings confirming the same ordering—and the WER control (all WER < 4% across accents) jointly rule out the most obvious confound (comprehension failure), making the bias claim unusually well-supported for a bias-audit paper. - The missing: Human validation is limited to the hiring domain with very small accent samples (4 British, 10–14 per other group), and no mitigation experiment or causal mechanism is provided—e.g., the MoE-routing explanation for Qwen3-Omni's reversal is pure speculation. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or audit speech-based evaluation systems, or work on speech fairness; skip it if you want mitigation techniques or causal analysis, since this is a measurement study only.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) rests on a genuinely new empirical finding — graded, content-controlled delivery penalties in deployment-grounded audio LMs — plus a new 52-speaker corpus. Rigor (70) is unusually strong for a bias audit: scripted-content design, WER controls, within-accent dispersion checks, judge validation, and honest exclusion of unstable models, though the self-measured WER, small human samples (4–14 per accent), and absent error bars cap it. Non-Obviousness (72) comes from the acoustic-distance correlation revealing an implicit American norm rather than a binary native/non-native artifact, plus the clever critical-framing methodology. Completeness (75) is high because limitations are confronted directly and non-minimally. Resilience (70) survives most standard objections (single TTS vendor and the speculative MoE explanation are the residual soft spots). Impact (62) reflects a reusable audit harness and released corpus, but no mitigation — the field's more urgent need. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*62 = 71.

Problem & Motivation: Audio LMs that natively process speech are entering high-stakes decision contexts—asynchronous AI interviews, automated oral-exam grading, and English proficiency scoring used for visas in Anglosphere countries (one test vendor alone administered ~1.2 million tests in 2023, and it uses AI speech scoring). Prior bias work in speech focused on ASR word-error-rate disparities; existing evaluations of audio LM bias either study behavior outside deployment contexts (e.g., word associations) or examine gender/voice associations, not geographic accent variation. Nobody has audited whether these systems replicate the well-documented human accent bias that skews judgments of competence and credibility—a gap with direct consequences for who gets shortlisted, graded well, or granted a visa. Key Idea: Holding the script identical across speakers while varying only the accent isolates the causal effect of acoustics on model judgment; pairing this with an acoustic-distance measure (XLS-R layer-14 DTW distance from a pooled American reference) lets the authors show that delivery penalties form a graded function of how far a speaker's pronunciation sits from an implicit American norm—not a binary native/non-native artifact of a particular prompt framing. The critical framing ("provide improvement-oriented feedback" with no comparison target) is the clever methodological move: it elicits the model's own implicit reference standard rather than one the experimenters impose. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Data: 599 synthetic recordings (30 ElevenLabs voices, 3 male + 3 female per accent, 19 hours) across three domains—hiring (4 scripted interview responses), academic presentations (4 subjects × student/researcher contexts), and English proficiency tests (read-aloud and image description)—plus a newly collected human corpus (52 speakers; 312 recordings, 4h46m) for the hiring domain with scripted and unscripted prompts. (2) Evaluation: six audio LMs (frontier: Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, GPT-Audio-1.5; open-weight: Qwen3-Omni, Voxtral-small-24B, Audio Flamingo 3; the last two excluded from the main text for unstable/unreliable outputs) rate delivery and content on 1–7 scales at temperature 0, under three framings (critical, ideal-X, native-speaker). (3) Analysis: per-speaker XLS-R acoustic distance from an American leave-one-out reference pool, Spearman correlation of distance with delivery score, WER computed against reference scripts to rule out comprehension failure, and LLM-judged sentiment of rating explanations (judge validated against 50 human-rated samples, ρ = 0.74, 84% within one point). Critical design decisions: scripted speech to isolate speaker effects (well-justified, with unscripted data as sanity check but not primary); nationality-level accent aggregation (acknowledged as coarse); use of a single commercial TTS vendor whose accent rendering may over/under-represent phonological features (acknowledged and partially checked via word-category analysis). Key Results: Four of the five accent-group comparisons are consistent: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and GPT-Audio-1.5 penalize Chinese and Nigerian speakers on delivery across domains and framings, with non-Western minus Western z-scored delivery gaps of −0.40 to −0.83 (hiring/human), −0.13 to −0.95 (hiring/synthetic), and the largest gaps in the English-test domain (e.g., −1.05 for Gemini 2.5 Flash). Qwen3-Omni is an exception: it sometimes gives Nigerian, Chinese, and Indian speakers equal or slightly higher scores than US/UK speakers on synthetic presentation and English-test speech (+0.29 to +0.32 gaps) but shows large disparities on human hiring speech. Delivery scores correlate negatively with acoustic distance from American English for all four main models on human hiring speech (ρ = −0.35 to −0.66, p ≤ 0.012) and in each model's most-biased synthetic domain (ρ = −0.39 to −0.72). WER is uniformly low across accents (1.7–2.5% overall, max 3.8% per group), and WER–delivery-score correlations (−0.15 to −0.37) are consistently weaker than acoustic-distance correlations, supporting the implicit-American-norm interpretation over comprehension failure. Explanations for Chinese/Nigerian speakers more often cite "mumbling" or "strong accent," while US/UK speakers are described as "clear" and "professional." Baselines are current frontier models (2025–2026 releases); scale is modest but ecologically grounded rather than toy. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (gated 52-speaker accent-labeled corpus). The genuinely novel contribution is the demonstration of graded, content-controlled delivery penalties in general-purpose audio LMs in deployment-grounded settings, and the correlation of penalties with acoustic distance from an American reference. The measurement machinery itself (LLM-as-judge ratings, XLS-R DTW distances from Bartelds et al. 2022, WER controls) is a competent combination of existing techniques applied to a new model class. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for a bias audit: XLS-R layer-wise ablation (accent rank order stable across layers 6–16), within-accent dispersion control to rule out diffuse representation of less-resourced accents (Indian English sits at the American baseline, so the Chinese/Nigerian gap is accent-specific), word-category analysis for consonant clusters and schwa reduction, LLM-judge validation against human raters, and exclusion analysis for the two unstable models (documented sign-flips in 15/30 Voxtral scores across runs). No multiple seeds or error bars on the core rating measurements—temperature 0 mitigates but does not eliminate run-to-run variance, and only Voxtral's instability was checked with repeated runs. Code is public (github.com/arunasrivastava/ImplicitAccentBias); the human corpus is on Hugging Face (multispeak) but gated behind an application and non-commercial-use agreement, which limits frictionless reproduction. One methodological concern: WER is measured using the same audio LMs being audited (self-transcription), not an independent ASR system, so "the model can transcribe it" and "the model heard it correctly" are not fully separated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement/audit study with a released corpus, not a deployed system). - Practical: Yes—runs against commercially available APIs and open-weight models on standard hardware. - Efficient: Not applicable as a method contribution; the audit itself is cheap (scripted audio + LLM inference), though human data collection took ~20 minutes per speaker. - Effective: The evidence convincingly shows a proxy harm (rating disparities on scripted speech), not measured downstream decisions like shortlisting or visa outcomes; the authors are explicit about this distinction. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 52 human speakers and 30 synthetic voices; the framework scales trivially since it is a prompting harness, but no 10× stress test exists. The work delivers a public code artifact and a gated dataset (52-speaker accent-labeled corpus), not a trained model or mitigation tool. Strengths: - The controlled-script design plus independent acoustic-distance measure turns a categorical bias claim into a graded, mechanistic one (penalty magnitude tracks XLS-R distance), which is a stronger form of evidence than most LLM bias audits produce. - The confound-killing sequence—scripted content, WER check, three prompt framings, human + synthetic voices, within-dispersion control—preempts nearly every standard objection to accent-bias claims. - Ecological grounding is real, not decorative: the three domains are modeled on documented deployments (asynchronous AI interviews, vendor AI-scored proficiency tests), and the paper cites specific evidence that these AI-scored systems exist. - Honest model selection: excluding Voxtral and Audio Flamingo 3 with documented diagnostics (sign-flips across runs, insensitivity to disfluencies) rather than silently dropping them is a credibility positive. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly. They state: human data covers only the hiring domain and is small and non-representative (4–14 speakers per accent group); scripts reduce spontaneity relative to real deployments; the exact integration of audio LMs into proprietary hiring/proficiency systems is unknown, so their setup approximates rather than replicates real use; the choice of single-TTS synthetic voices may misrepresent phonological features; and nationality-level accent categories are coarse and erase within-group variation. They also flag contested terminology ("native," "standard") and note in-situ user studies are needed for true deployment validation. This transparency is above the norm for bias-audit papers. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No mitigation experiment or even ablation of what would reduce the gap (accent-normalized audio, explicit rubrics), so the paper identifies harm without testing remedies it gestures toward. - The single TTS vendor (ElevenLabs) is itself trained on speech data and could encode accent artifacts that interact with model biases in unknown ways; a second TTS source would have strengthened the synthetic arm. - WER is measured by the audited models themselves, not an independent recognizer, partially weakening the comprehension-failure exclusion. - The MoE-routing explanation for Qwen3-Omni's reversal is offered without any evidence (no probing, no routing analysis) and relies on a single preprint citation—this is speculation presented alongside findings. - No statistical model controlling for speaker-level covariates (gender, age, recording device) in the human corpus, though device and age vary across accent groups (e.g., the single 55–64 speaker is Chinese); small-N correlations could partially reflect these confounds. - Scoring prompts were developed and iterated on the same models/accent sets they evaluate, with no held-out accent group to test generalization of the audit instrument itself. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying or auditing speech-based evaluation systems gains concrete, well-controlled evidence that current audio LMs penalize non-Anglosphere accents on delivery independent of content—and a reusable audit harness—making this worth reading despite modest human-sample sizes and the absence of any mitigation, which is the field's more urgent open problem.

WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training (30 ▲ )

Ziyang Zeng, Tingyang Chen, Jia Deng, Qiyao Wang, Shuo Tang, Yike Yang, Tao Ren, Wayne Xin Zhao, Feng Chang, Jujie He, Chuan Hao, Ran Tao, Bryan Dai · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WorkFactory, a pipeline that synthesizes 112,686 executable professional tasks across 612 occupations by planning backward from intended outputs via an "information support graph" and repairing broken task environments with probe executions, then uses the resulting teacher trajectories to train the WorkPilot SFT family (4B/27B/35B-A3B) that improves over its Qwen bases on four professional-work benchmarks. - Why it's important: Scaling supervised agent training beyond coding requires diverse professional tasks whose environments actually support the intended work — missing or contradictory task information silently corrupts teacher demonstrations, and this paper targets exactly that failure mode with an industrial-scale data engine. - How it does it: For each intent, a planner builds a graph over information units (not artifacts) with explicit dependencies and carrier bindings that mark what is supplied vs. left solver-derived; an isolated probe solver then attempts the task from solver-visible inputs only, and a refiner repairs blocker-level defects under work-preservation constraints before an independent teacher collects trajectories. - The good: The controlled 5K-task component ablation directly links pipeline components to outcomes — information-level planning cuts broken-derivation defects from 24.86% to 6.86%, repair cuts cross-file inconsistency from 25.74% to 4.84%, and downstream GDPval-AA Elo rises from 1245 → 1293 → 1326 across conditions — the clearest causal evidence in the paper. - The missing: The headline Elo numbers depend on a locally built two-anchor Bradley–Terry estimator with an LLM judge, and the authors release only a subset of task data; a full independent replication of the flagship 1565/1612 Elo results on the official leaderboard protocol is absent. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building synthetic task/environment pipelines for agent SFT — the information-support-graph representation, repair-loop statistics, and scaling curves are directly reusable — skip it if you only want another leaderboard result, which it only partially provides.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training "working agents" (agents producing professional deliverables like spreadsheets, reports, analyses) via supervised fine-tuning need large, diverse sets of professional tasks on which a teacher model can reliably produce demonstrations. The core difficulty is environmental coherence: all premises needed for the intended output must be present and consistent across files and the request, while intermediate and final results must remain unsolved for the teacher to derive. The paper's motivating example is a supplier-selection task where a missing freight-pricing clause makes lifecycle-cost comparison impossible, yet supplying the computed costs would remove the very work being supervised. Prior synthesis systems (NexForge, Synthetic Computers, and concurrent GraphForge/WorkGenesis) plan at the artifact or rubric level and do not explicitly represent the boundary between supplied information and solver-derived work. Key Idea: Plan tasks backward from the intended output using a graph over information units rather than artifacts: nodes carry provision status (supplied / externally acquired / solver-derived / internal-to-construction) and carrier bindings locating each unit (request, reference file, external resource, future deliverable), so the planner can guarantee complete solver-visible support while explicitly reserving derivations for the solver. This graph is then enforced operationally by execution: a probe solver attempts the task blind to the graph, and any blocker it diagnoses triggers a constrained repair that must restore support without changing the intended work (verified by construction checks plus an LLM work-preservation review). Methodology: Four-stage pipeline. (1) Intent synthesis: three routes — expansion of a BLS Standard Occupational Classification hierarchy, composition of skills from a public skill directory (skills.sh), and instruction backtranslation from real web-collected deliverables — filtered by an LLM review into a shared intent library. (2) Graph-guided construction: an LLM planner (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731) builds Ginfo = (Vinfo, Vcarrier, Einfo, Eloc) and compiles it into an artifact-level plan P = (u, A, D) with acyclic construction dependencies; an environment worker reuses/adapts/synthesizes files, checked programmatically and by LLM review (up to 3 retries, else discard). (3) Execution-based repair: a probe solver (same model, Claude Code harness, 1M context, graph/plan hidden) attempts the task and reports grounded issues with severity labels; only blocker findings trigger a refiner that edits the request and existing files without changing file count/types/dependencies, followed by construction checks, an LLM work-preservation review, and a fresh probe — up to 3 rounds, unresolved tasks discarded. (4) Trajectory collection: GLM-5.3 as an independent teacher solves each retained task in a clean sandbox (Stirrup harness for 94,077 tasks, Claude Code for 18,609), with lightweight validity filtering plus pairwise rejection sampling for the longest 5% of rollouts; supervision is masked autoregressive SFT (failed tool-call spans removed from the loss but retained in history). Critical design decisions: the supplied-vs-solver-derived boundary encoded in node status (well-motivated, central to the paper); probe blindness to prior diagnoses (justified — avoids anchoring); repair constrained to preserve file structure (justified, but the graph itself is not updated during repair, a possible source of drift). Construction costs ~11.656M model tokens per attempted task. Key Results: Corpus: 112,686 tasks, 612 occupations, 23 major occupational groups, 4.15 reference files/task, mean 57.4 assistant turns and 136.18K tokens per trajectory. Matched-base gains: WorkPilot-35B-A3B improves from 879 to 1565 on GDPval-AA (local two-anchor estimate; official base value), 28.91→62.35 on JobBench, 47.12→56.53 on Workspace-Bench-Lite, 7.14→21.18 on OmegaUse-OfficeVal; WorkPilot-27B reaches a locally estimated 1612 Elo, nominally above DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (1600 official) and 34 below GLM-5.3 (1646 official); WorkPilot-4B gains +714 Elo over Qwen3.5-4B. Scaling (2K–110K nested subsets): diminishing returns are model-dependent — for 35B-A3B the first 5K tasks add 447 Elo while 75K→110K adds 13; by 30K tasks, 35B and 27B capture 88% and 94% of their full gains. Execution length is non-monotonic: mean turns rise 24.87→162.88 at 2K then fall to 85.90 at 110K; code-execution failures drop 16.0%→6.3%, web-search failures 22.4%→10.4% after an early spike, while web-fetch failures stay at 40–48%. Teacher ablation (30K tasks): GLM-5.3-trained student reaches 1483 Elo [1455, 1510] vs. 1248 [1220, 1274] for a DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-trained student — both above the 879 base. Cost analysis places all three WorkPilot models on the non-dominated cost–Elo frontier, at ~$0.012, $0.031, and $0.396 per GDPval-AA task (standardized estimates). Baselines include current frontier models (GLM-5.3, GPT-5.6 Sol, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), so the comparison context is strong, though the headline claim rests on locally estimated Elo for the authors' own checkpoints. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD + NEW SYSTEM + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the information support graph with provision-status and carrier bindings — a representation that makes the supplied-vs-derived boundary explicit before materialization — combined with blind-probe diagnosis and work-preservation-constrained repair; this differs from concurrent artifact/evidence-graph approaches (GraphForge) and rubric-audited synthesis (WorkGenesis). The overall recipe (LLM task synthesis → probe → teacher trajectories → SFT) is a known template competently instantiated; the scaling curves (non-monotonic execution length, model-dependent diminishing returns) are useful but not conceptually surprising empirical findings. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong ablation design: a controlled 5K-task comparison isolates planning level and repair, reporting per-category defect incidence with explicit definitions (Table 6), repair-depth statistics (69.6% of tasks need zero repairs, only 0.48% discarded for unresolved blockers), and a downstream Elo delta for each condition — this connects environment quality to training utility rather than asserting it. Elo estimates carry task-bootstrap 95% CIs (e.g., WorkPilot-27B [1594, 1631]) and the two-anchor estimator is itself validated (MAE 24.11 Elo on a 7-model validation set, 19.00 on a 3-model held-out test). Decontamination against benchmarks is thorough (embedding similarity, 10-gram overlap, file hashes, manual review of flagged pairs). Concerns: no multiple training seeds or significance tests for the benchmark deltas other than the Elo CIs; the probe, planner, refiner, and judge are all LLM-based, so defect incidence is a proxy measured by the same class of models that built the environments (possible circularity in the defect metric); the component analysis uses only 5K tasks; only a subset of task data is released (weights and subset at github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory), limiting full reproduction; GDPval-AA local Elo for the authors' checkpoints is self-generated under a protocol whose calibration nodes include their own base model. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — a built data-construction pipeline plus trained, released models. - Practical: The trained models run on open Qwen backbones (4B–35B-A3B MoE), so inference is on commodity hardware; the construction pipeline requires frontier LLM API access (~11.7M tokens per attempted task). - Efficient: WorkPilot-4B at ~$0.012/task and 35B-A3B at ~$0.031/task undercut frontier APIs by 1–3 orders of magnitude at comparable mid-range Elo, per the authors' own accounting (excludes judge, sandbox, and tool fees). - Effective: Matched-base gains on four independent benchmarks with decontamination support real training utility, though the flagship GDPval-AA ranking of the 27B/35B models rests on local estimates rather than official leaderboard runs. - Scalable: Tested to 110K tasks (a genuine scaling study with nested subsets across three model scales), but the observed diminishing returns (88–94% of gains by 30K) suggest the framework's marginal value beyond ~10⁵ tasks is unproven, and the paper does not claim otherwise. Deliverables: WorkPilot model weights and a subset of task data (GitHub release), plus a reusable pipeline description; the full pipeline code and complete corpus are not stated as released. Strengths: - The information-support graph is a real representational contribution: separating what information supports what from where it lives and who derives it is a sharper formulation than artifact-level dependency planning, and the component ablation shows it matters (broken derivations 24.86%→6.86%, downstream +48 Elo). - The probe–repair loop is evaluated with unusual honesty for a data engine: defect taxonomies, repair-depth distributions, discarded-task rates, and a documented regression (leakage +1.44pp, self-inconsistency +1.18pp after graph planning) that the authors analyze rather than hide. - The teacher-choice ablation (1483 vs. 1248 Elo from the same tasks) is a valuable, transferable finding that trajectory-generation style, not just task quality, drives training benefit. - Honest treatment of estimator uncertainty: bootstrap CIs, a validation/test split for the Elo estimator itself, and explicit statement that intervals exclude method-form error. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two: (1) the GLM-5.3 teacher is text-only, so training and evaluation run in text-only mode and the Qwen vision components remain unused — multimodal professional work is unexamined; (2) training is SFT only, with RL on execution feedback left to future work. They confront both directly, and the ethics section appropriately flags that agent outputs in consequential settings need human review. Notably, they do not minimize the regressions in their own component analysis. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Evaluation circularity risk: defect incidence in the component analysis is diagnosed by the same model family (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731) that serves as probe/planner/refiner, so "environment quality" is measured by the pipeline's own judge; no human audit of defect labels is reported. - The flagship 27B (1612) and 35B (1565) Elo figures are self-estimated; the official leaderboard values cited are for other models. Given the estimator's ±20–30 Elo validation error, the claim of "frontier-level" performance for the 27B sits within the method's error band relative to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. - Training uses the same GDPval-AA harness (Stirrup) and tool protocol for 94,077 of the teacher trajectories that GDPval-AA evaluation uses, a protocol-level alignment with the primary benchmark that could favorably interact with evaluation, even with task-level decontamination. - Only a subset of the 112,686 tasks is released; the complete corpus and pipeline code availability are not stated, limiting independent verification of the central claims. - The 5% rejection sampling and filtering affect only the longest rollouts, and no ablation isolates the contribution of this trajectory-curation stage versus the task-construction components. - Seeds for SFT runs are not stated; benchmark deltas other than Elo CIs (JobBench, Workspace-Bench, OmegaUse) carry no uncertainty estimates. Bottom Line: For anyone building synthetic professional-task pipelines for agent SFT, this is currently one of the most complete and honestly ablated data-engine reports available and is worth reading for its information-support representation and repair-loop statistics; treat the frontier-ranking claims about WorkPilot-27B as self-estimated until an official leaderboard run confirms them.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SNAPPerf, a 12M-parameter tabular foundation model pretrained once on ~29 million synthetic configurable systems that predicts software performance for unseen configurations in-context from a handful of measurements, with no per-system training or tuning. - Why it's important: Performance prediction models currently must be retrained from scratch after every software update, hardware migration, or workload change — a cost that grows as coding agents accelerate release cadence; skip it if you only care about deployment-ready tooling, since the paper self-labels its results "preliminary" and ships no artifact.

Problem & Motivation: Highly configurable systems (databases, web servers, compilers, video encoders) expose hundreds of options whose combinations change runtime, memory, and energy by large factors — varying two VP8 options changes encoding time elevenfold, and exhaustively measuring 2,736 configurations takes ~18 hours. The established workflow measures a small sample, trains a per-system model (regression trees, DeepPerf, HINNPerf, DaL), and predicts the rest; but every software version bump, hardware migration, or workload change invalidates the model and forces new measurements, retraining, and tuning. Prior transfer/meta-learning reduces measurements but still trains a new model per target environment. The gap: no method predicts performance for an arbitrary system from a few measurements using a single frozen model. Key Idea: Encode knowledge of configurable software in pretraining data instead of in per-system model architectures. A generator ("prior") draws synthetic configurable systems — configuration spaces with binary and numeric options, alternative groups, and inter-option constraints, paired with sparse performance-influence models (log y = Σβᵢxᵢ + Σβᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ + ε) with nonlinear numeric effects and measurement noise — and a small transformer is pretrained from scratch on ~29M such systems to approximate Bayesian prediction (PFN-style). At deployment, measured configurations become the context of the frozen model, which predicts every unmeasured configuration in one pass. The insight is that the structural regularities of configuration spaces (sparsity of dominant effects, interactions, constraints) are learnable in advance, making per-system gradient updates unnecessary. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Offline pretraining: each training example is a synthetic system sampled from the prior; a 12-layer, 12M-parameter transformer (half the size of Nori) is trained for 38 hours on two NVIDIA H200 GPUs to approximate the Bayesian posterior over performance given the context table. (2) In-context conditioning: measured configurations are encoded as option vectors and given as context; no gradient step, no hyperparameter search, no validation split taken from the small sample. (3) Prediction: a single inference call outputs a full predictive distribution per unmeasured configuration; the point estimate minimizes expected relative error, and 90% prediction intervals contain 92% of true values in the median case. Critical design decisions: (a) building the prior from the performance-modeling literature with no access to evaluation systems — well-justified, with an explicit leak-prevention argument; (b) all model-selection decisions (prior, size, checkpoint, point estimate) made on synthetic data plus 16 development systems from other studies, with the benchmark used only for final evaluation — well-justified and unusually clean; (c) averaging eight predictions with different option orderings/encodings at inference — a reasonable but essentially unexamined trick. The framework is in-context Bayesian prediction via transformer pretraining (Prior-Fitted Networks), specialized to a software configuration prior. Key Results: On the DaL benchmark — 12 real systems across 6 domains (databases, web servers, video encoders, compression, scientific solvers, image processing), 39,866 measured configurations, 4 metrics (runtime, latency, energy, max load), 5 budgets covering 3%–22% of configurations, 30 random samples per case — SNAPPerf achieves 2.80% median MRE vs. 4.72% for DaL (38% lower; 37–40% stable gain across budgets) and 3.80% for Nori, the best of five general-purpose tabular foundation models (25% lower). It ranks in the top Scott-Knott ESD group in 55/60 cases (vs. 9 for DaL, 15 for the best general-purpose model), with mean error 9.8% vs. 21.7% for DaL; in the 5 non-winning cases its error is within 0.12 percentage points of the best. It matches DaL's full-sample accuracy with 54% fewer measurements on average (vs. 27% for Nori), though savings range from 10% (HSMGP) to 93% (SQLite, where all methods have high error). Against the best general-purpose model per case — selected with test-set knowledge, a favorable handicap — SNAPPerf still wins 54/60 cases. Baselines are current and strong: five recent foundation models (Nori, TabICL, TabPFN, TabFM, Mitra 2), rerun state-of-the-art DaL and HINNPerf, and tuned classical learners. Tested at standard benchmark scale (systems with hundreds to thousands of configurations), not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (first tabular foundation model specialized for configurable software, pretrained purely on a software-specific synthetic prior) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (per-system training is unnecessary for accurate configuration performance prediction). The PFN/in-context-learning machinery is standard (TabPFN lineage); what is genuinely new is the software-aware prior and the demonstration that it alone — not architectural tricks like DaL's space division or DeepPerf's sparsity — accounts for the gains. This is a real, non-obvious finding, not a routine re-skin. Rigor & Reproducibility: Evaluation hygiene is above average: 30 repetitions per case, Scott-Knott ESD grouping with the Vargha-Delaney effect size at 99% confidence, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test across runs, and a strict train/eval firewall (benchmark never touches the prior or model selection). However, component ablations are absent — the paper acknowledges the prior's elements (interactions, constraints, noise) are untested individually. Error bars appear only as interquartile-range bands in Fig. 2; no per-case significance beyond Scott-Knott is tabulated. No code, model weights, or prior implementation URL is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the central artifact. One residual concern: the 16 development systems come from the same research literature as the benchmark systems, so the prior could inherit soft bias toward these domains even without direct leakage; and all evaluation is on a single benchmark (DaL). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent artifact). Practical: Inference is a single forward pass of a 12M-parameter model on a table — runs on commodity hardware; only the one-time pretraining needed H200s. Efficient: Eliminates the per-change train-and-tune cycle entirely; cost per adaptation is a few measurements plus one inference call, strictly cheaper than retraining DaL or tuning XGBoost. Effective: The evidence shows prediction accuracy on a static benchmark (MRE), a proxy — the motivating scenarios (accuracy after an update or migration) and downstream value for tuning are explicitly deferred to future plans, and the paper itself cites evidence that surrogate accuracy does not guarantee tuning improvement. Scalable: Untested beyond ~thousands-of-configurations systems; behavior on systems with orders more options, continuous high-cardinality options, or multi-objective outputs is claimed only implicitly through the prior's generality. Deliverable status: paper form only — no released library, weights, or tool is mentioned. Strengths: (1) A genuinely novel reframing: moving software configuration knowledge from per-system model architectures into a synthetic pretraining prior, with the first quantified evidence that this works (38% error reduction over a retraining SOTA). (2) The measurement-savings result (54% fewer configurations to match SOTA) directly attacks the dominant cost — benchmarking time — which is the right metric for this field. (3) Disciplined evaluation design: prior built without benchmark access, model selection on disjoint development systems, 30 repetitions, effect-size-aware ranking — better leakage hygiene than most in this subfield. (4) Calibrated uncertainty for free (90% intervals covering 92% of true values in the median case), which most per-system learners lack and which enables active measurement selection later. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors label all results "Preliminary" and explicitly defer to a future agenda: ablating prior elements (interactions, constraints, noise) with held-out success criteria, handling software evolution by reusing measurements across releases, and integrating into tuners with the honest caveat (citing prior work) that better accuracy does not guarantee better tuning. They also note savings vary widely by system (10%–93%) and that on SQLite all methods have high error. This is a paper that confronts its boundaries directly — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The motivating scenario is never tested: there is no experiment measuring accuracy after a version update, hardware migration, or workload change — the entire case for retraining-free prediction rests on the static single-environment benchmark. (2) No ablation isolates why the software-specific prior wins; without it, the 25% gain over Nori could partly reflect prior hyperparameters tuned on the 16 development systems, which share provenance with benchmark-domain systems. (3) Single-benchmark evaluation (DaL only, 12 systems); generalization to larger or industrial-scale configuration spaces is unmeasured. (4) No released artifact, so the numbers cannot be independently verified, and the inference-time trick of averaging eight permuted-encoding predictions is unanalyzed. (5) Uncertainty calibration is reported only as a median; tail calibration, which matters if intervals guide active sampling, is not evaluated. Bottom Line: A short but rigorous and genuinely novel paper that practitioners in configuration performance learning and tabular foundation-model research should read now — the prior-specialization finding is real and well-evidenced — while practitioners seeking deployable tooling should wait for the ablations, evolution experiments, and released model the authors themselves schedule as future work.
