Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Diffusion LLMs generate text by iterative denoising of masked sequences with bidirectional context, and this generation mechanism differs fundamentally from left-to-right autoregression. Practitioners deploying safety-aligned AR models have known attack taxonomies, but AR jailbreak prompts transfer poorly to dLLMs (e.g., direct AutoDAN achieves 0.8–12.5% ASR on the four tested dLLMs), leaving the dLLM attack surface poorly characterized. The only prior dLLM-specific attack, DIJA, uses manually designed interleaved mask-text scaffolds that carry limited query-specific content. The gap: a general mechanism for reusing the large body of existing AR jailbreak machinery against dLLMs. Key Idea: A harmful response to a query, once ~80% of its tokens are masked at uniform intervals, is itself an effective jailbreak input: the sparse surviving tokens act as distributed query-specific anchors that steer the dLLM's bidirectional infilling toward reconstructing the harmful content. This recasts jailbreaking dLLMs as a masked-reconstruction task rather than a prompt-steering task, and lets any AR jailbreak method serve as a harmful-response generator. Methodology: Three-phase pipeline (Algorithm 1). (1) Source AR induction: run an existing AR jailbreak method A (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, ReNeLLM, RA) on a source AR model (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 or Vicuna-7B-v1.5) to obtain a query-specific harmful response r; crucially, only the response r is reused, not the attack prompt. (2) Masked template transfer: retain tokens at interval d = round(1/(1−ρ)) with a random initial offset (ρ = 0.8 by default), producing template r̄; then an auxiliary LLM (Qwen3-8B) prompted to only insert additional <mask> tokens removes any remaining visible harmful content, yielding r̂. (3) Target dLLM jailbreak: concatenate query q and template r̂ and let the target dLLM complete via its native masked diffusion decoding. Design decisions: (a) uniform vs. continuous masking — justified by a controlled ablation at fixed mask ratio showing uniform masking wins by up to 58.3 ASR points (HarmBench, ρ=0.8); (b) ρ = 0.8 chosen to roughly match DIJA's actual masking ratio (80.28% vs DIJA's 78.93% on HarmBench), a fair-comparison argument backed by Table 8; (c) the safety-filtering stage, motivated as avoiding direct exposure of harmful text, is plausible but its ablation contribution is not separately reported. No explicit objective function is optimized — the method is a training-free, inference-time construction. Key Results: Evaluated on HarmBench (HarmBench-Llama-2-13b classifier), JailbreakBench (Llama-Guard-4), and StrongReject, against four target dLLMs (LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, MMaDA-8B-MixCoT) and baselines Zeroshot, GCG, AutoDAN, AIM, PAIR, ReNeLLM, and DIJA. Headlines: HarmBench ASR 61.3–76.5% (best baseline DIJA: 47.3–60.5%); JailbreakBench ASR 77.0–84.0% (DIJA: 69.0–74.0%); StrongReject SRS 56.7–70.4 (DIJA: 47.6–63.3). RMT-JAILBREAK wins all 12 target-model–benchmark combinations. In the generalization study, converting AutoDAN-induced responses lifts MMaDA-MixCoT JailbreakBench ASR from 1.0% (direct) to 85.0%. An early motivation experiment (Table 1) shows that simply masking an LLaDA-8B-Instruct harmful response yields 85.5–97.75% ASR across mask ratios 0.3–0.9. Under the Self-reminder defense, HarmBench ASR only drops to 69.5–72.0% and JBB ASR increases. Baselines are current (2023–2025 methods, including the dLLM-specific DIJA); scale is standard 7–8B models on commodity RTX A6000 GPUs — no stress-scale testing. A notable counter-finding: higher ASR does not uniformly bring higher GPT-4o harmfulness scores, which the authors attribute to more reliable (rather than more extreme) jailbreak success. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the observation that query-specific harmful responses function as jailbreak templates under high-ratio uniform masking, and the response-mediated transfer bridge from AR jailbreaks to dLLMs. The components — uniform masking, LLM-based content filtering, concatenating query and template — are individually standard; the contribution is their composition and the transfer insight, not new algorithms. It clearly advances beyond DIJA's hand-designed generic scaffolds by making the template query-specific. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: mask ratio sweep (0.7–0.9), uniform vs. continuous masking at matched ratios, actual-mask-ratio comparison against DIJA (Table 8), robustness under Self-reminder, and a 48-combination generalization grid over attack method × source model × target × benchmark. Evaluation spans three independent benchmarks with different evaluators, which guards against single-evaluator gaming. Missing: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; no ablation isolating the safety-filtering stage's contribution; no code, data, or artifacts release is mentioned. The ASR metrics are LLM-judged (HarmBench classifier, Llama-Guard-4, GPT-4o harmfulness), so evaluator bias is possible but mitigated by using three distinct judges. No Goodhart-style development-on-the-benchmark issue is evident, though ρ=0.8 was chosen partly to match DIJA, which is a defensible fairness choice. The paper is an arXiv preprint (v2); peer review status is not stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training-free attack method run against live models). Practical: Yes — everything runs on RTX A6000 GPUs with 7–8B open-weight models and public benchmarks/evaluators. Efficient: Attack cost is dominated by running the AR jailbreak once per query plus one dLLM decoding pass; it avoids the expensive per-query optimization of GCG/AutoDAN-style attacks, though AutoDAN-based induction still carries that method's own cost. Effective: Strong, multi-benchmark evidence that the attack elicits harmful completions judged successful by independent classifiers — this is the paper's actual target claim, not merely a proxy. Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B dLLMs; behavior on larger future dLLMs or dLLMs with dLLM-specific safety training is only implied, not demonstrated. The work delivers no software artifact — it stops at paper form (prompts and algorithms are specified, so reimplementation is feasible). Strengths: - The central insight — harmful responses as high-mask-ratio jailbreak templates — is simple, verifiable (Table 1: 85.5–97.75% ASR from masking alone), and opens a transfer bridge that subsumes many prior attacks. - The generalization grid (2 AR attacks × 2 source models × 4 targets × 3 benchmarks, 48 combinations, all positive) is unusually thorough for an attack paper and shows the effect is not an artifact of one attack or one model. - The uniform-vs-continuous masking ablation at fixed mask ratio isolates a real mechanistic finding: distributing sparse visible tokens throughout a response is what enables reconstruction, not the total amount of visible text. - Fair-comparison discipline against DIJA: the authors match actual mask ratios (~80%) rather than claiming gains from a masking advantage. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors note that attack effectiveness declines as mask ratio increases (Figure 4), that the Self-reminder defense changes but does not eliminate attack success, and that higher ASR is not accompanied by uniformly higher harmfulness scores. They do not include a dedicated limitations section; the stated boundaries are mostly embedded in the analysis and are confronted honestly rather than minimized, but the paper does not proactively discuss defenses beyond Self-reminder or dual-use risk of publishing the method. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Defense coverage is thin: only Self-reminder, a prompt-level defense, is tested. No evaluation against output filtering, refusal training on infilling contexts, or masked-input-aware classifiers — the natural countermeasure of detecting or downweighting high-ratio-mask inputs is never discussed. - The method presumes a source AR model that can be jailbroken into producing the harmful response; the framework's end-to-end cost and reliability depend on this unstated prerequisite, and no failure analysis of the induction stage is given. - The safety-filtering stage (masking residual harmful tokens) lacks its own ablation — its contribution to either effectiveness or the 'no directly visible harmful content' property is unmeasured. - All target models are ≤8B research-grade open-weight dLLMs; extrapolation to larger or production dLLMs is unsupported. - No statistical treatment (seeds, confidence intervals) for LLM-judged ASR, where judge variance across runs can be several points. - The 97.75% ASR motivation experiment (Table 1) operates at low mask ratios (0.3–0.9 shown, 0.9 already at 85.5%), which slightly blurs the later claim that ρ=0.8 is a challenging operating point; the relationship between Table 1 and the final configuration could be tightened. Bottom Line: A safety researcher working on diffusion LLMs should read this paper — it establishes, with broad controlled evidence, that AR jailbreak attacks transfer to dLLMs through masked-response reconstruction and outperforms the only prior dLLM-specific attack — but defenders will find it a problem statement rather than a solution, and will need to supply their own mitigations.

MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors

R Tian, Z Khan, Z Wang, JCY Chen, M Bansal · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MiRL, an error-targeted RL recipe for terminal agents that profiles a policy's recurring error types, starts rollouts from trajectory prefixes where those misbehaviors occur, and rewards rollouts only if they pass the task tests and a behavior judge confirms the misbehavior is avoided. - Why it's important: Terminal-agent RL training currently scales by burning tens of thousands of environments (e.g., a TMax run samples 14.6K environments on eight H100 nodes for 2–3 days), so a recipe that matches or beats that performance with 35% of the rollouts directly cuts training cost. - How it does it: The trick is connecting step-level error profiling (localizer flags a wrong step, teacher corrects it so the rollout can continue, annotator LLM clusters errors into reusable types) with RL from intermediate states, plus a conjunction reward r = ro ∧ re that gates the outcome reward on misbehavior avoidance. - The good: Misbehavior-rate measurements on unseen prefixes with two independent judges (Gemini 3.8 Flash and Qwen3.8-27B) show targeted misbehaviors drop 43–57% (e.g., "Makes false claims about tests" from 26.7% to 8.1%), and pass@k analysis shows MiRL raises the capability ceiling rather than merely sharpening, unlike TMax-4B. - The missing: Training each recipe only once with a single 4B backbone and selecting the final checkpoint by best TB-Lite score (one of the two evaluation benchmarks) leaves both cross-model generality and evaluation-selection contamination unaddressed. - Read it or not: Read it if you train LLM agents with RL and care about data/compute efficiency; skip it if you only need standard RLVR pipelines, since the core techniques (prefix-started rollouts, LLM-judged rewards) are assembled from known parts.

Problem & Motivation: Terminal agents — LLM policies that solve long-horizon tasks by issuing shell commands in containers, evaluated by test suites on final container state — are trained predominantly by scaling environment counts, which is expensive: the TMax recipe samples from 14.6K environments and takes two to three days on eight H100 nodes. Error-targeted learning (identify named weaknesses, train against them, verify the fix) is an attractive alternative because it makes improvement legible, but existing error-targeted methods are designed for single-turn tasks where a wrong answer immediately yields a training signal. Terminal trajectories take dozens of steps; a failed task often hinges on one or two wrong steps; and most wrong steps are environment-specific, so fixing them one at a time does not transfer. Meanwhile, existing agent-failure taxonomies (MAST, AgentErrorTaxonomy, Who&When, AgenTracer) are used to debug and evaluate agents, not to decide what the agent trains on. The paper closes the gap of using failure analysis as the direct driver of RL data selection and reward design for multi-step terminal agents. Key Idea: The core insight is that a small set of generalizable misbehaviors — error types that recur across many environments — concentrates most of the policy's errors (8 types cover 52.1% of error steps and appear in 75.4% of 2,017 profiled environments), so RL can be made targeted and data-efficient by (a) starting each rollout group at a misbehavior prefix (reconstructed by deterministically re-running prefix commands in a fresh container, keeping only prefixes whose outputs match exactly) and (b) gating the outcome reward with a binary behavior reward from an LLM judge that checks only whether that specific misbehavior recurs in the next m=5 steps. Everything else is competent assembly of known components. Methodology: The pipeline has two phases. (1) Error profiling: the policy (Qwen3.5-4B) is rolled out with 2 seeds on 2,017 environments sampled from TMax's 14.6K-environment pool; a Qwen3.8-27B error localizer flags problematic steps (verified against an engineer-plausibility rubric in the prompt); a Qwen3.8-27B teacher corrects flagged steps so rollouts continue and expose later errors; a Claude Opus 5 annotator proposes error types over batches, keeps types recurring across batches (threshold: ≥1% of error steps), and labels all error steps — yielding 12,746 error steps and eight misbehaviors. (2) MiRL training: for each misbehavior, 80 prefixes are sampled (640 total); each prefix is validated by re-running its commands in a fresh container with exact per-step output matching (34% survive, yielding 219 prefixes from 189 environments); DPPO-style RL (TMax recipe, group size 16, 160 steps, 8 A100 80GB GPUs) starts rollout groups from these prefixes; reward is the logical AND of the test-suite outcome reward ro and a behavior reward re from Gemini 3.8 Flash judging the first 5 post-prefix steps against the misbehavior definition — the judge returns only a binary signal, no text for the policy to imitate. Critical design decisions: teacher corrections keep rollouts on-policy-adjacent and reveal downstream errors (justified by same-family model choice); the exact-match rerun check ensures live rollouts start from the intended state but discards 66% of prefixes (biases toward deterministic environments, acknowledged); conjunctive reward vs. weighted combinations is unexplored (acknowledged). One notable negative/nuanced ablation finding: selecting the misbehavior environments alone hurts (37.4% vs. 43.4% on TB-Lite) because they are harder (dead-group rate rises from 27.3% to 42.9%); environment selection is only valuable as a prefix source. Key Results: All numbers are the authors' own runs (mean ± standard error over 3 evaluation seeds) on Terminal-Bench Lite (100 tasks) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (89 tasks), on Qwen3.5-4B. MiRL reaches 51.8±0.1% on TB-Lite and 21.3±0.7% on TB-2.1, versus 47.4±0.9% and 20.6±1.3% for TMax-4B (released checkpoint re-evaluated on the authors' hardware; TMax's published scores were lower, 42.6/19.9), using 35% of TMax-4B's rollouts (26.2K vs. 75.9K), 39% of its GPU hours (202.8 vs. 526.6 A100 hours), and 56% of its total dollar cost ($1,960 vs. $3,522, including $737 in API fees for profiling/judging). Against same-budget baselines on 189 random environments: MiRL beats the best of TMax-189 (43.4/17.6), PivotRL (47.2/19.1), and RaR+ (47.6/19.1) by ≥4.2 points on TB-Lite and 2.2 on TB-2.1. Misbehavior rates on unseen prefixes (16 samples per prefix, two judges) drop for 3 of 4 measured misbehaviors; outcome-reward-only training (TMax-4B) leaves "Makes false claims about tests" nearly unchanged and increases "Prints a binary file as text" ~5× (4.1%→21.9%). Pass@16 on TB-2.1: MiRL 39.3% vs. base 33.7% (base catches up to TMax-4B's 34.8% by k≈11), suggesting capability-raising rather than sharpening. A 16-seed re-evaluation on TB-2.1 preserves the ranking (MiRL 21.14±0.53 vs. TMax-4B 20.22±0.73 vs. RaR+ 19.66±0.62). Scaling from 47 to 378 environments raises TB-Lite from 42.0% to 52.4%. MiRL's reward is sparser than baselines (42.2% dead groups vs. 27.3% for TMax-189 and 0.13% for RaR+), so it trains longer per unit of gain than PivotRL/RaR+, which cost $999 and $770 respectively but score ≥4.2 points lower. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (MiRL recipe) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the concentration statistics — 8 misbehaviors covering 52.1% of error steps — and the demonstration that error-targeted learning transfers to long-horizon terminal tasks). The genuinely new element is using automated error profiling outputs to simultaneously choose rollout starting states and condition the reward; the individual mechanisms — rollouts from intermediate states (R3, PivotRL) and LLM-judged process rewards (RaR, process reward models) — are standard, and the paper says so itself. This is a well-motivated recombination with a new selection principle, not a new algorithmic framework. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: each of the three components (environment selection, prefix start, behavior reward) is added one at a time to TMax-189, with prefix start contributing +7.9 and the behavior reward +6.5 on TB-Lite; the counter-intuitive result that environment selection alone hurts is reported honestly with a mechanism (increased dead-group rate). Standard errors over 3 runs are reported throughout, and the authors go beyond community norms with 16 extra evaluation seeds on TB-2.1 and an unbiased pass@k analysis. Code, checkpoint, data, and evaluation trajectories are released under Apache 2.0/ODC-BY at github.com/runchu-tian/MiRL, with full prompts and hyperparameters in the appendix. Methodological concerns: (1) the final checkpoint is selected by best TB-Lite score, and TB-Lite is also a headline evaluation benchmark — this is checkpoint-selection-on-test and inflates TB-Lite numbers (the effect on TB-2.1 is less clear since selection uses TB-Lite, but the asymmetry between the two benchmarks is suspicious); (2) only one backbone (Qwen3.5-4B); (3) each recipe trained once, so training-run variance is unmeasured; (4) the behavior judge used in training (Gemini 3.8 Flash) is also one of the two misbehavior-measurement judges, though the Qwen judge cross-check mitigates this; (5) TMax-4B's resource totals are partly estimated from published curves rather than measured, so the 35%-rollout efficiency claim mixes measured and reconstructed numbers. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (TMax, PivotRL, RaR are 2026 works, with RaR+ strengthened by the authors for fairness). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in the released pipeline). Practical: Yes — runs on 8×A100 80GB with an open-weights 4B policy; the caveat is dependence on commercial API judges (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5), so full reproduction requires paid API access (~$737). Efficient: 61% fewer GPU hours, 65% fewer rollouts, and 44% lower total cost than TMax-4B up to the best checkpoint, though it is roughly 2× the cost of the weaker PivotRL/RaR+ baselines. Effective: The evidence shows both proxy success (misbehavior rates drop under an independent judge) and task success (higher TB-Lite, matched TB-2.1), plus pass@k evidence against mere sharpening — this is unusually complete causal evidence for an RL paper. Scalable: Only partially tested — the authors run a 0.25×–2× environment-count sweep showing monotone gains to 52.4%/22.1% at 378 environments, but the method's behavior when misbehaviors shift after training (a moving-target problem: the initial profile is stale once the policy improves) is untested, and re-profiling cost at each refresh cycle is not analyzed. The work delivers a software artifact: released code, trained checkpoint, profiling data, and evaluation trajectories. Strengths: - Genuinely closes the loop the paper names: failure taxonomies that previously only diagnosed agents now parameterize the training signal (both the rollout start states and the reward), which is a real conceptual move beyond PivotRL (SFT-trajectory pivots) and RaR (generic rubrics). - The misbehavior-rate evaluation on held-out prefixes with two independent judges is the right experiment for the central claim and is rarely done in agent-RL work; the cross-judge consistency (drops under both Gemini and Qwen judges) rules out the most obvious judge-gaming explanation. - The pass@k analysis directly engages the "RL sharpens rather than teaches" critique with data showing TMax-4B exhibits the sharpening pattern while MiRL does not — a substantive, falsifiable side finding. - Cost accounting is unusually honest: API fees are counted against the method (which uses them and baselines partly do not), TMax's resource numbers are labeled as estimates, and the sparser-reward/dead-group disadvantage versus RaR+ is reported rather than hidden. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state four: (1) single model backbone, so cross-model generalization is unknown; (2) one training run per recipe with only 3-seed evaluation standard errors, which does not capture training-run variance; (3) reliance on external commercial LLMs in error profiling and the rerun check's discarding of non-deterministic environments, which may bias training data; (4) only the conjunction reward combination was tried. These are stated directly and candidly in a dedicated Limitations section — a credibility positive — and item (2) is partially remediated by the 16-seed evaluation study, though not by multiple training runs. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Checkpoint selection on an evaluation benchmark: the best checkpoint is chosen by TB-Lite score, and TB-Lite is also a headline result; this is textbook Goodhart contamination and is not acknowledged. Reporting a selection-free or dev-split-selected number would strengthen the headline claim. - Stale-profile / moving-target problem unexamined: MiRL fixes the eight misbehaviors of the initial policy; whether new misbehaviors dominate after training, and whether a second profiling round yields further gains or diminishing returns, is untested — this is the natural scaling story for the method and is absent. - Single-judge dependence in training: the behavior reward during RL comes solely from Gemini 3.8 Flash; no experiment tests sensitivity to judge choice or judge errors (false accusations of misbehavior would create reward noise). The dual-judge check exists only for measurement, not for the training signal. - Error-localizer precision unknown: no human validation sample of the Qwen3.8-27B localizer's good/bad verdicts is reported; 12,746 "error steps" could include substantial false positives, and the taxonomy statistics inherit that noise. - Comparison budget asymmetry: PivotRL receives ~300 A100 hours matched to TMax-189, but the number of training steps and reward-density differences (0.13% vs. 42.2% dead groups) confound the comparison; the paper notes this but does not run a reward-shaping control for MiRL (e.g., dense judge scores at prefix starts without misbehavior conditioning). - Hardware-dependence of benchmark scores (TMax-4B scoring 47.4 on their hardware vs. 42.6 published) is handled by re-running everything locally, which is good, but it also means the "beats TMax-4B" margin (4.4 points on TB-Lite with ±0.9/±0.1 SEs) rests on a benchmark known to be hardware-sensitive. Bottom Line: A practitioner training terminal agents with limited compute should read and likely try this: the recipe is well-ablated, open-sourced, delivers measured cost savings (44% cheaper than TMax-4B at equal-or-better benchmark scores) with unusually careful verification that the targeted errors actually shrink — but its single-backbone, single-training-run evidence and untested re-profiling loop mean it is a strong recipe candidate, not yet a validated general training principle.

TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents (8 ▲ )

Krishanu Adhikary, Prashant Devadiga · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 29 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TauIndianBankBench, a 1,000-task benchmark for evaluating tool-using conversational agents in Indian retail banking that scores sessions on both final database state and procedural compliance (required read-only calls plus absence of unrequested writes). - Why it's important: Final-state-only scoring understates procedural failures by 6.5–12.0 percentage points per model, meaning agents that skip mandatory steps (e.g., showing a closure quote before an irreversible deposit closure) are wrongly judged safe in regulated banking settings. - How it does it: Each session is scored by two deterministic checks — a final-state check against an oracle replay of the task's gold chain, and an action check requiring every gold-chain call (including reads) plus write purity (no unrequested writes, even if later reverted). - The good: The scorer was validated against an independent re-implementation (identical verdicts on 600 sessions and 705 paired tool calls), four scripted trivial agents pass zero tasks, and complementary-failure analysis with McNemar tests shows neither check subsumes the other. - The missing: The simulated customer (MiniMax-M2.7) shapes every conversation, and its own error rate was never measured, so all reported scores conflate assistant quality with simulator behavior. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or adapting customer-service agents in regulated domains, and essential for benchmark designers choosing between outcome-only and trajectory-aware scoring; skippable for researchers outside agentic evaluation or financial services.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (75) is above average for a benchmark paper: paired re-scoring of identical sessions isolates the scoring rule, McNemar tests establish check complementarity, an independent re-implementation audit shows exact scorer agreement, trivial agents score zero, and code/data are released. Novelty (68) and Non-Obviousness (65) are solid but bounded — the components compose existing τ-bench-family ideas, and the outcome-vs-procedure gap is quantified rather than conceptually deep. Resilience (72) is helped by bounded claims; the unmeasured simulator error rate and unvalidated LM-drafted gold chains keep Completeness (78) from higher. Problem & Motivation:** Indian banks currently serve customers through FAQ pages and scripted chatbots; LLM-based assistants could execute requests (blocking a card, booking a deposit) but only if they follow written bank procedure, where regulation mandates specific steps (RBI 2016 KYC renewal, TDS on deposit interest, statutory eligibility rules). Existing τ-bench-style benchmarks verify only the final database state, and many mandated steps are read-only: in this corpus, 962 of 1,000 tasks require at least one read-only call and 114 require no write at all, so an agent that skips the closure quote, minimum-balance check, or card-status lookup produces identical records and passes. Prior financial benchmarks (FinBen, PIXIU, FinEval) test knowledge and arithmetic, not live servicing under Indian banking rules; trajectory-scoring benchmarks (JourneyBench, TRAJECT-Bench) either cannot verify resulting state or use judge models. Nobody has measured the gap between outcome-scoring and procedure-scoring on the same sessions. Key Idea: The core insight is that a gold chain should include the policy-mandated read-only calls, and that the score should be the conjunction of two complementary checks: (1) gold-chain membership — every required call, in any order, with per-call argument matching — and (2) write purity — every write in the session must correspond to a gold-chain write, failing the session even if the agent reverts the change. This turns a pure outcome metric into a procedure-plus-outcome metric at negligible cost, because the same oracle replay that produces the expected final state also defines the required call set. Methodology: The benchmark runs as a τ²-bench domain: an assistant model converses with an LLM-simulated customer (MiniMax-M2.7 at temperature 0) acting on a fresh copy of a seeded synthetic bank (944 customers with accounts, cards, deposits, loans, mandates, KYC status, transaction history), with a written policy, 24 searchable knowledge-base documents, and 34 tools (21 reads, 13 writes including two non-mutating request tools). Each of the 1,000 tasks across 50 families specifies the customer persona, scenario, and a gold chain (mean 3.54 calls, range 1–6); tasks fall into four categories — sequencing (470), edge-case (266), rare-tool (152), and control (112). Scoring (Algorithm 1) is deterministic: sessions must end normally, the action check verifies gold-chain call membership under argument-matching rules that ignore run-dependent identifiers and free-text fields, write purity rejects unrequested writes, and the final-state check compares normalized record hashes against the oracle replay. Key design decisions: LM-drafted tasks admitted only through four filters (message diversity within a family at ≤40% repetition, ≥3-call chains for graded tasks, train/test disjointness, gold-chain replay passing both checks); no partial credit; numbered customer instructions that force step ordering in graded tasks, making call order task-determined. Tasks were constructed by a language model against the live environment — the paper does not report human review of task or policy correctness. Key Results: Six open-weight models were evaluated on the full 1,000-task base split with one attempt per task and a shared customer simulator: Qwen3.8-27B 0.849, Gemma 4 31B 0.776, 26B-A4B 0.714, 12B 0.699, E4B 0.607, E2B 0.479 (95% Wilson CI ≈ ±3 points). Scoring by final state alone inflates pass rates by 6.5–12.0 points across all six models; for the three strongest models these procedural violations significantly dominate one-check failures (b > c, all p < 10⁻⁸), while for the weakest model (E2B) the reverse holds (p < 10⁻³) — sessions with all required calls but wrong final records — demonstrating the two checks are non-substitutable. Rare-tool tasks are hardest for every model (0.388–0.559 for Gemma; Qwen reaches 0.757); pass rates on control tasks show no trend with model size (0.804–0.929, highest for 12B) while graded categories separate models by size, ruling out a general-capability explanation. Four scripted agents (including one that makes every available change and one that only claims completion) pass zero tasks. Loan tasks show the highest violation rate (20.8% pooled vs. 7.9–10.5% elsewhere), because no loan tool is a write. A second run shifts each Gemma pass rate by ≤2.7 points, but 14–26% of individual tasks change outcome between runs. Missing required writes and missing required reads dominate action-check failures; unrequested writes are least frequent for every model except Qwen3.8-27B. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) a first benchmark for customer servicing under Indian retail-banking procedure, and (b) the empirical quantification of the outcome-vs-procedure scoring gap on identical sessions. The mechanism itself is a competent composition of existing ideas — final-state checking from τ-bench, action matching from τ²-bench, read inclusion and write purity echoing ToolSandbox milestones, AppWorld collateral-damage checks, and JourneyBench zero-tolerance — applied in combination for the first time with both state and action verification, deterministic (non-judge) scoring, and a controlled demonstration of why the combination matters. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a benchmark release. Ablations over scoring rules are effectively the paper's core experiment (re-scoring the same recorded sessions isolates the scoring rule); statistical testing is present (two-sided exact McNemar tests, paired sign tests with p < 0.005, Wilson CIs); a scorer audit shows exact agreement with an independent re-implementation on 600 sessions and 705 paired tool calls, plus exact reproduction of 5,000 session scores and rank stability across a second model-serving setup. Code (github.com/npci/TauIndianBankBench) and data (huggingface.co/datasets/NPCI/tau-indian-banking) are publicly released. Concerns: tasks were LM-drafted and the paper does not report human validation of task or gold-chain correctness against the written policy; results rest on a single customer-simulator model whose fidelity is unmeasured; single attempt per task in headline results, with 14–26% task-level outcome flip between runs indicating high per-task variance; and the benchmark is developed and evaluated entirely within its own environment, so no external grounding for gold chains is available. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus evaluation runs). Practical: Runs against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via the standard τ²-bench harness on commercially available models. Efficient: Expensive — 1,000 live multi-turn conversations of up to 200 steps per run, with both sides LLM-served and pass_k estimates multiplying cost by k; a 200-task lite split is provided for development. Effective: Evidence shows the dual-check score detects procedural violations that outcome-only scoring misses, which is the stated problem; it is still a proxy for deployment safety, as the authors state a pass does not establish bank-readiness. Scalable: Untested — scaling to larger task sets, multiple simulators, or multiple attempts is claimed only through the lite/base split design, not demonstrated. The work delivers a software artifact (benchmark, scorer, harness domain, train/test splits) and released reference results, not just a paper. Strengths: - The paired re-scoring of identical sessions is the right experimental design for the claim being made: the 6.5–12.0-point inflation from final-state-only scoring is attributable purely to the scoring rule, not run-to-run noise. - Validity evidence beyond scores: trivial-agent baselines all score zero (per the agentic-benchmark checklist of Zhu et al.), the control category shows no size trend while graded categories do (excluding a general-capability confound), and the complementarity analysis with McNemar tests establishes that neither check subsumes the other — a genuinely non-obvious empirical finding. - Deterministic scoring with per-call argument-matching rules and normalization avoids the known biases of LLM-judge scoring, and the independent re-implementation audit is unusual rigor for benchmark papers. - Write purity that fails reverted changes (customer was affected while the change was in place) is a subtle and defensible scoring decision most trajectory benchmarks omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) scores depend on both the assistant and the unmeasured-error-rate simulator and hold only for MiniMax-M2.7; (2) all customer data are synthetic, so edge-case frequencies reflect generated records rather than real bank traffic; (3) version 1.0.0 covers Indian retail banking in English only; (4) evaluation is computationally costly (1,000 conversations of up to 200 steps per run). They confront these directly and provide the lite split as mitigation; the acknowledgment of simulator error being unmeasured is candid but the gap itself remains unaddressed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No human validation of the LM-drafted tasks and gold chains is reported; if the policy-to-gold-chain mapping is wrong anywhere, the action check penalizes correct behavior, and the 705-call scorer audit verifies implementation consistency, not task correctness. - The action check accepts gold-chain calls in any order, but ordering is enforced only indirectly through the simulated customer's numbered instructions; an agent served by a different or less cooperative simulator could make calls in a logically invalid order (e.g., closing before quoting) and still pass. - Only one customer-simulator model is tested, so the sensitivity of all rankings to simulator choice — a documented failure mode (Seshadri et al.) — is unquantified. - All evaluated models share a likely-pretraining-overlap-free Indian-banking environment, but no frontier closed-weight model is included, so the reported pass rates say nothing about where the strongest deployable agents would fall. - The paper does not measure inter-annotator or inter-model agreement on what counts as a required step under the written policy, leaving construct validity of "procedure" resting on the authors' encodings. Bottom Line: For anyone building customer-service agents or banking-domain evaluations, this is a well-validated, thoughtfully scored benchmark that convincingly demonstrates outcome-only scoring is insufficient in regulated domains; for others, τ-bench-family familiarity plus the headline finding (6.5–12.0-point inflation) likely covers most of what you need.

VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team (18 ▲ )

Wenbo Hu, Ken Li, Jiazhe Wei, Yukang Cao, Weiyi Hong, Jiayi Dai, Chenjun Bai, Jiajun Liang, Yucheng Liao, Ruichuan An, Zeyu Lou, Haofan Wang, Yueming Lyu, Jingkang Yang, Ziwei Liu, Chenyang Si · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VibeGame, a framework that turns natural-language prompts (and optional reference images) into complete, playable 2D game projects via an AI-native game engine, an eight-role adversarial agent team, and a training-free self-evolution mechanism that distills validated projects into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts. - Why it's important: End-to-end game development is harder than repository-level code generation because code, scenes, art, physics, and configurations must cohere and be verified by interactive play, so the paper targets the gap where vibe-coding agents can build but not reliably play-test and polish games. - How it does it: The core trick is representing the entire game project as schema-validated structured text (a Phaser-based scene-node-asset hierarchy) and exposing frame-synchronous runtime control (pause, step, inspect, inject actions, screenshot), so agents can verify running behavior at their own reasoning pace, with independent reviewer agents adversarially gating acceptance. - The good: On a 30-task GameCraft-Bench subset ported to Phaser, VibeGame with the weaker model (GPT-5.6-Luna, P2G) beats the strongest baseline harness by 11.70 overall points (49.99 vs 38.29), and with GPT-6.1-Sol it beats Codex (P2G) by 4.19 points (72.99 vs 68.80); a blind 30-participant user study (300 judgments) confirms a 72.7% average overall human win rate against all GPT-6.1-Sol baselines. - The missing: The evaluation rests on 30 tasks with an LLM judge (GPT-6.1-Sol) that the authors themselves show changes rankings versus another judge (GPT-5.5), and the strongest model is evaluated by a judge of the same family; self-evolution is also admitted (Appendix H) to sometimes degrade performance across game types without a fix. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build agent harnesses for interactive software generation or want a concrete design for agent-operable engines and multi-agent verification; skippable if you only care about model capability benchmarks, since the artifact is a harness around existing frontier LLMs.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. The AI-native engine interface (schema-validated state plus frame-synchronous runtime control) is a real, transferable contribution, and the Codex-graft ablation (+2.69) plus a 300-judgment blind human study give the claim credible support; Rigor (60) is held back by single-run evaluations, a small 30-task set, and an in-family LLM judge, while Practical Impact (78) benefits from released code and a usable engine artifact. Novelty (70) is solid but the eight-role team is a competent recombination of known patterns, and Completeness (70) is helped by unusually honest negative results (Appendix H). Weighted composite: 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*65 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*65 + 0.30*78 = 70.

Problem & Motivation: Non-programmers can now "vibe code" ordinary software with LLM coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenHands), but games are the hard case: a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, and many defects (broken controls, occluding UI, missing attack tells) emerge only during interactive play, not from static inspection. Existing engine-integrated generators (DreamGarden, AutoUE in Unreal) work around GUI workflows and binary assets that agents cannot consistently inspect or modify; world models like Genie produce no editable source; and agent-native systems like OpenGame limit runtime checks to build-and-run success. The gap the paper closes: no prior system lets agents inspect a structured project state, control execution frame-by-frame, verify behavior adversarially inside the development loop, and carry validated experience forward to future projects. Key Idea: Make the game engine itself "AI-native" — GUI-independent (all project state in plain-text, type-checked JSON scene/node/asset files with schema validation catching invalid references before runtime), runtime-accessible (frame-synchronous programmatic control that converts asynchronous real-time gameplay into a pausable, step-through-verifiable process), and source-available (uncompiled engine source copied into the project so agents read exact APIs). Once this interface exists, an adversarial separation of implementation roles from auditor/player/reviewer roles becomes enforceable, and validated projects can be distilled into reusable priors. Methodology: The framework has three layers. (1) The AI-native engine (built on Phaser 3) stores each game as a collection of scenes whose configurations live in type-checked JSON; nodes group visual appearance, collision geometry, behavior scripts, and configuration; a programmatic interface exposes pause/resume, frame-stepping, runtime property inspection/modification, semantic action injection (e.g., "press jump"), and screenshot capture. (2) The Adversarial Agent Team runs three stages: Intention Alignment (designer expands the request into a Game Design Document; artist generates concept art; both become shared ground truth after user confirmation), Parallel Development (orchestrator decomposes into components, retrieves skeletons/modules/contracts, and pipelines architect → programmer → auditor [static checks] → player [runtime play-testing plus VLM visual assessment]; the artist generates and registers assets via GPT-Image-2 and Nano Banana Pro), and Adversarial Correction (an independent reviewer gates the full project on functionality, visual quality, and playability, rejecting with specific reasons that become repair tasks). (3) Training-free self-evolution distills accepted projects into skeletons (runnable templates with error notes and art packs), modules (attachable behavior scripts with self-checking logic converting past runtime failures into static validation), and contracts (role-by-role coordination documents for recurring features). Design decisions: the three engine properties are well-motivated by named failure modes; the eight-role decomposition is plausible but the exact role count versus a simpler produce/verify split is not ablated; the demo-recording instruction hint added to all harnesses is disclosed and identical across conditions. Key Results: On the 30-task GameCraft-Bench subset (2 tasks × 15 game types, ported to Phaser), with GPT-5.6-Luna, VibeGame (P2G) scores 49.99 overall versus 38.29 for the best baseline (Qwen Code, P2G), leading all four rubric categories (M 58.31, D 43.15, V 39.07, A 57.82). With GPT-6.1-Sol, VibeGame (P2G) scores 72.99 overall vs Codex (P2G) at 68.80 (+4.19), trailing Codex by under one point in Core Mechanics and Functional Visuals but leading by 4.76 in Content Depth and 7.72 in Art & Presentation. VibeGame beats the strongest per-model baseline on 13 of 15 game types. Baselines are current (Codex, Qwen Code, Kimi Code, DeepSeek Harness, OpenGame) under both PA2G and P2G settings with the same underlying model and a 24-hour-per-task budget at xhigh reasoning effort. A blind user study (30 participants, 150 pairs, 300 judgments) gives VibeGame a 72.7% average overall win rate, agreeing with the LLM judge. Ablations (10 tasks): removing the engine costs 10.33 points (53.45 → 43.12), removing the adversarial review roles costs 4.63 (→ 48.82); adding experience evolved by GPT-6.1-Sol to GPT-5.6-Luna adds 2.92 (→ 56.37), suggesting cross-model transfer; grafting the engine onto Codex with GPT-6.1-Sol raises its score 2.69 points (64.44 → 67.13). Counter-intuitive admission: accumulated self-evolution experience can lower performance when the agent develops game types different from the experience source (Appendix H). Surprising finding: with the frontier model, general coding agents already close most of the core-mechanics gap, so VibeGame's value concentrates in content depth and presentation. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the AI-native engine with frame-synchronous agent control) and NEW METHOD (adversarial agent team with runtime-grounded verification; training-free experience distillation into skeletons/modules/contracts). The genuinely novel core is the engine interface design that converts real-time gameplay into agent-verifiable synchronous process; the multi-agent role specialization is a competent combination of existing ideas (ChatDev/MetaGPT role patterns, ReAct-style agents, OpenGame's build-repair loop) applied to a new setting, and self-evolution is a form of skill/memory accumulation without training. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover the three claimed components (engine, adversarial review, experience), including an engine-transfer experiment onto Codex that isolates the engine's contribution — this is the strongest ablation. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; the main table appears to be single-run results despite a 24-hour-per-task budget making repeat runs expensive. Code and project page are released (github.com/tettethu/VibeGame; vibegame.tettet.org). Methodological concerns: (a) judge sensitivity is real — the paper itself shows the GPT-5.5 judge produces different scores and rankings from GPT-6.1-Sol (Table 3 vs Table 1), so absolute numbers and margins are judge-dependent, though VibeGame ranks first under both; (b) the judge model GPT-6.1-Sol is the same model family as the frontier model VibeGame runs on, a possible self-evaluation affinity; (c) the benchmark was ported (Godot → Phaser), the judge replaced, and instructions modified, so results are not comparable to published GameCraft-Bench numbers — the authors disclose this explicitly; (d) the evaluation is demonstrable-only ("your source code is never read"), which structurally rewards demo-maximizing behavior that VibeGame's engine is uniquely positioned to exploit (the added hint encourages showing maximum distinct assets in demos); (e) the test set is 30 tasks and the ablation set only 10. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built engine-plus-agent harness, evaluated on a benchmark and demonstrations, with released code). Practical: Yes — it runs on headless browser containers with commercial LLM/image APIs and the code is open source; the engine is web-based (Phaser), so runtime needs no GPU. Efficient: Expensive — a 24-hour budget per task at xhigh reasoning effort, plus multi-image-generation calls, means per-game costs are far above a single vanilla coding-agent run; the paper gives no token/cost accounting. Effective: The evidence shows it produces demonstrably better playable games under both LLM-judge and human preferences on 2D micro-games; it does not show long-term playability or commercial-grade quality. Scalable: Not tested beyond 20-second, 2D, small-scope games; 3D scenes, larger projects, and the authors' own observation that accumulated experience can degrade cross-genre performance suggest scaling of the self-evolution component is unresolved. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (engine layer, agent workflow, released code), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The AI-native engine design — schema-validated structured project state plus frame-synchronous runtime control — is a real, transferable interface contribution that the Codex-graft experiment (+2.69 points) shows benefits even non-VibeGame harnesses. (2) The evaluation is unusually honest for a systems paper: the authors replace the benchmark's own judge, publish the judge-disagreement cases, and show VibeGame ranks first under both judges. (3) Human preference validation (30 participants, 300 blind judgments) corroborates the LLM judge rather than resting on it. (4) Appendix H's negative result on self-evolution across genres is a candid, useful finding that many papers would have buried. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: scope is 2D only; the framework is unvalidated on 3D scenes or complete commercial games sustaining long-term play; the AI-native principles are implemented on a web-based 2D engine and porting to established engines (e.g., Godot) so agents can operate existing projects remains future work; and self-evolution can degrade performance when developing game types unlike the accumulated experience (Appendix H). This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The judge (GPT-6.1-Sol) is the same model VibeGame runs on in the headline comparison — no judge from a competing vendor or human-only scoring without LLM-judge alignment analysis is provided to rule out judge-model affinity for same-family outputs. (2) The demonstrable-only scoring plus the shared "demo hint" instruction favors a system whose engine is purpose-built for frame-synchronous demo generation; a scoring protocol that also audits source code or requires live human play per feature would test whether quality extends beyond what demos show. (3) No variance reporting: with 30 (main) and 10 (ablation) tasks, margins like +2.92 for the experience ablation could plausibly fall within run-to-run noise; multiple seeds or per-task CIs are absent. (4) The eight-role AAT is never decomposed — the ablation removes auditor/player/reviewer jointly, so the marginal value of the designer/artist/architect orchestration versus a single strong agent with the same engine is unmeasured. (5) The "w/ Experience" ablation substitutes VLM-judge scores for user feedback during evolution, which differs from the claimed production loop. (6) Compute cost and wall-clock comparisons between VibeGame and baselines within the 24-hour budget are not reported, so it is unknown how much of the gain is simply better budget utilization. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agentic code-generation systems — especially anyone designing agent-computer interfaces for interactive software — should read this for the AI-native engine design and the honest negative results, even though the headline ranking gains ride on a small task set, an in-family judge, and single-run evaluations that leave the margin's robustness uncertain.

StructSynth: Dependency Graphs as Generation Plans for Low-Data Tabular Synthesis with Language Models

S Liu, Y Zheng, H Li, Y Zhang · aclanthology.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces StructSynth, a framework that induces a directed dependency graph from scarce tabular data and executes it as a prompt-level generation plan—dictating the order, conditioning context, and scope of each black-box LLM call—for synthetic tabular data generation. - Why it's important: In domains like healthcare and finance, practitioners often have only tens to hundreds of records; synthetic augmentation is only useful if inter-feature dependencies survive, and existing generators either memorize, learn unstable graphs from too few samples, or bury dependencies in flat text serialization. - How it does it: An LLM-guided BFS search fuses statistical association scores (Cramér's V, |Pearson r|, correlation ratio) with LLM semantic rationales to induce a DAG (with LLM-based cycle resolution), and synthesis then proceeds autoregressively in topological layers, conditioning each feature on its graph-specified parents. - The good: The strongest evidence is downstream utility: mean AUC/R² of 75.01 with average rank 1.00 across six datasets versus 73.36 for the best baseline (CLLM) and 71.54 for real-data-only, verified across four evaluator model families (best in 14 of 16 dataset–evaluator combinations), eight LLM backbones, and two post-knowledge-cutoff datasets. - The missing: Margins over the closest baseline CLLM are small relative to reported standard deviations on some settings (e.g., 0.856 vs 0.843 AUC with Qwen2.5-32B, ±0.012/±0.014), no significance testing is reported, and the privacy claim rests on a single nearest-neighbor distance metric rather than any formal disclosure-risk assessment. - Read it or not: Read it if you build LLM-based synthetic-data pipelines for small tabular datasets or work on structure-aware generation—the graph-as-plan idea and honest fidelity/privacy trade-off analysis are directly reusable; skip it if you need large-n synthesis, formal privacy guarantees, or bidirectional dependency modeling.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Completeness (72) is a strength — candid, specific limitations including the non-privacy-guarantee warning and boundary-condition analysis — as is Rigor (70): 10 seeds, the Bayesian-sampler control cleanly isolating that the plan organizes rather than replaces the LLM (−4.4 pts), eight backbones, post-cutoff datasets, and released code. Novelty (72) reflects a genuinely new design point (dependency graph as inference-time prompt plan for a black-box LLM), but missing significance tests and margins within one standard deviation of CLLM keep it out of the top band, and Practical Impact (65) is bounded by API dependence and untested wide-table scaling. Composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*65 ≈ 70.

Problem & Motivation: The paper targets low-data tabular synthesis: given as few as n=20–100 real records, generate additional rows that preserve inter-feature dependencies so downstream ML models actually gain predictive signal. The problem affects healthcare, finance, and education practitioners who cannot collect more data. Prior approaches close only part of the gap: deep generative models (TVAE, CTGAN, TabSyn) learn dependencies implicitly and fail to converge at small n; structure-aware methods (Bayesian networks, GOGGLE, DECAF) rely on graphs that become unreliable under scarcity, so graph errors propagate into generation; LLM methods (GReaT, CLLM, TabGen-ICL) serialize rows as flat text without explicit dependency direction or conditional-independence structure. Recent graph-aware hybrids—PAFT and GraDe (functional-dependency-aware fine-tuning) and SPADA (LLM-annotated graph driving KDE/normalizing-flow samplers)—do not execute a dependency graph as an inference-time plan for a black-box LLM without parameter updates. Key Idea: Treat a dependency DAG as a "generation plan"—the graph's topological layers fix the generation order, each node's parent set defines the conditioning context, and the local subgraph bounds the prompt scope of each black-box LLM call—so discovered conditional dependencies are explicitly enforced rather than incidentally induced by serialized feature order. Enabling this is a second idea: LLM semantic priors act as a structural regularizer on top of statistical association scores during graph induction, stabilizing structure discovery exactly where conditional-independence tests lose power (n≤100). Methodology: Stage 1, Evidence-Grounded Graph Induction: an LLM selects source nodes from few-shot rows (π_source prompt); a BFS loop dequeues each node, computes normalized pairwise association scores (Cramér's V with Bergsma bias correction for categorical pairs, |Pearson r| for continuous–continuous, correlation ratio for mixed), and queries the LLM (π_generate) with the current graph state plus these scores to propose directed successor edges with textual rationales; elementary cycles are detected and the LLM (π_resolve) removes the least-justified edge per cycle, guaranteeing a DAG. Stage 2, Graph-Planned Conditional Synthesis: nodes are partitioned into topological layers; per synthetic row, each layer is generated by one LLM call conditioned on all previously generated values, the local subgraph G[Lᵢ ∪ Γ⁻(Lᵢ)], and few-shot rows (Eq. 4); attributes excluded from the graph are generated in one final call conditioned on graph-based values (Eq. 5). No explicit loss function exists—this is prompt-orchestration, not optimization. Critical design decisions: (1) DAG rather than undirected/mixed structure, justified functionally (autoregressive generation needs a total order) and explicitly disclaimed as non-causal—well-argued in Appendix D; (2) separating discovery from generation so each stage uses different signals—plausible but the interaction is only tested via ablation on one dataset; (3) LLM-as-judge for cycle resolution by rationale strength—unjustified beyond the ablation's aggregate effect. Key Results: On six datasets (Adult, Anxiety, Compas, Salary, Obesity, Churn) at n=100 with 1,000 generated rows and XGBoost as the downstream evaluator, StructSynth scores a mean 75.01 (AUC/R²) with average rank 1.00 across 14 generators, versus CLLM 73.36 (rank 2.83), BN 70.09, GReaT 69.25, TabSyn 69.64, and real-data-only 71.54. Privacy risk (fraction of synthetic records whose nearest real neighbor comes from train; ideal 0.5) averages 50.95 (rank 1.50), while GReaT memorizes at 90.15 and SPADA-NF at 83.70; statistical fidelity is mid-pack (59.52, rank 9.50), which the authors argue is a fidelity–privacy trade-off. Ablations on Adult: removing structure costs 1.6 AUC pts, removing topological order 1.1, removing association scores 1.5, while replacing the LLM generator with a Bayesian sampler over the same graph costs 4.4. On three bnlearn benchmarks with ground-truth DAGs (Asia 8, Child 20, Insurance 27 nodes), StructSynth achieves lowest or near-lowest SHD across n∈{20,50,100,200}, beating FCI, GOGGLE, NoTears, and GraDe especially at n≤50. Gains hold across eight backbones (Llama-4 Maverick +0.028 AUC over CLLM, GPT-4o +0.002) with +31% total token overhead (+57% input, +2.7% output). Baselines are current (TabSyn ICLR'24, CLLM ICML'24, GraDe/SPADA EMNLP'25); notably, gains persist on two post-cutoff datasets, and the Anxiety dataset is explicitly labeled as synthetically generated in its source citation—an unacknowledged wrinkle for a data-scarcity benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: executing a learned dependency graph as a prompt-level plan (order, context, scope) for a black-box, non-fine-tuned LLM—the paper clearly differentiates this from PAFT/GraDe (structure during fine-tuning) and SPADA (graph for statistical samplers, no LLM generation). The components themselves are standard combinations: BFS-based LLM structure discovery exists (Jiralerspong et al. 2024), association-score prompting and LLM cycle resolution are known patterns, and layer-wise conditional generation is classic Bayesian-network sampling re-expressed as prompts; the contribution is the composition and the demonstration that the graph regulates a strong generator rather than replacing it. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed—seven variants isolate both stages, including the crucial Bayesian-Sampler control showing the plan organizes rather than replaces the LLM (−4.4 pts). Experiments repeat 10 times (seeds 42–51) with mean±standard deviation reported, but no significance tests appear, and several margins (e.g., Qwen2.5-32B: 0.856±0.014 vs 0.843±0.012) fall within one standard deviation. Code with reproduction instructions is released at https://github.com/ssui-liu/StructSynth; no model weights (not applicable—black-box APIs). Concerns: the main ablation is on one dataset (Adult) only; evaluation uses the authors' own pipeline end-to-end with a single primary downstream evaluator (XGBoost), though sensitivity across four evaluator families partially mitigates this; the SHD advantage is evaluated on synthetic bnlearn networks sampled from known DAGs, which structurally favors any method whose semantic prior matches these classic textbook networks; LLM-discovered graphs on real datasets have no ground truth, so the qualitative Adult graph comparison (vs a PC-plus-expertise reference) is the only real-data structural check. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a prompting framework with experiments; no new model is trained). - Practical: Yes—runs on any commercial LLM API (GPT-4o-mini, Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek all tested) with XGBoost downstream; no training infrastructure needed. - Efficient: Moderate—+31% total token overhead over CLLM (219.8K→287.9K tokens average), input-dominated (+57% input vs +2.7% output), which the authors correctly note reduces monetary cost since input tokens are typically cheaper. - Effective: The evidence supports improved downstream utility and privacy ranking at n≤200 on six datasets, but only via proxy metrics (AUC/R², pairwise fidelity, nearest-neighbor privacy)—no formal privacy guarantee or human/data-validation assessment. - Scalable: Not tested—evaluation caps at n=200 and 27-node graphs (Insurance); behavior on wide tables (hundreds of columns) or dense dependency structures, where BFS fan-out and prompt scope could explode, is unexamined; the authors explicitly leave larger n untested. The work delivers a software artifact (public GitHub repository with prompts and reproduction instructions) but depends on non-deterministic commercial APIs, which the authors flag as a reproducibility risk. Strengths: - The graph-as-generation-plan abstraction is a clean, genuinely new point in the design space between fine-tuned structure-aware generators (PAFT/GraDe) and statistical samplers on LLM-annotated graphs (SPADA): it requires no parameter updates and keeps structure discovery decoupled from generation. - The evaluation anticipates the obvious contamination objection by including two post-cutoff datasets (Anxiety, Salary) and by showing gains persist under schema anonymization (utility 0.865→0.850 on Anxiety), plus eight-backbone generalization with backbone-dependent effect sizes that behave sensibly (largest gains for mid-capability models). - The ablation separating "plan organizes the generator" from "plan replaces the generator" (Bayesian Sampler, −4.4 pts) is the intellectually honest control many LLM-synthesis papers omit, and the K.1/K.2 discussion explicitly reconciles high utility with mediocre pairwise fidelity. - The +31% token-overhead analysis decomposed into input vs output is rare and practically useful for cost planning. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly state three: (1) evaluation only covers n≤200, so advantage at larger samples is untested; (2) the DAG formulation cannot represent cyclic or bidirectional dependencies (e.g., reciprocal economic indicators) and must approximate them unidirectionally; (3) reliance on commercial LLM APIs raises cost and reproducibility concerns since API updates may change discovered structures. The Ethical Considerations section adds that StructSynth is not a formal privacy mechanism and that prompts containing real rows may leak data to providers. This is a credibility positive: the limitations are specific, and Appendix K.3 additionally identifies boundary conditions (opaque feature names, dense non-DAG structures) where the method should degrade—unusually candid. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Missing significance testing throughout; several headline comparisons (Qwen2.5-32B post-cutoff results, GPT-4o backbone +0.002) are within one standard deviation, yet are presented as consistent directional evidence. - The main ablation table covers only Adult; whether the component contributions (association scores, topological order, cycle resolution) transfer to other datasets is not shown. - The SHD evaluation on bnlearn networks (Asia, Child, Insurance) structurally favors LLM semantic priors, since these textbook medical networks are exactly the kind of canonical variable relationships in pre-training data—a dogs-not-barking omission is any real-world dataset with a known ground-truth graph or expert-validated structure. - The Anxiety dataset's own source citation describes it as "synthetically generated," which undercuts its use as a real low-data benchmark even if post-cutoff; this is never acknowledged. - Cycle resolution relies on LLM judgment of rationale quality with no measurement of how often cycles occur or whether the LLM picks the correct edge to remove. - Privacy is assessed by a single DCR-style nearest-neighbor metric; membership-inference or attribute-inference attacks—the standard bar for synthetic-data privacy claims—are absent, so "best privacy-risk ranking" should not be read as a privacy guarantee. - No comparison of generation wall-clock/latency against SPADA-NF, whose stated selling point is sampling speed; StructSynth's per-row multi-call loop could be orders of magnitude slower at scale. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing small-n tabular augmentation gains concrete, well-controlled evidence that an explicit dependency graph used as an inference-time prompt plan beats flat serialization and classical structure learning—but should verify the modest CLLM margins on their own data, budget for ~31% extra tokens and slow autoregressive sampling, and never mistake the privacy ranking for a privacy guarantee.

HarnessMM: Recursive Self - Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency

Y Jiang, C Xu, F Gao, L Zhao · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HarnessMM, a harness-level controller that stores a reasoning model's already-resolved future actions (with literal arguments and public guards), re-executes them when tool receipts satisfy their guards, and thereby substitutes native tool execution for repeated reasoning callbacks — reducing actor tokens by up to ~88% on coding benchmarks at preserved or improved success rates. - Why it's important: Agent harnesses (ReAct-style loops, Codex, etc.) repeatedly re-invoke the LLM after every tool result even when the next action was already decided, and token cost is the dominant operating expense for deployed agents; any method that removes redundant reasoning calls without hurting success directly cuts inference bills. - How it does it: The core trick is separating semantic resolution (slow reasoning fixes action + literal arguments once) from execution readiness (cheap CPU-checkable guards over observed tool receipts), packaged as Executable Decision Graphs (EDG), Guarded Decision Reuse (GDR), and Certified Callback Substitution (CCS), with receipt-bound certificates auditing that a registered slow call was actually omitted. - The good: The MBPP ablation cleanly isolates the mechanism (full 13.17k Tokens/task vs. 18.03k single-use-graph and 16.37k retained-callback conditions), and complete-task accounting charges authorship, selector, fallback, and failures — addressing the paper's own named 'Substitution Paradox'. - The missing: The integrated harness results conflate EDG/GDR/CCS with context management and finalization edits; the mechanism ablation's correctness intervals all include zero, and one condition (EDG disabled) actually scores higher accuracy (95.33% vs. 93.77%) at moderately higher cost; no head-to-head against ReWOO, LLMCompiler, Voyager, or ActionEngine is run. - Read it or not: Worth reading for agent-systems engineers building token-efficiency or fast/slow harness layers, because the resolved-vs-ready decomposition and complete-cost accounting discipline are directly reusable; skippable if you only want evidence of superiority over existing executable-planning systems, which the paper explicitly does not provide.
