Problem & Motivation Agent harnesses connect LLM reasoning to tool execution, and after each tool result they must decide whether the observation demands new reasoning or merely permits an already-decided action to run. In practice the harness re-invokes the reasoning model at nearly every boundary, regenerating decisions whose semantics have not changed — e.g., after writing a program, the compile command is already fixed, and after a successful compile, the test command is fixed. Existing efficiency work splits into prompt/context compression (LLMLingua, AgentDiet, trajectory reduction), fast–slow routing (Talker–Reasoner, CogRouter), and reusable programs/skills (Voyager, ActionEngine, ReWOO, LLMCompiler), but these either shrink individual calls or add a fast stage without removing the slow callback. The paper names this accounting failure the 'Substitution Paradox': a fast path saves tokens only when eliminated reasoning exceeds the added authorship, selection, and recovery cost, and prior systems rarely verify that elimination. The affected audience is anyone operating LLM agents where token cost is the binding constraint. Key Idea The core insight is that a decision becomes 'resolved' when prior reasoning has fixed its action and literal arguments; only execution readiness remains unknown until tool feedback arrives. Such resolved decisions can persist across feedback boundaries as guarded executable commitments: an EDG node stores (action, literal args, predecessor, public guard g: S_public → {true,false}), a receipt-checked eligibility predicate activates it (predecessor completed ∧ guard true ∧ args closed), and executing it through the native interface with a certificate binding (graph hash, decision id, predecessor receipt, exact args, tool receipt, bypassed callback id) proves a slow call was omitted. Crucially, guards consume only observed receipts — never predictions — and any new semantic decision, unsupported evidence, or selector abstention falls back to the original slow actor with fixed weights. Methodology The formulation fixes actor parameters θ and an existing harness h, unrolls execution into a computation graph with per-node model-token costs C(π) = E[Σ 1{v invoked} c_v], and optimizes min C(π) subject to capability regret R_b(π) = Q_b(h₀) − Q_b(h_π) ≤ ε_b against the original harness on the same tasks. Runtime follows a six-step loop: register the parent callback and ingest the public receipt; build the eligible set from unresolved nodes with completed dependencies, passing guards, and closed literal arguments; route deterministically if exactly one node is eligible, or via a Jev-style typed selector returning a candidate ID or abstention (single-token decoding when a model call is needed); execute the literal args through the original tool interface and emit an omission certificate only after verifying execution and absence of the registered slow request; otherwise invoke the slow actor, which may author a new graph; repeat under benchmark limits. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) runs orthogonally: training feedback proposes edits to companion harness configurations (instructions, context settings, finalization), disjoint validation selects among frozen candidates, and the winner is frozen before test. Critical design decisions: (1) literal-argument closure enforced by schema and candidate-membership checks — justified syntactically, but semantic correctness of the authored action remains an assumption measured only by task scoring (the paper states this explicitly, Eq. 12); (2) per-node guards authored at graph-creation time — reasonable, but a passing guard proves only its declared public condition, not task correctness; (3) complete-episode token accounting (Eq. 8) charging authorship, selection, fallback, and failed executions — well-justified and unusually honest, with development cost amortized separately (Eq. 9). Key Results All comparisons share one backbone (DeepSeek-flash), pinned harness versions (Codex CLI 0.142.5, DeepSeek Harness dsh-v0.2.0-rc.1), original tools, and scorer. On HumanEval (n=98): Codex preserves 90.82% success while Tokens/task fall 66.72k→47.02k (29.54% saving; 18 certified bypasses; McNemar p=1, i.e., no significant quality change); DeepSeek Harness rises 71.43%→85.71% while Tokens/task fall 96.28k→11.62k (87.93% saving; 147 bypasses; McNemar p=0.016). On MBPP-sanitized (n=257): DeepSeek 90.27%→91.83% at 53.98k→10.61k (80.35% saving, 472 bypasses); Codex slightly degrades 91.83%→90.66% at 129.55k→49.22k. The mechanism ablation (257 MBPP tasks, shared backbone): full HarnessMM 93.77% at 13.17k vs. w/o GDR (single-use EDG) 93.00% at 18.03k (26.91% cost saving, interval [4.01, 45.57]%) and w/o CCS (callbacks retained) 93.39% at 16.37k (19.52% saving, interval [−2.07, 38.68]%); disabling EDG execution yields 95.33% at 16.19k — HarnessMM uses 18.62% fewer tokens but solves four fewer tasks, and all three correctness intervals include zero. Companion configuration studies are mixed: on GAIA2 (480 scenarios) HarnessMM reaches 43.96% at 639.64k vs. No Skill 42.71%/730.22k but 2.92 points below SkillOpt; on AIME (560 questions) HarnessMM costs 5.90k vs. 4.59k for No Skill and scores below AutoSaddler (87.14% vs. 88.04%) — a negative result the authors report faithfully. MiniWoB++ RSI iterations show success rising 34.38%→90.63% over eight training-guided rounds with tokens falling 67.43%. Baselines are current within the harness-pair framing, but no external executable-planning baseline (ReWOO, LLMCompiler, Voyager, ActionEngine) is run. Scale is standard (tens to hundreds of tasks per benchmark), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the resolved-vs-ready decomposition with immutable literal arguments and receipt-activated public guards as a harness-level substitution contract, (b) receipt-bound certificates that structurally verify a registered slow callback was omitted, and (c) the Substitution Paradox framing with complete-cost accounting that prior fast/slow work ignores. The EDG itself is a standard acyclic executable action graph; GDR's eligibility logic and typed selection are competent combinations of known ideas (guard evaluation, abstaining selectors, program caching from Voyager/ReWOO/LLMCompiler), and RSI is a straightforward train/validate/freeze loop over configurations. The paper's own Appendix D.4 concedes this lineage. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are present and specifically designed to isolate persistence (w/o GDR) and callback removal (w/o CCS), though the certificate's independent benefit is not ablated. Uncertainty is handled unusually well for this area: task-paired bootstrap intervals with Bonferroni adjustment over contrasts, exact McNemar tests, floorplan-cluster intervals for ALFWorld, and explicit separation of task-level from run-to-run variation (single execution per task is acknowledged as a limitation). Development/validation/test splits are custom 20/20/60 (HumanEval 33/33/98, MBPP 85/85/257) with frozen selection; a pre-registered all-outcomes reporting rule is stated and negative results (AIME, GAIA2 dev, industrial RSI searches that rejected both candidates) are published. Methodological concerns: (1) the ablation originally reported (Appendix E.1, Table 5) showed the single-use control with slightly higher correctness and lower cost than full HarnessMM — the revised five-condition comparison in Table 3 reverses this, and the flip-flop across seeds/repairs is a fragility signal; (2) all benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, ALFWorld, SearchQA, AIME) are previously exposed public data with custom repartitions, acknowledged by the authors; (3) the headline 87.93% saving rests on an unusually weak DeepSeek Harness baseline (71.43% success, 96.28k tokens/task); (4) internal consistency checks exist (e.g., a TRAIN audit showing the v20 bank arm costs 79.68% more than baseline), which is a credibility positive. No public code URL is given; 'external reproduction artifacts' are referenced but their availability is not stated in the provided text. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a controller method run on real harnesses and benchmarks; no theorems, and no deployed production system). Practical: Yes — the controller runs on unmodified official Codex/DeepSeek Harness runtimes with a task adapter, CPU-executable guards, and at most single-token selector calls; no special hardware. Efficient: Substantial per-episode token reductions (29–88% on coding tasks), but savings are workload-dependent — on AIME the added input plus shared authorship makes HarnessMM 28.34% more expensive than No Skill, exactly the paradox the paper names. Effective: The evidence shows preserved/improved benchmark success with lower cost on coding tasks, but the certificate proves only call omission, not that the omitted call would have produced the same trajectory; correctness gains are within noise in the cleanest ablation. Scalable: Not tested beyond ~2,133-task ALFWorld and 480-scenario GAIA2; the adapter is task-specific (authors state 'public-state adapters are task specific'), so 100× generalization requires re-authoring adapters, and no experiment demonstrates this. The work stops at paper form plus referenced (non-public, as far as the text shows) reproduction artifacts; no library or trained-model release is stated. Strengths - The resolved-vs-ready separation is a real conceptual contribution: it gives a principled answer to when an agent may skip a reasoning call, distinct from compression (shrink a call) or routing (who reasons). - Receipt-bound substitution certificates turn an unfalsifiable efficiency claim ('we skipped reasoning') into a structurally auditable event, and the paper refuses to treat certificate validity as correctness evidence — a level of claim discipline rare in agent-efficiency work. - Complete-task accounting with separately amortized development cost, all-failures-included denominators, and pre-declared tolerance ε_b directly operationalizes the Substitution Paradox critique of prior fast/slow systems. - Negative and null results are reported in the main text and figures (AIME cost regression, w/o-EDG accuracy gain, rejected industrial RSI candidates), which materially raises confidence in the positive coding results. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The limitations section states: savings depend on provider input/cache accounting and on the availability of resolved actions; new semantic decisions always require slow reasoning; authorship, selection, and recovery can outweigh avoided calls; public-state adapters are task specific; and small development sets leave policy-level quality differences uncertain. Appendix D further concedes that guards prove declared conditions, not task correctness, that there is no statewise correctness guarantee, and that the paper does not compare against executable-planning systems experimentally. The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive. They also correctly separate companion-configuration studies (instructions, context) from the core mechanism and label each figure's evidence scope. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The headline industrial results are confounded: the Codex and DeepSeek Harness pairs bundle literal-bank reuse with context management and finalization changes, so the 87.93% HumanEval saving cannot be attributed to EDG/GDR/CCS from those rows alone; the clean ablation exists but shows no significant correctness effect and a competitor condition (EDG disabled) with higher accuracy. - Inconsistency across ablation versions (Appendix E.1's five-condition study vs. Table 3) — where the same contrasts change sign between studies — is not discussed, leaving the mechanism's cost benefit fragile across seeds and repair procedures. - The DeepSeek HumanEval baseline (71.43% at 96.28k tokens/task) is dramatically weaker than its own MBPP baseline (90.27% at 53.98k); no explanation is given for why the unmodified harness is so inefficient there, inflating the relative saving. - Single backbone family (DeepSeek-flash, plus Qwen/MiMo variants in companion studies) means no evidence of interaction effects with stronger or frontier actors, and guard quality under tool non-determinism or noisy receipts is untested. - No latency or energy measurement despite token savings being the proxy; the authors note this but it remains unaddressed. - The RSI component — the paper's title — is the least supported: the MiniWoB++ curve is training-set performance over eight iterations, not held-out RSI gains, and the industrial RSI searches rejected both candidates in both arms. Bottom Line A practitioner building agent harnesses should read this for the resolved-vs-ready contract, the certificate pattern, and the cost-accounting discipline — all directly portable — while treating the headline savings as workload- and baseline-dependent, since the cleanest ablation shows the method trades accuracy for cost on some settings and no comparison against ReWOO/LLMCompiler-class systems is offered.

CRM- Agent -Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments

M Banerjee, Z Lan, D Cao · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CRM-Agent-Bench, an execution-grounded benchmark of 555 stateful, multi-turn CRM tasks across nine business domains, where success is the strict conjunction of task-specific executable contracts covering actions, arguments, ordering, response content, target state, and forbidden effects. - Why it's important: Agents that mutate systems of record cause real business damage when they claim success without executing correctly or violate policy, and prior CRM benchmarks grade answer/retrieval quality rather than whether the underlying state change was carried out correctly and within policy. - How it does it: Each task declares a conjunctive contract over six check families graded on the recorded trace and terminal database state, with only response-content checks delegated to a fixed LLM judge that cannot override programmatic checks, plus on-policy user simulation and separated reporting of outcome, trajectory, cost/latency, and policy compliance. - The good: The quantified "saying vs. doing" gap is the strongest evidence: response-only grading overestimates strict success by 10.5–11.0 percentage points, and a documented trace shows a duplicated checkout passing response, action, and ordering checks while failing only the state check (loyalty balance 310 instead of 155). - The missing: The headline leaderboard uses a single run per task while the top eight systems sit within a 2.88-point band on 555 tasks, so most rank distinctions among leading systems are within run-to-run noise the authors only partially address in a three-round appendix. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or procure enterprise agents and need a template for contract-based execution evaluation; skip it if you only need answer-quality CRM evaluation, which CRMArena-Pro already covers.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Completeness (78) is the standout — direct, specific limitation acknowledgment (single-run snapshot, judge false negative, cache-neutral cost accounting) raises credibility. Novelty (70) rests on the conjunctive executable contract gating actions, ordering, state, and forbidden effects, which no surveyed benchmark combines. Rigor (68) is solid: three-round reliability analysis with SDs and rank correlations, released code with gold-path validation, careful measurement hygiene — but the vendor-authored self-run evaluation, unquantified simulator confound, and untested scaffold-agnosticism claim cap it. Resilience (68) and Impact (70) reflect honest leaderboard framing and an affordable, reusable artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*70 = 70.
empirical Novelty 70 Rigor 68 Non-Obv 65 Completeness 78 Resilience 68 Impact 70
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Once a language agent receives authority to update a system of record, failures become consequential business events: a refund claimed but never executed, a coupon applied to the wrong account, or a forbidden action on protected customer state. Prior benchmarks each cover a slice — BFCL (function calling), τ-bench/τ²-bench (on-policy dialogue over mutable databases), ToolSandbox (milestones/minefields), AppWorld (programmatic state checks), CRMArena/CRMArena-Pro (CRM retrieval and answer correctness) — but none jointly gate outcome, trajectory, policy compliance, and operational viability. The paper's motivating example (Figure 1) shows a real trajectory where response-only or action-only grading scores a failed, duplicated transaction as success. The target audience is enterprises deploying agent systems in CRM and adjacent SaaS workflows, where the cost of a silent wrong transaction exceeds the cost of a wrong answer. Key Idea: The core trick is the per-task conjunctive executable contract: each task declares only the checks applicable to it, drawn from six families (expected actions, argument constraints, ordering, semantic response, target state, and forbidden actions/arguments/state), and success is the strict product of declared checks — a persuasive reply cannot offset a missing transaction, and undeclared dimensions are absent rather than counted as passes. This single mechanism instantiates three of the four evaluation facets (outcome via response+state, trajectory via actions+arguments+ordering, policy compliance via forbidden-action/argument/state checks) while latency and cost are reported alongside rather than folded into the pass criterion. Methodology: Each task Ti = (ui, s0_i, Ci, di) induces a finite-horizon POMDP over a resettable synthetic CRM environment with typed tools (61 graph nodes, 122 canonical tool contracts across nine domains). The evaluation pipeline is: (1) fresh environment reset per trial; (2) an on-policy user simulator (gpt-5-mini, temperature 0) that generates each turn conditioned only on the agent's user-visible reply — not hidden state, tool calls, or results — with a 30-turn cap and 1,200-second timeout; (3) a graph-routed reference agent in which a per-turn classifier exposes exactly one capability node with scoped tools running a ReAct loop (≤10 iterations), plus a deterministic refusal route; (4) a conjunctive grader over four frozen evidence channels (dialogue, route log, tool trace, terminal state) applying only the task's declared checks; programmatic checks are authoritative, and the fixed LLM judge sees only user instruction and visible replies for semantic-response criteria. The objective is Yi = ∏_{c∈Di} c(τi, xT) ∈ {0,1}. Critical design decisions: (a) conjunctive rather than averaged scoring — well justified by the cascade analysis (Figure 6) showing each added check family removes tasks; (b) simulator sees only visible replies — sound for measurement hygiene but creates a simulator-dependence the paper discusses (Appendix E) without quantifying; (c) undeclared-checks-are-absent semantics — prevents artificial score inflation and is explicitly argued. Key Results: Sixteen systems were evaluated on the audited 555-task set with zero infrastructure exclusions. Strict success spans 64.32% (Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B, GPT-4.1 Nano) to 83.60% (Gemini 3.8 Flash, 464/555), with eight systems compressed into 80.72–83.60% and three tying exactly at 81.26% (451/555). Response-only grading overestimates strict success by 10.5–11.0 pp; the action check alone removes 45–50 of 555 tasks for the four systems in the cascade analysis. On the 165 policy-constrained tasks, systems pass applicable negative checks on 91.2% of 2,640 trials but the full contract on only 66.8%, versus 82.1% on the 390 tasks without negative assertions — compliance and completion are distinct axes. Customer support is the hardest domain (across-model mean 56.35%, 20.80 pp below travel at 77.15%), and domain leadership reshuffles rankings (Muse Glimmer 30B, 12th overall, is the sole strongest on customer support at 68.00%). Cost spans 89.3× ($2.14 for GPT-4.1 Nano to $191.00 for Claude Opus 5); Gemini 3.8 Flash is the sole Pareto-optimal point (83.60% at $16.12, 24.0k tokens/task). Three-round reliability: Gemini 3.8 Flash ranks first every round (mean 85.53%, SD 1.66 pp, pass³ = 78.20%); Spearman rank correlations across rounds are 0.869–0.934, but nearby systems exchange positions. Every system declines monotonically easy→hard (within-model drop 5.37–27.39 pp). Baselines are current frontier and open-weight systems evaluated under one frozen protocol, so comparisons are internally consistent, though the leaderboard is a single-run snapshot. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely novel element is the task-specific conjunctive executable contract that jointly gates required actions, ordering, resulting state, and prohibited effects, with component evidence retained for diagnosis and four facets reported separably — no surveyed benchmark (Table 1) combines on-policy users, agent-mutated state, required and no-extra final effects, forbidden trace events, trace-order enforcement, and a process-outcome hard gate. The ingredients are largely standard: on-policy simulation follows τ-bench, stateful environments and programmatic checks follow ToolSandbox/AppWorld, and the graph-routed reference agent is conventional ReAct-style orchestration; the concurrent EnterpriseOps-Gym targets a similar setting, and this paper's differentiation rests specifically on the conjunctive multi-family contract. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is present: the Figure 6 cascade shows how much each check family contributes, the Figure 14 grader matrix decomposes failure modes (action mismatch is the largest non-success category for all 16 runs, 54–157 tasks), and Appendix C reports three rounds with per-round scores, sample SDs (0.52–2.06 pp), Spearman correlations, and pass³. No significance tests are reported — the authors explicitly frame the leaderboard as descriptive, which is honest given one trial per task. Code and benchmark artifacts are released (GitHub: https://github.com/salesforce-misc/crm-agent-bench; project page: https://crm-agent-bench.github.io/), with release gates, gold-path validation, and content-addressed locks. Methodological concerns: (a) the benchmark is vendor-authored and all evaluations are self-run (Salesforce), though the tested systems span competitor families; (b) the reference scaffold is a fixed graph-routed agent, so reported scores measure model-in-scaffold — the paper claims the protocol is agent-agnostic but never evaluates an alternative orchestration to show scaffold insensitivity; (c) difficulty labels are author-assigned descriptive strata, not validated externally; (d) a documented judge false negative (Case D.2: contradiction_found=false despite an intermediate self-contradiction) shows the semantic judge is imperfect, but no aggregate judge-error rate is estimated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark with systems actually run, producing a reusable artifact). Practical: Yes — it runs entirely on synthetic state without a live CRM or vendor backend, using commercial APIs or self-hosted open-weight checkpoints. Efficient: Full-suite evaluation costs $2.14–$191.00 per system for 555 tasks (13 priced runs, cache-neutral list-price accounting excluding simulator/judge usage), so per-system evaluation is affordable even at the top end. Effective: It demonstrably measures execution integrity (the response-only vs. strict gap, the duplicate-checkout state catch), but the evidence that this proxies real deployed-CRM outcomes is construct-argument, not measured — no correlation with production metrics or human judgment is provided. Scalable: The extension interface (declarative YAML tasks, pluggable ToolEnvironments, four-step release gates) is designed for growth and 10× task counts look feasible, but contract authoring and per-domain grader maintenance are human costs the paper does not quantify. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: a runnable benchmark, environments, grader, audit script, and per-trace evidence files. Strengths: (1) The conjunctive-contract formulation is a real conceptual contribution — the Figure 1 duplicate-checkout case and the 10.5–11.0 pp response-only inflation quantify, rather than assert, the gap between saying and doing. (2) Measurement hygiene is unusually careful: the simulator sees only visible replies, the LLM judge cannot override programmatic checks and must cite verbatim evidence spans, undeclared checks are absent rather than passed, and model-attributable failures (hallucinated tools, verified non-convergence) stay in the denominator while infrastructure failures are excluded. (3) The multi-axis reporting exposes information a single headline number hides — the 89.3× cost spread at near-identical accuracy, per-domain leadership reshuffles, and the compliance-vs-completion split (91.2% negative-check pass vs. 66.8% full contract) are each actionable procurement findings. (4) Honest reliability analysis: the paper volunteers that a five-task lead (0.90 pp) separates ranks 1–2, that nearby systems swap positions across rounds, and that 30 of Gemini's task outcomes flip between two executions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the leaderboard is a single-run snapshot with descriptive (non-significance) comparisons; that three self-hosted open-weight runs have no metered cost ("n/a", explicitly not zero-cost); that cost accounting is cache-neutral list-price and excludes simulator/judge usage; that the capability-exposure audit is static (graph-wide reachability), with turn-level and attempted-behavior analysis planned but not reported; that difficulty labels are descriptive author strata; that Case D.2 exposes a judge false negative; that the semantic judge and simulator both use gpt-5-mini as a fixed instrument with sensitivity discussed in Appendix E; and (Appendix E, scope paragraph) that the benchmark covers controlled headless structured-tool workflows, with document-rich, visual, voice, and live-service workflows deferred to future extension. This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted directly and specifically rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (a) The simulator is a confound the paper never quantifies: all sixteen systems face the same gpt-5-mini user, and Case C shows simulator credential drift contributing to a timeout failure — no experiment varies the simulator to measure how scores move, despite citing SimulatorArena/RealUserSim work on simulator fidelity. (b) The "agent-agnostic protocol" claim is untested: all results come from the authors' graph-routed scaffold, and no alternative orchestration (flat tool list, different router) is evaluated to show conclusions transfer. (c) With 555 tasks, one task = 0.18 pp; the top-eight 2.88-point band spans ~16 tasks, and the three-round data show rank swaps among exactly those systems — the paper reports this but still presents the single-round ranking as the headline leaderboard. (d) Gold-path validation establishes executability of positive paths, but the paper concedes semantic and negative checks "still require their focused tests" — no reported validation of contract correctness beyond the reference agent passing. (e) No human-expert performance anchor and no external-validity check against real CRM outcomes. (f) Sales (18 tasks) and Marketing (21 tasks) domains are small enough that single-task flips move domain rankings, which the paper notes only in passing. Bottom Line: For anyone specifying, building, or buying enterprise agents, this is worth reading: the conjunctive-contract evaluation pattern and the quantified say/do and compliance/completion gaps are directly reusable and expose failure modes answer-quality benchmarks structurally miss — with the caveat that it is a vendor-authored preprint whose leaderboard precision among top systems is thinner than its four-facet framing implies.

Compiling Autoregressive LLM Control into Policy-Exact Parallel Inference for Hierarchical RAG

Z Lin, Q Shen, X Hao, S Cui, C Li, K Chen, B Tang… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a compilation technique that executes a grammar-constrained autoregressive LLM controller for hierarchical RAG as one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe forward pass, provably reproducing the serial greedy policy in exact arithmetic while decoding zero output tokens. - Why it's important: LLM controllers in structured pipelines currently face a three-way trade-off between error-prone free-form JSON (3–65% protocol failures), memoryless single-token scoring, and serial grammar-constrained decoding whose critical path scales with emitted tokens; this removes the serial latency penalty without giving up the history-dependent policy. - How it does it: The reachable future of a bounded-horizon (n≤3) constrained controller is a shallow action-prefix tree, which is evaluated in a single forward pass under a block-causal mask with serial position indices so each prefix state sees exactly the tokens, positions, and causal ancestry it would see under serial decoding — an equivalence proven by induction over layers (Lemma 1, Theorem 1). - The good: Evaluation across four document-disjoint QASPER splits, two model scales, and two accelerators shows 84–89% exact action-sequence agreement with the serial controller, with all 39 instrumented divergences confined to slots whose decision margin falls within the floating-point flip window predicted by Corollary 1, plus 35–47% control-latency reduction. - The missing: The only quality metric is evidence-coverage (AllEvidence@B) on QASPER — a single, small (60–120 question), scientific-paper dataset — and on the two fresh splits the compiled policy actually trails serial by 2.4 points (CI [−4.9, −0.4]), so the practical-quality parity claim rests substantially on non-fresh splits and an fp32 fallback. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building constrained-decoding or agentic-control serving stacks — the prefix-tree compilation idea and the honest floating-point divergence analysis generalize beyond hierarchical RAG — but quality-focused RAG researchers will find the evaluation too narrow to transfer conclusions directly.

Problem & Motivation: In hierarchical RAG, an LLM repeatedly traverses a document tree, selecting b of k ≤ 20 candidate sections per frontier; deployed systems execute this controller by autoregressive text decoding. This creates a three-way dilemma: free-form JSON output dominates the error budget (3–65% of questions fail on syntax, identifier, or cardinality errors per the authors' companion interface study); scoring all k single-token labels in one prefill (the "unary shortcut") removes protocol errors but destroys history-dependence, so selection cannot condition on earlier selections; and grammar-constrained decoding preserves both but pays one dependent forward pass per emitted token (n + m_syn ≈ 9 forwards for n = 3). The paper argues this serial bottleneck is an artifact of the execution model, not of the controller, and affects anyone deploying finite-action LLM controllers (tool selection, routing, agenda selection). Key Idea: The core insight is that a constrained greedy controller with horizon n has a bounded, enumerable reachable future — once the first action is fixed, at most k prefix states remain — so the action grammar can be compiled into its full prefix tree and all prefix-conditioned action distributions evaluated in one tree-causal forward pass. Because each tree row attends to the identical key/value set, token ids, and serial position ids it would have under serial decoding, the logits are arithmetically identical (up to floating-point reduction order), and the greedy chain is recovered by argmax rather than approximated or distilled. Serial depth (n + m_syn forwards) is exchanged for bounded parallel width Θ(N(k,n)) probe rows. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Root prefill: one pass over the prompt plus forced opening syntax produces slot-1 logits and a shared KV cache; a₁ resolves by greedy argmax over admissible-label masks. (2) Tree-causal probe: all N(k,n) = Σ₍d=0..n−2₎ (k−1)!/(k−1−d)! prefix continuations (each the exact forced token sequence serial decoding would emit) are concatenated into one query of a few hundred tokens and evaluated in a single forward under a block-causal mask; the last position of each row yields that prefix's action distribution. (3) Certified set inference: the probe exposes joint preferences, enabling exact order-marginalized posterior P(S|x) = Σ_σ ∏ₜ p(σₜ|x,σ₍<t₎) over permutations, with a branch-and-bound MAP certificate (unexpanded prefixes bound completions by P(ρ); expand ordered pairs until the lower bound of the best set exceeds all other upper bounds) and a Pinsker-based bound |E[PAR u] − E[PU u]| ≤ √(I_seq/2) on the expected-utility cost of the unary shortcut, where I_seq = KL(P_AR ∥ P_PU) is computable in closed form from the probe. The formal framework is layer-wise induction (prefix-state equivalence → policy equivalence under matched masks, candidate order, and first-maximum tie-breaking) plus a margin-stability corollary flagging flips within 2ε_max. Critical design decisions: replicating the trunk across probe rows so attended KV sets coincide (justified by the equivalence proof); marginalizing order for the decision while serializing the chosen set by its highest-probability ordering (reasoned, though order still enters packing); and a hardware-specific parity dial (serial replay of rounds with margin below θ) explicitly measured as too slow to be practical. Key Results: On QASPER with byte-verified evidence spans, Qwen2.5-7B/3B-Instruct in bf16, and one MetaX C500 (repeated on H800): compiled control matches the serial controller's full action sequences on 84–89% of questions (80/90, 101/120, 79/90, 52/60 across splits A/B/D/E; 87% at 3B) with zero output tokens and zero protocol failures, versus 11–13 mean output tokens for serial. Mean control latency falls 35–41% versus token-wise serial decoding (e.g., 0.56→0.36 s/question on split D; 0.63→0.37 s at 3B, a 47% cut) and 6–7% versus an idealized chunked serial engine (D=n) on real workloads (0.35 vs 0.37 s on D); the chunked-vs-compiled bootstrap CIs exclude zero, and a reversed arm order on E reproduces the gap. The certificate fires after expanding 24 of up to 380 pairs in every non-trivial round (527/527 across four splits); MAP certification adds 0.44 vs 0.37 s/question. Interaction mass is heavy-tailed (median 2.6, p90 8.3 nats), with only 14% of rounds below I_seq=0.5 — history dependence is pervasive, so the unary shortcut is rarely provably benign. Notably, the AR policy beat unary by only +5.9/+4.4 points at 2K budget on splits B/C and trailed by 1.1 on D, and embedding-MMR changed 84/90 selections — the quality case for history-dependence is distribution-dependent, which the authors state plainly. All 39 diverging rounds sit at margins ≤ 2.5 (inside the 2ε window); fp32 replay collapses mean logit deviation from 1.2 to 0.05 and restores 89/90 sequence agreement. On H800, latency ordering holds but cross-accelerator agreement of the serial engine itself is only 67–73% — the realized bf16 policy is backend-dependent regardless of compilation. Synthetic sweeps (k ∈ {4..20}, n ∈ {2,3,4}, prompts 1.4k–8.2k tokens) reveal a width wall at n=4 (362 rows, ~270× total compute; 0.4–0.6× vs serial at short prompts), and ablations show reading only slot-1 marginals collapses quality (42.2 vs 51.1 AllEvidence@1K). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (compilation of a frozen constrained controller's own prefix conditionals into a tree-causal probe with a proof of policy exactness) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (quantified cross-accelerator instability of bf16 greedy policies). The genuinely novel core is executing — not approximating — a frozen autoregressive policy on a shallower execution graph with an equivalence theorem and a certified MAP readout. Tree attention, speculative decoding, and grammar-constrained decoding are established primitives, and parallel structured-selection methods (Contextual Plackett–Luce, mean-field decoding, SimpleTool, LLMCompiler) either learn joint structure or retrain; the paper's positioning against these is fair. The theoretical results are elementary (layer-wise induction, Pinsker) but the application is non-obvious. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is unusually high for a systems-flavored paper: a preregistered split E (identity hashes recorded before gold was read), document-disjoint splits, document-cluster bootstrap CIs (10k resamples, fixed seed), per-run code-hash manifests, bit-identical repeat runs on fixed hardware, a reversed-arm-order control, two accelerators, a hierarchy-corruption stress test, ablations isolating each readout, and margin-instrumented replays tracing every divergence to the predicted flip window. The authors evaluate a technique partly on the splits where prompts were frozen (A is a development split), but D and E are fresh and the conclusion does not depend on A. Weaknesses: no error bars on the fidelity percentages beyond the raw counts, one run per device for the H800 repetition, no significance testing on fidelity, no public code or data at submission time (the compiler and benchmark harness are promised for release), and only one dataset (QASPER) and one model family (Qwen2.5) — the generality claim to "any finite-action controller" is asserted, not tested. Baselines are strong and current, including an idealized chunked engine the authors themselves designed to be a hard comparison. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — the compiler is built and run end-to-end, with measured wall-clock latencies on commercial accelerators (MetaX C500, NVIDIA H800). - Practical: Yes — runs on single commercial accelerators in bf16 with eager attention, using ordinary attention calls composable with existing tree-attention IO kernels. - Efficient: At the deployed frontier (k=20, n=3) it spends ~13× total compute (117 parallel positions vs 9 serial tokens) to cut critical path to 2 forwards, netting 1.3–2.8× wall-clock speedup; probe memory overhead is ≤5 MB at n≤3 but ~3.7 GB at n=4. - Effective: It reliably reproduces the source policy (84–89% exact agreement, all divergences precision-induced), but final evidence-coverage on fresh splits is 2.4 points below serial, so exact parity in bf16 is not achieved — only argued to be precision-limited. - Scalable: Explicitly not scalable past the greedy horizon: probe width grows factorially (N(k,n)), the n=4 probe loses to serial at short prompts and never catches the chunked engine — the paper measures and states this width wall rather than claiming otherwise. The work delivers a method plus a promised artifact: the compiler and benchmark harness "will be released" but no repo, URL, or trained model is available in this version. Strengths: - The reframing of constrained decoding as a compilation problem — evaluating a frozen policy's exhaustive reachable state space instead of accelerating guesses — is a genuinely non-obvious move that differs categorically from speculative decoding (nothing to reject, provable rather than distributional equivalence). - The equivalence theory (Lemma 1 + Theorem 1 + margin-stability Corollary) is simple, correct-looking, and — critically — paired with measurements that map every observed divergence onto the corollary's predicted flip window, closing the loop between claim and evidence. - Exceptional experimental hygiene for an industrial-lab paper: preregistration with pre-recorded hashes, reversed-arm-order controls, code-hash manifests, cross-accelerator repetition, and candid reporting that the compiled policy is 2.4 points worse on fresh splits and that the exact-parity dial is slower than just running serial. - The interaction-mass diagnostic (I_seq) is a useful, cheap-byproduct contribution: it converts the abstract question "does history-dependence matter here?" into a per-input closed-form quantity, and the finding that only 14% of rounds are provably unary-benign is independently interesting. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are direct about the two main limits: (1) probe width grows factorially beyond the greedy horizon — measured, not merely claimed, via the n=4 width-wall experiments — and (2) bf16 floating-point reduction orders cause near-tie divergences that fp32 narrows to 89/90 but does not eliminate. They further concede that exact parity via the margin-gated hybrid is slower than serial decoding, that θ and ε are hardware-specific (three gated flips escaped on H800), and that the realized bf16 policy is accelerator- and backend-dependent even without compilation. This candor is a strong credibility positive; the conclusion restates rather than minimizes the limits. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single dataset (QASPER, 360 questions total), single model family, and a single task shape (b-of-k section selection with n=3). The closing claim that "the guarantees transfer to any finite-action agent loop" is untested — no tool-calling, routing, or different-grammar instantiation is run. - The quality metric (AllEvidence@B coverage) is a retrieval-proxy metric; no downstream answer accuracy (QASPER's QA F1) is reported, so the reader cannot tell whether the 2.4-point coverage deficit on fresh splits matters for end-task quality. - The claimed latency win over the chunked engine is only 6–7% on real workloads and vanishes on the synthetic 8k-prompt sweep (both 2.09 s); the headline 35–47% is against the token-wise serial baseline, which a deployed system could partly replace with chunking at far less engineering cost — the practical value of the extra machinery over chunking is thin. - The companion "interface study" supplying the 3–65% protocol-failure motivation is under review and unpublished, so the motivating error budget cannot be verified from this paper. - The Pinsker bound via I_seq is presented as a diagnostic but the paper itself notes only 14% of rounds fall in the provably-benign regime, and it defers "predicting [unary cost] before compilation" to future work — the bound's actionable value is not demonstrated. - H800 and MetaX results each rest on one run per device per configuration; cross-accelerator agreement statistics (67–73%) are suggestive but under-powered. Bottom Line: A practitioner building grammar-constrained LLM controllers should read this for the compilation idea and the unusually honest precision analysis — it is the clearest demonstration I have seen that bf16 greedy policies are not even self-consistent across accelerators — but as a hierarchical-RAG latency fix, the marginal gain over a simple chunked engine is 6–7% on one small dataset, so most readers can wait for the promised release and a multi-dataset follow-up.

AutoEnergyDesign: An LLM-Driven Agent for Automatic Energy System Design Optimization

A Buonanno, S Fabozzi, M Valenti · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AutoEnergyDesign, an LLM-agent framework that searches for optimal building energy-system designs (technology selection and sizing) through iterative simulation, structured memory files, and git-based keep/revert state management, evaluated on a full 25-year Net Present Cost model of eight technologies. - Why it's important: Simulation-driven design optimization requires hundreds of expensive black-box evaluations, gives no explanation for its choices, and cannot absorb qualitative engineering knowledge; a cheaper, auditable, natural-language search would lower the expertise barrier for energy engineers. - How it does it: A coding-agent LLM (Claude Code) edits a design configuration file in a strict hill-climbing loop — proposing one-to-three coordinated parameter changes per experiment, learning from simulator feedback and cost breakdowns in context, with environment-enforced hooks that validate proposals and revert suboptimal designs via git commits. - The good: The paper includes a well-matched control — a (1+1) evolution strategy sharing the agent's exact acceptance rule and move-size constraints — isolating the LLM's contribution: the agent reaches the 1%-of-best band in 28/30 runs at a median of 18–27.5 simulations versus 5/10 seeds at a median of 192 evaluations for the ES. - The missing: Everything is evaluated on a single case study (one office building, one climate, one flat tariff, one NPC objective), and the agent exploits a cost breakdown in the simulator output that the black-box baselines never see, so the evidence base for generality is thin. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in LLM-driven optimization and simulation-based engineering design who want an unusually honest accounting of when LLM search beats classical baselines and when it does not; skip it if you need evidence on multi-building, multi-objective, or non-flat-tariff settings.

Problem & Motivation: Building energy-system design couples discrete technology activation (PV, wind, CHP, solar thermal, boiler, battery, heat pump, inverters) with continuous sizing and hourly dispatch under lifecycle economics. Each candidate design requires a year-long operational simulation, and the objective (25-year NPC with CAPEX, replacements, salvage, OPEX) is non-convex and mixed-integer, so black-box optimizers need hundreds of evaluations. Practitioners additionally lack traceability from classical optimizers, cannot inject qualitative domain knowledge without formalizing it mathematically, and need optimization expertise to configure the tools. The paper positions itself at a gap it argues is unfilled: LLM-as-optimizer applied to design-phase technology selection and sizing against a full techno-economic model, rather than to dispatch/control or model formulation. Key Idea: Treat the LLM agent itself as the search operator in a strict hill-climbing loop: the model, not a random mutation or a surrogate acquisition function, chooses which one-to-three logically related parameters to change next, exploiting information black-box methods cannot use — the simulator's cost breakdown (CAPEX/OPEX per technology), a domain-knowledge file (insights.md), and general design knowledge — while environment-enforced hooks (a pre-execution validator and a git-based post-execution accept/revert) guarantee that the working configuration is always the best feasible design found so far, independent of model behavior. The acceptance rule (Eq. 1: keep only strictly-lower-NPC valid designs) is deliberately shared with the (1+1)-ES baseline so the attribution question — acceptance rule versus move selection — can be answered empirically. Methodology: The framework has two parts. (1) Agent loop: a Claude model running inside Claude Code reads state files each experiment (CLAUDE.md procedural instructions, insights.md semantic domain knowledge, search_history.md and status files as episodic memory written by hooks, decisions.md decision log and agent_notes.md reflective note written by the agent), edits config.py, and runs a PyPSA/HiGHS simulator. Hooks enforce the design-space constraints (ranges, quantization, at least one thermal source) before simulation and apply the acceptance rule with git commit/revert after it. The memory taxonomy follows the CoALA framework; the reflective note (rewritten every Na=4 experiments) follows Reflexion. (2) Simulator: for a given design vector x (7 binaries + 18 quantized continuous variables), an hourly linear program over 8,784 hours minimizes variable cost (imports/exports, gas, CHP maintenance, 1000 EUR/kWh unserved-energy penalty) subject to electric, heat, and cooling balances, battery SOC dynamics with cyclic condition, CHP heat-to-power coupling, a shared heat-pump compressor constraint (heating + cooling ≤ rated capacity per hour), and inverter limits; NPC then aggregates discounted CAPEX with replacements and linear salvage, annuity-discounted fixed OPEX, and the LP's variable cost repeated flat over 25 years. Critical design decisions: (a) the environment writes reliable state and the agent writes only reasoning artifacts — well justified and ablated; (b) git-based rollback externalizes the acceptance rule from the model — sound, since rules-as-convention are verified post-hoc on transcripts while design-space rules are hook-enforced; (c) flat tariffs and a fixed COP/EER — simplifications the authors flag but which materially shape the optimum (battery valued only via self-consumption; efficiencies pushed to bounds because cost is efficiency-independent). Key Results: On a single case study (measured 2024 load/weather profiles for an office building near Naples; 703 MWh/yr electricity, 459 MWh/yr heat, 277 MWh/yr cooling), the best design found by any method has NPC = 3,525,522 EUR. All three agent models (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus 5.5, 10 runs each, budget 50 simulations) reach NPC in at least one run; Opus reaches it in 10/10, Sonnet 6/10, Haiku 1/10 (median 3,525,947 EUR, +0.012%). Baselines (10 seeds, 300 evaluations): random search median 4,052,571 EUR, TPE median 3,596,245 EUR (best 3,568,489), (1+1)-ES median 3,557,264 EUR (best 3,533,721). Within the 1% band of NPC: agent 28/30 runs at a median of 18 (Opus), 20.5 (Sonnet), 27.5 (Haiku) evaluations, versus 5/10 ES seeds at a median of 192 evaluations; TPE and random search never reach it. Feasible rates: 87.6–89.8% (agents), 70.1% (TPE), 73.3% (ES), 19.8% (random). Ablation: removing insights.md barely changes outcomes (Opus still finds NPC in 8/10 runs; the file mainly reduces run-to-run variance early on). Qualitative trace analysis documents the failure mode of two trapped Sonnet runs (premature conclusion that a 750–800 kW heat pump was the minimum, never retested) and rule-compliance statistics. Cost: 0.63–2.26 USD and 11–17 minutes per agent run versus ~35 minutes per 300-evaluation baseline seed — the agent is not cheaper in money, only in simulator calls and slightly in wall-clock time. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: applying the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm (OPRO/AutoResearch lineage) to design-phase building energy-system sizing with a full 25-year NPC lifecycle model, and the controlled attribution experiment against a same-acceptance-rule ES baseline. The components themselves are standard combinations — hill-climbing acceptance, Reflexion-style reflection, CoALA memory taxonomy, git rollback from AutoResearch, PyPSA dispatch — applied to a new domain setting. The claim of being "first" for this domain slice is plausible per the cited surveys but narrow. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above average for this genre. Ablations exist (insights.md removal, 10+10 runs) and the (1+1)-ES control is a thoughtful isolation of the LLM's contribution. Ten runs/seeds per configuration with medians and interquartile ranges; no significance tests, but the evals-to-band statistic (fraction of runs, median, max) is reported honestly, including non-reaching runs. Protocol asymmetries are disclosed: agents get pre-execution validation (out-of-range designs cost no evaluation) while random/TPE do not, and the agent sees a cost breakdown baselines never receive — the authors acknowledge both and show via the ablation that the insights.md half of the asymmetry is not decisive. The simulator output's cost breakdown advantage is not ablated away, however, since the dispatch LP still reveals marginal costs. No public code/data repository is stated in the paper (Not stated), though the entire trajectory is logged per-run and the full parameter tables are given. Compliance is verified on transcripts, not sandboxed — a mild audit rather than enforcement weakness. Main methodological concern: the case study's optimum is degenerate (PV, battery at admissible bounds; free inverters and efficiencies at upper bounds), which simplifies the search in ways that may not transfer. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built framework evaluated in experiments; no deployment). Practical: Yes — needs only a Claude Code session, PyPSA/HiGHS, and cloud LLM API access on commodity hardware. Efficient: 50 simulations at ~7 s each plus 0.63–2.26 USD of LLM calls per run; not cheaper than a 35-minute 300-evaluation baseline seed in money, so the economics only favor the agent when simulations are expensive (e.g., minutes-to-hours each), which the paper states explicitly. Effective: Within this single case study, yes — equal or better final NPC than all baselines with far fewer evaluations and auditable traces — but this is one building, one tariff, one objective. Scalable: Untested beyond this instance; higher-dimensional design spaces, larger technology portfolios, or noisy/slower simulators are unexamined, and the flat-repetition-of-year-one-cost assumption caps realism at any scale. Delivers a paper plus an implied scripts/files framework; no released artifact or URL is stated. Strengths: - The (1+1)-ES control sharing the agent's acceptance rule and one-to-three-change constraint is the paper's best move: it cleanly demonstrates that the gain (28/30 vs 5/10 runs reaching the 1% band, ~7–11× fewer evaluations) comes from LLM-chosen coordinated moves, not from the hill-climbing scaffold. - The environment-side enforcement architecture (pre-execution validator, git commit/revert, hook-written episodic state) makes the acceptance rule and feasibility handling model-independent — a robust design pattern that other agent-optimization papers leave to prompts. - Unusually candid reporting: the paper documents its own agents' reasoning errors (the Sonnet heat-pump fixation, Haiku's premature convergence claims), states that the agent is not cheaper in monetary terms, and explicitly disclaims superiority over exact MILP when a linear formulation exists. - The trace-audit of rule compliance (e.g., 32/500 Opus experiments changing ≥4 parameters, all technology switch-ons) provides qualitative evidence that is rare in agent papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Single case study (one climate, one tariff structure, single-objective NPC); one model family and one coding agent; the agent's access to the cost structure via insights.md is information the baselines lack (mitigated by the ablation, which the authors report honestly); possible contamination from design rules learned during pretraining that the experiments cannot separate from genuine reasoning; LLM calls add cost so total compute is not reduced. These are stated directly in Section 8 without minimization — a credibility positive. The authors also correctly note the case study uses LP dispatch to provide a controlled evaluation environment, not to prove MILP infeasibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The residual information asymmetry: even without insights.md, the agent reads a per-technology CAPEX/OPEX breakdown and unserved-energy detail from the simulator output each experiment, while TPE/random see only a scalar and the ES sees a scalar plus accept/reject. An ablation giving baselines the same per-evaluation feedback vector (e.g., TPE on the cost components) is missing, so the size of the genuinely "reasoning" advantage versus an information-advantage is not fully pinned down. - The problem instance is nearly free of the non-convexity the introduction stresses: efficiencies and inverters are cost-free so their optima sit at bounds, PV and battery hit admissible limits, and the tariff is flat. A harder instance (time-of-use tariffs, cost-coupled efficiencies, roof-area constraint making the PV bound inactive) is needed to test whether the agent's advantage survives when the landscape is genuinely multimodal. - No MILP-oracle check: since the dispatch LP is linear and the design grid is discrete, an exhaustive or near-exhaustive search over the 7 binaries with per-configuration LP could establish the true optimum of this instance; without it, "NPC*" is only the best-found value, and the 0.23% margin over the ES best seed is within the modeling uncertainty the authors themselves cite. - Scaling behavior of the agent's per-run cost (LLM tokens per experiment grows with context/history length) is not characterized, so the 10×-scale economics are unknown. - No code or data release URL is given, limiting independent reproduction despite the claimed full auditability. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing simulation-based energy-system design optimization gains real, transferable insight from this paper — particularly the hook-enforced accept/revert architecture and the honest attribution experiment — even though the single, rather benign case study means TPE or a well-tuned local search likely remains the safer default until the agent approach is shown to hold on harder, non-degenerate instances.

Span-Based Reasoning with Anonymous Knowledge Graphs

DG Olivares, L Quijano, F Liberatore · aclanthology.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GRASE, a knowledge-graph question answering framework that replaces iterative LLM-driven graph exploration with a frozen DeBERTa span encoder performing fuzzy matching between an Anonymous Knowledge Graph (AKG) derived from the query and candidate subgraphs, cutting LLM calls from ~16 to ~2.4 per query while matching or exceeding state-of-the-art accuracy (e.g., 73.9 Hits@1 on CWQ vs. 70.7 for PathMind). - Why it's important: LLM-agent KGQA pipelines make repeated LLM calls at every traversal step, which inflates latency (69.3s vs. 10.4s per query vs. ToG) and cost, making KGQA impractical in production; Problem & Motivation: Multi-hop KGQA requires grounding answers in knowledge-graph topology, but the dominant recent paradigm — LLM agents that iteratively decide which relation or entity to explore (ToG, ToG-2, PoG, EPERM) — calls the LLM at every hop, producing 5–16+ LLM calls, tens of seconds, and dollars per query. Prior efficiency fixes are unsatisfying: GNN-based retrieval (GNN-RAG) is expensive at realistic KG scale, RoG requires enumerating all relations in advance and matching LLM-planned paths exactly, SubGraphRAG leaves chain composition to the LLM with a sensitive top-K, and PathMind needs task-specific fine-tuning of its reasoning component. The gap GRASE closes is: can retrieval be decoupled from the LLM entirely, preserving global query structure, without per-relation training or repeated LLM scoring? Key Idea: Reformulate the natural-language query once — via a single LLM planning call — as an Anonymous Knowledge Graph: a small pattern graph in which unknown entities and relations are variables (e.g., Tom Hanks —acted_in→ X1 —directed_by→ X2). Exploration then becomes incremental fuzzy graph matching: a frozen span encoder embeds the triplets incident to the next unresolved variable and candidate KG spans, and a beam search resolves variables one by one using retrieve–rerank scoring plus a completeness classifier, with no LLM in the loop until one final answer-selection call. The AKG preserves global query structure (unlike sub-query decomposition) while deferring grounding to inference time. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Planning: GPT-4 (few-shot prompt, Fig. 6) converts the question into an AKG with anonymous variables, a resolution order, and an anchor entity, following ToG's entity-linking protocol. (2) Exploration: for each anonymous variable Xk, the system enumerates one-hop extensions of the current partial span, shortlists them with a bi-encoder (cosine similarity between f(T_Xk) and f(P')), reranks with a cross-encoder whose score is a sigmoid head over concatenated [CLS] embeddings plus the two span embeddings, and applies a three-class completeness classifier (STOP/CONTINUE/DROP) that, with Eq. 4, defines the search score; beam size b=10 and max depth D_max=3. The span encoder is DeBERTa-v3-Large fine-tuned with a triplet loss (margin α=0.15) on ~query–span pairs auto-generated by GPT-4 from SimpleQA, Natural Questions, and WikiHop train splits, with synonym rewrites, path truncation (for CONTINUE labels), corruption-based hard negatives, and explicit exclusion of all entities/relations appearing in any evaluation split. (3) Reasoning: one GPT-4 call receives STOP-labelled spans plus the resolved AKG and selects the answer; multi-answer queries run the resolved AKG as a traversal pattern. Critical design decisions: anonymizing the query pattern (well justified — Table 10 shows 79.2→81.8 Hits@1 and halved latency vs. sub-query decomposition); a shared frozen encoder feeding all three scoring heads (economical but makes classifier quality encoder-dependent); and GPT-4-generated training data with automatic augmentation (justified via leakage exclusion and the held-out-relation experiment, though correctness of GPT-4 labels is never human-verified). Key Results: On WebQSP, GRASE reaches 89.1 Hits@1 / 73.5 F1 (PathMind: 89.5/72.8; EPERM: 88.8/72.4); on CWQ, 73.9/61.8, beating PathMind (70.7/61.4) and PoG (70.9 Hits@1). On eight additional benchmarks it outperforms ToG-2 by 17.4 points on AdvHotpotQA (60.31 vs. 42.9) and 11.6 on QALD-10-en (65.67 vs. 54.1), and beats ToG on FEVER (79.12 vs. 52.7) though not on CREAK (92.77 vs. 93.8). Efficiency: 2.4 average LLM calls and 10.4s per query vs. ToG's 16.3 calls / 69.3s — an 85.3% call reduction and 85% latency reduction — with per-query cost bounded at D_max+2 LLM calls independent of beam width. Depth analysis shows graceful degradation: CWQ F1 of 0.780/0.648/0.422 at 1/2/3+ hops vs. RoG's 0.629/0.585/0.378. Robustness analyses: synonym substitution barely hurts AKG perturbation performance (F1 0.61→0.57 at 90%) but entity removal collapses it (0.50→0.01); holding out up to 50% of relations from encoder training costs only 0.019 F1. Baselines are current (PathMind is late-2025, SubGraphRAG/EPERM from 2025 venues), though three top baselines were scored from published numbers because their code is unavailable. Evaluation is at standard benchmark scale, not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (and arguably NEW FORMULATION). The genuinely novel element is the combination of anonymous query-pattern graphs with a frozen, retrieval–rerank–completeness encoder stack that fully replaces LLM scoring during graph exploration — the authors claim, credibly, to be the first within LLM-augmented KGQA to do so. Individual components (bi-encoder retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, beam search, triplet-loss training) are standard; the novelty lies in the AKG formulation preserving global query structure and the completeness-classifier-driven early stopping that caps LLM calls, not in any single piece. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong and well-designed: Table 4 isolates each module with LLM-equivalent replacements, and Tables 9–11 control for encoder capacity (DeBERTa sizes 22M–304M), AKG vs. sub-queries, and span encoder vs. a 2-layer GAT retriever. The authors report mean ± std over 5 runs, explicitly motivating this by LLM non-determinism at temperature 0 — a credibility positive. Concerns: (i) no code, data, or model release is mentioned anywhere, which is significant given the bespoke training pipeline; (ii) PathMind, EPERM, and SubGraphRAG results are transcribed from prior papers with different prompts, KG snapshots, and evaluation protocols rather than re-run; (iii) AKG correctness (Table 8, 78.4–96.5% by dataset) is judged by an LLM on only 200 samples per dataset, not human annotation; (iv) the three key baselines on the broader eight-dataset table are ToG/ToG-2/CoK rather than the strongest available systems, so some headline gaps are against weaker opponents. No Goodhart-style benchmark contamination is apparent — the leakage exclusion across all ten evaluation datasets is explicitly documented. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a framework run end-to-end in experiments). Practical: Yes — exploration runs on a two-A100 workstation and any planner LLM works (open-weight Llama-3 70B trails GPT-4 by only 1.6 QA average points). Efficient: 2.4 LLM calls and 10.4s per query, 6× fewer calls and 7× faster than ToG; encoder capacity scaling shows even a 22M-parameter encoder preserves 73.8 Hits@1 at 5.1s. Effective: The evidence covers standard KGQA and fact-checking benchmarks with consistent F1 gains, but the system is bounded by KG coverage and entity-linking quality — a proxy condition the authors acknowledge — and unseen-domain generalization is only tested within Wikidata/Freebase-style graphs. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested: per-query cost is capped by design (D_max+2 LLM calls), but there is no experiment on large production KGs (e.g., full Freebase traversal behavior, index size, or throughput under load). Deliverable status: paper only — no software artifact, dataset, or trained model release is reported. Strengths: - The core reframing — treating multi-hop KGQA retrieval as incremental fuzzy graph-pattern matching over an anonymized query graph, with the LLM confined to planning and final answer selection — is a clean, genuinely new point in the design space between fully agentic and fully learned-retrieval systems. - The ablation methodology is unusually rigorous for this literature: every disabled component is replaced by its exact LLM equivalent, so the component attribution (cross-encoder as the inflection point, cutting calls from 50.5 to 14.8) is directly interpretable. - The held-out-relation generalization experiment (stable F1 up to 50% unseen relations) and the AKG perturbation taxonomy (edge removal vs. synonym vs. entity removal) go beyond headline numbers and characterize failure modes the deployment community actually needs. - Honest baseline treatment: the paper flags which numbers are self-run vs. transcribed and runs GPT-4 across the board for fair comparison rather than cherry-picking the weakest prompt per baseline. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: no support for unstructured evidence sources (text, tables), which would need new alignment modules; performance is bounded by KG coverage and entity-linking quality at planning time; encoder components may require re-tuning on KGs with substantially different relation distributions (mitigated, they argue, by the 50%-held-out result); and residual dependence on the LLM in the single final reasoning call. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — each limitation is concrete and paired with either a mitigation or a future-work path. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No human verification of the GPT-4-generated training data (S_enc): the entire encoder and classifier learn from auto-generated, auto-augmented labels, so systematic GPT-4 labeling errors would be invisible and could partially explain the fuzzy-matching behavior. - The broader generalization table compares against ToG/ToG-2/CoK, not PathMind, EPERM, or GNN-RAG — the strongest known systems — on those eight datasets, so "substantially stronger" claims on AdvHotpotQA and QALD-10 are not established against the true frontier. - Wall-clock latency comparisons conflate different LLMs and serving stacks across systems (GRASE's 10.4s is measured on the authors' hardware with their own endpoint configuration), and the abstract's "up to 85% faster" headline is the most favorable single comparison. - No stress-scale experiment on a full-scale Freebase dump (Wikidata/Freebase are invoked, but traversal behavior, index footprint, and entity-linking accuracy at scale are unreported), even though scalability is a central motivation. - Beam search with b=10 and D_max=3 caps the reasoning depth of answerable questions; performance on queries requiring >3 hops (beyond CWQ's 3-hop slice) is untested, and the paper does not discuss what fraction of real queries this ceiling excludes. Bottom Line: For anyone building cost-sensitive KGQA or graph-RAG systems, this is worth a close read as the current best-published accuracy-per-LLM-call point and a template for moving LLM scoring out of the retrieval loop — but the missing code release, transcribed baselines, and absent large-graph stress tests mean its production claims should be validated independently before adoption.

#63 — Innovative (69)

Rethinking Time Series Tokenization from a Frequency Perspective

Z Tian, M Jin, B Du, S Pan · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TimeFT, a parameter-free, frequency-domain tokenizer for time series that partitions the spectrum into Nyquist-compliant sub-bands, shifts them to baseband, and samples, producing tokens with nearly lossless reconstruction of the input signal. - Why it's important: Tokenization via patching or downsampling is a default preprocessing step in essentially all modern time series models (including foundation models like Chronos and TimesFM), and the paper argues these tokenizers inject spectral leakage and aliasing that corrupt model inputs before learning begins. - How it does it: The core move is to reinterpret tokenization as a sampling problem: slice the RFFT of the sequence into blocks of bandwidth ⌊N/2S⌋ (so each block satisfies the Nyquist criterion at stride S), relocate each block to baseband, inverse-transform, and extract polyphase samples — all fixed, non-learned operations. - The good: The plug-in evidence is the strongest part: swapping the tokenizer in four backbones (PatchTST, PhaseFormer, PatchMLP, iTransformer) improves forecasting MSE by 1.4%–10.5% across seven datasets with no architecture changes, and a three-stage ablation shows every stage contributes. - The missing: The core theory is classical DSP (rectangular windowing, Dirichlet kernel convolution, aliasing, polyphase decomposition) applied verbatim, and the paper never tests the tokenizer on the pre-trained foundation models (TSFMs) where patch tokenization matters most — explicitly deferred to future work. - Read it or not: Worth reading for time series modeling researchers who want a defensible, plug-and-play tokenizer replacement and a clean DSP framing of why patching distorts spectra; skippable for readers seeking new theory beyond textbook signal processing or results at foundation-model scale.
Why this rank

The composite is held back by Non-Obviousness (62) — the core machinery is textbook DSP (Dirichlet leakage, aliasing, polyphase decomposition), and the reframing is useful but predictable to a signal-processing-literate audience — and Resilience (62), since the central causal claim that token-level spectral distortion harms models is asserted rather than demonstrated against a lossless-patching control, and anomaly margins sit within run variance. Rigor (72) is solid (ablations, multi-seed error bars, released code, current baselines) but discounted for the preprint status, the confounded headline Table 1, and the missing wavelet/low-pass baseline.
