Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the gap between what current open-ended agent benchmarks measure and what real computer science R&D looks like. Benchmarks like FrontierCS, ALE-Bench, and AtCoder hand the agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run; environment-based benchmarks like SWE-bench, MLE-bench, ResearchGym, MLS-Bench, and PaperBench grade against tests, leaderboards, rubrics, or reimplementations, and the cross-field ones stay within ML or never use the original authors' code as the bar. A researcher improving a published system instead inherits a working codebase, modifies a component, tests against the paper's own workloads, and is judged against the paper's own implementation. The authors — a large academic consortium led from UC Berkeley and Princeton — ask whether an LLM agent can perform under those conditions, which matters for anyone forecasting autonomous R&D capability. Key Idea: The core trick is "task building by subtraction": locate the code implementing a paper's contribution, delete it while leaving everything it depends on intact (with the deleted functions still declared and called), keep the deleted code privately as the human reference, and measure pass thresholds from the reference's own behavior on the paper's reported workloads. This yields a task with a guaranteed-correct oracle that runs in the original repository, plus a naturally calibrated bar, without any human having to author a solution or a rubric. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Task construction: from 48 source papers across 13 domains (9 ML, 9 database, 6 MLSys, 4 HPC, 4 PL, 3 each in architecture/network/cryptography, 2 each in security/robotics, 1 each in bioinformatics, SE, theory), the contribution-implementing code is deleted; the agent may edit only the files that held the contribution. One task (Structured LWE) is an original cryptanalysis challenge rather than a subtraction. Pass thresholds are set from reference measurements — e.g., for SVG-EAR, latency ≤ 0.96× the reference, PSNR within 0.25 dB, SSIM within 0.01, LPIPS within 0.005 — plus held-out final workloads (different seeds, queries, or graphs). (2) Judge architecture: agent and judge run in separate sandboxes linked only by a driver; the agent sandbox has no network except the driver (preventing it from downloading the authors' code), GPU tasks give the agent a development GPU while only the judge runs the measurement GPU, and the judge returns per-patch development-suite scores plus a sanitized threshold-count message. (3) Evaluation: 12 model-harness pairs run each task once for up to five hours; a run passes only if its self-chosen final submission meets every metric on every held-out workload. The FrontierCS Capabilities Index (FCI) adapts Epoch AI's item-response model, jointly fitting 13 agent strengths, 115 metric-group difficulties, and 48 task tie-levels from binary per-metric outcomes and censored Gaussian score margins over the reference, with a shared per-run random effect integrated via 64-node Gauss–Hermite quadrature, Laplace-approximated hyperparameter fitting, and 500-draw task-level bootstrap intervals (10 FCI points = 1 logit; Kimi K2.7 anchors 0). Key design decisions — self-selection of the final patch (well justified: patch choice is part of the researcher's job), measuring the bar on the paper's own workloads (reasonable, but couples thresholds to workloads that may leak into pretraining), and one harness per model (a confound the authors acknowledge implicitly by naming agents as model+harness). Key Results: The best agent, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, passes 58% of its 48 runs; GPT-6 Astra reaches 44%, Gemini 4 Argon 40% (with two provider-refused runs counted as failures), GPT-6.1 Sol 35%, GLM 5.3 25%, and Step 5 Preview 8%. No agent passes any of 16 tasks. FCI ranks agents nearly identically to pass rate: 55.7 (Claude Opus 5.5), 50.7 (GPT-6 Astra), 42.6 (GPT-6.1 Sol), down to 9.8 (Step 5 Preview); the tasks span a wider difficulty range than the agents, with the median task at roughly the strongest agent's FCI. A key measured finding: final score and pass diverge — mean score margins over the reference range from +9.4 (Claude Opus 5.5) to −10.6 (Step 5 Preview), yet most runs that beat the reference on the combined score still fail some metric or workload. Under test-time scaling, the leader changes with cost budget: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash leads at the lowest budgets (with costs that are lower bounds), Claude Opus 5.5 at the highest. Case studies show agents producing genuine designs (Muse Wonder 1.0 cutting QuarterPIR lookups from ~1,728 to 1,280 bytes via RAID-6-style dual checksums; Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon finding distinct faster FPGA clock schemes for the BBQ scheduler), and one task (SVG-EAR) where no run passes despite most runs beating reference latency — image-quality bands fail in two clips. Scale is standard per-task (single repositories, 5-hour runs, up to A100/H100 judge GPUs), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the score-versus-pass divergence and the cost-dependent leader). The genuinely novel elements are the subtraction-based task construction with the original authors' code as the measured oracle, and the privacy-separated judge that grades patches mid-run. The FCI is an adaptation of an existing item-response index to per-metric outcomes with censored margins — competent extension, not a new method; the judge/sandbox infrastructure is standard secure-evaluation engineering applied carefully. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations in the classic sense are absent (there is no system to ablate), but the FCI appendix specifies a 12-step fitting procedure with explicit priors, hyperparameter values (σ_u = 2.041 logits, α = 0.597), 500 bootstrap draws for agent intervals, and importance-weighted draws for task-difficulty intervals — this is unusually transparent for a benchmark paper. Error bars: 90% bootstrap intervals for FCI/FDI only; the headline pass rates from single runs per task carry no replication. Code and task infrastructure are released at github.com/FrontierCS/FrontierCS-2 with a public website (frontier-cs.org), and 100+ tasks are held private for future release — a meaningful contamination hedge, though the 48 public tasks are now themselves contamination-exposed. Methodological concerns: (1) each model is paired with exactly one harness, so model and harness effects are confounded by design; (2) one run per task-agent cell means pass-rate differences between adjacent agents may be noise; (3) several source papers are by the authors' own consortium (SVG-EAR, Continuum, FlashLib, FARGO), which aids task fidelity but complicates independence; (4) counting two provider-refused runs as failures is defensible but inflates Gemini 4 Argon's difficulty slightly. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built benchmark infrastructure with harness, judge, and sandboxing, evaluated by running 12 agents through it). Practical: Tasks run on commodity cloud resources — most tasks need 1–8 CPU cores and 2–32 GiB, with GPU tasks on L4/A10G/A100-80GB/H100 — so any lab with standard GPU access can use it. Efficient: A full 48-task run costs a mean of roughly $0.1–$20+ per run depending on agent (log-scale cost axis in Figure 5), with per-task judge compute bounded by listed GPU-hour budgets and 3–1800-minute final-eval limits. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark discriminates agents and elicits real engineering (the QuarterPIR and BBQ case studies), but whether passing predicts real R&D contribution is untested — pass is a proxy built from the papers' own thresholds. Scalable: Only claimed via the 100+ private task reserve; whether subtraction-based construction generalizes to papers whose contributions span whole subsystems, or where the reference cannot be cleanly deleted, is not demonstrated. The work delivers a concrete artifact: released code, 48 public tasks, judge infrastructure, and a reserved private task set. Strengths: - The subtraction construction is a real methodological idea, not just curation: it yields a guaranteed-correct, repository-native oracle with thresholds measured from the reference itself, removing the rubric-authoring and reimplementation-grading weaknesses of PaperBench/ResearchGym-style benchmarks. - The information separation between agent and judge (private evaluator, private reference, sanitized feedback, network-isolated agent sandbox) is carefully engineered against leakage, including blocking the agent from downloading the original code. - The FCI/FDI item-response fit is a substantive measurement contribution: it uses both per-metric outcomes and censored score margins in one likelihood, reports bootstrap intervals, and honestly shows the intervals separate only distant agents. - The case studies interrogate the benchmark's own metrics — showing the pass misses the best QuarterPIR solution, and the final score rewards a circuit that ignores FPGA size — which is rare critical self-analysis in benchmark papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly document that neither the pass nor the final score captures everything: the SVG-EAR run faster than the reference on every clip still fails two clips on image bands; the QuarterPIR checksum solution is invisible to both metrics; the BBQ score ignores circuit size. They state that such benchmarks "will need to report such side costs next to the pass." They also note DeepSeek's low-budget lead depends on how its tokens are priced, that FDI per-task intervals are too wide to order individual tasks, and that harnesses are part of what is measured. This is direct, non-defensive limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Pretraining contamination is the elephant: every deleted contribution is described in a published paper (with arXiv availability) that frontier models have likely ingested; an agent can partially reconstruct the "deleted" method from memory rather than by research. The network-isolated sandbox prevents downloading code but not recalling the paper. The private 100-task reserve mitigates future leakage, but the 48 reported results are not contamination-clean, and no decontamination analysis (e.g., probing whether models can recite the deleted method) is reported. - Single run per cell: with one run per agent-task pair, a 58% versus 50% pass-rate gap (Claude Opus 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Astra) rests on ~4 tasks; only the FCI intervals acknowledge uncertainty, and the paper itself shows FCI intervals overlap for mid-ranked agents. - Threshold construction couples the bar to the papers' workloads: thresholds measured on the workloads the paper reported may be easier or harder than the held-out workloads, and the paper does not report how often development-suite and final-suite outcomes disagree. - Harness confound: because each model ships with exactly one harness, statements about models ("Claude Opus 5.5 leads") are actually statements about model-harness bundles; no harness-controlled comparison exists. - No human baseline: the benchmark's motivating question is whether agents can do researcher-style R&D, but no human-under-same-conditions measurement is included; the reference code was written by the original authors with full context, not by time-boxed subjects. Bottom Line: For anyone building or selecting coding/research agents, this is currently the most realistic cross-domain R&D benchmark available and worth reading closely for its construction method and measurement discipline — but its headline rankings should be read as single-run, contamination-unclean, harness-confounded estimates, and the contamination question must be answered before the 58% figure can be interpreted as research ability rather than paper recall.

PSR: Efficient Knowledge Graph Question Answering via Plan-Guided Schema-Level Reasoning

M Li, Y Li, Y Bao, Y Sun, G Cheng · aclanthology.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PSR, a training-free retrieval-augmented framework for multi-hop knowledge graph question answering that answers each question with exactly three LLM calls, independent of retrieval depth. - Why it's important: Existing iterative KGQA methods invoke the LLM at every retrieval step (7–58 calls per question in reported baselines), making latency and API cost the dominant practical barrier to deploying KG-grounded RAG. - How it does it: The LLM generates a high-level retrieval plan once, and a Plan-Regularized Monte Carlo Tree Search (PR-MCTS) — driven by string-similarity to the plan plus an out-degree penalty on a compact schema tree — performs LLM-free path search, leaving only path selection and answer generation as LLM calls. - The good: With GPT-4, PSR reaches 89.17% Hits@1 on WebQSP and 72.83% on CWQ with 3 calls, versus ToG's 82.6%/67.6% at 15.9/22.6 calls, and the gains replicate across Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen-2.5-72B, and Qwen-2.5-14B backbones. - The missing: No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple-seed runs are reported, and the LLM-call baseline comparison mixes numbers self-reported across different papers and backbones rather than running all baselines under one harness. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building LLM-over-KG systems who cares about call-count/latency budgets; skip if you only want a new accuracy ceiling, since the accuracy story is incremental (PoG still leads on CWQ Hits@1, 75.0 vs 72.83).

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying RAG over knowledge graphs (KGQA) face two compounding costs on large KGs like Freebase: hop-by-hop agentic retrieval must expand exponentially many entity branches as depth grows, and guiding that expansion requires an LLM call per step (plus reflection/rollout calls), so interaction cost scales linearly (or worse) with retrieval depth D — the paper tabulates baselines at, e.g., ToG's 2WD+D+1 calls and DoG's D(a+1)+3(D−1) calls. The motivating question is whether multi-hop KGQA can run on a constant number of LLM calls without sacrificing accuracy. This targets anyone serving KGQA in production or with paid API access. Key Idea: Decouple the LLM from iterative retrieval by shifting search from the instance graph to the KG schema: use one LLM call to emit a textual plan (topic type → relation-label chain → answer type), then let a training-free MCTS over the compact schema tree use that plan as a soft semantic prior — a plan-alignment bonus (lexical similarity, normalized Levenshtein) added to UCT selection and an out-degree penalty (log(1+deg_out)) in both the selection score and expansion choice — so the expensive multi-hop search happens entirely without the LLM, and the plan is grounded back to instance triples only at the end. Methodology: Three stages, one LLM call each. Stage I: prompt the LLM with the question, topic entities, and their KG types to produce a plan set Π, each plan π = (c_topic, (r′_1..r′_L), c′_ans) of KG-agnostic text labels. Stage II: build a schema graph S = (C, R, E_S) where type-level triples generalize instance triples (Eq. 3), unroll S into a tree rooted at c_topic to depth k=3, and run PR-MCTS for B=500 simulations per plan with a plan-regularized UCT score Q + λ·exploration + α·LexSim(r, plan) − β·log(1+deg_out); expansion samples at most m=7 untried actions and instantiates the one minimizing H(a); terminal value is cosine similarity between a frozen encoder's embeddings of the node type text and the predicted answer type. Top-K=40 candidates (K by embedding similarity, Eq. 15) are passed to a second LLM call for fine-grained selection. Stage III: ground selected schema paths via a retrieval operator into instance triples F, and a third LLM call generates the answer set from (q, F). Design decisions: (1) lexical rather than embedding similarity during MCTS selection — justified as preserving domain prefixes and fine-grained constraints, but this is a weak similarity signal and unvalidated in isolation; (2) out-degree branching penalty — plausible for budget control, not ablated on its own; (3) fixed schema depth k=3 covering 4-hop instance questions — justified via schema compression of mediator nodes, only asserted. Key Results: On WebQSP with GPT-4: 89.17% Hits@1 / 80.17% F1 in 3 calls vs ToG 82.6%/75.79% at 15.9 calls, PoG 87.3% at 9 calls, DoG 91.0% at 30.9 calls (DoG collapses to 56.0% on CWQ). On CWQ: 72.83%/65.60% vs ToG 67.6%/60.2% and PoG 75.0%; PoG retains the CWQ Hits@1 lead at 2.17 points. Under open-source backbones the margins widen: with Llama-3.1-70B, PSR 86.1/68.9 Hits@1 vs ToG 68.3/37.1; with Qwen-2.5-72B, 87.38/70.67 vs ToG 79.0/44.2. Latency (Qwen-2.5-72B, real Freebase): 21.37s on WebQSP and 37.32s on CWQ, ~2.75–3.22× faster than ToG/PoG/ReKnoS; PR-MCTS plus encoding is only 8–10% of that latency. Retrieval quality (Gold Answer Recall): 87.6/81.2/86.6 on WebQSP/CWQ/GrailQA, beating ToG by +25.3/+29.2/+9.4 points. Ablations (Qwen-2.5-72B): replacing PR-MCTS with beam search costs −1.67/−4.27 Hits@1; removing embedding-based ranking −1.17/−4.49; removing LLM path selection −4.15/−4.98. Failure analysis of 100 CWQ errors: constraint missing 57%, schema error 40%, budget limit 3%. A proprietary TCM-KG dataset (1,000 auto-generated questions) shows 97.9–98.9% EM — a near-saturated, self-constructed evaluation of limited evidential value. Scale tested: standard public benchmarks (1,639–3,519 test questions), not stress-scale. Baselines are recent (2024–2025) and mostly strong, but results are compiled from original papers across different backbones rather than re-run uniformly (the authors report failing to reproduce DoG and ORT). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (PR-MCTS as a plan-regularized, training-free, LLM-free schema search) plus an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION framing (constant-3-call interaction pattern). The genuinely novel pieces are (a) injecting a textual plan into MCTS selection/expansion as a lexical prior instead of a trained value model, and (b) coupling that with out-degree-controlled expansion on a schema tree. The ingredients — schema-level search-space compression (from ORT), planning-as-guidance (RoG/PoG/FiDeLiS), and MCTS for KGQA (KBQA-o1, ReKG-MCTS) — all exist; PSR's contribution is a specific, well-executed recombination that removes the LLM from the search loop. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover all three main components and show each contributes; hyper-parameter analysis (m and K) is genuine and reveals non-monotonic behavior in m. Code is released at github.com/nju-websoft/PSR. Missing: no seeds/error bars/significance tests anywhere; main-table GPT-4 baseline numbers are taken from the baselines' original papers, so call-count and accuracy comparisons are not run under one harness, and some cells (F1 for PoG, DoG, ReKnoS; call counts for ORT, EPERM) are simply absent, making the efficiency-vs-accuracy frontier partially unverifiable. The proprietary TCM dataset evaluation is on the authors' own auto-generated data with no external baseline participation, and only the authors' chosen baselines (CoT, ToG, PoG) are run on it. The latency comparison is done carefully (re-running FiDeLiS on the real Freebase backend for transparency), which is a credibility positive. Prompt templates, hyper-parameters, complexity analysis, and full dataset statistics are in the appendix — good reproducibility hygiene. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a framework with run experiments and a released system). Practical: Yes — runs on 8×RTX 4090 with open-source 14B–72B backbones, and PR-MCTS needs only a frozen text encoder plus string similarity. Efficient: 3 LLM calls, ~188–430 output tokens, and 21–37s end-to-end latency per question, roughly 2–3× cheaper and faster than iterative baselines, with non-LLM overhead under 10%. Effective: The evidence supports solving the stated cost-accuracy problem on Freebase benchmarks (high GAR, strong Hits@1), but 57% of failures come from lost query constraints the plan cannot represent — so aggregate operators/comparisons in the motivating example remain a real weakness. Scalable: Not tested beyond Freebase's schema; the constant-call property is architectural, but behavior on KGs with noisy, flat, or missing type annotations (Wikidata, ad-hoc graphs) is acknowledged as untested. Delivers a software artifact (code on GitHub); no model weights or datasets beyond the code. Strengths: - The constant-3-call design is a real, verifiable architectural property, not a tuning trick — the interaction-complexity analysis (Table 6) rigorously derives call counts for every baseline, turning an efficiency claim into a provable structural statement. - PR-MCTS replaces trained value models used in prior MCTS-KGQA work with a plan-alignment prior, making the entire search training-free and portable across backbones — confirmed by consistent gains under four different LLMs including a 14B model. - Honest failure analysis with a taxonomy (constraint missing 57%, schema error 40%, budget 3%) and full worked case studies, including cases where the plan was correct and downstream stages drifted — this diagnoses where the schema abstraction breaks rather than hiding it. - The latency breakdown showing search+encoding is only 8–10% of runtime pre-empts the standard objection that MCTS merely shifts cost from LLM calls to graph search. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Two stated explicitly: (1) dependence on entity-type assignments — missing, incorrect, or overly flat type annotations in real-world KGs (Wikidata, ad-hoc extracted graphs) can exclude valid paths during schema induction; (2) dependence on plan-predicted relation labels — semantically deviant plans waste the search budget, with proposed future remedies (type-annotation-free induction, grounding-feedback plan revision). The authors confront these directly and concretely; the Limitations section also implicitly concedes the method is validated mainly on clean benchmark KGs. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline efficiency comparison is a patchwork of self-reported numbers from different papers/backbones; only ToG and PoG were re-run (under open-source backbones), and DoG/ORT were dropped after failed reproduction — the strongest GPT-4 comparisons are not under a uniform harness. - The plan format (a linear relation-label chain plus answer type) cannot express comparison, superlative, or aggregation operators — exactly the multi-constraint capability the motivating example showcases — and this accounts for 57% of failures, yet the framework offers no mechanism (e.g., SPARQL-style plan structure) to carry such constraints. - The out-degree penalty in expansion and the choice of Levenshtein similarity over embedding similarity inside MCTS are individually un-justified by ablation; the reported ablation swaps the whole search procedure for beam search rather than isolating these two priors. - The hyper-parameter optimum m=7 is tuned on CWQ with the same backbone used in the headline ablation results, a mild Goodhart risk, and no held-out tuning protocol is described. - Evaluation KGs are Freebase-derived with clean type systems; no experiment probes the acknowledged sensitivity to type noise, so the robustness claim in the limitations is untested rather than merely unaddressed. - No statistical rigor (seeds, variance, significance) despite LLM decoding at temperature 0.7, where run-to-run variance in path selection could be material. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM-based KGQA should read this: the constant-3-call plan-guided schema search is a deployable, code-released efficiency contribution with credible multi-backbone evidence, even though the accuracy frontier on complex questions (PoG) and the clean-KG assumption leave the accuracy-only reader better served by comparing against PoG/ORT directly.

#75 — Innovative (68)

JuDi: Revisiting Judge Decoding from First Principles via Training-Free Distributional Divergence

S Sun, Y Li, R Liu, W Lin, HL Zhen, X Yu, M Yuan, C Ma · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces JuDi, a training-free verification rule for lossy speculative decoding that replaces supervised "judge" classifiers with a threshold on token-level KL divergence between the draft and target model distributions. - Why it's important: Current judge decoding requires either expensive human annotation or heuristic mining (the authors measure >2,700 GPU-hours to mine AutoJudge labels for GSM8K with a 70B model), and the resulting classifiers generalize poorly under domain shift — removing the supervision bottleneck makes lossy speculative decoding practical for new domains and reasoning models. - How it does it: The core move is a first-principles argument, backed by a Fisher-information second-order expansion, that KL divergence and trained linear judges operate on the same logit-gap primitives Δ_ij(x) — KL aggregates them quadratically, the classifier linearly — so the divergence itself can serve as the criticality score, with a zero-cost top-1 confidence fallback (target confidence > 0.9 reverts to standard speculative sampling). - The good: The domain-shift result is the strongest evidence: on MATH-500-Hard and MMLU-Pro, where the AutoJudge classifier was trained only on GSM8K, KL thresholding improves MAT from 13.93→32.02 (1B/8B) with <1% accuracy drop while AutoJudge degrades to near the weak Top-K baseline. - The missing: The theoretical result is an approximation that holds only when draft and target logits are close (‖δ‖ small, i.e., after prior acceptances), the empirical correlation evidence is shown only on GSM8K, and evaluation subsets are small (400 GSM8K, 100 MMLU-Pro examples) with no error bars or significance tests. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or deploy speculative decoding systems and want to drop judge-training pipelines entirely; skip it if you seek strong lossiness guarantees or large-scale (405B+) evidence, which the paper explicitly does not provide.
Why this rank

The core Non-Obviousness (80) is high — demonstrating that the field's expensive judge-supervision pipeline is redundant with free draft-target KL divergence, backed by a shared-primitives argument and a domain-shift experiment that is the right test. Novelty (78) anchors on this reframe of the subfield. Rigor (55) is the main drag: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, eval subsets as small as 100 examples, an unexplained accuracy discrepancy between tables, and missing 2025 judge-decoding baselines. Completeness (72) and Resilience (62) benefit from honest negative results and anticipatory ablations, tempered by the structurally favorable domain-shift setup and the untested small-δ approximation. Problem & Motivation: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates LLM inference by verifying draft tokens in parallel, but its strict lossless criterion rejects semantically equivalent tokens ("6+1=7" vs "6 plus 1 equals 7"), capping speedup. Judge decoding (Bachmann et al., 2025) relaxes verification using a learned classifier that separates "critical" errors from harmless deviations, but the field faces a supervision dilemma: manual annotation is labor-intensive, subjective, and coarse (span-based labels smear criticality over all tokens after an error, obscuring the true logic-pivoting token), while automatic mining (AutoJudge) costs thousands of GPU-hours and produces noisy labels — the authors measure that only 25.4% of tokens keep a consistent criticality label across four generation trials. Practitioners deploying judge decoding for new domains or reasoning models inherit this cost and brittleness. The paper asks whether the criticality signal can be obtained without any supervision at all. Key Idea: The key insight is that the "criticality" a supervised judge learns is not a new signal but a proxy for draft–target distributional divergence that is already computable for free. Empirically, binned AutoJudge scores on GSM8K rise monotonically with token-level KL divergence (while entropy shows no correlation). Theoretically, via a Bregman-divergence/Fisher-information expansion, KL(P_t‖P_d) ≈ ½δᵀF(P_d)δ, which decomposes as a Fisher-weighted quadratic sum over pairwise logit-gap primitives Δ_ij(x) = (z_t(i)−z_t(j))−(z_d(i)−z_d(j)); any linear classifier over the concatenated hidden state can be re-expressed as a linear combination of the same primitives (since V ≫ d makes the primitive directions an overcomplete frame). KL thresholding is therefore a quadratic-in-primitives surrogate for the judge's linear partition — same signal, no training. Methodology: The method plugs into the standard draft-then-verify loop of speculative decoding. Stage 1: the draft model M_D produces γ candidate tokens with stored logits. Stage 2: the target model M_T verifies all candidates in one forward pass. Stage 3 (the contribution): for each position, compute D_KL(P_T‖P_D) over the full vocabulary; if the target's top-1 probability exceeds a confidence threshold τ_c = 0.9, apply standard speculative sampling (exact match); otherwise accept the draft token if its KL divergence falls below a threshold τ, and reject/truncate at the first violation. Stage 4 appends a bonus token when all γ drafts are accepted. The framework is greedy decoding with a threshold-based relaxation; no loss is trained. Critical design decisions: (1) token-level rather than step-level KL — the authors justify this with an ablation showing Step-KL loses 2–5% accuracy at matched MAT due to signal dilution and collateral rejection; (2) full-vocabulary rather than Top-K KL — justified by profiling showing full-vocab is 1.8× faster (0.068 ms vs 0.125+ ms) because Top-K selection/gather breaks memory coalescing, and by accuracy degradation of Top-K at low thresholds; (3) the top-1 confidence fallback — shown to trigger on <5% of decisions (<0.4 per query) and to be negligible when added to AutoJudge, so gains are attributable to the KL signal itself. The theoretical analysis assumes ‖δ‖ is small (conditioned on accepted prefixes), making the quadratic expansion a local approximation. Key Results: Evaluated on GSM8K, MATH-500-Hard (authors' Level-5 subset of MATH-500), LiveCodeBench, and MMLU-Pro with Llama-3.2-1B/Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-8B/Llama-3.1-70B, and Qwen3-0.6B/Qwen3-8B pairs; baselines are Vanilla SP, Top-K (Bachmann et al.), AutoJudge, and two entropy-based methods (Wang et al., 2025) — current and representative for this subfield. Headline MAT gains over Vanilla SP: +63.5% (10.61→17.35, ~2% accuracy drop) on GSM8K 1B/8B; +128.8% (13.35→30.55, ~1% drop) on GSM8K 8B/70B; +104.0% (8.83→18.01) and +53.7% (11.49→17.66) on LiveCodeBench. Under domain shift (AutoJudge trained only on GSM8K), KL thresholding reaches MAT 32.02 (1B/8B) and 26.67 (8B/70B) on MATH-500-Hard with ≤1.5% accuracy drop, while AutoJudge degrades to Top-K-level accuracy. In vLLM end-to-end deployment, KL thresholding achieves 1.3× speedup over Vanilla SP (which itself runs ~2× over autoregressive decoding) within a 1–2% accuracy budget, matching AutoJudge's Pareto position; the best configured point reaches 1.60× (1B/8B, δ≤5%) and 1.45× (8B/70B, δ≤3%). On reasoning models (Qwen3-0.6B/8B), MAT rises 2.77× (6.91→19.15) with ~2% accuracy drop. Counter-intuitive findings: Top-K vocabulary truncation hurts both wall-clock speed and low-threshold accuracy, and step-level aggregation underperforms token-level KL by 2–5% accuracy. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + NEW METHOD (with a supporting formal result). The genuinely novel contribution is the empirical demonstration and theoretical account that supervised judge criticality is redundant with intrinsic draft–target KL divergence, plus the training-free KL-thresholding acceptance rule this enables. The theoretical machinery (Bregman expansion, Fisher metric, overcomplete-frame representation of linear classifiers) is a competent assembly of standard tools applied to a new question, and the decoding loop itself is standard speculative decoding with one substituted criterion — the novelty lies in the replacement and its justification, not in new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the top-1 fallback (Tables 4–5), Top-K truncation (Table 2, latency profiling in Fig. 17), and Step-KL vs Token-KL (Fig. 12) each isolate a design decision. Code is released at https://github.com/sunshy-1/JuDi. Concerns: (1) no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; (2) evaluation subsets are small (400 GSM8K test examples, 100 MMLU-Pro examples), and accuracy figures differ between Table 1 (82.50% Vanilla SP) and Table 2 (87.75%) without clear reconciliation, suggesting different subsets or settings; (3) the headline domain-shift comparison is structurally favorable — AutoJudge is deliberately starved of in-domain training data, which is exactly the regime the paper argues for, so it demonstrates the failure mode of trained judges rather than a like-for-like capability gap; (4) the theory's small-δ premise is an approximation invoked rather than validated quantitatively on real token distributions; (5) the empirical KL–AutoJudge correlation (Fig. 6) is shown only on GSM8K. The appendix includes useful negative results (LLM-as-annotator via Qwen3-Max at ~$10 underperforms AutoJudge mining in the low-loss regime) that strengthen the paper's honesty. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built system artifact — a vLLM integration). Practical: Yes — runs on standard hardware with existing Llama/Qwen checkpoints in vLLM, adding no parameters. Efficient: The KL computation adds per-token overhead (0.068 ms per call at V=128,256), which the authors concede is unoptimized (no fused Triton kernels) and may bottleneck achievable speedup; even so it matches AutoJudge's end-to-end trade-off. Effective: The evidence shows it preserves benchmark accuracy while raising MAT and wall-clock speedup, but this is a lossy-decoding proxy — correctness of the target model's own errors is explicitly out of scope, and no human evaluation of output quality beyond benchmark scores is given. Scalable: Tested up to a 70B target; the authors admit they have not evaluated at 405B scale, and the mining-cost argument implies KL's advantage grows with model size, but this remains a claim, not a measurement. The work delivers a software artifact (GitHub repository plus vLLM integration), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) A genuinely useful negative result: the field's expensive supervision pipeline for judge decoding is largely redundant, established by both a measurable correlation and a shared-primitive theorem — this reframes the subfield's assumptions. (2) The domain-shift experiment is the right experiment: it directly demonstrates the generalization fragility of trained judges that the theory predicts. (3) Unusual engineering diligence for an algorithm paper — memory-access profiling showing full-vocab KL beats Top-K, and a negative result on their own Step-KL extension — makes the design choices credible rather than arbitrary. (4) The appendix analysis of the fallback mechanism and the LLM-annotator alternative preempts obvious reviewer objections with data. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two limitations directly: (1) no evaluation on very large models (e.g., Llama-3.1-405B), so scalability claims rest on extrapolation; (2) the KL computation adds inference overhead and their implementation lacks fused Triton kernels, so reported speedups understate the potential but also reflect an unoptimized integration. They confront these honestly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. They also explicitly bound scope in Appendix A.8: like all draft-then-verify methods, KL consistency cannot detect errors shared by both draft and target. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Statistical rigor: no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing, on eval sets as small as 100 examples (MMLU-Pro) — reported accuracy deltas of 1–2% at the operating points emphasized in Tables 6–7 are within plausible noise. (2) The unexplained discrepancy between Vanilla SP accuracy in Table 1 (82.50%) and Table 2 (87.75%) on nominally the same GSM8K/1B-8B setup needs reconciliation. (3) The correlation study (Fig. 6) covers one dataset; the KL–criticality alignment on code or knowledge domains is asserted via downstream results but never shown directly. (4) Theorem 4.1 is a local approximation whose accuracy at realistic δ magnitudes (rejected tokens are precisely large-δ cases, but the accept/reject boundary sits at moderate δ) is untested. (5) Missing baselines from the 2025 judge-decoding wave — SelfJudge, R2R, Pivot-Aware Speculative Decoding — are cited but not compared, so the claim of matching "complex trained judges" is validated against only AutoJudge and Top-K. (6) No measurement of output-length or formatting drift under lossy acceptance across domains, which matters for the paper's own "semantically equivalent token" motivation. Bottom Line: For anyone shipping speculative decoding beyond a fixed benchmark domain, this paper is worth reading — it deletes the judge-training pipeline entirely with a one-line criterion, matches AutoJudge's trade-off in-domain and beats it out-of-domain, and its honest ablation culture outweighs the missing statistical rigor; a practitioner focused solely on in-domain, small-model settings already served by AutoJudge gains less.

Controllable Text-Attributed Graph Generation via LLM-Based Substructure Modeling

R Mao, J Chen, B Li, Z Zhang, Y Zhang, F Wang · aclanthology.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a controllable substructure generator (CSG) that trains a lightweight LLM (Qwen2.5-3B) to jointly generate text, labels, and edges of connected graph substructures — the first approach to learn the joint distribution p(A, X_text, Y) over text-attributed graphs rather than prompting or agent simulation. - Why it's important: Real-world text-attributed graphs (TAGs) are limited in scale, balance, and diversity, and no prior generator supports both raw-text node attributes and generation-time control over structural/label statistics, blocking uses like GNN augmentation and controlled synthetic testbeds. - How it does it: Each subgraph is losslessly serialized as an Eulerian-circuit token sequence; averaging next-token loss over all N start-node traversals optimizes a variational lower bound on the permutation-invariant substructure likelihood, followed by fine-tuning with masked control-prefix conditioning (degree, clustering, homophily, dominant-label proportion). - The good: The multi-start variational objective is validated by a controlled ablation — multi-start CPT achieves the lowest held-out SFT loss on all five datasets and raises aggregate parse/lossless validity to 83.3/79.4% versus 80.6/74.4% for single-start. - The missing: Generated node text quality is never evaluated — no semantic-fidelity metric, no comparison of generated text distributions against the reference — so the joint text–structure claim is only half-verified (structure) while the text half rests on the lossless round-trip property alone. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in graph generation or LLM-for-graphs who need to see how causal LMs can be adapted to combinatorial structure; skippable if you need deployable graph augmentation today, since gains are modest and a per-dataset retrain is required.

Problem & Motivation: Text-attributed graphs underpin citation retrieval, e-commerce recommendation, and knowledge-graph-based RAG, but real TAGs are small, imbalanced, license-restricted, or static snapshots. Practitioners need synthetic TAGs whose text, labels, and structure they can specify at generation time — for GNN augmentation with genuinely new text-and-structure samples, for controlled distribution-shift studies, and for counterfactual graph analysis. Prior work fails this: structure-only generators (GraphRNN, GRAN, EDGE, DiGress) ignore node text; attributed-graph generators (GraphMaker, GDSS) use pre-extracted categorical/numerical features, not raw text; LLM-based methods either use text as a coarse domain prompt (LGGM), simulate agents without a learned distribution (GAG), or generate isolated nodes with post-hoc edges (LLM4NG). None learn the joint distribution over unbounded natural-language node text, edges, and labels. Key Idea: Two coupled ideas: (1) shift the modeling target from whole graphs to connected substructures, which sidesteps the context-length barrier (a 10k-node TAG serializes to millions of tokens) and makes enumerating all N per-node serializations tractable; (2) treat the Eulerian traversal order as a latent variable and average next-token cross-entropy over the N start-node circuits, which Theorem 1 shows exactly maximizes a variational lower bound on log p(G_sub) under a uniform variational distribution — turning "how many traversals to enumerate" into a principled knob rather than a heuristic. The serialization itself is lossless: Eulerization edges are tagged as <e_jump> and stripped at decoding. Methodology: The pipeline is: (a) sample connected substructures from the reference TAG by random walks; (b) Eulerize and serialize each as token sequences with special node/edge/attribute tokens; (c) continual pretraining (CPT) on all N start-node serializations under the uniform-q ELBO to learn the unconditional graph grammar (no labels); (d) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) where attribute blocks carry {label, text} and a masked control prefix (avg degree, clustering coefficient, homophily, dominant-label proportion) is prepended, with stratified start-node sampling and binning to balance the corpus; (e) single-pass inference with a logits processor enforcing the first-occurrence attribute invariant. The framework is autoregressive causal LM training (full-parameter fine-tuning, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, bfloat16) with an explicit variational objective (Equation 1), plus a monotonicity proof that the tightest bound improves as serializations are added (Proposition 2). Two applications reuse one trained generator: distribution-aligned generation assembles packets with a PI controller on prefix targets and VGAE-predicted inter-packet edges; TAG-AUG augmentation conditions on one-hop ego statistics of decision-boundary anchor nodes found by an oracle GCN and attaches packets to semantically nearest real anchors. Critical design decisions: substructure-level modeling (justified by tractability of full enumeration), uniform-q instead of optimal-q variational weights (justified as a deliberate simplification avoiding repeated q updates), and Eulerian rather than arbitrary traversal (needed for losslessness). All three are reasonably justified, though the uniform-q choice leaves measurable bound slack. Key Results: On five TAGLAS graphs (Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, WikiCS, a curated ogbn-Products subset; train/test graphs node- and edge-disjoint via METIS community-stratified 0.66/0.34 split), the raw generator achieves 83.3% strict parse rate and 95.3% conditional lossless round-trip over 180 held-out generations. Control adherence is coarse: clustering is reliably steerable (Pearson 0.98 on Products, 0.84 on WikiCS), homophily is strong on WikiCS (0.89) but unstable elsewhere, and requested degrees of 16–21 yield realized degrees of 4–6 on WikiCS. On structural fidelity (Gaussian-EMD MMD over degree/clustering/4-orbit/spectral statistics of 200-node BFS subgraphs), the method is best on degree MMD on most splits and spectral MMD on several versus GraphRNN, GRAN, DiGress, GraphMaker, and GAG — notably beating diffusion on dense WikiCS (best on all four metrics per split) while structure-only baselines win some motif columns on sparse citation graphs. GAG is markedly weaker on its two comparable datasets. For augmentation (GCN, five seeds, test on disjoint real graph), Macro-F1 changes are +2.93 (Cora), +0.57 (PubMed), +4.14 (Products), +1.34 (WikiCS), and −0.27 (CiteSeer) versus DropEdge, GAug, GraphSHA, and LLM4NG, several of which are negative on multiple datasets (GraphSHA: −15.96 on Products). Cross-dataset CPT (Cora↔CiteSeer) improves held-out SFT loss over SFT-only in both directions. Tested scale is small: all generated graphs are capped at 4,000 nodes; training used two RTX A6000s at 2.2–4.3 h CPT and 1.2–2.4 h SFT per dataset. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a NEW FORMULATION component. Genuinely novel: training a language model to model the joint p(A, X_text, Y) of raw-text TAGs with control-prefix conditioning, and the multi-start Eulerian-serialization ELBO at the substructure level. Not novel: the Eulerian serialization is explicitly borrowed from GraphGPT (used there for discriminative tasks), the variational-ordering idea follows Liao et al. (2019) and Chen et al. (2021), and the PI-controller/VGAE assembly is standard control engineering plus a 2016 autoencoder — competent engineering of known components. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: w/o-CPT comparison (full model more stable across degree/clustering/orbit MMD columns), a size-matched single-start vs multi-start comparison isolating traversal diversity (same substructures, token counts, optimizer steps), and bidirectional cross-dataset CPT transfer. Augmentation results report mean ± std over five random seeds; no significance tests. MMD evaluation averages five sampling repeats. Code is released at github.com/Ridge-yz/taggen, and hyperparameters, corpus statistics, and per-dataset settings are documented in appendices. Concerns: (1) generated text quality is unmeasured — structural MMDs say nothing about whether the node text is coherent, diverse, or label-consistent beyond parseable JSON; (2) GAG is comparable on only two datasets and unavailable on three, weakening the LLM-baseline comparison; (3) controllability correlations are computed on grid-level averages over just three requested percentile levels and four samples each, so Pearson values rest on n=3 points per descriptor; (4) each dataset gets its own separately tuned generator with dataset-specific clip ranges, which risks tuning components against the very MMD metrics used for evaluation. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with experiments, not a deployed tool). Practical: Yes — a 3B model fine-tuned on two RTX A6000 GPUs in under ~7 hours per dataset is within reach of most academic and industry labs. Efficient: Full-parameter fine-tuning of 3B (not LoRA) plus per-dataset retraining is moderately expensive; inference is a single autoregressive pass per packet, but distribution-aligned generation needs many packet queries plus VGAE assembly. Effective: Partially — the evidence shows valid parseable substructures and coarse descriptor control, but degree control fails in extreme regimes and the paper itself routes graph-level targets through feedback control rather than direct generation. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the substructure design is motivated by context limits of 10k+-node graphs, yet all evaluations are on train graphs of 1.8k–35k nodes and generated graphs capped at 4,000 nodes; behavior at 10×–100× is untested. The work delivers a code artifact (GitHub repo with configurations) plus per-dataset trained generator checkpoints; no pretrained universal model. Strengths: - The variational treatment is genuinely principled: Theorem 1 and Proposition 2 connect a concrete, cheap training change (enumerate all N start-node circuits) to a provable bound on the permutation-invariant likelihood, and the size-matched multi-start ablation empirically confirms the prediction on all five datasets — a rare theory-predicts-practice loop in this literature. - The lossless serialization with tagged Eulerization edges plus a runtime logits processor yields 95.3% conditional round-trip fidelity, directly addressing hallucination in structured generation without retraining. - Honest evaluation design: the disjoint train/test protocol is deliberately harder than transductive settings, the paper reports its own negative result (CiteSeer −0.27 Macro-F1) and unstable homophily control, and it decouples packet-level from assembled-graph MMD to attribute gains correctly. - One trained generator supporting two heterogeneous applications (synthesis and augmentation) via target-side adaptation alone demonstrates real reusability of the conditioning interface. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly concede: (1) control is coarse and aggregate — some descriptors track better than others, and instance-level constraints (motif counts, degree sequences) are out of scope; (2) scope is static, undirected, node-attributed graphs on five citation/web/e-commerce datasets, with no claim of transfer to molecular or knowledge graphs; (3) a separately tuned generator per dataset is required, and control correlations are only within-dataset. They confront these directly and name concrete future directions, which is a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge the absence of any text-quality evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' acknowledgments, a critical reviewer would flag: (1) no evaluation of generated text whatsoever — no perplexity, no embedding-distribution distance, no human or model-judged coherence, no check that generated text matches its assigned label beyond the model's own training signal, which leaves the headline contribution (joint text–structure modeling) half-verified; (2) the augmentation comparison never asks whether generated text is semantically useful — attaching packets via BERT-similarity could work with templated text, so the LLM's contribution to the GNN gains is unisolated (an ablation with ablated/shuffled text is absent); (3) the oracle GCN used to derive boundary profiles shares architecture with the evaluated GCN, possibly inflating augmentation fit; (4) controllability statistics are computed on n=3 grid points, making the reported Pearson correlations fragile; (5) the 'first to train an LLM for TAG generation' claim is defensible but sits close to concurrent prompting/agent work, and the comparison set omits any whole-graph diffusion baseline adapted to text attributes via frozen embeddings, which would test whether joint text modeling is actually necessary for the structural-fidelity results; (6) no analysis of how augmentation gain scales with packet budget. Bottom Line: A technically substantive first step that convincingly establishes the feasibility of LLM-trained controllable TAG substructure generation with a genuinely principled variational trick, but practitioners seeking graph augmentation should treat the +0.6–4.1 point Macro-F1 gains as preliminary evidence, and no reader gets an answer on text quality — the field still lacks stronger alternatives here, so this is the current reference point for the problem.

OASIS: Online Anchor-calibrated Self - Improvement System

W Wang, F Laakom, L Nanbo, Y Dai, Y Wang, Y Xu… · aclanthology.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces OASIS, a system that reformulates recursive self-improvement of LLM agents as online learning over non-stationary task streams and validates self-modifications via paired comparisons against a continuously-run anchor agent using Beta-posterior credible intervals, raising SWE-Bench Pro solve rate from 51.6% to 56.9% and DeepResearch Bench from 35.18 to 39.31. - Why it's important: Existing self-improving agents (Darwin/Huxley-Gödel Machine, STOP) are optimized offline on fixed benchmarks, but deployed agents face sequential, shifting task distributions where raw rewards conflate agent quality with task difficulty, causing premature reversion or over-optimistic continuation. - How it does it: The core trick is running a reference (anchor) agent on every incoming task so each branch's reward is paired with a matched control, then gating reversion and anchor promotion on non-overlapping posterior credible intervals instead of absolute subtree rewards. - The good: The ablation cleanly separates mechanisms: replacing OASIS's branch control with the SSA rule drops performance by 4.4 points (56.9%→52.5%), while removing best-of-two selection costs only 1.1 points, attributing most of the gain to anchor calibration; a Westfall-Young adjusted sign-flip test (p=0.031) supports the trajectory advantage. - The missing: Every configuration is run exactly once (no seeds, no hyperparameter search, explicitly due to the ~USD 4,000 / 5,000 A100-hour budget), so the headline 5.3-point gain carries no variance estimate, and no offline-RSI baseline (e.g., DGM/HGM adapted to the same streams) is compared. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building self-improving or online-adapting agent systems who need a concrete, statistically grounded answer to the branch-comparability problem; skippable for practitioners wanting a ready-to-deploy tool, since code is only promised, not released.

Problem & Motivation: Deployed LLM agents receive tasks sequentially from live streams with shifting domains and difficulties, but recent recursive self-improvement (RSI) systems treat self-improvement as offline search: variants are generated, evaluated on fixed benchmark protocols, and the best frozen artifact is reported. In the online regime, performance is cumulative reward over the stream, exploration is not free, and a central difficulty emerges that the authors call branch comparability: different lineages of self-modifications encounter different task subsets, so raw rewards conflate agent capability with task difficulty. The closest prior method, Schmidhuber's Success-Story Algorithm (SSA, 1997), validates modifications by requiring monotonic improvement in raw subtree-average reward along the active path; on non-stationary streams this yields wide-but-shallow search trees with repeated revert cycles, discarding useful modifications when later tasks happen to be harder. The problem matters for anyone deploying self-modifying agents where a bad modification degrades live performance. Key Idea: Replace absolute-reward validation with task-matched paired comparison against an adaptive anchor agent. The anchor is run on every incoming task regardless of which branch is active; for each subtree, the branch's rewards are paired with the contemporaneous anchor rewards on the same tasks, and reversion/promotion decisions are made only when Beta-posterior credible intervals of the paired normalized rewards separate (revert when the branch's upper credible bound falls below the anchor's lower bound; promote when the reverse holds, with a wider interval for promotion). The anchor doubles as a deployment fallback whose solution can be submitted when the active branch is under-evaluated, and as a promotable reference that improves over time. Methodology: The paper first formalizes online RSI: tasks τ₁...τ_T arrive sequentially, each with an evaluator returning reward (and optional feedback) after submission; self-modifications grow a tree G_t of agents; the system must choose which agents to run, which solution to submit (only the submitted reward counts toward the objective), and where to move the active pointer. SSA is shown to be the special case Q_t = {active agent} with a raw-reward monotonicity condition. OASIS instantiates this framework with: (1) an anchor agent run alongside the active agent each round; (2) Beta(2,2) fractional-count posteriors over normalized rewards for branch and matched anchor evidence sets, with central α-level credible intervals; (3) three confidence-gated decisions — promotion (checked before reversion, requiring LCB_branch > UCB_anchor at level α₂=0.6, deepest qualifying node wins), reversion (UCB_branch < LCB_anchor at α₁=0.4, earliest qualifying non-root node triggers revert to its parent), and best-of-two solution selection via an LLM judge. Self-modifications are represented as Claude Code skills and generated once per batch; candidates are validated by re-running the modified agent on the same task in a fresh container, and the candidate with the largest strictly positive validation gain is added to the tree. Critical design decisions: the asymmetric α₁/α₂ settings (well-motivated — promotion should require stronger evidence — but supported only by a single sensitivity run at α₁=α₂=0.95 giving 53.9%); the Beta(2,2) independence prior (stated as an assumption, not tested); and per-batch rather than per-task self-modification for wall-clock efficiency (justified pragmatically). Key Results: On 11 SWE-Bench Pro repository streams (20–29 sequential steps each, 96 down to 20 tasks) with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: initial agent with best-of-two 51.6%, SSA 52.0%, compute-matched SSA (SSA + best-of-two against the initial agent) 52.5%, OASIS 56.9%, OASIS without best-of-two 55.8%, OASIS with α₁=α₂=0.95 53.9%. On two DeepResearch Bench streams (25 steps, 50 tasks each, English and Chinese) with Gemini 3 Flash and the RACE metric: initial 35.18, SSA 37.03, OASIS 39.31, versus a best reported non-Deep-Research leaderboard score of 38.22. The 56.9% SWE-Bench Pro result exceeds reported numbers for MiniMax M2.7 (230B-A10B, 56.2%), Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (50.9%), GPT-5.3-Codex (56.8%), and Qwen3.6-Plus (56.6%), though those systems use different scaffolds. Trajectory analyses show OASIS reaches ~10× deeper maximum effective depth than SSA and a growing future solve-rate advantage, with the global one-sided sign-flip null rejected at p=0.031 and checkpoints 16–18 individually significant (adjusted p=0.031–0.037). Baselines are thin but honestly compute-matched; the strongest claim (beating much larger proprietary systems) is a cross-scaffold comparison the authors themselves flag. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel elements are (a) framing recursive self-improvement as online learning with cumulative reward as the objective, and (b) the anchor-calibrated paired-comparison mechanism for branch control with confidence-gated promotion/reversion. The underlying statistical machinery (Beta credible intervals, dueling-bandit-style matched comparisons, LLM-as-judge best-of-k selection) is standard; the contribution is their composition in the self-modification-tree setting, plus reviving the 1997 SSA as the only applicable online baseline. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the compute-matched SSA variant isolates branch control from test-time selection, and the α-sensitivity run probes the calibration thresholds. Statistical testing is unusually careful for this area (exhaustive 2¹¹ sign-flip enumeration preserving within-stream dependence, Westfall-Young family-wise adjustment), but it is applied only to the trajectory metric, not the headline solve rates. No error bars or repeated seeds exist anywhere: Appendix C.5 states each configuration was run once because a full stream sweep costs ~USD 1,800 and 2,200 A100-hours for OASIS alone, and no hyperparameter search was performed. Code, prompts, materialized streams, agent trees, and resumable histories are described in detail but only planned for release — no URL or repository is given. Methodological concerns: (1) task streams are constructed by the authors (random permutation for SWE-Bench Pro, alphabetical topic ordering for DeepResearch Bench), so the non-stationarity being exploited is partly designed rather than naturally occurring; (2) the LLM judge used for solution selection is never itself evaluated, and judge errors directly contaminate the online reward; (3) comparisons against MiniMax/GPT-5.3-Codex/Qwen3.6-Plus involve different scaffolds and are self-reported relative positioning rather than controlled experiments. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system run end-to-end on real benchmark streams). - Practical: Yes — the SWE-Bench Pro configuration runs a 35B-A3B MoE locally via vLLM on NVIDIA A100 GPUs, and the DeepResearch configuration uses commercial APIs. - Efficient: The anchor roughly doubles task-solving rollouts, plus a validation re-run per self-modification candidate; total project cost was ~USD 4,000 API + 5,000 A100-hours, which is substantial for what is still a small-scale evaluation. - Effective: Evidence on the two target benchmarks is consistent and ablation-supported, but both are benchmark streams replayed deterministically rather than genuinely live deployments; effectiveness in a real production stream is untested. - Scalable: Not tested — streams top out at 29 online steps and ~96 tasks, and the authors acknowledge that longer runs are needed to see whether gains compound or regress late; the 10×-deeper-spine claim concerns tree depth, not deployment scale. The paper stops at paper form: code and streams are promised but no artifact is released at publication time. Strengths: - The branch-comparability diagnosis is a genuine insight: identifying that raw subtree-reward validation (SSA) mistakes task difficulty for agent quality, and demonstrating the resulting shallow-revert failure mode empirically (Figure 1's 10× effective-depth contrast). - The compute-matched ablation design is exemplary — giving the plain SSA baseline the same best-of-two + LLM-judge budget removes the most common confound in agent-system papers, and the result cleanly attributes ~4.4 of the 5.3 points to anchor calibration. - The statistical treatment of the trajectory claim (exhaustive sign-flip permutation test with Westfall-Young adjustment that preserves within-stream dependence) exceeds the rigor norm for agent papers. - The formulation itself (Section 2) is a clean, reusable formalization of online RSI that positions SSA and Gödel-machine-style systems as special cases and gives successors a common vocabulary. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that OASIS assumes a relatively structured environment with identifiable tasks and reproducible evaluations; that the method depends on usable (non-sparse, non-subjective, non-delayed) reward signals, and measured gains may not capture robustness or safety; that the evaluation horizon is short and longer runs are needed to test compounding and late-stage regressions; and that maintaining an anchor adds inference cost creating a deployment-dependent trade-off. Appendix A further concedes that anchor calibration is a reliability mechanism, not a safety guarantee, and that reward hacking or evaluator blind spots can still validate harmful modifications. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run results throughout: with no seeds and no variance estimates, a 4.4-point gain over compute-matched SSA (52.5% vs 56.9%) could plausibly fall within run-to-run noise for stochastic agentic systems; the paper's own honesty about this does not remove the concern. - The non-stationarity is partially self-constructed: permuting tasks within a repository and alphabetically ordering topics manufactures the distribution shift the anchor is designed to handle; no naturally occurring non-stationary stream (e.g., time-ordered issues) is evaluated. - The LLM judge is a silent single point of failure: it picks between two candidates per task, yet its accuracy, bias toward the anchor's outputs, and interaction with the reward signal are never measured. - Missing baseline family: offline RSI methods (Darwin/Huxley-Gödel Machine, self-improving coding agents) are discussed as the offline paradigm but never adapted to the online streams, so it is unknown whether a simpler offline-then-deploy strategy would match OASIS's cumulative reward. - The Beta(2,2) independence assumption for subtree rewards is almost certainly violated (nested subtrees share task records), and no experiment checks whether the credible intervals are actually calibrated. - The headline cross-model comparison (beating GPT-5.3-Codex etc.) compares different scaffolds and is not an apples-to-apples result, though the authors flag this more carefully than most. - DeepResearch Bench rests on only two streams (50 tasks each) with an LLM-judged RACE score, the weakest evidence in the paper. Bottom Line: A practitioner building adaptive agent systems gains a genuinely useful and well-ablated mechanism for the branch-comparability problem that offline-style self-improving agents will hit the moment they deploy, but the single-run evidence, manufactured non-stationarity, and unreleased code mean the 5+ point gains should be treated as promising rather than established — read it for the formulation and ablation design, verify the numbers yourself before adopting.

Self-Evolving Continual Learners

Xiaoyin Chen, Yizheng Huang, Yinglun Xu, Ziyun Zhao, Emmett McQuinn, Julie Liu, Hope Yao · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a formal continual-learning evaluation framework for nonparametric self-evolving LLM agents and empirically shows, across four drifting task streams and three representative methods, that current self-evolution improves aggregate performance but trades plasticity against stability (r = -0.72, p = 0.008) through cross-task interference, prompt overwriting, and retrieval collision. - Why it's important: Agents deployed over long horizons must absorb new tasks, tools, and workflows after weights are frozen, and per-session gradient updates are prohibitively expensive and erode general capabilities; if harness-level self-evolution silently destroys earlier skills, the dominant paradigm for cheap agent adaptation is unsound as deployed. - How it does it: The core move is recasting the agent's evolver (the function that rewrites prompts, memory, skills, and code) as a continual learner on task-free drifting streams, then decomposing stream advantage into within-block plasticity and cross-block stability (pre-block interference + post-block forgetting), with mechanistic forensics on prompt character-share, retrieval provenance, and behavior rates. - The good: The mechanistic evidence is unusually concrete: e.g., GEPA's prompt-share tracking shows BIRD-F1 rules falling from 59.5% to 4.1% of prompt characters while its accuracy gain decays from +4.0 to 0.0, and the retrieval-collision analysis shows BFCL-Miss/BFCL-Base nearest-match cross-group similarity (0.835-0.840) is statistically indistinguishable from within-group similarity (0.834-0.837), proving no similarity threshold can separate conflicting workflows. - The missing: All experiments use a single base model (Gemini 3.6 Flash), only three methods, blocks fixed at 50 tasks, and no error bars, seeds, significance tests, or released code are reported; the paper diagnoses the failure but proposes and tests no mitigation. - Read it or not: Anyone building self-evolving, memory-based, or prompt-optimizing agents should read it — it is the first rigorous continual-learning audit of this paradigm and quantifies failure modes (global-edit interference, retrieval collision, behavioral reversal) that will shape system design; pure continual-learning theorists can skip it since the metrics are adaptations of Lopez-Paz & Ranzato-style decomposition.
