Problem & Motivation: LLM agents are deployed in environments where new tasks, tools, and workflows arrive after the model weights are frozen, and they must learn each new task without erasing earlier ones — the classical continual learning problem, but at the timescale of individual interactions. Gradient-based adaptation is too expensive per session and is known to erode general capabilities when fine-tuned on small recent windows. Nonparametric self-evolving agents, which rewrite their own harness (system prompt, memory, skills, controller code) from task feedback while keeping weights frozen, are a natural alternative — but both existing paradigms (self-modification à la GEPA; experience augmentation à la ReasoningBank) were validated only on stationary, single-domain benchmarks. Whether they accumulate durable gains or suffer compounding interference on heterogeneous task streams was unknown. The paper closes this gap by asking: are current self-evolving agents effective continual learners? Key Idea: Formalize the agent's evolver f as the continual learner (c_{t+1} = f(c_t, H_t) on the frozen-weight harness c), run self-evolving methods designed for a single task family (K=1) on drifting multi-family streams, and decompose the advantage over the seed harness into within-block plasticity P and cross-block stability S = -(Ī + F̄). The negative result — a consistent plasticity-stability trade-off — is the paper's central insight: where a method writes its updates (one shared prompt vs. a retrieval-localized store) determines which failure mode it exhibits, but no placement avoids both. Methodology: The paper defines a task family F = (X, D, Y, R) with binary task-success reward, a K-family stream with piecewise-constant one-hot weight schedule (contiguous blocks of 50 tasks per group, no group labels or boundary hints revealed — a task-free setup), and evaluates the evolver via checkpoint accuracy A[t,k] on disjoint hold-out sets, offset by seed baseline B_k. Metrics: terminal advantage, average advantage Δ̄, plasticity P (advantage at each family's own block end), and stability S combining pre-block interference Ī and post-block forgetting F̄. Four streams built from BIRD, BFCL v4, and ScienceWorld isolate topic drift (three BIRD databases, T=150, K=3), workflow drift (BFCL-Miss → BFCL-Base: same APIs, conflicting requirement to ask vs. not ask for missing arguments, T=100, K=2), domain drift (ScienceWorld → BFCL-Base → BIRD-F1, T=150, K=3), and compound drift (all four groups, T=200, K=4), plus an interleaved uniform Mix reference stream. Three methods spanning both paradigms run on Gemini 3.6 Flash in a ReAct loop with binary success feedback: ReasoningBank (distills episodes to memory items, retrieves top-1 by gemini-embedding-2 cosine similarity), GEPA (rewrites a shared strategy prompt section via reflective mutation), and Meta-Harness (a coding-agent proposer in the opencode harness edits system prompt, memory/skill files, and controller code, gated by validation accuracy on the active sub-block). Checkpointing at every block boundary with 8 rollouts per hold-out instance. Critical design decisions: (1) the frozen base model across methods, isolating evolver effects — well-justified; (2) task-free streams with hidden group labels, mirroring realistic deployment — well-justified; (3) Meta-Harness's proposer running in a different harness (opencode) than the agent under test — a potential confound that is stated but not ablated. Key Results: Self-evolution improves stream performance in most settings — four-stream overall terminal advantage is +3.7 pp for GEPA, +2.5 for ReasoningBank, +1.4 for Meta-Harness (seed accuracies 43.2-79.2% per group) — but only topic drift yields near-zero or negative gains (-1.7, +0.3, -1.5 respectively). The central quantitative finding is the plasticity-stability trade-off: GEPA has the highest plasticity (+6.2 pp average, up to +11.0 on workflow drift) and the largest stability loss (-4.3 average), while ReasoningBank has the highest stability (-1.9) at roughly half the plasticity (+3.3); across 12 scenario-method points, P and S correlate at r = -0.72 (p = 0.008). Mechanistically: (a) self-modification causes pre-block interference — training on two BIRD blocks degrades unseen BFCL-Miss by 6.8 pp under GEPA and 4.8 under Meta-Harness before any BFCL task arrives — and post-block overwriting, with GEPA condensing seven BIRD sections (3,386 chars) into one (1,034 chars) and erasing BIRD-F1's +4.0 gain; (b) behavioral reversal under conflicting workflows: GEPA's clarification-asking rate on BFCL-Miss goes 3.8% → 29.8% (after the Miss block, +15.5 gain) → 11.2% (after the Base block, 13.0 pp accuracy drop), and Meta-Harness shows the same pattern (60.8% → 8.5%, 10.2 pp drop); (c) retrieval collision: 52% of BFCL-Miss and 46% of BFCL-Base evaluation episodes retrieve memories from the opposite workflow at stream end, dropping BFCL-Miss by 8.0 pp on workflow drift, because cross- and within-workflow embedding similarities (0.835-0.840 vs. 0.834-0.837 nearest-match) are indistinguishable. Interleaving all groups uniformly does not fix contention — GEPA's terminal advantage falls from +5.8 (blocked) to +0.9 (Mix). Tested scale is small and standard: streams of 100-200 tasks, 50 training tasks per block, 50-90 hold-out tasks per group. Baselines are current, representative methods (GEPA, ReasoningBank published 2025; Meta-Harness 2026), though only three are covered. A surprise: GEPA spontaneously adopts additive (append-only) prompt updates on domain drift, achieving zero forgetting, but this behavior emerges unreliably and is replaced by compression on compound drift. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a secondary NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK contribution (the four drifting stream configurations and the P/S decomposition adapted to harness evolution). Genuinely novel is the framing of harness-level self-evolution as a continual learning process and the identification of retrieval collision as a failure mode specific to similarity-based memory. The individual ingredients — standard continual-learning metrics (Kemker et al., Lopez-Paz & Ranzato), off-the-shelf self-evolving methods, and established benchmarks — are standard combinations applied to a new setting; the value is in the synthesis and the forensic analysis, not in new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation design is careful: metrics are formally defined, per-group interference/forgetting are fully decomposed (Table 3), and the mechanistic claims are backed by direct measurement (prompt character-share attribution, retrieval provenance percentages, clarification-asking rates over 400 rollouts per cell) rather than anecdotes. However: no error bars, no multiple seeds, and no significance tests are reported despite binary rewards and 8-rollout averages over 50-90 instances; several per-group effects are 1-2 pp, within plausible noise bands. No code, prompts, or stream configurations are stated as released (Not stated). Methodological concerns: (1) single base model — all conclusions rest on Gemini 3.6 Flash, so model-family generality is unverified; (2) the paper develops and evaluates its framework on the same three benchmarks it draws its conclusions from, though the conclusions are negative and unlikely to be Goodharted; (3) block length is fixed at 50 with no sensitivity analysis; (4) Meta-Harness's proposer runs in opencode, introducing a harness confound; (5) only three methods are sampled, so the plasticity-stability correlation rests on n=12 points from three design points. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (an evaluation study with a reusable benchmark construction, not a deployed system). Practical: Yes — all components run against a commercially available API model (Gemini 3.6 Flash) and public benchmarks. Efficient: Harness updates are cheap relative to gradient updates, but the protocol is evaluation-heavy (8 rollouts per checkpoint per group at every block boundary), which is a research cost, not a deployment cost. Effective: The evidence shows self-evolution partially solves the aggregate adaptation problem but demonstrably fails the stated continual-learning objective (no method achieves both high P and high S) — the paper is honest that the answer to its title question is "not yet." Scalable: Untested and questionable: streams are 100-200 tasks, and the observed failure modes (unbounded additive prompt growth to 7,621 characters, prompt contention) would plausibly worsen at 10× the number of groups; the paper claims no scalability. Deliverable: the paper stops at paper form plus a reproducible stream-construction recipe; no code artifact, library, or trained model release is stated. Strengths: - The formalization is genuinely useful: casting the evolver as a continual learner on task-free drifting streams connects two literatures (self-evolving agents; continual learning) with definitions precise enough to reconstruct the entire experimental protocol. - The mechanistic forensics are the paper's best execution — the prompt character-share tracking that shows accuracy decay in lockstep with rule displacement, and the retrieval-collision analysis showing cross-workflow similarity statistically identical to within-workflow similarity, convert vague worries about "agent memory" into measured, reproducible failure modes. - The behavioral-reversal finding (clarification rate 3.8% → 29.8% → 11.2% with matching accuracy swings) is a clean, quantified demonstration that conflicting workflows in a shared domain are the hardest drift case — a non-obvious and actionable result. - Honest negative control: the paper reports where self-evolution does not help (topic drift) and includes the interleaved Mix stream showing interleaving does not cure prompt contention, preempting the obvious "just shuffle the data" rejoinder. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state directly that current self-evolving agents are "incomplete continual learners" and that the findings call for mechanisms that isolate task-specific updates and condition retrieval beyond query similarity. They acknowledge that Meta-Harness's apparent stability on topic/workflow drift is an artifact of its validation gate rejecting updates (verified by the gate-removal ablation: stability drops from -0.3 to -3.1 on topic drift), that GEPA's additive update behavior is unreliable, and that no method escapes the trade-off. They do not include an explicit limitations section discussing scale, single-model generality, or seed variance; the confrontational honesty is at the finding level but thin at the methodology level. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-model results: every conclusion is conditioned on Gemini 3.6 Flash; whether the plasticity-stability trade-off is a property of self-evolution in general or of one model's in-context plasticity is untested. - No mitigation is proposed or tested — the paper diagnoses three failure modes but leaves the prescriptive question (e.g., task-conditioned retrieval, gated or modular prompt sections, per-domain workspaces) entirely open, limiting practical uptake. - No variance quantification: with 8 rollouts per instance on 50-90 instances and binary rewards, several reported 1-2 pp effects (e.g., ReasoningBank's -1.2 interference on domain drift) sit within plausible confidence intervals, yet no error bars or seeds are given. - Only three methods, each representing one point on the "editable surface" axis; the trade-off claim would be stronger with a fourth design point (e.g., scoped per-domain prompts) that could plausibly dominate the frontier. - The retrieval-collision analysis uses one embedding model (gemini-embedding-2); a stronger embedder or metadata filtering might separate the BFCL workflows, so "no similarity threshold can separate the two groups" is shown for one embedding space only. - Block length (50) and stream length (100-200) are fixed; whether the trade-off persists or amplifies at deployment-realistic horizons is extrapolated, not measured. Bottom Line: Practitioners building self-evolving agents, memory systems, or prompt-optimization pipelines should read this — it is the first rigorous continual-learning audit of the paradigm, its retrieval-collision and behavioral-reversal findings are directly actionable for system design, and despite single-model scope and missing variance analysis, no competing work covers this ground.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Sensorimotor Alignment (S²), a training-free offline metric that measures how closely a robot foundation model's image-text sensory representation aligns with the geometry of end-effector motion trajectories, and shows it correlates with closed-loop task success. - Why it's important: Closed-loop rollout evaluation of robot policies is slow, noisy, and expensive, and prior offline proxies (VQA scores, video-quality metrics) fail to predict downstream manipulation success, so a reliable pre-evaluation filter saves substantial compute and lab time. - How it does it: The core trick is a mutual k-nearest-neighbor overlap (a centered CKNNA variant from the Platonic Representation Hypothesis literature) between sensory embeddings (cosine distance) and end-effector trajectories (Dynamic Time Warping over 7D pose-plus-gripper sequences with SO(3) geodesic rotations). - The good: The correlation replicates across four model families (12 VLAs r=+0.717; 8 raw VLM backbones r=+0.681; 6 WAMs r=+0.718; 5 real-robot policies r=+0.831), transfers across reference datasets and horizons, and a deliberate embodiment-mismatch negative control collapses the correlation from r=+0.999 to +0.246 as it should. - The missing: All correlations are computed post-hoc on 3–12 models per family with one-tailed unadjusted p-values; the real-robot result at the reported horizon (h=110, r=+0.831) is an exploratory choice — the prespecified horizon gives r=+0.429, p=0.236 (disclosed only in the appendix) — and no prospective test of S² as a selection rule is run. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on VLA/world-model evaluation or representation-based model selection in robotics; skip it if you want a validated, deployable selection procedure, since the authors themselves position S² as correlational and not yet a training-time objective.

Problem & Motivation: Robot foundation model developers (VLA, VLM-backbone, and world-action-model builders) currently must run costly closed-loop rollouts in simulation or on physical robots to know whether a model is any good; these evaluations are slow, high-variance, and benchmark-specific. Existing offline proxies measure the wrong thing: VQA scores measure language/visual understanding and FID/SSIM/PSNR measure pixel-level generation quality, but neither captures whether a representation is organized for action. The paper targets the gap of predicting which models (or which VLM backbones before fine-tuning) will succeed at manipulation, without ever executing the policy. Key Idea: The single core insight is a PRH-inspired claim: motor trajectories are another projection of the same underlying world that vision and language representations model, so more capable embodied models should have sensory representations whose neighborhood geometry matches the neighborhood geometry of executed motion trajectories. Alignment is then measurable, training-free, as the overlap between k-nearest-neighbor sets computed in sensory space and in trajectory space. Methodology: For each of N sampled episodes from a reference dataset (DROID Franka Panda, N=6,000; BridgeDataV2 WidowX, N=3,245; bimanual ALOHA for WAMs, N=839), the paper builds (1) a sensory representation z_i from one sampled image frame plus the task instruction, encoded and mean-pooled by the model under test, and (2) a motor representation τ_i ∈ R^{h×7} of end-effector position, SO(3) orientation, and gripper state over the next h steps. Sensory distance is 1−cosine; motor distance is symmetric2 Dynamic Time Warping with a weighted local cost (position ℓ2 + quaternion geodesic + gripper difference, unit weights). Alignment is scored with the unbiased centered kernel nearest-neighbor alignment (CKNNA) estimator from Huh et al.'s PRH work (k=10), a centered, normalized variant of the plain neighbor-overlap count m_NN. Critical design decisions: (a) DTW to compare trajectories at different speeds — well-justified and ablated (removing DTW changes r by at most ±3.2%); (b) CKNNA rather than global CKA to emphasize local structure — adopted from prior work, not independently justified against alternatives; (c) absolute rather than anchor-relative poses as the default — the ablation actually shows anchor-relative gives a slightly higher r (+0.752 vs +0.717), a choice the authors admit is for simplicity. Key Results: (1) 12 fine-tuned VLAs vs SimplerEnv success: Pearson r=+0.717, p=0.004, model-bootstrap 95% CI [+0.436, +0.912]; the correlation survives leave-one-out over all five architecture groups (r from +0.526 to +0.785) and a CogACT-only within-family check (r=+0.826, n=3). (2) 8 raw VLM backbones (VLM4VLA recipe): S² correlates with post-fine-tuning SimplerEnv success at r=+0.681 (p=0.031), whereas aggregate VQA scores correlate at r=−0.154 — the headline contrast. (3) 6 WAMs on bimanual ALOHA vs RoboTwin 2.0 success: r=+0.718, but p=0.054 (not significant at 0.05); on the 3 WAMs that generate video, S² reaches r=+0.999 (n=3) versus SSIM +0.558, PSNR +0.468, and FID correlating in the wrong direction (+0.680, i.e., better FID→worse success). (4) 5 real-robot policies from MolmoB0T's shared 120-trial evaluation: r=+0.831 at the exploratory horizon h=110; the prespecified h=7 yields r=+0.429, p=0.236 (appendix only). (5) 14 frozen vision encoders from Hu et al.: S² correlates with BC success at r=+0.677 and visual-reward RL at r=+0.774, but not with RL-from-task-reward (r between −0.193 and −0.002) or large BC budgets (r=+0.236). (6) Robustness: correlation holds across both reference datasets (r≈+0.7), all horizons h∈{1..220} for joint features (r=+0.610 to +0.717), and all implementation variants (r=+0.634 to +0.752). (7) Diagnostic findings: fine-tuned VLAs' success correlates with vision-feature S² (r=+0.694) but not text-feature S² (r=+0.237), reversing before fine-tuning; freezing the ViT drops S² by ~41% and success by ~40%; WAM S² is flat (≤6% variation) across the denoising schedule and peaks at mid-depth Block 14 in all 3 WAMs. Success rates are taken from published reports/repositories rather than re-run by the authors. Baselines (VQA, FID/SSIM/PSNR) are the standard alternatives in this space and are current. Note this is an arXiv preprint (v2, Oct 2026); results are not peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a modest NEW METHOD (the S² metric as a robotics-specific instantiation) and a NEW PROBLEM framing (extending the Platonic Representation Hypothesis to motor data). The genuinely novel element is the hypothesis itself — treating end-effector trajectories as a third Platonic modality and validating the convergence prediction against closed-loop success — plus the representation-level explanations of known VLA/WAM phenomena. The machinery (CKNNA from Huh et al., DTW, standard feature pooling) is a competent combination of existing tools; the WAM denoising-step and mid-depth-block findings confirm rather than extend prior behavioral observations. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is one of the more rigorous correlation papers in this genre. Ablations are extensive: leave-one-out over architecture groups, confound control via a fixed fine-tuning recipe, within-family scale check, horizon sweeps over 10 settings, five implementation variants (k, normalization, weights, rotation distance, pooling), a DTW-vs-lockstep ablation, and a genuinely informative negative control (embodiment mismatch collapses r from +0.999 to +0.246). Code and project page are public (github.com/yunfeixie233/sensorimotor-alignment). However: all p-values are one-tailed and unadjusted; three of four families have n≤8, with the WAM result failing the 0.05 threshold (p=0.054) and the r=+0.999 result resting on 3 points; success rates are self-reported from external papers/repos rather than re-evaluated under one protocol; and — the sharpest concern — the real-robot correlation of r=+0.831 in the main text comes from an exploratory horizon (h=110), while the prespecified h=7 gives r=+0.429, p=0.236, a post-hoc-selection pattern the authors disclose in Appendix B.5 but do not surface in the headline claim. No prospective test (select models by S², then verify with rollouts) is run. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement/diagnostic method validated by correlation, not a trained system). - Practical: Yes — S² is training-free and runs on a single GPU over public checkpoints and public datasets (DROID, BridgeDataV2, ALOHA); no robot hardware needed. - Efficient: Cheaper than any alternative by construction — it replaces closed-loop rollouts with offline embedding plus DTW, whose O(N²h²) pairwise cost on N≈6,000 episodes is the only nontrivial compute; no runtime numbers are stated. - Effective: The evidence shows correlation, not problem-solving — S² ranks models imperfectly (similar S² can yield different success rates, per the authors), and the real-robot ranking is fragile to the horizon choice, so it solves only a proxy of the stated filtering problem. - Scalable: Not tested — nothing addresses whether S²–success correlation holds over 100+ models or datasets beyond the three reference sets; the metric's value at cohort scale is claimed, not demonstrated. Deliverable: a software artifact — released code, project website, and a reusable metric; no trained model or dataset is contributed. Strengths: - A genuinely new empirical claim with a clean conceptual frame: PRH extended to a generated modality (motion) rather than observational ones, tested with a concrete, cheap, implementable metric. - The paper distinguishes what it claims from what it measures unusually well, and the diagnostic section converts a correlation into representation-level explanations (vision-dominance after fine-tuning, frozen-encoder S² deficit of 41% matching a 40% success drop, flat S² across denoising) that are independently interesting to VLA/WAM builders. - Robustness work exceeds the norm for correlation studies: cross-dataset transfer, full horizon sweeps, implementation ablations, and an embodiment-mismatch negative control that behaves exactly as a sound metric should. - Honest disclosure of the h=110 exploratory horizon and the frozen-encoder RL-variability failures in the appendix, rather than burying them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) the S²–success relationship is correlational and they have not shown S² can be optimized during training to improve success; (2) models with similar S² can differ in success, so S² is only a pre-screening proxy with closed-loop evaluation still final; (3) evaluation covers limited model families, benchmarks, recipes, few models per comparison, and a single real-robot setting. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment of the right limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The main-text headline r=+0.831 for real robots rests on a horizon chosen after seeing results; the prespecified, non-significant r=+0.429 belongs in the main claim, and a skeptical reader should discount that panel entirely. - Success rates are compiled from heterogeneous external reports and repos rather than re-run under one controlled protocol, so evaluation-protocol variance is confounded with S². - The WAM comparisons use 3 or 6 models; an r=+0.999 on three points is not evidence of a strong relationship, and the family-level p=0.054 misses significance. - Potential circularity: several evaluated models (e.g., StarVLA variants, GR00T bridges) fine-tune on BridgeData or DROID-family data, so sensory features of better models may be closer to the reference trajectories themselves for reasons of data overlap rather than capability; the paper does not test S² on models trained entirely outside the reference data distribution. - No comparison against other representation-alignment proxies (e.g., plain CKA to trajectories, RDM-style distance correlation), so it is unknown whether CKNNA specifically matters or any sensory-vs-motor alignment statistic would work. - The claim that S² "explains" instruction-grounding failure is an inference from a missing text-feature correlation; no direct intervention (e.g., prompt perturbation) validates the causal story. Bottom Line: A practitioner evaluating VLAs, VLM backbones, or world action models gains a cheap, well-validated screening signal that beats VQA and video-quality metrics by a wide margin, but should treat it strictly as a pre-filter with the real-robot headline discounted and closed-loop evaluation retained — there is no stronger offline alternative covering the same ground today.

Problem & Motivation: Developers deploying coding/CLI agents face a gap between benchmark performance and real-world usability: users rarely provide complete, fixed specifications, instead adding information, revising constraints, and deciding whether to authorize high-impact actions mid-execution. Existing benchmarks either assume autonomous execution with upfront instructions (SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE, Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench) or treat user interaction as an aid to task completion rather than a separate evaluation target (Ambig-SWE, SWE-INTERACT, SWE-Together, Dialogue SWE-Bench). No prior benchmark unifies task effectiveness and multi-dimensional collaboration quality under identical tasks and environments, which blocks systematic answers to (RQ1) what task outcomes and collaboration quality agents achieve when users participate and how the two relate, and (RQ2) how behavior differs between autonomous and collaborative execution on the same tasks. Key Idea: Treat collaboration as a first-class, independently scored evaluation axis via a paired-task design: the same task instance (environment, verifier, acceptance criteria) is run twice — once with the full specification upfront (EXEC) and once with a scripted user who releases the specification in ~16 slices and fires six scenario probes timed to execution state (COLLAB) — so that deltas in task success and collaboration profiles are attributable to the interaction itself rather than task difficulty. The second half of the idea is evidence-based collaboration scoring: expected behaviors are decomposed into binary checklist items where environment evidence overrides dialogue claims, with strict timing anchors (remedial correctness after a probe scores 0) and an all-or-nothing aggregation through a 75% cross-task consistency threshold. Methodology: The pipeline has two stages. (1) Base instance synthesis: real CLI logs are compressed into task patterns, converted into skills, and synthesized into containerized tasks with instructions, reference solutions, and verifiers (56 Python assert, 34 Bash, 11 VLM-judged); quality checks require reference solutions to pass and no-op baselines to fail, followed by multi-agent multi-run rollouts that separate task issues from infrastructure issues and profile difficulty (only medium/hard instances are retained). (2) Interactive instance synthesis: each base task gets six assigned collaboration scenarios, an interaction script (opening, ~16 information slices, six probes with checklist items, closing), validated by static checks, semantic review, end-to-end pilot runs with judge review, and human expert curation. Formally, each task is a tuple (E, s0, ω, V); the two modes differ in action/observation spaces, with COLLAB adding communication actions and user messages. Scoring uses a four-level aggregation: binary scenario perfection (Level 1), cross-task scenario consistency with a 0.75 threshold (Level 2), equal-weight sub-dimension and dimension means (Level 3), and S_COLLAB as the mean of five dimension scores; J_COLLAB = R_COLLAB × S_COLLAB. The user simulator is GLM-5.3 driven by a detailed verbatim guide with append-only ledger auditing; the judge is Claude Code running Claude-Opus-4.8, which separately scores agent checklists and simulator script fidelity, flagging contaminated sessions. Critical design decisions: (a) environment evidence taking precedence over dialogue claims — well-justified against inflated self-reports; (b) the strict 75% cross-task consistency threshold and all-or-nothing Level-1 scoring — justified as enforcing reliability, but the threshold is arbitrary and un-ablated; (c) multiplicative J_COLLAB — justified as penalizing unsafe-but-effective agents, but it conflates task and collaboration regressions into one number. Key Results: Across 33 configurations (11 models × 3 scaffolds: Claude Code 2.1.140, Terminus-2, Codex 0.142.0; avg@3, 600-turn cap, 6h/10h budgets) on 101 tasks: the best average task reward is 49.2% (Claude Opus 5), followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 45.6%; peak J_COLLAB is 37.6% (Opus 5 on Terminus-2). Task effectiveness and collaboration diverge sharply: GPT-5.6 Sol reaches R_EXEC of 58.5% on Codex but J_COLLAB drops 50.0 points to 8.5%, with Trust Calibration at 7% and Safety at 0% on two scaffolds. User interaction is not a uniform gain: on matched Claude Code runs, aggregate pass rates are nearly identical (46.8% interactive vs. 47.4% autonomous), but 17.9% of runs flip failure→success while 18.5% flip success→failure; gains concentrate in Data Analysis and Software Engineering (+up to +50.0 pp per model), regressions in System Operations, Models & Algorithms, and Office Suite. Collaboration is dimensionally imbalanced: Understandability and Observation & Recovery score relatively high (e.g., Opus 5/Terminus-2: 85·40·89·43·43 in U·S·OR·TC·SR), while Steerability, Trust Calibration, and Safety are weak. Behavioral diagnostics: 80.2% strict pass on updating plans after blockers vs. 51.7% on recognizing scope expansion; 98.8% on following the latest request vs. 54.4% on retaining early constraints and 29.3% on resolving conflicting instructions; among successful interactive trajectories, 91.0% fail at least one collaboration check; constraint-retention failures are 91.3% artifact mismatches, and 53.3% of those still pass all communication checks (saying without doing). Interactive trajectories are 1.43×–3.62× longer in median tool calls across models, and 59.9% of runs with more interactive calls and sub-1.0 reward do not improve reward. Baselines are current frontier models (mid-2026 releases: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, DeepSeek V4.1, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 Max), so the comparison set is strong. Tested at a standard benchmark scale (101 tasks, 606 scenario instances), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW FORMULATION: the genuine novelty is the paired EXEC/COLLAB design on identical task instances with collaboration scored as an independent axis against a five-dimensional taxonomy grounded in HCI theory, plus the evidence-based (environment-over-dialogue) checklist scoring protocol. The constituent techniques — LLM-simulated users, progressive information disclosure, probe-based scenario testing, containerized CLI environments — are combinations of existing ideas from SWE-INTERACT, UnderSpecBench, and Terminal-Bench applied to a unified setting; the taxonomy itself is a competent synthesis of Amershi et al. (2019) and Shneiderman (2020) guidelines rather than new theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is partially present: the paired design itself is a controlled comparison, and there are strong auxiliary audits — simulator script-fidelity checks (94.9–100% per configuration, 98.0% no-harmful-deviation overall), a separate judge evaluation of simulator contamination, and NA handling that excludes scenarios whose triggers never occurred. Runs use avg@3 to mitigate trajectory stochasticity, but no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, and with 101 tasks the per-cell differences (e.g., many ±10–20 pp category-level swings on 7–16 tasks) have wide uncertainty. The scoring methodology is unusually transparent for an LLM-judged benchmark: the full judge prompt, simulator guide, and checklist semantics are reproduced verbatim in appendices, and 33.5% of checklist items (555/1,658) use deterministic environment evidence. Code and data are referenced via GitHub and Hugging Face links on the title page, but no specific URLs or a released leaderboard are verifiable from the text. Methodological concerns: the judge is a frontier Claude model scoring Claude-family and competitor agents — self-judging bias cannot be ruled out and no judge-validation or human-agreement study is reported; the 75% consistency threshold and equal weighting of dimensions are un-validated design choices; and benchmark construction used agent rollouts for difficulty profiling, so instances are partly filtered by the same class of models being evaluated (Goodhart-adjacent, though a held-out split is used for headline numbers). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built benchmark with an execution harness, scripts, verifier, and judge infrastructure, evaluated by running 33 agent configurations through it). - Practical: Yes — tasks run in isolated Docker containers with any of three mainstream open scaffolds and API-accessible models; a research group with API budget can run it. - Efficient: Not cheap — COLLAB runs get 10-hour budgets, up to 600 turns, and interactive trajectories are 1.43×–3.62× longer than EXEC, so a full 33-configuration sweep with avg@3 is a substantial compute/API expenditure. - Effective: The evidence convincingly shows the benchmark measures something outcome-only benchmarks miss (91.0% of task-successful runs fail collaboration checks), though whether S_COLLAB predicts real human preference for an agent is untested — it is a proxy validated only against the authors' own construction. - Scalable: Task count (101) and the LLM-judge-LLM-simulator stack are the bottleneck; scaling to thousands of tasks would multiply judge and simulator costs, and judge consistency at scale is unexamined — the paper tests only what it built, making no scaling claims. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (benchmark package with instance layout, interaction scripts, oracle contracts, judge templates) plus GitHub and Hugging Face release pointers; the five-dimension taxonomy and checklist protocol are reusable evaluation techniques independent of the specific instances. Strengths: - The paired-task design is the paper's real contribution: running the identical task, environment, and verifier under autonomous and scripted-collaboration modes enables causal, within-task attribution of interaction effects, which no prior CLI benchmark does (Table 1 comparison is accurate on this point). - The collaboration-scoring protocol is unusually well-engineered: environment evidence overrides dialogue claims, timing anchors make remedial correctness score 0, NA handling removes un-triggered scenarios from denominators, and simulator contamination is separately audited and flagged — this directly addresses the two standard failure modes of interactive benchmarks (lenient judges and simulator error). - The failure-mode analysis goes beyond leaderboard numbers and yields actionable findings: the say-do gap (53.3% of artifact mismatches pass all communication checks) and the cross-turn goal-maintenance deficit (29.3% conflict resolution vs. 98.8% latest-request following) are specific, quantified, and diagnostic for training-data and post-training work. - Construction discipline is above average for LLM-synthesized benchmarks: reference-solution-must-pass / no-op-must-fail checks, multi-agent multi-run diagnosis separating task from infrastructure issues, and end-to-end pilots verifying that each intended collaboration behavior is actually elicitable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper's explicit limitation statements are thin; it concedes that user interaction "is not a reliable gain" and that its benefits "vary by task type and model," and implicitly acknowledges the difficulty of simulator control by building the entire audit apparatus (Part B of the judge, ledger auditing, contamination flagging, degraded-probe semantics) — which is itself an admission that simulator fidelity is a live risk. It does not include a dedicated limitations section addressing judge bias, scorer validity, or benchmark size; on this point it minimizes rather than confronts. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No validation that the LLM judge (Claude Opus 4.8) scores collaboration checklists correctly: no human-annotated agreement sample, no comparison of judge verdicts against expert labels, and a same-family judge evaluating Claude models creates a plausible self-model bias that is unexamined. - The user simulator is itself an LLM (GLM-5.3), so measured "collaboration quality" is agent-behavior-under-one-simulator; simulator stylistic quirks (e.g., pressure phrasing) could systematically trip or favor particular models, and no cross-simulator robustness check is run. - The 75% cross-task consistency threshold (Eq. 5) and equal dimension weighting are arbitrary; no ablation shows results are robust to these choices, and the all-or-nothing Level-1 scoring makes the metric sensitive to single checklist failures on tasks with few triggered scenarios. - Category-level pass-rate swings (Figure 4) are reported in percentage points on cells of 7–16 tasks without any uncertainty quantification; several headline contrasts (e.g., ±40 pp flips) may not survive averaging noise despite avg@3. - Benchmark construction used agent rollouts and judge review during curation; although headline numbers use a held-out split, the extent of distributional overlap between curated tasks and the models' post-training data (notably for the Claude family used in the toolchain) is not discussed. - The planted-secret and injection scenarios test a narrow, pre-specified set of safety behaviors; whether checklist performance on these scripted probes transfers to unscripted safety failures is asserted, not shown. Bottom Line: A practitioner building human-in-the-loop coding agents should read this paper — the paired evaluation design, the evidence-based checklist protocol, and the quantified say-do gap are directly reusable and expose failure modes that SWE-bench-style scores structurally cannot see — but the LLM-judge validity and simulator-dependence issues mean its collaboration scores should be treated as a well-instrumented proxy pending independent human validation, not ground truth.

UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents (47 ▲ )

Jujia Zhao, Jiakai Tang, Jing Yu, Wen Chen, Jian Wu, Han Zhu, Fei Sun, Suzan Verberne, Zhaochun Ren · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces USERARENA, an interactive e-commerce benchmark of 64,729 real session trajectories from 11,010 users (566,102 items, 577,670 actions, 13 action types) paired with a five-level simulator-fidelity protocol and offline validation against a production A/B test, plus a training method (On-Policy Trajectory Distillation, OPTD) that achieves the best fidelity among evaluated simulators. - Why it's important: Post-training and evaluating agentic recommendation policies currently relies on simulators whose long-horizon behavioral fidelity is unmeasured, so offline simulation conclusions may not transfer to production — costing platforms expensive online A/B tests and misleading policy development. - How it does it: OPTD combines on-policy distillation (teacher supervision on student-generated rollouts rather than ground-truth prefixes) with a trajectory-level intent summary given as privileged context to the teacher, constrained per-token by a trust-region interpolation bounded by a KL divergence budget (ε = 0.02) against an unconditioned reference. - The good: The offline validation against a real production A/B test is the standout: OPTD reproduces the production ΔPV-CTR policy effect at 0.713× versus 0.020×–0.297× for task-specific baselines and 1.576×–2.154× for GPT-6 models, an effect error 50.2% lower than the next-best simulator. - The missing: The A/B validation uses a single policy pair on a single platform; all fidelity metrics and the distillation method are developed and evaluated on the same benchmark (Goodhart risk), and even OPTD underestimates the production effect by 28.7%. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate user simulators, recommendation world models, or offline policy evaluation for agentic recommendation; skip it if you need general web-agent benchmarks or methods validated beyond e-commerce shopping feeds.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is the top dimension — production A/B validation of simulator-based policy deltas is unprecedented among interactive recommendation benchmarks, and the privileged-intent trust-region distillation is a genuine twist on on-policy distillation. Non-Obviousness (75) follows: task-specific simulators attenuating real effects 3–50× while frontier models overestimate 1.6–2.2× is an important, unpredictable finding. Problem & Motivation: Agentic recommendation requires a scalable "recommendation world model" — an executable environment plus a user simulator — to support offline, counterfactual, and RL-based policy optimization without running costly online experiments. Who has this problem: e-commerce platforms and researchers developing recommendation agents and user simulators. The paper identifies two gaps in prior resources: (1) at the data level, existing datasets (Amazon Reviews, Qilin, OmniBehavior, OPeRA, USB) rarely provide long-horizon trajectories that align user profiles, visual observations, product context, and actions across repeated sessions; (2) at the evaluation level, next-action agreement measures step-wise choices in isolation and does not test whether simulated trajectories preserve long-horizon behavioral tendencies, nor whether simulator-based policy comparisons agree with production A/B outcomes. Table 1 shows no prior benchmark combines real traces, visual context, full action space, long-horizon scope, and production A/B validation. Key Idea: Two ideas, one per contribution. For the benchmark: reconstruct the production shopping environment offline (pre-rendered feeds, viewport cropping on scroll, interactive detail pages) so that every logged decision is step-aligned with what the user actually saw, then evaluate simulator fidelity hierarchically — L0 output validity, L1 local next-decision, L2 sequential dynamics, L3 personalized population heterogeneity, L4 aggregate outcome/CTR fidelity — with a Replay mode (predict logged action at recorded states) and a Rollout mode (free-running generation). For OPTD: extract an abstract trajectory-level intent z_u from the full training trajectory (excluding products, prices, actions, outcomes) and give it as privileged context only to a frozen teacher, whose token-level distributions on the student's own rollouts provide dense supervision; a per-token trust region interpolates the intent-conditioned teacher distribution with an unconditioned reference in log-probability space so intent can shift the target by at most ε nats of KL per token. This simultaneously addresses sparse exact-match supervision (replaced by full-vocabulary JSD targets) and exposure bias (training on student-generated prefixes). Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Benchmark construction: normalize raw platform logs into a 13-action space, reconstruct feed and item-detail pages in an offline React environment via batch rendering, stratify users 8:1:1 into train/validation/test, and link 59,378 sessions from 5,768 users into cross-session trajectories (mean 10.29 sessions, 86.36 actions per user). (2) Evaluation: five fidelity levels with metrics including Replay/Rollout valid-action rates, macro-F1 and exact-match accuracy (L1), decision-mix JSD and trajectory-length error (L2), cohort-based population fidelity across eight behavioral blocks (L3), and ΔCTR/ΔACR errors plus terminal-state JSD (L4); the A/B validation compares ΔPV-CTR of a fixed policy pair across simulators against production values with 10,000 users split 5,000/5,000. (3) OPTD training: SFT warm-up (rationale + structured action targets, rationales generated by Qwen3.5-397B), then on-policy distillation with loss L = L_dist + γ·L_GT where L_dist is a per-token generalized JSD against the trust-region-regularized teacher target q^λ_t,k and L_GT is a teacher-forced cross-entropy grounding term (γ = 0.1, β = 0.5, λ_t,k found by 8-iteration bisection). Critical design decisions: (a) privileged intent only in the teacher, preventing it from becoming an answer key — well-motivated but the leakage-control rules are validated only by construction; (b) the trust region ε = 0.02 — reasonable but chosen without a sensitivity sweep reported in the main text; (c) shared Qwen3.5-2B backbone for all baselines — a good controlled-comparison choice isolating method from scale. The framework is on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024) adapted with trajectory-level conditioning and per-token trust regions; the JSD objective is bounded, avoiding unbounded per-token losses. Key Results: On the eight L1–L4 metrics in the single-session setting, OPTD (Qwen3.5-2B) ranks first on all eight: macro-F1 0.4178 (vs. Customer-R1 0.4108, STA 0.4030), accuracy 0.3204, DM-JSD 0.0156 (vs. STA 0.0245), trajectory error 1.72, population fidelity 0.8692, ΔCTR 0.0026, ΔACR 0.0430, T-JSD 0.0387. In the cross-session setting, OPTD ranks first on five of eight and second on two; STA leads macro-F1 (0.3556 vs. 0.3456) and ΔCTR. A/B Agent shows poor valid-action rates (0.4113 RVA single-session), suggesting limited transfer to the fixed action protocol. In production A/B validation, OPTD reaches an effect ratio of 0.713× (effect error 0.287), vs. STA 0.297×, Customer-R1 0.191×, Shop-R1 0.162×, AlignUSER 0.020×, base Qwen3.5-2B 0.004×, and GPT-6-Sol/GPT-6-Luna at 1.576×/2.154× (overestimation). Ablations show each component (on-policy sampling, intent, trust region, grounding, SFT warm-up) contributes, with w/o SFT degrading most. In a Turing-style blinded evaluation (200 pairs, 3 annotators, Fleiss' κ = 0.528), OPTD has the lowest human win rate (38.7%, i.e., hardest to detect) and highest "model win" rate (26.3%). Baselines are current (2024–2026 methods including RL-tuned Shop-R1/Customer-R1 and GUI-based STA/A/B Agent), and the shared-backbone design is strong. Scale is moderate: 2B-parameter students, ~64K sessions, 10K-user A/B simulation pool. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the combination of step-aligned visual observations with a full action space, cross-session long-horizon trajectories, and offline validation against a controlled production A/B test is, per the paper's Table 1 and this reviewer's knowledge of the cited works, unprecedented among interactive recommendation benchmarks; the trajectory-level-intent-conditioned teacher with per-token trust-region interpolation is a new twist on on-policy distillation. The distillation machinery itself (on-policy rollout, JSD targets, teacher/student split) is a direct application of Agarwal et al. (2024) to a new domain; the five-level protocol is a sensible assembly of existing metric types (JSD, F1, cohort comparison). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover all five OPTD components with fixed settings, though each ablation reports only one representative metric per level. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for the main Table 2 comparisons, and margins between OPTD and STA on several cross-session metrics (e.g., PF 0.8929 vs. 0.8911, ΔCTR 0.0099 vs. 0.0357 reversed in STA's favor) are small. Code and data are stated to be publicly available (github.com/RecGPT-Team/UserArena; project page recgpt-team.github.io/UserArena-Page), with extensive metric definitions (Appendix A.3), hyperparameters, and prompt templates — a strong reproducibility posture. Methodological concerns: (1) OPTD and all metrics are developed and evaluated on the same benchmark with no external validation set; (2) the A/B validation covers one policy pair from one platform, and the production reference window/users differ from the simulation setup; (3) intent-extraction quality (Qwen3.5-397B) is not independently validated; (4) L1 accuracy excludes scroll actions by an argued but consequential design choice. The benchmark derives from Alibaba production data — effectively a vendor-affiliated dataset, though de-identification and release under a data use agreement mitigate this partially. Deployability (4-property check): Profile — EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component via the released benchmark/environment). - Practical: Runs on standard GPU infrastructure (BF16, Qwen3.5-2B student, vLLM serving, Megatron-Core training); the A/B simulation used a frozen 10K-user pool. - Efficient: Step-wise token and latency analysis shows OPTD uses fewer total tokens than STA with closely aligned latency, so fidelity gains do not cost extra per-step inference, though on-policy distillation training requires teacher inference at 397B scale. - Effective: Evidence supports fidelity to logged behavior (L1–L4 sweep) and directional agreement with one production policy effect, but even OPTD errs 28.7% on that effect — useful for relative comparisons, not yet for absolute effect prediction. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — scaling to larger catalogs, more concurrent policies, or multi-policy A/B sweeps is untested; RL training on the simulator (the stated end use) is not demonstrated. The work delivers a software artifact (benchmark, environment, code, data) plus trained checkpoints implied by the release, not just a paper. Strengths: - The production A/B validation is a rare and genuinely valuable evaluation axis: most simulator papers never test whether simulated policy deltas match reality, and the result (task-specific simulators attenuate the effect 3–50×, frontier general-purpose models overestimate 1.6–2.2×) is an important empirical finding in itself. - The privileged-intent-plus-trust-region design is a clean solution to a real tension — using trajectory-level information during training without leaking it to the student at inference — and the per-token KL budget makes the leakage constraint explicit and tunable rather than implicit. - Controlled comparison design: identical backbone (Qwen3.5-2B), identical action schema and prompts for trainable baselines, and both Replay (isolating local fidelity) and Rollout (exposing compounding errors) modes. - The benchmark's step-aligned visual reconstruction (viewport cropping from pre-rendered full feeds, interactive detail pages for any exposed item) enables counterfactual evaluation that log-replay datasets structurally cannot support. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that all evaluated simulators, including OPTD, still underestimate the production effect (OPTD by 28.7%), and that A/B Agent's low valid-action rates limit its transfer to the fixed protocol. They frame the Turing evaluation's Fleiss' κ (0.528) as measuring annotator consistency rather than attribution correctness — a careful, credible framing. The conclusion scopes future work to leaderboard development and stronger long-horizon simulators. The limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Benchmark-method circularity: the fidelity metrics, intent extraction, and OPTD are all co-designed on USERARENA; a simulator optimized for these metrics could game them (e.g., matching DM-JSD and terminal-outcome distributions without modeling per-user choice), and no held-out external environment tests this. (2) Single policy pair, single platform, single observation window for the headline A/B validation — generalization of the 0.713× calibration to other policies or effect sizes is untested, and with 5,000 users per arm the production ΔPV-CTR estimate itself carries variance that is not propagated into the effect ratio. (3) No statistical uncertainty on Table 2 or Table 3, so the OPTD-vs-STA margins on several metrics may not be meaningful. (4) The end-use claim — supporting RL-based policy optimization in the simulator — is never demonstrated by training a policy in simulation and validating it online. (5) Intent extraction relies on a 397B LLM with no human validation of intent quality, and extraction cost at training scale is unreported. (6) 92% of clicked items appear only once and 54.9% of clicks are apparel, so item-level generalization and category coverage may be weaker than headline counts suggest. Bottom Line: For anyone building or trusting LLM-based user simulators for recommendation, this is currently the most credible evaluation substrate available — the A/B validation alone justifies reading it — but its findings should be treated as platform-specific until the single-policy-pair, single-benchmark circularity is broken by independent replication.

Trajectory2Gym: Decision-Grounded Compositional Interaction Synthesis for Tool-Use Agents (336 ▲ )

Yihao Hu, Zhihao Wen, Yitong Lin, Siyuan Lu, Pan Wang, Wei Wu, Jiang-Ming Yang, Tao Lin · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Trajectory2Gym, a pipeline that synthesizes tool-use interactions around under-represented multi-step dependency structures, certifies each supervised action against the agent-visible history, and trains with a parent-normalized SFT objective, raising the Tau1/Tau2/BFCL three-benchmark mean by 16.9–29.8 points across five Qwen3 scales (1.7B–30B-A3B). - Why it's important: The dominant practice of collecting success-filtered trajectories produces supervision where 40.9% of interactions contain at most two supervised decisions and only 10.0% contain a certified decision after an authentic error, so agents systematically fail to learn cross-step dependencies and recovery — the very behaviors stateful benchmarks score. - How it does it: The core trick is a decision-level supervision mask that separates native execution validity from decision-time grounding (identifier-like arguments must trace to prior visible evidence), combined with deficit-guided synthesis in native environments and weighting each semantic trajectory equally regardless of how many rendered examples it produces. - The good: The evidence is built on strict paired comparisons — each post-trained model versus its own public Qwen3 initialization under identical benchmarks, interfaces, and scorers — with the 4B post-trained model (69.17 Tau2) surpassing the public 30B-A3B initialization (28.33) and matched 8B ablations isolating each stage. - The missing: Every ablation arm and every benchmark task is run once with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests (the authors concede gains of a few points are only "directional"), and the largest headline gains come from the full recipe rather than from any single isolated component. - Read it or not: Practitioners building tool-use training pipelines should read it for the grounding-mask formulation, the parent-normalization finding, and the honest accounting of what outcome filtering misses; readers seeking RL-based agent training or theory will find little beyond SFT.

Problem & Motivation: Teams fine-tuning tool-use agents typically supervise on trajectories filtered by task completion or per-call execution, but success certifies that an episode ended well, not that each imitated action was justified by what the learner could see at decision time — a collector can invoke an identifier the student never observed, and the environment accepts it anyway. The result is supervision that under-represents compositional dependencies (observation → later action), recovery from authentic errors, and workflow ordering, and prior work shows fine-tuning on logged trajectories can even fall below initialization. The problem hits anyone training agents on interactive stateful benchmarks (τ-bench-style customer service, multi-turn function calling), where later decisions depend on earlier observations. Key Idea: Decompose trajectory value into two certifiable properties — compositional coverage (the dependency structures an interaction actually realizes) and decision grounding (whether each supervised action follows from the learner-visible history) — and operationalize them as a binary mask m_t = R_τ · 1[q_τ ⪯ A_τ] · g_t with g_t = e_t·v_t, so that failed calls remain visible context without imitation loss while grounded recoveries become targets. Once this framing is accepted, the rest follows: synthesize tasks to realize missing paths, mask non-grounded decisions, and normalize training mass per semantic trajectory rather than per rendered row. Methodology: Three coupled stages. (1) Compositional interaction synthesis: a shared capability vocabulary abstracts native tools into canonical paths; a generator produces requests and initial states conditioned on under-supported paths, and a teacher executes them in native environments, with certification requiring that the intended dependencies actually appear in the executed log. (2) Grounded supervision: each executed log yields student contexts containing only native-interface-visible events; target eligibility requires execution validity AND visible argument provenance AND workflow-order consistency (ordered subsequence check); authentic errors are retained as context but masked from the loss. (3) Structural-support learning: greedy deficit-driven selection maximizes capped per-path support at a scale-dependent depth d_s (1, 2, 3, 4, 8 for 1.7B–30B-A3B), with proved submodularity for the pure-budget case; training uses parent-normalized SFT (each semantic trajectory gets weight 1/|D_s| distributed over its certified tokens), proved rendering-invariant. Critical design decisions: masking rather than discarding failed calls (well justified via recovery examples and an entropy-floor argument in Proposition 1); the depth schedule (admittedly non-monotonic in the sensitivity study, weakly justified); exclusion of teacher-only hints from student traces (well justified). Key Results: On Tau1+Tau2, paired gains in domain-averaged success range from +20.04 (1.7B) to +40.92 (14B) points; the post-trained 30B-A3B reaches 84.17 Tau2 average, within 1.2 points of reported Claude-4.5-Opus (85.31) and GPT-5.2 (84.76) references. Against re-evaluated public agent-training checkpoints (Simia, MUA-RL, LoopTool, EnvFactory, MidTool-RL), the 8B model reaches 74.17 Tau2 — at least 28 points above every one, including the 32B MUA-RL — and holds the highest equal-weight three-benchmark mean (67.97 vs. at most 57.17). BFCL Overall improves +3.35 to +11.93, driven by Multi-turn Base (+7 to +41 points); the 30B-A3B model posts 80.93 Overall, numerically above the reported Gemini-3.0-Pro (79.97). One consistent regression: Live Simple drops 6–13 points at four of five scales. Ablations at 8B favor all four proposed choices, with parent normalization the largest isolated gain (+8.04 mean). The depth sensitivity study is non-monotonic (depth 2 gives 72.28 mean vs. 70.55 at depth 3). Scale tested: standard research scale (11.6k–19.9k trajectories, 13–24M target tokens, one epoch). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new elements are the decision-grounding mask formalizing collector-privileged versus student-visible information as a supervision criterion (distinct from outcome or per-call filtering), and the empirical finding that parent normalization alone accounts for an 8-point mean gain. Deficit-guided synthesis, submodular selection, and SFT itself are standard machinery; thedafuq-combination is coherent but each ingredient has close precedents (e.g., DAgger-style privileged/student separation, TopoCurate's topology-based curation, Patches-to-Trajectories' prefix grounding). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: strict paired protocol against each model's own initialization; matched stage-wise ablations with explicitly stated matching conditions; sensitivity study with a predeclared schedule; qualitative cases including one retained failure. Weaknesses: every run is a single run and every benchmark task is evaluated once — no seeds, no error bars, no significance tests; the authors themselves downgrade few-point ablation gains to "directional." The targeted-expansion ablation does not fix the target-token budget, so it confounds targeting with data volume. Tau1 Airline is admitted to be a seen-task, transductive setting. External checkpoints are re-evaluated but not matched in data, family, or compute, and closed-source BFCL numbers are reported references under foreign protocols. Homepage, code, and Hugging Face links are indicated, but no concrete URLs appear in the provided text. A homepage/code/weights artifact appears to exist but is not verifiable from the paper text alone. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (training-data construction plus SFT experiments the authors actually run). Practical: Yes — full-parameter SFT of Qwen3 models up to 30B-A3B (MoE) with a global batch size of 8 is commodity multi-GPU work. Efficient: Favorable — one epoch over 11.6k–19.9k trajectories (13–24M target tokens) yields gains that outpace model scale, though the synthesis pipeline's teacher-generation cost is never quantified. Effective: The evidence supports the claim on stateful and multi-turn tasks (Tau2 +28 to +70 points paired), but the Live Simple regression and the near-zero transfer of pure function-calling skill to stateful tasks show the recipe trades off narrow reactivity. Scalable: Only claimed — the depth sweep shows returns are non-monotonic at 8B, and nothing is tested beyond 30B-A3B or outside the τ/BFCL environment family. The work delivers (per page-one links) a code and dataset artifact; the paper text does not confirm release status. Strengths: - The collector-visibility vs. student-visibility distinction, formalized as a supervision mask with an information-theoretic justification (Proposition 1: an ungrounded target imposes a log-loss floor of I(A;Z|C) on any student), is a clean, reusable formulation that reframes data curation at the decision level rather than the trajectory level. - The parent-normalization result is a genuinely useful, cheap finding: identical renderings and masks, only the loss-averaging granularity changed, produce an 8.04-point mean improvement — evidence that the semantic interaction, not the rendered row, should be the unit of training mass. - Measurement discipline: paired self-comparisons, matched ablation controls, a predeclared depth schedule, and explicit disclaimers that external checkpoints are references, not matched controls — unusually honest for a results-heavy paper. - The qualitative analysis retains a failure case (Figure 11) and correctly labels constructed dialogues as behavior illustrations rather than identical-context comparisons. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that ablation gains are directional only (single runs, one task moving the mean by 0.56 points); that the targeted-expansion comparison does not hold token budget fixed; that Tau1 Airline is transductive; that external checkpoints and closed-source rows are not matched comparisons and preclude component attribution; that support depth is not monotonic and the schedule is a predeclared choice rather than an optimized one; that grounding checks do not prove every admitted action is uniquely determined by visible history; and that BFCL closed-source numbers follow foreign protocols. This is direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Problem & Motivation: RL with verifiable rewards improves long-context reasoning, but the training data must be long, require evidence retrieval, be difficult, and have automatically verifiable answers. Human annotation of such data is expensive; natural long-context QA is too scarce; and existing synthesis pipelines extend short QA datasets with distractors (LoongRL), write questions over real corpora (QwenLong-L1, SPELL), build tasks from knowledge graphs, or use a stronger teacher — all external dependencies. Real-world documents add a confound: models can answer from parametric knowledge rather than the context. Meanwhile, zero-data RL (Absolute Zero, R-Zero, SPIRAL) has succeeded only on short-context tasks, where the long context itself does not need to be synthesized and kept consistent with the question. The open problem is whether a model can bootstrap long-context reasoning ability from literally no external data. Key Idea: Invert the generate-then-ask order: have the policy first write a compact structured specification of a fictional world — entities, atomic facts, distractor facts, multi-hop questions with answers — and only then expand the already-fixed evidence into long multi-document prose. Because the answer exists before any long text, correctness is guaranteed by construction, and residual risk is confined to the expansion step (caught by a programmatic faithfulness gate that requires the answer to appear verbatim). Difficulty is then controlled by the policy's own inconsistency: only questions the model sometimes answers correctly and sometimes incorrectly are kept, which is exactly the band where GRPO receives non-zero gradient signal. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Data synthesis: for reasoning data, the policy writes a world specification (JSON: entities including confusable names, 4 question chains of 3–5 hops, 2–3 distractors per chain sharing a bridge entity), plans which of 8 documents state which facts (spreading a question's supporting facts across documents and placing distractors away from the facts they imitate), then expands each document independently to 2,400–4,500 words; a program shuffles documents and discards questions whose answer no longer appears verbatim. For retrieval data (MRCR-style), the policy generates a pool of ~434K responses to template requests, and a program assembles ~11K-token conversations with 8 near-duplicate needles, so the reference answer (prefix + k-th needle) is correct by construction. (2) Difficulty filtering: the policy answers each question in waves of 2 samples, up to W=4; a question is kept as soon as it receives both a correct and an incorrect answer, and discarded if its first 4 answers agree. From ~14.4K–19.5K filtered questions per model, 17.7% (Qwen3-4B) / 13.1% (Qwen3-8B) fall in the unstable band. (3) RL: GRPO (verl implementation) with DAPO-style token-level loss, dual-clip clipping, k3 KL estimator (β=0.001), rule-based rewards (whole-word answer matching for reasoning; difflib SequenceMatcher ratio against the needle for retrieval), 64 prompts × 8 responses per step, 72–108 steps (~1.3–2 epochs). Key design decisions: fictional worlds to eliminate parametric-knowledge shortcuts (well-justified by the knowledge-conflict literature); specification-before-expansion ordering (the central, well-motivated insight); and a 2:1 reasoning-to-retrieval mixture (justified only post-hoc by ablation, not by a principled selection rule). The stated difficulty model Difficulty ∝ |x|·H·K is explicitly a design heuristic, not a fitted or validated relation. Key Results: Tested on two base models (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, Qwen3-8B thinking) against the base model, Enhanced HotpotQA (5,120 distractor-augmented HotpotQA questions, LoongRL pipeline), and Teacher-synthesized QA (questions by Qwen3.5-397B-A17B over Ultra-FineWeb clusters, SPELL verification), all sharing the identical RL configuration and checkpoint step. Five benchmarks: LongBench multi-doc QA (F1), LongBench v2 (503 questions), FRAMES (824 questions), AA-LCR (100 questions, 72K–115K inputs), LongReason 32K (794 questions). On Qwen3-4B, LongZero reaches 57.42 average vs 56.57 (Enhanced HotpotQA), 55.99 (teacher-synthesized), 54.68 (base), winning 4/5 benchmarks (e.g., FRAMES 55.76 vs 51.27 base; AA-LCR 39.50 vs 36.50). On Qwen3-8B, gains are much smaller: 45.66 vs 45.03 (Enhanced HotpotQA) and 44.63 (base); both baselines fall below base on two benchmarks each, LongZero on one (LBv2). Ablations (Qwen3-4B): reasoning data alone 55.38, retrieval alone 53.85 (below base), 1:1 mixture 55.95, 2:1 mixture 57.42. Training contexts are ~11–19K tokens, yet gains transfer to LBv2 (120K-truncated) and partially to AA-LCR. Counter-intuitive finding: the 397B teacher-written baseline underperforms self-synthesized data, attributed to ability mismatch between question writer and policy. Baselines are current (2025–2026 methods) and reasonably strong; the notable weakness is that all models score near zero on AA-LCR with Qwen3-8B (120/200 responses contain no answer due to token exhaustion), making that column uninformative for the 8B model. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING). The genuinely novel element is the specification-before-expansion inversion for zero-data synthesis of long-context tasks — prior zero-data RL methods (Absolute Zero, R-Zero) target short contexts, and prior long-context RL methods all source contexts/questions externally. The surrounding machinery is a competent combination of known ideas: GRPO/DAPO training from existing work, MRCR-style retrieval tasks from OpenAI's benchmark, difficulty filtering analogous to LoongRL's pipeline, and fictional-world QA from the knowledge-storage literature. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for the data mixture (reasoning-only vs retrieval-only vs two mixtures) and per-dataset breakdowns are provided, but there are no ablations for the difficulty-filter window W, the faithfulness gate, or the specification format — the components most likely to matter. Each benchmark is run twice and only the mean is reported; no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, which matters for gains of 0.2–3 points on benchmarks with 79–603 questions. All three RL methods share hyperparameters and checkpoint steps, and the authors state no hyperparameter was tuned on evaluation benchmarks — a good contamination control. Code and data are released at https://github.com/zhennan1/LongZero. Concerns: (i) the paper develops and evaluates on overlapping task styles (MRCR-format retrieval training vs MRCR-style long-context skills), though the headline benchmarks are external; (ii) AA-LCR judging uses GPT-5.6-Luna, introducing judge variance without repeated judging; (iii) the case studies (Appendix C.3) show defective questions pass difficulty filtering, and the rate of such leakage into training is never quantified. Baseline data for the teacher baseline mixes in the same self-synthesized retrieval data, so the comparison isolates only the reasoning-question source — fair but narrower than a full pipeline comparison. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (method with experiments; no standalone system deployment). Practical: Yes — the full pipeline runs on 8×A800-80GB (~27–29 hours, 213–230 GPU-hours per model) plus ~100 GPU-hours per evaluation round, using only the policy model with vLLM. Efficient: Data synthesis is the dominant cost and scales with the policy's size, not a teacher's; but the unstable-band yield is low (13–18% of questions kept; Qwen3-8B needs ~75K filtered answers for 2,560 questions), so synthesis cost is nontrivial and grows as the model gets stronger. Effective: The evidence supports improved long-context reasoning on real benchmarks (transfer from fictional to Wikipedia-based tasks, and from ≤20K-token training contexts to 115K-token evaluation inputs), but the effect is modest and shrinks on the weaker base model. Scalable: Not tested — the authors propose iterating synthesis-training cycles and longer contexts as future work; whether a second self-play round continues to help (or collapses) is unverified, as is behavior beyond Qwen3-family models. Delivers a software artifact: code, prompts, and synthesized data on GitHub; no trained model weights are mentioned as released. Strengths: - The specification-before-expansion inversion is a real, transferable insight: it converts the hard problem of verifying consistency in long generated text into a short-text verification problem plus a programmatic string-matching gate, cleanly sidestepping the self-verification circularity that plagues zero-data long-context methods. - The difficulty filter is elegantly aligned with the training objective: keeping only GRPO-informative (unstable) questions doubles as a defect filter, since consistently-failed questions are frequently ill-posed — a claim supported by concrete case studies of all three question categories (kept, discarded-defective, leaked-defective). - The baseline design is unusually fair: all methods share the identical RL configuration, prompt, reward, checkpoint step, and retrieval-data mixture, so differences isolate only the reasoning-question source; the result that a 397B teacher's questions lose to the policy's own is a substantive empirical finding about ability-matched data. - Demonstrated transfer on two axes that matter — fictional-to-real documents and short-to-long contexts — rather than only improving on in-distribution synthetic validation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that Qwen3-8B shows no improvement on LBv2, that AA-LCR is effectively broken for Qwen3-8B (72–115K inputs exhaust the output budget; 120/200 responses contain no answer), that benchmark gains are smaller than validation gains due to distribution shift, that defective questions can pass difficulty filtering when the model sometimes reproduces the reference answer (with a worked example, C.3, and a proposed but unimplemented fix: consistency-checking the specification before expansion), that gains are larger on the stronger model, and they list unexplored directions (iterative regeneration, longer contexts, new question types, stronger correctness guarantees). They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical treatment of 1–3 point average gains over two runs on benchmarks of 79–603 questions; several per-benchmark differences (e.g., LB1: 67.22 vs 67.04 vs 66.59) are plausibly within noise, and the honest headline is really the cross-benchmark consistency rather than any single number. - Only two Qwen3 models are tested, and the larger gain goes to the model with the better base long-context ability; whether the method helps models below some competence floor (or whether yield collapses to zero) is unknown, and the Qwen3-8B result hints the method may be marginal there. - The leakage rate of defective-but-unstable questions into training (category C.3) is never quantified — the method's central correctness guarantee has a known, unmeasured hole. - Only one iteration of the self-synthesis loop is run; the headline "zero data" claim is strongest at round one, and the literature on self-play (e.g., R-Zero) suggests later iterations behave differently. - The 2:1 data mixture appears to be selected after seeing ablation results on the evaluation benchmarks themselves, a mild Goodhart risk the paper does not flag (the authors state no hyperparameters were tuned on benchmarks, but the mixture ratio is arguably a tuned choice). - No comparison against other zero-data RL methods adapted to long context, and no comparison with a fictional-world teacher baseline, which would disentangle "self-generated" from "fictional/clean" as the source of the advantage over the teacher baseline. Bottom Line: A practitioner in long-context post-training should read this paper for the specification-before-expansion idea and the honest evidence that ability-matched self-generated data can beat a 397B teacher's questions, but should not expect the reported 1–3 point gains to be individually significant or the method to work equally well beyond strong base models.

Instruction Capacity: Behavior and Degradation of Language Models under Controlled Load (1 ▲ )

Hennadii Kutomanov · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 29 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a psychophysics-style instrument and statistical framework that measures a language model's "instruction capacity" — the number of simultaneous atomic rules a model executes at a given success probability, reported with an uncertainty — and delivers a first passport for GPT-4o mini. - Why it's important: Instruction-following degradation under load is well documented but has never been expressed as a comparable, uncertainty-carrying quantity in units of load; without one, models cannot be compared on "how many instructions can it hold" the way effective context length compares long-input use. - How it does it: The load unit is a word-replacement rule applied to a meaningless text of single-token nouns, making every rule application a Bernoulli trial with a program-computed reference answer; a binned logistic mixed model (GLMM) fits degradation profiles per load axis, and capacity is solved as an inverse dose–response problem via the delta method. - The good: The design eliminates judge-model error and confounding of instruction count with task difficulty, and the measurement is large and reproducible — 2,958 requests and 642,430 trials on GPT-4o mini, with every passport number recomputable from published points via task seeds. - The missing: Only one model (GPT-4o mini) is measured, so the central claim — that the capacity is a comparable model parameter — is never demonstrated across models, and the proposed "meter" for arbitrary prompts remains a proposal. - Read it or not: Read it if you build LLM evaluation benchmarks or study instruction-following degradation — its nine-criteria methodology critique and trial-level design are directly reusable; skip it if you need practical prompt-load numbers for other models today.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (76) is high — instruction capacity as an inverse dose–response problem is a genuine new problem formulation, and the nine-criteria deconstruction of prior benchmarks is itself a substantive methodological contribution. Rigor (65) reflects careful, reproducible statistics (GLMM, delta-method uncertainty, out-of-sample checks) reduced for the single-model scope that undercuts the 'comparable parameter' framing, the unauditable closed adaptive point-selection, and the lack of peer review as a preprint.
