Problem & Motivation: Discrete diffusion language models (LLaDA, Dream) predict many masked positions in parallel but still need dozens of iterative decoding rounds, and each round is a full transformer forward pass. Existing decoders choose which positions to commit using per-position confidence or entropy, i.e., local predictability. The authors argue this is the wrong criterion: a peaked, easy token may add no information, while a moderately uncertain token may resolve dependencies that make many other positions predictable. They support this empirically: on correct GSM8K responses from LLaDA, revealing an uncertain token (p<0.5) makes 5.1× more other positions "ready" and lowers their surprisal 4.7× more than revealing a confident one, and responses with larger accumulated uncertainty area need more forward passes (Pearson r=0.73). The gap is that no prior decoding/distillation method optimizes the downstream utility of a commitment. Key Idea: Reframe unmasking as a context-construction problem and score each candidate reveal by how much it reduces uncertainty (surprisal) at the other masked positions, not by the candidate's own confidence. Concretely, from the total accumulated uncertainty area A(π;y) = Σ_r Σ_{j∈M_r} h_j(s_r) as the objective, greedily promote the plausible candidate (top-k=10, p≥0.02) whose reveal maximizes Σ_{j≠i} [h_j(s_r) − h_j(s(i)_r)]. This produces optimized unmasking trajectories that are then distilled into the model, shifting schedule search from inference time to training time. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Schedule construction (offline, teacher): using the frozen base model on verified correct responses, at each round enumerate plausible candidates (Eq. 5: rank ≤10, p ≥0.02), score each by total surprisal drop at other positions (Eq. 6), promote the best positive-scoring candidate, and record the trajectory τ(y); candidates outside the filter are excluded to avoid promoting tokens the model has effectively ruled out. (2) Distillation (student): LoRA fine-tuning (rank 256, all attention/FFN projections, 4×A100, 6 epochs) on intermediate states of optimized trajectories with a cross-entropy reconstruction loss plus a confidence-sharpening term (entropy minimization on positions where the student is already correct) — L+ (Eq. 7). (3) Selective KL anchoring: because sharpening cannot distinguish right from wrong on unseen states, failed trajectories are retained and the student is pulled toward the frozen base model's distribution on them — L− (Eq. 8), β=1 — while correct trajectories are KL-free. Decoding uses multi-block parallel decoding (d3LLM-style) with confidence threshold 0.90–0.95, block size 32, max 256 tokens. Critical design decisions: excluding the revealed position itself from its score (well-justified: prevents trivial self-term dominance); promoting low-probability tokens (justified by Table 10 — committing promoted tokens with p∈[0.02,0.1) leaves accuracy unchanged and saves ~6.5 forward passes); using failed* rather than disjoint correct trajectories for KL (justified by ablation — using disjoint correct data drops accuracy 78.94→77.10 and TPF by 30.5%). The per-candidate scoring in Eq. 6 requires one forward pass per candidate per round, so teacher-side schedule construction is expensive, but this cost is paid offline. Key Results: Evaluated on GSM8K (0-shot), MATH (4-shot), MBPP (3-shot), HumanEval (0-shot) with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, against Fast-dLLM, D2F, dParallel, and d3LLM — recent, strong baselines (2026 ICLR/arXiv-era), averaged over 3 runs with lm-eval-harness. Headline: GSM8K TPF of 10.12 (LLaDA) and 5.12 (Dream) vs. 1.0 for base models, with accuracy preserved or improved (78.9% vs. 78.8%; 83.6% vs. 82.1%). Highest AUP (accuracy-under-parallelism) on all 8 benchmark×backbone cells, e.g., 761.67 vs. 571.28 for d3LLM on LLaDA GSM8K (+33.3%); MATH gains are smaller (119.55 vs. 107.59 AUP on LLaDA). Wall-clock (appendix, LLaDA GSM8K, batch 1): 249 tokens/s vs. 15 for base (16.6×) and 220 for d3LLM (13.2% higher), with a custom CUDA-graph static KV cache raising it to 313 tokens/s. Calibration analysis on 250 GSM8K samples: dSpark is confident-when-wrong 15.5% of the time vs. 22.9% (d3LLM) and 21.7% (dParallel), with ECE 8.2% vs. 19.2–20.4%. Ablations confirm the schedule drives parallelism (natural schedule without KL: 7.6 TPF vs. 11.4 with surprisal-reduction promotion) and KL regularization drives accuracy (74.2→78.9%); the KL weight β=1 is selected from a sweep (β∈{0,0.5,1,2}). Gains hold at generation lengths 128/256/512 and general knowledge (MMLU 63.1 vs. 63.0; ARC-C 47.2 vs. 47.6) is preserved. Tested at standard academic-benchmark scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (schedule distillation via downstream-uncertainty scoring) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the 4.7–5.1× quantification that uncertain tokens are more useful to reveal than confident ones). The closest prior work — dParallel's certainty-forcing distillation and d3LLM's pseudo-trajectory distillation — also distills toward earlier commitment, but selects what to distill by confidence; the surprisal-reduction promotion criterion (Eq. 6) and the failed-trajectory-selective KL anchoring are the genuinely new pieces. The overall skeleton (teacher trajectories → trajectory distillation → KL anchor → multi-block decoding) is a competent combination of known ingredients applied to a new selection rule; the uncertainty-area objective A(π;y) is a diagnostic, not a directly optimized loss. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough and target the right questions: training-recipe ablation (schedule vs. KL vs. both), promotion-strategy ablation (natural/random/highest-surprisal/surprisal-reduction, showing the proposed criterion beats highest-surprisal promotion on accuracy, 78.9% vs. 77.8% at high TPF), KL data ratio (4:1 chosen from a 6-point sweep), KL weight sweep, candidate-filter analysis, generation-length robustness, and general-knowledge retention. Evaluation is averaged over 3 runs with a standard harness; code is released at github.com/VILA-Lab/dSpark (trained weights not explicitly stated as released). Concerns: (1) trajectory construction uses GSM8K/PRM12K/NuminaMath data and evaluation includes GSM8K — in-domain distillation-to-evaluation proximity is not dissected (e.g., no MATH-only or code-only training ablation); (2) headline "speedups" are TPF ratios, a proxy metric — wall-clock is reported only for LLaDA GSM8K in the appendix; (3) TPF normalization means "10.12×" is relative to a base model decoding one token per pass, so cross-method wall-clock gains are more modest; (4) no error bars or significance tests beyond 3-run averaging; (5) the AUP metric (Eq. 10) comes from the d3LLM authors and involves a discount function with hand-set α=3, which advantages methods evaluated at one operating point — though the Pareto plots (Fig. 4) independently support the conclusion. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained/fine-tuned models with benchmark evaluation; a small systems component in the appendix KV cache). Practical: Yes — fine-tuning used 4×A100 GPUs and inference runs on A100s at batch size 1; LoRA keeps training cheap. Efficient: Training requires offline teacher schedule search with one forward pass per candidate per round (cost not quantified), but inference cost drops to 249–313 tokens/s, 13–17× the base model in wall-clock. Effective: Evidence shows it solves the proxy (TPF/AUP) and the real objective (wall-clock throughput at matched accuracy) on math/code benchmarks, but only for verifiable, ground-truth-checkable training data — free-form generation is untested. Scalable: Only 7–8B backbones and ≤512-token generations were tested; behavior at 10× context length or larger models is claimed by extension, not measured. Delivers a software artifact: released code plus configurations; models are LoRA adapters merged at evaluation time. Strengths: - A crisp, well-measured empirical finding with practical consequence: the predictability-vs-utility distinction is quantified (4.7× surprisal drop, 5.1× newly-ready positions, r=0.73 area-vs-passes correlation) before any method is proposed, so the design is evidence-driven rather than intuition-driven. - The selective KL anchoring is a genuinely clever mechanism: the sharpening term is knowingly unsafe off-distribution, so the authors confine the KL penalty to failed trajectories — the ablation showing that KL on correct trajectories instead costs 30.5% TPF validates the asymmetry. - The calibration analysis (Table 8, Fig. 5) goes beyond accuracy/TPF and explains why dSpark tolerates aggressive commitment (90.8% precision at p≥0.9 vs. ~82% for baselines), which most competing distillation papers omit. - Baselines are current and strong (Fast-dLLM, D2F, dParallel, d3LLM), evaluation uses a standard harness, and ablations cleanly decompose the contribution into schedule (parallelism) and regularization (accuracy). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Implicitly, the authors acknowledge that schedule construction depends on verified correct responses (the framework builds trajectories only for correct y and needs failed trajectories as KL anchors) and that aggressive parallel commitment risks confident errors, which they address with the KL term and analyze via calibration. They also note KV-cache interactions are nontrivial (Fast-dLLM caches can increase forward passes for short prompts). However, there is no dedicated limitations section; scope boundaries such as ground-truth dependence, benchmark narrowness, and model-size coverage are not confronted directly — this is a mild credibility negative. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - In-domain training contamination is not dissected: the distillation corpus includes GSM8K-derived trajectories and GSM8K is a headline benchmark; a leave-one-domain-out experiment (e.g., train on math only, evaluate on code) is needed to show the gains transfer rather than partially reflect domain-adapted fine-tuning. - The schedule-search teacher cost is never reported (forward passes per trajectory, total GPU-hours beyond "4×A100, 6 epochs"), so the train-time vs. infer-time trade-off central to the paper's argument ("shifts computation into training") is asserted, not measured. - Only two instruct models of similar scale (8B, 7B) are tested; nothing about smaller/larger models, base (non-instruct) variants, or long-form generation where multi-block decoding and the 256-token training cap may diverge. - Wall-clock results are appendix-only and LLaDA/GSM8K-specific; the Dream wall-clock story and behavior with batching (all throughput numbers are batch size 1) are absent, yet batching is where dLLMs are actually deployed. - The "10.12×" framing invites over-reading: it is tokens-per-forward relative to a baseline decoding one token per pass; a practitioner comparing to d3LLM sees 13.2% wall-clock improvement, a materially different number. - No comparison to the training-free lookahead methods (LEAP, Ripple-Pivot Search) that the related-work section identifies as closest in spirit to utility-based selection. Bottom Line: A practitioner accelerating diffusion LLMs should read this: the utility-based promotion criterion, the failed-trajectory KL trick, and the calibration evidence are concrete and reproducible improvements over confidence-only distillation — but treat the 10× headline as a tokens-per-forward metric, since the honest wall-clock gain over the strongest existing baseline is roughly 1.13× on the one configuration reported.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LPDS, a conditional generative inverse-design framework that maps desired implosion outcomes and pellet parameters directly to laser pulse shapes for direct-drive inertial confinement fusion, using a diffusion model and autoregressive variants trained with a frozen differentiable LILAC-surrogate loss plus an energy-conservation penalty. - Why it's important: Laser pulse design currently requires repeated radiation-hydrodynamic simulation sweeps and expert iteration; Problem & Motivation: In direct-drive ICF, implosion performance (energy yield, areal density, burn width, ion temperature) depends nonlinearly on the ~3 ns laser pulse shape (LP) and target pellet configuration. Designing an LP traditionally means forward simulation with LILAC — a 1-D Lagrangian radiation-hydrodynamics code — plus manual expert refinement, which is computationally expensive, one design at a time, and bottlenecked by limited facility access. The gap LPDS closes is the inverse direction: given desired outcomes and pellet parameters, produce candidate pulses directly, with diversity (the inverse problem is ill-posed — many pulses yield similar outcomes), physical feasibility, and interactive control (fixing picket power, inpainting pulse regions) that one-shot black-box optimizers (Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES) and low-dimensional parameterized optimization do not provide. The intended users are ICF design scientists at facilities like OMEGA. Key Idea: The core trick is treating generative inverse design as amortized neural posterior estimation of p(l | m, p) — with LILAC too expensive to query online — and closing the physical-fidelity gap by injecting a frozen differentiable surrogate of the simulator into the generator's training loss, so the generator is explicitly optimized onto the physically valid solution manifold rather than merely conditioned on (pulse, outcome) pairs. The multi-objective loss O(θ) = λL·L (reconstruction/likelihood) + λS·S (surrogate outcome consistency) + λP·P (excess-energy integral penalty) simultaneously handles non-identifiability (reconstruction regularizes toward the feasible manifold), outcome targeting, and energy budgeting. Exploiting DDIM's non-Markovian û0 estimate lets the surrogate loss apply at intermediate diffusion steps. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Offline: 1 million LILAC simulations over a 20-D input space (5 pellet parameters + internal pulse parameterization), sampled as random valid draws plus perturbations of known high-performing implosions to concentrate on the unknown high-performance manifold; LPs are 256-dim real sequences, outcomes are 12-dim. A 4-layer MLP surrogate Sϕ (1.4% avg outcome error; benchmarked against FNO at 1.43% and a physics-informed MLP at 2.31%) is trained and frozen. (2) Inverse-model training: conditional DDIM diffusion model εθ(ln, n, m, p), and autoregressive LSTMs/Transformer with Gaussian, Mixture-of-Gaussians (K-component), or 128-bin categorical output heads; predictive (MSE) and generative (NLL) AR variants. The surrogate loss S(θ) = E‖m − Sϕ(Gθ(m,p), p)‖² and hinge-style energy penalty P(θ) are added with weights λS=0.5, λP=0.25, λL=0.25. (3) Generation without simulator/surrogate calls, plus three control mechanisms: (a) constraint-adaptation via a small embedding network Bδ fine-tuned for 10 epochs on a new constraint c (e.g., picket/foot power) while freezing the diffusion backbone, with constraint values injected through the timestep-embedding channel; (b) model-agnostic post-generation gradient descent on the differentiable pulse, trading surrogate loss against a constraint loss with clipping; (c) inpainting via masked DDIM resampling (Eq. 19) or AR prefix completion. Design optimization (Section 5.5) sets a 10%-higher yield target, generates 20 candidates per baseline, filters by surrogate-predicted yield, energy budget, and a frequency-domain (DFT magnitude) similarity constraint τ=0.1, then validates survivors in true LILAC. Critical design decisions: frozen surrogate inside the training loop (justified via the OOD-correlation analysis in Appendix G, Spearman ρ=0.353 between novelty and surrogate error, and novelty statistics showing generated pulses are no farther off-manifold than held-out test pulses); reconstruction weighting to tame non-identifiability (justified by the λL–λS Pareto ablation); and manifold-focused data sampling (justified qualitatively, not ablated). Key Results: On a held-out simulation test set, LPDSDiff achieves 1.93% ± 0.046 surrogate outcome error, diversity 0.64 ± 0.077 (upper bound 1.9 from random pulse pairs), 5.6% reconstruction error, 1.59% energy violation; the deterministic LPDSLSTM achieves 1.65% ± 0.09 outcome error and 0.1×10⁻³ reconstruction error but zero diversity. Ablations: removing the surrogate loss S more than doubles outcome error (Diff: 1.93%→4.50%; Transformer: 1.94%→4.40%); removing the energy penalty roughly doubles energy violation for the diffusion model (1.59%→3.21%). True LILAC validation for the two best models: LPDSDiff 2.07%, LPDSLSTM 2.01% — confirming surrogate-to-simulator transfer. Against seven off-the-shelf baselines (VAE, GAN, TabSyn, VLD, cINN, CSGM, FNO-inverse) under identical data and metrics, all baselines without physics feedback show 4.97%–16.60% outcome error, while CSGM reaches 2.58% only by collapsing diversity to 0.01; LPDS is the only method combining <2% outcome error with high diversity and <2% energy violation. Yield optimization: across 60 high-performing baseline pulses validated in true LILAC, LPDSDiff achieves a 17.74% mean energy-yield gain (~1.18× neutron yield) at unchanged energy budget with 86% of pulses exceeding the 10% target, versus 2.79% for the AR variant. Constraint adaptation: gradient-based MAPE 2.5% ± 0.12, diffusion-adapter 3.4% ± 0.14, with outcome error unaffected. Inpainting: 2.00% (diffusion) and 1.55% (LSTM) outcome error. Pellet-stratified generalization: 2.02% vs. 2.02%/1.93% random-split baseline and a 1.53% surrogate floor on held-out pellet clusters. Transfer study: 300 experimental OMEGA shots (complete historical set), 70/30 split, surrogate 8% error, LPDS outcome error 8.8% ± 0.05, reconstruction 0.0068, energy violation 1.78%. Scale: 1M simulations, 4×H100 node, ~400 GPU-hours total, 29.6 h diffusion training per run, 1939 samples/s diffusion inference; evaluation over 5 training runs × 10 seeds per model. Note this is a NeurIPS 2026 submission preprint (arXiv 2610.33096), not peer-reviewed at time of posting. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION flavor). Genuinely novel: the instantiation of surrogate-in-the-loop generative inverse design for 256-dimensional structured LP output under per-sample hard physical constraints with interactive editing — the authors state (plausibly) that no prior work does this for direct-drive LP design, and the 17.74% LILAC-validated yield gain over expert-designed baselines is a substantive empirical finding. Standard components: DDIM, LSTM/Transformer AR heads, few-shot adapter fine-tuning, masked-diffusion inpainting, and MLP surrogates are all established techniques recombined; the contribution is the framework and its domain demonstration rather than a new generative algorithm (flow matching is explicitly deferred to future work). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for an applied ML paper. Ablations isolate both loss terms (S and P) across model families; a λL–λS sweep maps the fidelity–diversity Pareto frontier; evaluation covers 5 training runs × 10 seeds with reported standard deviations; surrogate-architecture choice is benchmarked (MLP vs. FNO vs. physics-informed MLP); a pellet-stratified split addresses train/test leakage within perturbation families; an OOD-correlation analysis (Spearman ρ=0.353, novelty distributions in Table 11) probes surrogate reliability off-manifold; and — critically — the headline claims (LILAC error, yield optimization) are validated in the true simulator rather than only via the surrogate, explicitly acknowledged as the surrogate's 1.4% error floor. A constrained-optimization alternative (12-parameter) is benchmarked and loses (10% vs. 1.93% outcome error). Concerns: code and data are not released (promised "upon publication"; NeurIPS checklist answer [No]); the simulation dataset is proprietary to LLE and not reproducible externally; the ablation of loss terms was run on only a subset of models due to compute; LILAC validation is limited to 2 models / 60 pulses because simulator access is scarce; and the experimental transfer study (300 shots, retrospective) has no error-bar provenance on the surrogate's 8% figure beyond the stated split. No Goodhart-style red flags: the method is developed and evaluated on the same simulator family, but the simulator itself is the ground truth in this field, and true-simulator validation partially de-risks surrogate gaming (the authors also analyze adversarial surrogate exploitation in Appendix F.3). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact component — a design pipeline, though not publicly released). - Practical: Yes — all models train and run on a single H100 GPU (13 h diffusion, 7 h LSTM per run); the framework needs a simulation archive rather than special hardware. - Efficient: Inference is fast (1939 samples/s diffusion, up to 34,666/s AR) and training cost (~30 GPU-hours) is negligible against month-scale ICF experimental cycles, though 1M LILAC simulations for the offline dataset dominate the true cost and are not priced in the paper. - Effective: Strongly evidenced for the simulated regime (true-LILAC-validated yield gains and outcome error), partially evidenced for experiments (retrospective 300-shot study with 8.8% outcome error); the 17.74% yield figure is simulator-predicted, not facility-demonstrated. - Scalable: Untested beyond 1M simulations and the 20-D/256-point design space; the authors claim broader applicability to other inverse-design domains but provide no cross-domain experiment — 10× data or a move to 2-D/3-D hydrodynamics would require re-validating the surrogate-error assumptions entirely. The work delivers a methodology and internal pipeline in paper form; no code, dataset, or trained model is released at submission time. Strengths: - True-simulator validation discipline: instead of reporting only surrogate-screened numbers, the authors spend scarce LILAC access to confirm the two best models (<2.1% outcome error) and to validate the yield-optimization headline (17.74% mean gain over 60 expert-quality baselines), which is the difference between an ML claim and a physics claim. - Honest treatment of the ill-posed inverse problem: the λL/λS ablation explicitly maps the fidelity–diversity Pareto frontier and the deterministic-vs-generative trade-off is surfaced rather than hidden (the highest-fidelity model has zero diversity). - A genuine head-to-head baseline study: seven off-the-shelf conditional generators under identical data and metrics, with a clear two-failure-mode analysis (no-physics-feedback methods miss outcome consistency; test-time optimization collapses diversity), which substantiates the framework's positioning rather than asserting it. - Unusual thoroughness on surrogate-risk analysis for an applied paper: adversarial-exploitation analysis, OOD correlation study, novelty-distance statistics, and a pellet-stratified generalization test with an explicit error floor. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive: (1) surrogate bias is named as "a central limitation" since most training and evaluation route through the learned surrogate; (2) the experimental study is small, noisy, and retrospective — "prospective validation on new facility shots remains future work"; (3) the energy-conservation penalty does not guarantee full facility-level feasibility or robustness to out-of-distribution target requests; (4) safety is addressed (a mis-designed pulse degrades performance rather than creating a runaway condition, and generated pulses would undergo standard facility review). No minimizing language is apparent. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The dataset-sampling strategy (perturbations of known high-performing implosions) is never ablated; the entire 1M-simulation corpus is biased toward a known manifold, so LPDS's "novel" designs may be restricted to neighborhoods of expert designs — consistent with the generated pulses' novelty statistics actually sitting slightly below held-out test pulses (0.7048 vs. 0.7125), a point the authors present as a virtue but which also bounds discovered-design novelty. - LILAC is 1-D hydrodynamics; real direct-drive implosion performance depends on 2-D/3-D asymmetry and laser-imprint physics absent from both the simulator and the model. The yield gains are therefore LILAC-gains, and the gap between 1-D prediction and facility yield (a known, large effect in this field) is not discussed in the limitations. - The experimental transfer study conditions on measured outcomes of past shots but generated pulses from that regime are never run — the transfer claim rests on surrogate/reconstruction consistency, not on any closed-loop or prospective evidence. - Statistical reporting is inconsistent in places: the LILAC error column is a single number with no seed/run variance (understandable given simulator cost, but it is the paper's most important column), and the 17.74% yield gain has no confidence interval or per-baseline distribution reported. - No comparison against a classical baseline that matters in practice: Bayesian optimization or CMA-ES directly against LILAC on a per-design budget, which is what a design scientist would otherwise do; the appendix only benchmarks constrained optimization against the authors' own surrogate. Bottom Line: A practitioner in ML-for-fusion or constrained scientific inverse design gains real value from this paper — the simulator-validated yield results and the honest surrogate-risk analysis set a credible template — but its impact hinges on 1-D-simulator fidelity and unreleased artifacts, so it should be read as a strong domain demonstration rather than a validated design tool.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FOCUS, an actor-critic reinforcement-learning method for long-horizon LLM agents that treats rollout allocation as active learning for a value critic, branching continuations at the states expected to most reduce value-estimation error. - Why it's important: Long-horizon agents trained with sparse outcome rewards waste rollout compute and assign credit poorly across dozens of tool calls; efficient intermediate value estimates are the bottleneck for scaling agentic RL. - How it does it: It scores each resumable state (naturally supplied by context-compaction boundaries) with a Beta-posterior acquisition function estimating marginal MSE reduction in critic error, then blends sampled-continuation evidence with critic predictions into recursive value backups that supply both segment-level TD advantages for the actor and supervision targets for the critic. - The good: Under a matched per-step generation budget, FOCUS ranks first among trained methods on all three benchmarks at Qwen3.5-9B, with +7.2 points on BrowseComp-Plus held-out accuracy (55.4 vs. 48.2 for GRPO) and a diagnostic showing its allocation rule reduces critic MSE faster than random or residual-based scheduling. - The missing: Several headline-adjacent comparisons have 90% bootstrap CIs crossing zero (DeonticBench Hard subset, where FOCUS is 1.4 points worse than GRPO; SARA-N; LocBench File@5), results use best-held-out-checkpoint selection, and the baselines omit the tree-allocation methods (TreeGRPO, TRACE, PaTR) the paper itself cites as closest related work. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agentic RL or credit-assignment systems — the active-learning framing of rollout allocation and the honest Appendix E/E analysis are genuinely instructive — but practitioners wanting validated large-scale results should treat the gains as preliminary.

Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon language-model agents (deep search, code localization, statute reasoning) are trained with RLVR, but a single terminal verifiable reward must be smeared across hundreds of tokens when most had no effect on the outcome. Learned critics give intermediate value estimates but are inaccurate; Monte Carlo refinement via branching from intermediate states is accurate but expensive. The unaddressed question is where to spend a finite branching budget: uniform allocation ignores that critic error varies enormously across states in a trajectory. The work targets anyone training tool-using agents on multi-step tasks under a fixed rollout compute budget. Key Idea: Cast the choice of where to branch during RL rollouts as an expected-error-reduction active learning problem for the critic: allocate each additional continuation to the state maximizing an analytically derived acquisition score g(c) = (2κ²ê² + (N−κ)σ̂²)/(κ+N)³, built from a Beta posterior mixing the critic prediction with observed continuation outcomes — and, critically, using raw observed outcomes rather than recursive backups for selection, because backups attenuate critic–outcome discrepancy geometrically along a chain (Appendix E shows a factor-of-4 shrink per edge under κ=1). Methodology: The pipeline runs per training round: (1) collect initial episodes with a policy-generated context-compaction operator whose trigger points create resumable tree states; (2) seed continuations from candidate states; (3) iteratively allocate the remaining budget B: score nonterminal states with the critic, compute the acquisition score from posterior statistics (Eq. 6), run CONTINUE from the argmax state to termination, and update observed-outcome counts/means; (4) bottom-up refine values Ṽ(c) = (κV_φ(c) + n·Ḡ(c))/(κ+n) via TreeRPO-style one-level backups; (5) train the critic on recursive targets Ḡ (fixed during the update, Eq. 3) and the actor on clipped PPO with segment-level TD(λ) residuals (λ=0, i.e., δ_i = R_i + γd·Ṽ(c_i) − Ṽ(c_{i−1})) applied to task and compaction tokens with observations masked. Design decisions: κ=1 pseudo-observation weight (admitted to be a heuristic — optimal only if critic error equals outcome variance); binary-outcome Beta model for selection; modular separation of allocation, context management, and credit assignment (validated by swapping compaction operators). The asynchronous variant with bounded per-node concurrency (C=2) is described but its effect is not ablated. Key Results: On Qwen3.5-9B with matched per-step generation budgets: BrowseComp-Plus held-out 55.4 (FOCUS) vs. 48.2 (GRPO) vs. 46.6 (VinePPO); DeonticBench overall 56.5 vs. 52.4 vs. 49.4; LocBench File@1 72.4 vs. 70.1 vs. 67.8 and File@5 81.6 vs. 80.5 vs. 79.3. At Qwen3.5-27B (LoRA, DeonticBench only), FOCUS still leads (76.3 vs. 74.3/74.9) but the margin shrinks to +2.0. Notably, FOCUS is worse than GRPO on the DeonticBench Hard subset at 9B (26.8 vs. 28.2, Δ=−1.4, CI crossing zero). Diagnostics: the acquisition score g(c) falls ~50% from update 1 to 32 on MATH L4–5; FOCUS allocation reduces critic MSE faster than random or residual-priority scheduling under both degenerate (constant, random) critic inits; critic Spearman ρ against an n=16 MCTS ground truth improves over LocBench training. FOCUS also generates shorter evaluation outputs than GRPO/PPO on MATH (2,782 vs. 5,747/7,207 tokens at update 32), and avoids GRPO's late-training collapse into premature submit-after-compaction behavior (documented with concrete trace examples in Appendix G). Baselines are credible but narrow: GRPO and VinePPO are standard, though multiple 2025–2026 tree-search RL methods in the paper's own related-work section are absent. Tests are at 4B–27B scale with 1-epoch training — standard, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (active-error-reduction allocation of rollout branching, with the observed-outcome-vs-backup selection analysis) plus an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (the modular compaction-coupled rollout controller). The genuinely new element is the acquisition function for allocating continuations by marginal critic-error reduction and the Appendix E argument for why selection must use observed outcomes; the surrounding machinery — tree-structured rollouts, one-level backups (TreeRPO), critic-blended values (AlphaGo-style), compaction-based state forking, PPO clipping — is a competent combination of existing ideas applied to a new allocation problem. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover the compaction operator (in-context vs. in-memory workspace perform similarly), refinement rollouts (removal hurts, especially early, on BrowseComp-Plus), and compaction prompt structure (free-form vs. structural), and diagnostics isolate the allocation rule against random and residual-priority schedules — the components do matter and are tested individually. Uncertainty: 90% paired bootstrap CIs on all main deltas, with a transparent Appendix B describing resampling details; however, intervals are marginal without multiple-comparison correction, and several key comparisons cross zero. Two methodological concerns: (1) BrowseComp-Plus and LocBench results use the best held-out checkpoint over training, which the authors explicitly note their CIs do not account for — this is selection on the evaluation set; (2) each method is trained and evaluated on splits of the same benchmark (e.g., 498 BrowseComp-Plus train tasks), a Goodhart exposure. Code is released (https://github.com/zipJiang/FOCUS) with harness details, prompts, and per-run hyperparameter tables in appendices. The work is an arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Runs on commercially available hardware (2×H200 training, 4–6×H100 rollouts, 1 GPU for the critic) — substantial but accessible cluster-scale resources. Efficient: FOCUS beats GRPO under a matched per-step generation budget and shortens evaluation outputs, but adds a separate critic model, refinement rollouts, and a sequential allocation loop whose wall-clock cost relative to GRPO is not reported. Effective: Evidence on held-out benchmark splits supports the credit-assignment claim, though checkpoint selection on held-out data and near-zero CIs on several subsets weaken it. Scalable: Untested beyond 9B full-parameter and 27B LoRA; the shrinking 27B margin and the authors' own future-work list (larger models, longer budgets) indicate scaling is claimed, not shown. Deliverable: a software artifact — a modular rollout controller with interfaces for alternative harnesses and adapters for Slime and Tinker; no trained model weights are stated as released. Strengths: - The core intellectual contribution — recasting rollout allocation as expected-error-reduction active learning for the critic, with the acquisition score derived analytically rather than hand-tuned — is a clean, transferable framing. - Appendix E is the paper's best section: it proves that recursive backups attenuate critic–outcome discrepancy (factor 4 per edge at κ=1) and therefore must not drive selection, plus candid admissions that κ=1 is suboptimal in general and that the acquisition score is a heuristic. This level of self-scrutiny is rare. - The evaluation spans three genuinely different long-horizon domains (statute reasoning, deep search, code localization) with matched generation budgets, identical training-data order across methods, and a documented failure-mode analysis (GRPO's premature submission collapse with verbatim traces). - The modular decoupling of rollout allocation from context management is validated by an actual operator swap, not just asserted. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the 27B margin shrinks (attributed to a higher untuned starting point); κ=1 is optimal only when critic error equals outcome variance and the acquisition score is a heuristic, not an exact expected-error reduction; the unbiasedness argument does not extend to adaptively chosen stopping times; bootstrap intervals are marginal, unadjusted, and do not account for held-out checkpoint selection, training-seed variation, or stochastic decoding; and future work must scale to larger models and longer budgets and adopt stronger uncertainty quantification. They confront limitations directly — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Baseline set is stale relative to the paper's own related work: TreeGRPO, TRACE, PaTR, IGRPO, and SIGHT are all cited as tree-allocation or budget-routing methods for agentic RL, yet none is compared. FOCUS's allocation rule is only beaten against random and residual scheduling, not against competing allocation heuristics (information gain, process scores) — so the claim that error-reduction allocation is the right objective is untested against its nearest rivals. - Reporting the best held-out checkpoint (BrowseComp-Plus: "each the best held-out checkpoint over training"; LocBench GRPO uses checkpoint 1 for one metric and 89 for another) is evaluation-set selection; a fixed-final-checkpoint or validation-selected protocol would make the headline +7.2 number more trustworthy. - The paper trains on splits of the evaluation benchmarks themselves, so "held-out" gains may partly reflect benchmark-specific adaptation; no transfer to an untouched benchmark is shown. - The diagnostic ground truth for critic error (n=16 MCTS continuations) is itself a Monte Carlo proxy, and the MATH preliminary uses different question counts per method (PPO 64, GRPO 16, FOCUS 16 with a 64-edge budget) whose compute-matching rationale is asserted rather than cost-verified in dollars or GPU-hours. - DeonticBench Hard — the subset where accurate credit assignment should matter most — is the one place FOCUS loses to GRPO at 9B, and the paper offers no analysis of why. - Wall-clock overhead of the sequential allocation loop and the cost of the extra critic GPU are never quantified. Bottom Line: A researcher working on agentic RL credit assignment gains real, reusable insight — especially from the allocation-as-active-learning framing and the backup-attenuation analysis — but should not adopt FOCUS over competing tree-allocation methods until the gains are reproduced without held-out checkpoint selection and against the baselines the paper itself identifies as closest.

MAS-on-the-Fly: In-Context Structural Adaptation of LLM-Based Multi- Agent Systems

G Liu, H Wang, Q Yao · aclanthology.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MASFly, a framework that lets a frozen-LLM multi-agent system generate a query-specific configuration (agent roles, tool assignments, communication topology) at test time via retrieval-augmented SOP instantiation, and reconfigure it mid-execution via a Watcher agent that monitors against distilled failure experience. - Why it's important: Existing LLM multi-agent systems either deploy one fixed structure that cannot match query diversity, or require expensive training of a meta-agent, and nearly all run open-loop pipelines that cannot recover from agent failures or prompt attacks during execution. - How it does it: It treats structured experience as in-context conditioning: hybrid retrieval over an SOP repository instantiates a tailored system per query, while a Watcher agent with a Personalized Experience Pool of failure attributions detects anomalies and intervenes by corrective feedback or agent replacement — with no parameter updates. - The good: The evaluation is broad and unusually honest for this subfield: TravelPlanner final pass rate of 61.7% (Sole-Planning) and 39.4% (Two-Stage) with bootstrap CIs that exclude the best baseline, three-run mean±std on GAIA/HumanEval/MBPP/MBPP Pro, a manual Watcher intervention-quality audit (precision 0.806, recall 0.893, F1 0.847), efficiency Pareto analysis, and a Qwen3-32B backbone generalization check. - The missing: The SOP/PEP repositories are built from labeled training data via reflection that uses ground-truth correctness — the paper does not test cross-domain transfer of the repositories or quantify how performance degrades when labeled experience is absent or domain-shifted, despite claiming general adaptability. - Read it or not: Read it if you build LLM multi-agent systems and want a well-ablated, end-to-end reproducible framework covering both test-time system construction and runtime self-repair; skip it if you only need the incremental insight, which is essentially RAG plus process supervision applied at the MAS-organization level.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are used for complex tasks (planning, QA, code generation), but existing constructions fall into three inadequate categories: handcrafted SOP frameworks (MetaGPT, ChatDev) that are rigid; search-based automation (ADAS, AFlow, AgentSquare, SwarmAgentic) that finds a single fixed system and cannot adapt per query; and training-based meta-agents (MAS-GPT, FlowReasoner) that need substantial data/compute and still run open-loop at execution time. None adapt after deployment: they cannot tailor structure to a specific query at test time or correct malfunctioning agents mid-execution, making them brittle under errors, unexpected tool feedback, or adversarial prompts. The authors target practitioners who need a resilient MAS whose structure adapts in context — analogous to how in-context learning adapts a single frozen model — without parameter updates. Key Idea: The core move is extending the in-context-learning conditioning principle from model behavior to system structure: retrieved structured collaboration experience (successful SOP templates and failure attributions) serves as context that conditions both how a frozen-LLM MAS is instantiated per query and how it is reconfigured during execution. Retrieval narrows a combinatorially large design space (the SOP repository has fewer than 100 entries), and the Watcher's runtime supervision is grounded in an experience pool of past failures with agent-level error attributions and improvement strategies. Methodology: MASFly is a closed-loop three-stage pipeline: (1) Query-Driven System Instantiation — an LLM generates a need analysis n for query q, hybrid retrieval scores repository cases by s(q,ci)=λ·Sim(q,qi)+(1−λ)·Sim(n,ni) (cosine similarity of embeddings, λ=0.3, K=2 retrieved SOPs), and the LLM synthesizes a query-specific operation procedure (OP) defining agent composition, prompts, tool assignments, and a directed communication graph; (2) Process-Supervised Execution — a global Watcher agent, triggered every M communication rounds (M = half the agent count) or every L=5 environment steps, performs dual-level supervision (inter-agent communication conformity, agent–environment tool usage) against the OP and ~2 retrieved PEP records (~30% of the Watcher prompt), intervening via experience-guided feedback or dynamic agent replacement with full log purging; (3) Reflective Experience Distillation — offline on labeled training data only, successful executions are abstracted into reusable SOPs added to the repository, failures are diagnosed into agent-wise error attributions added to the PEP, and failed OPs are iteratively revised. The framework is retrieval-augmented LLM prompting over an experience store, not learning; no explicit loss/objective beyond LLM reflection is defined. Critical design decisions: (a) retrieve-then-instantiate rather than retrieve-as-configuration — justified by the w/o SOP-Inst ablation (GAIA-L2 drops 41.5→35.8); (b) hybrid query+need retrieval — justified by Table 12 (λ=1 yields 44.0 vs 49.5 hard-constraint pass on TravelPlanner), though gains from need-similarity are modest; (c) heuristic supervision timing — acknowledged by the authors as suboptimal. Key Results: All methods share the Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 backbone, tool interfaces, and sandbox. On TravelPlanner (180 test queries), MASFly reaches 61.7% final pass rate in Sole-Planning mode ([54.4, 68.9] bootstrap CI) versus 31.1% for the strongest baseline SwarmAgentic, and 39.4% Two-Stage versus 24.4% for G-Memory — a relative improvement the authors state as 98% and 62%. On GAIA (110 test questions), MASFly averages 39.7% accuracy (Level 1: 46.3, Level 2: 41.5, Level 3: 16.7) versus 36.0 for G-Memory and 35.1 for AgentSquare. On coding: HumanEval 98.7, MBPP 93.3, MBPP Pro 85.6 Pass@1, all within one point of the best baselines on the easier sets but ahead on MBPP Pro; LiveCodeBench-v5 results in the appendix also favor MASFly. Baselines are current (2024–2025 methods) and strong. Scale is standard (per-benchmark test sets of 16–367 instances; training repositories of 2–20 labeled samples; <$0.31/query API cost). Notable findings: zero-shot (empty repository) MASFly already beats all baselines on TravelPlanner; under a forced-empty-output prompt attack on MBPP Pro and a prompt-injection attack on TravelPlanner, MASFly retains near-baseline performance while baselines collapse; supervision frequency shows a non-monotonic trade-off, with moderate frequency optimal; even a Qwen3-8B Watcher recovers most of the supervision benefit. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (in-context structural adaptation, extending ICL conditioning to MAS organization) plus NEW METHOD (the combined retrieval-augmented SOP instantiation + experience-enhanced Watcher supervision loop). The ingredients are individually standard — RAG-style retrieval over experience stores (cf. G-Memory, Agent KB), process supervision, and runtime agent replacement (cf. MegaAgent's hierarchical monitoring) — and the novelty lies in their integration into a closed loop with per-query structural customization, plus the explicit problem framing. The framing paper positions this against training-based MAS generation, which is a genuine gap in the literature. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for this subfield. Ablations isolate each component (SOP-RAG, SOP instantiation, Watcher, PEP), showing the largest drop from removing SOP-RAG (TravelPlanner hard-constraint 49.5→18.6). Three independent runs with mean±std are reported for GAIA and coding tasks; task-level bootstrap CIs (200,000 resamples) are given for TravelPlanner. A hyperparameter sweep covers λ, K, supervision frequency, and Watcher backbone scale. Code and data are released at https://github.com/LARS-research/MASFly. A notable credibility positive is the manual audit of 50 Watcher calls reporting precision/recall/F1 including a concrete false-positive case analysis. Methodological concerns: (1) repositories are built using ground-truth labels on training splits, so the method quietly assumes labeled data availability — the "labeled data" budget is matched across baselines but the philosophical claim of parameter-free adaptivity is weakened; (2) evaluation is entirely on benchmarks whose training data seeds the repositories, so contamination-adjacent adaptation within-domain is tested, not out-of-domain transfer; (3) GAIA Level 3 has only 16 test questions (±3.6 std), so the Level 3 number is statistically fragile; (4) TravelPlanner is a single full run despite the bootstrap CI addressing sampling but not run-to-run variance. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a framework the authors run end-to-end with API-based LLMs). - Practical: Yes — runs on commercial API access to Qwen3-235B, with a demonstrated lighter configuration (Qwen3-32B backbone, Qwen3-8B Watcher). - Efficient: Moderately — total API cost is $0.31/query on TravelPlanner and $0.07 on GAIA, with instantiation <5% and supervision 12–16% of cost; execution time is higher than open-loop baselines but the paper shows MASFly sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on HumanEval and MBPP Pro (baserun baselines on TravelPlanner are faster but far less accurate). - Effective: Yes for the stated in-distribution problem — closed-loop supervision demonstrably fixes tool-bypass and agent-failure modes, and the intervention audit (F1 0.847) shows supervision is not arbitrary; effectiveness on truly novel domains is untested. - Scalable: Not tested beyond ~100-entry repositories and small test sets; the authors only claim clustering-based scalability of the repository for future larger scenarios — this is a claim, not an experiment. The work delivers a software artifact (code and data repository) rather than a trained model. Strengths: - The in-context structural adaptation formulation is a clean conceptual contribution that productively reframes the search-based vs. training-based dichotomy in automated MAS design. - The evaluation rigor exceeds subfield norms: bootstrap CIs, three-seed variance, a component-wise ablation where removing SOP-RAG causes a 3× drop in hard-constraint pass rate, and a manually annotated intervention-quality audit that surfaces real failure modes (e.g., the Watcher's false-positive "Brooklyn/San Francisco" case). - The robustness experiments (forced-empty-output attack, prompt injection causing tool bypass) directly test the runtime-repair claim rather than leaving it anecdotal — baselines collapse while MASFly holds. - Cost transparency (per-stage token breakdown, Pareto plots against clock time and API cost) is unusual and lets a practitioner judge the actual price of the Watcher loop. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) supervision triggering relies on heuristic rules (interval = half the agent count) that may be suboptimal; (2) repository construction needs labeled training instances and domain-limited experience may bias or negatively transfer on substantially different settings; (3) the Watcher has incomplete visibility into agent–environment interactions and may issue unnecessary interventions (confirmed empirically: 6 false positives in 50 calls); (4) supervision and reconfiguration add inference cost. They confront limitations directly and propose future directions (automated anomaly detection, principled experience selection, budget-aware adaptation) — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No experiment on cross-domain experience transfer: the limitation about negative transfer is acknowledged but never measured, even with a simple TravelPlanner-repo-on-GAIA test. - The experience distillation stage uses ground-truth evaluation on training data, meaning the "in-context" framing parallels ICL but with a supervision signal that vanilla ICL does not require; a comparison against training-free alternatives that use the same labeled budget differently (e.g., simply retrieving full successful trajectories rather than distilled SOPs) is absent. - Single-run TravelPlanner evaluation contrasts with the three-seed protocol elsewhere, and the headline 61.7% figure carries no run-variance estimate. - The Watcher's own LLM-based judgment creates a potential circularity (same backbone supervising agents generated by the same backbone) that is not analyzed; the C.7 ablation varies Watcher scale but not model family. - Ablations report only the Watcher intervention policy on TravelPlanner; the interaction between supervision frequency and adversarial settings is not studied. Bottom Line: This is the most complete empirical treatment to date of test-time structural adaptation and runtime self-repair for LLM multi-agent systems, and a practitioner building agentic pipelines should read it for its evaluation template alone — but its dependence on labeled in-domain experience means the "general adaptability" framing should be treated as unproven beyond the three evaluated domains.

Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models (19 ▲ )

Xilin Wei, Shengyuan Ding, Xinyu Fang, Tiancheng Gu, Yuchi Wang, Zhixun Li, Ziyu Liu, Yuhang Zang, Weixiang Yu, Cheng Lu, Chonggao Sun, Tong Zhou, Dahua Lin, Hang Zhang, Shuai Bai, Dayiheng Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Co-Design Bench, a reference-free benchmark of 273 real-user application-revision tasks (100 Multimodal Editing, 173 Repository Editing) with 2,331 hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria, plus a judge-then-refute evaluation protocol combining source-code and browser evidence with adversarial verification. - Why it's important: Existing web-coding benchmarks either use synthetic/predefined edits, require gold code or target screenshots, or evaluate single-shot generation, so the field lacks a realistic testbed for whether agentic coding agents fully deliver compound revisions drawn from actual user sessions. - How it does it: Tasks are recovered from 26,314 real coding sessions with runnable pre-edit applications, and grading uses a fixed agentic evaluator over source diffs, screenshots, and Playwright traces, followed by a separate LLM verifier that challenges positive verdicts (checking for stubs, hardcoding, unreachable functionality) and mandatory evidence audits (screenshots for visual claims, recorded actions for interaction claims). - The good: The headline finding is well-measured and consistent across ten endpoints: the best model (gpt-6-astra) averages 69.9% strict criterion completion but fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks, cleanly exposing the gap between partial requirement coverage and complete delivery. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the LLM-judged scores; the human validation of the judge (200 task-model outputs by two experts) reports no agreement statistics, and the benchmark/data release status beyond a project page is not stated in the provided text. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate agentic coding systems and need a realistic, contamination-resistant evaluation of web application editing; skip it if you only need another coding-agent leaderboard, since the per-model results are descriptive under one fixed harness.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building coding agents for web application co-design need to know whether an agent can take a real user's revision request — often combining image, audio, video, or document attachments with changes spanning layout, interaction, and application state — and produce a fully working revision of an existing application. Prior benchmarks cover reference reconstruction (Design2Code, WebSight-Test, WebRenderBench, IWR-Bench), synthetic page-level edits (MT-Web2Code, WebCompass-edit, DesignBench), or repository issues/freelance tasks (SWE-bench, SWE-Lancer), but none combine real-user compound revisions, runnable starting states, reference-free acceptance, agentic evaluation, and adversarial verification. The authors also show execution conditions distort existing scores: switching qwen3.7-plus from single-shot to agentic execution on 150 WebCompass-edit tasks raises mean graded feature completion from 73.6% to 95.1% under identical rubric, judge, and rendering pipeline — meaning single-shot evaluations understate agentic capability while still masking incomplete delivery. Key Idea: The core insight is that acceptance for application revisions can be grounded in the pre-edit application rather than gold code or target screenshots: hidden expert criteria specify requested outcomes relative to a runnable baseline, and an adversarial judge-then-refute protocol (primary agentic grader → independent LLM verifier that attacks PASS/PARTIAL verdicts → mandatory evidence audits that abort scoring when visual/interaction claims lack render or action evidence) prevents source-code presence from being credited as working functionality. A second framing insight is reporting criterion-level Strict/Graded Completion alongside Full-Pass Rate, since the two metrics diverge sharply when unmet requirements are spread across many tasks. Methodology: Data construction: (a) recover runnable starting states — from 39,325 queries in 26,314 sessions, deduplicate to 37,463, anchor each candidate to an edit turn, restore repo/assets/context via source-hash snapshots, and gate on dependency, build, container launch, and Playwright render checks (with scripted/agentic repair and pruning of unrecoverable services); (b) select and author — normalize requests, apply hard filters F1–F6 (environment-blocked, chatter, vague, non-editing), rank by r(q) = d + v + f (difficulty 0–5, verifiability 0–3, historical failure signals 0–2), consolidate ≤3 queries per session into bounded intervals, and have experts author hidden criteria. The task form is t = (S, I, C): runnable baseline + containerized environment, request/attachments/history, and hidden rubric; a solver harness maps (S, I) to an edited application and trajectory. ME (100 tasks, 553 criteria, mean 5.5/task) covers localized edits with optional image (4), audio (32), video (27), or document (17) attachments; RE (173 tasks, 1,778 criteria, mean 10.3/task, max 46) covers coordinated multi-file edits — 96% of RE tasks require multiple edit types. Evaluation: build/render in an isolated sandbox, extract evidence (source diffs, DOM, screenshots, Playwright action logs), grade each criterion PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL (scored 1/0.5/0), then a separate LLM verifier refutes positive verdicts; render/browser-log audits abort evaluation on violations. Scoring reports Strict (R̄), Graded (Ḡ), and Full-Pass Rate (F) with equal task weighting. Failure attribution uses a parallel baseline render and a solvability probe (minimal sandbox patch with stubbed network endpoints) to classify model vs. environment vs. artifact defects, without altering raw scores. Critical design decisions: hidden rubrics that admit multiple valid implementations (justified by reference-free acceptance), mandatory evidence audits (well-motivated by the source-presence ≠ reachability argument), and a fixed solver harness (Claude Code) — though Appendix H shows model×harness interactions are large, which the fixed-harness choice controls for but does not resolve. Key Results: Ten endpoints under a shared harness: gpt-6-astra leads with combined strict completion 0.699 (ME 0.754, RE 0.667) but Full-Pass of only 26.4% (ME 41.0%, RE 17.9%); opus-5 0.661/18.3%, qwen3.8-max-0902 0.653/16.5%, qwen3.8-27b 0.644/15.0%, down to grok-4.6 at 0.511/6.6%. Cross-track Spearman ρ = 0.818, but rankings shuffle (qwen3.8-27b: 5th on ME, 2nd on RE). All ten endpoints score lower on RE tasks spanning 3–4 edit types (pooled strict 0.591) than 1–2 types (0.654); zero-pass rates rise from 0.9% to 5.8%. By modality, pooled strict ranges 0.584 (audio) to 0.652 (documents), yet document tasks fully pass in only 18.2% of pairs vs. 37.0% for text-only. By capability, Functional Implementation (126 tasks) has the highest pooled strict (0.619) but lowest full-pass (10.3%). Execution profiles: ME video tasks need a median 44 turns vs. 27 for text-only; gpt-6-astra reaches ME 0.754 with 1.24M tokens/case while glm-5.2 spends 7.29M tokens for 0.572. Harness sensitivity (Appendix H): the kimi-k3 minus qwen3.8-27b gap swings 10.0 pp on ME and 16.2 pp on RE across three harnesses, with harness ranking inverted on ME (ρ = −1.00). The WebCompass-edit ablation shows single-shot scores saturate (opus-4-8 at 99.4% graded completion agentic) while Co-Design Bench leaves 35.1 points of headroom. Baseline comparisons are against contemporary frontier endpoints, though all are vendor-served API models; the benchmark itself is the contribution, so external baselines are the ten evaluated endpoints. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW METHOD (evaluation protocol) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (criterion-satisfaction vs. complete-delivery gap under agentic execution). The genuinely novel elements are the real-session provenance with runnable pre-edit states, reference-free hidden rubrics spanning five input modalities, and the judge-then-refute protocol with mandatory evidence audits; the underlying machinery (Playwright sandboxing, LLM-as-judge, Agent-as-a-Judge-style evaluation, containerized SWE-bench-style harnesses) is a competent combination of existing techniques applied to a new problem setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover three axes: execution regime (single-shot vs. agentic, paired on 150 WebCompass-edit tasks), evaluator sensitivity (four judge configurations shift absolute graded scores by ≤0.053 with stable ordering for the two test solvers), and harness robustness (three harnesses, revealing large model×harness interactions). Human validation exists (two frontend experts reviewing 200 task-model outputs) but no agreement rate or inter-rater statistics are reported. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests appear for the main grid, and the text acknowledges that a fixed configuration does not make LLM judging deterministic. Release status: a project page (https://codesignbench.github.io/) is given and stored trajectories/outputs are described as retained; no explicit code/data/model-weight repository URL for the benchmark artifacts is provided in the text. Methodological flags: the benchmark is authored and evaluated by the same group with hidden rubrics, so rubric quality cannot be independently audited; endpoint results come from vendor APIs (self-reported naming/versions, no open weights for most); and token accounting mixes different vendor conventions, which the authors correctly note is not a common monetary cost. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus evaluation system, run at scale). - Practical: Runs on standard containerized infrastructure (Vite/static builds, headless Chrome/Playwright) plus API access to model endpoints; nothing requires exotic hardware. - Efficient: Each solver run is capped at 3 hours and 120 turns with 0.45M–7.29M tokens per case, so a full 10-endpoint grid (2,730 pairs, 135,370 tool calls) is a substantial but bounded compute investment; the judge pipeline adds render + LLM grading per criterion. - Effective: Evidence supports that it measures the stated phenomenon — the criterion/full-pass gap and edit-breadth degradation are consistent across all ten endpoints — but the absolute scores are LLM-judged with unreported human agreement, so "effective" rests on the (reasonable) validity argument plus a 200-sample expert check without published statistics. - Scalable: 273 tasks is a moderate benchmark size; scaling rubric authorship and the refute-audit pipeline to thousands of tasks has not been demonstrated, though the pipeline is largely automated and the paper makes no explicit scalability claims to test. The work delivers (or describes) a benchmark artifact, evaluation harness, and stored trajectories; a public artifact URL beyond the project page is not stated in the provided text. Strengths: - Real-user provenance with runnable baselines: recovering buildable pre-edit applications from 26,314 production sessions, with a build/launch/render gate, is a genuine curation contribution that most editing benchmarks lack (WebCompass uses predefined edit operations; DesignBench uses version-pair screenshots). - The judge-then-refute protocol with evidence-type-specific audits directly targets the most common LLM-judge failure (crediting hardcoded or unreachable code), and retained verdict/evidence traces make scores inspectable. - The dual-metric framing (Strict/Graded vs. Full-Pass) surfaces a phenomenon single-number leaderboards hide, and the 69.9% vs. 26.4% divergence is a memorable, actionable finding for agent builders. - The negative controls are unusually honest for a benchmark paper: the cross-harness study showing model rankings invert across harnesses (ρ = −1.00 on ME) and the paired single-shot/agentic ablation are the kind of self-skeptical analysis most benchmark papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) task-group comparisons (modality, edit breadth, capability) are descriptive and confounded by task content, not causal estimates; (2) cross-benchmark score comparisons use different task pools and protocols; (3) the refutation pass cannot by itself establish correctness of every verdict, and a fixed judge configuration is not deterministic; (4) tasks evaluate a fixed request and do not simulate iterative user feedback during execution; (5) the evaluator-sensitivity check is descriptive and may differ from production in sampling/serving; (6) endpoint generations are not exactly reproducible from endpoint names alone; (7) token counts are execution measures, not monetary costs; (8) small groups (e.g., 4 image tasks, 4 Motion & Adaptation tasks) yield unstable numbers, which they grey out. This is a direct, non-defensive treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No inter-rater or human–judge agreement statistics are reported despite the 200-output expert audit; without an agreement rate, the validity of PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL verdicts is asserted rather than measured. - Only one primary solver harness (Claude Code) is used for the main leaderboard, while the paper's own Appendix H shows harness effects of 10–16 pp — so the headline rankings are conditional on an untested-for-most-models scaffold choice. - The judge model identity/configuration is not stated in the provided text, and the separate verifier's false-refutation rate (correctly overturning genuine passes) is unmeasured — only the failure direction the authors care about (false positives) is characterized. - Rubrics are authored by the benchmark creators who also run the evaluation; no external rubric audit or contamination check against solver training data is described, and real-session tasks may appear in vendor training corpora (a dogs-not-barking omission given the 2026 endpoints). - ME is heavily imbalanced across modalities (4 image tasks vs. 32 audio), making modality conclusions fragile; single-task strata are already greyed out, but 4-task strata receive headline-adjacent comparisons. - Cost analysis stops at tokens; no wall-clock distribution, dollar cost, or success-per-cost comparison is provided despite large effort differences (e.g., glm-5.2's 7.29M tokens for ME 0.572). Bottom Line: For researchers benchmarking agentic coding and multimodal editing systems, this is a meaningfully better evaluation instrument than WebCompass-edit, DesignBench, or SWE-bench-M for the co-design setting — its real-session provenance and adversarial, evidence-audited grading are worth adopting wholesale — but its leaderboard numbers should be read as one-harness, LLM-judged estimates pending released artifacts and human-agreement validation.

EAST: Embodied AI Safety Testing via Systematic Fault Injection in Digital Twins

Y Tian, T Li, L Zhou, D Towey, Z Fan, W Wu, R Huang… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EAST, a three-stage framework that converts literature-grounded safety knowledge into executable fault-injection tests (eight operators targeting perception, instruction, scene, action, and timing interfaces) run in the RoboTwin digital twin, with runtime realization verification and safety oracles that judge safety independently of task success. - Why it's important: Task success does not imply safe execution for embodied AI — a robot can complete a manipulation task while violating a safety constraint mid-trajectory — and existing robustness benchmarks and safety benchmarks do not systematically translate safety knowledge into controlled, reproducible, traceable fault injections. - How it does it: A safety-fault model (7 taxonomy classes abstracted from 81 evidence entries in 15 papers) is mapped many-to-many onto 8 executable fault operators; constraint-aware generation (applicability, validity, semantic, context, deduplication, diversity checks) produces fixed test specifications whose runtime realization is verified from recorded evidence before safety oracles classify outcomes into six exclusive categories. - The good: Methodologically disciplined evaluation — 14,728 budgeted records across 6 experiments, matched-budget comparisons with paired bootstrap CIs, sign-flip tests and Holm correction, zero no-op false positives, 100% exact-replay consistency, and full ablations attributing up to +20.42 pp valid-test yield to individual generation mechanisms. - The missing: EAST's advantage over simple Random-Legal generation is coverage (74/74 vs 59–63/74 task–policy–operator combinations), not effectiveness — Random-Legal matches its challenge exposure and safety-failure rates and even finds more distinct failure signatures (39 vs 27), so the core claim that systematic generation beats cheaper randomization is only weakly supported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building embodied-AI safety evaluation infrastructure who want a rigorous template for fault-injection methodology and metrics; skip it if you need evidence on frontier VLA models, physical-robot transfer, or a released tool, since none of these are present.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The statistical discipline (matched budgets, bootstrap CIs, sign-flip tests, seed-matched ablations) and the candid limitations section are excellent, but two dimensions pull the composite down: Novelty (62) is framework engineering — the realization/exposure/violation decomposition is useful, yet the unsafe-success finding is confirmatory of prior benchmarks — and the paper's own data undercuts its central comparative claim (Random-Legal matches SFTR and finds more failure signatures, so the coverage advantage is partly by construction), capping Non-Obviousness (55) and Resilience (76). Practical Impact (38) is low: no released code, dataset, or tool despite meticulous protocol documentation. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*74 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*76 + 0.10*38 = 66.
