Problem & Motivation: Multi-hop QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, MultiHopRAG) requires assembling complementary evidence from multiple graph regions, but practitioners building graph-based RAG systems organize evidence by independently ranking candidate reasoning paths by query relevance. Because BFS/beam exploration from anchor nodes generates many structurally overlapping paths from the same locally relevant region, independent ranking fills the limited evidence context with redundant paths and suppresses evidence for other reasoning sub-goals. The paper targets the evidence-organization stage — not path exploration — arguing this stage is under-optimized relative to retrieval and traversal work. Key Idea: Treat evidence organization as constrained maximum-coverage-style subgraph optimization: define explicit reasoning targets (LLM-decomposed sub-questions), measure each path's coverage of each target via truncated cosine similarity between path-node and target embeddings, and greedily select paths by marginal coverage gain — so redundant paths score near zero — under node-budget and connectivity constraints. The key insight is that diminishing returns over reasoning targets, rather than relevance scores, should drive evidence selection. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) build a sentence-level document graph (nodes = sentences, edges = semantic/discourse relations); retrieve anchor nodes with a dense retriever (BGE-large-en-v1.5) or BM25; extract candidate paths via BFS (depth 5, up to 20 paths per anchor, 20 anchors). (2) Reasoning Coverage Construction (RCC): prompt the backbone LLM to output atomic single-hop sub-questions plus question type and key entities; embed these as targets. (3) Coverage-aware Reasoning Optimization (CRO): greedy selection (Algorithm 1) maximizing the monotone submodular objective F(S) subject to a node budget B (default 4) and at most K connected components (default 2, enforced with Union-Find); complexity O(n·l̄·m + n²·m). Theoretical analysis proves NP-hardness via reduction from Maximum Coverage (Appendix B) and monotone submodularity of F (Appendix C), invoking Nemhauser et al.'s (1−1/e) greedy guarantee — though the authors correctly note this bound strictly applies when connectivity is non-binding. Design decisions worth flagging: (a) truncated-cosine coverage is a semantic proxy, not logical entailment — the authors acknowledge this; (b) the connectivity constraint is empirically shown to hurt when strict (K=1 degrades EM), so its default of 2 is only weakly justified; (c) target decomposition quality is never independently measured. Key Results: With BGE-large-en-v1.5 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct default: HotpotQA EM 52.60 / F1 65.49 (SentGraph: 48.80 / 62.92); 2WikiMultiHopQA EM 47.53 / F1 57.00 (SentGraph: 42.00 / 52.26); MuSiQue EM 30.80 / F1 43.33 (SentGraph: 26.80 / 40.36); MultiHopRAG accuracy 67.40 (SentGraph: 65.60), at 2.62 average evidence units vs. 2.70 (SentGraph) and 3.00–5.00 for passage baselines. Under BM25: HotpotQA EM 47.20 vs. 43.80; 2Wiki EM 39.80 vs. 32.20; MuSiQue EM 20.80 vs. 16.00 — the largest relative gains in the weaker retrieval regime. Baselines include Retrieval Only, RankLlama, SetR variants, LightRAG, KGP, and SentGraph; SentGraph (the strongest baseline, and the authors' own prior work) and KGP are current and reasonably strong, though no GNN-RAG or ToG/RoG-style traversal baselines appear in the main table. Ablations: removing RCC drops 2Wiki EM from 47.53 to 41.80; removing both RCC and CRO drops it to 41.00 (MuSiQue EM falls 30.80 → 26.80 → 25.60). Budget sweeps show saturation around B=3–5 (HotpotQA EM 39.80 at B=1 → 51.80 at B=3). Exhaustive search on ≤20-path instances (400 samples): average approximation ratio >0.9977, minimum 0.9395 (2Wiki); HotpotQA ratio 1.0000. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with a modest theoretical contribution. Genuinely novel: casting the evidence-organization stage of graph-RAG as constrained coverage maximization over reasoning targets with structural constraints, plus the exhaustive-search validation of greedy quality in this setting. What is standard: greedy submodular maximization, MMR-style diversity, LLM question decomposition, BFS path extraction, and sentence graphs (the latter from the authors' own SentGraph) are all established; the contribution is their principled combination applied to graph-based multi-hop QA, not a fundamentally new algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Reasonably rigorous for an empirical NLP paper: ablations of both core components (Table 3), budget and connectivity sweeps (Figures 4–5), two retrievers, four backbone LLMs (7B–32B), and an exhaustive-optimal-search comparison (Appendix D). Three seeds (42, 123, 456) with temperature-0 decoding and full hyperparameter tables are reported; however, no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests appear in any table. Code, prompts beyond one template, or data splits are not stated as released — a reproducibility gap. Concerns: (1) the coverage proxy is evaluated on the same benchmarks used for tuning defaults (B=4, K=2), inviting mild Goodhart risk; (2) the approximation-ratio analysis measures greedy quality on the coverage objective, not on downstream QA accuracy, so near-optimal coverage does not directly establish near-optimal answer quality; (3) the closest baseline (SentGraph) is the authors' own prior work, making it hard to audit baseline tuning fairness; (4) the theory guarantee and the connectivity constraint are in tension — the guarantee needs the constraint non-binding, yet connectivity is presented as a design feature. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (training-free inference-time method with experiments; small theory appendix). Practical: Yes — runs on 8× RTX 4090 (24 GB) with 7B–32B open-weight LLMs, so no exotic hardware. Efficient: O(n²·m) greedy loop plus one LLM decomposition call per question; cheaper context (≈2.6 evidence units) reduces generation cost, but per-candidate-path embedding and marginal-gain computation add overhead the paper does not quantify in wall-clock terms. Effective: Evidence supports it on four standard benchmarks with two retrievers and four backbones, though the mechanism is validated through a semantic-coverage proxy, not direct measurement of reasoning completeness. Scalable: Untested — experiments use standard QA corpora; behavior on graphs or candidate sets orders of magnitude larger, where the O(n²·m) loop and LLM decomposition latency would matter, is only claimed implicitly. Deliverable: paper only; no library, CLI, dataset, or model weights are reported as released. Strengths: - A clean, correct reframing: the paper identifies a real failure mode (redundant top-ranked overlapping paths) and shows the fix follows from a classical optimization lens, with the NP-hardness and submodularity proofs done properly rather than decoratively. - The exhaustive-search validation (approximation ratio >0.9977 average, ≥0.9395 worst-case on ≤20-path instances) is an unusually honest empirical bridge between the theory and the algorithm, and the BM25 results (e.g., MuSiQue EM 20.80 vs. 16.00) show the gains are not an artifact of a strong dense retriever. - Consistent improvement at lower evidence cost (2.62 vs. 2.70–5.00 units), which matters for context-limited deployment, and stable gains across 7B–32B backbones suggesting orthogonality to model scale. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) CROG cannot recover evidence missed by upstream path extraction, so recall is bounded by the candidate set; (2) semantic- similarity coverage does not verify logical correctness of the reasoning; (3) evaluation is English-only and general-domain. They confront these directly and name concrete future directions, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical uncertainty: three seeds are used but no variance, error bars, or significance tests are reported for any headline number, despite margins over SentGraph of ~3.8 EM points that are plausibly robust but unverified. - The approximation analysis optimizes coverage, not QA accuracy — greedy could be near-optimal on a flawed proxy; no experiment links approximation ratio to downstream EM/F1. - The (1−1/e) guarantee is invoked while the connectivity constraint (a selling-point contribution) is exactly the part that voids it, and the paper does not analyze greedy quality when the constraint binds. - Missing baselines: no comparison against LLM-based set-selection alternatives beyond SetR, no GNN-RAG/ToG/RoG numbers in the main table, and no baseline that simply diversifies top-ranked paths via MMR — the most direct competitor to the marginal-gain mechanism. - RCC prompt quality depends entirely on the backbone LLM; no analysis of decomposition failure rates or of how errors in sub-question generation propagate into coverage errors. - No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits independent verification given the authors' authorship of the strongest baseline. Bottom Line: A practitioner building graph-RAG systems gains a concrete, well-validated, training-free upgrade to the often-overlooked evidence-selection stage, but the lack of released code, absence of significance testing, and proxy-based validation mean it should be adopted as a design pattern to reimplement rather than a verified drop-in tool.

#100 — Innovative (65)

Efficient Streaming Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction for Real-World Acoustic Scenes (149 ▲ )

Wendi Sang, Kai Li, Yifan Li, Jianqiang Huang, Xiaolin Hu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 29 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RealSSA, a two-part audio-visual target speaker extraction (AVTSE) benchmark pairing a controllable simulation suite (1–5 near-field plus 10–15 far-field interferers, reverberation, sudden noise) with an 84-minute real-recorded evaluation set, and Falcon, a 0.5M-parameter causal AVTSE model trained with a new encoder-space speaker contrastive loss. - Why it's important: Latency-sensitive deployments (video conferencing, hearing aids) currently validate causal AVTSE models on fixed two-speaker, anechoic benchmarks that say little about real scenes, and heavy causal architectures exceed edge compute budgets. - How it does it: Falcon performs frequency-, time-, and joint time-frequency modeling at four scales in a single encoder–decoder pass (replacing SwiftNet's iterative re-invocation), and adds a contrastive loss in the STFT-encoder space that repels the estimate from each near-field interferer during training only, at zero inference cost. - The good: The efficiency result is decisive: vs. causal AV-TFGridNet, Falcon cuts parameters by 91.9%, MACs by 95.0% (20.2×), and GPU latency by 11.1× (567.8→51.3 ms per 2 s clip) while matching or exceeding its SI-SNRi on all four simulated benchmarks. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, and the headline quality margin over AV-TFGridNet on the new benchmark is only 0.1 dB SI-SNRi (7.7 vs. 7.6), within plausible run-to-run noise. - Read it or not: Read it if you build streaming or on-device speech separation/extraction systems or need a realistic AVTSE evaluation substrate; skip it if you only care about offline, large-scale multi-channel separation, where its single-channel scope limits relevance.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Practical Impact (75) is the strongest dimension — a released benchmark with regenerable splits, model code, demo page, and the best documented quality-per-FLOP causal AVTSE model (20.2× compute, 11.1× latency reduction demonstrated, not claimed). Rigor (62) is dragged down by single-run results with 0.1 dB headline margins, no seed variance, proxy-only real-data evaluation, and Falcon-vs-RealSSA co-design inviting Goodhart alignment. Novelty (68) reflects a genuinely new benchmark axis coverage plus a reusable contrastive loss, but the architecture is competent recombination; Non-Obviousness (60) is moderate (the crowding-dominates-difficulty finding is mildly counter-intuitive). Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Causal (streaming) AVTSE — extracting a target speaker's voice from a mixture using lip video as an enrollment cue — is needed for hearing-assistive devices and video conferencing, but the field has two coupled gaps. First, existing benchmarks (LRS2-2Mix, LRS3-2Mix, VoxCeleb2-2Mix, plus the LRS3+WHAM! noisy protocol) fix the speaker count at two, use anechoic or inherited acoustics, include no sudden noise events, and are evaluated only on held-out splits of the same source videos, so reported gains do not predict deployed behavior. Second, causal architectures with strong quality (AV-TFGridNet, AV-Mossformer2) are too heavy for edge hardware, while lightweight iterative models (SwiftNet) reclaim capacity by repeatedly invoking a small separator, multiplying per-frame FLOPs. The SI-SNR training objective also never explicitly pushes the estimate away from spatially close interferers, leaving near-field leakage that grows with the number of active talkers. Key Idea: Two ideas. (1) Architecture: collapse multi-scale time-frequency modeling into one asymmetric U-Net traversal — a TFRB (bidirectional frequency LSTM → unidirectional time LSTM → block-causal 2D self-attention) at the bottleneck plus level-specific TFRBs at each decoder resolution, with global-context-injection gating skips — so four TF scales are modeled in a single pass instead of via iterative cycles. (2) Training: an encoder-space speaker contrastive loss that reuses the model's own STFT encoder (with stop-gradients on references) to pull the masked estimate toward the clean target and push it away from each near-field interferer, with a softmax-weighted, margin-based (m=0.5) repulsion whose temperature τ is annealed 0→1; the branch is discarded at inference, so the quality gain is free. Methodology: Pipeline: frozen FRCNN visual backbone (from CTCNet) extracts 96×96 mouth-crop features; a STFT audio encoder (window 256, hop 128, real/imag/magnitude 3-channel input) produces A0; audio and visual blocks refine each modality; fusion adds the frequency-expanded visual feature to the audio feature; the Separator predicts a complex TF mask applied to A0 by complex multiplication, and iSTFT reconstructs the waveform. The Separator is a 4-level causal U-Net (Ch=64): stride-1/stride-2 depthwise convolutions downsample, TFRB at the bottleneck forms global context G, GCI modules inject G into each skip via a gated, depthwise-convolution formulation, and decoder TFRBs recover resolution coarse-to-fine; all temporal padding is left-aligned (no lookahead). The objective is L = −SI-SNR(ŝ, s) + λspk·Lspk with λspk=1.0; Lspk pools encoder features to unit-norm speaker embeddings and applies Eq. (10)'s attraction-plus-repulsion form. Critical design decisions: (a) depth fixed at 3 downsampling stages, justified by the 120 ms visual lookahead budget (a 4th stage would break audio-visual alignment) — well-justified and ablated; (b) excluding far-field interferers from the contrastive negatives, justified by arguing their residual falls below the SI-SNR error floor — plausible but asserted rather than ablated; (c) LSTM over GRU/SRU inside TFRB — ablated (7.7 vs. 7.3–7.4 dB SI-SNRi). Key Results: On RealSSA-Sim, Falcon reached 7.7 dB SI-SNRi / 8.2 dB SDRi vs. 7.6/8.1 for AV-TFGridNet (6.2M params) and 7.3/7.8 for Swift-Net-12 (same 0.5M params); per-scene breakdowns show Falcon best on 11 of 16 (scene × speaker-count) cells. On public benchmarks it led all four: LRS2-2Mix 14.1/14.7, LRS3-2Mix 16.4/16.7, VoxCeleb2-2Mix 10.5/11.8 SI-SNRi/SDRi, with the largest gain (+1.1 dB SI-SNRi over Swift-Net-12) on VoxCeleb2-2Mix. On RealSSA-Real it tied Swift-Net-12 for the best DNSMOS (3.276), ranked second in WER (32.74% vs. AV-Mossformer2's 32.00%), and led target-speaker similarity (42.23 vs. 40.04 for Swift-Net-12; ground-truth reference on sim is 64.69). Efficiency on 2 s clips (RTX 3090): 0.5M params, 10.6 G MACs, 51.3 ms GPU / 1361.2 ms CPU latency, 125.3 MB RAM / 364.7 MB GPU memory — the lowest in every column among the five compared models. A useful counter-intuitive finding: outdoor (near-anechoic) scenes are the easiest and crowded small meeting rooms the hardest, showing near-field talker crowding, not reverberation, dominates difficulty. Baselines were retrained under a common protocol and include recent 2025–2026 models (Dolphin, AV-Mossformer2), so they are current; LRS2/LRS3 baseline numbers are taken from the Swift-Net paper rather than retrained. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (RealSSA is the first AVTSE benchmark jointly varying speaker count, near/far-field geometry, reverb, environmental and sudden noise, with a real-recorded eval set) + NEW METHOD (single-pass multi-scale causal separator) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the encoder-space contrastive loss transfers across three backbones at zero inference cost). The separator is a competent recombination of known components (TF-GridNet-style TF blocks, U-Net skip design, SwiftNet's causal protocol); the genuinely new elements are the benchmark's joint acoustic-axis coverage and the reusable contrastive-loss formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover separator depth (7.1→7.7 dB across 1→3 stages), the contrastive loss on three architectures (+0.2 to +0.4 dB), the τ annealing schedule, recurrent unit choice, output parameterization, speech-overlap ratio, and missing-visual robustness — unusually thorough. However, no multi-seed runs, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and several headline margins (e.g., 0.1 dB over AV-TFGridNet on RealSSA-Sim) are small enough that seed variance could matter. Reproducibility is strong on paper: a fixed master seed (42), bit-for-bit regenerable splits, full metadata (room geometry, RIR hashes, SIR values), full hyperparameter tables, a demo page, and a stated commitment to release generation scripts, dataset, and code (https://cslikai.cn/Falcon/); whether weights are public is not stated. Methodological concerns: (1) the flagship model and the flagship benchmark are co-designed and co-evaluated — Falcon's design choices (contrastive negatives restricted to near-field, 3-stage depth) were developed in the same distribution RealSSA-Sim defines, inviting Goodhart-style alignment; (2) RealSSA-Real evaluation relies entirely on non-intrusive proxies (DNSMOS, NISQA, ASR-WER, speaker similarity) since no isolated ground truth exists; (3) the causalized Dolphin and AV-Mossformer2 baselines are the authors' own re-implementations; (4) the latency numbers are batch-of-one forward-pass medians amortized over a 2 s clip, not measured streaming per-hop latency — the authors honestly flag this in Appendix E. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trains and evaluates models) with a SYSTEMS artifact (released benchmark + model). - Practical: Runs on a single RTX 3090 with 0.5M parameters and 364.7 MB GPU memory, and 1361 ms CPU latency for a 2 s clip (5.44 ms/hop amortized) is borderline for real-time CPU-only edge use. - Efficient: 20.2× less compute and 11.1× less GPU latency than the strongest quality baseline at equal or better quality — the paper's central, well-measured claim. - Effective: Evidence covers simulated quality (SI-SNRi/SDRi with clean references) and real-data proxies, but no human listening test or on-device end-to-end streaming measurement, so real-world effectiveness is shown by proxy only. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 2 s clips and single-channel audio; 100× scale (multi-channel arrays, hours-long streams, on-device quantization) is untested and only implied. Deliverables: benchmark dataset (RealSSA-Sim/Real), generation scripts, model code, and demo page — a substantive software artifact, not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The benchmark fills a real, well-argued hole: Table 1's three-axis analysis shows no prior AVTSE benchmark varies speaker count, acoustics, and evaluation realism jointly, and the four-scene design with per-scene Hive semantic noise assignment is carefully grounded (critical-distance threshold, Sabine/gpuRIR pipeline, EBU R128 loudness). (2) The efficiency-versus-quality trade is demonstrated, not claimed: Falcon dominates AV-TFGridNet on all four simulated benchmarks while using 3.1% of its GPU latency, and the per-scene grid (Appendix G) shows the single-pass design specifically rescues the crowded-near-field cells where iterative lightweight models collapse (RTFSNet-12 <4 dB on every small-meeting cell). (3) The contrastive loss is a genuinely reusable contribution: it needs no extra encoder, no architecture change, and transfers (+0.2–0.4 dB) to SwiftNet-12 and Dolphin, with an embedding-space visualization supporting the mechanism. (4) The limitation section is candid — single-channel scope, the 84-minute/10-participant real set, and the contrastive loss's dependence on clean simulated interferer waveforms are all stated plainly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) Falcon is single-channel; the four-element simulated array is left for future multi-channel work; (2) RealSSA-Real is only ~84 minutes over 10 participants and 8 environments; (3) the contrastive loss requires clean per-source near-field interferer waveforms available only in simulation, and extending it to unlabeled real recordings is future work. They also disclose (Appendix E) that per-hop streaming latency and end-to-end scheduling overhead were not measured, and (Appendix A.2) that outdoor scenes are approximated by a near-anechoic closed-room simulation. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Statistical rigor: single-run results with 0.1–0.2 dB margins over the strongest baseline and no seed variance or significance testing; the "matches or exceeds" claim on RealSSA-Sim rests on the thinnest of margins. (2) The contrastive-negative exclusion of far-field interferers is argued, not ablated — a one-row experiment would settle it. (3) RealSSA-Real's ground-truth-free evaluation means all real-world conclusions route through proxy models (DNSMOS/NISQA/Mega-ASR/WeSpeaker), each with their own domain shift; no small-scale human listening test is provided. (4) Training on RealSSA-Sim and evaluating on RealSSA-Real still leaves a 20.9-point speaker-similarity gap to the ground-truth reference (43.05 vs. 64.69) and a 13.6-point WER gap (25.47% vs. 11.83%), which the paper reports but does not confront as a ceiling on simulated-to-real transfer. (5) The Falcon-versus-RealSSA co-design concern above: the paper does not report whether Falcon's design choices were tuned on RealSSA-Sim's test distribution. (6) CPU latency of 1.36 s per 2 s clip undercuts the "edge deployment" framing unless GPU or NPU offload is assumed; the paper does not test any embedded target hardware. Bottom Line: For anyone building causal, single-channel speech extraction or seeking a realistic AVTSE evaluation substrate, this paper delivers both a usable benchmark and the best quality-per-FLOP causal model currently documented, and is worth reading despite thin statistical rigor and untested streaming latency; no existing alternative covers the same realistic-conditions ground.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training LLM software-engineering agents need large corpora of executable tasks—repository environment, problem statement, and fail-to-pass/pass-to-pass (F2P/P2P) tests. Existing sources fail on one of three axes: hand-curated sets like SWE-Gym are tiny (2.4k instances, 11 repositories); synthetic generators like SWE-Smith and SWE-Mirror scale but produce distributions biased toward simple bug types (the paper shows SWE-Smith is dominated by logic errors and underrepresents API mismatches and state-synchronization bugs); and automated miners like SWE-rebench cap out at 7.5k executable instances over 3.5k repositories. The three hard sub-problems are heterogeneous environment setup across repositories, repositories lacking usable unit tests, and PR descriptions that are missing, post-hoc, or leak the fix. Key Idea: Replace rigid rule-based dataset-mining rules with a sandboxed multi-agent system in which each agent interacts with the repository at execution time: the environment builder iteratively installs dependencies inside Docker and distills its trajectory into a reproducible Dockerfile; the unit-test creator writes pytest files verified by a "time travel" procedure (must fail on the parent commit, pass on the merge commit, calling only public APIs to avoid overfitting); and the problem-statement writer receives the generated F2P tests as input so the issue narrative is semantically aligned with the validation criteria while explicitly withholding implementation details. Environment cost is contained by building at most ten environments per repository and reusing the "nearest" environment (proxied by PR ID) for additional PRs, discarding PRs that fail validation. Methodology: The pipeline runs: (1) repository selection (top 15k PyPI packages ∪ 9,062 SEART repos, ≥500 stars, ≥5 contributors, permissive license, LLM-as-judge filtering → ~23k repos), excluding all SWE-bench-Verified repositories to prevent contamination; (2) PR filtering (6M merged PRs, LLM-as-judge on diff/description/commit message → ~1M processed); (3) EBA builds Docker environments; (4) UCA generates 2–10 F2P tests per PR with iterative execute-analyze-refine loops and fails the instance unless the time-travel criterion holds; (5) PSWA (Gemini 3 Pro, chosen after an ablation showing GPT-5 and DeepSeek v3.2 leak solution information) writes leak-free problem statements; (6) rule-based checks require all P2P pass and F2P fail pre-patch, all pass post-patch. This yields 100k verified instances (median 3 files modified, 43 added lines, 5.7 F2P and 209 P2P tests per instance). For training, 71,498 trajectories (~3.5B tokens) are distilled from DeepSeek-V3.2 (5 samples/instance, temperature 0.95, 100-turn budget, only test-passing trajectories kept) and used to SFT Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct (lr 1e-5, batch 128, 3 epochs, 131k context, loss masked to well-formed assistant actions). Critical design decisions: test-grounded problem statements (justified by the leakage ablation, Table 6: Gemini 50.8 vs. GPT-5 44.4 vs. DeepSeek 43.6 at 2k trajectories); environment reuse via nearest-PR matching (justified by cost, but correctness of reuse is only indirectly validated by the pass/fail rule); and public-API-only test generation (plausible but not ablated against implementation-level tests). Key Results: On SWE-bench-Verified, Scale-SWE-Agent (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct backbone) reaches 64.0% resolved vs. 22.0% for the base model, beating same-size competitors Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B (51.6%) and GLM-4.7-Flash (59.2%), and open-weight leaders including SWE-Lego-32B (52.6%), SWE-Mirror-LM-32B (52.2%), and KAT-Dev-32B (62.4%), though below proprietary systems (GPT-5.2 Thinking 80.0%, Claude Sonnet 4.5 77.2%). On SWE-bench-Pro (Python), Scale-SWE distilled from "DeepSeek v4 High" reaches 43.9% vs. 8.5% for the base model and 22.6% for GLM-4.7-Flash, with the stronger teacher adding 11.2 absolute points over DeepSeek v3.2 distillation (43.9 vs. 32.7). Under an identical distillation+SFT pipeline, Scale-SWE data beats SWE-Gym (64.0 vs. 54.8) and SWE-Smith (54.6) on SWE-bench-Verified. Training-size scaling is monotonic: 50.8 (2k trajectories) → 58.2 (10k) → 64.0 (71k). Manual audit of 100 sampled instances by four PhD students found 94 valid. Baselines in Table 1 are current (2025–2026 models); evaluation uses the OpenHands scaffolding uniformly. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW METHOD (the agent-based construction pipeline) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (real-world data at scale beats larger synthetic corpora under a controlled training pipeline; teacher quality strongly modulates distillation gains). The core trick—using agentic, execution-grounded exploration instead of static rules to mine real PRs—is a genuinely new point in the design space; the downstream SFT, distillation sampling, and evaluation protocol are standard combinations of known techniques, and the agent components (SWE-agent scaffold, OpenHands, Docker sandboxing) are off-the-shelf. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is unusually strong on controlled comparison: the same distillation and SFT pipeline is applied to SWE-Gym and SWE-Smith, isolating dataset quality as the variable, and the problem-statement generator is ablated across three frontier models. Code and dataset are promised at https://github.com/AweAI-Team/ScaleSWE (the paper states "will release" for the dataset with attribution). Concerns: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; the human audit is 100 instances out of 100k (94/100 valid, with 4 of 6 failures from overly strict F2P tests—suggesting a tail of test-quality issues the audit is too small to characterize); LLM-as-judge filtering and LLM-generated bug taxonomy are validated only anecdotally; and evaluation relies on SWE-bench-Verified, a benchmark whose repositories were excluded from training (good hygiene) but whose task style the pipeline's problem-statement format closely mimics, leaving an open question of format-specific advantage. The prompt appendix is thorough and supports reproduction. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (and SYSTEMS, as a data-construction pipeline). - Practical: Yes—runs on Docker containers with open-weight models (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and public scaffolding; construction uses API access to DeepSeek and Gemini but consumption of the artifact does not. - Efficient: The 30B-A3B (3B activated) model beats 70B+ baselines, and environment reuse (~10 envs per repo, ~19 instances per repo) is the key cost lever; absolute construction compute for 6M PRs is not reported. - Effective: Strong proxy evidence—gains transfer to an out-of-distribution benchmark (SWE-bench-Pro) and to a controlled comparison against alternative datasets—though whether mined instances match the epistemic quality of human-authored issue-solving tasks is not directly measured. - Scalable: The pipeline is the scaling claim and was demonstrated at 100k instances/5.2k repos, a 13× repository increase over the next-largest real dataset; a 10× further jump is asserted by design but not tested, and the nearest-environment reuse heuristic is the most likely failure point as repository heterogeneity grows. The work delivers a concrete artifact: the Scale-SWE-Data dataset, distilled trajectories, Docker environments, and full agent prompts, with a public GitHub repository; the paper itself is peer-reviewed (Findings of EMNLP 2026). Strengths: - The controlled dataset-quality experiment (same pipeline, same base model, three datasets) is the right design and yields the paper's most credible claim: real-world mined data at 100k instances beats a 50k-instance synthetic dataset (SWE-Smith) that under identical training yields only 54.6%. - Test-grounded problem-statement synthesis (PSWA consuming the F2P tests) is a sharp, well-motivated fix for the statement–test misalignment problem, backed by a direct ablation quantifying leakage differences across statement generators (up to 7.2 points). - Honest, specific contamination hygiene: SWE-bench-Verified repositories are excluded from training, and an explicit git-history sanitization script (Appendix D) blocks solution leakage via `git log` during evaluation—details many dataset papers omit. - Full prompt disclosure (Appendix E) plus the bug-taxonomy analysis against BugPilot's ten categories makes the pipeline unusually reproducible for a dataset paper. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly that the dataset is Python-only, justified by Python's ecosystem diversity, and that extension to other languages is necessary future work to prove generality—they do not minimize this. They also acknowledge in the audit section that overly strict F2P tests and low-quality PRs account for the 6% invalid rate. The ethical section commits to license-compliant release with attribution. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: the headline 64.0% vs. 62.4% (KAT-Dev-32B) margin is ~1.6 points on a 500-instance benchmark (~8 instances) with no seeds or significance testing, so the "state-of-the-art open-source" claim is statistically unsupported. - LLM-generated F2P tests create a subtle validity risk the paper does not quantify: tests written by the same model family that later distills trajectories could encode solvable-by-the-generator patterns, and the time-travel criterion alone does not rule out tests that pass for the wrong reason post-patch. The 100-instance audit cannot detect this at scale. - The nearest-environment reuse heuristic (PR-ID proximity as a timeline proxy) is a potential correctness hazard for fast-moving repositories—dependency drift between a PR and its borrowed environment is not analyzed. - Contamination against SWE-bench-Pro is not discussed (only SWE-bench-Verified repositories were excluded), yet SWE-bench-Pro is used as the generalization evidence. - Training-scale experiments vary only trajectory count; no ablation isolates dataset scale from trajectory quality, and the claimed data-scaling trend rests on three points. - Inference at 262k context vs. 131k training length is mentioned but not ablated, and the SWE-bench-Pro comparison restricts all models to one scaffolding, which may disadvantage models tuned for other harnesses. Bottom Line: For anyone constructing SWE training data or training open-weight coding agents, this paper delivers the strongest publicly documented dataset-construction recipe and evidence that real-PR mining at scale beats synthetic generation, and it is worth reading despite the unsupported statistical precision of its headline comparison.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a lifecycle carbon-cost model comparing a time series foundation model (Chronos-2) against supervised alternatives (LightGBM, PatchTST) across a deployment horizon, and then prunes one encoder block from Chronos-2 to cut its inference cost. - Why it's important: Industrial forecasting deployments (data-center UPS units, electrical transformers) face a real sustainability trade-off: an expensive, rarely-queried TSFM may never repay its pretraining carbon cost versus a periodically retrained classical model, and no prior work quantified this break-even. - How it does it: The core moves are (1) closed-form cumulative cost equations parameterized by number of assets, query frequency, and retraining cadence, with carbon measured via CodeCarbon, and (2) a gradient-free pruning criterion — cosine similarity between each encoder block's input and output (adapted from LLM layer-collapse work) — that ranks blocks by redundancy. - The good: The pruning result is validated on 19 held-out tasks never used for calibration: removing one block (7.9% of parameters) yields consistent 5.97–8.72% reductions across four independent cost metrics (params, FLOPs, CO2, latency) at roughly one skill-score point of MASE change (22.99 → 21.87) and a slight WQL gain (+0.29). - The missing: Chronos-2's pretraining cost Cpr — the parameter driving every break-even conclusion — is extrapolated from a single measured step using another model's (Chronos T5-base) publicly documented schedule, and is admitted to be a lower bound; all break-even numbers scale linearly with this guess (18 months at Na=1,000 becomes ~15 years at 10×). - Read it or not: Worth reading for ML-sustainability practitioners and anyone deciding between TSFM and per-asset classical forecasting deployments — the break-even analysis is genuinely useful decision tooling, but the pruning contribution is a thin, single-model application of a known technique.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations deploying forecasting across many industrial assets (e.g., hourly forecasting on data-center UPS units or electrical transformers) must choose between zero-shot time series foundation models (TSFMs like Chronos-2) and classical/task-specific models (LightGBM, PatchTST) that must be retrained per asset as data drifts. TSFMs carry a large, one-time pretraining carbon cost; classical models carry recurring per-asset retraining costs. Prior carbon-accounting work (Strubell et al. 2019, Green AI) never compared cumulative lifecycle carbon of TSFMs versus specialized forecasters across pretraining, retraining, and inference. The gap: no decision rule telling a deployer when the TSFM's upfront cost amortizes, and what to do when it does not. Key Idea: The core insight is a break-even framing: the TSFM's fixed pretraining cost Cpr is repaid at a constant monthly rate equal to its inference-cost saving over LightGBM, so break-even time is linear in Cpr and inversely sensitive to query frequency — yielding simple closed-form conditions on (number of assets, duration, inference frequency). The secondary idea is that encoder-block redundancy in a TSFM can be detected gradient-free by measuring input-output cosine similarity per block, and the most redundant block can be deleted outright with no fine-tuning while preserving zero-shot accuracy. The adaptation is non-trivial in one respect: Gromov et al.'s layer-removal criterion targets causal decoders via last-token similarity, and the authors extend it to a bidirectional encoder by averaging cosine similarity across all patch positions. Methodology: Two pipelines. (1) Carbon lifecycle model: Measured per-operation costs (CodeCarbon on a single A100 80GB, grid intensity ~56 gCO2/kWh in Île-de-France; 10 runs for training measurements, 20 for inference) feed closed-form cumulative cost equations: M_L(t, Na) sums per-asset retraining events (every T_tr months, window sizes W_i ~ U[a,b]) plus inference (n_inf forecasts/month/asset × H=24 sequential LightGBM calls), while the TSFM cost is Cpr + ⌊t⌋·Na·n_inf·C_inf^T with optional periodic LoRA or full fine-tuning terms. Cost parameters come from ETTh1 (12,026 training windows). Four drift scenarios (T_tr ∈ {1, 6, 12, ∞}) × three inference frequencies (n_inf = 720, 30, ~4/month) are swept. (2) Pruning: Cosine similarity between input and output is computed per encoder block over 6 calibration tasks (up to 30 series each, median within task, equal weight across tasks), blocks ranked once, and the k most redundant removed as a group (time attention + group attention + FFN together). Compression budget k ∈ {0,...,6} selected on the 6 calibration tasks by aggregated skill score; final evaluation on 25 of 27 Chronos Benchmark II tasks (ETT tasks excluded due to a dataset-loading incompatibility), strict univariate mode, MASE/WQL skill scores relative to Seasonal Naive via geometric-mean ratios. Three notable design decisions: equal task weighting to prevent 100k+-series tasks dominating; budget selection on calibration tasks with 19 held-out tasks for confirmation (good); and the single-block granularity that cannot attribute redundancy to attention vs. FFN sub-layers (acknowledged, not justified as optimal). Key Results: Cost model: Chronos-2 inference is one order of magnitude more carbon-intensive than both baselines (6.1×10⁻⁵ vs 6.6×10⁻⁶ and 6.8×10⁻⁶ gCO2 per call); full pretraining (~200k steps, extrapolated to 65.17 gCO2, a stated lower bound) is ~60× PatchTST's training carbon. At Na=1,000 assets under the daily-inference baseline, Chronos-2 zero-shot breaks even with LightGBM at 18 months; break-even shifts to <1 month at hourly queries, 49 months at weekly queries, 180 months at Na=100, and never (within 100 years) at Na=10. PatchTST trained per asset never becomes competitive. Inference frequency shifts the break-even up to 49×, far more than drift/retraining cadence. Pruning: Removing block 6 (cosine score 0.963, the most redundant; 119.48M → 110.04M parameters, −7.90%) gives FLOPs −8.15% (59.52 → 54.67 G), CO2 −8.72% (1.221±0.037 → 1.114±0.002 gCO2eq), latency −5.97% (19.43±1.02 → 18.27±1.00 ms). On the 25-task set: MASE skill 22.99 → 21.87 (−1.12 points, ~5% relative), WQL skill 41.24 → 41.53 (+0.29), MASE win rate 40%, WQL win rate 52%. Ablation confirms the criterion: removing block 11 (score 0.576, least redundant) collapses MASE skill from 9.57% to −47.30% on calibration tasks; removing block 6 slightly improves it (10.24% vs 9.57%). Baselines (LightGBM, PatchTST) are standard and reasonably chosen, though with untuned fixed budgets. Tested at standard scale (120M-parameter model, single GPU), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the lifecycle break-even analysis of TSFM pretraining amortization is, per the authors and a literature check, genuinely unreported) plus a modest NEW METHOD application (gradient-free cosine block pruning adapted from Gromov et al. 2024 to a bidirectional time-series encoder — a principled but small transfer of an existing LLM technique to a new setting, ~15 lines beyond changing last-token to all-position averaging). The cost equations themselves are straightforward accounting, and the pruning pipeline is a competent combination of known ideas; the closest prior pruning work on TSFMs (Zhao et al. 2025) has a different goal (task-specialization), so the zero-shot cost-preserving angle is new. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and genuinely informative: per-block cosine scores with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p = 0.016) for block 11, single-block removals of blocks 5/6/11, and a compression-budget sweep. Carbon/latency measurements carry standard deviations over 10–20 runs (5 repetitions for the pruning cost comparison); the CO2-vs-latency-vs-FLOPs agreement within 6–9% is a convincing cross-check. No significance test is run on the headline Table 2 comparison (single deterministic zero-shot run per configuration, acknowledged in the checklist). Code is NOT released ([No] on the NeurIPS checklist — "While the code is not available, we describe all the steps to reproduce it"); data (Chronos Benchmark II via HuggingFace autogluon/chronos_datasets) is public. Methodological concerns: (a) the driving parameter Cpr is extrapolated, not measured — though the sensitivity analysis (T* ≈ 18k months) is honest and correctly notes the lower bound favors Chronos-2, strengthening the negative conclusion; (b) configuration selection and criterion validation share 6 calibration tasks, partially mitigated by 19 held-out tasks; (c) each baseline is costed under its intended usage pattern, so the comparison is explicitly not at equal informational footing (a shared-PatchTST variant would change conclusions); (d) the MASE-vs-WQL split in Table 2 is unexplained. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent decision tool in the cost equations). - Practical: Yes — a 120M-parameter model on one A100, LightGBM on CPU; the entire study runs on a single commercial cloud VM. - Efficient: The pruned model saves 6–9% of an already-modest footprint (Chronos-2 inference is ~6×10⁻⁵ gCO2/call, ~10× LightGBM); gains are real but small in absolute terms. - Effective: The break-even tool answers the stated deployment question credibly; the pruning preserves zero-shot quality on a 25-task public benchmark, but only in strict univariate mode — the multivariate/in-context (cross-learning) capability, a headline Chronos-2 feature, is untested after pruning. - Scalable: The cost equations extrapolate analytically to any Na and t (the authors' break-even table spans Na=10 to 5,000), but the underlying per-operation measurements come from one GPU, one dataset (ETTh1), one grid intensity; multi-GPU pretraining cost, the realistic case, would inflate Cpr beyond the stated lower bound. Delivers: no software artifact — no code, CLI, or pruned checkpoint release; the reusable output is the cost-model methodology and the pruning recipe as described in the paper. Strengths: - The lifecycle break-even framing is a genuinely new empirical question for TSFMs, and the answer has actionable structure: the 49× swing in break-even from inference frequency alone (hourly vs weekly at Na=1,000) is a non-obvious, decision-relevant finding. - Unusually candid treatment of the weakest link: the authors identify Cpr as "the parameter driving every break-even result," derive T* ≈ 18k months analytically, and show their optimistic lower bound strengthens rather than weakens their conclusion that TSFMs do not always amortize. - The pruning ablation is well designed: the criterion's negative case is validated (removing the lowest-cosine block 11 catastrophically degrades skill score from 9.57% to −47.30%), and the confirmation on 19 calibration-free tasks avoids the benchmark-gaming trap most pruning papers fall into. - Cross-metric consistency (parameter count, analytical FLOPs, measured CO2, measured latency all in the 6–9% band) is a credibility check most compression papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensive and direct (Appendix E + checklist): single hardware/dataset/grid-intensity for all carbon measurements; TDP-based CPU power estimation that disproportionately affects LightGBM; Cpr as an extrapolated single-GPU lower bound; the unequal-footing comparison (shared-PatchTST would change the picture); untuned baseline hyperparameters; two excluded ETT tasks; block-level granularity that cannot isolate attention vs FFN contributions; no comparison of the cosine criterion against alternative pruning criteria; univariate-only evaluation with cross-learning untested; CO2/latency measured on a cost subset rather than the full evaluation set; single-run performance comparison; one high-variance measurement (Chronos-2 CPU inference) reported as-is. The authors confront limitations head-on rather than minimizing them — a strong credibility signal. Notably, the untested multivariate/cross-learning capability after pruning is buried in an appendix rather than flagged as a headline caveat. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The pruned model's multivariate and in-context (cross-learning) capabilities — arguably Chronos-2's core selling point over classical models — are never evaluated after pruning; a 7.9% block removal could disproportionately damage group-attention behavior, and the single-block ablations only cover univariate calibration tasks. - Only ONE block-removal configuration is validated at scale (k=1); the intermediate budgets k=2–5 are explored only on the 6 calibration tasks, so the "performance degrades gradually up to 3 blocks" claim rests on a small sample. - The cost model treats Chronos-2 inference cost as independent of batch/asset count, but real TSFM deployments serving many assets could batch requests — potentially reversing the per-call cost comparison against LightGBM's 24 sequential calls; batching is never discussed. - Hardware heterogeneity is ignored at the decision level: LightGBM on CPU vs Chronos-2 on GPU implies different deployment infrastructure whose embodied carbon (manufacturing, idle power) is excluded from the model, systematically favoring the TSFM's total footprint. - The win rates (40% MASE, 52% WQL) reveal the pruned model loses on a majority of tasks by the point metric; the paper's "essentially no cost" framing rests entirely on the aggregated geometric-mean convention, and per-task losses up to +0.123 MASE (monash_fred_md 0.469 → 0.592) are visible in Table 11 without discussion. - No comparison pruning criterion (gradient-based, activation-based) is run, so it is unknown whether the 6–9% saving is the best achievable at zero quality cost — the authors note this but a single alternative criterion would have been cheap to test. Bottom Line: A practitioner deciding how to deploy forecasting across an asset fleet gains concrete, hard-to-find decision numbers (break-even curves versus asset count, query frequency, and drift) from the first half and a verified but modest 6–9% compression recipe from the second; the cost model alone justifies reading it, even though the pruning half is a thin transfer of Gromov et al. to a new architecture and no code is released.

DualPace: Decoupled Scheduling and Cooperative GPU--CPU Decoding for LLM Serving

YX Lin, KQ Wu, K Chow · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DualPace, an LLM serving runtime that gives host memory and AMX-enabled CPUs the status of an independently scheduled decode engine, with profile-guided "GPU Dense Assist" for selected dense stages, instead of treating CPU work as a GPU-gated offloading stage. - Why it's important: Existing CPU-offloading servers leave CPU-resident requests stuck waiting for GPU scheduler overlap windows, so paid-for host memory and CPU compute sit idle under load and tail inter-token latency (ITL) inflates exactly when capacity is most needed. - How it does it: Split scheduling authority across two engines (GPU owns prefills and GPU-resident decodes; CPU owns CPU-resident decodes with its own queues and clock), coupled only at explicit model-stage boundaries where the GPU can execute dense operators for CPU-owned batches without transferring request ownership or KV residency. - The good: A targeted head-to-head against NEO (the strongest current CPU-offloading baseline) shows DualPace sustains 7.3–50.5% higher request rates at the same P99 ITL target while preserving NEO's P99 TTFT advantage over vLLM, plus a mechanistic diagnosis (bursty CPU-resident progress with plateaus) that directly ties the scheduling flaw to the tail-latency symptom. - The missing: No public code release is stated, evaluation covers only two Azure trace workloads with fixed 2,000-request samples and three server configurations, and no comparison against other heterogeneous systems (FastDecode, APEX, OmniServe) beyond NEO. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or operate LLM serving systems with KV-cache pressure and AMX-capable hosts — the scheduling-decoupling diagnosis alone is instructive — otherwise skip it, as the techniques are unlikely to transfer to CPU-less deployments.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Practical Impact (55) is capped by the absence of any released artifact despite the contribution being a runtime, and by the niche hardware requirement (AMX-capable Xeon + constrained GPU). Rigor (65) is solid on ablations and honest negative results (Azure-Code) but is held back by a single trace source, one arrival seed, no error bars, no code, and only NEO as a heterogeneous baseline. Novelty (72) reflects a genuinely new scheduling architecture (decoupling authority from placement, ownership-preserving Dense Assist) built from standard components; Non-Obviousness (70) rests on the crisp 'GPU assistance ≠ GPU scheduling control' insight backed by a mechanistic diagnosis. Completeness (70) and Resilience (70) benefit from unusually direct limitation handling. Weighted composite: 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*70 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*70 + 0.30*55 = 65.

Problem & Motivation: Operators serving LLMs (chat, coding assistants) hit a KV-cache capacity wall: GPU HBM bounds concurrent decodes, and long contexts or high load exhaust it. CPU-offloading systems (FastDecode, NEO) move KV state to host memory and run attention near it, expanding capacity, but the CPU remains a pipeline stage inside a GPU-controlled scheduler. NEO admits CPU attention only when predicted CPU attention fits within GPU linear-stage work from another sub-batch and the pipeline beats GPU-only execution; with decode-dominated iterations (little prefill to provide GPU linear work), these admission conditions fail repeatedly, so CPU-resident requests stall for multi-second intervals and eventually plateau. The paper identifies this "GPU-gated CPU offloading" as the root cause of intermittent host-side progress and inflated P99 ITL, and argues the missing ingredient is scheduling authority, not host capacity or CPU compute. The affected audience is serving-infrastructure builders on constrained GPUs (e.g., single RTX 4090 nodes) with AMX-capable Xeon hosts. Key Idea: Decouple scheduling authority from execution placement. Each CPU-resident request has exactly one owner engine; the CPU engine advances its batches on its own clock without GPU admission, while the GPU can still accelerate CPU-owned computation through "Dense Assist" — operator-level requests issued at fixed model-stage boundaries (after pre-attention, after the final layer) that never enter the GPU scheduler's queues and never change KV residency. The insight that GPU assistance need not imply GPU scheduling control is what makes both independence and acceleration simultaneously achievable. Methodology: DualPace is a Python/PyTorch runtime (FastAPI/Uvicorn front end, DistServe-style async engine, Ray actors for GPU/CPU workers, shared-memory control and KV pools, oneDNN BF16 AMX dense kernels, custom AVX512-BF16/OpenMP CPU PagedAttention, FlashInfer on GPU). Three components: (1) Residency-aware dual-engine scheduling — each engine runs its own event loop with local step semantics (schedule, execute one batch, apply state) and no shared iteration barrier. A shared KV-safety envelope constrains four host obligations: used + planned + finish-growth of CPU-running decodes + migration reserve for potential GPU evictions (Equation 2). GPU rounds handle Prefill-to-GPU vs. Prefill-to-CPU (layer-wise async KV transfer through temporary staging), swap-out/swap-in gated by finish-peak footprints to prevent residency oscillation. (2) Stage-boundary cooperation — a two-threshold routing policy π(P,F) selects Full-CPU, Split-Final (one assist for the post-layer), or Fused-Assist (per-layer post-attention assists) by CPU batch size; the GPU worker services ready Dense Assist requests at non-preemptive stage boundaries before dequeuing the next GPU-main stage. (3) Offline profile-guided configuration — profiling derives routing thresholds via a routing score S_r(b) = T_CPU_r(b) + λ_GPU·D_GPU_r(b) that jointly penalizes CPU-visible time and displaced GPU service, an ε-regret threshold enumeration (Algorithm 1), a GPU batched-token limit from an isotonic-regression plateau fit (1,024 tokens in the tested config), and a CPU decode batch limit (256). Critical design decisions: migration minimization via finish-peak admission (well-justified to avoid PCIe thrash), the four-term global KV envelope (well-justified, addresses a real overcommitment hazard unique to dual schedulers), and a fixed λ_GPU = 1 in the routing score (asserted, not ablated). Appendices give complete per-engine scheduling procedures and score-construction details with calibration of launch/finalize overheads. Key Results: Tested on three configurations: Llama-3.1-8B on one RTX 4090 + 12-core Xeon Silver 4510; Qwen3-14B on 2×H20 + 24-core Xeon Platinum 8469C; Qwen3-32B on 4×H20 + 48-core. Workloads: first 2,000 requests each of Azure-Conversation (mean prompt 1,599, mean output 114 tokens) and Azure-Code (mean prompt 2,348, mean output 22 tokens) with Poisson arrivals. Baselines: vLLM 0.22.1 (chunked prefill, no host offloading) and NEO (patched for Qwen protocol compatibility). Headline numbers at a 1 s/token normalized-latency target on Azure-Conversation: DualPace sustains 43.2%, 6.9%, and 18.1% higher request rates than NEO and 90.6%, 11.5%, and 23.8% higher than vLLM across the three configurations. At a 1.5 s P99 ITL target: 50.5%, 15.2%, 7.3% higher request rates than NEO; P99 TTFT roughly matches NEO. Ablations: CPU TP=2 raises sustainable request rate 15.0–29.7% over TP=1 depending on metric; host KV capacity of 120 GiB beats 30/60 GiB by 18.5–28.7% on throughput/TTFT, with 240 GiB showing no further gain (CPU bandwidth becomes the bottleneck). Dense Assist overhead when idle is 2–5 µs/layer; CUDA execution dominates assist time (60–70%), with host launch/finalization 30–40%. Azure-Code (short outputs, prefill-dominated) is an honest negative-to-mixed result: vLLM is favored in the Qwen3 configurations, and the paper explicitly frames this as the workload boundary of the approach. Baselines are current and appropriate; testing is at standard single-node scale, not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (and arguably NEW PROBLEM framing). The genuinely novel element is the separation of scheduling authority from execution placement for heterogeneous LLM serving — dual independently-scheduled engines with ownership-preserving GPU Dense Assist and the four-term global KV-safety envelope. The constituent techniques are standard: CPU attention near host-resident KV (FastDecode/NEO), AMX BF16 dense kernels (LIA), PagedAttention (vLLM), chunked-prefill-style plateau profiling, Ray/FastAPI plumbing. The contribution is a new scheduling architecture, not new kernels or a new algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: routing-threshold selection is visualized (Figure 7), CPU tensor parallelism and host KV capacity are swept, and Dense Assist cost is decomposed into CUDA vs. host orchestration components. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; the Poisson arrivals use a single fixed seed per configuration. The offline profiler is calibrated end-to-end against the serving runtime, which mitigates (but does not eliminate) profile-reality mismatch. No code, data, or model release is mentioned — a significant reproducibility gap for a systems paper whose value depends on implementation details like shared-memory handshake protocols and event-loop semantics. Methodological concerns: only two workloads, both from the same Azure trace with 2,000-request samples; prefix caching disabled due to synthetic length-preserving prompts; the migration of finish-peak footprints and routing thresholds could interact with the specific trace distribution. NEO required author patches to run Qwen3 models, which the authors disclose but which introduces a small risk that the patched baseline is not fully tuned. Positive: the authors report an unfavorable workload regime (Azure-Code) in the main text rather than burying it. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: SYSTEMS (a built runtime, evaluated by serving workloads), with EMPIRICAL evaluation methodology. - Practical: Runs on commodity hardware — one RTX 4090 plus an AMX Xeon is a consumer-prosumer configuration; the main hardware requirement is Sapphire Rapids-or-newer AMX support. - Efficient: CPU-side decode is strictly slower per token than GPU decode (roughly one order of magnitude from the microbenchmarks), so the system trades per-token speed for admission capacity; Dense Assist displaces 0.6–0.8 ms of GPU time per assisted stage at batch 256, a modest but non-zero tax on GPU-main work. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem — sustained CPU-resident progress and 7.3–50.5% higher request rates at fixed P99 ITL versus NEO — with the honest caveat that the benefit vanishes for prefill-dominated, short-output workloads. - Scalable: Not tested beyond single-node, ≤4 GPUs, ≤48 cores, single NUMA node per CPU allocation; behavior under multi-node serving, larger traces, or higher request rates is claimed by mechanism, not measured. The work is described as an open-source-comparable runtime built on Ray/PyTorch, but no artifact URL is given; as presented, it stops at paper form. Strengths: - A crisp, falsifiable diagnosis: the paper isolates "GPU-gated CPU offloading" as a scheduling-authority problem and supports it with a directly interpretable measurement (bursty CPU-resident token progress with plateaus in NEO, Figure 1) plus the algebraic admission conditions of NEO's pipeline (Equation 1) that predict exactly when stalls occur. - The Dense Assist mechanism is a genuinely useful primitive — GPU acceleration without ownership transfer — and the two-threshold routing policy with ε-regret tie-breaking is a clean, deployable instantiation of it. - The global KV-safety envelope (Equation 2 with used/planned/growth/migration terms) addresses a real coordination hazard unique to dual schedulers that prior single-scheduler designs never had to face; this is thoughtful systems design, not decoration. - Honest workload-boundary reporting: Azure-Code results are presented in the main text and explicitly bound where the approach wins, and the KV-capacity sensitivity correctly identifies CPU bandwidth as the next bottleneck rather than implying monotone scaling. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the approach is most effective when GPU KV pressure coincides with sustained decode work, and that prefill-dominated/short-output workloads (Azure-Code) favor GPU-only serving. They acknowledge per-token ITL/TPOT on CPU-decoded requests intrinsically exceeds GPU-resident execution, so vLLM retains lower per-token tail latency; DualPace's win is only over other offloading systems. They note host KV capacity is an admission-control knob, not a monotone ITL knob, and that Dense Assist incurs measurable GPU orchestration cost (30–40% of assist component time). They disclose the NEO patches needed for Qwen3 and Codex-assisted development. They confront limitations directly; nothing material is minimized or hidden. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No artifact release: for a paper whose contribution is a runtime, the absence of code or a repository URL materially limits verification and adoption. - Only one trace source (Azure 2024) with 2,000-request subsamples and one arrival seed; no sensitivity to arrival-process shape (e.g., bursty arrivals), prefix-sharing workloads, or longer runs, all of which could interact with the finish-peak admission logic. - No comparison against FastDecode, APEX, OmniServe, or a GPU-only system with swap-based preemption (vLLM with offloading disabled is the only vLLM variant tested), so the claim that decoupled scheduling is the differentiator is established only against NEO. - The offline profiles (routing thresholds, batched-token limit, CPU batch limit) are derived per hardware/model pair; the paper does not test robustness to workload drift or whether profiles transfer across workloads, and λ_GPU = 1 in the routing score is not ablated. - Single NUMA node per allocation is noted as a resource constraint, but NUMA-crossing behavior — likely important at 48 cores and 240 GiB — is unexplored. - Fairness of the migration-reserve mechanism under adversarial workload mixes (repeated prefill pressure forcing permanent eviction reserve) is argued by construction but never stress-tested. Bottom Line: A credible and well-motivated systems contribution — decoupling scheduling authority from execution placement demonstrably fixes real tail-latency pathology in CPU-offloading LLM serving — but without released code and with only NEO as the heterogeneous baseline, practitioners in exactly this niche (AMX hosts + constrained GPUs) benefit most, and everyone else can get the core insight from Section 3 plus Figures 1 and 10.

Regularization Paths for Continuous DAG Learning

D Li, F Wang, K Gan · cs.cornell.edu · Fei Wang, FAMIA, FIAHSI, FACMI - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DAG-flow, an exact path-following framework that characterizes and computes the entire regularization path of stationary solutions for the three dominant continuous DAG learning formulations (NOTEARS, GOLEM, DAGMA), replacing grid-based re-optimization over sparsity parameters. - Why it's important: Practitioners tuning the ℓ1 sparsity parameter in continuous DAG learning currently solve many independent nonconvex optimizations, which is computationally expensive, statistically unstable, and gives no view of how the estimated graph changes across tuning levels. - How it does it: The core move is showing that, once the active support and acyclic stratum are fixed, stationary solutions obey explicit (for NOTEARS/DAGMA, column-decoupled affine; for GOLEM, linear-in-velocity coupled) matrix-valued ODEs in λ, with closed-form event conditions for edge insertion/deletion and regime changes, so the path is traced by solving linear systems and integrating ODEs instead of repeated nonconvex solves. - The good: The path exactness is verifiable: DAG-flow achieves zero stationarity residual in all tested settings where warm-start grid search leaves residuals of 0.1–0.72, while cutting wall-clock time by roughly 3–10× on real benchmarks (Table 2) and by growing margins as n and d scale. - The missing: All evaluation uses test negative log-likelihood as the quality metric; no structural recovery metrics (e.g., SHD, F1) against known ground-truth graphs are reported even though DREAM4 and SynTReN provide reference networks, and the only baseline is the authors' own warm-start grid search. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in continuous/Differentiable DAG learning and homotopy/solution-path methods, since it is the first exact path theory for these formulations; skippable for applied causal-discovery users until nonlinear-model extensions and structure-recovery evidence exist.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (with substantial theoretical content). Novelty (82) is the driver — the first exact, closed-form regularization-path characterization for NOTEARS/GOLEM/DAGMA, correctly diagnosing and circumventing the first-order degeneracy that breaks naive homotopy, is a real theoretical advance with sharp, checkable thresholds. Rigor (62) is supported by ~50 pages of proofs and 20-split standard deviations, but is pulled down by evaluating only stationarity residual and test NLL with no SHD/F1 against available ground-truth graphs, a single self-implemented baseline, no code release, and the gap between the analyzed constrained formulations and the augmented-Lagrangian solvers actually used in practice. Completeness (55) suffers from the same missing structure-recovery evidence and vacuous finiteness bounds; Resilience (60) and Impact (50) are limited by the linear-SEM-only scope and absence of any released artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*82 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*50 = 65.4 ≈ 65.

Problem & Motivation: Continuous DAG learning (NOTEARS, GOLEM, DAGMA) recasts combinatorial DAG structure learning as differentiable optimization over weighted adjacency matrices, but the recovered skeleton is highly sensitive to the ℓ1 regularization parameter λ. Standard practice solves the nonconvex problem independently (or warm-started) at a grid of λ values and picks one via validation — computationally wasteful, statistically unstable, and blind to the continuum of solutions between grid points. Classical exact solution-path machinery (LARS, glmnet-style homotopy) does not transfer because DAG learning violates its assumptions simultaneously: the acyclicity constraint is a global non-convex constraint whose feasible set is a union of strata indexed by topological orders, the acyclicity function is first-order degenerate on the DAG space (breaking naive implicit-function-theorem homotopy), and the ℓ1 term is nonsmooth. The open problem is whether an exact, structured regularization path even exists for these objectives and can be computed cheaper than a grid. Key Idea: Work on a fixed acyclic stratum (frozen topological order and sign pattern of the active support): there, the exact DAG constraint degenerates to a linear support restriction, the acyclicity term contributes no multiplier force (NOTEARS/DAGMA), and the stationarity system becomes a linear matrix ODE in λ — for NOTEARS/DAGMA it decouples column-by-column into per-node Lasso-type flows, (1/n)X⊤_:,Aj X_:,Aj · dW_Aj,j/dλ = −sign(W_Aj,j), making each path segment piecewise affine with closed-form next-transition values; for GOLEM the soft acyclicity penalty yields a coupled but linear-in-velocity system L_λ2[V] = r solvable by a single linear factorization per step. Kinks (edge drops/insertions, topological transitions, GOLEM domain/turning events) are located in closed form, and finitely many such segments suffice almost surely. Methodology: The paper is primarily theoretical with an algorithmic instantiation. (1) Characterization: for NOTEARS (Eq. 1, least squares + λ‖W‖₁ s.t. tr(e^{W⊙W}) = d), it proves a closed-form zero-solution threshold λmax (Theorem 3.1, sharp), real-analyticity of the branch between transition points (Thm 3.2), the column-decoupled affine matrix flow (Thm 3.3), and closed-form nearest-transition candidates λdrop, λenter (Thm 3.4). (2) GOLEM (Eq. 3, log-likelihood + log-det + soft penalty h(W)): a two-parameter surface W(λ1, λ2) analyzed along both coordinate paths, with a shared linear operator L_λ2 whose factorization serves both sweeps (Thms 4.1–4.4). (3) DAGMA: corollaries showing the NOTEARS results carry verbatim to the log-determinant acyclicity constraint on its effective domain. (4) Algorithm: DAG-flow (Algorithms 1–2) alternates between integrating the segment flow, detecting the minimum of {λdrop, λenter, domain/turning events, λmax}, updating the active set/signs/topological stratum, and warm-started re-optimization only when the branch is discontinuous (9–27% of events in experiments). (5) Finite convergence: Theorem 6.1 gives an almost-sure explicit upper bound on transition points (for NOTEARS/DAGMA, roughly 1 + d!·[½·Σ_{k=0}^{d−1}(Σ_{r}2^r C(k,r)) − 1]; for GOLEM a combinatorial bound over sign/support patterns). Key design decisions: tracking stationary points rather than local/global optima (justified as community convention for nonconvex objectives, but not deeply defended); freezing the topological order per stratum (well-justified by the degenerate-gradient analysis); choosing the outgoing tangent by minimal angle with the incoming tangent at branching events (a heuristic, acknowledged implicitly via the warm-start fallback). Critical limitation: linear SEMs only; everything is exact for the stated objectives, not for augmented-Lagrangian variants actually used in practice. Key Results: Synthetic (three linear-SEM DGPs, n up to 5000, d up to 160): under a matched wall-clock budget, DAG-flow reaches zero active stationarity residual at every tested λ, while Grid-WS (warm-started re-optimization) leaves residuals of 0.11–0.72 (NOTEARS), 0.11–0.34 (GOLEM), 0.14–0.73 (DAGMA); only 9–27% of transition points required warm restarts. Full-path computation time favors DAG-flow increasingly with n and d versus Grid-WS with 30/50/70 points. Real/semi-real benchmarks (Sachs, DREAM4-10, DREAM4-100MF, SynTReN-300; 20 random 70/20/10 splits): DAG-flow achieves lower validation-selected test NLL than Grid-WS-50 across all 12 dataset/model pairs (e.g., NOTEARS on Sachs 0.986 vs 1.01; SynTReN-300 GOLEM 1.36 vs 1.42) with 3–10× less runtime (e.g., SynTReN-300 NOTEARS 1.52×10⁴ s vs 9.85×10⁴ s). The baseline (warm-start grid search) is the standard practice, so it is current, but it is the only baseline; no comparison to other path or model-selection methods, and no structure-recovery accuracy against ground truth. Notably, all gains are on linear objectives; the method was not tested on the nonlinear/neural DAG variants that dominate current applications. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (first exact solution-path/continuation framework with explicit matrix-flow dynamics and event characterization for NOTEARS, GOLEM, and DAGMA) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (exact paths beat warm-start grid search on both compute and validation-selected fit). The building blocks — homotopy continuation, ℓ1-path event analysis (LARS, generalized lasso), and implicit-function arguments — are classical; the genuine novelty is proving they survive the interaction of a nonsmooth sparsity term with a globally non-convex, first-order-degenerate acyclicity constraint, and the discovery that the path is piecewise affine and column-decoupled for the hard-constrained formulations. Rigor & Reproducibility: Theory is thorough: full proofs are included for all main theorems (roughly 50 pages of appendices), thresholds are proven sharp, and finiteness is established with explicit (if extremely loose) bounds. Experiments report standard deviations (20 splits for NLL, 20 runs for timing, multiple seeds in Table 1). Ablations are implicit rather than explicit — the algorithm is dictated by the theory, but no study isolates which event-handling components matter. Concerns: (i) evaluation quality is judged only by stationarity residual (a proxy) and test NLL; no SHD/F1 against known ground-truth graphs despite using benchmarks (DREAM4, SynTReN, Sachs) that have reference networks; (ii) the only baseline is the authors' implemented Grid-WS — no comparison with other path-based or stability-selection approaches cited in related work; (iii) Theorem 6.1's GOLEM bound sums over all sign/support subsets and is almost certainly vacuous in practice, and the NOTEARS/DAGMA bound carries a d! factor. Code availability is not stated in the provided text. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (with substantial THEORETICAL content). Practical: Yes — linear algebra (Gram blocks, linear solves, off-the-shelf ODE integrators) on standard hardware; no GPU or special infrastructure indicated. Efficient: 3–10× faster than a 50-point warm-start grid on real data, with the gap widening with n (up to 5000) and d (up to 160); GOLEM paths require a global coupled linear solve per step, so cost grows with active-set size. Effective: Evidence supports exact path tracking and better validation-selected fit than grid search, but effectiveness at the actual task — recovering the correct causal graph — is unmeasured; NLL on a refit linear SEM is a proxy. Scalable: Tested to d = 160 nodes; the per-segment cost involves Gram matrices of active columns (NOTEARS/DAGMA favorable via column decoupling) and full active-system solves (GOLEM), and the paper claims rather than demonstrates scalability to thousands of nodes; behavior under many transition points in high dimensions is untested. The work delivers a method plus (implicitly) an algorithmic scheme; no released library, dataset, or trained model artifact is mentioned. Strengths: - Genuinely new theory: first exact, closed-form characterization of regularization paths for the three canonical continuous DAG objectives, including the insight that hard-constrained paths are piecewise affine and column-decoupled while the acyclicity constraint contributes no multiplier force on a fixed stratum. - The technical obstacle is correctly diagnosed and handled: the first-order degeneracy of tr(e^{W⊙W}) on the DAG space, which breaks naive KKT homotopy, is circumvented by stratum-local analysis. - Sharp, checkable results: the zero-solution thresholds are proven both sufficient and necessary, and transition events have closed-form candidate values, enabling an algorithm with no inner nonconvex optimization loop. - Honest experimental design in one respect: the restart percentage (9–27%) quantifies where the pure continuation method fails and needs re-optimization, rather than hiding it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that DAG-flow tracks one stationary branch from a given initialization and does not guarantee coverage of all stationary branches in nonconvex landscapes; discontinuous transitions and turning points may force warm-started re-optimization (though empirically infrequent); and the theory covers only linear SEMs and one-dimensional regularization paths, with nonlinear models, nonparametric objectives, and multi-parameter continuation left as future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitation statement — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No structure-recovery evaluation (SHD, F1, precision/recall) against ground-truth graphs, even for benchmarks that have them; the paper's own framing emphasizes edge-level stability and skeleton quality, yet never measures skeleton accuracy. - Single-baseline evaluation: only the authors' warm-start grid search; no comparison with alternative model-selection strategies (stability selection, bootstrap ensembling) or with other path-based structure-learning methods cited in related work (e.g., top-k solution path of Manjunath et al. 2025), so the claimed downstream advantage over the field is not fully substantiated. - Practical NOTEARS/DAGMA pipelines use augmented Lagrangian solvers rather than the exact constrained formulation analyzed; the paper explicitly notes Corollary 5.4 does not extend to augmented-Lagrangian paths, leaving a gap between the theory and how these methods are actually run. - The GOLEM two-parameter surface is only explored along coordinate paths; no guidance is given on how to navigate the (λ1, λ2) plane for model selection. - The finiteness bounds of Theorem 6.1 are super-exponential (d!-type) and the GOLEM bound is a raw combinatorial count, so the compactness claim rests on empirical transition counts, not the stated bounds. - Initialization cost: obtaining the initial stationary point at λ0 requires solving the nonconvex problem once; the paper does not report how sensitive the resulting path is to this initialization or its share of total runtime. Bottom Line: For anyone working on continuous DAG learning or solution-path methods, this is a foundational and technically strong paper whose exact path theory is a real advance, but practitioners seeking better causal graphs should note the evidence stops at likelihood proxies and linear models, so its practical payoff remains unproven until structure-recovery and nonlinear extensions are demonstrated.

CapGeo-Bench: Decoupling Visual Perception from Reasoning and Evaluating Geometric Understanding

Y Li, S Qian, H Liang, L Zheng, R An, L Sun, J Zhang… · aclanthology.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds CapGeo-Bench, a benchmark of 4,641 human-annotated geometric figure–caption pairs with a keypoint-based F1 metric across elements, spatial relations, and numerical attributes, and uses a caption-assisted reasoning probe (CapGeo) to show that visual perception, not reasoning, is the bottleneck of multimodal geometric reasoning in MLLMs. - Why it's important: Frontier models that solve IMO-level text problems still fail geometry diagrams, and no existing metric measures geometric caption quality, so practitioners lack a diagnostic instrument for where to invest (perception vs. reasoning training). - How it does it: The core move is a controlled input-modality comparison (Image-only vs. Caption-only vs. Caption+Image) using oracle-quality GPT-o3 captions to isolate perception, plus an LLM-extracted keypoint-matching F1 metric that scores captions along three fine-grained dimensions. - The good: The perception-bottleneck result is large and consistent — supplying captions lifts Qwen2.5-VL-72B from 8.6% to 66.4% on MathVerse Vision-Only — and CapGeo-Bench scores correlate strongly with downstream reasoning accuracy (r = 0.900–0.953 in the best settings, with leave-one-out robustness checks). - The missing: The evaluation metric itself is an LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-pro) whose scoring was validated by human expert review on only 200 captions, and the benchmark is drawn entirely from Chinese K-12 textbooks (86.7% plane geometry, 2.2% solid geometry), limiting generalization claims. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate MLLM perception (geometric or diagram-understanding) or need a reward signal for perception-targeted RL; skip it if you only care about reasoning-side improvements, since the headline finding is now well-corroborated in adjacent work.
