Problem & Motivation: MLLMs (including GPT-o3 and Gemini-2.5-Pro) succeed at text-only mathematical reasoning (IMO, IPho) but fail geometric problems, producing visual hallucinations and entity mismatches that derail downstream reasoning. The paper targets two communities: (1) researchers training multimodal reasoners who need to know whether to invest in perception or reasoning, and (2) the captioning community, which lacks any quantitative, fine-grained metric for geometric descriptions — general caption metrics (CIDEr, SPICE) and existing geometric datasets (MathVerse, MathVista, GeoQA) measure end-task accuracy, not the fidelity of visual information extraction. Key Idea: Decouple perception from reasoning by substituting an oracle caption for the model's own visual encoding: if a reasoning model given only a high-quality caption matches or beats its image-only performance, the image pathway — not the reasoning machinery — is the failure point. The second key idea is that geometric captions decompose into a finite keypoint set (elements, spatial relations, numerical attributes) aligned with Geometric Formal Language, enabling keypoint-by-keypoint macro-F1 scoring instead of holistic caption metrics. Methodology: Two artifacts. (1) CapGeo, a two-stage probe: a captioner converts a geometric figure into a formal natural-language description, then a reasoner answers A = MLLM(Q, I, C) under three masking conditions (Img, Cap, Cap+Img). Four captioners × eight reasoners (five MLLMs, three text-only LLMs) on MathVerse (Vision-Only and Vision-Intensive), MathVista geometry subset, and 200 sampled GeoQA problems at temperature 0.0. Two ablations isolate confounds: Caption-only vs. MathVerse's native Text-only setting (rules out textual priors) and natural-language vs. rigid JSON-schema captions (rules out template exploitation). (2) CapGeo-Bench: 5,000 diagrams harvested from Chinese K-12 textbooks via DocLayout-YOLO, filtered to 4,641; 24 vetted STEM annotators ($10/figure) write bilingual captions under a construction-logic protocol (constructive elements only, explicit definitions over deductions); a 3-expert review loop re-annotates failures (18.3% first-round rejection; Fleiss' Kappa 0.83/0.87/0.91 post-training). Scoring: an LLM (Gemini-2.5-pro) extracts keypoint sets E, R, N from both ground-truth and model captions, performs semantic-equivalence matching to form TP sets, and computes per-dimension macro F1. Design decisions: natural-language over JSON captions (justified by the ablation showing JSON degrades reasoning by 0.4–3.2 points); caption-only difficulty grading by diagram complexity; the choice to score only constructive (not derivable) elements is asserted by protocol but not empirically validated. Key Results: On MathVerse Vision-Only with GPT-o3 as captioner, Caption+Img lifts Qwen2.5-VL-72B from 8.6% to 66.4% and Claude-Opus-4 from 44.8% to 73.0%; text-only LLMs given captions (DeepSeek-R1 68.2%) rival or beat MLLMs reading images. On CapGeo-Bench, the best model (GPT-o3) averages only 38.4% F1 overall; the Numerical dimension is weakest (GPT-o3 20.4%, Qwen2.5-VL-7B 7.4%) and drops to 0.0 at difficulty T4 for several models. Baselines are current frontier models (GPT-o3, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Qwen2.5-VL), so the tested scale is standard but not stress-scale. Two counter-intuitive findings: (a) modality conflict — adding the true image to a weak captioner's output collapses strong MLLM accuracy (GPT-o3: 75.4% Cap-only → 46.6% Cap+Img with Qwen2.5-VL-7B captions); (b) rigid structured JSON captions consistently underperform natural prose. Correlation between CapGeo-Bench scores and downstream reasoning: r = 0.900 (Cap Only, Vision-Only, N=32), r = 0.953 (Cap+Img, N=20), r = 0.708/0.633 for Vision-Intensive, with leave-one-out analysis showing r stays 0.726–0.983 after removing extreme captioners. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the first dedicated geometric-caption benchmark with a three-dimensional keypoint-level F1 metric, and a quantified modality-conflict phenomenon (strong-perception MLLMs degraded by contradictory images). The perception-bottleneck conclusion itself is a competent, well-controlled confirmation of claims already present in Slow Perception, Describe-then-Reason, and recent perception-reward RL work; the keypoint metric is a domain adaptation of keypoint-style evaluation ideas from general captioning. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and meaningful — the Text-only control (66.1% vs. 62.2% for Qwen-72B) directly quantifies extracted visual information versus prior knowledge, and the JSON-caption ablation addresses template gaming. Correlation analysis reports Pearson r with two-tailed p-values (e.g., p = 3.87×10⁻¹¹) and leave-one-out robustness. Temperature 0.0 removes run-to-run variance, but no repeated-seed error bars are possible or reported for the LLM-judge scores, and the expert validation of the judge covered only 200 of 4,641 captions. Code and data are released at https://github.com/YuYingLi0/CapGeo. Methodological concerns: (1) the evaluator (Gemini-2.5-pro) and one evaluated captioner (GPT-o3) are closed-source black boxes, so the metric inherits LLM-judge opacity and potential self-preference; (2) the correlation analysis has small effective N (4 captioners, at most 8 reasoners) despite pooled point counts of 20–32; (3) CapGeo-Bench is developed and evaluated on the same K-12 textbook distribution it was built from, with no out-of-distribution captioning test. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (probe experiments plus a released benchmark). Practical: Yes — all evaluation runs on commercially available APIs and open-weight Qwen models served via vLLM. Efficient: Caption-assisted reasoning roughly doubles inference cost (captioning pass + reasoning pass), and the benchmark's LLM-judge adds a Gemini-2.5-pro call per scored caption; no cost figures are reported. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark measures a proxy (caption quality) that correlates with, but does not itself demonstrate improvement of, end-task reasoning; the bottleneck diagnosis is well-supported on three standard benchmarks. Scalable: Not tested — the benchmark is fixed at 4,641 items and the correlation study uses only 4 captioners; claims about the metric serving as an RL reward signal are purely speculative. Delivers a software/data artifact: benchmark, evaluation prompts, and code on GitHub. Strengths: (1) The Text-only control ablation is a genuinely clean identification strategy — it separates extracted visual content from textual prior in a way most caption-assist papers omit. (2) The keypoint-based metric is interpretable and error-typed by construction (missing elements vs. mismatched relations vs. wrong numbers), and the finding that numerical attribution ("floating" values lacking explicit pointers to their geometric subjects) is the dominant failure mode is a concrete, actionable diagnosis. (3) Annotation quality control is above the norm for academic benchmarks: two-round training, 18.3% re-annotation rate, post-training Fleiss' Kappa of 0.83–0.91, expert cross-review, and disclosed fair pay. (4) The modality-conflict analysis (weak captioner + true image hurts strong-perception models) is a surprising, reproducible observation with direct implications for pipeline design. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that limited time and compute prevented exhaustive evaluation across all frontier models and datasets, and that manual annotation may contain residual errors despite quality controls. This is a fairly thin limitations section — it acknowledges scope but does not confront the LLM-judge dependency, the narrow data distribution, or the small-N correlation analysis, which are the more substantive constraints. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Circularity risk in the metric: the same class of MLLM (Gemini-2.5-pro) both generates candidate captions in some settings and judges all captions; human validation of judge agreement is limited to 200 samples with no reported agreement statistics (only that experts "confirmed validity"). (2) The correlation study's support is 4 captioners — the r = 0.900–0.953 headline rests on very few independent caption-quality levels, and pooled N=32 conflates captioner and reasoner effects. (3) Severe class imbalance (Plane 86.7%, Solid 2.2%) and difficulty skew (only 197 T4 items) mean the T4 and Solid-Geometry cells rest on tiny samples where several models score 0.0. (4) In the CapGeo probe, captions for MathVerse Vision-Only apparently restate the question text alongside figure content, so caption quality and problem-restatement quality are entangled; the Text-only ablation partially addresses this but does not decompose caption content vs. question restatement. (5) No evaluation of specialized geometric models (G-LLaVA, fine-tuned perception models) or of whether CapGeo-Bench scores discriminate among models trained specifically for geometric perception — the claim that the metric guides RL training is untested. (6) The claim that perception ("under current difficulty levels") is the bottleneck is scoped in the abstract's framing but the conclusion states it unconditionally, extrapolating beyond where ceiling effects might reverse. Bottom Line: For anyone diagnosing or training MLLM visual perception on diagrams, CapGeo-Bench is currently the only game in town for graded geometric-caption evaluation and is worth adopting despite its LLM-judge fragility and K-12 skew; for readers seeking reasoning-side methods or perception-bottleneck theory, the exploratory half of the paper mostly confirms what Describe-then-Reason and perception-reward RL papers already argued.

CARL: Chat Assisted Reinforcement Learning

S Das, H Khadilkar, S Mittal, D Ostrov, J Sisk · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CARL, a human-AI co-design system that walks a domain expert through a structured ten-step conversational workflow to specify a Markov decision process, then autonomously generates, trains, and debugs an end-to-end RL pipeline with an iterative post-training revisit loop. - Why it's important: Applied RL projects fail disproportionately at problem formulation (the "specification gap") rather than at algorithms, and domain experts who cannot formalize an MDP currently get unreliable results from unguided LLM code generation. - How it does it: Each of ten workflow steps is governed by a single markdown "skill file" with a checklist; only compact per-step decision summaries (not full transcripts) carry forward into memory, and an assistant persona ("Trillian") pre-drafts domain-expert-style replies that the user can accept, edit, or reject. - The good: A controlled 6-method × 7-scenario comparison on a path-dependent goals-based wealth-management problem shows CARL-PartSpec reaching 7.94 mean utility versus 7.36 (Claude Code + custom skills) and 4.19 (Claude Code only) under identical incomplete specifications, over 1,000,000 Monte Carlo episodes with shared random number streams. - The missing: The "domain expert" in the interactive sessions appears to be the system's own authors, there is no user study, no error bars or significance tests on the RL comparisons, and evaluation covers only two low-dimensional, fully observable problems. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build agentic coding workflows or deploy RL in domains with non-expert users; skip it if you want novel RL algorithms or rigorous benchmarking of LLM agents — the RL machinery (PPO, Double DQN, beta-distribution policies) is entirely standard.

Problem & Motivation: Domain experts in finance, engineering, and elsewhere increasingly want RL solutions but cannot formalize states, actions, rewards, and constraints themselves; handing a well-written domain brief to a "vibe coding" tool (e.g., Claude Code) produces code that runs but optimizes the wrong problem due to reward hacking, state aliasing, and constraint violation. The paper posits that the bottleneck for applied RL is the "RL specification gap" — translating human intent into a formal MDP — plus a "performance gap" where experts cannot verify or retune results. Prior conversational coding assistants lack a stepwise workflow for large systems, and the authors argue (citing Hamadanian et al. 2022 and HCI literature) that iterative, human-controlled specification is the missing piece. Key Idea: Enforce interactive specification prior to code generation by decomposing MDP design into ten sequential, single-topic conversation steps, each locked to one skill file, with the accumulated state of the design carried forward as compact decision summaries rather than raw conversation — so the autonomous implementation phase executes an audited contract instead of re-interpreting intent. The core asymmetry motivating this: "a correct implementation of the wrong MDP optimizes the wrong problem." Methodology: CARL is a Python orchestration layer (Flask web UI plus terminal client) over AWS Bedrock's Converse API, model-agnostic by design; at the time of writing it uses Claude Opus 4.7 for the main workflow, Haiku 4.5 for the Trillian reply-suggestion persona, and Sonnet 4.6 for report generation. Steps 1–7 are interactive (problem definition, references, optional literature search, parameter exploration, state design, action design, reward design, hyperparameter confirmation); Steps 8–9 are autonomous (artifact validation with a rule-based heuristic warm-up, then training/evaluation); Step 10 is an optional revisit loop that inspects logs, plots, and checkpoints and triggers new iterations. Context management feeds only decision summaries from `memory.md` to later steps (token budgets per step range from ~350 to ~5,500). Auxiliary features include resume mode, Semantic Scholar-based literature grounding with hallucination guards, autonomous-step user interjections, and LaTeX report generation. Evaluation uses six methods (CARL-FullSpec/PartSpec, Claude Code with custom skills FullSpec/PartSpec, Claude Code only FullSpec/PartSpec, all on Opus 4.7 at xhigh thinking) on two domains: (1) a goals-based wealth management problem with conditional utility bonuses Ûi = Ui(1 + 0.25ki) that make it path-dependent and thus ineligible for dynamic programming, evaluated on 7 scenarios × 1,000,000 shared-randomness Monte Carlo episodes; (2) a Goddard rocket problem with a hard dynamic-pressure constraint, evaluated on 18 deterministic scenarios against bang-bang, MC-Local-Greedy search, and the analytic unconstrained bang-arc-bang optimum. Key Results: In GBWM, CARL variants cluster at the top: in the increasing four-goal scenario CARL-PartSpec achieves 7.94 mean utility vs. 7.36 (CC-Custom-Skill-PartSpec) and 4.19 (CC-Only-PartSpec, which reaches only 34.2% of maximum attainable utility); in the decreasing four-goal case 5.78 vs. 5.27 and 5.45. CARL-PartSpec essentially matches CARL-FullSpec (7.94 both), supporting the claim that the interactive phase closes the partial-specification gap. In Goddard, CARL's final policy is within 3.1% of the best method per scenario across all 18 scenarios, exceeds CC-Only by 19.9% on average, and runs inference 100–253× faster in wall-clock than MC-Local-Greedy — though MC-Local-Greedy achieves higher apogee in every constraint-binding scenario (e.g., 49,707 m vs. CARL's 47,140 m at 4000 kg / 15,000 Pa). The revisit loop improved CARL's Goddard performance by 4.1% (Revisit 1) plus a further 6.9% (Revisit 2), an 11.4% total gain, with Revisit 2 best in 16 of 18 scenarios. A notable mechanistic finding: unimodal beta policy heads (softplus+1) cause entropy collapse because they cannot put probability mass at throttle endpoints u∈{0,1}, which matters because the optimal policy is bang-arc-bang; CARL's boundary-mode head (softplus+0.01) fixes this, while both Claude Code baselines, which chose unimodal heads non-interactively, suffered from it. On the demonstration optimal-stopping problem, CARL's policy achieves expected value 43.52 vs. the analytic optimum 43.55 (99.93%). A striking baseline failure: CC-Custom-Skill collapses to 293 m in one light-fuel scenario it should handle easily. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the interaction architecture: step-gated skill files, decision-summary memory, a hybrid interactive/autonomy authority boundary, and a self-updating reply-suggestion persona applied to RL specification — and the empirical demonstration that interactive specification (not skill libraries alone) is what recovers performance under partial specification. The underlying components (PPO, Double DQN, beta policy heads, Claude Code, retrieval-augmented literature search, reward shaping) are standard; the Goddard and GBWM problems are variants of known problems. Rigor & Reproducibility: The GBWM experiment is well-controlled — six methods share identical random number streams over 1,000,000 episodes per method-scenario pair, and seven held-out evaluation scenarios are not seen in training. The Goddard comparison benefits from deterministic dynamics and a shared RK4 evaluation environment, with a credible analytic upper bound. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported (the authors argue the GBWM shared-noise design makes differences attributable to method, which is only convincing for within-run comparisons, not for RL training variance). No ablation isolates Trillian's contribution, the resume/report features, or individual skill files. Code is released at https://github.com/srdas/carl. Key concerns: the "domain expert" driving the interactive dialogues appears to be the authors themselves, so the system is evaluated by its designers on problems partially of their own construction (the GBWM problem extends their own prior work, Das et al. 2022/2026); in the Goddard Revisit 2, the burnout target ttarget is numerically fitted from MC-Local-Greedy's behavior on the evaluation parameter grid, blurring the train/evaluation separation the paper otherwise maintains. Baselines are current (Claude Opus 4.7, October 2025-era tooling) and the three-level skill-access design is a thoughtful ablation of the automation axis. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, deployed tool evaluated on empirical tasks). Practical: Yes — the Goddard evaluation ran CPU-only on an AWS ml.t3.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GB), with the main cost being commercial LLM API calls. Efficient: Inference is fast relative to per-instance search (100–253× cheaper than MC-Local-Greedy at rollout), but total token cost of the interactive workflow (roughly ~20k tokens of skill prompts per iteration plus multi-turn dialogue and LLM training compute) is not reported. Effective: The evidence shows viable policies on both tested problems and — more importantly — diagnostic value (the beta-head fix, burnout penalty, GBWM allocation sharpening), but only for small, fully observable MDPs; the specification-gap claim is not tested on hard RL domains. Scalable: Not tested — both examples have ≤14-dimensional observations and 1–2-dimensional actions; behavior on partially observable, high-dimensional, or multi-agent problems is only speculated. The work delivers a software artifact (open-source repository) plus a reusable design template; the paper itself documents rather than independently validates the interaction quality. Strengths: - The controlled PartSpec comparison is the paper's best evidence: it separates the value of skill libraries (modest) from the value of interactive clarification (large), showing a 3.6× utility gap (7.94 vs. 4.19) attributable to unresolved specification under identical LLMs. - The beta-distribution boundary-mode analysis is a concrete, transferable technical insight — a policy-parameterization failure mode (entropy collapse at action boundaries) that directly explains the non-interactive baselines' Goddard underperformance and would apply to any [0,1]-bounded control problem. - The decision-summary memory design (compact audited contracts rather than full transcripts) is a clean, generalizable mechanism for context management in long agentic workflows. - The Goddard example is honest about limits: the authors show MC-Local-Greedy beating CARL wherever the constraint binds and explicitly position CARL as producing reusable policies, not as superior to model-based search. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that both examples have "compact state descriptions, low-dimensional action spaces" and inspectable evaluation structures; that broader usability evidence and a diverse user base are needed (listing interaction-burden metrics they have not measured); that CARL does not replace specialized optimization or model-based planning; and that evaluation protocols for problems without analytical optima remain undeveloped. They confront limitations directly — the Goddard section explicitly includes the scenarios where their method loses. One limitation they minimize: they never acknowledge that the expert-in-the-loop in all reported sessions is almost certainly a co-author, which weakens the HCI/generalizability claims considerably. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Designer-as-user evaluation: Every interactive session is run by the system's designers on problems (GBWM) closely related to their own prior publications; the claimed benefit for real domain experts is unmeasured, and the detailed clarification dialogues may reflect hindsight not available to genuine users. - No training-variance treatment: RL training is notoriously seed-sensitive (the paper says so itself in the introduction), yet no repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or seed ablations are reported for any learning-based method; single-run differences like 7.94 vs. 7.36 could sit within training noise. - Possible evaluation leakage in Goddard: The Revisit 2 quadratic burnout target is fitted from MC-Local-Greedy behavior tied to evaluation-grid parameters, and the ttarget calibration references fixed evaluation thrust (Tmax = 200,000 N), partially contaminating the train/evaluation separation. - Missing baselines: No comparison against other structured specification or agent-orchestration frameworks (e.g., other spec-driven development tools, or an ablation where a human writes the full spec for Claude Code without CARL's workflow), so the value of CARL's specific ten-step structure versus any structured human effort is unquantified. - Scale of the claim vs. scale of the evidence: Two toy-to-medium problems cannot support the paper's broad conclusion that "unguided, fully autonomous code generation fails" in general; the failure modes demonstrated (unimodal beta heads, greedy goal-taking) are specific and might be fixed in baseline prompts. Bottom Line: Practitioners building human-in-the-loop agent workflows or deploying RL for non-expert domain experts will gain concrete, reusable design patterns (step-gated skill files, decision-memory contracts, the beta-boundary insight), but the empirical claims rest on two small problems, single training runs, and self-administered evaluation — read it as a well-documented systems and design paper, not as rigorous evidence that CARL beats alternatives at scale.

#107 — Innovative (65)

EXPERIENCE-HANDOFF REINFORCEMENT LEARNING

R SELF · openreview.net · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ACE-RL, an RL method that trains a single LLM for all three roles of the ACE agent harness — actor, reflector, and playbook curator — by rewarding each handoff artifact (reflection, playbook edit) with the verifier score of a fresh actor rollout executed with the resulting playbook. - Why it's important: Outcome-only RL (GRPO/PPO) compresses a trial into one scalar and never trains the reflection/curation behavior, so small open models deploy inside self-improvement harnesses write experience that is worth less than simply resampling; this work shows that gap is trainable away. - How it does it: The key move is making the handoff verifiable — executing each candidate playbook with a fresh rollout and reading the task verifier — combined with a sparse sampling tree that gives each role its own GRPO comparison group (reflections compared against reflections of the same trajectory, edits against edits of the same insight), derived as an approximation to the full-tree policy gradient of the harness-level objective. - The good: The cleanest evidence is Figure 2 and Section 5.2: an actor-only GRPO checkpoint's harnessed RSI@3 falls below its own vanilla pass@1 at 12/29 Mastermind and 19/40 AppWorld checkpoints, while ACE-RL's RSI@3 exceeds GRPO's at 29/29, 24/29, and 36/40 evaluated checkpoints on Mastermind, MBPP, and AppWorld respectively. - The missing: Every method was trained once per benchmark with a single run (no seed variance), the failure of the delayed-joint PPO baseline is explicitly not isolated, and the per-role-group ablation (Appendix B) shows the core design choice (groups vs. chains) yields differences within the 95% task CI on all four benchmarks. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone training small/mid-size open models for agentic scaffolds or working on test-time self-improvement; readers focused on frontier-scale RL can skim Section 5.3 for the pass@K vs. RSI@K comparison and Appendix D.1 for the credit-assignment derivation.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners post-training LLM agents currently have two disconnected channels of experience handoff: RL, which distills a trial into a scalar reward that updates weights but discards error logs, tool outputs, and discovered constraints; and harnesses (Reflexion, ACE, Dynamic Cheatsheet, skill libraries), which pass rich model-written artifacts to future rollouts but never train the model that writes them. The authors show (Figure 2) that Qwen3-0.6B's frozen-weights ACE harness stops improving after attempt 2 and underperforms independent resampling — the harness is only as good as the frozen model writing the reflections. The missing piece is training the model for the harness it actually runs in: both to act and to write experience its future rollouts inherit, using only task outcomes. This targets the regime of small open models, where harness quality is bounded by the writer. Key Idea: Score intermediate model-written artifacts by their downstream causal effect: a candidate playbook's reward is the verifier score of one fresh actor rollout conditioned on it; a reflection's reward is the mean value of the playbooks curated from it. This turns the two-stage handoff into an RLVR-style problem with no learned reward model, and a sparse sampling tree (one seed trajectory reflected on with M=4 candidates, one reflection curated with C=4 candidates, one evaluation per candidate) supplies each role a within-input GRPO comparison group, so a failed trajectory can still yield a positively-advantaged reflection. This is a genuinely identifiable core idea, distinct from prior work that credits summaries through chain outcomes or learned critics. Methodology: The ACE harness runs three calls of one shared policy πθ per handoff iteration on task q with incumbent playbook P: actor generates trajectory τ, reflector reads a formatted trace and emits insight z, curator emits structured edits u (add/update/remove tips) producing P′ = Apply(P, u). The objective is the harness-level J(θ) = E[R(τ̃)] where τ̃ is a fresh actor attempt under the updated playbook. One training step (per 8 tasks): sample N=8 actor rollouts; pick one uniform seed; sample M=4 reflections of it; pick one reflection; sample C=4 edits of it plus one edit per other reflection; execute every admissible candidate playbook once; assign rewards per Eq. (7); normalize advantages within each role's group; apply one joint clipped token-level GRPO update (no critic, no KL, asymmetric clip δ = (0.2, 0.28), dual clip c=3). Critical design decisions: (1) verifiable playbook reward via execution — well justified, it is what distinguishes the working method from the collapsing learned-critic baseline; (2) per-role groups vs. chain-wise sampling — the authors derive both as estimators of the same gradient direction (Appendix B) and honestly report the empirical difference is within CI, which undercuts the headline framing somewhat; (3) treating the seed trajectory as fixed evidence (conditional handoff learning) — explicitly acknowledged as a local approximation to the full delayed gradient, with a careful Appendix D.1 analysis of what the sparse estimator preserves and what it does not (the finite-group normalization, admissible-only reflector averaging, and token-count weighting all break exact equivalence). Key Results: Tested on Qwen3-0.6B (Mastermind, MBPP) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (AppWorld, MiniSWEBench), one training run per method, 95% CIs over held-out tasks. Final test reward (RSI@3 for harness methods, vanilla pass@1 for actor-only, each in its own mode): ACE-RL 0.736±0.025 Mastermind, 0.973±0.026 MBPP, 0.649±0.125 AppWorld, 0.227±0.083 MiniSWEBench, versus GRPO 0.643, 0.668, 0.529, 0.120 and PPO 0.664, 0.868, 0.174, 0.007. Delayed-joint PPO (authors' adaptation of CompactionRL) collapses: 0.004/0.000/0.000/0.051, below the base model on MBPP, despite its critic reaching explained variance near 1. Scaling: at equal actor episodes, RSI@K matches or exceeds pass@K on 3 of 4 benchmarks; on MBPP a single ACE-RL harnessed visit scores 0.95 vs. 0.86 for 8 independent GRPO samples, though that gain precedes any handoff (prompt-fit effect); AppWorld is the exception (RSI@8 0.77 vs. pass@8 0.81). Notably, the Appendix B ablation shows delayed-joint ACE-RL (chain-wise, same reward) achieves 0.746/0.973/0.580/0.242 — statistically indistinguishable from the headline method. Baselines are current (GRPO, PPO with learned critic per recent agentic-RL practice), and the token cost is 2.6–3.3× GRPO in generated completions, 1.6–1.9× in gradient tokens. Scale is modest: 0.6B/4B models, 60–400 training steps, ≤100 held-out tasks per benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (experience-handoff RL: training all model calls in a fixed harness from task outcomes) plus NEW METHOD (ACE-RL: verifiable playbook reward + per-role comparison groups via sparse sampling tree). The genuinely novel elements are the executed-playbook reward for intermediate text and applying group-relative credit to the dependency tree of a harness rather than a single rollout. The ingredients are standard: GRPO advantages, RLVR verifiers, the ACE harness, and the principle of grouping at shared inputs (GiGPO/AT-GRPO); the contribution is their specific composition and the credit-assignment derivation, not new primitives. Closest precedents the authors cite and differentiate from: Reflect-Retry-Reward, ERL, Memory-R1, JERP (downstream credit for intermediate text, but none train a two-stage handoff with a persistent editable artifact and per-stage groups), and CompactionRL/Composer 2 (chain-wise credit through own summaries, with learned critics). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partially present and unusually honest: Appendix B directly tests the paper's main methodological claim (per-role groups) and finds it does not matter within CI on any benchmark — a result that weakens the headline novelty but strengthens credibility. Error bars are 95% CIs over held-out tasks, but no multiple training seeds (explicitly stated: one run per method) and no significance tests beyond overlapping CIs. Concerns: (1) single-seed runs for all methods including the collapsing PPO baseline, whose failure the authors admit they cannot isolate; (2) evaluation-mode asymmetry — harness methods are evaluated RSI@3 (which uses 3× the actor episodes of vanilla pass@1 in Table 2), though Section 5.3 correctly re-compares at matched episode budgets; (3) MBPP's harness can carry forward the exact displayed asserts, which the authors flag; (4) no code release yet — promised upon publication; prompts, hyperparameters, and statistical protocols are fully listed in Appendices C–F. The delayed-joint PPO baseline is the authors' own adaptation, not the original CompactionRL system, so the learned-critic result should be read as "a reasonable critic-based instantiation fails," not "the published method fails." Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained checkpoints, measured rewards). - Practical: Yes — runs on 2 H100/H200 GPUs per run with open-weight Qwen3 models. - Efficient: Costly relative to actor-only RL: 2.6–3.3× GRPO's generated tokens per training step and up to 7 extra evaluation rollouts per task-step, though ~40–45% of generated tokens receive no gradient. - Effective: The evidence supports the claim on the training distribution and its held-out splits (three of four benchmarks), but the MiniSWEBench gain over GRPO (0.23 vs. 0.18) is within task CI, so the long-horizon claim is only weakly supported. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 4B parameters and ≤400 steps; whether the rollout-tree sampling cost remains tolerable for 30-turn MiniSWEBench episodes at larger scale, or whether the one-rollout playbook estimate is too noisy for harder tasks, is unexamined. The work delivers a method and promised code ("harness-optimization" repo referenced for prompts) plus trained recipes; no model weights or released artifact are stated as available yet. Strengths: - The verifiable-handoff-reward insight is real and consequential: it removes the learned reward model from training intermediate agent text, and the paper shows concretely what it buys (actor-only GRPO deployed in the harness is often worse than its own pass@1; ACE-RL is never worse on 3 of 4 benchmarks). - Appendix D.1 is a genuine credit-assignment contribution: it derives the full-tree gradient of the harness objective, states exactly which approximations (one evaluation per candidate, finite-group normalization, admissible-only averaging, token-mean role weighting) break exact equivalence, and quantifies the reduced sampling (296 → 26 outputs per task-step). This level of derivation transparency is rare. - The negative result on delayed-joint PPO (test reward 0.00 on MBPP with near-perfect critic explained variance) is a useful, well-documented failure mode for critic-based training through model-written context. - Honest handling of inconvenient findings: the per-role-group ablation, the AppWorld RSI-vs-pass@K loss, the MBPP prompt-fit confound at K=1, and the single-run limitation are all reported by the authors themselves. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that results come from one training run per method with uncertainty only over tasks; that the delayed-joint PPO failure's cause is not isolated ("the results favor this implementation, but do not isolate the cause"); that the conditional treatment of seed trajectories is an explicit local approximation (Appendix D.1); that the implemented update is not provably equal to the full-tree gradient; that playbooks in the 0.6B runs carry little task information (Appendix G); and Appendix H discusses safety scoping for agents that self-write their future context. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. The Conclusion also narrows the scope to "especially under ACE harness," a candid hedge of generality. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged items: (1) the headline Table 2 comparison evaluates each method in its own mode, giving harness methods 3× the actor episodes of vanilla-evaluated baselines; the matched-budget comparison (Figure 5b) is fairer and shows AppWorld favors independent sampling — the abstract's "faster convergence and higher converged performance" claim glosses over this asymmetry; (2) the per-role-group mechanism, presented as a core contribution, is empirically indistinguishable from the simpler chain-wise variant on all four benchmarks, so the paper's methodological novelty is thinner than its framing suggests; (3) no ablation on group sizes (M, C), reset interval F, or playbook cap beyond the fixed choices; (4) the delayed-joint PPO baseline omits CompactionRL's context-replacement and advantage-correction mechanisms, so the learned-critic conclusion is drawn from a deliberately reduced stand-in; (5) the verifiable-reward requirement limits applicability to environments with cheap, deterministic verifiers — nothing is said about domains without them, which is where most real agent deployments live; (6) reflection quality on MBPP could partly exploit the displayed-asserts shortcut acknowledged for the harness but not analyzed for the reflector specifically. Bottom Line: For researchers training open models to operate inside self-improving agent scaffolds, this is worth reading for its verifiable-handoff-reward formulation and unusually rigorous credit-assignment appendix; for the broader RL community, the single-run evidence, matched-budget ambivalence on long-horizon tasks, and the null ablation on per-role groups mean the core practical recipe matters more than the methodological packaging.

ForesightSafety-SAGE: A Fully Automated Scenario Generation and Safety Evaluation Framework for LLM Agents

L Jia, H Tong, F Zhao, J Li, D Liang, P Wu, Q Zhang… · aclanthology.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ForesightSafety-SAGE, a fully automated framework that generates 1,072 executable multi-turn safety evaluation scenarios for LLM agents from a five-dimension risk taxonomy and uses them to measure process-level unsafe behavior during simulated task execution. - Why it's important: LLM agents now execute real operations (tool calls, state changes, API actions) where failures are consequential and emergent during execution, yet most safety benchmarks still rely on static prompts and final-answer judgments that miss how unsafe behavior forms mid-task. - How it does it: The framework pairs LLM-generated, scenario-family-constrained executable tool environments with an adaptive attacker that pressures the target agent over multiple turns, then judges whole episodes as safe/unsafe from the recorded execution trace using both programmatic tool-call flags (UTR) and LLM trajectory judgment (ASR). - The good: Evaluation is at meaningful scale (25,728 target-agent episodes across 12 models and 2 authority contexts) with unusually thorough validation: multi-judge agreement above 0.85, independent human trajectory audit (78.1–85.2% judge–human agreement), a paired 4-turn vs. 10-turn long-horizon analysis with McNemar tests, and a safety–utility joint analysis (Spearman's ρ = −0.853 between ASR and task completion). - The missing: The same model (GPT-5.4) generates scenarios, drives the attacker, and serves as the main judge — a generation–judgment circularity that could inflate measured vulnerability, and all tool execution is simulated rather than real. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or benchmark LLM agents and need a concrete template for executable, process-level safety evaluation; skip it if you already work with ToolEmu, AgentHarm, or Agent-SafetyBench and only want a new leaderboard — the delta is the automated scenario-generation pipeline and authority-context analysis, not a fundamentally new judging method.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The released artifact (code, 1,072 scenarios, executable tool environments) and unusually strong validation — multi-judge agreement, human trajectory audits, McNemar-tested long-horizon analysis — support Completeness (76) and Impact (68). The composite is pulled down by Rigor (62) and Resilience (60): the generation–judgment circularity (GPT-5.4 writes scenarios, plays the attacker, and is the main judge, with no cross-family control) and judge–target role conflicts mean the headline 47.1% ASR is conditional on the generator's own biases, and no comparison to ToolEmu or Agent-SafetyBench calibrates difficulty. Novelty (62) is a competent combination in territory adjacent to existing agent-safety benchmarks; Non-Obviousness (64) rests on the Trust/Warning and UTR/ASR-divergence findings. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*64 + 0.15*76 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*68 = 65.
empirical Novelty 62 Rigor 62 Non-Obv 64 Completeness 76 Resilience 60 Impact 68
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Developers and deployers of LLM agents lack safety evaluations that observe how unsafe behavior emerges during task execution — through tool calls, environment feedback, authority boundaries, and supervision pressure — rather than in a single harmful response. Existing approaches fail along three axes: static-prompt benchmarks (SafetyBench, HarmBench) test only response-level safety; scenario-based evaluations (R-Judge, Agent-SafetyBench) depend on manually written cases that don't scale across risk mechanisms, domains, and tool environments; and capability-oriented agent benchmarks (AgentBench, Tau-bench) assess task completion while treating safety as a post-hoc or indirect signal. The paper targets this gap: scalable, executable, process-level evaluation of whether agents preserve goals, authority boundaries, and supervision constraints across a multi-turn episode. Key Idea: Convert abstract behavioral risk categories into executable evaluation episodes by anchoring LLM-assisted scenario expansion in hand-designed "scenario families" (per-subcategory specifications of failure mechanism, safe/risky behavior paths, tool patterns, attacker pressure, and judge criteria) plus seven human-written seed scenarios each, then judge the whole recorded execution trace — not just the final answer — with both programmatic tool flags (Unsafe Tool-call Rate) and LLM episode-level judgment (ASR). The scenario family schema is the load-bearing idea: it constrains generation so that 1,000+ automatically expanded scenarios stay aligned with the intended risk mechanism while remaining executable in a simulated tool environment. Methodology: The framework has three stages. (1) Automated scenario generation: a five-dimension taxonomy (Interaction Understanding, Goal–Norm Misalignment, Robustness, Supervision/Control, Autonomy/Authority) is split into 16 subcategories; for each, a scenario-family specification plus 7 expert seed scenarios condition GPT-5.4 (temp 0.7) to produce 100 candidates; LLM-assisted structured scoring (Claude-Opus-4.7) plus rule-based checks and coverage-constrained top-k selection retain 60 per subcategory, yielding 67×16 = 1,072 scenarios. (2) Interactive evaluation pipeline: each scenario instantiates an episode x = (s, e, T, a, j); a simulated tool environment exposes only target-visible schemas (hidden risk conditions and judge fields withheld), an adaptive attacker (GPT-5.4, temp 0.7) generates pressure conditioned on the running trajectory, and the loop runs up to 4 turns (10 in a supplementary study), recording attacker messages, tool calls, observations, state flags, and the final response. (3) Episode-level judgment: UTR counts episodes containing predefined unsafe tool calls; ASR is the fraction of episodes labeled unsafe by the GPT-5.4 judge (temp 0.0) given the full trace, runtime state, and scenario-specific judge criteria. Each scenario runs under two authority contexts — Trust ("trusted to operate independently") vs. Warning ("out-of-scope actions are strictly prohibited") — a deliberate ablation of prompt-level safety framing. Critically, all judged models are pure targets; none of them (except the separate judges) participate in the generation loop. Key Results: Across 25,728 episodes (12 agents × 2,144 episodes), the overall average ASR is 47.1%, with Llama-3.3-70B, Doubao-Seed-1.6, and Gemini-2.5-Flash exceeding 70% (Llama-3.3-70B above 80%) and Claude-Sonnet-4.6/Claude-Haiku-4.5 below 10%. Highest-risk subcategories are process-oriented: Misleading Context Vulnerability 77.9%, Long-Horizon Instability 71.5%, Objective Drift 67.7%, Inducement Vulnerability 64.7%, Negative Side Effects 61.9%; boundary-clear violations (Unauthorized Decision-Making, Privilege Escalation, Interruption Failure) score markedly lower. Warning Context reduces ASR for most models and dimensions, but not uniformly — Robustness risks are barely mitigated, and low-ASR models show floor effects. In the paired 10-turn study (180 scenarios, 5 models), overall unsafe rate rises from 43.3% to 49.4% (McNemar p = 0.035), with Long-Horizon Instability jumping 62.9% → 80.0% (p = 0.031). The safety–utility analysis on 2,688 seed episodes finds ASR negatively correlated with task completion (ρ = −0.853, p < 0.001), i.e., safer models do not systematically refuse more, but over-refusal varies widely among similarly safe models (Claude-Sonnet-4.6 at 17.0% vs. GLM-5.1 at 8.9%). Multi-judge pairwise agreement exceeds 0.85; UTR–ASR agreement is 0.81–0.85, with systematic divergence (UTR > ASR for safe models, ASR > UTR for unsafe ones) that the paper interprets sensibly. Trace-grounded failure analysis of 170 unsafe episodes attributes 84.1% to four causes, and 54.7% of failures emerge within the first two turns. Baselines are current frontier and open-weight models (GPT-4o-mini through Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Qwen3.6-Plus), though several are version-dated snapshots. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel elements are the scenario-family schema that makes large-scale executable scenario generation taxonomy-faithful, the joint UTR (programmatic tool-level) + ASR (trajectory-level) judgment pairing with systematic agreement analysis, and the Trust/Warning authority-context experimental design. The underlying machinery — LLM-generated test cases (Self-Instruct, Evol-Instruct), LLM red teaming (Perez et al.), LM-emulated tool sandboxes (ToolEmu), and LLM-as-a-judge — is a competent combination of existing techniques applied to process-level agent safety, where ToolEmu and Agent-SafetyBench already occupy adjacent territory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations and validation are unusually strong for a benchmark paper: multi-judge validation (4 judges), independent human audit of both scenario quality (95.9% pass, 91.9% inter-annotator agreement on 160 sampled scenarios, 16.7% of expansions) and trajectory judgments (78.1% human–judge agreement, rising to 85.2% on agreed pairs), a paired long-horizon study with exact McNemar tests, and a safety–utility joint analysis with Spearman correlation. Per-judge ASR heatmaps are reported for transparency. Code and data are released at https://github.com/LuJia-USTB/ForesightSafety-SAGE. Concerns: (1) the generation–judgment pipeline shares GPT-5.4 across scenario expansion, attacker, and main judge — scenarios are tuned on the same model family that scores them (Goodhart-adjacent circularity), and no experiment isolates this (e.g., scenarios generated by a different model family); (2) DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-4o-mini serve as both evaluation targets and validation/utility judges in places, an unacknowledged conflict of interest in those rows; (3) only 16.7% of expanded scenarios receive human quality inspection; (4) error bars in Figure 5 are min/max across judges rather than seed-based confidence intervals, though episode counts are large enough that sampling noise is probably minor. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark-generation system with a large measurement campaign; no real-world deployment). Practical: Runs entirely on commercial LLM APIs plus simulated Python tool environments — no special hardware; anyone with API access can reproduce the pipeline. Efficient: Cost is not quantified, but 25,728 multi-turn episodes at ≤4 turns plus judging is nontrivial API spend; UTR offers a cheap programmatic signal that the paper shows correlates ~0.81–0.85 with judged ASR. Effective: The evidence convincingly shows the framework discriminates between models and surfaces process-level failures, but only against simulated tools — whether ASR here predicts unsafe behavior with real APIs, real file systems, or real permitting workflows is untested. Scalable: Scenario generation is by construction scalable (the paper's stated goal), and 1,072 scenarios is demonstrated; but scaling to more dimensions depends on expert-written scenario families and seeds, and 10-turn episodes already expose budget sensitivity, so longer horizons multiply cost and ambiguity. The work delivers a concrete artifact — released code, 1,072 scenarios, and executable tool environments — not just a paper. Strengths: - The scenario-family specification + seed conditioning is the right solution to the central problem of automated benchmark generation (drift from intended risk mechanisms), and the 95.9% human pass rate on sampled scenarios suggests it actually works. - The dual-metric design (UTR as programmatic behavioral ground truth vs. ASR as semantic trajectory judgment) with a systematic agreement analysis is more rigorous than most LLM-as-a-judge safety papers, and the documented UTR/ASR divergence for safe vs. unsafe models is an informative empirical finding in its own right. - The Trust vs. Warning authority-context experiment turns a deployment-relevant question (do explicit safety reminders help, and for which risk types?) into a controlled comparison across 12 models — the finding that Robustness risks resist prompt-level mitigation is actionable. - The failure analysis is genuinely diagnostic rather than descriptive: 84.1% of 170 unsafe episodes trace to four named causes (weak authority reasoning, attacker-pressure susceptibility, context misinterpretation, insufficient consequence reasoning), with per-model and per-subcategory safeguard suggestions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section states that (1) all evaluation happens in controlled simulated environments that cannot reproduce real-world ambiguity, tool unreliability, or completion-vs-safety incentive tension, with a staged roadmap toward sandboxed and real-workflow evaluation; and (2) results are a snapshot of fast-moving model versions, not a permanent ranking. The Ethical Considerations section acknowledges dual-use risk of publishing unsafe-behavior patterns and describes mitigation (controlled environments, minimized examples). The authors confront the simulation-vs-reality gap directly rather than minimizing it, which is a credibility positive — though they do not quantify how the simulation gap might bias ASR in either direction. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Generation–judge circularity: GPT-5.4 writes the scenarios, plays the attacker, and judges the episodes. A cross-family experiment (e.g., scenarios authored by Claude models judged by GPT and vice versa) is needed to rule out that scenario style is tuned to GPT-5.4's judgment biases; this is the single most important missing control. - Judge–target role conflicts: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-4o-mini appear as both targets and judges in multi-judge and utility analyses; self-judging bias for those cells is unexamined. - Attacker strength is unbounded relative to the defense being measured: the adaptive attacker is a frontier model applying calibrated social pressure; the paper does not report any robustness check of how ASR varies with attacker model capability, so results are conditional on one (strong) pressure profile. - No comparison of ASR on ForesightSafety-SAGE vs. existing benchmarks (ToolEmu, Agent-SafetyBench) for overlapping models, leaving open whether the 47.1% average is a property of agents or of this benchmark's difficulty calibration. - The human–judge agreement of 78.1% (85.2% on agreed pairs) leaves meaningful borderline ambiguity, particularly for Supervision-dimension risks, and no sensitivity analysis shows how ASR rankings change under disagreement flips. Bottom Line: Practitioners building or auditing LLM agents should read this for its executable scenario-generation template and the Trust/Warning authority-context finding, but should treat the headline ASR numbers as conditional on GPT-5.4-authored pressure and judgment — rerun the released pipeline with a disjoint generator/judge before treating the 47.1% figure as a calibrated risk estimate.

Principia: Test-Time Hypotheses to Principle Construction for Scientific Discovery (27 ▲ )

Dongki Kim, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Soyeong Jeong, Sung Ju Hwang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PRINCIPIA, an LLM-based framework that constructs comparative causal hypotheses from paired observations, generalizes them into inductive principles via similarity-based clustering, and continually revises both through new observations during test-time scientific discovery. - Why it's important: Constructing empirical scientific principles from accumulated experimental observations is a bottleneck requiring substantial domain expertise, time, and labor; automating this could accelerate drug discovery, protein engineering, and gene perturbation studies. - How it does it: The core mechanism is a three-stage loop: (1) generate comparative causal hypotheses from reference-to-target input pairs and their observed outcomes, (2) inductively synthesize principles by clustering similar inputs and generalizing recurring relationships, and (3) apply the knowledge to new tasks, then revise hypotheses using new observations to reconstruct principles. - The good: PRINCIPIA consistently outperforms all evaluated baselines—including those using external knowledge (WebSearch, DeepEvolve), experience summaries (ExLLM), and internal principles—across 13 tasks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, with a 55% reduction in oracle evaluations versus ExLLM on Syn-3bfo. - The missing: The paper does not evaluate whether the induced principles transfer to genuinely novel domains or out-of-distribution scientific spaces; all tasks use pre-defined oracles and the knowledge construction is evaluated only within the same task where the observations were collected. - Read it or not: Researchers working on LLM-based scientific discovery agents or automated hypothesis generation should read this for the structured memory design and revision loop; practitioners primarily interested in optimization performance alone may find the gains modest on some tasks (e.g., Valsartan AUC@10 of 0.106 vs 0.188 for ExLLM).

Problem & Motivation: In complex scientific discovery processes (drug discovery, protein engineering, gene perturbation), the underlying scientific principles governing input-output relationships are usually unknown and must be constructed empirically from progressively accumulated experimental observations. Human researchers currently perform this hypotheses-to-principle translation manually, requiring substantial domain expertise, time, and financial resources—creating a bottleneck that limits the pace of discovery. Existing LLM-based discovery systems either do not construct reusable knowledge from observations (MolLEO, REINVENT), rely on external retrieval that may not match the specific task (WebSearch, DeepEvolve), or summarize experience without explicit causal structure (ExLLM, Textual summary). The gap is that no prior framework explicitly constructs and continually refines structured causal hypotheses and generalized principles from test-time observations. Key Idea: The single core technical insight is that pairwise comparative evidence—two similar inputs and their differing outcomes—provides a stronger basis for an LLM to identify causal factors than a single input-outcome pair. This comparison narrows the hypothesis space (when outcomes differ, the differing characteristics are candidates for causation; when outcomes match, shared characteristics are candidates for maintaining the outcome). These comparative hypotheses are then grouped by input similarity and inductively merged into broader principles, with a revision loop that grounds hypothesis updates in new observations obtained by applying the knowledge. Methodology: PRINCIPIA operates as a continuous loop with four stages. (1) Comparative evidence construction: For optimization tasks, it compares a generated candidate x′ with its parent input x, using oracle outcomes to form comparative evidence (x, O(x), x′, O(x′)). For prediction tasks, it selects up to three nearest-neighbor references by domain-specific distance (Tanimoto for molecules, Hamming/Jaccard for proteins, cosine on text-embedding-3-large for genes). (2) Comparative causal hypothesis generation: An LLM generates a textual hypothesis explaining how similarities/differences between the two inputs account for their observed outcomes, stored as directed edges in a graph-structured hypothesis memory Mh. (3) Inductive principle construction: Inputs are clustered via soft-balanced k-medoids (≈10 inputs per cluster); for each cluster, an LLM generalizes recurring relationships across the cluster's hypotheses into a principle, stored in Mp. (4) Hypothesis revision: Retrieved hypotheses and principles guide candidate generation or prediction; new observations from these actions are used by an LLM to revise (retain/strengthen/revise/remove/add) the used hypotheses, then principles are reconstructed. The framework wraps around a population-based evolutionary optimization architecture (crossover + LLM mutation, based on MolLEO). For prediction, knowledge is built over six sequential rounds of a training split, then frozen and applied to a held-out scaffold-split test set. No explicit mathematical loss or objective function is optimized—the framework is a prompting-based knowledge construction pipeline. Critical design decisions: (a) Comparative rather than single-input hypothesis generation—justified by ablation showing comparative generation improves AUC@10 by +0.092 to +0.135 on GB1 and Syn-3bfo over non-comparative variants; (b) Diversifying retrieval by fitness direction (improvements + declines)—justified by ablation showing mixture retrieval achieves 0.452 AUC@10 on GSK3β versus 0.341 for no retrieval and ≤0.379 for directional-only retrieval; (c) LLM-based knowledge retrieval over fixed selection—justified by ablation showing removal drops GSK3β AUC@10 from the full system's performance to 0.364. Key Results: - Molecular optimization (PMO benchmark, 5 tasks, 1,000 oracle calls, 3 seeds): PRINCIPIA achieves an average AUC@10 of 0.279 and Avg@100 of 0.340, outperforming MolLEO (0.222/0.235), ExLLM (0.250/0.254), WebSearch (0.230/0.245), DeepEvolve (0.232/0.248), and PiFlow (0.157/0.139). On JNK3, PRINCIPIA achieves 0.350 AUC@10 versus 0.234 for the next best (DeepEvolve); on GSK3β, 0.452 versus 0.421 (WebSearch). - Protein sequence engineering (3 tasks, 200 oracle calls): PRINCIPIA achieves average AUC@10 of 0.605 versus 0.575 (ExLLM), with GB1 Avg@50 of 0.398 versus 0.236 for the next best. On Syn-3bfo, PRINCIPIA reaches 0.084 Avg@50 versus negative values for all baselines. - Gene perturbation (2 CRISPR tasks): PRINCIPIA achieves average AUC@10 of 0.605 with hit ratios of 0.308 (Scharenberg22) and 0.114 (IFNG), outperforming all baselines. - Molecular property prediction (8 TDC tasks, 3 seeds): PRINCIPIA achieves average accuracy 69.75% and macro-F1 69.03%, versus 63.95%/62.30% for best few-shot baseline (k=7) and 63.26%/61.03% for textual summary. Individual task gains are largest on CYP2C9 (76.67% acc vs 70.33% for k=3 few-shot) and DILI (70.49% vs 62.85% for k=5 few-shot). - Budget efficiency: PRINCIPIA matches ExLLM's final performance with ~55% fewer oracle evaluations, and matches WebSearch/MolLEO/DeepEvolve with ~84–86% fewer evaluations on Syn-3bfo. - Robustness: Results hold across four backbone models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash/Pro, GPT-5.6-Luna, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite) in supplementary experiments. - Baselines are recent and current (2024–2025 publications); some are reimplemented by the authors rather than using official numbers. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely novel element is the explicit two-level knowledge structure—comparative causal hypotheses stored as graph edges and inductive principles induced per cluster—with a grounding revision loop that ties hypothesis updates to new observations. This is distinct from prior experience-summarization (ExLLM) or external-knowledge retrieval (WebSearch, DeepEvolve) approaches. The underlying evolutionary optimization backbone (MolLEO) and LLM prompting are standard; the contribution is the knowledge construction layer applied on top, which is a formulation-level innovation rather than an algorithmic or theoretical one. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and cover each major component: comparative vs non-comparative hypothesis generation (Table 4, Fig. 3), principle construction removal, hypothesis revision removal (Fig. 4), retrieval strategy diversity (Table 6), and LLM-based vs no retrieval (Fig. 6). Results are averaged over three random seeds with standard deviation shown in trajectory plots (shaded regions). The paper does not report statistical significance tests or confidence intervals beyond mean±std. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia. Several baselines are reimplemented (marked with *) rather than using published numbers, which introduces potential for suboptimal baseline configurations—though the authors provide detailed reimplementation settings in Appendix C. The knowledge construction and evaluation use the same tasks (no transfer evaluation), which is a Goodhart risk: the principles may be overfit to each task's specific oracle. However, the prediction evaluation uses a held-out scaffold-split test set, which partially addresses this for that setting. PiFlow performs dramatically worse than other baselines (Syn-3bfo Avg@50 of -32.149), suggesting possible implementation or configuration issues that inflate PRINCIPIA's relative advantage. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component via the released code). - Practical: Yes—requires only API access to a commercial LLM (GPT-5-mini) and standard scientific oracles/benchmarks; no specialized hardware. - Efficient: The knowledge construction adds LLM calls per generation (hypothesis generation, principle induction, revision, retrieval) beyond the base optimizer's calls; the paper does not report wall-clock or token cost overhead, so the inference-cost multiplier relative to MolLEO is unknown. - Effective: The evidence shows improvements on oracle-based proxy tasks with restricted budgets; the paper does not demonstrate real wet-lab validation or show that constructed principles match human expert-derived principles quantitatively (only qualitative plausibility checks against literature). - Scalable: All tasks are bounded (200–1,000 oracle calls, ≤200 training molecules per class for prediction); the framework's behavior at much larger observation scales (e.g., millions of molecules) is untested, and the k-medoids clustering plus per-cluster LLM calls could become bottlenecks at 10–100× scale. The work delivers a software artifact (GitHub repository with code and prompts) and a reusable framework design. Strengths: - The comparative evidence mechanism is a genuine conceptual contribution: grounding hypothesis generation in paired inputs with differing outcomes is a simple but non-obvious trick that directly addresses the underdetermination of causal factors from single observations. - The two-level memory (episodic graph edges for hypotheses, clustered semantic principles) with a revision loop grounded in applied observations is architecturally clean and well-motivated by the human scientific process analogy, going beyond flat experience summaries. - The budget-efficiency analysis (55–86% fewer oracle evaluations to match baseline performance) directly addresses the real-world cost constraint in scientific experimentation, which most prior LLM-discovery work does not measure. - Ablations systematically isolate each component's contribution, and the retrieval-strategy ablation (Table 6) provides a non-trivial finding that mixed-direction retrieval (+0.111) substantially outperforms directional-only retrieval (+0.025 to +0.038). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper does not include a dedicated limitations section. Implicitly acknowledged limitations include: (a) observations cover only a small fraction of the input space, making hypotheses potentially incomplete or incorrect (addressed by the revision mechanism but not fully resolved); (b) the qualitative principle-plausibility check is limited to a single example (Ames mutagenicity) linked to prior literature. The authors do not explicitly confront scope boundaries such as oracle realism, transfer to new domains, or computational overhead. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evaluation of principle transfer or generalization across tasks or domains—each task constructs its own knowledge from scratch, so the framework's claim of building "reusable scientific knowledge" is never tested for actual reuse. - The molecular property prediction evaluation uses only up to 200 training molecules and 50 test molecules per class per run, a small sample that limits confidence in the accuracy differences (which are 5–8 percentage points over baselines). - PiFlow's catastrophic underperformance (e.g., -32.149 Avg@50 on Syn-3bfo) suggests a potential misconfiguration or unfair adaptation, which inflates the apparent advantage over the only other principle-aware baseline. - No reporting of LLM inference cost (token count, wall-clock time, number of LLM calls) relative to baselines, which is essential for assessing the practical efficiency claim. - The "principles" are free-text LLM generations without formal verification or constraint; there is no mechanism to prevent plausible-but-wrong principles from persisting and misleading optimization, beyond the revision loop's reliance on new observations—which may be too sparse to detect subtle errors. - The paper does not evaluate on any real experimental platform or human-in-the-loop setting; all results use pre-recorded oracles or lookup tables. Bottom Line: A researcher building LLM-driven scientific discovery agents gains concrete design patterns—particularly the comparative hypothesis mechanism and the two-level memory with revision loop—that demonstrably improve sample efficiency over existing alternatives on standard benchmarks, making this worth reading despite the lack of real-world validation and the open questions about cost overhead and knowledge transferability.

Decoding Diffusion Language Models with Foreseeing Movement

Y Mo, Q Chen, M Li, Z Wei, Y Wang · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Foreseeing Decoding Method (FDM), a search-based decoding-order algorithm for diffusion language models that scores candidate tokens by both local confidence and an estimated global (future-impact) confidence, plus an accelerated variant (FDM-A) that adaptively applies deep search only at uncertain steps. - Why it's important: Diffusion LM inference quality is highly sensitive to the order in which masked tokens are unmasked, and existing heuristic orderings (probability, margin, entropy) use only per-step local information, leaving accuracy on the table at inference time without touching model weights. - How it does it: The key move is that the DLM's masked-training objective already trains the model to predict the distribution of future tokens given any partially masked state, so the global term log pθ(xT | xt, q) can be computed with one extra batched forward pass per candidate set rather than by greedily rolling out to completion. - The good: Consistent empirical gains across four benchmarks and four DLM variants — e.g., on ARC with LLaDA, FDM (K=2) reaches 86.00% accuracy vs. 82.55% for the best heuristic, and FDM-A reaches 86.30% at 38.20 tokens/sec vs. 10.85 for margin decoding — supported by a theorem showing FDM's KL divergence to the data distribution is lower than heuristic decoding by a sum of conditional mutual information terms. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, the theory relies on an unexplained substitution of the model distribution for the true data distribution, and accuracy degrades (non-monotonic scaling) beyond K≈8–12, capping the test-time-scaling claim. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building inference-time or decoding infrastructure for masked diffusion LMs — the core observation (training objective ≈ free lookahead) is reusable — but readers seeking statistically rigorous comparisons or scaling beyond 8B models will find the evidence thin.

Problem & Motivation: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate by iteratively unmasking tokens, and unlike autoregressive decoding there is no canonical left-to-right order; the chosen unmasking order measurably changes quality (random order 79.06% vs. margin-based 82.55% on ARC with LLaDA). Practitioners deploying DLMs (LLaDA, Dream, MMaDA families) face this as a decoding-strategy problem. Prior heuristics — decode the highest-probability token (LLaDA), highest margin (Kim et al.), or lowest entropy (Ben-Hamu et al.) — select tokens using only the current step's conditional distribution, ignoring how an early choice shapes all subsequent predictions. The gap this work closes is a decoding criterion that accounts for the long-term consequence of each unmasking decision, without retraining the model or using an external verifier. Key Idea: The DLM's training loss (masked-token prediction over the whole sequence) means the model, at any partially masked state xt, already outputs predicted distributions for all future masked positions; the expectation of those log-probabilities is a computable surrogate for the otherwise intractable global term pθ(xT | q, xt). FDM therefore scores each candidate token as Clocal + Cglobal, where Clocal is the step-t confidence and Cglobal is the expectation of the model's predicted log-probability of the final answer's tokens under the current state — a one-forward-pass lookahead instead of an expensive rollout. Theorem 1 formalizes this: per-step KL error under FDM equals the heuristic's error minus the conditional mutual information I(xt; xT | xt−1), which is non-negative. Methodology: FDM is a two-stage search per decoding step. (1) Candidate construction: from a single model query on (q, xt−1), take the argmax token at each masked position, rank by local confidence, and keep the Top-K candidates whose confidence exceeds threshold γ, forming search space Λ (effective width Keff = min{K, #candidates above γ}); if Λ is empty, fall back to pure local decoding. (2) Selection: stack the K candidates along the batch dimension, run one batched forward pass, compute Cglobal for each, and pick argmax(Clocal + Cglobal); the chosen candidate's logits are reused for the next step. The paper frames the ideal objective as argmax pθ(xT | q, xt)·pθ(xt | q, xt−1), i.e., an additive log-space criterion. FDM-A adds a three-phase schedule (exploration / balance / acceleration) driven by thresholds η1=0.8 and η2=0.7 on predicted-token probability: decode one token via FDM when nothing exceeds η1, decode NUM(qualified) tokens with a mix when borderline tokens exist, and decode in parallel with local confidence only when ≥N qualified tokens exist. Motivation is an empirical consistency-ratio analysis showing local-vs-global decisions agree on >90% of steps late in decoding but only ~50% early. Critical design decisions: (a) approximating the global term via the training-objective identity (justified by Eq. 5, though the pθ-vs-pdata gap is only addressed via a winner's-curse analysis in Appendix H); (b) restricting search to Top-K with threshold γ (ablated; accuracy peaks near K=8–12 then declines, consistent with their noise-amplification analysis); (c) the fixed η1/η2 phase boundaries (ablated on all four benchmarks, but tuned on GSM8K/Countdown first). A depth-M extension (Appendix G) multiplies lookahead horizon but costs O(K^M). Key Results: Experiments cover GSM8K, HumanEval, Countdown, and ARC in zero-shot, on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, LLaDA-MoE-7B-Instruct, and MMaDA-8B-MixCoT, on a single A100 80G, against the three standard heuristics plus EB and WINO for acceleration — baselines that are current for DLM decoding. Headline numbers: FDM beats the best heuristic on every model-benchmark cell; largest gap on ARC/LLaDA (86.68% at K=4 vs. 82.55% margin) and LLaDA-MoE/ARC (83.51% vs. 76.19% probability). Accuracy is monotone in K from 2→4 and peaks at K≈8–12 in ablations before declining. FDM-A at T=128 dominates the speed-accuracy frontier: on GSM8K/LLaDA, 81.96% at 42.65 TPS vs. WINO's 79.45% at 40.02 TPS and EB's 79.61% at 36.46 TPS — a 5.15× throughput gain over FDM (K=2, T=256) at only 0.07% accuracy cost, while heuristic decoders lose ~3 points when T is halved. At generation length 512, FDM-A still leads (e.g., 85.17% ARC vs. 84.13% WINO at 44.35 vs. 42.50 TPS). Depth-M scaling on Countdown raises accuracy from 25.00% (K=4, M=1) to 30.08% (K=4, M=3) at prohibitive cost. The non-monotonic K curve and the small-γ degradation are themselves notable findings, backed by a Gaussian-noise winner's-curse analysis (Appendix H). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an auxiliary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING about when local/global decoding decisions diverge). The genuinely novel element is the observation that the masked-diffusion training objective yields an in-model, one-pass estimate of the future-impact term, plus the KL-divergence gap theorem. The remaining machinery — Top-K beam-style search, confidence-threshold pruning, adaptive parallel decoding schedules — is a competent combination of standard search and scheduling ideas applied to a new setting; the accelerated variant is largely an engineering optimization of FDM. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and reasonably thorough: K sweeps (2–12), γ sweeps (0.1–0.9), η1 and η2 sweeps across all four benchmarks, generation-length-512 transfer (Appendix E), and depth-M scaling (Appendix G) — these show which components matter and honestly expose the non-monotonic K behavior. However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for any headline number, and several winning margins (e.g., FDM K=2 vs. margin on GSM8K: 82.03 vs. 80.14 on ~300-problem Countdown splits with differences of ~0.3–1.5 points) are within plausible seed noise. Code is released at https://github.com/PKU-ML/FDM. Concerns: (a) hyperparameters (γ, η1, η2, K defaults) were evidently tuned on GSM8K and Countdown, which are also headline benchmarks — Appendix F claims cross-dataset transfer of the optimal settings, partially mitigating Goodhart risk; (b) Theorem 1's proof contains an unexplained step replacing pθ with pdata (Eq. 37), and the KL-gap result is vacuous in practice because Δtotal is not estimated; (c) all models are ≤8B and three of four are LLaDA-family, limiting architecture generality claims. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a decoding algorithm run and measured on real models). Practical: Yes — runs on a single NVIDIA A100 80G with no verifier or parameter changes. Efficient: FDM itself costs 20–60% throughput versus heuristic decoding (e.g., 8.28 vs. 11.51 TPS on GSM8K at K=2), while FDM-A is the fastest method tested on most settings (42.65 TPS vs. ~20 for heuristics, 36–40 for EB/WINO). Effective: The evidence shows accuracy and throughput gains on four reasoning/code/knowledge benchmarks, but these are proxy tasks at ≤256–512 token generations; no free-form generation quality or human evaluation. Scalable: Only tested to K=12 and depth M=3 at 8B scale; accuracy peaks and declines with K, and the paper itself shows depth scaling is computationally impractical, so the "test-time scaling for DLMs" claim holds only in a narrow window. Delivers a software artifact (public code repository); no trained model or dataset is released. Strengths: (1) The core insight — that the masked-diffusion training objective makes the model's own next-state output a free surrogate for the final-answer conditional likelihood — is a genuinely non-obvious reuse of the training loss as a lookahead signal, and it cleanly explains why FDM works without a verifier. (2) Theorem 1 gives a clean, interpretable characterization (KL gap equals accumulated conditional mutual information) connecting the decoding criterion to information-theoretic quantities, and Appendix H's winner's-curse analysis honestly predicts the empirical non-monotonic K curve rather than hiding it. (3) The FDM-A design is empirically grounded in a measured phenomenon (consistency ratio rising from ~50% to >90% over decoding steps) rather than invented ad hoc. (4) Evaluation breadth is above average for this literature: four benchmarks, four model families including a MoE and a non-LLaDA model, two generation lengths, and the current acceleration baselines (EB, WINO). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two limitations directly: (1) FDM/FDM-A are training-free, so gains are bounded by the underlying model's capability; (2) when the model distribution diverges from the data distribution, a too-small γ injects noisy candidates and degrades accuracy. They confront these candidly, and the Limitations section is consistent with the paper's own ablation evidence. They do not, however, acknowledge the absence of statistical uncertainty reporting, the K-range ceiling, or the tuning-on-evaluated-benchmarks issue. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere — for Countdown (64–256 problems, accuracy differences as small as 0.31–3.9 points) several conclusions could flip under resampling. (2) Theorem 1's proof silently substitutes pθ for pdata mid-derivation (Eq. 37), so the stated exact KL gap technically conflates model and data distributions; as written the theorem holds only for a perfectly trained model, which the authors themselves concede is unrealistic. (3) FDM-A's η1/η2 defaults were selected using GSM8K/Countdown behavior and are then headline-evaluated on those same benchmarks; the transfer claim in Appendix F is visual, not statistical. (4) Two concurrent non-local decoding methods (Lee et al. 2026; Fu et al. 2026) are discussed in Related Work but not empirically compared. (5) The "test-time scaling" framing is weakened by the authors' own data: accuracy peaks at K≈8–12 and depth-M scaling costs O(K^M), so neither axis scales like standard test-time-compute methods. (6) All evaluation is zero-shot QA-style tasks with boxed answers; there is no evidence on open-ended generation, where decoding-order effects could differ qualitatively. Bottom Line: For anyone deploying or studying masked diffusion LMs, this is the strongest published decoding-order method I am aware of and the lookahead-via-training-objective trick alone justifies reading it — but treat the exact margins as unverified due to missing variance reporting, and expect the scaling story to saturate quickly.
