TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows, through exact objective analysis plus a frozen-policy experiment on sixteen simulated actuator laws, that fast clipped-quadratic actuator identification yields only modest controller restoration (medians 0.9084/0.8966) and fails a declared full policy-recovery capability gate — even a true inverse model does not restore the actor. - Why it's important: It demarcates a concrete boundary between a cheap model-maintenance component (adaptation) and useful closed-loop behavior (policy recovery), warning against interpreting good system-identification metrics as control-value guarantees. - How it does it: It exploits piecewise quadratic structure: within fixed clipping-region assignments the clipped least-squares objective reduces to convex quadratic subproblems solved by enumeration with constraint-based pruning, complemented by a finite-difference counterexample (Proposition 1) proving ordinary empirical Gram statistics cannot represent the clipped loss. - The good: The matched-controller design is disciplined — paired-reset normalization, law-level bootstrap uncertainty (10,000 resamples), pre-declared acceptance criteria, and complete negative results reported rather than cherry-picked, including the decisive finding that true inversion (0.9123/0.8977) also misses the two-family gate. - The missing: The evaluation rests on one frozen soft actor-critic policy, one scalar actuator family, and one simulation environment, with no significance tests, no comparison to modern adaptive-control or meta-learning baselines, and no evidence the boundary extends beyond this specific setup. - Read it or not: Read it if you work at the intersection of system identification and learned control and care about honest negative results and identification-evaluation separations; skip it if you want broadly validated methods, since the scope is deliberately narrow and single-lab.

Problem & Motivation: When an actuator's response changes, a system must both identify the new response and keep the controller useful under it. The identification problem can be low-dimensional and well-posed while the behavioral problem remains unsolved. The paper studies this separation under deliberately favorable conditions — known mechanics, continuous force sensing, a low-dimensional source prior, and an inherited policy — asking whether accurate, compact model adaptation suffices for policy recovery. This matters for anyone building adaptive control systems on top of learned policies, where a model-fit metric is often implicitly trusted as a proxy for control performance. Key Idea: The core insight is twofold. (1) For a scalar stable-lag actuator with clipped static drive, sorted commands and a coefficient-monotone response imply saturations form a lower prefix and upper suffix with one interior block, so the clipped objective decomposes into (n+1)(n+2)/2 region assignments, each a convex quadratic program with linear consistency constraints — an exact finite-region reduction, not a generic convex formulation. (2) Clipping is parameter-dependent, so sufficient statistics retained for an unclipped objective (empirical Grams) provably cannot evaluate the clipped loss (Proposition 1, via the seventh finite-difference identity on binomial-weighted moment-matched datasets). The second is the paper's sharpest theoretical point: statistics must match the objective actually deployed. Methodology: The identification pipeline parameterizes a first-order force recurrence (pole ρ constrained to [0, 0.85]) with a clipped static drive whose coefficients are expressed as a source-mean plus scaled prior-direction correction (equations 1–2). Without clipping the prediction is affine in (ρ, a), giving a quadratic objective with linear monotonicity constraints; with clipping, region enumeration yields per-assignment convex QPs, pruned via lower bounds from dropped constraints, with batched Hessian construction. An exact response Gram (equation 7) is derived in closed form for the unclipped geometric transient under a uniform reference measure, shown PSD by inner-product construction. The evaluation is a matched-policy panel: a frozen calibrated SAC actor (611,088 source training transitions plus 126,000 validation plus earlier 20-million-transition pretraining; no target policy-gradient updates) is held fixed across seven arms — identity, frozen 16-row RLS, online RLS, six-coordinate polynomial-prior inverse, six-coordinate shared-prior inverse, true inverse, nominal dynamics — over two actuator families (asymmetric lag, compound lag), 8 fresh law seeds each, 8 paired resets per law, 1,000 steps per episode. Metrics are paired-reset normalized returns with law-level bootstrap (10,000 resamples) and pre-declared gates: 0.90 restoration median, 0.80 all-law floor, ≥0.02 gain over each cheap comparator. Critical design decisions: the frozen-actor protocol isolates the inverse adapter (well justified); the 0.02 pre-declared gain criterion (justified as pre-registration, though arbitrary in magnitude); the true-inverse arm as an intervention diagnostic rather than an upper bound (well justified and underused in this literature). Note the shared-prior and polynomial-prior arms share a cardinal carrier but their geometry and subspace selection are not separately ablated — the authors admit this. Key Results: Shared-prior inverse achieves median restoration 0.9084 (asymmetric lag) and 0.8966 (compound lag), with paired gains over frozen RLS (0.8850/0.8722) of 0.02124 and 0.02292 (positive law-bootstrap lower bounds), but gains over the polynomial prior (0.8999/0.8901) of only 0.00747 and 0.01164 fall below the declared 0.02 criterion, so the capability gate fails. The true inverse under the same actor scores 0.9123/0.8977 and also fails two-family restoration — the paper's most consequential negative finding, showing inverse-fitting refinement alone is not the bottleneck. Identity baselines are 0.2295/0.2579. Timing: on a reused 576-fit panel, 90 of 96 six-actuator cases finish below 100 ms but the worst takes 133.39 ms, so an all-case timing gate fails; maximum common fitting takes 15.488 ms, activation is always step 17, numeric state is 651,900 bytes, evaluator RSS is 317.672 MiB. Audits confirm all 898,048 evaluator transitions and 1,536 scalar-fit reproductions pass recurrence and immutability checks. Baselines (RLS, polynomial prior) are simple, deliberately cheap comparators rather than state-of-the-art adaptive controllers. Scale is toy-to-standard: sixteen scalar actuator laws in simulation, one actor, no hardware. The counterintuitive headline — perfect inversion does not restore performance — is genuinely surprising and correctly highlighted. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the true-inverse failure under a frozen policy) plus a modest NEW FORMULATION (the finite-region exact quadratic reduction for clipped scalar identification) and a small theoretical contribution (the Gram-insufficiency counterexample). The components — Hammerstein-style identification, RLS baselines, SAC as the inherited policy, kernel/Gram machinery — are all standard; the novelty lies in the careful statement of where the quadratic reduction is exact, what statistics the clipped objective actually requires, and the disciplined negative experimental result, not in any new algorithm or architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: Pre-declared acceptance criteria (0.90 restoration, 0.80 floor, 0.02 comparator gains) are stated before the analysis, and the paper reports complete results including failures — a strong practice. Uncertainty is handled via law-unit bootstrap with 10,000 fixed resamples and paired law-difference medians, though no formal significance tests or seed-level error bars on the policy side are given. Ablations are incomplete: the shared-prior vs. polynomial-prior distinction is not isolated from geometry/subspace selection, as the authors concede. Numerical audits (898,048 transitions, 1,536 fit reproductions) are described but no code, data, or model weights are stated as publicly released — no URL or repo appears in the text. Methodological concerns: single simulation environment and single frozen actor (evaluation on the authors' own setup throughout); the policy's 20M-transition pretraining means the 'sixteen-row fitting' framing understates total data cost, which the authors themselves flag; the bootstrap is descriptive, not inferential; and the timing gate failure (133.39 ms worst case) is reported but not analyzed for cause. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation experiments plus small theoretical results), with a minor SYSTEMS component (the identification pipeline). Practical: Everything runs on a local machine with 317.672 MiB evaluator RSS and sub-150 ms fits, so commercially available hardware suffices for simulation, though no real-time hardware control deadline is demonstrated. Efficient: The quadratic-region pipeline is cheap (15.488 ms common fit, 90/96 cases under 100 ms) versus generic nonlinear optimization, but the all-case timing guarantee fails at the current scale. Effective: Evidence supports modest restoration improvement (medians ~0.90) but explicitly not the full policy-recovery objective — the paper measures a proxy success and honestly reports gate failure. Scalable: Not tested beyond sixteen scalar laws and one actor; behavior at 10× the actuator diversity or with retrained policies is unclaimed and unexplored. The work delivers no released software artifact, dataset, or trained model — it stops at paper form; the finite-difference counterexample technique is reusable as a proof tool for statistics-vs-objective mismatches. Strengths: - Proposition 1 is a clean, verifiable obstruction result: two moment-matched datasets (agreeing through degree six by the finite-difference identity) with divergent clipped losses, establishing that the clipping partition — not floating-point error — makes ordinary Gram statistics insufficient. This is a crisp, transferable point about matching retained statistics to the deployed objective. - The true-inverse intervention arm converts a plausible confound (maybe the fit just isn't good enough?) into a decisive negative finding (0.9123/0.8977 still fails the gate), which most papers in this space omit. - Pre-registration-style gates, paired-reset normalization, law-unit bootstrap, and full disclosure of failed criteria (timing gate, comparator-gain gate, capability gate) represent above-average experimental hygiene for a single-author manuscript. - The exact closed-form response Gram (equation 7) with PSD proof, and explicit demarcation of where the quadratic reduction is and is not exact, prevents the common overclaim of 'convex identification.' Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually direct: the result is not a safety guarantee, unknown-change detection system, or demonstration of robotic self-improvement; timing receipts are local simulation numbers, not hardware deadlines; floating-point pruning is not a formal exact-arithmetic certificate; the true inverse is an intervention, not an optimal-policy upper bound; the agent cannot be described as learned from sixteen examples given 20M+ transition pretraining; geometry and subspace selection between the two prior arms are not separately isolated; and any change of controller, observation interface, or disturbance family would constitute a different study. This candor is a strong credibility positive — the paper is structured around its own negative result rather than minimizing it. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' notes: (1) only one frozen actor is tested — the central claim (a boundary between identification and recovery) could be an artifact of this particular policy's response distribution, and no second actor or actor family probes generality; (2) no modern baseline from adaptive control, meta-learning, or system identification (e.g., kernel-based Hammerstein methods the paper itself cites) is run — only RLS and a polynomial prior; (3) the 0.02 comparator-gain threshold is pre-declared but its justification is unstated, and with 8 laws per family the bootstrap on 8 units has limited power, making the 'positive lower bounds' claim fragile; (4) the counterexample, while correct, uses a constructed binomial-weight dataset — its prevalence on natural excitation signals is unquantified, so the practical severity of the Gram-insufficiency problem is unknown; (5) the compound-lag family's qualitative difference from asymmetric lag is never explained mechanistically; (6) no released code or environment specification, so the exact audit and gates cannot be independently reproduced from the manuscript alone. Bottom Line: A practitioner building adaptive controllers around learned policies gains a genuinely useful cautionary result and two reusable analytical tools (finite-region quadratic reduction, statistics-vs-objective obstruction) from this honest single-environment negative-result study, but should not expect broadly validated methods here — the scope is narrow, the baselines are minimal, and peer review has evidently not occurred for this self-published manuscript.

Problem & Motivation: Operators of LLM-powered systems face an "alignment lag": safety policies (regulations, platform rules, domain moderation requirements) change frequently, but fine-tuned guardrails (LlamaGuard, ShieldGemma, WildGuard, xGuard) bake a fixed harm definition into weights, and adapting them requires new labeled data and retraining. Generic LLM judges are flexible but anchor decisions in parametric priors rather than a user-supplied rule set. Naive RAG over raw policy text fails in safety contexts because adversarial inputs avoid policy keywords and chunked retrieval strips global context and exceptions. The paper targets zero-shot policy adaptation: can a judge stay competitive on standard safety evaluation while changing its decision boundary at inference time from an external document? Key Idea: Compile the policy once into a structured, modular representation (the PMPD: global module G plus category modules c_i = (id, name, definition, rules, exceptions)) and render two different runtime prompt views from it — a permissive routing view and a compact judging view. Two sub-ideas carry the adaptation result: (1) the router has zero label authority and only decides policy relevance, so deleting a category from the roster architecturally guarantees zero leakage on that category, and (2) empty routing short-circuits to SAFE, making policy narrowing instantaneous. Ablations show this structure matters: a monolithic 28,000-token policy-in-prompt baseline reaches 86.63% raw accuracy but suffers 7.9% parser failures (79.74% effective) versus 87.43% with zero failures for the modular runtime, and Kg=1 top-1 routing collapses accuracy to 0.69. Methodology: Three-stage pipeline. (1) Offline compilation: a governance PDF (MLCommons AILuminate) is parsed to Markdown and extracted to structured JSON modules M = T(d) = (G, C). (2) Routing: an LLM mapper g_φ(x, V_route(M)) returns up to K_g=3 candidate categories, union-of-fields, instructed to over-route; empty set → default SAFE. (3) Judging: K independent judges see the record, compact global guidance, and label contract, returning (label, support map, reasoning); for K=3, outputs aggregate by mean label support, then vote count, then fixed label order. Two runtime configurations are studied: 1-judge GPT-OSS-20B and 3-judge Ministral-3B. Critical design decisions: (a) routers cannot judge and judges cannot see full category dossiers — justified by internal ablations showing scoped-specialist prompts were costlier and less accurate (Appendix J); (b) response-primary judging with union-of-fields routing — argued for, not ablated directly; (c) accepting a static-accuracy cost (0.85 vs 0.90 for router-off) to gain the adaptation capability — explicitly framed as the price of controllability. The formalism is prompt-engineering and routing logic, not a learned objective; no loss function exists. Key Results: (1) Intra-domain adaptation (390-example JailJudge slice, four staged MLCommons removals: S2, S10, S7, S5): PMPD GPT-OSS-20B averages 0.84 Acc / 0.82 F1 across five policy conditions vs 0.79 / 0.75 for GPT-OSS-Safeguard-20B, the best baseline; static guardrails degrade to 0.54–0.77 accuracy ranges; zero removed-category leakage across all stages. (2) Policy-aligned attack suite (850 examples, 9 attack families, Fleiss' κ=0.79): 0.915 Acc / 0.896 F1, within 0.4 points of JailJudge-MultiAgent-GPT-OSS-20B (0.919 / 0.901) at 3,926 vs 4,519 tokens/sample, clearly above GPT-OSS-Safeguard-20B (0.869 / 0.849). Ministral-3B (3 judges) reaches 0.780 / 0.749, beating LlamaGuard 4 (0.76 / 0.72). (3) Eight-dataset public benchmark suite (1,785 examples, audited labels): 0.87 Acc / 0.85 F1 — competitive with WildGuard (0.88 / 0.87) and JailJudge-Finetuned (0.88 / 0.87) but trailing JailJudge-MultiAgent-GPT (0.90 / 0.89), with high specificity (0.93) hurting recall on benchmarks broader than the active policy. Cost sits between single-call judges (~620 tokens) and multi-agent pipelines (~4,519 tokens). Baselines are current and reasonably strong (Qwen3Guard, GPT-OSS-Safeguard, WildGuard, LlamaGuard 4). The ablation finding that router-off judging (0.90/0.90) beats the full system on static accuracy is honestly reported. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus a NEW FORMULATION of safety judging as policy-memory/prompt-view decoupling; secondary NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the 850-example policy-aligned attack suite and the audit methodology for benchmark–policy mismatch). The genuinely novel element is the treatment of the policy artifact itself as a swappable, modular database supporting distinct routing and judging projections with an architectural zero-leakage guarantee. The individual components — LLM routing, LLM judging, multivote aggregation, prompt compilation — are standard; the contribution is their composition around the policy-swap abstraction, positioned against GPT-OSS-Safeguard's monolithic policy-in-prompt approach. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (monolithic-prompt baseline with parse-failure accounting, router-off condition, K_g sensitivity from 1 to ≥2, plus a Table 12 lineage of eight architectural variants with token/latency costs). However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; temperature 0.7 is used, so run-to-run variance is unaddressed. Code is released (https://github.com/Court-Guard/CourtGuardPMPD). Two methodological concerns stand out. First, Goodhart-adjacent evaluation construction: the attack suite labels and the "audited" benchmark labels (96 of 1,785 flipped, up to 15% on BeaverTails) were produced by the authors under MLCommons — the exact policy the system is compiled from — so the primary evaluation surfaces are partially authored by the system designers; the pre-audit/original-label results are relegated to diagnostics even though on original labels PMPD drops behind several baselines (0.83 Acc vs WildGuard 0.84, JailJudge-Finetuned 0.86, Ordinary Judge GPT-OSS 0.86). Second, cost accounting is asymmetric: PMPD rows use direct execution logs while external baselines use "standardized tokenizer accounting" over reconstructed inputs, a comparison the authors themselves flag as incomplete. The adaptation ground truth is also author-designed (relabeling rule is deterministic given category tags), which favors routing-based systems by construction. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a released SYSTEMS artifact). - Practical: Yes — runs via OpenRouter API on GPT-OSS-20B or Ministral-3B, all commercially accessible checkpoints. - Efficient: Moderate — 3,926 tokens/sample (1-judge) is 6× an ordinary judge and 2.3× GPT-OSS-Safeguard, though cheaper than multi-agent debate (4,519); the Ministral 3-judge config costs 6,732 tokens, so ensemble-of-small is less efficient than one large judge. - Effective: The evidence shows it follows policy edits and stays competitive on policy-aligned data; effectiveness on arbitrary third-party policies (only MLCommons is tested) and on labels not authored by the system designers is unproven. - Scalable: Not tested beyond ~1,800-example suites and 12 policy categories; behavior with many concurrent categories, long policies, or high-throughput routing latency (20–29 s/sample in ablation table) at 10–100× scale is claimed nowhere. Delivers a software artifact: released framework including the PMPD compiler and routing runtime, plus the annotated attack suite. Strengths: - The staged category-removal protocol is a genuinely new evaluation paradigm for safety judges: it measures whether a decision boundary follows a policy edit on held-constant examples, a property no static baseline can even express, and the metric design (leakage tracking) is clean. - The architectural zero-leakage guarantee (router sees only active categories) is a rare example of a safety property obtained by construction rather than by training, and the paper correctly distinguishes the guarantee from its empirical verification. - The ablation lineage in Appendix J (monolithic 28k-token prompt with 7.9% parse failures vs 0% for modular views; Kg=1 collapse to 0.69; router-off at 0.90 but non-adaptable) gives concrete evidence for why structure beats prompt dumping. - Honest trade-off framing: the paper explicitly concedes it does not win every benchmark, quantifies the token cost premium, and separates "benchmark leadership" from "policy faithfulness" as distinct objectives. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state four: (1) the PMPD store does not cover every benchmark's category space, causing structural recall loss (JailJudge's 14 vs 12 categories); (2) performance depends on compilation quality, with errors propagating to routing and judging; (3) competitor cost comparisons are incomplete because external baselines lack comparable token traces; (4) the attack suite was labeled by the paper's own authors, mitigated only by independent first-pass labeling and reported pre-resolution Fleiss' κ (0.79), with external annotation deferred to future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The audited benchmark labels are author-produced under the authors' own reference policy, and the main tables use only audited copies; the original-label table (Appendix G.2) shows PMPD falls from 0.87 to 0.83 accuracy and behind WildGuard, JailJudge-Finetuned, and Ordinary GPT judges — the headline "highly competitive" claim depends on the authors' own relabeling. - Only one policy document (MLCommons AILuminate) is ever compiled; there is no test that the compiler generalizes to a second, differently structured governance document, so "model-agnostic" is demonstrated but "policy-agnostic" is not. - Adaptation is only tested in the narrowing direction (category removal); adding a new category, merging categories, or editing a definition — arguably the more common policy change — is never evaluated. - No inter-run variance despite temperature 0.7, no confidence intervals on any headline number, and the 5-point adaptation margin over GPT-OSS-Safeguard is reported without significance testing. - Single-judge GPT-OSS-20B is both the backbone of the proposed system and the backbone of the strongest generic baselines, which is good for control, but the paper does not test whether PMPD's routing stage adds failure modes (e.g., under-routing on adversarial inputs that avoid category keywords — the very RAG failure the introduction criticizes) is never directly measured; routing recall/error rates are not reported. - The Ministral ablation rows show an unexplained anomaly (label-first multivote at 0.60/0.71 vs rebuilt gated judges at 0.77/0.79) that is presented without analysis. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying LLM moderation should read this for the policy-swap abstraction and the staged-removal evaluation protocol, which are genuinely useful and reusable, but should treat the absolute accuracy numbers skeptically given the author-constructed ground truth — and GPT-OSS-Safeguard remains a simpler alternative if monolithic policy prompting suffices for their update cadence.

#113 — Innovative (64)

Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities (55 ▲ )

Yunhang Shen, Zhangquan Chen, Xiaotian Li, Zhongpeng Cai, Qing Zhou, Zekai Zhang, Kun Zhang, Zezhong Wu, Jian Hu, Haihan Gao, Heting Gao, Xin Li, Yinsong Liu, Deqian Jiang, Di Yin, Haoyu Cao, Xing Sun, Bing Liu, Yanqiu Qu, Yunfei Wu, Kun Yin, Zhixiang Wei, Yongxiang Hua, Qianyu Li, Xiaoxing Hu, Peiyuan Zhang, Lijiang Li, Dong Xu, Zhenchuan Yang, Yiliang Jiang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Youtu-Parsing-Omni, a 5B-parameter omni-modal parser that converts documents, natural images, charts, geometry, chemical structures, sheet music, audio, and video into a single JSON schema with spatial bounding boxes or temporal timestamps, and reports state-of-the-art results on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall) and the best open-weight score on OmniParsingBench (75.08). - Why it's important: LLM agents increasingly consume documents, images, audio, and video, and a single grounded text record lets any downstream LLM — including text-only ones — read, locate, and cite evidence once instead of re-encoding raw pixels or waveforms per query. - How it does it: The two core moves are (1) replacing the usual separate vision and audio towers with one shared Transformer initialized from a pre-trained text LM, using an axis-factorized (t, h, w) rotary encoding so frames and audio tokens share one time axis, with a few fusion layers letting frames attend to concurrent audio, and (2) a self-evolving on-policy distillation (OSAD) in which a reference-conditioned copy of the model provides token-level targets, with JS divergence for content tokens and forward KL for structure tokens, refreshing the teacher every round. - The good: The ablation program is unusually credible: a controlled comparison shows text-LM initialization beats an identical randomly initialized encoder by 130.6 points on OCRBench at 300B tokens, and OSAD accounts for 1.75 of the 1.99 points gained after SFT on OmniDocBench (vs. 0.24 from RLVR), with gains at every one of six rounds. - The missing: OmniParsingBench results come from the authors' own evaluation toolkit (the benchmark ships without a complete one), with schema repair before scoring, corrected ground truth, and excluded subsets, so the headline 75.08 is not comparable to benchmark-author numbers and the scoring pipeline itself favors schema-conformant outputs. - Read it or not: Read it if you build document/multimodal parsing systems or design post-training for structured generation — the OSAD recipe and the encoder ablations are directly reusable; skip it if you want rigorous cross-task ablations of the schema itself or latency/throughput numbers, which are absent.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Impact (85) leads: open code, open weights, a single 5B checkpoint covering ten tasks at specialist-competitive level is real practitioner value. Novelty (60) is honest recombination — unified encoders, on-policy distillation, teacher refresh are all known, and the summary's own classification concedes the novelty is in the combination for grounded omni-modal parsing. Rigor (65) is undermined by the OmniParsingBench headline being scored with the authors' own toolkit, with schema repair structurally favoring schema-conformant outputs (a Goodhart risk on the headline 75.08), encoder ablations at proxy scale, no error bars or seeds, and no fusion-mechanism or OmniSchema ablation. Non-Obviousness (55) is modest — the text-LM-initialization and OSAD-over-RLVR attributions are useful but predictable. Completeness (65) is helped by candid per-split loss reporting and direct limitation acknowledgment; Resilience (60) reflects toolkit-dependent margins and missing latency figures despite a deployment framing. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*85 = 64.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents need a perception layer that turns non-text inputs into structured, grounded records their outputs can cite. Prior parsers cover this only partially: document parsers are strong on pages but leave chemical structures and sheet music to specialists, omni-modal models are built for captioning/QA rather than grounded structured output, and the one existing omni-modal parser (Logics-Parsing-Omni) pairs two separately pre-trained encoders. Two-tower designs have three costs the authors identify: each modality is encoded in isolation with no fusion during perception; frame and audio positions are indexed on independent timelines; and each new modality requires a new tower with its own pre-training lineage. Separately, optimizing one model across ten heterogeneous parsing tasks is awkward: SFT trains on reference prefixes, and RLVR needs a scalar reward that is hard to define across content accuracy, grounding, and schema validity. Key Idea: Unify perception and supervision around a single coordinate system and a single schema. (1) One encoder: a shared bidirectional Transformer (initialized from Qwen3-0.6B-Base) reads a packed mix of image patches, video frames, and log-mel audio tokens under one axis-factorized RoPE budget split into T/H/W segments (21/21/22 of 64 slots), where audio tokens write (t, 0, 0) and vision tokens write (frame index, patch row, patch column) so both modalities share one time axis; four designated fusion layers let frame and audio tokens of the same instant attend to each other within short (I+A*) windows. (2) One schema: OmniSchema serializes all ten tasks as JSON whose every token is classifiable as structure (constrained JSON grammar) or content (free-form values), which enables OSAD — on-policy distillation where a frozen teacher copy of the model, conditioned on the reference parse as privileged information, scores the student's own rollouts with role-specific divergences, and the teacher is refreshed from the merged student weights every round. Methodology: Pipeline: modality-specific stems (linear patch projection for vision; strided convolutions on log-mel at 13 tokens/second for audio) → shared 28-layer bidirectional Transformer → per-modality merger/projector → dense 4.5B decoder (Youtu-LLM recipe, MLA attention, 1D RoPE, 128k context). Training has seven stages over 2.24T pre-training + 0.6B post-training tokens: Stage 0 aligns randomly initialized stems/projectors to frozen decoder on dense captions/transcripts (4k sequences, no fusion); Stage 1 unfreezes everything at 1.28T tokens with 4 fusion layers; Stage 2 anneals LR 10⁻⁴→10⁻⁵ over 512B tokens with layer-wise LR decay (γ=0.9) and stochastic fused-route probability p_fus=0.8; Stage 3 extends to 128k sequences/512 frames. Post-training: SFT (16B tokens) establishes OmniSchema serialization; schema-routed GRPO-style RLVR uses reward R = 1[decodes]·1[payload]·clip(Ω·core_ν) where Ω combines format validity with repetition and under-coverage penalties and core_ν is task-specific grounded-field accuracy; OSAD then runs six rounds of LoRA-based on-policy distillation with admission-gated rollouts (JSON-validity, schema-conformance, box-syntax, repetition checks), loss L = mean of all-token JS + weighted content-JS (α_c rising 0.50→0.80) and structure-KL (α_s 0.10→0.08) terms, adapters merged into base weights at each round boundary. Critical design decisions: text-LM initialization of the encoder (justified by a controlled ablation), the chunked (vs. interleaved) axis-factorized RoPE (justified only by "preliminary runs" for ≤64 frames), and fusing only within short audio-visual windows (sensible but the fusion-layer count/depth is not ablated on the final model). Key Results: Single checkpoint, single inference configuration, ten tasks. OmniDocBench v1.6: 96.96 Overall (best of 24 systems; Text Edit 0.0271, Formula CDM 96.80, Table TEDS 96.79, Reading Order Edit 0.1104), edging TeleOCR at 96.91. PureDocBench: best end-to-end Avg3 at 76.29 (+8 over predecessor on each track). OmniParsingBench (authors' toolkit, all systems re-scored): 75.08 avg vs. 72.26 for Logics-Parsing-Omni and 77.44 for Gemini-3-Pro, with gains concentrated on temporal splits (audio 78.08, natural video 74.18, text-rich video 75.62) and losses on static splits (natural image 62.84 vs. 67.53; geometry 74.33 vs. 76.34 for Logics-Parsing-Omni). ChemOCR: Tani@1.0 54.2 vs. 49.6 for DeepSeek-OCR 2 (Avg. Sim. 74.6 vs. 74.9 — slightly worse). PDMX-Synth: CER 22.73, beating the specialist LEGATO (23.30, as self-reported in its paper) and far ahead of GPT-5.6 (45.02) and Gemini-3-Pro (54.26). Video-MME-v2 (no subtitles): group score 11.5, mid-pack, with a distinct L1 (cross-frame aggregation) lead of ≥5 points over all non-thinking baselines. Baselines are current (TeleOCR, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6, MinerU2.5-Pro, Gemini-3-Pro, GPT-5.x, Qwen3-Omni) and strong. Surprising findings: ASR is the model's weakest perception skill (77.94 on audio, lowest of compared models; 67.80 on natural video vs. Gemini's 84.06), yet overall leads persist via temporal localization; RLVR contributes only 0.24 of 1.99 post-SFT points, with OSAD dominating. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (unified text-initialized perception encoder with shared space-time RoPE and in-encoder audio-visual fusion for grounded parsing) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and, secondarily, NEW FORMULATION (schema-role-based token-adaptive on-policy distillation). The individual ingredients are known — unified multimodal encoders (VATT, Meta-Transformer), text-LM-initialized vision backbones (DeepSeek-OCR 2, TrOCR), on-policy distillation (GKD), reference-conditioned self-distillation (OPSD), privileged information (Vapnik & Vashist), and teacher refresh (born-again/Noisy Student) — the genuine novelty is their combination for grounded omni-modal parsing with schema-aware divergence assignment, which the ablations support as effective rather than as conceptually new machinery. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-targeted for the two headline ideas: unified vs. two-tower encoder, text-init vs. random init (16 vision/ASR benchmarks, matched schedules), and OSAD vs. RLVR vs. SFT with per-round increments. However, encoder ablations run at 0.4B encoder + Qwen3-4B decoder on general multimodal data — a proxy scale, not the deployed 5B system — and the OSAD ablation is measured only on OmniDocBench, so the self-evolution claim is not verified on audio/video tasks. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere. Methodological concerns: (1) OmniParsingBench is scored with the authors' own toolkit built from metric definitions, with schema repair before scoring and corrected ground truth — these numbers are internally comparable but not comparable to benchmark-author results, and the repair-then-score design structurally favors schema-conformant models like this one (a Goodhart risk on the headline metric); (2) camera-video subset excluded for annotation issues and 136 of 3,874 samples dropped; (3) OmniDocBench/PureDocBench/Video-MME-v2 numbers are leaderboard-sourced, mixing evaluation configurations; (4) LEGATO's comparison number is from its own paper, and GPT-5.4/Qwen3.5 run only on image splits. Code (github.com/TencentCloudADP/youtu-parsing) and weights (huggingface.co/tencent/Youtu-Parsing-Omni) are publicly released, which substantially aids reproducibility. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained and evaluated system). Practical: Yes — a dense 5B model with a 0.4B encoder, 128k context, and published weights runs on a single commodity accelerator-class node; no exotic hardware is implied. Efficient: Mixed — 5B total is competitive with 0.8–1.2B document specialists on cost and far below 30B MoE rivals, but the authors concede throughput is worse than their own 2.5B predecessor because dense structured content (tables) decodes autoregressively without the predecessor's parallel decoding. Effective: The evidence shows grounded parses across ten modalities/tasks with benchmark-level accuracy, though temporal reasoning beyond parsing (Video-MME-v2 L2/L3) and knowledge recognition on natural images remain weak, so it solves the parsing proxy convincingly but not general omni-modal understanding. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — inference at 64 frames despite Stage 3 training to 512 frames, and no throughput/latency measurements or cost analysis at 10–100× input scale. Deliverable: software artifact (open code + open model weights); the OSAD recipe is described at reproducible detail (pseudocode, schedules in Appendix C). Strengths: - The controlled encoder study is the paper's best science: identical schedules, single-variable comparison, showing text-LM initialization closes most of the vision gap (within 0.4 Avg-6 points of pre-trained towers with two-thirds the perception parameters) and dominates OCRBench (+130.6 at 300B tokens), cleanly attributing the benefit to reading rather than spatial perception (scratch encoder wins BLINK by 9.5). - OSAD is a well-motivated middle ground between SFT and RLVR for structured output, and the attribution is precise: 1.75 of 1.99 post-SFT points from OSAD vs. 0.24 from RLVR, with monotone per-round gains (95.21→96.96 over six rounds). - Honest per-split reporting: the paper states where it loses (natural images, geometry, ASR, L2/L3 reasoning, chart Cognition) and explains why, rather than only aggregating. - A single checkpoint genuinely covering chemical structures (Tani@1.0 54.2) and sheet music (CER 22.73, beating the LEGATO specialist) at specialist-competitive level is a substantive demonstration that breadth need not cost depth. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that Youtu-Parsing-Omni lacks the predecessor's inference acceleration (feature reuse and parallel/query-level decoding), decodes autoregressively with a larger decoder, and therefore will have lower throughput on dense structured content such as tables; they commit to porting parallel decoding in future work. Within the evaluation they also disclose weaker knowledge recognition on natural images (attributed to the smaller parameter budget), weaker geometric-relation perception, weaker ASR relative to baselines, weaker higher-level video reasoning without a thinking mode, and all-systems degradation on physically recaptured documents. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation of the fusion mechanism itself: the four fusion layers, the (I+A*) window granularity, and p_fus=0.8 are never compared against a no-fusion or full-fusion variant of the final model, so the causal claim that in-perception audio-visual fusion drives the temporal-split advantage is correlational (single encoder vs. two towers conflates sharing, timeline, and fusion). - The OmniSchema unification is never ablated as a variable: no experiment compares training with OmniSchema against task-specific output formats at fixed data, so "one schema enables one objective" remains an architecture argument, not a measurement. - OSAD's admission gate masks rejected rollouts entirely; the interaction between teacher refresh and possible self-reinforcement (teacher = previous student) is not analyzed for drift or collapse on tasks not covered by the OmniDocBench ablation. - Audio/ground-truth pipelines are model-annotation-heavy (consensus of ASR systems, VLM captions, SAM-3 boxes), so benchmarks where the model's own training distribution matches the annotation tooling could be favorably biased — this is not discussed. - Training data scale per task and the composition of the post-training mixture are not disclosed in the level of detail needed to reproduce OSAD's data conditions. - No latency, memory, or token-cost figures anywhere in the paper despite the deployment framing ("perception layer for agents"). Bottom Line: For practitioners building parsing-backed agent perception stacks, this is currently the strongest open omni-modal parser and the OSAD recipe plus text-initialized-encoder ablations are worth stealing wholesale; but treat the OmniParsingBench margin over Logics-Parsing-Omni as toolkit-dependent, expect weak ASR and slow table decoding, and look to Logics-Parsing-Omni or TeleOCR if static-image parsing or throughput is your bottleneck.

RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain (33 ▲ )

Minghao Zhu, Bohan Hou, Kun Xiang, Zixuan Wang, Yinzhou Tang, Yifei Yang, Zhikai Wang, Tianyi Zhang, Kehan Li, Haoyu Zhao, Siteng Huang, Leigang Qu, Sicong Leng, Dongchi Huang, Mingxiu Chen, Shijian Lu, Yue Wang, Xiaodan Liang, Zhenyu Zeng, Deli Zhao, Chengju Liu, Jianfei Yang, Xin Li · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model (8B autoregressive reasoner + 8B diffusion video generator) that performs interleaved video-language reasoning for long-horizon visual planning, an RL-trained agentic extension that decides when to invoke video generation for answering embodied questions, and a World-Action Model (WAM) extension for robot control, plus two new benchmarks (Rynn-VP, Rynn-GEU). - Why it's important: Embodied agents need understanding, world prediction, and action in one system; if visual prediction genuinely improves reasoning and planning over long horizons, this reduces the need for separate world models, planners, and VLA stacks and addresses error accumulation that breaks current unified models during multi-step rollouts. - How it does it: The core trick is cross-chunk scene memory (four persistent reference frames plus a continuous video prefix from the previous clip) combined with self-forcing-style training on degraded/self-generated conditioning, so each diffusion-generated clip stays consistent with prior context, and a Branch-Conditional Policy Optimization (BCPO) scheme using within-branch GSPO plus a soft routing loss trained on the reward difference between direct and generation-assisted answering. - The good: The agentic RL result is the most credible headline: the RL-trained agent lifts Rynn-GEU average from 44.0 to 50.0 (beating GPT-5.6-Terra at 45.1), whereas the same interleaved-generation trick applied to baselines BAGEL, RxBrain, and Cosmos 3 Nano degrades their Rynn-GEU scores (31.4→28.6, 37.3→33.5, etc.) — a controlled contrast showing the gain is not from generation alone. - The missing: Rynn-VP is scored by an LLM evaluator (GPT-6-sol in a Codex harness) built by the same authors, with no independent validation beyond internal human review, and the robot-control headline (51.5%) comes from an author-selected 20-task subset of RoboCasa365 where baseline numbers on the subset were re-run by the authors; no ablation isolates the contribution of scene memory versus self-forcing versus duration prediction. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on unified multimodal/embodied models, world-model-conditioned control, or RL for tool-use routing — the BCPO formulation and the negative results for naive generation-assisted reasoning in baselines are genuinely informative; skip it if you only want validated robot-control recipes, since the WAM evidence is thin (3 real tasks, 20 trials each).
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Practical Impact (80, 10% weight) is high — model weights, code, and two new benchmarks are publicly released — and Novelty (70) reflects the transferable BCPO routing recipe plus the informative cross-model negative controls showing naive generation-assisted reasoning degrades baselines. Rigor (50) pulls the composite down: no error bars or significance tests anywhere, an author-built LLM judge scoring the authors' own benchmark, a test set filtered to favor the proposed mechanism, and no component ablation attributing Rynn-VP gains to scene memory vs. self-forcing vs. duration prediction. Resilience (55) is limited by these benchmark-validity concerns; the thin robot-control evidence (3 real tasks, 60 trials) further bounds the claims. Problem & Motivation: Robotics and embodied-AI researchers lack unified models that can both understand the physical world and predict how it evolves across successive subtasks. Existing unified multimodal models (UMMs) that jointly model understanding and generation degrade over long horizons as scene changes and prediction errors accumulate, and static video predictions overlook intermediate dynamics. A second, related gap: nobody knows whether generated video actually helps answer embodied questions about unobserved future states — dedicated benchmarks for sustained visual planning and for the marginal value of video prediction in embodied reasoning are absent. The paper targets practitioners building "robot brains" who currently stitch together separate understanding, world-model, and action modules. Key Idea: The central insight is that long-horizon visual planning can be factored into an autoregressive reasoner that emits a structured, duration-specified video prompt (next subtask + anticipated visual evolution + duration) and a rectified-flow generator that predicts the corresponding clip, with a cross-chunk scene memory (4 independently encoded reference frames + a continuous temporal prefix from the previous clip's tail) keeping predictions consistent, and self-forcing (condition degradation, cached offline endpoint replacement, history replacement) training the generator to continue from its own imperfect outputs. A second key idea is BCPO: learn when generation helps by supervising a soft routing head with the stop-gradient reward difference between direct and generation-assisted branches, while optimizing each branch with sequence-level GSPO. Methodology: The pipeline is Cosmos3's Mixture-of-Transformers: an 8B AR reasoner and 8B diffusion generator sharing joint attention. Stage 1 fine-tunes the reasoner (autoregressive loss on assistant tokens, Eq. 2) on ~2.0M understanding samples plus curated spatial/physical/affordance/trajectory data, teaching subtask prediction, world-model prompt writing, and video-conditioned QA. Stage 2 freezes the reasoner and fine-tunes the generator with a flow-matching loss (Eq. 3) restricted to prediction positions, over 1,083,458 video clips (~1,370 hours), using I2V, FL2V, and cross-chunk continuation modes with scene-memory token placement (Eq. 1) and the three self-forcing variants. Stage 3 (BCPO) trains an 8B agent from the reasoner with GSPO clipping (Eq. 5), a soft routing target qG(x) = sigmoid((µG−µD)/T) (Eq. 6), combined loss LRL = LGSPO + λroute·Lroute + β·LKL − η·H, and task-grounded rewards r = F·Ak with a cubic shaping function on normalized error (δ=0.30); 22,007 training questions, 512 trajectories per update, 344 updates. The WAM extension adds a subtask-latent conditioning path and an 18-block flow-matching action head (At ∈ R^48×12) reading all 36 generator layers, trained in three stages (reasoner → generator → action head, Eq. 10–13) on ~1,600h atomic + 177h composite RoboCasa365 trajectories. Critical design decisions: (1) token-group concatenation for scene memory instead of a separate memory encoder — justified as avoiding new modules, but no ablation against alternatives; (2) generator frozen during agentic RL — reasonable for stability but caps the gains; (3) LLM-based relabeling of subtask boundaries (Qwen3.6-27B) and prompt rewriting (GPT-5.6-Terra/Luna) — introduces unquantified label noise. Key Results: On 10 public embodied benchmarks, RynnUnify averages 57.9 among UMMs (vs. Cosmos 3 Nano 53.2, RxBrain 44.9, BAGEL 28.0), leading on 6/10 metrics and beating all compared models on EmbSpatial (83.0), RefSpatial-Bench (60.3), and ShareRobot Trajectory (0.27). On Rynn-VP (200 egocentric tasks), it scores 54.80 overall vs. 45.05 for Cosmos 3 Nano (PI 45.66 vs 30.50), though below the composed GPT-5.6-Terra + MiniMax-H3 system (65.71). On Rynn-GEU, direct answering scores 44.0; the agentic extension reaches 50.0, with large per-task gains (Area 35.9→66.2, Mess 8.5→29.1) and +8.4 on MindCube — while the same rollout protocol lowers BAGEL/RxBrain/Cosmos 3 Nano Rynn-GEU averages. The WAM achieves 52.0%/50.0% on RoboCasa365 Composite-Seen/Unseen and 51.5% on the author-selected Selected-20 mobile-manipulation tasks (vs. CMA 47.0, Xiaomi-Robotics-1 46.0, Cosmos 3 45.0); on a real Astribot S1 it averages 46.7% complete-task success over 3 tasks × 20 trials (vs. GR00T N1.7 26.7%, π0.5 25.0%). Baselines are current (2025–2026 models). Notably, the paper honestly reports that fine-grained spatial scores (position, distance, size) decrease after agentic rollout, and that a subset of Rynn-GEU was filtered to favor future-evidence-sensitive questions. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (cross-chunk scene memory with token-group conditioning; BCPO for learn-when-to-generate routing) + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (Rynn-VP, Rynn-GEU) + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (16B unified embodied model with WAM extension). The genuinely novel elements are BCPO's branch-conditional reward-difference routing and the memory-conditioned long-horizon rollout; the base architecture is inherited from Cosmos3, self-forcing is adapted from prior work, and the WAM is a competent integration of latent planning plus flow-matching action heads — the contribution is the system integration and the empirical demonstration that generation helps only when selectively invoked. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the paper contrasts agentic vs. direct answering and analyzes why baseline rollouts fail, but provides no component ablation for scene memory, self-forcing variants, or duration prediction — the attribution of Rynn-VP gains to these mechanisms is argued, not measured. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; real-robot results are 20 trials per task without confidence intervals. Code, model weights, and benchmark materials are released (GitHub: alibaba-damo-academy/RynnUnify; HuggingFace collection; project page). Methodological concerns: (1) Rynn-VP scoring relies on an author-built LLM evaluator (GPT-6-sol with a custom "Skill"), creating potential self-favoring bias, partially mitigated by 300 human-review assignments; (2) Rynn-GEU test questions were filtered by whether a model answers better with the reference future video — a selection criterion aligned with the proposed method's mechanism; (3) Selected-20 RoboCasa365 tasks are author-chosen and author-run for all baselines (full-split baselines are taken from published reports); (4) heavy reliance on GPT-5.6/Qwen judges for training-data labels and RL rewards. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component). - Practical: Runs on accelerator hardware the authors control; 16B parameters with video generation at 480p/24fps and 35–50 diffusion steps per segment is within reach of commodity multi-GPU setups, though closed-loop control additionally needs a real-robot stack. - Efficient: Not favorable — the paper itself flags that interleaved generation is too costly for closed-loop control; each agentic answer requires a multi-step diffusion rollout, and the WAM mitigates this with a single denoising step plus feature reuse. - Effective: Evidence supports improved embodied understanding and planning versus UMM baselines, but the robot-control evidence (3 tasks, 20 trials, selected simulation subset) shows capability on a narrow slice rather than general manipulation competence. - Scalable: Untested beyond 16 steps of planning rollout and 3 real tasks; the paper claims future work on computational cost and cross-task generalization but provides no scaling experiment. The work delivers a real artifact: model weights, code, and two benchmarks are publicly released. Strengths: - The BCPO routing formulation is a clean, transferable contribution: using the stop-gradient reward difference between direct and generation-assisted branches as a soft supervision target for tool invocation is a general recipe for learn-when-to-use-generation, beyond embodied settings. - The cross-model contrast is unusually informative: applying identical generation-assisted rollouts to BAGEL, RxBrain, and Cosmos 3 Nano hurts Rynn-GEU scores, isolating that RynnUnify's gains come from selective routing, robust video interpretation, and precise prompt formulation rather than from generation per se. - Self-forcing adaptation (condition degradation, cached endpoint replacement, joint history replacement) is a well-motivated answer to the train/test mismatch of autoregressive clip chaining, and the honest reporting of spatial-score regressions after agentic rollout adds credibility. - Building the WAM by reusing the UMM's generator video features for action prediction (single denoising step, 18-block cross-attention head) is an economical design that connects world prediction to control without a second large model. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that generated videos distort fine-grained geometry (evidenced by post-rollout drops on position/distance/size tasks), that simulator-free visual planning performance needs broader physical-execution validation across tasks and environments, and that the computational cost of interleaved generation is prohibitive for closed-loop control. They also disclose that Rynn-GEU's future-oriented sample filtering is a heuristic (stochastic responses make the selection non-definitive) and that baseline Selected-20 numbers were obtained by their own evaluation. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Rynn-VP's evaluator is an LLM judge designed by the same team, scored with weights the same team chose; agreement statistics with humans (beyond "feedback guided refinement") are not reported, so the 9.75-point margin over Cosmos 3 Nano could partly reflect evaluator bias toward the authors' generation style. - No ablation decomposes the Rynn-VP gain into scene memory, self-forcing, duration prediction, and embodied data scaling — the causal story in Section 7.2.2 is plausible but unverified. - Rynn-GEU's test set was explicitly filtered for questions where future video changes the answer, which structurally advantages generation-assisted methods on the benchmark the authors also train on (the training data and test data come from the same construction pipelines with scene-level separation only). - The real-robot WAM keeps the reasoner frozen and trains on demonstrations from only the target platform; generalization to unseen real tasks, longer horizons, or other embodiments is untested, and the 46.7% average rests on just 60 trials total. - RL reward quality depends on Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 semantic judgments; no measurement of judge accuracy against human labels is provided. - Generator failure handling ("missing feedback") and the routing mask conditions could mask cases where the agent learns to avoid generation due to infrastructure flakiness rather than task difficulty; no analysis of learned routing behavior (e.g., what fraction of questions route to G) is reported. Bottom Line: For researchers building unified embodied or world-model systems, this paper is worth reading for the BCPO routing recipe, the scene-memory/self-forcing machinery, and the rare negative controls showing naive generation-assisted reasoning fails — but the robot-control claims should be treated as preliminary, and the benchmark results deserve independent replication before being taken as the new reference point.

CoEvoLoop: Closed-Loop RL Training of Customer-Service Agents by Co-Evolving Environment , Reward, and Policy

H Cai, J Chen, Y Zhou, W Ren, CZW Marcus, TLH Faith… · aclanthology.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CoEvoLoop, a closed-loop training system in which a customer-service assistant policy, an LLM user simulator (the RL environment), and an LLM grader (the reward model) are all retrained each round under a fixed-budget expert calibration loop, and demonstrates the loop lifts strict all-15-dimension pass rate from 0.879 (SFT) to 0.904 on 241 held-out cross-border-payment profiles. - Why it's important: Enterprise RL for dialogue agents requires LLM proxies for customers and rewards, and these proxies are exploitable — the paper shows RL against an uncalibrated grader actively degrades the policy below its SFT starting point, a failure mode that silently wastes training compute and ships worse agents. - How it does it: Each round, experts annotate a sampled subset of trajectories (~20, under 4 expert-hours), the annotations update both simulator and grader (SFT/DPO), and the assistant is retrained with GRPO against the newly calibrated grader, closing the reward-exploitation loophole that freezes proxies leave open. - The good: Blind two-expert human evaluation on 40 trajectories per system (480 ratings total) tracks the grader-measured gains at Pearson r = 0.93, so the improvement is not merely metric gaming against the authors' own reward model. - The missing: All evaluation is on one proprietary cross-border-payment domain with a custom strict-agg@eval metric and no online deployment metrics (CSAT, escalation rates), and there are no error bars or significance tests despite per-profile stochastic runs. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building RL-trained enterprise dialogue agents who must decide how to allocate scarce expert annotation between reward calibration and environment realism; skippable for readers seeking general RL methodology, since every component (SFT, DPO, GRPO, LLM-as-judge) is standard.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Non-Obviousness (65) is the standout: the quantified reward-exploitation failure (training reward rising while calibrated score falls below SFT) is a concrete instance of a failure practitioners suspect but rarely measure, and the fixed-budget expert-calibration loop is a transferable reframing. Rigor (60) is solid on ablation decomposition and cross-grader evaluation discipline but weakened by no variance reporting despite 5 stochastic runs, an unreported inter-annotator agreement, and a custom self-graded primary metric. Practical Impact (65) reflects the MIT-licensed demo artifact and unusually actionable expert-cost accounting (~10 expert-hours for the measured gain); Completeness (70) is a credibility positive with direct, non-minimizing limitations. Weighted composite: 0.15*60 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*65 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*62 + 0.30*65 = 64.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying RL-trained customer-service agents cannot train on real customers and lack a ground-truth reward for enterprise-specific quality and compliance, so they substitute an LLM user simulator and an LLM-as-judge grader. Prior pipelines treat at least one of these proxies as frozen infrastructure. The paper's motivating observation is a failure mode with real cost: while training against a frozen grader, the policy's training reward rose monotonically while its expert-calibrated score fell below its own supervised starting point — the policy learned the grader's blind spots rather than better service. A frozen simulator compounds this by rehearsing customer behaviors the policy has already mastered, and a single scalar reward cannot express the tension between helpfulness and strict compliance or attribute which rule was broken. The problem is squarely industrial: organizations with compliance-gated, multi-turn service workloads (here, cross-border payments) where a failed dimension (e.g., PII leak, unauthorized promise) is a costly defect. Key Idea: The core insight is that the RL environment, the reward model, and the policy should all be trainees of a single expert-anchored loop: per-round recalibration of the grader by a small fixed-budget set of expert annotations closes the reward-exploitation gap that frozen proxies allow, and the same annotations refresh the simulator so rollouts track the policy's current weaknesses. This is a systems-level reframing rather than a new algorithm — the trick is treating expert calibration as a recurring, budgeted loop component rather than a one-time setup cost. Methodology: The system composes three learned components plus a human annotation stage. (1) User simulator (Qwen3-8B): generates 6-turn dialogues conditioned on structured user profiles (background, knowledge gap, action history, problem description) reverse-engineered from anonymized real dialogues; trained with SFT on ~15,312 dialogues (real H2H plus synthetic reactions to assistant failures) then DPO on 419 preference pairs contrasting robust vs. undesirable reactions to flawed assistant behavior. (2) Grader (Qwen3-32B, split into knowledge-intensive and non-knowledge sub-models): scores 15 binary dimensions across four pillars (Security & Compliance, Information Correctness, Logical Reasonability, Service Quality) and emits critiques; trained via difficulty-aware SFT on teacher pseudo-labels (Qwen3-235B/80B-Next with cross-rollout consistency as confidence, low-confidence instances discarded) followed by stability-enhancing DPO on borderline cases. (3) Assistant (Qwen3-32B): SFT on ~500 grader-filtered dialogues distilled from Gemini 2.5 Pro, then trajectory-level GRPO maximizing G = Ragg + Rfmt + Rlen, where Ragg = max(0, 1 − 0.2·nz) is a stepped degradation over the number of failed dimensions nz, Rfmt is a binary <think>-format penalty, and Rlen is a DAPO-inspired soft length penalty. (4) Expert calibration: a fixed per-round budget of ~20 sampled trajectories (prioritized by grader uncertainty and historical disagreement) reviewed on the same 15-dimension rubric, with turn-level corrections feeding both the grader/simulator updates and SFT. Critical design decisions: binary dimensions chosen because merged dimensions lowered inter-annotator agreement in pilots (justified); the stepped 0.2-per-dimension reward penalty (partially ablated in Table 6, where the stricter variant underperformed); and scoring all variants with the final calibrated grader rather than the grader each variant trained against (a good anti-self-evaluation safeguard). The framework is standard RL post-training (SFT → DPO → GRPO) orchestrated in a loop; the contribution is the orchestration, not any new optimization objective. Key Results: Evaluation covers 241 held-out profiles × 5 stochastic runs = 1,205 trajectories per system, disjoint from 2,906 RL training profiles and the grader's 414-dialogue held-out benchmark. Strict-agg@eval (all 15 binary dimensions must pass): base Qwen3-32B 0.821; +SFT 0.879; RL with no loop 0.855 (below SFT); RL with frozen simulator but evolving grader 0.892; frozen grader but evolving simulator 0.863; full loop 0.904. Frontier baselines without fine-tuning score 0.867–0.875 (Claude-3.5-Haiku, Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5.2). Blind human evaluation (2 experts × 40 trajectories × 6 systems = 480 ratings): 85.00% (SFT) → 88.75% (full loop), correlating with grader scores at r = 0.93. Over three rounds, simulator Turing score rises 0.722 → 0.958 (real humans score 0.967 under the same protocol), grader Cohen's Kappa rises 0.498 → 0.663 (92.44% accuracy vs. experts). The most striking finding is the reward-exploitation result: the round-1 policy improved its training reward while its calibrated score dropped below the SFT baseline, and per-round recalibration reversed this. The ablation is honest but weakens the simulator's role: grader co-evolution alone captures 0.892 of the 0.904, so simulator co-evolution contributes only +1.2 points. Baselines are current frontier models but are not domain-fine-tuned, making the comparison favorable to the authors' system; tested scale is small (hundreds of profiles, one domain). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the demonstrated co-evolution of environment, reward, and policy under recurring expert calibration with a fixed annotation budget, together with the quantified failure mode of reward exploitation against a frozen grader (calibrated score falling below the SFT baseline while training reward rises). Every constituent technique — profile-driven LLM simulation, SFT, DPO, GRPO, LLM-as-judge with multi-dimension rubrics, human-in-the-loop data refinement — is standard; prior work (e.g., policy–reward co-adaptation, simulator–policy joint training) covers pairs of these components, and the paper positions itself accordingly. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and load-bearing: the loop is decomposed into no-loop / frozen-simulator / frozen-grader / full-loop variants, plus a reward-design ablation (model size 8B vs. 32B, Ragg vs. Ragg-strict, length buffers 200/300 vs. 500/1100). Data hygiene is explicit: disjoint held-out profiles, grader benchmark, and assistant evaluation set; all variants scored by the same final grader to avoid self-evaluation artifacts. No error bars, multiple-seed variance, or significance tests are reported despite 5 stochastic runs per profile. Human validation is spot-check scale (480 ratings, 2 experts) and inter-annotator agreement for the human evaluation is not reported. Demo code is released under MIT (github.com/ant-intl/CoEvoLoop) with a demo video, but customer-derived training/evaluation data are withheld for privacy, so full reproduction is impossible. Methodological concerns: the primary metric (strict-agg@eval) is a custom, non-comparable metric scored by a model the authors trained; the paper mitigates this credibly with blind human evaluation, but at small n. The authors openly flag the custom metric and single-domain scope in Limitations, which is a credibility positive. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built training system with an industrial evaluation). Practical: Runs on 1 node × 8 GPUs with Qwen3-8B/32B backbones — modest, commercially available hardware. Efficient: Expert cost is explicitly bounded (~10 min/trajectory, ~79 expert-hours one-time, under 4 hours/round, ~10 total hours for the full three-round gain), though GPU cost of the loop rounds is not reported. Effective: Blind human evaluation at r = 0.93 with the automated metric supports real effectiveness on the proxy task, but no online indicators (CSAT, escalation-to-human rates) exist yet, so production effectiveness is unproven. Scalable: Untested beyond one domain and ~3,000 training profiles; whether the fixed annotation budget suffices as business policies and failure modes diversify is claimed but not shown. The work delivers a software artifact (MIT-licensed demo system and interfaces), though not the trained models or data. Strengths: (1) The reward-exploitation demonstration — rising training reward coinciding with a calibrated score drop below the SFT baseline — is a concrete, quantified instance of a failure practitioners suspect but rarely measure, and it directly motivates the loop design. (2) The ablation cleanly attributes the gain: grader co-evolution is the dominant factor (0.863 → 0.892 frozen-simulator variant) and the simulator adds a smaller but positive increment, an honest decomposition many system papers omit. (3) The cross-evaluation discipline (never scoring a variant with the grader it trained against) plus blind human evaluation at matching correlation is the strongest available evidence design for a paper whose reward model is also its judge. (4) The cost accounting for expert calibration (~10 expert-hours for the entire measured improvement) makes the human-in-the-loop requirement actionable rather than aspirational. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: human validation is spot-check scale and no online indicators (customer satisfaction, escalation rates) exist; the loop assumes qualified domain experts and requires bootstrapping a QA function where none exists; strict-agg@eval is custom and not cross-paper comparable; experiments cover a single proprietary cross-border-payment domain; and data cannot be released. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, and the four practical findings (instruct over thinking models for simulators/graders, H2H/H2M distribution mismatch, helpful-assistant priors ruining user simulation, reward-design sensitivity) are candid failure-mode reports that add credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No variance reporting: with 5 runs per profile and per-dimension binary scores, confidence intervals on the 0.904 vs. 0.892 gap (and the +3.75-point human gain on 40 trajectories) are computable and absent — the headline margins may not be significant. (2) Inter-annotator agreement between the two blind human evaluators is unreported, so the human-evaluation noise floor is unknown. (3) The frontier baselines (GPT-5.2, Gemini-2.5-Pro) are used zero-shot; a domain-SFT'd frontier model would isolate whether the loop beats simply fine-tuning a stronger base. (4) Grader-drift risk is unaddressed: since all variants are scored by the final grader, a systematic bias in that final grader would flatter the full-loop system, and the human check covers only 40 trajectories per system. (5) The loop's convergence behavior beyond three rounds is unexplored — whether calibration and policy improvement reach equilibrium, or oscillate, is not shown. (6) Compliance gains are claimed, but no per-pillar breakdown (e.g., Security & Compliance failure rates before/after) is reported to verify that the strict compliance dimensions, not just service-quality dimensions, improved. Bottom Line: For teams building RL-post-trained enterprise dialogue agents with LLM proxies for users and rewards, this paper offers a directly transferable, cost-quantified recipe and a memorable warning about frozen-reward exploitation; for readers outside that niche, the methodological novelty is thin and the single-domain, self-graded evaluation limits what can be generalized from it.

Are LLM-Generated Formal Specifications Faithful to Their Requirements? A Study on Bimodal Formal Specification Generation

W Wang, S Chen, Z Sun, S Feng · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents the first empirical study of LLM-based formal specification generation in a bimodal setting — given both a natural-language requirement and a C implementation of unknown correctness — and releases a 1,403-program ACSL/Frama-C benchmark that pairs correct and incorrect human-written implementations with the same requirement. - Why it's important: Existing LLM specification generators assume the code is correct and treat verifier pass as success, but the actual purpose of verification is to check code against requirements — so a specification that passes on buggy code is a dangerous false positive, and until now nobody had measured how often this happens. - How it does it: The authors build a filtered and I/O-rewritten benchmark from CodeContests, generate ACSL specifications with three LLMs under four research questions, and classify specification faithfulness on buggy code using an E-ACSL runtime-checking taxonomy (correct/wrong/weak/misled) calibrated against human analysis, plus a two-stage requirement-first prompting workflow called RULER. - The good: The central negative findings are quantified and robust: code-only prompting verifies more specifications (22.73%) than requirement+code (18.47%), only ~24–26% of buggy implementations receive a faithful specification, and formal specifications as correctness classifiers lose badly to the non-formal HoarePrompt (average MCC 0.58 vs. −0.45). - The missing: Every configuration is run once with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests despite acknowledged LLM nondeterminism, and the taxonomy thresholds (Cohen's kappa 0.51–0.57 against humans, rising to 0.67–0.72) plus a large 'Other' bucket (41.7% of GPT-5.5's syntactically valid specs) leave the headline faithfulness rates uncertain. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-based specification generation, deductive verification, or requirement-code consistency checking — it defines a new evaluation setting whose negative results should reshape how these systems are benchmarked; skip it if you only want verified-generation techniques, since it proposes no method that fixes the problem it identifies.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Practical Impact (40) suffers because no code, data, or benchmark release URL is stated despite the paper's evaluative mission.
