Problem & Motivation: LLM-based specification generation (SpecGen, AutoSpec, FormalBench, etc.) overwhelmingly generates specifications from source code alone and implicitly assumes the implementation is correct, treating verification pass as success. This inverts the purpose of formal verification: the semantic oracle should be the requirement, not the code. If the implementation is buggy, a code-derived specification merely encodes the bug, and a verifier will happily 'confirm' incorrect software. Prior work either generates non-verifiable assertions from requirements (Endres et al.) or uses specifications from correct programs to catch mutants (Richter & Wehrheim), leaving open whether LLMs can generate verifiable ACSL specifications that are faithful to the requirement when implementation correctness is unknown. The stakeholders are researchers and practitioners building LLM-assisted verification pipelines who currently have no benchmark or metric for requirement faithfulness. Key Idea: Reframe specification generation as a bimodal problem where verification pass is not a success signal: since Beh(S) = Beh(R) is the goal, a faithful specification must fail verification on incorrect code, so passing verification on buggy code indicates the specification is either too weak (Weak) or was 'misled' into encoding the buggy behavior (Misled). This reversal of the standard pass/fail oracle — plus a runtime E-ACSL-execution proxy (ValidRate, WrongAcceptRate, RightAbortRate, TimeoutRate with calibrated thresholds) for automating the otherwise-hard semantic classification — is the conceptual core that lets the authors measure faithfulness at scale. Methodology: The pipeline has four parts. (1) Benchmark construction: from 10,000 CodeContests problems, filter to C99-compatible C++ solutions with complete natural-language descriptions and 'wrong answer' buggy solutions (1,083 problems), rewrite scanf/printf I/O into a `__solve` function with argument/return interfaces via static analysis plus LLM-based rewriting (gpt-5.4-mini, up to 3 fix rounds validated against test cases), yielding 500 problems / 1,403 programs (500 correct, 903 incorrect) stratified into four control-flow complexity tiers (CF-1 no branches to CF-4 nested loops; avg. 32.8 LOC). (2) Generation: GPT-5.5, gpt-5.4-mini, and DeepSeek-v4-pro produce ACSL specifications ⟨precondition, postcondition, auxiliaries⟩ under three input modalities (Req.+Code, Req.+Signature, Code only); Frama-C 32.0 with the WP plug-in (Alt-Ergo + Z3, 30s timeout) checks syntax and discharges proof obligations. (3) Faithfulness taxonomy: for buggy code, each specification is executed on up to 40 test cases under E-ACSL instrumentation; rates computed from outcome cells A–E are thresholded (θ_v=0.5, θ_t=0.6, θ_w=0.6, θ_r=0.10, calibrated against 50 human-labeled specs per model) to assign Correct/Wrong/Misled/Weak/Other labels, with sensitivity analysis showing ≤2.06% label change under threshold perturbation. (4) Interventions and comparison: RULER (requirement-only reasoning stage, then generation with Frama-C feedback and an LLM judge that may stop on verification failure), AutoSpec adapted without refinement, and a reimplementation of HoarePrompt for C, compared as requirement-code consistency classifiers using balanced accuracy, TPR, FPR, and MCC on a 200-problem/557-implementation subset. Critical design decisions: using contest 'wrong answer' programs as buggy implementations is well-justified (behavioral deviation from requirement); the E-ACSL proxy for semantic classification is only moderately validated (kappa 0.51–0.57 vs. humans) but sensitivity-tested; treating Frama-C pass as 'Correct' prediction in RQ4 conflates verifiability with faithfulness on correct code, which the authors do not fully justify. Key Results: RQ1 (500 correct programs × 3 models): Code-only achieves the highest aggregate verification rate at 22.73% (341/1,500), vs. 18.47% for Req.+Code and 9.27% for Req.+Sig.; conditionally on syntactic validity, 38.19% vs. 30.57% vs. 19.61%. GPT-5.5 verifies 36.60% under Code-only but only 10.40% under Req.+Sig. Verification collapses with complexity: Code-only verifies 61.11% (CF-1) down to 5.23% (CF-4). RQ2 (903 incorrect programs): only ~24.25–26.02% of implementations receive a syntactically valid, requirement-consistent specification; GPT-5.5's 'Other' bucket holds 41.68% of its valid specs, so its true faithfulness is uncertain; false positives skew toward Misled over Weak (misled = 81.82% of GPT-5.5's false positives) — the specification actively mirrors the bug rather than merely under-constraining it. RQ3: RULER two-stage decomposition alone hurts (277→248 successes on correct code); adding iterative refinement raises success from 18.47%→24.27% on correct and 24.95%→29.49% on incorrect code, but GPT-5.5 degrades on incorrect code after refinement (256→251), and wrong/misled/weak categories do not consistently decrease over repair iterations. RQ4 (557 implementations): HoarePrompt with GPT-5.5 reaches BA 0.9053 / MCC 0.8124, while the best formal pipeline (RULER+refine) averages BA 0.2688 / MCC −0.4452, with TPR as the bottleneck (correct implementations rejected because the LLM cannot produce verifiable faithful specs). The verification failure rate is a poor proxy for faithfulness in both directions — the study's most consequential quantitative finding. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (bimodal specification generation with unknown implementation correctness), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first ACSL benchmark pairing requirements with both correct and incorrect human implementations, verified with Frama-C), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (verifier pass is not a success signal; misled specifications dominate weak ones), and NEW METHOD for the RULER workflow, though RULER is a straightforward assemble of known moves (task decomposition + verifier-feedback refinement + LLM judge) and its contribution is the judge's stop-on-failure criterion. The genuinely novel element is the problem framing and the faithfulness taxonomy; the prompting machinery is a competent combination of existing ideas, and the E-ACSL-based automated classifier is an engineering contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partially present: threshold sensitivity (Table 5, ≤2.06% label change), a human-vs-automatic calibration study (50 specs per model, kappa reported per model), modality comparisons, complexity-tier breakdowns, and three models spanning capability levels. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere — each cell reflects a single generation run despite the authors' own acknowledgment of LLM nondeterminism, which is the study's biggest internal-validity weakness. No code, data, or benchmark release URL is mentioned in the paper. Methodological concerns: the E-ACSL proxy agrees only moderately with humans (kappa 0.51–0.57 overall), and the authors candidly flag that the large 'Other' bucket (especially for GPT-5.5) is conservatively excluded, potentially understating faithfulness; the HoarePrompt comparison is a reimplementation at 557 samples 'due to the extremely costly nature' of the baseline; the benchmark derives from CodeContests (likely in LLM pre-training data, partially mitigated by heavy rewriting); the I/O rewriting itself is an uncontrolled semantic-transformation risk the authors acknowledge. Baselines are current and appropriate (AutoSpec, HoarePrompt, SpecGen-style refinement). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (an empirical study plus a benchmark artifact; RULER is a workflow, not a shipped tool). Practical: Yes — everything runs on commodity LLM APIs plus Frama-C with open-source SMT solvers, no special hardware. Efficient: Specification generation is cheap (7K–110K tokens per classification for the formal pipelines) versus HoarePrompt's 46K–217K, but the low token cost buys negative MCC, so efficiency is moot at current quality. Effective: The evidence shows the current approach does not solve requirement-code consistency checking (MCC < 0 for all formal variants) — the paper's value is in demonstrating this, not in a working capability. Scalable: Untested beyond 32.8-LOC contest programs; the authors claim, without evidence, that industrial-scale verification is too hard to attempt, so behavior on realistic codebases is unknown. Deliverable: the paper describes a benchmark and taxonomy, but no released artifact (repository, dataset, or tool) is stated; it stops at paper form as far as the text shows. Strengths: (1) The problem framing is genuinely new and correct: redefining verification pass as a potential failure signal, and defining the bimodal task with Beh(S) = Beh(R) as the oracle, is a conceptual contribution the specification-generation literature has ignored. (2) The Misled-vs-Weak distinction, operationalized through calibrated E-ACSL runtime checking, is an insightful and reusable measurement technique — the finding that LLMs more often encode the bug than merely under-specify is the kind of result that should change how these systems are evaluated. (3) The benchmark is carefully engineered (I/O rewriting, test-validated LLM refinement, complexity stratification, wrong-answer-only buggy programs) and the first to pair requirements with both correct and incorrect implementations under a real verifier. (4) Honest negative results across all four RQs, including self-critical interpretation of the RULER gains and the GPT-5.5 'Other' ambiguity. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The threats-to-validity section is direct: (internal) I/O rewriting may change semantics in ways test cases miss, and LLM nondeterminism is unmitigated beyond fixed setup; (construct) verification outcomes and E-ACSL rates are only proxies for semantic faithfulness; (external) contest problems are small, well-specified, and unrepresentative of industrial requirements and codebases. The authors also candidly flag the large 'Other' rate for GPT-5.5 and that RULER refinement can push specifications toward the faulty implementation. This is a credibility positive — the limitations are confronted, not minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No repeated runs or variance estimates anywhere, so headline gaps like 18.47% vs. 22.73% (RQ1) and the RULER deltas are single-sample comparisons that could plausibly fall within run-to-run LLM variance. (2) RQ1 only classifies faithfulness on incorrect code; specifications verified on correct code are never checked for being weak or misled — a code-only specification that mirrors the implementation trivially verifies even when it under-constrains the requirement, so 'Code-only verifies best' may partly reflect verifier-gaming, which the paper's own framing implies but does not measure. (3) The RQ4 'Success' metric treats Frama-C pass as a correct-classification prediction, conflating verifiability with faithfulness, and the formal pipelines are denied a fairness adjustment (e.g., an abstain option) that might improve their classifier metrics. (4) Only one buggy program per problem category depth is sampled (max 2 incorrect per problem), and buggy programs are restricted to 'wrong answer' failures, excluding crashes/timeouts — a narrower bug population than real requirements violations. (5) No release URL for the benchmark, taxonomy code, or prompts, which limits reproducibility of the calibrated thresholds. (6) The HoarePrompt reimplementation quality is not independently validated on this benchmark. Bottom Line: Anyone building or evaluating LLM specification generators should read this paper for its benchmark, taxonomy, and the clear demonstration that verifier pass rates are the wrong metric — but practitioners seeking a deployable requirement-faithful generation method will not find one here, and the field currently has no stronger alternative to this evaluation framing.

Evolving Agent Interfaces

Saaket Agashe, Yuzhe Yang, Gonzalo Gonzalez-Pumariega, Bhuvan Chandra Koduru, Chih-Lun Li, Jiachen Yang, Ang Li, Xin Eric Wang · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Agent S4, a meta-agent system that autonomously evolves repositories of computer-use agent interfaces (executable tools plus usage knowledge) from synthetic task trajectories, using population-based mutation/crossover with held-out validation for parent selection. - Why it's important: Human-designed agent interfaces are a manual bottleneck that cannot keep pace with new applications and models, and interface-task mismatch forces agents to burn test-time compute on brittle GUI-only strategies. - How it does it: A meta-agent reads task-agent trajectories on ungraded synthetic tasks, writes revised interface repositories as code (mutation or crossover of two parents), and a binary-tournament population search selects parents by validation scores the meta-agent never sees — separating construction evidence from selection evidence. - The good: The asymmetric evaluation design (construction on verifier-free synthetic trajectories only, selection on held-out validation tasks) is a credible defense against benchmark overfitting, and the qualitative trajectory analyses concretely show what evolved interfaces change (e.g., a browser.api helper that reads a mailbox via the logged-in tab's API in 3 calls versus ~90 GUI calls). - The missing: The headline "3.8× improvement" conflates a harness change with evolution: the same model under the authors' Prime Agent harness with no repository already scores 15.74% binary (versus 5.56% for the Qwen CUA baseline), so the isolated effect of evolution over the seed repository is 19.44%→21.30% binary (+1.9 points) and 44.90%→46.90% partial (+2.0 points) on OSWorld V2 — and each condition is a single run with no error bars. - Read it or not: Worth reading for agent-framework researchers and anyone building self-improving agent systems, but skip if you only want the benchmark claims — the frontier-model comparisons are not apples-to-apples, and the genuine contribution is the evolution machinery, not the leaderboard position.

Problem & Motivation: Computer-use agents (CUAs) act through observation and action interfaces that are human-designed and frozen before deployment. The authors identify three consequences: (1) interface progress requires manual trajectory analysis and framework re-releases, which does not scale with task diversity; (2) a fixed interface mismatches many tasks — an agent types shell commands character-by-character through a GUI and reads occluded terminal screenshots when a direct shell interface would be faster and more reliable, and extra sampling compensates wastefully; (3) skill/memory methods compose only what the preset interface allows, so distillation cannot extend the interaction surface. The stakeholders are CUA framework builders; the domain is open-ended desktop automation. The gap closed is that prior systems (Agent S/S2/S3, UI-TARS, CoAct-1, AXIS) treat code, APIs, or tools as one predefined action type designed by humans, or as within-task throwaway programs — not as persistent, cross-task artifacts that an agent itself can design and improve from experience. Key Idea: The core insight is that interfaces are code, so an agent that can read trajectories and write code can redesign them — and this redesign can be run as an evolutionary search over complete repository versions, with a strict information firewall: the meta-agent constructing repositories sees only synthetic, ungraded training trajectories, while disjoint validation task scores (hidden from the meta-agent) determine which repositories become parents. This asymmetric evidence access plus a persistent repository containing executable interfaces and usage knowledge (docstrings encoding when/how to use them) is the trick. The optimization target is max over repositories R of E_{x~D}[J(A,R,x)] for a fixed task agent A = (model, harness). Methodology: Agent S4 maintains a population of repository variants R = (executable interfaces, knowledge), initialized from a 550-line, 15-function seed (GUI wrappers, accessibility tree, Chrome tab listing, OOXML readers). Each of N=30 evolution steps: (1) an operator schedule picks mutation (one parent) or crossover (two parents) via binary tournament on validation score; (2) a meta-agent (same Qwen3.8-27B model in a modified Prime Agent harness with persistent IPython kernel, 131,072-token context) studies the parents' saved synthetic-task trajectories, diagnoses failures/inefficiencies, and writes one descendant repository under a two-hour (OSWorld V2) or one-hour (ScienceBoard) construction budget, optionally with a scratch VM to test code; (3) the frozen descendant is run by the fixed task agent on synthetic training tasks (30 for OSWorld V2, 48 for ScienceBoard, all verifier-free with constant-zero placeholder evaluators) and 15 official validation tasks; (4) the descendant joins the population regardless of score, preserving the lineage DAG. Final repository selection is by validation performance, then evaluation on the full benchmark. Synthetic tasks are authored and reviewed by separate LLM agents (GPT-6 Astra coordinator, GPT-5.6-Sol authors/reviewers) with explicit overlap checks against official benchmark tasks. Critical design decisions: verifier-free construction (justified by the placeholder-evaluator protocol in the prompts), the training/validation firewall (justified by analogy to evolutionary curtailment), and keeping the harness in control of execution, permissions, and budgets. ScienceBoard adds a periodic denoising step re-evaluating the top-3 variants because single validation runs on 15 tasks are noisy — the paper shows one repository whose first-eval score of 73.3% fell to a 60.0% mean on re-evaluation. Key Results: On the full 108-task OSWorld V2 benchmark, Qwen3.8-27B with the evolved repository (no scratch VM) reaches 21.30% binary success and 46.90% partial score at $1.10/task; with a scratch VM, 19.44% binary and 51.06% partial at $1.27/task. The same model with the fixed Qwen CUA interface scores 5.56% binary / 20.69% partial at $1.39. Compared against reported numbers from the OSWorld V2 paper, this exceeds GPT-5.5 (13.0% binary, $25.50) and Claude Opus 4.8 batched (20.6%, $72.40) at 4.3% and 1.5% of their costs. On the full 169-task ScienceBoard benchmark, evolution raises success from 55.03% (seed) to 58.58% (99/169 vs 93/169 tasks), versus 41.4% for Qwen CUA, with the largest gain on KAlgebra (48%→68%); the repository grows from 15 to 64 functions. Ablations (Table 4) show the harness plus seed repository already achieves 19.44% binary / 44.90% partial, so evolution's isolated gain is +1.86 binary / +2.0 partial; population beats linear evolution on partial score with a scratch VM (51.06% vs 47.17%), and the no-scratch-VM run achieves the best binary success. These are single-run results without error bars on the test set; external baselines are self-run for Qwen CUA but transcribed from the OSWorld V2 reference paper for frontier models, under a different reference harness with a 500-step budget versus the authors' 300-step budget. The cost figures exclude repository-construction compute and assume an 80% input-cache hit rate. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (population-based evolution of interface repositories from verifier-free experience with asymmetric construction/selection evidence) applied to a partially NEW PROBLEM (autonomous, cross-task interface design as an agent capability). The genuinely new elements are the firewall between construction trajectories and selection scores, and evolving whole repositories (interfaces + usage knowledge + configuration) rather than prompts (GEPA), coding-agent code (Darwin Gödel Machine, ADAS), or within-task tools (LATM, SkillWeaver). The underlying machinery — LLM-driven code mutation, tournament selection, population retention, validation-based early curtailment — is a competent recombination of established ideas from neuroevolution, AlphaEvolve/ShinkaEvolve, and genetic programming, instantiated for computer-use interfaces. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and useful: seed vs. no repository vs. evolved, three evolution strategies (population/linear × scratch-VM), a denoising/re-evaluation analysis with explicit per-repository validation scores, full lineage graphs with per-variant scores, and tool-call/execution-efficiency comparisons that honestly report where savings do not materialize (all-task call counts are flat: 163.2 vs 162.1). No multiple seeds or significance tests are reported for the final full-benchmark evaluations — each headline number is one run, and the paper itself acknowledges "substantial run-to-run variance" on long-horizon tasks, which makes the 1.9-point evolution-over-seed gain on OSWorld V2 difficult to distinguish from noise (validation-task counts are only 15). Code is open-sourced at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s; synthetic task instructions are reproduced. Methodological concerns: (1) the final evaluation on OSWorld V2 includes the 15 validation tasks used for repository selection — mild selection leakage, acknowledged in framing but not quantified by excluding them; (2) the evolved-vs-baseline comparison crosses harness boundaries (Prime Agent vs. reference harness, 300 vs. 500 steps), so frontier-model comparisons are indicative rather than controlled; (3) construction cost is excluded from per-task cost claims; (4) synthetic tasks are authored by the authors' chosen LLMs following the benchmark's own design taxonomy, a subtle distributional coupling. Note this is a preprint (arXiv 2610.28601) with vendor-affiliated authorship (Simular), though the Qwen3.8-27B numbers are self-run rather than vendor-reported. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system built and run, with benchmark deployments). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on a single 27B open-source model via a commercial API (Parasail) on standard AWS VMs, no frontier-model dependency. - Efficient: Task-solving costs $1.10–$1.27/task, roughly 1/3 of the Qwen CUA baseline's failure-prone trajectory cost and 1.5–4.3% of frontier-model costs, but each evolution run adds 30 meta-agent constructions (up to 2 hours each) plus rollout costs that the paper excludes. - Effective: The evidence supports that evolved interfaces solve benchmark tasks better than the seed repository, but the effect size over the seed is small (+1.9 binary on OSWorld V2) relative to run-to-run variance; the large headline margins come mostly from the harness and seed. - Scalable: Not tested — 30 descendants and 30–48 training tasks per run; behavior at 10× evolution steps, larger populations, or larger task distributions is unexamined, and the paper does not claim it. The work delivers a software artifact (open-source code and evolved repositories) plus reusable design patterns (asymmetric evidence access, verifier-free construction), not just a paper. Strengths: - The training/validation firewall is the paper's real intellectual contribution: forcing repository construction to rely solely on ungraded synthetic trajectories while using held-out scores only for selection is a concrete, transferable mechanism against the Goodhart failure mode that plagues agent self-improvement, and it is argued with lineage evidence. - The qualitative analysis is unusually honest and mechanistic: the paper reports where efficiency claims break down (flat all-task call counts, the 11 common full-credit tasks where calls increase from 87.8 to 103.2), rather than cherry-picking. - The verifier-free setup — dummy constant-zero evaluators, no reference solutions, no success labels — is a strictly harder and more realistic training condition than most self-improvement work, making the positive results more meaningful. - Denoising analysis (Figure 6) exposes and then fixes a concrete selection pitfall: a 73.3% first evaluation on if-003 collapsing to a 60.0% mean, demonstrating the noise magnitude reviewers should demand in this area. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that validation tasks are drawn from the same benchmark and influence selection (while test tasks were never seen during construction); that a single validation run can overrate a repository (motivating denoising, run only on ScienceBoard due to OSWorld V2 cost); that the case studies are "not controlled comparisons" and "illustrate interface use rather than estimating a treatment effect"; and that full-credit subset comparisons involve different task subsets. They also transparently document the harness/interface mismatch with reference evaluations (300 vs. 500 steps, different action backends). This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted directly in the text rather than buried, though the abstract and Figure 2 still lead with the frontier-model comparison that these caveats undermine. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central framing ("3.8× the same model with fixed interfaces") compares the evolved repository against a different harness (upstream Qwen CUA), not against the same harness with no/seed repository; the controlled comparison in Table 4 shows only +1.86 binary / +2.0 partial from evolution over the seed. This gap between the framing and the controlled evidence is the paper's most significant presentation issue. - No multiple evolution runs or seeds: the entire pipeline is stochastic (LLM construction, tournament selection), so the 21.30% vs. 19.44% difference on 108 tasks (~2 tasks) carries no uncertainty quantification. - The test set includes the 15 validation tasks used for selection; the paper does not report results excluding them, leaving possible selection overfitting unquantified. - Qwen CUA baseline on ScienceBoard (41.4%) sits far below the authors' own seed repository (55.03%); whether that baseline is tuned fairly is not established. - Interface evolution is only demonstrated with the same model family for both meta-agent and task agent; transferability of an evolved repository across models or harnesses — the property that would make this most useful — is untested despite the repository being advertised as reusable "with compatible agents and harnesses." - Synthetic task authoring uses a capability taxonomy from OSWorld V2's own paper, so the distribution of evolved interfaces may be implicitly shaped by the benchmark's design, a subtler coupling than direct task overlap. Bottom Line: This is a genuinely interesting and honestly analyzed system with a transferable core idea (evolving interface repositories under a construction/selection firewall), but a practitioner should read it for the machinery and the ablation discipline, not for the headline frontier-model comparison — the controlled evidence for evolution itself is a ~2-point gain on 108 tasks from a single run, so treat the strong alternative reading (a better harness plus a good seed repository does most of the work) as currently unresolved.

Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs (5 ▲ )

Anita Kriz, Antonin Berthon, Nicolás Astorga, Mihaela van der Schaar · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 29 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AR-BED, a method that amortizes sequential Bayesian experimental design into a reasoning LLM by training its reasoning traces with expected information-gain rewards computed under an external, policy-independent generative model. - Why it's important: LLMs are known to gather information poorly in multi-turn settings — ignoring experimental feedback and relying on priors — and inference-time BED fixes this only at 61× the computational cost, which blocks real-time deployment. - How it does it: The core trick is decoupling the experimental generative model (a fixed finite contrastive hypothesis set plus a separate large LLM as semantic likelihood evaluator) from the policy being trained, then rewarding the policy's reasoning-plus-question outputs with a Rao-Blackwellized expected EIG that marginalizes exactly over the finite hypothesis and outcome spaces, accumulated over K-step rollouts with GRPO. - The good: The gains are consistent and cost-justified: the trained Gemma-4-E4B-it policy beats both inference-time BED-LLM (2376 s vs 38.9 s per game, a 61.1× speedup) and training-time ASIG (2.9× slower per step), generalizes to unseen categories, and transfers positively to the MediQ clinical benchmark (90.5%→94.7% accuracy on held-out dermatology, 84.8%→90.2% on out-of-domain specialties). - The missing: All headline results come from a single training run of a small (~E4B-scale) model evaluated on a toy game whose in-distribution evaluation targets are drawn from the same 200-animal contrastive set used to compute the training reward; error bars are SEM over three evaluation repeats, not training seeds. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM agents, active questioning, or RLVR post-training — it is the clearest demonstration to date that information gathering can be trained as a transferable reasoning skill; skip it if you need large-scale or real-user evidence, which it does not provide.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (74) and Non-Obviousness (74) are the strengths: decoupling the experimental generative model from the policy, with an exactly computable Rao-Blackwellized expected-EIG reward and the D.6 gradient decomposition, is a consequential and reusable insight that out-performs both inference-time BED (61× faster) and training-time ASIG. But Rigor (55) pulls the composite down: no training seeds anywhere, in-distribution evaluation drawn from the same 200-animal contrastive set that defines the reward (a Goodhart-adjacent design), a fully simulated GPT-5 MediQ loop, and no code or artifact release. Completeness (72) is helped by unusually careful confound separation and direct limitation handling, but Resilience (62) is reduced because the central oracle-corruption assumption is untested and the headline solve rate partly measures fit to the reward model's support. Impact (45) is low — a paper-only deliverable with no library, dataset, or checkpoint. Weighted composite: 0.20*74 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*74 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*45 = 64.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents must often acquire information adaptively — a clinician narrowing diagnoses, an assistant disambiguating a task — yet empirical work (Gupta et al. 2025; Krishnamurthy et al. 2024; Laban et al. 2026) shows LLMs are insensitive to experimental feedback and perform poorly in multi-turn settings. Inference-time BED methods (BED-LLM, Kobalczyk et al.) select questions by estimated EIG but require maintaining a posterior and a doubly-intractable EIG estimate at every step of every interaction, plus they derive the generative model from the LLM's own predictive distributions, which may misrepresent the experiment. Training-time amortization (DAD, Blau et al., ASIG) shifts cost offline, but prior LLM instantiations either use LLM-induced generative models or skip reasoning entirely. The gap: no prior method trains an LLM's reasoning process against an information-theoretic objective computed under a trustworthy, external model of the experiment. Key Idea: Because training-time amortization never needs the generative model at inference, the EIG used as the RL reward can be computed under a generative model chosen by the designers — a fixed uniform prior over a finite contrastive set ΘC and a separate oracle LLM providing the full distribution p(y|θ,x) over a small enumerable outcome space — rather than induced by the policy LLM. Since both hypothesis and outcome spaces are finite and enumerable, the one-step reward can be marginalized exactly (the Rao-Blackwellized expectation of the realized sPCE reward, Eq. 7), making the reward equal to the one-step EIG under the specified finite model rather than a noisy single-sample estimate, and removing a moving-target pathology: with a decoupled model, policy updates change which states are visited but not what counts as informative (Appendix D.6 derives the policy-induced vs. external gradient decomposition explicitly). Methodology: The policy is factorized as π(z_t, x_t | h_{t-1}) = π(z_t | h_{t-1})·π(x_t | h_{t-1}, z_t), jointly generating a reasoning trace and a question. Training proceeds in three stages: (1) roll out the current policy from sampled histories; (2) score the first design using the external generative model — posterior over the fixed contrastive set is computed exactly via cumulative likelihood products C_{t,ℓ} (assuming conditional independence of observations given hypothesis and design), and the expected reward r^EIG_t (Eq. 7) is the exact one-step EIG under this finite model; (3) optimize with GRPO over K-step returns R = Σ γ^k r^EIG_{t+k} (γ=0.5, K∈{1,2,3}), which recovers multi-step EIG in expectation. Concretely: Gemma-4-E4B-it with rank-16 LoRA, 4-bit loading, batch 128, 8 rollouts/state, 250 steps, GPT-5 (gpt-5-2025-08-07) as the semantic likelihood oracle, trained on 1,200 partial Twenty Questions trajectories over 100 animal targets with a 200-animal contrastive set; likelihoods are cached and low-weight hypotheses pruned. Three critical design decisions: (a) decoupling the generative model from the policy — well justified both intuitively and via the gradient decomposition in D.6, and ablated indirectly through the ASIG comparison; (b) expected vs. realized rewards — well justified by Rao-Blackwellization and confirmed empirically (Sec. B.2), with a honest derivation in D.5 showing the two diverge non-trivially when training targets and contrastive prior differ; (c) finite-horizon rollouts instead of a learned critic — motivated by the cost of critics over natural-language state-action spaces, but only validated at K≤3. Key Results: On Twenty Questions (50 games × 3 seeds per domain), AR-BED1 achieves the best final solve rate across all four categories and the highest average EIG per question on Animals, Plants, and Countries; with the 200-animal set it reaches 43.3% solve rate and 0.330 nats/question EIG on Animals and 40.7% on Plants (vs. 28.0% with the 100-animal set). Notable negative controls: adding inference-time reasoning to the base model hurts solve rate; the non-reasoning direct-amortization policy (AR-BED^Direct) improves in-distribution but transfers inconsistently. Against baselines: BED-LLM (inference-time, recent) improves only modestly over base and is 61.1× slower per game (2376 s vs 38.9 s); ASIG (training-time, with LLM-induced generative model) is 2.9× slower per training step and stays below AR-BED1 on Animals, Plants, and Countries. Ablations: a mammals-only contrastive set collapses solve rate to 16.7% (from 41.3%) and hurts even on mammals, showing coverage sensitivity; expected rewards beat realized rewards on Animals (0.330 vs 0.290 nats; 43.3% vs 34.0%) and Plants/Countries but not Celebrities; multi-step training gives small downstream gains (+0.0062/+0.0116 nats/question at horizons 2/3 for K=2), while the controlled Cube-NM environment shows a strong non-myopic effect (75.0% vs 30.2% MAP solve rate after five tests for K=2 vs K=1). Transfer: a separately trained medical policy improves MediQ accuracy from 90.5% to 94.7% on held-out dermatology and 84.8% to 90.2% on other specialties, with Brier scores dropping 0.165→0.120 and 0.227→0.157, using a GPT-5 patient and a GPT-5 decider. The contrast that inference-time reasoning alone can degrade performance, while training reasoning against an external information objective helps, is the most interesting finding. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel pieces are (i) decoupling the training-time generative model from the policy LLM for EIG-based RLVR — prior LLM-BED work (BED-LLM, ASIG) derives it from the policy's own predictive distributions — and (ii) the exact, Rao-Blackwellized expected-EIG reward made possible by enumerable hypothesis/outcome spaces, applied to rewarding reasoning traces. The surrounding machinery is a competent combination of existing ideas: sPCE per-step rewards from Blau et al. (2022), DAD-style amortization from Foster et al. (2021), and GRPO from DeepSeekMath, instantiated on a reasoning LLM. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: contrastive-set size (100 vs 200) and coverage (mammals-only), expected vs. realized rewards, training horizon K (with the useful distinction between training horizon and evaluation horizon), and a controlled Cube-NM mechanism check that cleanly demonstrates the non-myopic credit-assignment mechanism. Weaknesses: no independent training seeds anywhere — all SEMs are over three evaluation repeats of fixed checkpoints, and the Cube-NM result is explicitly single-seed; in-distribution Twenty Questions evaluation targets are drawn from the same 200-animal contrastive set that defines the training reward, so ID numbers partially reflect the reward model's own support (a Goodhart-adjacent concern the authors partially mitigate with held-out-label MediQ and truly-OOD domain tests); the MediQ evaluation relies on GPT-5 as both patient and decider, i.e., a fully simulated pipeline with vendor self-reported model components; no code, data, or checkpoint release is mentioned. Baselines (BED-LLM 2025, ASIG 2026) are current and appropriate. The theoretical derivations (D.3–D.6) are careful and honest about when the expected reward ceases to equal EIG. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained policy evaluated in simulated interactive environments). Practical: Yes at inference — the trained policy is a small LoRA adapter answering with a single forward pass per turn, requiring no oracle at deployment; training does require GPT-5 API access as the likelihood oracle. Efficient: 38.9 s vs 2376 s per game against inference-time BED (61×), and 2.9× cheaper per training step than ASIG, with 4-bit LoRA training of a small model. Effective: The evidence supports the stated claim within simulated settings — improved acquisition and transfer — but the clinical result is against an LLM-simulated patient and LLM-judged diagnosis, not real clinicians or patients. Scalable: Not tested — contrastive sets cap at 200 hypotheses, horizons at K=3, and the authors state that extending to longer horizons while keeping a reliable signal is open; the reward requires |ΘC| oracle likelihood queries per candidate design per step, which will strain scaling beyond small enumerable hypothesis sets. Deliverable form: paper only; no library, dataset, or checkpoint artifact is stated as released. Strengths: - The decoupled-generative-model insight is real and consequential: it converts BED from an inference-time posterior-maintenance burden into a stationary training objective, and the D.6 gradient decomposition (policy-selection vs. reward-model effects) gives the community a reusable analytical lens on why policy-induced EIG objectives are unstable. - The Rao-Blackwellized expected-EIG reward is a clean, exactly computable variance-reduction move enabled by the finite design, and the matched ablation (0.290→0.330 nats on Animals) supports it; the D.5 analysis of when realized and expected rewards diverge (the DKL term under mismatched target distributions) is a genuine theoretical contribution. - The evaluation separates confounds unusually well for this literature: reasoning-at-test-time vs. training-reasoning controls, direct vs. reasoning policies, training-horizon vs. evaluation-horizon in the multi-step analysis, and the Cube-NM environment that isolates the non-myopic mechanism from open-ended question generation. - Positive cross-task transfer from a synthetic game to MediQ (including +5.4 points on out-of-specialty cases) is the strongest evidence that the learned behavior is a generalizable skill rather than domain-tuned questioning. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that rollout horizons are short and that extending to longer horizons while maintaining a reliable training signal is open; they also acknowledge sensitivity to contrastive-set coverage under misspecification (demonstrated by the mammals-only experiment) and flag the size, composition, and weighting of the contrastive set as an open design question. The appendix further qualifies the multi-step results as modest and non-monotonic in K, labels Cube-NM as a single-seed mechanism check, and repeatedly distinguishes diagnostics from optimality claims. This is direct, non-defensive limitation handling — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - In-distribution evaluation targets come from the same 200-animal contrastive set used to define the reward, so the 43.3% headline solve rate partly measures fit to the reward model's support; the truly held-out evidence is the OOD domains and MediQ, where absolute solve/accuracy is reported but EIG-per-turn against a matched external model is not. - Single training run per configuration throughout the main results; with the acknowledged contrastive-set sensitivity, run-to-run variance in the learned policy could be material and is unmeasured. - The oracle likelihood (GPT-5) is itself the ground truth for information gain in training; no experiment probes what happens when the oracle's p(y|θ,x) is systematically wrong relative to the true environment answering the policy's questions at evaluation time — the method's central assumption is untested under oracle corruption. - MediQ evaluation is a fully simulated loop (GPT-5 patient, GPT-5 decider, GPT-5-scored probabilities); the accuracy deltas could partly reflect prompt/formatting interactions rather than better information gathering, and no human-clinician or real-record validation is attempted. - Baselines are tuned for fairness in compute but ASIG is run without its task-outcome reward component; a stronger ASIG variant with the combined objective, or a DAD-style sPCE baseline without LLM likelihoods, is not tested. - The release question is unaddressed: no repository, dataset, or checkpoint URL appears in the text, which limits reproducibility of a method whose reward pipeline (oracle prompts, caching) carries much of the engineering risk. Bottom Line: For anyone post-training LLMs to ask better questions, this is worth reading now — the decoupled-generative-model-plus-expected-EIG recipe is a concrete, well-ablated advance over BED-LLM and ASIG at a fraction of the cost — but the single-run, small-model, simulation-only evidence means practitioners should treat the MediQ transfer numbers as promising direction, not deployable fact.

Volatility-Corrected Prediction Intervals: Locally Adaptive Uncertainty Quantification for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting

JB Cho, DS Matteson · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes Volatility-Corrected Prediction Intervals (VCPI), a post-hoc calibration method that fits GARCH-family models to the standardized forecast residuals of a black-box time-series forecaster and applies a multiplicative scale correction to produce locally adaptive prediction intervals. - Why it's important: Time-series foundation models (Chronos, Moirai, TimesFM) increasingly ship uncertainty estimates used in high-stakes domains (energy, finance, climate), yet their intervals can hit nominal marginal coverage while undercovering by >20 points during high-volatility regimes — a failure mode the authors name local scale miscalibration. - How it does it: VCPI extracts a Gaussian reference scale from the forecaster's predictive quantiles by least squares, standardizes residuals by that scale, fits a GARCH/GJR-GARCH/EGARCH(1,1) model (with normal or skewed-t innovations, selected by validation coverage error) to forecast the residual scale correction, and multiplies the base scale by this correction with quantiles from the fitted innovation distribution. - The good: VCPI achieves the lowest rolling root mean squared coverage error (RMSCE) in nearly all 36 dataset × model × horizon-block cells at 80% coverage (e.g., on Colorado River/Chronos, RMSCE 0.062–0.116 vs. 0.171–0.210 for ACI, 0.188–0.263 for SPCI), with marginal coverage within ~0.05 of nominal, backed by a theorem showing GARCH's first-step interval is asymptotically closer to the post-volatility-jump oracle than quantile tracking as jump size Δ→∞. - The missing: Evaluation covers only four univariate series (one per domain), there is no comparison against the obvious cheap baseline of an EWMA/rolling-standard-deviation scale correction (which would isolate whether full GARCH machinery is needed), and no code release or error bars on metric differences are reported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone deploying conformal or native uncertainty estimates on top of time-series foundation models, or working on sequential calibration — it clearly documents a real failure mode and offers a simple, theoretically motivated fix; skip if you only need point-forecast accuracy or work exclusively outside heteroskedastic settings.

The composite is pulled down by Rigor (58) and Resilience (58): no seeds, bootstrap CIs, or significance tests anywhere; four hand-picked heteroskedastic series (one per domain); no code release; and — most damaging — no EWMA/rolling-SD ablation, so the paper cannot show that the GARCH machinery behind its central theoretical claim is what earns the empirical wins rather than any volatility smoother. Novelty (75) is genuinely high — reframing post-hoc interval calibration as volatility forecasting of standardized residuals is a real new formulation — and Non-Obviousness (72) is solid, but Completeness (60) suffers from the narrow evaluation and the missing simple baseline, and Practical Impact (45) reflects a compute-heavy (~100 CPU-days) method with no artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*45 = 63.

Problem & Motivation: Probabilistic forecasters are typically evaluated by marginal coverage — the long-run fraction of observations inside the interval. But forecast errors in time series are serially dependent and heteroskedastic, so intervals can attain near-nominal average coverage while alternating between overcoverage and undercoverage in local windows. The motivating example: on Capital Bikeshare data, the 80% native intervals from Chronos, Moirai 2, and TimesFM 2.5 drop below 60% empirical coverage during summer peaks. This matters most for zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) used in finance, energy, demand, and climate applications, where uncertainty is most consequential exactly during stress and regime change. Existing model-agnostic fixes (ACI, quantile tracking, EnbPI, SPCI) manipulate a scalar coverage-control parameter or calibration quantiles but do not explicitly model the temporal dynamics of residual variance. Key Idea: Treat the volatility of the base forecaster's standardized residuals as its own forecasting target. Because TSFMs already report a predictive scale, the residuals normalized by that scale should be roughly unit-variance; any remaining temporal variation in their magnitude is a multiplicative scale correction st, which GARCH-type recursions forecast well because the squared-error term lets a newly observed large shock immediately inflate the next interval — unlike conformal updates (ACI, QT) whose step size is fixed and independent of shock magnitude. Methodology: VCPI is a post-hoc, model-agnostic wrapper (it consumes only forecasts and observations, never re-querying or retraining the base model). Stages: (1) extract a reference scale σ̂t from the forecaster's predictive quantiles via the least-squares fit in Eq. (1) (a weighted summary of interquantile spreads; equals the standard deviation under Gaussian quantiles); (2) form normalized residuals et = (Yt − f̂t)/σ̂t; (3) fit a GARCH-family variance model (standard/GJR/EGARCH at order (1,1), with normal or standardized skewed-t innovations, selected by validation coverage error on a chronologically held-out 20% of the 256-observation calibration window, using the R rugarch package) and forecast the scale correction ũs t+h; (4) build intervals as f̂ ± σ̂ · s̃ · F̃−1(α/2), preserving the forecaster's location and baseline scale. A separate model is fit per horizon h = 1,…,16. The theory section analyzes the one-step GARCH update after an abrupt upward volatility jump Δ: under Assumptions 1–3 (iid symmetric innovations, local baseline stability, fitted GARCH coefficients bounded with ˆa+ˆb ≤ 1−κ), the GARCH half-width is within cα[1 − a(1−ρ)]Δ + Op(1) of the oracle while quantile tracking's error is at least cαΔ − Op(1), so VCPI's first post-shock interval is asymptotically closer to the oracle with probability → 1 conditional on the shock event. Critical design decisions: multiplicative (not additive) correction on top of the forecaster's own scale — well-motivated since TSFM scales already capture some structure; per-horizon model fitting — sensible but 16× the compute; model selection by validation coverage error — direct alignment with the evaluation target, though it risks overfitting the selection to the same coverage metric used downstream. Key Results: Three released TSFM checkpoints (Chronos-Bolt Small, Moirai-2.0-R Small, TimesFM-2.5 200M) × four daily univariate series (Bike Rental, Colorado River streamflow, NYISO electricity demand, Pasadena NO2), rolling-origin protocol with 256-step context, horizons 1–16, ~3,000 origins per dataset. At 80% nominal coverage, VCPI attains the smallest RMSCE in nearly every cell — e.g., Bike Rental/TimesFM horizon 1–4: RMSCE 0.045 vs. 0.073 native, 0.108 ACI, 0.105 QT, 0.112 EnbPI, 0.103 SPCI; Colorado River/Chronos horizon 9–16: 0.085 vs. 0.173 (ACI) and 0.165 (SPCI). Marginal coverage stays near nominal (mostly 0.78–0.85) with mild overcoverage; widths are competitive with or narrower than native intervals on two datasets and substantially narrower than ACI/QT (e.g., Colorado River at 90%: VCPI ~2,845 vs. ACI ~8,101 at horizon 9–16). SPCI produces narrower intervals on NO2/Electricity but by undercovering, worsening RMSCE. At 90% the advantage holds across the board; at 95% it holds mainly at horizons 1–4, with ACI competitive at longer horizons on some datasets — attributed to multi-step GARCH mean reversion and tail misspecification. Sensitivity analyses over ACI/QT learning rates (3 values each) confirm neither approaches VCPI's RMSCE under any setting. Baselines are current and standard (ACI NeurIPS 2021, QT NeurIPS 2023, SPCI ICML 2023); experiments are at standard, not stress, scale, and all findings are preprint (arXiv 2610.31621), not peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD, with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel move is reframing post-hoc interval calibration as volatility forecasting of standardized residuals — importing the econometric ARCH/GARCH toolbox to correct black-box forecaster uncertainty rather than to model the data-generating process — plus the asymptotic first-step adaptivity result contrasting GARCH and quantile-tracking updates. The ingredients (least-squares scale extraction, GARCH(1,1) fitting, quantile interval construction, model selection by validation coverage) are each standard; the contribution is their composition into a wrapper for TSFMs and the empirical demonstration that conformal methods systematically lose on local calibration. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist in the form of the GARCH-family/specification selection (validated on held-out data) and learning-rate sensitivity analyses for ACI and QT, but there is no ablation isolating the value of GARCH versus simpler scale smoothers, and no decomposition of which variance model choices matter. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; differences are shown point-estimate only. No code or data release is mentioned — VCPI is described in an appendix algorithm but no repository URL is given (base model checkpoints are public on HuggingFace). Methodological concerns: (1) RMSCE is the authors' own proposed primary metric, though it is a reasonable and clearly defined diagnostic; (2) the four datasets were hand-picked for pronounced heteroskedasticity (stated explicitly), which flatters a volatility-based method; (3) conformal baselines were run at learning rates following their original papers' conventions rather than tuned to the setting, though sensitivity tables partially mitigate this; (4) each domain contributes a single univariate site, so cross-series generalization is untested. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a theoretical analysis of a stylized regime, so the theory does not carry the primary claims). Practical: Yes — runs on CPU only (GARCH fits via R rugarch; base TSFMs are small checkpoints runnable on one CPU with 16 GB); no GPU required. Efficient: Calibration is the bottleneck — roughly 100 CPU-days total across ~3,000 origins × 16 horizons × 3 models × 4 datasets because a GARCH is refit at every origin and horizon; per-fit cost is seconds, but this is materially heavier than ACI/QT scalar updates. Effective: The evidence shows it fixes the stated problem (local calibration stability) on the authors' chosen heteroskedastic series while preserving marginal coverage and width — but effectiveness on weakly heteroskedastic or i.i.d.-like series is not shown. Scalable: Not tested or claimed beyond these settings; the per-horizon refitting scheme would scale linearly in horizons and origins, and high-frequency (intraday, millions of series) deployment is unaddressed. Delivers no released software artifact — the method exists at paper form with a precise algorithmic recipe; conformal baselines used official implementations (EnbPI/SPCI) and ACI/QT were reimplemented in R. Strengths: (1) Identification and naming of local scale miscalibration as a distinct failure mode — the motivating Figure 1 (native coverage dipping below 60% while marginal coverage is ~80%) is a clean, reproducible demonstration that marginal coverage is the wrong sole metric for TSFM uncertainty. (2) The theory is honest about its scope (first post-shock step, conditional on a shock event, fixed Δ→∞ asymptotics) and delivers a genuinely interpretable mechanism: GARCH consumes shock magnitude, conformal updates consume only miss indicators. (3) Empirically, VCPI dominates on the primary metric in nearly every cell across three foundation models and four domains, with the width column showing the stability gain is not bought by blanket widening — a non-trivial trade-off handled well. (4) The limitations section confronts the parametric misspecification risk and the multi-step GARCH mean-reversion failure directly, including pinpointing where ACI becomes competitive (95% level, longer horizons). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that VCPI inherits specification bias when the GARCH scale dynamics or the standardized error distribution F are misspecified, and that this trades flexibility for first-step adaptivity; they specifically flag multi-step GARCH mean reversion degrading the correction beyond horizons 4–8 and tail sensitivity at 95% coverage — consistent with the observed loss to ACI on Colorado River at 95%/long horizons. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations and adds credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The missing ablation: an EWMA or rolling-window standard-deviation scale corrector would cost one line to implement and would test whether GARCH's shock-responsiveness — the paper's central theoretical claim — is what drives the empirical wins, or whether any volatility smoother suffices. (2) Only four series, one per domain, all selected for pronounced heteroskedasticity; no panel of weakly-varying-volatility series to establish that VCPI does not degrade calibration when GARCH fits noise. (3) No distribution of results (seeds, bootstrap CIs, or per-dataset variance) supporting the claim of consistent dominance, though margins are often large enough to be visually credible. (4) No code release, limiting reproducibility of the ~100-CPU-day pipeline. (5) The conformal baselines manipulate only interval width; a hybrid that combines conformal guarantees with volatility scaling is an obvious next baseline not explored. (6) The theoretical result is confined to a single step after the jump; behavior over the subsequent adaptation transient (where conformal methods might catch up) is not analyzed. (7) Dataset selection and metric (RMSCE) both favor volatility-tracking methods by construction; a Winkler/interval-score or CRPS comparison is absent. Bottom Line: A practitioner wrapping uncertainty estimates around foundation-model forecasts on volatile real-world series gains a concrete, theoretically motivated, and empirically dominant post-hoc fix here, and the paper is worth reading for the local-coverage diagnosis alone; it is not the last word, though, because the missing simple-smoother ablation and single-series-per-domain evaluation leave open how much of the GARCH machinery is actually earning its keep.

UCVE: Graph Structured Retrieval for Compliance Validation

E Chen, M Menachery, R Nenavath, H Kumar… · aclanthology.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces UCVE, a framework that represents a domain's legal obligation space as a Contextual Requirement Graph with reinforcement-learning-weighted edges and retrieves violated requirements via low-pass spectral reranking over the graph Laplacian. - Why it's important: Compliance review costs are asymmetric — a missed violation carries regulatory or litigation risk while a false alarm costs only extra human review — so high recall over the obligation space is the binding constraint on automating legal compliance work. - How it does it: RL-trained scalar weights over six metadata edge types reshape a k-NN-sparsified graph's community structure so that projecting cosine similarity scores onto the bottom eigenvectors of the Laplacian (with α=0.8 blend) lifts lexically dissimilar but structurally co-relevant obligations and suppresses false positives. - The good: The component ablation (Table 5) demonstrates a genuinely conditional dependency — spectral reranking on the cosine-only graph and BFS on the RL-weighted graph each underperform, while their combination wins across all three domains — cleanly isolating why the method works rather than just that it works. - The missing: The tested requirement spaces are tiny (24–82 nodes), the headline gains shrink and lose statistical significance on the two larger/denser domains under the tuned-stopping robustness check, and a heat-kernel baseline marginally beats the method on OPP-115 under an unmodified stopping rule. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on compliance automation or graph-based RAG and care about exploiting inter-requirement structure for recall; skip it if you need methods validated at realistic obligation-space scale, since the authors themselves show the mechanism degrades as graphs grow.
Why this rank

Completeness (75) is unusually high — the authors volunteer that heat-kernel beats them under the unmodified stopping rule, that CLAUDETTE differences are insignificant, and that RL failed to converge on ESRS — and Non-Obviousness (70) is anchored by the well-isolated conditional-dependency finding that RL-weighted edges and spectral reranking each fail alone. However, Rigor (58) is capped by requirement spaces of only 24–82 nodes, headline CIs missing on the main table, and per-domain tuning on validation data of the test benchmarks, while Resilience (55) reflects fragile margins outside the smallest domain and Practical Impact (45) reflects no released artifact and a validation stage that collapses precision to 0.204 on ESRS. Problem & Motivation: Legal compliance teams (privacy offices, consumer protection authorities, ESG reporting functions) must verify that a document satisfies, violates, or leaves unaddressed every obligation in a predefined requirement space — a coverage problem, not a per-clause classification problem. Existing legal NLP systems (ContractNLI-style NLI, closed-set GDPR checkers, regulatory knowledge-graph RAG systems like PrivComp-KG and GraphCompliance) treat obligations as independent retrieval or classification targets, so they miss violations whose evidence lacks lexical overlap with the requirement text or is distributed across clauses. The authors argue the retrieval step, not the classifier, is the bottleneck: a requirement missed at retrieval is silently treated as satisfied, so retrieval recall sets the ceiling on end-to-end violation detection. Key Idea: The core insight is a conditional dependency between two components: reinforcement learning over typed metadata edges reshapes the graph Laplacian's community structure so that spectral clusters correspond to requirements that genuinely co-occur as relevant, and low-pass spectral filtering over that reshaped Laplacian is the mechanism that converts the learned structure into recall gains. Neither piece alone suffices — this is the paper's central, and best-supported, empirical claim. Methodology: UCVE is a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 builds a per-domain Contextual Requirement Graph: nodes carry requirement text, a natural-language validation question, and programmatic positive/negative class definitions; edges combine cosine similarity (threshold τ=0.5, weight fixed at 1.0) with six metadata edge types (e.g., same_category, same_sub_attribute, same_fairness_tier) whose learned scalar weights λ_t are trained by ϵ-greedy BFS traversal with credit assignment from ground-truth violation status (step-decaying credit +1.0→0 for hitting a violation, +0.1 within 3 hops, −0.05 otherwise), gradient ascent with learning rate 0.05 over 30 epochs, weights clamped to [0, 3]. This is RL in only a weak sense — it is gradient ascent on six scalars, not a traversal policy; the authors acknowledge this and defend it as appropriate for graphs of 24–82 nodes. Stage 2 retrieves: k-NN sparsification of the dense RL-weighted graph (k=3 for OPP-115/CLAUDETTE, k=5 for ESRS, chosen on validation data), eigendecomposition of the unnormalized Laplacian retaining the bottom n eigenvectors (n=5 or 12), and reranking by ŝ = 0.8·V_n V_n^T s + 0.2·s, with an adaptive stopping threshold of 0.75. The full pipeline passes retrieved nodes to a Llama-3.3-70B validator producing binary verdicts. Critical design decisions: (1) restricting RL to edge-type weights rather than policies — justified by graph size; (2) k-NN sparsification to prevent propagation methods degenerating to flat cosine — justified and ablated; (3) domain-general sentence encoders (all-mpnet-base-v2) — supported by an encoder-sensitivity appendix showing gains hold under bge-large-en-v1.5. Key Results: Across three domains — OPP-115 (24 nodes, privacy policies), CLAUDETTE (53 nodes, unfair ToS clauses), ESRS-CID (82 nodes, sustainability disclosures) — CRG + Spectral achieves matched-K recall of 0.792, 0.860, and 0.755 respectively, versus flat cosine at 0.748/0.806/0.723, heat-kernel diffusion at 0.747/0.817/0.744, Leiden community retrieval at 0.766/0.841/0.675, and a cross-encoder at 0.781/0.825/0.465. Average lift over flat cosine is +4.3% (range +3.2 to +5.4%); lift over Leiden is +2.6% and +1.9% on OPP-115 and CLAUDETTE. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (BM25, cross-encoder reranking, PPR à la HippoRAG, heat-kernel diffusion, GraphRAG-style communities). The full-pipeline results are notably weaker: Llama-3.3-70B validation loses 25.7% of retrieval recall on OPP-115, 4.3% on CLAUDETTE, and 22.8% on ESRS, with ESRS precision collapsing to 0.204 due to ~3% positive class rate. A surprising robustness finding in Appendix D.4: under an unmodified adaptive stopping rule, heat-kernel diffusion reaches 0.795 vs. 0.791 for CRG + Spectral on OPP-115, and on CLAUDETTE all matched-K differences have bootstrap CIs crossing zero; the ESRS gap to heat-kernel (−0.016) is reported as unconfirmed. On the positive side, the method's margin over the cross-encoder widens with graph size (cross-encoder needs 44.9 retrieved nodes vs. K=17 to match recall on ESRS). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (compliance validation as closed-set coverage over an obligation graph under asymmetric error costs) plus NEW METHOD, with a genuine empirical finding about component conditional dependence. The individually novel parts are modest: spectral reranking is textbook manifold ranking / fast spectral ranking (Iscen et al. 2018; Zhou et al. 2011) applied to a new setting, and the "RL" is gradient ascent on six edge-type scalars rather than learned graph construction or traversal policies (contrast AutoGraph-R1, GraphRAG-R1). The genuine contribution is the demonstration that task-rewarded edge weighting and spectral filtering are jointly necessary — a non-obvious interaction — plus the document-level recall evaluation protocol, which the authors state no prior compliance system has adopted. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: component analysis (Table 5) separates graph type × retrieval method; per-edge-type removal (Table 4) quantifies each metadata type's contribution; hyperparameter sensitivity sweeps cover k∈[1,10], n∈[2,15], α∈[0,1]; encoder sensitivity is checked across two embedding lineages. Paired bootstrap 95% CIs (2,000 resamples) are reported in the appendix robustness check but not on the headline Table 1 numbers, and no multiple-seed variance is reported for RL training. The matched-K protocol is thoughtfully designed to prevent budget-inflated recall, and the authors transparently report where tuned baselines erode their margins. However, the main significance evidence is confined to two of three domains; on CLAUDETTE (the domain with the largest claimed lift, +4.1%) differences are not statistically significant, and ESRS lacks confidence intervals entirely. No code, data, or model release URL is mentioned. All graphs are built from dataset-provided expert metadata, and hyperparameters are tuned per domain on validation data of the same benchmarks used for testing — a mild Goodhart risk. The graph-document-alignment baseline is an adaptation, not a faithful reimplementation of GraphCompliance, which the authors flag. This is a peer-reviewed workshop paper (ACL NLLP 2026), not a preprint, but from an industry lab with self-run evaluation. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system framework with experiments, no formal results). - Practical: Yes — the pipeline uses off-the-shelf sentence encoders, eigendecomposition of graphs with ≤82 nodes, and open-weight Llama validators, all runnable on commodity hardware. - Efficient: Cheap relative to LLM-centric graph-RAG (one eigendecomposition per graph, six learned scalars), though the validator stage dominates cost; the cross-encoder baseline needs 2.6× the retrieval budget on ESRS to match recall. - Effective: Retrieval-stage evidence is solid on the smallest domain and mixed on the others; end-to-end effectiveness is only partially demonstrated — validation loses 20–26% of retrieval recall on two of three domains and ESRS precision (0.204) is far below workflow-usable. - Scalable: Not tested — the authors themselves report the spectral gap shrinking (λ2 = 0.04 on ESRS vs. 0.19 on OPP-115), RL failing to converge on ESRS (needing a fixed category boost), and identify a compounding scarcity of positive labels as graphs grow; claims that real deployments use 50–150-node spaces are asserted, not measured. The work stops at paper form; no library, tool, or dataset artifact is released. Strengths: - The conditional-dependency finding is the paper's real intellectual contribution: RL-weighted edges and spectral reranking each fail alone (BFS×RL: 0.710 on OPP-115; Spectral×Cosine: 0.759) while combining to 0.792 — a mechanism-level result, not just a leaderboard delta. - Evaluation honesty is unusually high for an industry paper: the authors volunteer that heat-kernel diffusion beats their method under an unmodified stopping rule on OPP-115, that CLAUDETTE differences are insignificant, and that ESRS RL learning did not converge. - The matched-K evaluation protocol is a substantive methodological contribution that prevents the budget-inflation confound common in retrieval comparisons. - The qualitative spectral community analysis (Appendix B) connects the mechanism to data — e.g., CLAUDETTE's five unfair-clause types each forming a pure spectral cluster explains where and why the method gains most. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility. They acknowledge: poor path efficiency (0.10–0.18) from spectral reranking scoring most of the node set; sensitivity to hyperparameters with up to 4.37% additional lift from tuning; small requirement spaces (24–82 nodes) with degrading spectral signal at scale; the compounding problem that larger compliance corpora have sparser positive labels, weakening the RL reward (forcing a fixed boost on ESRS); dependence on expert-curated metadata schemas rather than automated graph construction from regulatory text; the untested LLM query-expansion baseline; and the non-significant CLAUDETTE / heat-kernel-on-OPP results under tuned stopping. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline Table 1 lacks error bars or significance tests; the sobering robustness-check results (Appendix D.4) live in an appendix while the abstract cites the 4.3% average lift without qualification — a framing asymmetry a reviewer should flag, since on two of three domains the margin over heat-kernel diffusion is statistically unconfirmed or reversed under the alternate protocol. - Table 5 mixes protocols: matched-K for baselines but "natural stopping" for spectral conditions, which partially undercuts the clean component-dependence narrative. - Only 2–3 of six metadata edge types carry any weight per domain, and one (same_category on ESRS) is a hand-set fixed boost rather than learned — raising the question of whether a simpler hand-tuned weighted graph over one or two metadata types would match the RL machinery. - The end-to-end system is effectively broken on ESRS (precision 0.204, far below the ~3% base rate needed to beat random positive prediction) yet the paper leads with retrieval numbers; a practitioner deploying this would face the validation-stage problem, which receives less analysis than retrieval. - No baseline uses LLM-based query expansion or a strong LLM zero-shot retriever over the requirement space, which is the most obvious practical alternative in 2026 (acknowledged but untested). - All three domains are public benchmarks with dataset-provided metadata that directly supplies the graph's structural edges; no experiment tests the framework on a domain where metadata must be authored, so portability claims rest on architecture, not evidence. Bottom Line: A practitioner building compliance-automation retrieval should read this for the well-isolated finding that task-rewarded edge weighting and spectral filtering are jointly necessary and for its honest evaluation protocol, but should not treat the 4.3% recall lift as settled — the margins are fragile outside the smallest domain and the framework's scalability beyond ~100 obligations is asserted rather than demonstrated, so stronger general graph-RAG baselines (heat-kernel diffusion in particular) cover much of the same ground with less machinery.

Learning to Compose

Y Chen, F Liu, Z Wang, ZJXZL Ruan, W Han · cocacola-lab.github.io · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Recursia, a recursive self-improvement framework in which a coding agent iteratively repairs and extends a versioned, four-layer shared executable stack (tools, skills with execution contracts, handoffs, verifiers) on source robot tasks, then freezes the stack for zero-shot execution on unseen long-horizon compositions. - Why it's important: Individually competent robot skills frequently fail when composed — a completed pick can leave the scene violating the next skill's preconditions — so long-horizon manipulation reliability is bottlenecked at skill boundaries, not just per-skill competence. - How it does it: First-failure attribution over source execution traces localizes the broken stack layer; candidate patches must pass generality checks, mechanism tests, and paired selection-plus-regression gates against the parent stack before being accepted. - The good: The frozen-stack transfer results are concrete: 28.4% (Pos) and 53.4% (Task) on LIBERO-Pro Long versus 22.6%/38.3% for ASPIRE, plus a +40-point mean gain over a Skill-Document-Only baseline on three physical Franka FR3 tasks (66.7% vs 26.7%). - The missing: The improvement loop depends on simulator ground-truth diagnosis and controlled resets, and all baselines are copied from prior papers despite an acknowledged grasp-backend mismatch (Contact-GraspNet vs ASPIRE's AnyGrasp), so both the real-world applicability of the improvement procedure and the headline comparison carry caveats. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-driven skill libraries, self-improving embodied agents, or compositional transfer in robot programming; skip it if you need a statistically rigorous VLA comparison — the baseline table is inherited, not rerun.

Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (75) and Completeness (75) are the strengths: the shared-stack-as-unit-of-improvement hypothesis with layer-attributed repair, the dual acceptance gates, and exceptionally honest protocol accounting (backend mismatch, shadow verifier, Scene5 exposure) are real contributions. However, Rigor (48) is the primary drag — no error bars or repeated evaluations, a physical evaluation of 3 tasks × 10 trials with manual scoring, and every headline comparison relying on baselines copied from ASPIRE under a different grasp backend, making the margins uninterpretable. Resilience (58) falls because the central transfer claim collapses to 'suggestive' under adversarial questioning about the backend confound, and the core hypothesis (shared repairs transfer; task patches do not) is never tested with a controlled arm. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*48 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*50 = 63.
