Problem & Motivation: Large e-commerce platforms must detect listings with suspiciously inflated prices. The right signal is the underlying procurement cost — not the selling price — inferred from heterogeneous multimodal evidence (product image, structured attributes, comparable products, pricing knowledge). General-purpose VLMs can reason about this but fail industrial constraints: serving cost at high QPS, 3–8 s API latency, and verbose rationales that complicate auditing and rule integration. Prior LLM-based pricing work (e.g., LLP, Wang et al. 2025) targets selling-price prediction, not cost estimation for risk control. This gap — a compact, auditable, cost-estimating model usable as a production auxiliary signal — is what the paper addresses. Key Idea: The core trick is a supervision-shaping pair: (1) adaptive-depth rationale distillation — keep only the shortest teacher-CoT prefix with which a frozen evaluator still prices within ε=0.20, so each training example carries minimal-sufficient evidence rather than redundant reasoning; and (2) an asymmetric verifiable reward — clip(0.5 − w·e, −0.5, 0.5) with w=1.5 for over-estimates — that directly counters the systematic upward bias induced by anchoring on transaction-priced comparables. Supporting this, a segment-normalized SFT loss (separate mean cross-entropy for format/rationale/answer segments, weighted 0.5/0.5/2.5) prevents the long rationale from drowning out supervision of the numeric answer. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Progressive pricing-data construction: a teacher (Gemini-3-Pro Preview) generates structured long-CoT rationales (≤1024 tokens) from the multimodal input; a frozen evaluator (Qwen3-VL-32B, zero-shot) prices each prefix, and the shortest prefix with relative error ≤0.20 is retained. Rationales with no sufficient prefix (~18%, the hard cases) keep the full chain; average rationale length drops 1,722→1,246 characters (27.6% compression). (2) Segment-normalized SFT: the assistant response is partitioned into format/think/answer segments; the objective is a weighted average of per-segment mean cross-entropies (Eq. 6), with hard-case retention trained identically. (3) GRPO: group-normalized advantages over G sampled rollouts, clipped importance ratios, KL to the SFT reference; the reward parses the <answer> number and applies the asymmetric clipped MAPE score (Eq. 7). Pricing knowledge K comes from a category-conditioned cost knowledge base retrieved via category/attribute-aware RAG. Critical design decisions: prefix-probing for rationale compression (justified by an ablation showing consistency collapses to 20.1% when training on full long CoTs); segment normalization (justified: consistency 36.83%→84.90% at near-identical MAPE); asymmetric over-estimation penalty (justified: symmetric reward plateaus at 30.90% MAPE). Data hygiene is addressed via product-ID-level splits that remove test products from training comparables and restrict K to category-level priors. Key Results: On the in-house benchmark (~25K instances, 105 fine-grained categories, 18.75K/2.5K/3.75K split), Cost-LLM achieves MAPE 29.47%, Acc@10 19.73%, Acc@20 40.42%, consistency 100%, format 0.9994. Baselines under identical prompts/evidence: Doubao-Seed-1.6 (MAPE 30.28), Qwen3-VL-235B (31.81), Qwen3-235B-A22B (32.80), Gemini-3-Flash-Preview (33.94), Qwen2.5-VL-72B (36.75), and the non-LLM regressor PriceBERT (71.58). The ablation on the same 7B backbone: zero-shot 33.43, SFT-only 35.30 (consistency drops to 36.83), GRPO-only 33.04, full pipeline 29.47 — showing SFT and RL are jointly necessary. Paired-bootstrap (10,000 resamples) shows the 0.81-point gap over Doubao-Seed-1.6 is not statistically significant; gaps over all other baselines are significant. Teacher/evaluator sensitivity: swapping the proprietary teacher for open Qwen2.5-VL-72B yields 30.10% MAPE. Online, on 121,395 matched live listings, Cost-LLM (threshold pred_ratio≥2.5, audited on ~1,000 human-labeled flags to precision-match the baseline) flags 2,810 anomalies of which 2,344 (30.73% of the baseline's 7,628) are exclusive, with only 466 in the intersection — the two signals catch largely different candidates, concentrated in long-tail categories with sparse same-item price references. Serving: single A100-80G with vLLM at 0.4–0.8 s/listing vs. 3–8 s for external APIs. Baselines are current and strong (2025–2026 frontier models); testing is at realistic industrial, not research-toy, scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (procurement-cost estimation as a distinct multimodal reasoning task, vs. selling-price prediction) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION and a modest NEW METHOD. The genuinely new elements are the asymmetric over-estimation-aware MAPE reward tied to a domain-specific bias mechanism, and the minimal-sufficient-prefix rationale construction; segment-normalized SFT, GRPO, RAG-grounded knowledge, and teacher-distillation are standard ideas competently combined. The most transferable contribution is arguably the deployment methodology (precision-matched operating-point calibration, consistency-as-diagnostic), not the modeling itself. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: same-backbone stage ablations (Table 2), component-level ablations isolating the SFT objective, reward design (including symmetric and MSLE alternatives), and hard-case retention (Table 4), plus teacher/evaluator swap experiments (Appendix A.5). Paired-bootstrap significance with 10,000 resamples is reported, and the authors explicitly decline to claim a decisive win over Doubao-Seed-1.6 — a credibility positive. No data or code release: the dataset is withheld for commercial sensitivity, so exact reproduction is impossible; the training recipe, prompts, and parsing rules are documented in Appendix A.1. Methodological concerns: (a) the method is developed and evaluated on the authors' single proprietary dataset — no external benchmark corroborates the offline numbers; (b) reference costs contain acknowledged label noise from temporal drift, unquantified; (c) the online "30.73%" is a relative detection count, not recall, and the audited precision match rests on a ~1,000-label finite sample; (d) several Appendix figures (bucket MAPE, error distributions) are referenced but their underlying values are not fully stated in text. None of these are hidden — the authors flag most of them in Limitations. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a deployed production signal, with offline empirical evaluation). Practical: Yes — a 7B model on a single A100-80G with vLLM, well within commercially available hardware. Efficient: 0.4–0.8 s per listing vs. 3–8 s for external APIs, with no per-call fees, though the authors correctly note the latency comparison spans different serving stacks. Effective: The evidence supports it as a complementary flagging signal at precision-matched operating point, but effectiveness is measured against an unknown ground-truth anomaly base rate, so it solves the operational problem only partially (no recall estimate exists). Scalable: Not stress-tested — the online study covers 121K listings in one sampling window; behavior at 10–100× QPS or under distribution drift is claimed only implicitly via the production framing, not measured. Deliverable: a trained 7B model and serving stack deployed internally; no public artifact (no weights, code, or data release). Strengths: - Unusually honest statistical treatment for an industry paper: the authors run paired-bootstrap tests and then explicitly disclaim their headline accuracy advantage over the strongest baseline, reframing the case on latency, cost, and complementary detections. - The component-level ablations (Appendix A.2) actually isolate which design matters — the segment-normalized loss fixes a real, diagnosed failure mode (rationale tokens dominating the gradient, consistency 36.83%→84.90%), and the reward ablation (symmetric 30.90% vs. asymmetric 29.47% MAPE) substantiates the over-estimation-bias mechanism rather than asserting it. - The asymmetric reward is grounded in a concrete causal observation — transaction-priced comparables embed margin and channel costs, biasing cost estimates upward — which makes the 1.5× penalty a motivated fix, not a tuned hyperparameter. - The deployment methodology (precision-matched threshold selection via ~1,000-label human audit, consistency as a runtime diagnostic, explicit product-ID-level leakage prevention in the data split) is a reusable playbook for vertical-domain LLM post-training under serving constraints. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length: (1) the dataset is proprietary and unreleased, limiting reproducibility, and reference costs carry temporal/supply-chain label noise; (2) rationale faithfulness to the internal decision process is not claimed — consistency and format are monitors, not rewards; (3) progressive construction depends on teacher/evaluator quality, and shortest-prefix selection biases the corpus toward easy cases, only partially mitigated by hard-case retention; (4) the 30.73% online figure is not recall, audited precision has finite-sample uncertainty, and long-term pipeline effects require further A/B study. This candidness is a credibility positive; nothing significant is minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) no external or public-benchmark evaluation of any kind — the claim that domain post-training beats parameter scaling rests entirely on one platform's data and label conventions, so generalization across marketplaces or pricing regimes is untested; (2) the consistency metric is defined against the model's own rationale, not against ground truth, so 100% consistency certifies self-agreement, not correctness; (3) the online operating point (pred_ratio≥2.5) is chosen from an audited subset and then evaluated on the same-style production sample — mild selection-on-the-eval-set risk the paper does not discuss; (4) the baseline API models receive "identical prompt and evidence inputs," but a stronger comparison — fine-tuning a competing open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B SFT) on the same data — is absent, leaving open how much of the win is the recipe vs. any 7B-specific advantage; (5) per-bucket MAPE claims against the production baseline and Kimi-K2.5 are shown only as figures without reported numbers, and Kimi-K2.5 appears only there due to API-quota limits. Bottom Line: For practitioners building compact, auditable LLM systems in vertical risk-control or pricing domains, this is a genuinely useful deployment case study with unusually honest evaluation; for anyone seeking a reproducible modeling advance, the closed dataset and non-decisive accuracy margins mean the published recipe ablations, not the headline results, are the real contribution.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the "illusion of passing tests": the risk that visible unit-test success is mistakenly treated as sufficient evidence to deploy LLM-generated code that crosses a security-relevant trust boundary. The intended audience is the Secure Program Synthesis (SPS) community and anyone operating AI coding agents in security-sensitive settings. The gap it targets is that code-generation benchmarks measure whether a model can emit a passing artifact, not whether a tests-only release signal is safe; meanwhile, complete formal specifications for arbitrary systems do not exist (citing Dodds), so end-to-end verification is unrealistic. The paper argues the bottleneck is shifting from generation to verification and that deployment authorization under bounded evidence is an unsolved, first-class systems problem. Key Idea: Treat specifications not as prompt decoration but as executable oracles — frozen, hidden checks (day-2 harnesses and template-generated adversarial payloads) applied post-generation to a fixed candidate pool — and triage each artifact into three operational decisions (accept, reject, escalate to review) rather than a benchmark score. The escalate outcome, informed by Trusted Computing Base (TCB) literature, is the distinguishing structural move: it makes "passed all automated checks" and "safe to ship" explicitly distinct states. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Task suite: 24 narrow-waist, security-relevant Python components (8 development, 16 confirmatory) covering authorization logic, rate limiting, parser boundaries, and resource scoping, plus a 24-task expansion suite; hidden evidence comes from frozen day-2 harnesses on an owned internal slice and deterministically generated hidden oracles (benign + adversarial payloads, e.g., rejecting "../secret" in path validation) on a secure slice, with oracle hashes logged. (2) Candidate pool generation: multiple prompt templates (requirements-first, invariants-first, self-critique, regression-preservation) produce a varied pool of 1,405 candidate rows; the specific LLM(s) used are not stated. (3) Dual-stage evaluation: visible harnesses first, then hidden oracles, with anonymized selector inputs and identical fixed pools across competing selectors to isolate evaluation quality from generation variance. (4) Triage and adjudication: decisions logged in append-only ledgers, executed under the Inspect AI framework for runtime provenance; 138 rows received deep manual adjudication. A bounded repair arm (one bounded patch under equal compute) is compared against fresh generation. Critical design decisions: fixing candidate pools (well-justified for isolating triage efficacy), freezing oracles before confirmatory execution (well-justified), and a three-way triage policy with human escalation (motivated by TCB arguments but with author-defined, subjective escalation criteria). No explicit loss function; this is a decision-procedure evaluation, not an optimization method. Key Results: On the 16 confirmatory tasks, every task had candidates that passed visible tests but failed hidden checks, with security-relevant hidden failures on 8 tasks. A tests-only selector falsely authorized insecure artifacts on 7 tasks; specification-aware selection reduced this to 1 (6 tasks improved). Of 72 triage decisions, 6 selected artifacts that passed all automated oracles were escalated to human review (wrapper dependencies, interface assumptions, under-specified edge cases). The support bottleneck: candidate pools contained a hidden-correct solution on 8 tasks and none on 9; the spec-aware selector beat the tests-only baseline on only 2 of these tasks. Under equal compute, bounded repair won 0 times against fresh generation. A Dafny overlay on 150 candidates yielded 52 formally verified artifacts, yet all 52 received the lowest task-level judge score because failures surfaced at the Python operational boundary. A 6-task Lean 4 formal-evaluator slice reduced bounded-slice false-accept tasks from 3 to 0 once support existed, and a 2-task follow-up produced a formal-pass/review-required case (timing-safe compare not certifiable without compare_digest). Scale is small (24 primary tasks, 72 triage decisions); there are no accuracy-percentage metrics, no external baselines, and no comparison against other gating approaches. All baselines are author-constructed; none are drawn from prior literature. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK component (the frozen 48-task suite). The genuinely novel element is the three-way deployment-gate framing (accept/reject/escalate) operationalizing TCB critique for LLM code, plus the quantified visible-pass/hidden-fail demonstration. The underlying techniques — hidden tests, specification-based filtering, best-of-n selection — are standard; the contribution is their packaging as a deployment decision procedure on self-authored tasks, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper's evidentiary hygiene is above average for a hackathon report: frozen tasks and oracles before confirmatory execution, append-only ledgers, Inspect AI runtime provenance, oracle hashes, manual adjudication of 138 claim-bearing rows, an equal-compute repair control, and a published repository (github.com/davidkimai/sps_evals) with a documented reviewer quickstart. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported (small task counts make this largely moot but should be stated). Methodological concerns: (1) circularity — the authors designed the tasks, the visible harnesses, the hidden oracles, and the failure taxonomy, so the 7→1 result partially measures their own test-design choices; (2) no independent or external baseline for what a "secure" oracle should check; (3) the generating LLM is unnamed, limiting reproduction; (4) escalation criteria are author-defined and not validated against independent security review; (5) it is an unrefereed hackathon paper, not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a workflow and decision procedure, run and measured, with no formal theorems of its own). Practical: Yes — the gate runs on ordinary Python tooling plus Inspect AI, on tasks an individual built in a hackathon, so hardware needs are trivial. Efficient: Cheap relative to generation (evaluation of fixed pools); the paper reports no runtime or cost figures, so efficiency is unevaluated. Effective: Within its bounded setting, the evidence (7→1 false accepts, 6 justified escalations, 138 adjudicated rows) shows the gate blocks insecure code that visible tests admit, but the criterion of "secure" is the authors' own oracle, so it solves the stated problem on a proxy it constructed. Scalable: Untested beyond 48 narrow tasks; the authors explicitly disclaim extension to monolithic or stateful systems, and the 9-task support vacuum suggests scaling difficulty will come from generation, not the gate. Deliverable: a real software artifact — the sps_evals repository with task specs, oracle modules, ledgers, and logs — though as a hackathon substrate, not a hardened tool. Strengths: - The headline finding is operationally concrete and quantified: visible-test success hid security-critical failures on 8 of 16 confirmatory tasks, and spec-aware triage cut false accepts from 7 tasks to 1 — a result directly relevant to anyone gating agent-generated code. - Unusually honest boundary-mapping for this genre: the paper reports its own negative results (selector wins on only 2 supported tasks; repair won 0 of equal-compute comparisons; all 52 Dafny-verified artifacts scored worst at the Python boundary) rather than burying them. - The three-way triage with explicit escalation is a genuinely useful reframing — it converts TCB theory into an operational decision state, and the Lean 4 timing-safe-compare case is a well-chosen concrete demonstration that formal-pass ≠ deploy-safe. - Strong provenance discipline for a hackathon setting: frozen denominators, hashed oracles, append-only ledgers, Inspect AI logs, and a documented reviewer audit path. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length, which is a credibility positive. They acknowledge: (1) the narrow-waist design trades broad applicability for operational clarity and does not scale to monoliths, stateful systems, or codebases lacking local invariants; (2) evaluation cannot resolve the generation bottleneck — selection is impotent when pools lack a hidden-correct candidate; (3) bounded repair is not a rescue mechanism under compute parity; (4) no end-to-end formal synthesis or whole-system proofs are offered; (5) hidden checks are only as strong as the specifications they operationalize and can both under- and over-constrain. Appendix C adds dual-use analysis (the same methods could teach proxy gaming) and interpretation boundaries (a pass is not "the system is safe"). Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged narrow scope, a critical reviewer would flag: (1) oracle circularity — the same team authored tasks, visible tests, hidden oracles, and failure labels, so the proxy-target gap is partly constructed rather than discovered; no independent security expert validated the oracles or the 6 escalations; (2) no named generator model, model count, or decoding configuration, making the support-vacuum results (8 vs 9 tasks) impossible to situate against known capability levels; (3) no comparison against any existing secure-code evaluation or gating method — the tests-only selector is the only baseline, and it is a weak straw man by the paper's own argument; (4) selection effects in the "confirmatory set": how these 16 tasks were chosen from the development process is not described, leaving room for favorable task selection; (5) the Dafny and Lean 4 overlays are on different task denominators with different judge metrics and are explicitly not comparable, so the formal-methods claims rest on 2–6 task anecdotes; (6) no false-reject rate is reported — the cost side of the gate (how often spec-aware triage rejects acceptable code) is never quantified, which matters for any real deployment decision. Bottom Line: A practitioner building deployment gates for AI-generated security code gains a useful framing, an honest negative-result inventory, and a reusable small benchmark suite, but the empirical claims are self-referential and hackathon-scale — treat this as a well-documented position paper with a pilot study, not as validated evidence that specification-aware triage is ready for operational use.

L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (34 ▲ )

Jinhyeok Choi, JoungBin Lee, Jongmin Lee, Minkyeong Jeon, Jiyoung Kim, Kaeun Han, Yoonjin Yoon, Seungryong Kim · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces L3G-World, a real-time interactive world-generation system that maintains a compact latent 3D Gaussian scene memory updated in place by a feed-forward updater, and shows it sustains spatially consistent generation at 9.02 FPS over 481-frame loop-closure trajectories where baseline memory representations OOM or drift. - Why it's important: Existing world models lose spatial consistency over long explorations or blow up in memory/rendering cost because their scene memory grows with generated stream length rather than scene extent, blocking practical minute-long interactive exploration. - How it does it: The core trick is a persistent set of 3D Gaussians that each store a VAE latent feature, so a feed-forward updater spawns Gaussians only in uncovered/high-error regions, refines existing ones via residual (gated) updates, and renders the memory directly into the diffusion transformer's latent space with no VAE re-encoding. - The good: The efficiency evidence is strong and internally consistent — 33K vs. 8.7M–150M primitives, 40 vs. 0.1–12.5 reconstruction FPS, and ~1,087 vs. ~0.06–3.1 VAE-conditioning FPS against the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline per metric, alongside the best loop-closure self-consistency (LPIPS 0.547 on DL3DV) and best FID (40.57). - The missing: No released code or model weights are stated, no error bars/multiple seeds, and the baselines were substantially re-engineered by the authors for the single-image setting, so the comparisons rest on author-modified implementations of competitors. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building long-horizon, camera-controllable world models or latent-space 3D memory representations; skippable if you only care about dynamic scenes, since the method is explicitly static-scene only.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The latent-Gaussian memory idea (per-Gaussian VAE features splatted directly into the DiT latent space) is a real Novelty (68) and Non-Obviousness (68) contribution — reframing memory update as selective spawn plus gated residual refinement — and ablations credibly attribute gains. Rigor (60) is pulled down by training/evaluation dataset overlap (DL3DV/RealEstate10K used for both training and evaluation), substantially author-modified baselines, no seeds or error bars, and no stated code/weight release. Resilience (58) suffers because the 'infinite generation' claim is analytical, never tested beyond 481 frames, and absolute loop-closure PSNR (~16) suggests all methods, including this one, reconstruct poorly. Impact (48) is limited to a paper and project page with no shipped artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*48 = 62.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Interactive video world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions (camera trajectories, keyboard controls) and are aimed at real-world simulation, interactive game generation, and embodied simulation. Two failure modes block long-horizon use: (1) temporal-context methods (KV caches, retrieved history frames) have memory and attention cost that grows linearly with generated stream length and resolution, eventually OOM-ing — the authors report Yume 1.5 at 66.7 GiB peak GPU memory and WorldKV failing outright at 400 frames; (2) explicit 3D-memory methods either accumulate dense per-pixel point clouds/Gaussians per frame (redundant primitives pile up over revisited regions, rendering slows, errors persist) or use optimization-based reconstruction that is too slow for real time (ArtiFixer at 0.10 FPS). The gap is a memory whose size scales with explored scene extent (O(S)) rather than generation length, that supports online refinement, and whose conditioning of a latent video generator avoids VAE re-encoding. Key Idea: Treat the 3D scene memory as a living representation rather than an append-only buffer: each 3D Gaussian stores both appearance parameters and a 16-channel VAE latent feature, so the memory can be splatted directly into the DiT's input latent space under target cameras. Combined with (a) an opacity/error-based spawn mask that allocates a K-means-clustered spawning budget only to memory-insufficient regions and (b) gated residual refinement of visible existing Gaussians, this converts memory maintenance from accumulation to selective revision. This is the key insight — everything else is competent assembly of known components (feed-forward token-based Gaussians, rectified-flow DiT, flow-map distillation). Methodology: The pipeline alternates two modules autoregressively over windows of V∈{1..9} frames. (1) L3G-Mem (1.7B params, initialized from ZipSplat, with a Depth Anything 3 geometry backbone trained end-to-end): renders the previous memory M_{k-1} under current cameras; a spawn mask (patch error > τ_E=0.05 or opacity < τ_α=0.25) selects geometry features for K-means-initialized spawn queries; visible Gaussians are retrieved via depth/opacity probes and yield refinement tokens; both streams (3 blocks each of cross-attention, self-attention, plus a global self-attention over concatenated tokens) are processed by one transformer; a separate VAE-lifting branch produces latent tokens channel-concatenated with spawn tokens; MLP heads decode 32 Gaussians per token plus residuals (δµ, δs, δq, δα, δc, δz) with independent gates. (2) L3G-Gen (Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B backbone, frozen, with rank-16 LoRA + UCPE camera conditioning): rendered memory latents and alpha are channel-concatenated with noisy target latents, up to three pose-proximate reference latents are prepended with offset temporal RoPE, and RayRoPE camera encodings are added; trained with rectified flow on target latents only. A distilled student (AnyFlow flow-map + on-policy DMD-style distribution matching, 4 denoising steps, no CFG) enables real-time inference. Training uses stop-gradients through M_{k-1}, supervises renderings from all windows up to k with ℓ1 RGB + LPIPS + depth + VAE latent MSE + visibility losses (Eq. 5). Critical design decisions: (i) adaptive spawn vs. accumulate — justified by the Tab. 3 ablation (1.8× more Gaussians and worse quality without it); (ii) direct VAE latent rendering vs. RGB render + re-encode — justified by a 349–359× throughput gain and Tab. 3/4 ablations, though it makes the memory representation coupled to the specific Cosmos VAE; (iii) gated residual refinement — justified by Tab. 4, where removing it degrades self-consistency PSNR from 15.11 to 14.82 and TransErr from 0.278 to 0.314. Key Results: On DL3DV and RealEstate10K test splits with 481-frame loop-closure trajectories at 480×832, L3G-World stores 25–33K primitives (vs. 655K–150M for baselines; 266–417× fewer than NeoVerse), 8.91–11.88 MiB memory, 38.9–40.1 reconstruction FPS, 460–577 RGB render FPS, and ~1,087–1,102 VAE-conditioning FPS — a 349–359× VAE-conditioning speedup over the best baseline (NeoVerse at ~3.1). Peak GPU memory is 7.4 GiB vs. 11.7–66.7 GiB for baselines; total throughput 9.02 FPS on one H100 vs. 0.10–1.99 for baselines (real-time only for L3G-World). Self-consistency (loop-closure frame pairs): best PSNR 16.00 / LPIPS 0.547 on DL3DV and 18.36 / 0.518 on RealEstate10K. Generation quality: best FID 40.57 (DL3DV) and 36.09 (RealEstate10K), best LPIPS, SC and BC; baselines include recent systems (Yume 1.5, Matrix-Game 3.0, GEN3C, Spatia, SPMem, Lyra 2.0, 3DScenePrompt, NeoVerse, all 2025–2026), i.e., current and strong. Caveats: absolute PSNR values are low (~16), other methods beat it on pose error and MEt3R on RealEstate10K (e.g., Lyra 2.0 TransErr 0.091 vs. 0.216), and the distilled L3G-World Fast loses ~1.4 PSNR. Scale is standard (2 indoor/outdoor scene datasets, minute-length rollouts) — "infinite" generation is a design claim, not an experiment. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. Genuinely novel: per-Gaussian VAE latent features enabling direct latent-space splatting into a video DiT (eliminating VAE re-encoding), and a spawn-mask-driven selective updater that keeps memory O(S) with in-place residual refinement in a fully feed-forward pipeline. Standard combinations: token-based feed-forward Gaussians (ZipSplat), geometry backbone (DA3), DiT backbone and distillation recipe (Cosmos-Predict2.5, AnyFlow), camera conditioning (UCPE, RayRoPE) — all existing ideas integrated in a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative at both component level (L3G-Mem variants in Tab. 3: adaptive spawning, refinement, global self-attention, RGB loss, VAE lifting) and system level (Tab. 4: refinement and VAE lifting within the full generation loop), clearly attributing gains. A separate online-NVS comparison (Tab. 6) against dedicated online 3DGS methods (ReCoSplat, OF3GS) honestly concedes that ReCoSplat at 480×480 achieves higher reconstruction fidelity, positioning the memory as fit-for-purpose rather than best-in-class reconstruction. Concerns: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; the two evaluation datasets (DL3DV, RealEstate10K) are also the training datasets for L3G-Gen (and DL3DV for L3G-Mem), so generation-quality metrics partly measure in-domain generalization — a Goodhart risk; baselines required substantial author modification (modified initialization for SPMem/3DScenePrompt, a from-scratch autoregressive pipeline for NeoVerse, action-space conversion for Yume 1.5/Matrix-Game 3.0), which is disclosed but leaves comparison fidelity unverifiable; efficiency is measured on A100 while the headline 9.02 FPS is on H100. No public code/weights release is stated beyond a project page URL (https://cvlab-kaist.github.io/L3G-World/). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built, running system with deployment-relevant measurements). - Practical: Runs on a single H100 at 9.02 FPS and a single A100 for evaluation — commercially available datacenter hardware, though not consumer GPUs. - Efficient: 7.4 GiB peak GPU memory and 25–33K primitives are an order of magnitude below all tested baselines; the 2B DiT with 4-step distillation is the dominant compute cost. - Effective: Evidence covers loop-closure consistency and quality on two scene datasets, but only for static scenes with ground-truth camera trajectories — the stated use case of user-driven interactive exploration is only partially proxied (camera control is measured via pose-error estimation, not user studies). - Scalable: Not tested — the O(S) scaling argument is analytical; the longest evaluation is 481 frames, and the authors themselves note memory can still grow under very large-scale exploration without having run such an experiment. Deliverable: currently a paper plus project page; no library, CLI, or released model weights are stated. Strengths: - The latent-lifting design — storing splattable VAE features per Gaussian so the memory conditions the DiT in its native input space — is a real, well-motivated contribution that converts a 349× overhead problem (RGB render + re-encode) into a non-issue, and it is ablated from both sides (render quality and end-generation quality). - Reframing memory update as selective spawn + gated residual refinement (rather than accumulation) directly targets the O(TR) vs. O(S) scaling distinction, and the Tab. 4 ablation shows refinement specifically fixes self-consistency and pose accuracy, not just compactness. - The loop-closure evaluation protocol (compare frames at identical poses from outgoing vs. returning trajectories) is a clean, direct test of exactly the consistency property being claimed, and the qualitative figure set (Fig. 6/8) shows distinct, diagnosable failure modes per baseline. - The efficiency table is measured on the authors' own system and all baselines under aligned depth/scale conditions, and the appendix honestly positions L3G-Mem as worse than dedicated online 3DGS at pure reconstruction — resistance to overclaiming. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The appendix (Sec. E) states three: (1) the memory is designed for static scenes and does not model independently moving objects; (2) memory can still grow under extremely large-scale exploration, motivating pruning/hierarchical representations; (3) geometric errors from long-horizon autoregressive generation may still propagate through subsequent memory updates despite refinement. The authors confront these directly and concretely — a credibility positive. They do not acknowledge the training/evaluation dataset overlap or the author-modified baselines as limitations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Training/evaluation overlap: L3G-Gen is trained on DL3DV and RealEstate10K and evaluated on their test splits with no held-out third dataset for generation quality; the out-of-domain claim in Tab. 6 covers only the memory updater, not the full generation system. - Baseline comparability: action-conditioned baselines (Yume 1.5, Matrix-Game 3.0) were driven through a discrete-action conversion of continuous camera trajectories, and NeoVerse's autoregressive pipeline was built by the authors — both conversions could disadvantage those systems in ways the metrics cannot distinguish. - The reported self-consistency PSNR ceiling (~16–18) suggests no method, including L3G-World, actually reconstructs the start scene well at loop closure; the paper frames relative wins without discussing this absolute floor. - Robustness of the spawn-mask thresholds (τ_E=0.05, τ_α=0.25) and K-means budget N_q across scene types is not studied; no failure case analysis of the spawning mechanism is provided. - Interaction is limited to camera trajectories plus a text prompt; the keyboards/WASD controls in the teaser figure are not evaluated, and no user study or downstream-task evaluation is reported. Bottom Line: For anyone building long-horizon, camera-controllable world models, this is worth reading — the latent-Gaussian memory idea and the O(S) selective-update mechanism are genuinely useful and empirically well-supported, but the untested "infinite" scaling claim, dataset-overlapped evaluation, and static-scene restriction mean the practical recipe still needs independent reproduction on held-out domains before it displaces existing memory designs.

#130 — Innovative (62)

Agent Chronoception: Temporal Validity and Useful Persistence

A Yuan, Z Su · aojieyuan.com · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This position paper proposes an evaluation standard for "agent chronoception" — requiring LLM agents to show stability under decision-equivalent temporal changes (e.g., seconds vs. milliseconds) and selective adaptation when timing changes alter plan value — and backs it with an exact constructed counterexample plus several small pilot experiments showing a simple scheduler matches model controllers' quality at lower time cost. - Why it's important: Agent evaluations judge punctuality, duration reporting, or raw persistence, none of which distinguish a genuinely useful continuation decision from wasteful waiting or premature abandonment — a gap that matters for delegated coding and assistant work where user waiting time has real cost. - How it does it: The core move is a joint test design that pairs equivalence interventions (unit conversion, coherent world rescaling) with consequential interventions (tool slowdown/recovery that reverses the utility ordering of two feasible plans), evaluated against an equally informed explicit scheduler, with all deliberation time charged against the user's deadline. - The good: The exact constructed witness (Table 2, Appendix A) proves by arithmetic that a policy can be perfectly punctual and unit-invariant yet incur mean regret ≥ 0.02, establishing that punctuality and invariance jointly underdetermine useful adaptation — a clean, unanswerable-by-fiat contribution. - The missing: There is no public code/data release ("this preprint releases the manuscript only"), no error bars or significance tests, models from a single provider, tiny authored task sets (2–4 mechanics, 2 repetitions per cell), and the headline negative finding (scheduler ≥ model controllers) rests on 34 valid exploratory episodes. - Read it or not: Read it if you design agent benchmarks or evaluate long-horizon LLM agents — the evaluation taxonomy and counterexample are directly reusable — but skip it if you want validated model behavior findings or a new method; the authors themselves state no stable intervention effect was established.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The score is pulled down by Rigor (45) — no error bars or significance tests anywhere, 2-4 authored mechanics with 2 repetitions per cell, single-provider models, interrupted and resumed batches, and no code/data release — and by Impact (30), since the manuscript-only release means the reusable protocol that constitutes the paper's value cannot actually be adopted. The counterexample and evaluation taxonomy earn Novelty (68) and strong Non-Obviousness (72), while Completeness (80) and Resilience (75) are high: the limitation disclosure is exemplary and claims are carefully bounded, but this also reveals the empirical section as exploratory feasibility work. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Personal-assistant, coding, and collaborating agents must decide whether further work is worth the user's wait: when to verify, deliver a checkpoint, keep working, or stop. Existing evaluation practices — deadline adherence, task quality, runtime matching, or rewarding persistence — cannot distinguish a timing-sensitive policy from one that succeeds on a familiar timing regime, nor identify whether early stopping reflects saturation, lost authorization, or abandonment of a valuable continuation. The authors argue that current criteria (punctuality and invariance) are jointly insufficient to establish transferable temporal competence, and that no existing framework tests whether an agent's continuation decision survives temporal interventions that preserve versus reverse the value ordering of feasible plans. Key Idea: Temporal interventions must be split into decision-equivalent transformations (unit conversion; fully coherent world rescaling), under which the policy's action distribution should be invariant, and consequential latency changes (a tool slowdown or recovery that reverses the preferred plan's utility ranking), under which it should adapt — and an agent must pass both jointly, with every decision charged its own deliberation time against a root deadline. The formal witness: a full plan (quality 0.90, 4 units fast / 9 units slow) versus a targeted plan (quality 0.80, 2 units always), utility U = q − 0.02Δ, gives any regime-independent policy regret R(p) = 0.03 − 0.01p ≥ 0.02, while both it and an informed selector are punctual and unit-invariant. Methodology: The paper delivers three artifacts: (1) a joint evaluation standard with formal diagnostics — expected total variation on equivalent pairs (E_eq) and state-conditional candidate-set regret (R(x)) estimated separately on preference-reversing, preserving, and uncertain pairs; (2) a portable temporal record R_k = (C, t_obs, t_dispatch, P̂_k, G_k, v_k) capturing the contract, observation/dispatch times, forecasts, dependencies, and delivered artifact, plus a serial execution ledger separating inference, tool, and waiting intervals; (3) an attribution protocol comparing model replanning, a conditional runtime controller, and an equally informed deterministic scheduler. The candidate learning objective L(θ,φ) combines delivered utility, a proper duration score with censoring for timeouts, and a consistency divergence on validated equivalent pairs — proposed, not trained. Executed pilots include: a 16-case virtual-clock decision probe (Qwen2.5-3B vs. Sonnet 5.5 vs. scripted control), 24-episode coding/browser integration screens, a 32-selection measured-delay diagnostic, a 64-episode budget-aging/handoff screen, a 128-episode two-model factorial on new task mechanics, a 36-condition slowdown/recovery paid-controller screen (34 valid), a 32-trajectory three-milestone multistage study, and a 972-state exact grid stress test of five admission rules. Key design decisions: charging deliberation time to the root deadline (well justified by the observed late decisions), scoring only the artifact actually delivered (prevents best-checkpoint oracle credit), and treating timeouts as right-censored durations (correct, and frequently violated elsewhere). Key Results: All results are explicitly exploratory. The exact counterexample (authored constants) shows mean regret ≥ 0.02 for any timing-insensitive policy. In the 36-condition paid-controller screen, all 34 valid episodes matched the disclosed regime, and the deterministic scheduler achieved identical delivered quality to Sonnet 5.5 replanning/conditional controllers while being faster in all 22 matched comparisons (replanning +2.68 s, conditional +2.81 s on average). In the 32-trajectory multistage study under the changing regime, mean delivered quality was 1.000 (immediate scheduler), 0.833 (delayed scheduler), 0.750 (replanner, 4 late milestone attempts), 1.000 (conditional control). In the 128-episode factorial, no revision was infeasible at request time and the discovery-phase failure did not replicate; 37 checkpoint-retention responses arrived after the deadline (late control responses, not lost artifacts). In budget-aging screens, the model gate upgraded 0/4 tight-budget browser checkpoints versus 4/4 for the explicit expected-utility gate. The 972-state grid shows a dispatch-time VETO rule eliminates late continuations but still admits 183 zero-or-negative-value continuations that an exact-value rule avoids. The 972-state grid and witness run no model at all. Baselines (equally informed scheduler, scripted control, moving-average estimator) are appropriately strong for the claims; the 128-condition screen and 36-condition screen froze protocols locally but without external preregistration. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (a joint evaluation standard pairing equivalence and consequential interventions) plus a modest NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (model controllers cost time without quality gain on these fixtures) and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (measurement harness, temporal record). The paper is unusually candid that every ingredient — clock access, duration prediction, deadline propagation, metareasoning overhead, scale-invariant time representations — has prior work (Timely Machine, On the Clock, AgentTime, Gaia2, Tempora, Russell & Wefald), and that the genuinely new element is only the controlled diagnostic comparison and its attribution protocol; it explicitly disclaims inventing scheduling, clock propagation, or the concept of chronoception. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: forecast substitution, timestamp-metadata, and freshness-instruction arms exist but produced null or underpowered contrasts the authors report as such. No error bars, seeds-based confidence intervals, or significance tests appear anywhere; the paper explicitly forswears them given non-independence. Code and data are not publicly released — "a complete public code and data release is not yet available," some source files are temporarily inaccessible, and independent end-to-end reproduction has not been reverified (checksums on result summaries establish record integrity only). Methodological concerns: all models come from one provider (Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5); tasks are 2–4 authored mechanics with 2 repetitions per cell; execution was interrupted (DNS error, HTTP 400, insufficient-credit errors) and resumed in separate blocks with disclosed service-condition differences; the discovery batch was adaptively selected before the follow-up screens. Counterbalancing these, the paper's failure disclosure is exemplary — truncated outputs, schema failures (2/12 conditional-planning schema failures with valid-only means flagged as optimistic), an invalidated earlier diagnostic version retained for audit, and a consistent refusal to impute outcomes. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (small live model pilots plus exact offline constructions, in service of a position). Practical: Yes — runs on CPU (Jetstream) and standard API endpoints; nothing requires exotic hardware. Efficient: The central finding is itself an efficiency verdict — model-based control added ~2.7–2.8 s per decision over an equally informed scheduler with zero quality gain, and one browser parent summary alone consumed ~10 s of an 11-s budget. Effective: Evidence shows the measurement pipeline works and that simple schedulers suffice on these fixtures; it does not show that any agent (or the proposed standard) improves delivered utility on realistic tasks. Scalable: Not tested — long-horizon transfer, multi-agent coordination, RL training, and independent task families are all explicitly prospective. The deliverable is currently paper-form only (no released library, dataset, or trained model); the reusable artifacts described (witness, record schema, protocol) are not yet externally available. Strengths: - The exact constructed witness is a genuine, verifiable contribution: it proves punctuality and unit-invariance jointly underdetermine useful adaptation, which blocks a whole class of weak evaluation claims by construction rather than by experiment. - The attribution discipline — comparing model replanning against an equally informed scheduler with all deliberation time charged — yields the paper's most useful empirical signal: model control was strictly dominated in cost at equal quality in all 22 matched comparisons, a negative result with direct design implications. - Exceptional evidential hygiene: interrupted batches, schema failures, parser-version changes, and an invalidated earlier diagnostic are all disclosed in the record rather than cleaned away, and the paper repeatedly separates claims from evidence status ("constructed tests clarify diagnostic distinctions rather than model capability"). - The taxonomy separating expired decisions, forecast-use errors, missing evidence, and costly deliberation (plus the censored-timeout treatment and the delivered-artifact-only scoring rule) is immediately adoptable by benchmark builders. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensively acknowledged, to an unusual degree: the tasks are short authored workflows with prepared candidates and supplied quality increments; no timestamp-prompt advantage was established; the 34/36 valid-episode screen is descriptive; models share one provider; repeated conditions are not independent task families; the 128-episode study had a documented execution continuation with differing service conditions; no RL result is reported as completed; long-horizon transfer, personalized waiting preferences, and RL benefits remain open; and the release ships the manuscript only with reproduction not reverified. The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — this candor is itself a credibility asset, though it also means the empirical section is largely a feasibility report. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No released artifacts despite the paper's core value being a reusable protocol; without the harness, the "portable temporal record" and intervention designs cannot be independently adopted or verified. - The utility functions (e.g., 0.02/s waiting cost, 0.05/s in the selection diagnostic) are entirely authored; no evidence is offered that any human user's preferences resemble them, so the "useful to the user" framing rests on synthetic preferences throughout. - The equivalence test is operationalized via total variation on a canonical option set, but with prepared candidates and near-tied actions the interpretation of TV divergence as a failure signal is untested — no example shows what a realistic magnitude looks like on a real agent. - Model comparisons (Qwen2.5-3B on cached CPU at 16 tokens vs. Sonnet 5.5 via API at 256 tokens) use non-comparable inference/formatting settings, as the authors note, but Table 4 invites cross-model reading anyway. - The distinction between "chronoception" and ordinary robustness/adaptive control is defended rhetorically (Section 12) but never empirically demonstrated to carve nature at a joint that existing terms like "budget-aware control" do not already cover. Bottom Line: A rigorous, unusually honest position paper whose evaluation framework and counterexample any agent-benchmark designer should absorb, but whose experimental content is exploratory feasibility work with a null-to-negative verdict on model-based temporal control — read it for the standard, not for the results, and note that Timely Machine, On the Clock, and AgentTime already cover adjacent ground that this paper positions against rather than outperforms.

Semantic Atoms for Scalable Text Analysis in Data Analytics in the Era of LLM-Based Agents

J Xie, Z Li, R Ding, B Zhou, S Han, D Zhang · arxiv.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces two query-driven semantic atoms — Tagging (N→N, one string per text item) and Categorization (N→M, a category table) — as the uniform output contract of every semantic LLM call in an analytical agent, materialized as reusable table state that SQL/Python consumes, and builds TADA-Agent plus the 40-request TABench benchmark to evaluate this interface. - Why it's important: Real analytical tables mix free-text columns with structured data, and existing composite semantic operators (semantic sort, semantic filter) hide intermediate semantic values, forcing agents to recompute the same semantic variable — wasting LLM calls and risking inconsistent downstream results. - How it does it: The trick is placing the neural–symbolic boundary at the semantic output and making reusable state (a row-aligned column keyed by row id, or a category table keyed by category id) the default return of every semantic call, with MapReduce-style chunking and a Hoeffding-bound/bootstrap-planned retention budget handling inputs beyond one context window. - The good: The evaluation is unusually honest and well-instrumented: 3 independent runs per configuration, case–run cluster-bootstrap intervals, a stratified human calibration of the LLM judge (78.8% majority agreement, Cohen's κ = 0.68), and a cost ledger showing ≥41.8× fewer semantic-model requests than the LOTUS semantic-operator baseline across 120 task-runs. - The missing: There is no ablation that holds prompting, batching, and skill guidance fixed while swapping only the atom interface for semantic operators — so the measured gains cannot be causally attributed to the interface rather than to the surrounding agent scaffolding (the authors acknowledge this). - Read it or not: Read it if you build semantic query engines, LLM data-analysis agents, or LLM-based text annotation pipelines — the interface-design argument and cost accounting are directly actionable; skip it if you want new algorithms, since the atoms deliberately add no expressive power over a semantic map.

Problem & Motivation: Analysts working with text-bearing tables (e.g., a customer-support table with a complaint-text column alongside resolution time and region) need to derive semantic variables — frustration scores, themes — from text columns and then feed them into exact operations like sorting, filtering, aggregation, and regression. The authors call this workload TADA (Text Analysis in Data Analytics). In the agentic setting, the user's natural-language query dynamically specifies the semantic processing, and execution interleaves neural (LLM) and symbolic (SQL/Python) steps. Two gaps motivate the work: (1) composite semantic operators in systems like LOTUS, Snowflake AI functions, and Databricks package semantic processing with a specific analytical action and expose only the final artifact — a semantic sort returns an ordering but not the row-level scores the next regression needs, inviting recomputation; (2) large tables exceed a single reliable LLM context window, and naive chunk-and-concatenate fails because local processing can drop globally important categories, use synonymous names, or choose inconsistent granularity. The relevant audience is the database-systems and LLM-agent communities building semantic query processing. Key Idea: The core insight is an interface idea, not an algorithmic one: make reusable semantic state the default output of every semantic call by reducing the semantic surface to exactly two fixed output shapes — Tagging (N→N, materialized as a row-aligned column) and Categorization (N→M, materialized as a separate category table) — while leaving all exact computation (filter, sort, GroupBy, regression) in the symbolic runtime. Tagging is functionally identical to a semantic map; the contribution is that the map-first decomposition becomes the plan the interface offers by default, rather than an alternative the agent must discover among composite operators. The paper is explicit and repeated about this: the atoms add no expressive power over semantic-operator systems with a semantic map. Methodology: Three layers. (1) Interface: Both atoms take a text sequence X and an atom-level query q (which the agent derives from the user's analytical query). Tagging returns S = (s1,…,sN) preserving order and length; Categorization returns M category objects (name + optional description). Materialization writes Tagging output as a column keyed by row identifiers and Categorization output as a category table keyed by fresh category ids. A taxonomy (Table 1) shows how 16 representative requests decompose into atom compositions plus symbolic code, recovering semantic map/filter/grouping/ranking/summarization and going beyond single operators (hierarchical topics, group-wise loops, constrained scoring, regression on discovered features). (2) System: TADA-Agent exposes ta.tag and ta.categorize as Python APIs inside a code-execution environment via Programmatic Tool Calling (Anthropic, 2025), so data-dependent loops keep intermediate state inside the runtime instead of unfolding into orchestrator round trips; a strong reasoning model (Claude Opus 5) orchestrates while lightweight models (Claude Sonnet 5) execute atom calls, guided by a text-analysis skill adapting CAST's Algorithmic Prompting and Thinking-before-Speaking. (3) Scale: Large-scale Categorization partitions N rows into balanced chunks of n=1,000, retains local top-r candidates (r ≥ k) per chunk, and semantically consolidates synonyms into the final top-k. Retention is formalized as a top-k preservation problem with a Hoeffding-based sufficient bound, Pr(T̂k = Tk) ≥ 1 − B(C−r)Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ exp(−n_min·Δ²ᵢ,ᵣ/2), and a paired Jeffreys-Dirichlet bootstrap over pilot samples selects the smallest r meeting a 0.95 recovery target. Joint Tagging (shared output domain) reduces to discover-then-assign: large-scale Categorization first, then independent chunk-wise Tagging reassembled by rid. Critical design decisions: the fixed two-shape output contract (justified by composition analysis, but admittedly not a completeness claim — semantic joins and pairwise structures fall outside it); Programmatic Tool Calling over peer-tool registration (justified by the loop-unfolding argument, Figure 2); and a bootstrap planner rather than the plug-in bound, which the authors themselves show is vacuous at their operating points. Key Results: Evaluation on TABench (40 complete analysis requests over spreadsheet tables of 89–201 rows, 7,890 rows total, 10 of 12 scenario classes scored), with five configurations × three runs against a frozen held-out TADA reference and a GPT-5.5 judge. (1) Row-level quality: TADA-Agent and LOTUS-based semantic operators are near ceiling on classification (98.6 vs 97.5) and field extraction (98.9 vs 98.2); semantic operators better reproduce the reference's absolute ranking scale (86.6% vs 81.9% adjacent-agreement) while TADA-Agent has higher ordering agreement (Spearman ρ 0.801 vs 0.752, overlapping four-case intervals); TADA-Agent leads on constrained generation (89.1 vs 78.6). (2) Artifact reliability: TADA-Agent has higher complete-artifact preservation than semantic operators in all five classes (e.g., 12/12 vs 6/12 aggregation/summarization, 8/9 vs 5/9 grouping), though a plain Claude Code agent matches TADA-Agent in three of five classes. (3) Cost: 451 dedicated semantic-model requests for TADA-Agent vs ≥18,852 for semantic operators across 120 task-runs — a ≥41.8× reduction (explicitly a lower bound on the operator side and framed as implementation-level fan-out, not intrinsic). (4) Scale: End-to-end Tagging on 32,179 Play Store reviews reaches 0.973±0.000 accuracy (sentiment) and 0.942±0.002 (topic assignment) in 33 batched requests and 12–37 minutes, vs Claude Code at 0.817±0.047 and 0.856±0.116 respectively; LOTUS's per-row sem map extrapolates to 32,179 calls (~975× TADA's count) and 36–42 hours. In the controlled retention study over six 32K-row synthetic populations with C=20 canonical categories, r=k fails under narrow cutoff gaps (recovery drops to 73.9%), and the pilot bootstrap selects r=10 (oracle r=9–10), achieving 98.5–100% recovery at the selected budget. (5) Transfer:* CUAD clause extraction F1 of 0.787 vs DocETL 0.753 and LOTUS 0.619; BioDEX 0.230 RP@5 / 0.246 RP@10 / 0.385 term recall vs DocETL 0.201/0.196/0.305 and LOTUS 0.194/0.200/0.334 — with single protocol-matched baseline runs, an acknowledged repetition imbalance. Baselines (LOTUS, DocETL, CUAD, BioDEX) are current and appropriate; scale testing is modest (≤32K rows, i.e., one to two orders of magnitude below industrial warehouse scale). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (making reusable semantic state the uniform default output contract of semantic calls, framed as an interface-design principle for agent-planned workflows), NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (TADA-Agent with Programmatic Tool Calling and scale-transparent atom libraries), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (TABench, 40 complete agent-facing analysis requests), and partial NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the request-fan-out and artifact-preservation measurements). Genuinely novel: the reframing of the neural–symbolic boundary as an interface-boundary problem and the top-k retention planner connecting concentration bounds to a bootstrap-selected budget. Standard combination of existing ideas: Tagging is exactly a semantic map, Categorization is MapReduce-style hierarchical reduction, Programmatic Tool Calling is Anthropic's existing mechanism, and the Hoeffding bound application is textbook — the authors state all of this themselves. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is a careful evaluation by the standards of agentic-systems papers. Ablations: the five configurations partially isolate components (Code-only removes semantic judgment; Claude Code removes atoms but keeps scaffolding), but — admitted by the authors — no experiment swaps only the interface while holding prompting/batching/skill fixed. Statistics: three independent runs per configuration, 10,000-resample case–run cluster bootstrap intervals, descriptive Wilson intervals for artifacts, and an explicit refusal to aggregate classes or claim significance from overlapping intervals. Judge validity is calibrated: 39-unit stratified human study with six annotators (78.8% majority agreement, κ = 0.68, judge agreement within the annotator pool's own range). Code/data/model weights: no public release URL is mentioned — not stated. Methodological concerns: (a) the evaluation reference is a held-out TADA run, which the authors candidly flag as favoring TADA-Agent's run-to-run consistency in the ordering metric; (b) the semantic-operator baseline's ≥41.8× request count is a strict lower bound reconstructed from incomplete logs, and LOTUS's optimizer does not cover semantic maps, so the per-row execution path may not represent an optimized operator deployment; (c) TABench was constructed by the authors (mostly generated workbooks) and is evaluated against their own judge; (d) BioDEX baselines are single runs. The paper distinguishes claims from measurements unusually well, with metering caveats (Appendix G) and explicit statements that request-count reduction does not imply total-cost reduction. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built SYSTEM component — TADA-Agent is a running agent over a code-execution runtime). Practical: Yes — it runs on commercially available frontier APIs (Claude Opus 5 orchestrator, Claude Sonnet 5 atoms, GPT-5.5 judge) plus standard pandas/numpy/scikit-learn in a sandboxed Python runtime. Efficient: Batched execution (n=1,000) uses 1.2–1.6M tokens and 12–37 minutes per 32K-row run, versus an extrapolated 4–6M tokens and 36–42 hours for the per-row LOTUS path; the atoms trade a modest orchestration-model overhead for a 1–3 order-of-magnitude reduction in semantic-model calls, though total system cost including host-agent reasoning is not reconciled. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on TABench and three scale workloads, but quality is measured against a self-produced reference run and an LLM judge, so it is a proxy for analyst-verified correctness; the human calibration (κ = 0.68) partially mitigates this. Scalable: Tested to 32K rows end-to-end and 32K rows in the retention study — a real but modest multiple of the TABench scale; asymptotic cost, provider variance, and latency beyond this are explicitly not established, and consolidation of B local category lists into one reducer call will eventually hit its own context budget (the implementation rejects oversized reducer inputs rather than handling them). Deliverable: the paper describes a system and benchmark; no public repository, library, trained model, or dataset release is stated. Strengths: - The interface argument is made with unusual intellectual honesty: the paper repeatedly concedes the atoms add zero expressive power over a semantic map and locates the contribution precisely in the default — that materialized semantic state is what every call returns — which is the correct, falsifiable framing for an interface contribution. - The scale story is layered correctly: a Hoeffding-style sufficient condition with a proof (Appendix C), a bootstrap planner that the authors show must supersede the vacuous plug-in bound, and a controlled retention study (six populations, 5,000 held-out partitions per candidate r, no LLM calls during evaluation) that cleanly isolates one stage — rather than a single end-to-end anecdote. - Evaluation hygiene exceeds field norms: per-run telemetry tables exposing a provider-failure anomaly (105 request events vs 33 planned) rather than hiding it, a strict-lower-bound treatment of the opponent's request count, disclosure of two engineering accommodations to the LOTUS baseline, and three boundary cases (semantic join, text-to-table, imputation) reported as out-of-contract rather than silently dropped. - The failure-mode analysis of baselines (lexicon sentiment missing sarcasm, TF–IDF clustering producing incoherent categories, artifacts delivered with missing workbook mutations) is concrete and connects the artifact-preservation metric to observable errors. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility. They state: the two atoms are not a universal algebra and cannot express pairwise joins, global matching, graph outputs, or comparison-based ranking; the evaluation compares complete systems without isolating the interface from prompting/batching/skill; the reference-run protocol makes the Spearman comparison a consistency measure for TADA and an agreement-with-a-different-system measure for baselines; artifact denominators are small and intervals overlap; large-scale Categorization with open discovery is not evaluated end-to-end (only the retention stage under exact assignments); request counts measure implementation fan-out, not total cost; materialized state can propagate a single mistaken value into multiple downstream steps, and the cost of repairing intermediates is unmeasured; BioDEX baseline repetition is uneven; TABench covers 40 of 43 requests and 10 of 12 classes. This is an unusually complete self-audit. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged issues: (1) The headline request-reduction comparison is structurally confounded — LOTUS's native sem map is per-row by default and the authors note its optimizer does not cover maps, so the 975× figure partly measures a chosen, unbatched execution path of the baseline rather than a property of operator interfaces; an operator system that emits per-chunk map calls is not tested. (2) TABench is small (40 cases, 3–5 per class, mostly ~200-row generated workbooks), self-authored, and scored by the authors' own judge against their own reference run — the entire quality story rests on one LLM-judge pipeline, and no second independent judge or human-scored full case set is provided (the 39-unit calibration sample is a mitigation, not a substitute). (3) The cost accounting never reports total dollars/total tokens for the TABench comparison (token totals were not persistently recorded for the operator baseline), so the 41.8× request reduction could coexist with comparable token spend given TADA's larger batch prompts. (4) The neural–symbolic boundary diagnostic (Appendix D) uses a single GPT-4.1 execution per scale point against a raw monolithic prompt — a strawman illustrating mechanism, which the authors admit, but it is the only direct evidence for the boundary claim motivating the whole design. (5) Concurrency is not reported for the large-scale runs, making the 12–37 minute wall times hard to interpret or cost. (6) No release of TADA-Agent, the atom library, TABench, or prompts is mentioned, which caps reproducibility of a paper whose contribution is an interface. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM-based data-analysis or semantic-query systems gains a genuinely useful design lens — materialize semantic outputs as reusable table state by default, and batch beyond the context window behind a fixed API — supported by honest cost telemetry, even though the atoms themselves are a re-packaging of the semantic map and the evaluation's self-referential reference protocol and unreleased artifact mean LOTUS-style operator systems with good escape hatches remain strong alternatives for single-operator workloads.

#132 — Innovative (62)

SkillRubricsRL: Evolving Skill-Grounded Agents with Rubric-Guided Reinforcement Learning

Z Huang, J Pan, YF Zhang, T Chen, J Lin, K Ruan, X Xu… · aclanthology.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SkillRubricsRL, a skill-augmented reinforcement learning framework that attaches an applicability-aware rubric to every retrieved skill, decomposing per-skill credit into a rubric-based fulfillment reward (did the agent execute the skill?) and a dropout-based counterfactual utility estimate (did the skill help task success?). - Why it's important: Existing skill-augmented RL treats retrieved skills as unobserved prompt context supervised only by a trajectory-level outcome reward, so retrieval errors — irrelevant or harmful skills — cannot be detected or corrected during training. - How it does it: Each skill carries a dual representation (prompt principle + weighted rubric criteria); rubric scores from an LLM judge are added to the GRPO reward as a dense intrinsic signal, while stochastic skill replacement within the existing rollout group yields per-skill utility estimates that drive retrieval ranking and LLM-driven skill-bank evolution. - The good: A human validation study (3 annotators, 60 trajectory–skill pairs, trajectory-clustered bootstrap CIs) shows the LLM judge agrees with human consensus on skill execution (Cohen's κ = 0.776, F1 = 0.928), and ablations show every component matters: removing rubric reward, dropout utility, or skill evolution drops ALFWorld average success from 97.7% to 91.4%, 94.5%, and 87.5% respectively. - The missing: Evaluation is confined to two benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop) with a single seed per configuration and no error bars on the headline numbers, and the rubric judge is a proprietary ByteDance model (Doubao-1.8), so the reward-quality claim is not independently reproducible. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building skill- or memory-augmented agentic RL systems — the per-skill credit assignment framing and the skill-on/skill-off internalization diagnostic are directly transferable — but it can be skipped if you work outside agentic RL or process-reward design.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (58) is mixed: the human-validation study with clustered-bootstrap CIs and judge-agreement statistics (κ = 0.776) sets a standard most rubric-reward papers skip, but single-seed main results make the 2–3 pp headline margins unreliable, the proprietary Doubao judge blocks reward-channel reproduction, and the counterfactual utility estimator's variance is uncharacterized. Novelty (68) is the strength — casting retrieved skills as per-skill rewardable units with a fulfillment/utility decomposition is closer to a new formulation than a new method — and the skill-off internalization finding adds Non-Obviousness (65). Resilience (58) is dented by the unaddressed Heat-category anomaly, which is exactly the failure mode the utility channel should prevent. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*60 = 62.
