Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents increasingly carry external procedural memory (skill banks retrieved into prompts). In current skill-augmented RL systems (SkillRL, D2Skill, RetroAgent, etc.), the environment returns only a terminal success/failure reward, so the training signal is blind to how knowledge was used: whether each retrieved skill was executed, ignored, or actively harmful. The authors audit SkillRL on ALFWorld and report that outcome-only RL reaches 89.9% task success while executing only 15.6% of retrieved skills — retrieval mixes useful and useless skills and the policy follows the wrong ones (illustrated by a two-pan task where the agent loops over cabinets for 30 steps because low-utility skills bias it away from stove burners). The open problem is per-skill credit assignment: a single scalar r(τ) cannot identify the marginal role of each skill in the context. The beneficiaries are anyone training agents that couple policy optimization with growing external memory. Key Idea: Treat each skill as a dual-use object: its prompt view guides behavior while its reward view — a weighted set of observable trajectory-level criteria, gated by an application condition — makes execution itself a rewardable unit. Fulfillment (rubric-scored execution) and utility (counterfactual outcome change when the skill is swapped out) are deliberately separated, because a skill can be faithfully followed yet irrelevant. The prompt channel and reward channel are generated from the same skill specification, preventing them from drifting apart. Methodology: The pipeline runs inside a GRPO loop on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. (1) A retriever (embedding similarity, top-3 general + top-2 task skills) selects skills for each task prompt. (2) After rollout, an LLM judge (Doubao-1.8) scores the full action–observation transcript against each retrieved skill's rubric R(s) = {(c_j, w_j)}, giving r_intr(τ) = mean over applicable skills of the weighted criterion scores; the training reward is r(τ) = λ_env·r_env(τ) + β·r_intr(τ) with (λ_env, β) = (1.0, 0.2). (3) Utility Δ(s,t) is estimated counterfactually by reusing the GRPO rollout group — one trajectory anchors the full skill set, the others each drop one skill — and measuring the outcome difference; utilities are EMA-aggregated into weights w_n(s) that re-rank retrieval by cos(s,t) + α·w_n(s) and archive skills with w_n(s) < τ. (4) Every K steps, an LLM (Gemini-3.1) proposes new skills from failure pools, with strict anti-overfitting constraints (no object–location priors), budget-limited admission, embedding/title deduplication, and conservative merging (max 1 merge/update, LLM-verified scope match). (5) After step 75, rollouts mix 50/50 skill-on/skill-off prompts so the policy learns both to use and internalize skills. Critical design decisions: fulfillment enters the policy gradient while utility only shapes retrieval/bank (justified — dropout variance would be dangerous in the reward); rubric criteria are capped at 2 per skill (prevents reward bloat); utility probes reuse existing rollout groups (zero extra external tokens). The λ/β weight choice and the cap of 2 rubric items are stated but not sensitivity-analyzed. Key Results: On ALFWorld, SkillRubricsRL reaches 97.7% average success (skill-off) vs. 94.9% for RetroAgent, 90.6% for D2Skill, and 89.9% for SkillRL — a 2.8 pp gain over the strongest multi-skill baseline; skill-on achieves 96.1%. On WebShop, skill-on achieves 84.4% success (82.8% skill-off) vs. 80.5% (D2Skill) and 82.9% (Skill1). Skill execution rate improves by over 50 percentage points versus the outcome-only baseline's 15.6%. Ablations on ALFWorld (skill-off 97.7% reference): no rubric reward 91.4%, no dropout utility 94.5%, no skill evolution 87.5% (largest drop). Notable counter-intuitive finding: skill-off beats skill-on on ALFWorld (97.7 vs. 96.1), which the authors interpret as successful procedural internalization rather than failure of the skill mechanism; on WebShop skill-on retains an edge (84.4 vs. 82.8), attributed to instance-specific attribute constraints. Baselines include current 2025–2026 methods (GiGPO, SkillRL, D2Skill, RetroAgent, Skill1, Skill0), so the comparison set is strong, though all run on the same 7B-scale policy. The 77.9% Heat-category score under skill-on (vs. 100% skill-off) is an anomalous cell the authors do not discuss. Test scale is standard for the field (ALFWorld per-category suites, WebShop full test set); no stress-scale testing. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel move is casting retrieved skills as per-skill rewardable units with a two-channel (fulfillment/utility) decomposition — prior rubric-as-reward work scores single responses, and prior skill-augmented RL supervises only outcomes. The ingredients are individually standard: rubric-based LLM judging, dropout-style counterfactuals, GRPO, failure-driven skill curation; the contribution is their composition into a coherent credit-assignment framework plus the empirical finding that skill-off can match skill-on performance, evidencing internalization. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and isolate each of the four components (rubric reward, dropout utility, contribution-aware retrieval, skill evolution) with per-category breakdowns. The human-validation study is unusually careful: 3 annotators, trajectory-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs, Fleiss' κ = 0.601–0.671 for inter-annotator agreement, judge validity reported with CIs (κ = 0.776 [0.570, 0.947]; F1 = 0.928 [0.853, 0.984]; Spearman ρ = 0.792; MAE = 0.127). Training configuration, prompt templates, token costs (~103–127M judge tokens, ~$2.47–$3.02 judge cost), and an honest accounting-boundary caveat are provided; code is at https://github.com/gminiheimdallr-a11y/SkillRubricsRL. Concerns: (a) main results report no seeds, error bars, or significance tests — single-run differences of 2–3 pp on ALFWorld/WebShop may not be robust; (b) the rubric judge is Doubao-1.8, a proprietary ByteDance model unavailable to the public, undermining full reproduction of the reward channel; (c) the counterfactual utility estimate rests on a single anchor trajectory per group, a high-variance estimator whose noise properties are unquantified; (d) rubric quality and skill evolution are co-developed and evaluated on the same two benchmarks, so reward-design Goodharting cannot be ruled out — partially mitigated by the human agreement study. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained systems with benchmarks; a released code artifact). Practical: Runs on a 7B policy with GRPO plus API calls to two commercial LLMs, so it is deployable on standard multi-GPU training setups, though two of the three LLM roles depend on vendor APIs. Efficient: Judge cost is ~$2.47–$3.02 per environment run and utility probes add zero external tokens by reusing rollout groups; total end-to-end training cost (actor compute, rollouts) is not reported. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on the tested benchmarks (skill execution +50 pp, success +2.1–2.8 pp over strong baselines), but the internalization claim rests on a mixed-prompt training regime the authors themselves engineered, and no out-of-distribution transfer is tested. Scalable: Untested beyond 7B policies and two environments; skill-bank growth is bounded by strict budgets, but behavior at 10–100× task diversity or bank size is claimed, not measured. Delivers: released code + prompt templates; the skill bank and rubric banks are environment-specific artifacts, not portable models. Strengths: (1) A crisp, well-motivated problem decomposition — fulfillment vs. utility — that cleanly explains a real failure mode (89.9% success with only 15.6% skill execution) and is validated by an audit rather than assumed. (2) The mechanism-consistent experimental design: the 50/50 skill-on/off rollout mixing turns "does the policy internalize skills?" from a hand-wave into a measurable comparison, and the skill-off result (97.7%) is a genuinely interesting finding. (3) The human-validation appendix sets a standard most rubric-reward papers skip, with clustered-bootstrap CIs and honest reporting of moderate annotator agreement. (4) Ablations show a full gradient across all four components, with skill evolution mattering most (−10.2 pp), supporting the paper's central claim that static skill banks are insufficient. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that evaluation covers only two environments and broader testing is future work, and that the rubric formulation is instantiated only for procedural skills, with declarative/compositional skills left open. They confront these directly and do not overclaim beyond ALFWorld/WebShop — a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge single-seed reporting, judge-model dependency, or the anomalous Heat-category result. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No multi-seed variance on main tables: 2.1–2.8 pp margins over D2Skill/RetroAgent/Skill1 are within plausible run-to-run noise for RL on ALFWorld/WebShop. (2) The utility estimator's variance — one anchor trajectory per GRPO group, binary environment reward — is never characterized; EMA smoothing helps but noisy Δ estimates could silently corrupt retrieval rankings, and no analysis of estimate stability is given. (3) The reward-weight hyperparameters (λ_env, β = 1.0, 0.2) and the 2-criterion rubric cap are unjustified choices with no sensitivity analysis. (4) Skill-on Heat dropping to 77.9% while skill-off hits 100% is a dogs-not-barking anomaly suggesting retrieved skills can actively hurt specific task families — exactly the failure mode the utility channel should prevent — yet it is unmentioned. (5) The judge (Doubao-1.8) and skill updater (Gemini-3.1) are proprietary/frontier vendor models; an open-weights ablation of judge quality would establish whether the framework depends on a top-tier judge. (6) The internalization narrative partially conflates the effect of the mixed training regime with the effect of rubric rewards — a skill-off-only training control is absent. (7) Compute-matched comparison against GiGPO alone (no skills) is unclear; GiGPO already reaches 90.8% ALFWorld without any skill machinery, so the marginal value over simply improving the RL algorithm is not isolated. Bottom Line: A thoughtful and unusually well-validated contribution to agentic RL that turns retrieved skills from opaque context into supervised rewardable units — practitioners building skill/memory-augmented agents should read it and adopt the fulfillment/utility decomposition, but the 2–3 pp headline gains on two benchmarks from single runs warrant waiting for independent replication before treating it as the new default.

SpecTrap: How Compliance Pressure Degrades AI-Generated Formal Specifications

R Kumar · pys8vc40ox3z7qxp.public.blob.vercel-storage.com · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that structural compliance instructions (e.g., "generate at least 8 properties, do not refuse") drop file-level soundness of GPT-4o-generated Hypothesis property-based tests from 60.0% to 13.3% (p = 1.76×10⁻⁴, Cohen's h = 1.025), and releases SpecTrap, a pip-installable tool with Z3 cross-validation for testing AI spec generators under such pressure. - Why it's important: AI-assisted verification pipelines routinely prompt models to "be comprehensive, cover all edge cases," and an unsound property lifted into a verification obligation certifies a false claim — making LLM compliance failure modes part of the trusted computing base of formal verification workflows. - How it does it: A factorial pressure design (baseline, uncertainty prohibition, quantity mandate, benign pressure, escape hatch) generates tests for 7 Python functions with known contracts, then classifies each generated file as sound/unsound/errored/vacuous by executing it under Hypothesis with a fixed seed. - The good: The two headline degradations survive Bonferroni correction with large effect sizes (h = 1.025 and h = 0.796), the failure taxonomy (IEEE 754 NaN violations, hallucinated Hypothesis strategies, vacuous quota-filling) is concrete, and every number traces to released data in a public repository. - The missing: Only 7 target functions, 3 models, and 15–30 generations per cell — and the file-level soundness metric may be structurally confounded with the quantity mandate, since a "minimum 8 properties" instruction mechanically increases the chance that any single file contains at least one false property. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in LLM robustness and AI-for-formal-methods who want a transferable negative result on prompt-based remediation; practitioners wanting broad evidence across model families and spec languages should wait for larger-scale replication.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building AI-assisted verification pipelines use LLMs to generate formal specifications, property-based tests, and verification conditions. Prior work (The Compliance Trap, Kumar 2025, arXiv preprint) showed frontier models fabricate facts under "do not refuse"-style compliance pressure in Q&A domains, but nobody had tested whether this soundness degradation extends to structured code output — where a fabricated property becomes a false verification obligation that the prover faithfully proves. The gap: soundness checking in verification pipelines happens at the property level, not at the spec-generation level, so a model asserting false properties under production-style prompts ("generate at least 8 properties, don't leave anything untested") is invisible to the pipeline. Key Idea: Treat Hypothesis execution as an automated soundness oracle for AI-generated specifications, and apply a factorial compliance-pressure design to measure how specific prompt components (uncertainty prohibition vs. quantity mandate) causally degrade file-level soundness — with the corollary insight that prompt-based escape hatches ("skip if unsure") cannot transfer to code generation because code output has no syntactic analog of "I don't know." Methodology: (1) Target selection: 7 Python functions (JSON roundtrip, Base64, sorting, URL encoding, set algebra, plus real cryptographic code — Fernet and SHA-256) with 33 validated ground-truth Hypothesis tests. (2) Pressure conditions: 5-level factorial — D (baseline), G3 (uncertainty prohibition), G4 (quantity mandate + do-not-refuse), F (benign framing), G3E (G3 + escape hatch), with exact prompts in the released code. (3) Generation: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini via OpenAI API, Claude Sonnet 4 via OpenRouter, all at temperature 1.0, 252 generations total. (4) Validation pipeline: ast.parse syntax check → property counting → pytest execution with --hypothesis-seed=0 → classification as sound/unsound/errored/vacuous. (5) Statistics: two-proportion z-tests, Cohen's h effect sizes, Bonferroni correction at k = 3 (α = 0.0167), file-level soundness as the primary metric (justified because pressure conditions inflate property counts, diluting per-property rates). (6) Z3/SMT cross-validation of common unsound patterns. Critical design decisions: file-level rather than property-level metric (defensible but interacts with the quantity mandate — see gaps); temperature 1.0 for comparability with prior work (acknowledged as a variance risk); only 2–3 epochs per condition per function (statistical power limitation the authors concede). Key Results: GPT-4o file-level soundness drops 60.0% (18/30) baseline to 13.3% (4/30) under G4 (Δ = −46.7pp, h = 1.025, p = 1.76×10⁻⁴, survives Bonferroni). GPT-4o-mini drops 53.3% (8/15) to 16.7% (5/30) under G3 alone (Δ = −36.7pp, h = 0.796, p = 0.011, survives Bonferroni). Claude Sonnet 4 degrades 70.0% → 30.0% at G4 (p = 0.074, borderline, n = 10). The models show differential vulnerability thresholds within the same family: GPT-4o-mini collapses at G3, GPT-4o only at G4. The escape hatch fails to transfer: G3E 13.3% (2/15) vs G3 16.7% (5/30), a −3.3pp negative result despite the same remediation giving +15.6pp in factual Q&A. On cryptographic code, GPT-4o falls from 100% (4/4) to 25% (1/4) soundness under pressure, though n is too small for significance. Failure taxonomy: false float-roundtrip universals (NaN), hallucinated APIs (st.dict, st.raises) at 4× baseline rate under G3, vacuous quota-filling, and false universals. Baselines are the same models under default prompting rather than alternative spec-generation methods; scale is small (7 functions, 252 generations). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (compliance-induced fabrication extends to code/specification generation, with domain-specific failure modes and per-model pressure thresholds) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (SpecTrap) and a genuinely new methodological use of Hypothesis as an automated soundness oracle for LLM output. The factorial pressure design and the compliance-trap phenomenon itself are imported from the author's own prior preprint; the transfer-failure of the escape hatch is the most non-obvious finding, but the contribution is an extension of one prior finding to a new domain rather than a new mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation structure is present and appropriate — the factorial design isolates which pressure component (uncertainty prohibition vs. quantity mandate) triggers collapse, and per-model thresholds are separately tested. Statistical discipline is real: two-proportion z-tests, Cohen's h, Bonferroni correction, and both headline results survive correction. Code and data are publicly released (https://github.com/rkstu/spectrap), with a reproduction script and pre-computed results traceable to a single JSON artifact. Concerns: sample sizes of 10–30 per cell with only 2–3 epochs; uneven cell sizes across conditions (e.g., GPT-4o G4 has 30 generations, GPT-4o-mini G4 has 15); the key prior work it builds on is the author's own single-author preprint, unreplicated externally; only 3 models (no Gemini, Llama, or DeepSeek despite the prior work covering 11 models); Claude results do not reach significance; and all evaluation is on the authors' own 7-function suite, though the functions are standard-library and shipping-crypto code rather than adversarially curated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a small systems artifact). Practical: Yes — runs on commodity hardware via OpenAI/OpenRouter APIs; the tool is pip-installable and validates ground-truth tests and Z3 cross-validation without any API keys. Efficient: 252 generations is trivially cheap; the pipeline is pytest + Hypothesis + Z3 execution, not model training. Effective: The evidence convincingly demonstrates the problem exists, but offers no working mitigation — the one tested remediation fails, so the paper solves the diagnosis, not the cure. Scalable: Not tested beyond 7 functions and 3 models; whether threshold behavior generalizes to other spec languages (Lean, Coq, Dafny) or larger function suites is unclaimed and untested. Delivers a software artifact: pip-installable tool, reproduction script, and released data/model outputs; no trained model. Strengths: - The escape-hatch negative result is the standout: it converts a promising remediation finding from Q&A into a domain-dependence claim with a plausible mechanism (code has no uncertainty-token output channel), which is a genuinely useful and falsifiable insight for the prompting-robustness literature. - The factorial design correctly attributes collapse to different prompt components for different models (G3 for GPT-4o-mini, G4 for GPT-4o) rather than treating "compliance pressure" as a monolith. - The failure taxonomy is actionable — hallucinated Hypothesis strategies and NaN-universal properties are specific, checkable failure modes a pipeline could lint for. - End-to-end reproducibility discipline: fixed Hypothesis seed, all 252 generations regenerable, numbers traceable to one released JSON file. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: sample sizes of 15–30 per cell limit power for small effects; temperature 1.0 may inflate variance; baseline soundness is only 53–60% (they frame the contribution as differential degradation, not absolute reliability); the escape-hatch negative result may be wording-sensitive; and only Python/Hypothesis is tested, with Lean/Coq/Dafny left open. This is a direct, non-defensive limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Metric confound: the file-level soundness metric structurally penalizes the G4 condition — a "minimum 8 properties" mandate mechanically raises the probability that any file contains at least one false property, independent of per-property fabrication rate. A per-property analysis or a matched-property-count control is needed to fully attribute the G4 collapse to fabrication rather than arithmetic of the metric. - Uneven generation counts across cells (10/15/30) and only 2–3 epochs per function-per-condition raise questions about epoch-level variance; no multi-seed variance decomposition is reported. - The Claude Sonnet 4 result rests on n = 10 per cell, and the paper's "partially robust" characterization for Claude is not statistically supported. - All cited compliance-trap evidence ultimately traces to the author's own unreplicated preprint; no independent replication of the underlying phenomenon exists. - The vacuous-property classification interacts ambiguously with file-level soundness — under G4 the model produces vacuous quota-fillers, and the paper does not state clearly whether vacuous files count as unsound, which changes the headline numbers' interpretation. - The claim that production verification workflows "are operating at G4-equivalent pressure" is asserted from prompt similarity, not measured from real workflow prompts. Bottom Line: A careful, well-instrumented, if small-scale study that meaningfully extends compliance-pressure fabrication findings to specification generation and delivers a valuable negative result on remediation transfer — worth reading for LLM-robustness and AI-for-verification researchers, but its 7-function, 3-model, single-preprint-lineage evidence base needs independent replication before it should drive pipeline design decisions.

StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent (245 ▲ )

Chengzhi Liu, Yuxiang Lai, Yuzhe Yang, Yanqing Liu, Jiheng Hou, Yue Cao, Haonan Wang, Ruixi Fan, Lan Wang, Sheng Liu, Songyou Peng, Yale Song, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Xin Eric Wang, Jui-Hsin Lai, Youbao Tang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces StreamVibe, a three-part contribution for streaming video agents — StreamVibe-Bench (4.1K evaluation / 85K training samples with annotated help points spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamically evolving user intents), StreamVibe-VL (a streaming policy trained with adaptive-weight SFT and localized trajectory RL), and StreamVibe-Harness (an external state-tracking layer with intent lifecycles and hierarchical memory). - Why it's important: Real assistants must infer unstated goals, track what has already been done, and adapt as users change their minds — behaviors current proactive video models, which respond only to explicit one-shot requests, completely lack, so this defines and measures a gap that blocks deployment of always-on video assistants. - How it does it: The core moves are (i) localizing GRPO rollouts around annotated help points with a one-to-one-matched timing×content reward instead of full-trajectory optimization, and (ii) separating response generation from persistent intent/task-state bookkeeping kept in an external harness with hierarchical memory retrieval. - The good: The benchmark construction is unusually rigorous — Gemini-proposed annotations verified by four independent human reviewers under a detailed rubric, with Fleiss' κ of 0.82–0.87 and a methodologically correct agreement audit, plus both pointwise (gold history) and trajectory (self-generated history) protocols that cleanly isolate local decision quality from sustained-interaction degradation. - The missing: Absolute trajectory performance remains low (best Timing F1 19.96–26.51 on the authors' own benchmark, Content F1 8.75–10.83), and on pointwise explicit intents Gemini-3.8-Flash (Timing F1 67.81, Content F1 66.93) still beats StreamVibe-VL RL (60.88 / 39.31), so the headline "10.7% improvement" claim needs scrutiny; no seed variance, no latency measurements, and no released code/weights URL are reported. - Read it or not: Researchers working on streaming/proactive video agents or agent memory should read the benchmark protocol and diagnostic findings (the pointwise-vs-trajectory degradation analysis is genuinely informative); practitioners seeking a deployable assistant can skip it since absolute performance is far from usable.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses sustained proactive assistance in streaming video, where an agent watches a 1 FPS stream and must decide when and how to intervene without an explicit request. Three gaps in prior work motivate it: (i) implicit intents ("help me finish this task") must be inferred from observations; (ii) prior responses change task state, so a once-correct response becomes wrong later, and models lack up-to-date state tracking; (iii) user intents evolve mid-interaction (revisions, added constraints, interruptions), which existing streaming models ignore. The intended audience is builders of video agents for physical (egocentric, procedural) and digital (GUI/computer-use) settings; the closed gap is that prior proactive benchmarks (ProactiveVideoQA, EgoProactive, IPIBench, GuideMe, etc.) cover single intent types, single environments, and evaluate responses independently. Key Idea: Two ideas anchor the work. First, for the model: localized trajectory RL — instead of optimizing whole interaction trajectories (diffuse credit assignment), construct short causal rollouts around annotated help points and reward GRPO with a one-to-one-matched product of timing score τ(Δ) and LLM-judged content score ρ, aggregated as R_align = (1+α)Σ τρ / (N_pred + αN_gt), blended with a trajectory-level coherence reward (λ=0.7). Second, for the system: treat user intents as first-class persistent state objects with explicit lifecycles (evidence-waiting → matched → delivered → closed/retired) maintained outside the policy by a harness that supplies a compact integrated context, so bookkeeping about "which requests are still valid" is not the policy's job. Methodology: The pipeline has three parts. (1) StreamVibe-Bench: task videos from ~15 public sources (Assembly101, HoloAssist, Ego-Exo4D, AgentNet, GUI-World, etc.) are annotated by Gemini-3.8-Flash with candidate help points (response windows, preferred times, reference replies), then filtered by unanimous four-reviewer human approval; streams are serialized causally at 1 FPS so future frames are unavailable. Dynamic samples add timestamped intent revisions/compositions/interruptions. (2) StreamVibe-VL: a streaming video LLM trained in two stages — adaptive streaming SFT (Eq. 1) with per-token weights that balance silence/response decision tokens against the training distribution's class ratio, then localized GRPO as above with point-level (R_align) and trajectory-level (R_glob) rewards. (3) StreamVibe-Harness: a separate process running Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct off-the-shelf for memory summarization (32-second chunks, 5 mid-term summaries consolidated into up to 8 long-term blocks, FIFO eviction), maintaining state S_t = ⟨A_t, P_t, R_t⟩ with typed event updates and source-specific constraints (a request is not evidence of occurrence), and retrieving via purely lexical overlap (no embeddings, ≤3 facts + 3 transitions per decision). Design decisions generally justified: asymmetric RL reward accounting for over/under-response is well motivated; the fixed 10-skill library is admitted to be hand-written; the λ=0.7 and chunk/retention hyperparameters are asserted without ablation. Key Results: On StreamVibe-Bench (±2s tolerance), under trajectory evaluation StreamVibe-VL RL reaches Timing F1 of 26.51 (explicit), 26.26 (implicit), 19.96 (dynamic), with Content F1 10.83/19.13/8.91, versus streaming baselines at Timing F1 7.15–32.37 and Content F1 0.62–16.51 — ViSpeak actually posts the highest explicit Timing F1 (32.37) while StreamVibe wins on implicit/dynamic and answer quality. Under pointwise evaluation with gold history, Gemini-3.8-Flash leads on explicit intents (Timing F1 81.00, Content F1 66.93 vs StreamVibe RL 72.01/61.28 on implicit — StreamVibe wins implicit but loses explicit). RL reduces false positive rates substantially (e.g., FPR 46.19 vs 47.90 explicit pointwise; Monitoring subtype FPR −15.3pp). The harness adds 12.3% on trajectory proactive performance (e.g., implicit Timing F1 20.61→22.48 SFT, RL Content F1 10.65→14.22 dynamic). Diagnostic findings are striking: Timing F1 collapses with duration (0.262 at <1min to 0.041 at >5min); trajectory Timing F1 drops ~2–5× versus pointwise (63.5–75.6 → 12.1–28.2 across models); Recall drops from early to late trajectory halves (e.g., RV 0.641→0.464). Baselines are current (2026 Gemini-3.x, GPT-Realtime-2.1, Qwen3-VL-8B) and strong, though streaming baselines score near zero on several metrics, suggesting possible under-tuned implementations. General video understanding is preserved (OVO-Bench 59.29–59.44, MVBench ~70.6 vs base ~69.3). The paper reports these as measured results, but the "10.7% over baselines" headline is a claim that does not hold uniformly against proprietary pointwise scores. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first benchmark unifying explicit/implicit/dynamic intents across physical and digital environments with both pointwise and trajectory evaluation) plus NEW METHOD (localized trajectory RL with matched timing-content rewards, and adaptive decision-token weighting in SFT) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (StreamVibe-Harness). The harness itself is a competent combination of known ideas — persistent memory, hierarchical summarization, lexical retrieval, prompt-based state injection — applied to a new problem; the genuinely novel elements are the intent-lifecycle formulation and the localized RL reward structure. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist at the component level (SFT vs RL vs +Harness, per category), and the agreement audit for annotation is methodologically careful (Fleiss' κ 0.84 overall, correctly computed on pre-filter candidates). However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere; the general timing evaluation set is drawn from JoyAI-VL's public training data (held out from StreamVibe training, which mitigates but does not eliminate contamination questions); the benchmark was annotated by Gemini-3.8-Flash, which is also a reported baseline (creating incentive-compatibility tension, partially addressed by the κ=0.73–0.79 Gemini–human audit); content quality is judged by a single LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6) at 0–4 scale without human validation of the judge on this task; several hyperparameters (λ=0.7, α, chunk sizes, skill list) lack ablations; the paper is a preprint (arXiv 2610.34662v2), not peer-reviewed. A project page (stream-vibe.github.io) is cited, but no explicit code, data, or model-weight release URL is stated in the provided text — reproducibility of the model side is therefore uncertain. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark + trained model + evaluated system), with a SYSTEMS component in the harness. - Practical: Runs on streaming video at 1 FPS with an 8B-scale policy and a separate Qwen3-VL-4B inference process — commercially feasible hardware, though the second process adds infrastructure complexity. - Efficient: Not evaluated — no latency, throughput, tokens/second, or memory-footprint numbers are reported for either the policy or the harness; the harness's per-chunk summarization calls are an unquantified recurring cost. - Effective: Evidence is a proxy at real-world scale: it solves the authors' benchmark reasonably (best trajectory Timing F1 ~26, Content F1 ~19) and transfers partially to EgoProactive/IPIBench, but absolute trajectory performance remains far below what a deployed assistant would need, and timing F1 below 0.05 on long videos indicates the sustained-interaction problem is far from solved. - Scalable: Only claimed implicitly — the hierarchical memory bounds context growth, but nothing is tested beyond ~5-minute videos and 8-minute average samples; 100× longer interactions or concurrent intents are untested. The work delivers a benchmark (artifact, pending release confirmation) and a trained model; it stops at paper form plus a project page otherwise. Strengths: - The benchmark's evaluation design is the real contribution: separating pointwise (gold history) from trajectory (self-generated history) evaluation cleanly quantifies how much of the failure is local decision-making versus error propagation — the ~3–5× F1 collapse between the two settings is a finding other groups can build on immediately. - Annotation quality control exceeds community norms: four-reviewer unanimous approval, a 7-criterion rubric, and a correctly specified inter-annotator audit (κ computed on pre-filter candidates, explicitly noting that computing κ on retained samples would be invalid). - The localized trajectory RL reward is a concrete, transferable technique: one-to-one matching with asymmetric penalty for over-response (α term) directly targets the recall-vs-FPR trade-off that plagues proactive agents, and the measured FPR reductions (e.g., −15.3pp on Monitoring) show it works. - Honest diagnostic analysis: the paper's own figures expose its model's weaknesses (duration sensitivity, in-trajectory forgetting on Revision intents) rather than burying them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion explicitly states that real-world proactive interaction "may involve richer intent evolution and tighter coupling between user needs and environmental changes than captured in our current setting," and that feedback between intents and environment over longer horizons is left to future work. The harness section admits the skill library is a fixed set of ten hand-written read-only behavioral specifications, and that state updates require "sufficient" evidence without defining a learned threshold. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment of scope — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline "10.7% improvement over existing baselines" is not uniform: Gemini-3.8-Flash beats StreamVibe-VL on explicit-intent pointwise Timing F1 (81.00 vs 72.01) and Content F1 (66.93 vs 61.28 on implicit), and ViSpeak beats it on explicit trajectory F1. The claim holds only in aggregate on the authors' own benchmark. - The annotation model (Gemini-3.8-Flash) is also a scored baseline, and the benchmark construction pipeline could structurally favor responses in Gemini's annotation style; the κ audit covers review decisions, not stylistic fit of reference answers. - Content scoring relies entirely on Claude Sonnet 4.6 as judge with no human validation of judge fidelity on this task; Content F1 differences of a few points may be judge noise. - Offline baselines collapse under trajectory evaluation (Qwen3-VL F1 6.54–15.66), which may partly reflect wrapping offline models in a streaming harness rather than genuine capability gaps; the paper does not disentangle this. - Base model identity for StreamVibe-VL is not clearly stated in the main text, hurting reproducibility; no code/weights URL is confirmed. - Ablations for the harness's individual components (memory hierarchy vs lifecycle vs skill projection) are absent — the 12.3% harness gain is reported only as a monolith. Bottom Line: Researchers in proactive/streaming video agents gain real value from the benchmark protocol and the degradation diagnostics even if they skip the model, because no alternative benchmark covers implicit and dynamic intents with trajectory evaluation — but the modeling contribution is a solid-but-early system whose absolute performance and unverified headline gains mean practitioners should treat StreamVibe-Bench as the contribution and the rest as a promising first attempt.

Tempo-Zero: Recursive Self-Play in Executable Worlds for Video Reasoning

J Zhu, Y Zou, X Li, J Bailey, D Phung, T Yu, Y Hou… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Tempo-Zero, a self-play framework that trains video-capable vision-language models entirely on programmatically rendered videos, where executing a program produces both the video and exact ground-truth answers and evidence time intervals, eliminating majority-vote pseudo-labels and manual annotation. - Why it's important: Temporal annotations for real videos are expensive, and existing video self-play derives noisy labels from the model's own consensus, which this paper shows would mislabel about 52.5% of its Solver training groups — a failure mode that propagates systematic errors through training. - How it does it: A single shared policy plays both Questioner and Solver inside a library of 12 executable environment families; rewards are computed from the program's execution trace (answer correctness, evidence-line F1, interval IoU, and a Bernoulli-variance learnability term), while a pass-rate curriculum and policy-selected rule changes re-execute programs to generate new event dynamics with recomputed labels. - The good: The training only ever sees simple rendered videos, yet the resulting checkpoints improve all 28 reported temporal-grounding metrics at 4B/8B across four real-world benchmarks (e.g., ANet-RTL mIoU +14.48 at 4B, Charades-STA mIoU +9.40 at 8B) and beat the strongest baseline, Video-Zero, on 26 of 28 — evidence that execution-verified supervision transfers from synthetic to real content. - The missing: No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for the main results, code is promised but not yet released, and there is no comparison against annotation-supervised temporal-grounding methods (e.g., Video-R1-style RL on labeled data) to position the zero-annotation recipe against the ceiling of supervised training. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on self-improvement, RL post-training, or video reasoning and need to understand how executable environments can replace pseudo-labeling; skip it if you only want a stronger off-the-shelf grounding model and can use annotated data.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners training video-LLMs for temporal reasoning face a data bottleneck: videos with accurate temporal annotations (event intervals, evidence spans) are costly to collect and verify. Self-play reduces annotation needs but, in existing forms (Video-Zero, EvoVid), trains on fixed sets of recorded videos, where labels come from majority voting over the model's own samples — risky because correlated model errors get reinforced — and where the underlying event dynamics cannot change as the learner improves. Conversely, pre-built programmatic video environments (SynRL, SIMS-V) give exact labels but freeze task templates, difficulty, and event dynamics before training. The gap this paper closes: video self-play that has both verifiable ground truth (including exact time intervals) and an adaptive training distribution. Key Idea: Make the video itself the output of an executable program, so that the same execution trace that renders the video also compiles the ground-truth answer and evidence interval for every question — and let the trained policy mutate the program's rules and re-execute, so the environment, its labels, and the curriculum all co-evolve with the learner. The verifiable-label guarantee is enforced by two programmatic screens: every ground-truth value is recomputed on the timestamps of the frames actually sampled (discarding 403 of 49,525 compiled criteria, under 1%), and criteria whose answers are invariant to reversed or permuted event order are removed (9.01%), keeping only questions that are both visible and temporally dependent. Methodology: The framework is an EMPIRICAL pipeline with three stages. (1) Executable environments: 12 hand-designed program families (Billiards, Dominoes, Shell game, Traffic lights, etc.) with parameterized difficulty levels, rule configurations, and playback scales; execution yields a trace that compiles into a video, verification criteria (question stem, ground-truth option, ground-truth interval, distractor domain), and a canonical question. (2) Execution-verified self-play: one LoRA-adapted policy acts as Questioner (proposes questions bound to a criterion, gated programmatically for format/option-validity/leakage) and Solver (M=8 rollouts with timestamped evidence lines). Rewards are computed from the trace: rS = answer correctness + mean(statement-level F1, grounded interval IoU where credit requires the cited line to state the correct event); rQ = gate × mean(learnability 4p̃(1−p̃), novelty). Both feed a single joint GRPO update with mean-centered advantages and KL regularization to the base model (LoRA rank 64, lr 5e-5, 5 rounds × 20 steps, 8 GPUs). (3) Environment evolution: decayed pass rates reallocate instances across (family, task) pairs and move difficulty levels (advance at pass rate ≥0.80, retreat at ≤0.20); the policy selects rule changes from a bounded menu, which the executor validates and re-executes. Critical design decisions: interval credit conditioned on statement match (well-justified — Figure 7B shows ~50% of content-blind overlap credit would fall on wrong-event lines); frame-timeline recomputation of labels (well-justified — 28.56% of level-2 events fall between sampled frames); and free-form proposal generation constrained by a criterion (the criterion fixes ground truth while the stem/options vary). Key Results: Evaluated zero-shot on 12 real-world benchmarks (temporal grounding: ANet-RTL, ActivityNet Captions, Charades-STA, NExT-GQA; long-video: LongVideoBench, MLVU, Video-MME-Long, LSDBench; reasoning: LongVideoReason, MMVU, VideoMathQA, VideoMMMU) against the instruction-tuned base model, VisPlay, V-Zero (image self-play), and Video-Zero (recorded-video self-play) — a recent but narrow baseline set with no annotation-supervised comparison. Headline: at 4B, ANet-RTL mIoU rises 16.86→31.34 (+14.48); at 8B, Charades-STA mIoU 36.70→46.10 (+9.40) versus Video-Zero's +0.64. Overall (average of all 12 benchmarks) reaches 50.81 vs. base 44.81 at 4B. Gains extend to long-video understanding and reasoning (13 of 16 metrics best at 4B/8B) and hold on Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B (MoE) and Gemma-4-E4B (21 of 22 metrics improved each). Ablations at 4B: removing the Questioner costs the most Overall (50.81→47.71); answer-only reward costs the most grounding (−5.70 points); removing rule selection costs 1.77 grounding points. Analysis shows majority voting would mislabel 52.5% of 7,420 Solver groups (21.3% with unanimous wrong agreement at 4B), and held-out synthetic accuracy rises 25.9%→42.8% at 8B. A transfer check fine-tunes the base 4B model on bank data: evolved-rule data beats initial-rule data (31.78 vs. 30.73 grounding mIoU), showing rule-selected data carries training value outside the loop. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel move is closing the recursive loop — policy-selected rule changes re-executed to regenerate videos and exact labels — applied to video self-play; prior work offered either self-play on fixed videos (Video-Zero, adaptive questions, noisy labels) or fixed programmatic environments (SynRL, SIMS-V, exact labels, no adaptation). The components themselves are standard combinations: GRPO, LoRA, PLR-style pass-rate curricula (Prioritized Level Replay, ACCEL), SPADE-style adaptive executable environments, and Absolute-Zero-style Questioner/Solver self-play — the contribution is their integration with video-specific label verification (frame recomputation, order-dependence screen, statement-conditioned interval credit), which is competent and non-trivial but built from known ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough and well-designed: seven single-component variants under identical budget, each attributing a distinct effect, plus a separate transfer experiment (Table 4) that decouples the data value of rule selection from the training loop. The verification analyses are unusually careful: majority-vote error rates computed over all 7,420 Solver groups, criterion discard rates reported per level, and 270/270 menu alternatives verified to compile. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests appear anywhere, and single-run results at 4B/8B with gains sometimes under 1.3 points (e.g., 8B LongVideoReason +0.16) are hard to distinguish from noise. Code is promised but not yet released ("Code will be made publicly available"); the project page exists. A minor concern: the protocol follows Video-Zero's evaluation setup, and all baselines are self-improvement methods — the absence of any annotation-supervised RL baseline makes the ceiling of the approach unverifiable from this paper. This is a preprint and should be weighted accordingly. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor via the environment library). - Practical: Runs on 8 GPUs with LoRA adapters (rank 64, language model only), within reach of most academic labs. - Efficient: Budget is modest (3,200 instances, 100 GRPO updates, 5 rounds) but inflated by the rollout pattern — every question answered 8 times with up to 2,048 response tokens and video rendering in the loop; the paper does not report wall-clock or cost relative to baselines. - Effective: The evidence shows real transfer — training on purely synthetic rendered videos improves 22 of 24 metrics at 4B/8B on real benchmarks, with the largest gains exactly where the method targets (temporal grounding); but absolute grounding mIoU (31–34) remains low, so the stated problem is mitigated, not solved. - Scalable: Tested only up to 30B-A3B (3B active) and 5 rounds; the paper claims continued improvement as environments evolve but tests no longer horizons, larger environments, or more families, and whether the hand-designed family library scales is asserted, not shown. Deliverable: paper plus a promised-to-be-released artifact — a 12-family executable environment library, the self-play training loop, and LoRA-adapted checkpoints; no public weights or code at the time of this preprint. Strengths: - The core diagnostic result is convincing and reusable beyond this method: execution labels contradict majority-vote labels on roughly half of Solver groups (52.5% pooled, 14.8% unanimous-wrong), a concrete quantification of the pseudo-label failure mode that motivates the whole line of work. - The two programmatic label screens (frame-timeline recomputation, reversal/permutation order-dependence check) are simple, cheap, and address the exact gap between simulation-clock ground truth and what a frame-sampled model observes — with measured discard rates (under 1% recomputation, 9.01% static-screen) reported rather than assumed. - Statement-conditioned interval credit is a sharp design: gating IoU credit on whether the cited line states the correct event is validated directly (Figure 7B: ~50% of content-blind overlap credit would land on wrong-event lines). - Generalization across architectures (dense Qwen3-VL 4B/8B, sparse MoE 30B-A3B, Gemma-4-E4B) and the decoupled SFT transfer check (Table 4) strengthen the causal story that evolved environments produce better data, not just loop effects. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) backbones inherit pretraining abilities, so the method only shapes the self-play stage; (2) environments cover 12 hand-designed physical families with fixed task schemas and rule menus, far below natural video's perceptual and commonsense breadth; (3) supervision requires deterministic rendering and exact temporal coordinates, and evidence scoring only credits statements matching verification criteria. These are confronted directly in Appendix G and are accurate. Notably absent from their list: absence of supervised baselines, lack of statistical rigor, and the closed nature of the rule menu (rule changes are bounded to menu alternatives, not free program edits). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No annotation-supervised baseline (e.g., RL with ground-truth temporal annotations, or standard SFT on grounded video data) — the reader cannot tell how much of the annotation-cost savings comes at a performance ceiling cost. - No seeds, variance, or significance testing; several 8B long-video gains are within ~1 point of baselines, and the claim that Tempo-Zero "outperforms baselines on average" rests on single runs. - The 12 environment families all model toy physics and discrete state transitions; the sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on benchmarks whose tasks (interval localization, event counting) structurally resemble the training tasks, so benchmark-task alignment may inflate transfer — the four reasoning benchmarks improve by much smaller margins (0.2–5.5 points) than grounding (up to 14.5 mIoU), a pattern the paper does not probe. - Rule selection operates over a menu of at most three alternatives per family, and rule selection is described as at-inference with no gradient; the "policy selects rules" claim is weaker than open-ended environment design (à la SPADE), and the paper does not test whether more expressive rule mutation helps. - 12% of criteria pass the static-question screen only as "undetermined" (transformations not evaluable); the effect of keeping these on label quality is not measured. Bottom Line: For researchers building self-improvement or zero-annotation video-LLM training pipelines, this is one of the most convincing demonstrations that executable environments with exact, learner-adaptive supervision beat consensus-labeled video self-play — read it — while practitioners who can afford annotated temporal data still have stronger, better-characterized supervised options.

Organon: From Evolutionary Search to Recursive Self-Improving Agents for Scientific Discovery

C Ahmed, Z Zhang, K Mao, Y Zhang, Z Zhou · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Organon, a single persistent LLM-driven evolutionary agent that rewrites its own search policies, diagnostic tools, memory, and worker coordination at runtime, and applies it to 21 program-discovery tasks. - Why it's important: Existing LLM-guided evolutionary search frameworks (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, EvoX, ShinkaEvolve) adapt only a design-time-fixed subset of their pipeline, so when progress stalls outside those levers the system cannot diagnose or fix the cause — Organon targets that ceiling. - How it does it: The agent's entire operational stack is exposed as replaceable components in a dynamically composable runtime (DeepSeek Harness + Cordis spatiotemporal composability); between bounded search calls the agent inspects its accumulated population/history, activates tracked, revertible component revisions, and keeps population and history intact across revisions. - The good: On ALE-Bench Lite it wins all 10 tasks, with mean held-out private performance of 2478.6 vs 2056.3 for the strongest baseline (EvoX, +20.5%), and the anatomy section documents concrete self-corrections (e.g., an inverted survival rule in AHC025 whose fix revived the ancestor of the final winner). - The missing: Every headline result comes from a single run per task with no seeds, error bars, or ablation isolating the benefit of recursive self-improvement over a strong fixed composition, so the central causal claim — that self-revision causes the gains — is supported only by trajectory narrative. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building adaptive evolutionary or self-modifying agent systems who want a concrete runtime architecture and qualitative trajectory analysis; practitioners seeking statistically grounded method comparisons should treat the rankings as provisional.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is dragged down by Rigor (48) — no ablations, single run per task, no significance tests, unreported LLM costs, and wins that partly trace to harness-specific quirks a self-modifying agent can exploit but baselines were structurally denied — and by Resilience (54), since the central causal claim (self-revision causes the gains) is supported only by trajectory narrative, as the authors themselves concede. Novelty (75) is the strongest dimension: unrestricted recursive editability of the agent's own diagnostic and assessment procedures, plus state-preserving revertible composition, is a real advance over fixed-lever meta-evolution. Completeness (74) is a notable positive given Section A.13's explicit refusal to overclaim causality and the candid reporting of losses and undetected agent errors. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*48 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*74 + 0.15*54 + 0.10*60 = 62.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses non-stationarity in LLM-guided evolutionary program search: a strategy that yields early gains often concentrates effort in a narrow solution family and stalls long-horizon progress. Two prior camps each have a flaw — meta-evolutionary frameworks (ShinkaEvolve, PACEvolve, AdaEvolve, EvoX, Dream-RSI) adapt only designated components through fixed update procedures, bounding adaptive scope at design time; autonomous research agents (Autoresearch, CORAL, SwarmResearch) make unconstrained step-by-step decisions that drift toward greedy leader-following and premature consensus because they lack diagnostic instruments and explicit revisable mechanisms. The gap closed is the middle ground: an agent whose accumulated task experience can restructure its entire investigative process — including the procedures it uses to evaluate its own future changes — while preserving search state. Key Idea: The core trick is to make the agent's whole operational stack an editable, dynamically composable artifact: every component (evolutionary loop, parent selection Sel_r, variation Var_r, evaluation Eval_r, survival Sur_r, tools T_r, memory M_r, worker coordination W_r, execution loop Φ_r) registers into a live runtime context via tracked, revertible effects (equation 8–9), so a revision activates between bounded search horizons, cleanly withdraws if ineffective, and leaves the persistent population/history H and remaining budget B untouched. Because adopted diagnostics and assessment procedures become part of the next composition C_{r+1}, self-improvement becomes recursive — the agent can rewrite the instruments through which it judges subsequent revisions. Methodology: The formal setup is evolutionary search over programs X maximizing a fixed evaluator f within budget B (equation 1). The agent alternates two coupled levels: (i) candidate evolution — a bounded search call L_r(H; C_r, f, k) runs up to k delegated worker attempts (workers in isolated sandboxes that cannot execute code), evaluates via the official f plus any agent-added diagnostics, and updates the population/history per equation 5; (ii) capability evolution — after each call the agent diagnoses limitations from H (score progression, lineage concentration, worker findings) and constructs a component revision (add/replace/withdraw anything in C_r), implemented via reactive coeffects and revertible effects on DeepSeek Harness so changes take effect without losing state (equations 6–8). Three critical design decisions: (a) revisions occur only between bounded calls, not mid-search — justified as preserving evidence continuity; (b) workers are denied shell/execution access so that execution-based checks arise only when the agent itself invents them — well-argued as matching baselines but artificial relative to real deployments; (c) spatiotemporal composability for state-preserving reversion — motivated but never compared against a simpler checkpoint/rollback implementation. Key Results: Across 21 tasks with all methods on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and B=100 attempts (run through SkyDiscover): ALE-Bench Lite — best private score on all 10 tasks, mean 2478.6 vs EvoX 2056.3 (+20.5%) and OpenEvolve 1922.6; the largest single margin is AHC026 (3451.0 vs ShinkaEvolve 2083.0). KernelBench — best on 3 of 4 workloads (VGG16 3.34× vs OpenEvolve 2.10×; ConvDiv 5.58× vs 3.34×; LayerNorm 18.70× vs 17.44×), losing ConvMax to EvoX (2.29× vs 2.75×). Mathematical construction — best third-order autocorrelation among methods (1.4562828, AlphaEvolve reference 1.4556428), but loses circle packing (2.635314 vs ShinkaEvolve 2.635987) and Heilbronn (0.0365035 vs 0.0365299). Systems — best mean on all four tasks, but margins are 0.136% (EPLB) and 0.0045% (Cloudcast), with PRISM a four-way tie; the authors honestly flag that these tiny margins make variability decisive. Baselines are current (2025–2026 methods) and strong, but all were run by the authors. Scale is standard (100 attempts/task), not stress-scale. The anatomy section is the most distinctive evidence: 2–22 activated revisions per run (median 11), no two runs revised the same capability subset, on 7 of 21 tasks zero initial-composition candidates improved on x_0, and 12 runs explicitly withdrew or reversed earlier revisions. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (recursive self-improvement of the full evolutionary stack during live search, enabled by NEW SYSTEM/TOOL infrastructure — state-preserving component composition) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (trajectory analysis of what an agent actually revises about itself). The genuinely new elements are (i) unrestricted editability of the agent's own diagnostics and revision procedures, beyond EvoX's fixed set of evolvable strategies, and (ii) revertible, state-preserving runtime composition. The underlying loop — LLM variation plus population-based evaluation — is standard FunSearch/AlphaEvolve machinery; the contribution is the self-modification layer wrapped around it. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations in the strong sense are absent: the paper's own conclusion concedes that future work should "isolate the contribution of individual revisions through repeated runs and controlled ablations." One run per task; no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests on the method comparison (selected programs are evaluated 3× for ALE-Bench and systems tasks, which controls evaluation noise but not search stochasticity). The trajectory analysis is unusually candid — Section A.13 explicitly states revisions are temporal associations, not causal estimates, and documents undetected agent errors (a sign error in LLM-SQL, arithmetic inconsistencies in Cloudcast). Code is released at https://github.com/cheikh025/Organon. Methodological concerns: all baselines were re-run by the authors through SkyDiscover, so configuration subtleties could favor the proposed system; the sandboxed workers (no execution) make Organon's advantage partially an artifact of the controlled setting — the agent's invented pre-evaluation checkers (e.g., AHC026's local simulator validated against official scores) are a capability the baselines were structurally denied the opportunity to develop, though this is arguably the paper's point. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system evaluated through benchmark experiments; SYSTEMS elements in the runtime infrastructure). Practical: Yes — it runs on the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash API plus standard evaluation harnesses (Modal for KernelBench); no exotic hardware. Efficient: Not measured — LLM token/compute cost per run is unreported, and the paper notes worker generation takes minutes per candidate against seconds-to-minute evaluations, with concurrency tuned empirically (e.g., 8→5 workers when throughput dropped); relative cost vs baselines is claimed equal only via the shared attempt budget. Effective: Evidence supports effectiveness on algorithm design and kernel tasks; the near-tie systems results and losses on two of three math tasks show the advantage is task-dependent, and all gains are on benchmark objectives with fixed evaluators (a proxy for open-ended scientific discovery). Scalable: Not tested — the budget is fixed at 100 attempts everywhere; behavior at 10–100× budget, where revision overhead may amortize differently, is unexamined. Deliverable: open-source software artifact (GitHub repo) built on DeepSeek Harness and Cordis, plus reusable trajectory-analysis records; no trained model weights. Strengths: - The recursive scope is real, not rhetorical: the paper documents the agent correcting or withdrawing its own diagnostic instruments (AHC011's completion check, Heilbronn's budget reader corrected twice, each correction preceding a new record), which goes beyond prior work where the improver is never itself improved. - State-preserving reversion is a genuine systems contribution — e.g., Cloudcast reactivates an earlier component version while carrying forward the population and diagnostics accumulated under its replacement — cleanly formalized via revertible effects. - Section 5 and the appendices constitute the most detailed published anatomy of agent self-modification I am aware of: verbatim recorded diagnoses (Table 10), a defect/correction inventory (Table 11), and per-run timing data (median first revision at 4 attempts; 80% of post-first calls followed a revision). - The evaluation protocol anticipates obvious objections: workers are sandboxed so Organon's self-built checkers don't silently substitute for the attempt budget, and the authors route a footnote-disclosed 38 candidates to a stronger model on 3 tasks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront the causal-inference weakness (Section A.13: single run per task, revisions applied in combination, improvements are temporal associations, some revisions contained undetected errors and were never activated or used). The conclusion names two concrete limitations: inability to isolate individual-revision contributions without repeated runs and controlled ablations, and the fact that capabilities do not transfer across tasks (self-improvement compounds only within a run). The paper also candidly reports losing circle packing and Heilbronn to EvoX/ShinkaEvolve and flags the tiny EPLB/Cloudcast margins. This level of self-scrutiny is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation against a strong fixed-composition baseline with matched tuning: the headline claim requires showing that EvoX with a well-engineered static configuration (or EvoX given the same revision opportunities but restricted to its three designated levers) does not close the 20.5% gap. Single-run variance alone could plausibly account for parts of the ALE-Bench margins, which range from 40 points (AHC024) to 1368 (AHC026). - The sandboxes-equal-for-all design may systematically favor a self-modifying agent: Organon's wins in kernels (LayerNorm, ConvDiv) trace substantially to discovering the harness's Triton import-detection quirk — a path only an agent that can build its own evaluators can take, and one that rewards harness-specific diagnosis rather than general search skill. - LLM cost is unreported despite wildly different inference profiles (some runs use streaming/pipelined concurrency, one task routed to a stronger model); "equal budget" is defined only in attempt count. - The abstract and framing invoke "scientific discovery," but all 21 tasks have fixed scalar evaluators; nothing is tested on open-ended or human-in-the-loop discovery where the Baconian framing would actually bind. - Whether Organon's revisions are reproducible is unexamined — a second seed might revise entirely differently (the authors show no two runs revised the same subset), which is interesting science but undermines any claim of reliable capability emergence. Bottom Line: A practitioner building adaptive evolutionary or self-modifying agent systems should read this for the composability architecture and the exceptional trajectory analysis, but should treat the quantitative rankings as single-run, self-administered evidence pending the ablations the authors themselves call for — the architectural ideas, not the leaderboard, are the durable contribution.

Collaborative OS of Multi- Agent Systems

J Kang, R Zhao, D Lin, G Li, T Bai · aclanthology.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MAS-OS, a memory-centric 'operating system' framework for LLM multi-agent systems that jointly learns dynamic agent scheduling and fine-grained context allocation via reinforcement learning over a structured memory graph. - Why it's important: Existing multi-agent workflows either broadcast full noisy histories (raising token cost and 'lost-in-the-middle' degradation) or pass narrow fixed windows (losing global state), so long-horizon collaboration is both expensive and unreliable. - How it does it: A Memory Manager maintains a memory graph (temporal + semantic edges, cosine-similarity thresholded) plus a rolling global summary; an RL-trained Agent Scheduler (RLOO + PPO with KL regularization) picks the next agent from that summary, and an RL-trained Context Allocator selects K memory units from an M-sized candidate set for the active agent. - The good: On Llama-3.1-8B it reaches 0.315 accuracy on GSM-hard (+14.01% over the best baseline) and 0.278 on SciBench (+35.51%), and a budget-matched comparison against Self-Consistency and Reflection (including SC with a 70B backbone) shows the gains come from the architecture rather than extra compute. - The missing: RL training is never run at 70B due to compute constraints — the 70B results are from the untrained MAS-OS(-RL) variant — and with Llama-3.1-8B on MMLU-Pro the framework (0.376) actually loses to the raw base model (0.390), so the headline '17.42% average improvement' covers only three of four benchmarks. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building adaptive/learned multi-agent orchestration, since the joint scheduling+allocation RL formulation and memory-graph design are directly reusable; skip it if you only need a turnkey MAS framework, as the evaluated setting is limited to fixed agent rosters and benchmark-specific rewards.

The joint RL formulation of agent scheduling and per-step context allocation over a shared memory graph is a real formulation-level contribution with released code, budget-matched controls, ablations, and significance tests (Novelty 65, Rigor 68, Impact 65). The composite is pulled down by Resilience (55) and Completeness (60): the headline '17.42% average improvement' silently excludes MMLU-Pro where the framework loses to the raw base model, RL was never run at 70B yet scalability is claimed, the allocator's reward relies on unvalidated self-labeled usefulness (a reward-hacking path), and training/evaluation share benchmark-specific rewards (Goodhart risk). Non-Obviousness (58) is moderate because the 'operating system' framing is largely naming over standard memory-management and RLOO/PPO components. Problem & Motivation: LLM-driven multi-agent systems underperform on long-horizon tasks because inter-agent information distribution is handled statically: full-context broadcasting floods agents with redundant tokens and noise, while direct context passing isolates agents from global objectives and long-range dependencies. Additionally, most MAS use rigid, hand-designed workflows that cannot invoke a corrective agent when execution deviates from plan. The relevant audience is anyone deploying multi-agent LLM pipelines (reasoning, code generation, knowledge QA) where both accuracy and token cost matter. Prior work fixes only one side — RCR-Router routes context but keeps a static topology; Puppeteer dynamically orchestrates agents but shares global histories without fine-grained filtering — leaving joint optimization of scheduling and context allocation underexplored. Key Idea: Frame multi-agent collaboration as an OS-style resource-management problem in which a shared, structured memory state (graph + rolling summary) simultaneously drives two learned policies: which agent to activate next and which slice of memory that agent should see. The unifying trick is conditioning both the scheduler and allocator on the same evolving memory state, so scheduling and communication are optimized jointly rather than as separate mechanisms. Methodology: MAS-OS is a sequential decision process. (1) The Memory Manager converts each agent's raw output into a memory unit (raw content + LLM-generated summary), appends a temporal edge to the previous node, adds semantic edges to earlier nodes whose summaries exceed cosine similarity τ=0.80 (BGE-M3 embeddings), and updates a rolling natural-language global summary. (2) The Agent Scheduler samples the next agent index σt from policy πθ conditioned on [task, global summary, previous summary, previous agent, agent pool], or outputs 'Done'. (3) The Context Allocator builds a candidate set of ≤M=7 memory units by backward traversal over temporal/semantic edges, then samples a subset of size K=3 via policy πϕ conditioned on the task, candidates, global summary, and agent identity. (4) RL training follows MARTI's alternating collection/optimization loop: N=16 rollouts per prompt, RLOO leave-one-out baselines, PPO clipped surrogate (ε=0.2), and a KL penalty (β=0.001) to a frozen reference model. Rewards are composite: the active agent self-labels each allocated memory item as useful (hit-rate reward Ragent), the allocator gets α·Ragent + η·Rtask (α=0.25, η=1), and the scheduler gets Rtask − λ·ct with ct the activated agent's token count (λ=5e-5). Critical design decisions: joint rather than separate RL of the two policies (justified by the 10.21% average gain of the full system over the -RL variant); LLM-based self-reported memory usefulness as the allocator's shaping reward (weakly justified — circularity risk, no external validation of hit-rate labels); and candidate-set construction via graph traversal capped at M (justified by the hyperparameter sweep in Appendix E showing M=7, K=3 is optimal, with performance plateauing/degrading beyond that). Key Results: Tested on four benchmarks (GSM-hard, SciBench, SRDD, MMLU-Pro) with Llama-3.1-8B and 70B backbones (plus Qwen3-8B in Appendix D), against a current set of baselines (AFlow, DyLAN, MacNet, EvoAgent, Puppeteer, 2024–2026). With Llama-3.1-8B, MAS-OS scores 0.315 on GSM-hard vs. AFlow's 0.276 (+14.01%, p<0.05), 0.278 on SciBench vs. EvoAgent's 0.205 (+35.51%, p<0.05), and 0.713 on SRDD vs. EvoAgent's 0.694 (+2.75%, p<0.05), but 0.376 on MMLU-Pro vs. the base model's 0.390 — all agentic methods underperform the base model there at 8B. RL contributes an average +10.21% over the untrained MAS-OS(-RL) variant. At 70B (no RL training performed), MAS-OS(-RL) beats the best baselines on all four tasks (+21.89% over AFlow on GSM-hard). Ablations on 8B show removing the Context Allocator costs 26.1% on GSM-hard, Memory Manager 20.2%, Agent Scheduler 10.6%. Efficiency: MAS-OS consumes 38,635 total tokens (highest execution/input side at 34,156 but lowest output at 2,179) versus DyLAN's 48,381 and MacNet's 10,343, with 49.03s latency. Budget-matched comparisons (Table 5) show MAS-OS (8B) at 0.315/0.278 on GSM-hard/SciBench versus SC@28 (8B) at 0.175/0.158, SC@8 (70B) at 0.270/0.245, and Refl@8 (8B) at 0.252/0.225. Scheduler-scaling experiments (3B→70B scheduler, fixed 8B workers) show MAS-OS gains +214.5% versus Puppeteer's +72.9% at 70B. Base-model accuracy on GSM-hard at 8B is 0.0021, so absolute baseline levels there are low. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel element is the joint RL formulation of next-agent selection and per-step context allocation over a shared structured memory state; prior systems (Puppeteer, AnyMAC, RCR-Router) learn or design only one of the two. The individual ingredients — memory graphs with temporal/semantic edges (extending the authors' prior MemoryOS for single agents), RLOO/PPO post-training, hit-rate-style rewards, rolling summaries — are standard, and the 'operating system' framing is largely a naming abstraction over known memory-management components applied to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover all three components, hyperparameter sweeps exist for M/K and scheduler scale, statistical significance is reported (paired two-sided t-test, p<0.05, marked per-benchmark), and a budget-matched comparison rules out the 'more compute' confound — all above typical venue standards. Code is released at https://github.com/BAI-LAB/MAS-OS with an anonymous.4open.science mirror and detailed hyperparameters. Concerns: (1) the allocator's shaping reward relies on the active agent self-reporting memory usefulness, an unvalidated, potentially gameable signal developed and evaluated on the same benchmarks; (2) at 70B, results are only for the untrained variant, so the headline 'RL improves MAS' claim is untested at the stronger scale, and Puppeteer is excluded there; (3) the abstract's '17.42% average improvement' for Llama-3.1-8B averages only three of four benchmarks — MMLU-Pro shows no improvement over the base model; (4) rewards are benchmark-specific (binary correctness for three datasets, SRDD's own composite), so learned policies may not transfer without retraining. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (an RL-trained framework evaluated on standard benchmarks, not deployed as production infrastructure). Practical: Yes — runs on open-weight Llama/Qwen backbones with BGE-M3 embeddings, though training an RL policy requires GPU resources the authors themselves lacked for 70B. Efficient: Mixed — 34,156 input tokens per task (3–5× MacNet's overhead from scheduler/allocator/memory prompts) offset by the lowest output tokens (2,179) and a favorable accuracy-per-dollar trade-off under Cloudflare Workers AI pricing. Effective: Strong evidence on math/science/code reasoning against current baselines and budget-matched alternatives, but it fails to beat the raw base model on MMLU-Pro at 8B and was never trained at 70B, so 'general-purpose reasoning amplifier' is partially supported at best. Scalable: Untested beyond 70B backbones and fixed 10-agent rosters; sequential activation means throughput grows linearly with agent count, and the authors only claim (do not test) behavior with heterogeneous agents. Delivers a software artifact: an open-source code repository; no trained model weights are reported as released. Strengths: (1) The joint RL optimization of scheduling and context allocation is a real formulation-level contribution — the ablation and the +10.21% RL gain over the prompting-only variant both isolate that this joint training, not just dynamic orchestration, drives performance. (2) The budget-matched comparison against Self-Consistency (including a 70B backbone) and Reflection is an unusually honest control that most MAS papers omit. (3) The memory graph with dual edge types plus rolling global summary is a concrete, reusable mechanism for balancing recency and semantic relevance in multi-agent state. (4) Component-level ablation cleanly ranks what matters (Allocator > Memory Manager > Scheduler), giving deployers actionable guidance. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) the memory-centric mechanism adds token overhead, limiting latency/cost-sensitive use; (2) sequential agent activation forgoes parallelism among independent subtasks; (3) experiments use predefined agent roles and benchmark-specific reward signals, deferring heterogeneous agents and broader real-world tasks to future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The allocator's hit-rate reward is self-labeled by the active agent that received the memory — no independent check that these usefulness labels correlate with actual contribution, creating a possible reward-hacking path the RL policies could exploit. (2) The abstract's 17.42% average claim silently excludes MMLU-Pro, where MAS-OS underperforms the base model at 8B; the paper explains this as 'over-reasoning' but offers no mechanism to detect or suppress it. (3) RL was never run at 70B, yet the paper claims model-agnostic scalability — the strongest result scale uses an untrained policy, so the interaction between RL and larger backbones is unknown. (4) Training and evaluation share benchmarks with benchmark-tailored rewards (correctness binary for three datasets), raising Goodhart risk for any cross-task generalization claims. (5) The efficiency comparison shows MAS-OS has the highest input-token cost among several methods (5× MacNet); the cost-benefit analysis uses one vendor's pricing where output tokens dominate, and conclusions would flip for APIs with different input/output price ratios. (6) All worker agents come from a fixed 10-role roster shared with Puppeteer's setup, so the scheduler's effective action space is narrow — the framework's value with open-ended agent pools is unexamined. Bottom Line: A practitioner building learned multi-agent orchestration should read this for its joint scheduling-plus-allocation RL formulation, honest budget-matched controls, and open code — but should discount the headline improvement figure (it excludes the one benchmark where it loses to the base model) and expect to re-derive the reward design for any task outside math/science/code reasoning, where Alternatives like AnyMAC or a well-tuned single-agent workflow may cover much of the same ground at lower input-token cost.

Scaling Enterprise Cloud Agents to Thousands of APIs: An Empirical Study of Agent Architecture and MCP Tool Boundaries

S Ghoshal, K Mrini, M Assi, Y Fan, J Singh… · aclanthology.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Operation-Visible Agent Architecture, which pairs a centralized ReAct loop with parallel tool calling and a deterministic Operation-Resolver MCP (find_operations / describe_operation / invoke_api), and shows it beats a production lead-worker Tool-Planner baseline on 91 proprietary cloud-management tasks (77% vs. 68% full success) while cutting total tokens 54.1%, median latency 43.3%, LLM calls 37.8%, and tool errors 52.4%. - Why it's important: Enterprise cloud agents must ground user requests across ~8K SDK operations from 280+ clients, where poor tool-boundary design directly drives production cost, latency, and invocation failures;
