Problem & Motivation: Subject-to-video (S2V) generation conditions a video diffusion model on reference images of a specific subject. When the commanded camera path reveals surfaces absent from the references — e.g., a 360° orbit driven from a single front view — the model must invent the subject's back side, producing inconsistent silhouettes, duplicated parts, and identity drift. Prior multi-view extensions exist: MV-S2V feeds four references but provides no explicit 3D structure and trains on camera-controlled generated videos where viewpoint changes are not tied to a shared geometry; 3DreamBooth achieves 3D consistency via per-subject optimization, costing a test-time optimization pass per subject and sacrificing generalization. The gap this work targets is training on geometrically guaranteed viewpoint changes and conditioning on explicit geometry at inference, without per-subject optimization. Key Idea: Render the training target videos from actual 3D assets (so viewpoint changes are geometrically true by construction), and at both training and inference give the model a reconstructed surface-normal "turntable" — a 25-pose orbit of normal maps rendered from a feed-forward 3D reconstruction of the reference views — as a temporally concatenated in-context condition. Because the turntable is a fixed trajectory-independent yaw sweep while the target video follows an arbitrary prompt-specified path, imposing per-frame correspondence would be wrong; instead the normal latents occupy their own span (7 latent frames) alongside 4 reference-image latents and 20 target latents, with a binary mask marking which positions are clean context versus noised target. Methodology: The system has a data-synthesis stage and a generation stage. Data synthesis: 3D meshes from Objaverse, Digital Twin Catalog, and Google Scanned Objects pass four curation gates (a mesh heuristic plus three VLM gates using Gemini 2.5 Flash with binary rubrics, ~29,000 gate calls, ~$120 total). Blender renders each accepted asset along one of 88 trajectory configurations (4 orbit-family motions × 4 rotation amounts, plus 8 framing motions × 9 transitions) and 4 reference views at 90° yaw intervals; the subject is composited into prompt-driven scenes via VACE-style video inpainting that keeps rendered subject pixels fixed; captions are produced by Tarsier2-7B. Critically, the geometry condition is reconstructed from the rendered reference views (masked, pointmaps via a multi-view estimator, fused into 3D Gaussians, rendered at 25 poses at 15° elevation, depth-to-normal), not from the source mesh, ensuring train/inference condition parity. Generation: Wan2.1 I2V-14B-480P is LoRA-tuned (rank 128) with a rectified-flow objective; the input stacks three 16-channel streams (noised latents, mask, clean condition) for 36 channels; the loss averages velocity error over target-video latent elements only. Training: 33,000 steps, batch size 2 on 4× NVIDIA B200, ~50 hours, seed 42. Design decisions worth noting: (i) normal maps rather than textured renders of the reconstruction — justified by ablation showing textured color competes with reference images for appearance; (ii) separate-span rather than channel-wise geometry conditioning — argued but not directly ablated against a channel-wise alternative; (iii) reconstructing from references rather than source meshes — well justified for train/test consistency. Key Results: On SHOWCASEBENCH (50 held-out subjects, four 360° trajectories) and NAVI (35 real subjects), against Phantom-MV, MAGREF-MV, MV-S2V, and 3DreamBooth (all recent, 2025–2026, all given the same 4 references): OmniShowcase achieves DINO 0.799 / CLIP 0.925 / MEt3R 0.190 / GT-CD 0.0824 on held-out, and 0.828 / 0.918 / 0.249 / 0.0975 on NAVI — best on all identity and 3D metrics on both sets, with GT-CD roughly 2× better than the nearest baseline. ViCLIP text alignment (0.259/0.260) and VBench imaging quality (74.29/74.58) are best or competitive; aesthetic quality is slightly below some baselines. Reference-count ablation shows graceful degradation from 4 to 1 views (n=1 GT-CD 0.1704 on held-out). A training-data comparison shows Uni3C-generated clips score worse than the authors' renders on the same metrics (DINO 0.717 vs. 0.803). Scale is modest: 4K training videos, 480×832 resolution, 80 target frames (~5 s at 16 fps). A user study (44 participants, 24 videos) gives 70.9–79.4% preference share. Notably, the ablation "None" (no geometry conditioning) still reaches GT-CD 0.2092/0.1987 — beating most baselines — indicating the data pipeline alone contributes substantially. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (geometry-conditioned S2V via a reconstructed normal-turntable in-context span without temporal alignment) + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (SHOWCASE-4K and SHOWCASEBENCH with mesh/camera ground truth) + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (the fully automated render-composite-curation pipeline). The genuinely novel piece is the misalignment-tolerant normal-turntable conditioning; the components themselves — feed-forward reconstruction, Gaussian splatting, LoRA on an I2V backbone, VLM-gated synthetic data — are standard ideas combined competently in a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: geometry condition type (None/Textured/Sparse, Table 3), reference count (1–4, Table 4), and training-data source (Uni3C vs. own renders, Table 5). However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; everything runs under a single seed (42) and a single 33,000-step checkpoint. The authors commit to releasing data, benchmark, code, and pipeline prompts (project page justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase), and appendices document prompts, rubrics, and gate pass rates unusually thoroughly. Methodological concerns: (i) SHOWCASEBENCH is generated by the same synthesis pipeline as SHOWCASE-4K, so the headline held-out numbers benefit from train/eval domain match — Goodhart risk is mitigated but not eliminated by the NAVI results, where the method still leads but the geometry-condition ablation shows metric-specific inconsistencies (e.g., on NAVI, "None" yields the lowest GT-CD among ablations, 0.1987 vs. 0.0975 for full conditioning, an anomaly the paper notes without explaining); (ii) GT-CD relies on π³ lifting whose failure modes could interact with the method's own outputs; (iii) baselines Phantom and MAGREF are pushed into a non-native multi-reference mode (single-view variants are also reported in Appendix F for transparency, a credibility positive); (iv) the VLM curation gates are the same models class of judge that could bias corpus statistics, though gates are stated to be unused at evaluation. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained generative system with quantitative and human evaluation). Practical: Requires a 14B-parameter video DiT; training used 4× B200 GPUs, and consumer-hardware inference is not stated — likely needs high-end accelerators, though LoRA artifacts are small. Efficient: Unusually cheap for the subfield — 4,000 synthetic videos and ~50 GPU-hours of LoRA tuning versus ~1M real videos for Phantom; curation costs ~$25 per thousand kept clips. Effective: Strong evidence the system solves the stated problem on synthetic and real subjects, but the evaluation stresses camera trajectories around rigid, object-centric subjects at 480p and ~5 s clips — not the open-ended video regime. Scalable: Not tested beyond 4K videos; the authors claim corpus expansion scales with ~$25/1000-clip cost, which is plausible but unverified at higher volume or resolution. Deliverables: promised public release of dataset, benchmark, data-synthesis code, and training code; at paper form these are commitments, not yet shipped artifacts per the text. Strengths: - The train/inference condition-parity insight — reconstructing geometry from the rendered references rather than the source mesh — is a clean, correctness-driven design decision that most synthetic-data pipelines get wrong. - The misalignment-free in-context conditioning formulation (normals as a temporally separate masked span) is a genuinely reusable technique for injecting auxiliary sequences of different length/semantics into an I2V transformer. - Achieving the reported 3D-consistency margins with only 4K training videos, against baselines trained on up to 1M videos, is a strong data-efficiency result attributable to geometrically grounded supervision. - Unusual transparency: per-gate pass rates, dollar costs, verbatim VLM rubrics, single-vs-multi-view baseline extensions, and a frank training-data ablation against a camera-controlled generator are all disclosed. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two: (1) backgrounds sometimes look synthetic because only the subject is physically rendered while the surrounding scene is inpainted, so subject-background light transport was never consistent in training data; (2) non-rigid subjects are not handled — four references of a subject in different poses fuse into one rigid reconstruction, producing averaged poses or 3D tangles when motion is requested (Figure 13, Appendix H, with a mechanistic diagnosis). They explicitly defer both to future work and confront the failure mechanisms directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. They also note the aesthetic-quality metric slightly favors baselines. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline benchmark shares a synthesis pipeline with the training corpus; the paper does not report how much of the SHOWCASEBENCH margin survives under strictly out-of-pipeline synthetic data (NAVI partially covers this but its 35 subjects are described as "small and largely convex," which the authors themselves note favors fewer references — an easier geometry regime). - The paper does not ablate the channel-wise-alignment alternative for conditioning (normals appended to target latents), so the central architectural claim (separate span > channel-wise) rests on argument, not evidence. - No statistical treatment anywhere: single seed, single checkpoint, no variance across the 50-subject benchmark; the NAVI ablation anomaly (None best on GT-CD) goes unexplained. - Identity metrics (max DINO/CLIP similarity to references over generated frames) are gameable by copying reference appearance near reference viewpoints; the geometry metrics carry the result, but RotCoverage is self-described as auxiliary and alignment-dependent. - Resolution (480p), duration (80 frames), rigid-object scope, and the fixed 15°-elevation yaw turntable (regardless of commanded non-orbit trajectory) bound the claim of "omnidirectional" generation more tightly than the framing suggests. - The user study covers 24 videos with forced choice among five methods; no inter-rater agreement or confidence intervals are given. Bottom Line: A practitioner building subject-driven or camera-controllable video systems should read this: the normal-turntable conditioning recipe and the geometrically-grounded synthetic-data playbook are immediately reusable and demonstrably data-efficient, even granting that the headline margins are partly a home-turf effect and that rigid-object 480p clips are the proven envelope.

EnerVision AI driven digital twin for predictive energy intelligence and sustainable manufacturing

M Thakur, I Goyal, A Chalva · link.springer.com · digital twins for enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds "EnerVision," an AI-driven digital-twin platform that unifies interpretable production–energy regression, benchmarked ML/LSTM forecasting, exploratory generator-activation alerting, statistical anomaly detection, what-if scenario simulation, and a decision-support dashboard for energy management in small and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises (SMEs). - Why it's important: SMEs constitute ~90% of firms and up to 40% of GDP in emerging economies but lack affordable, integrated energy-decision tools, forcing costly and carbon-intensive diesel-generator reliance during grid outages. - How it does it: It integrates standard components (OLS regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM, rolling 2σ anomaly detection, deterministic dispatch rules) into a five-layer platform fed by a real plant's daily production, grid-energy, and generator-energy records. - The good: The paper's strongest, most credible finding is its own negative result — under 5-fold cross-validation on 59 daily records, simple linear regression (CV R² = 0.49 ± 0.26) beats Random Forest (0.17), gradient boosting (−0.03), XGBoost (−0.23), and the LSTM loses to a naive 3-day moving average (held-out RMSE 546 vs. 417 kWh) — a refreshingly honest benchmarking that justifies the framework's interpretable-model emphasis. - The missing: All savings and CO₂ figures are scenario estimates, never measured realized savings; the dataset is a single facility with 59 daily observations, no code/data release is confirmed, and the dashboard received no usability evaluation. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building or evaluating energy-decision tools for resource-constrained manufacturers — the honest small-data model comparison and the integrated-system framing are instructive — but skip it if you seek novel algorithms, large-scale validation, or causal energy modeling.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile (built platform, case-study evaluated). Rigor (60) is unusually strong for an integration paper — 5-fold CV with error bars, six forecasting baselines including naive ones, bootstrap CIs, and econometric diagnostics — and the honest negative result (LSTM losing to a 3-day moving average; ensembles overfitting at n=59) is the kind of credible, non-cherry-picked benchmarking the field needs. Completeness (75) and Resilience (70) benefit from extensive, direct limitation acknowledgment and well-bounded claims. The composite is held back by Novelty (45) — an integration of standard components by the authors' own admission — and Impact (50), since the platform ships as a described artifact with no public code, data, or measured realized savings. Weighted composite: 0.15*45 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*50 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.30*50 = 58.

Problem & Motivation: SME manufacturers face a grid-vs-diesel-generator trade-off (cheap but outage-prone grid at 6 MU/kWh vs. expensive, CO₂-emitting generator at 15 MU/kWh and α = 0.8 kg CO₂/kWh), yet existing digital-twin and energy-analytics research targets large plants or residential loads. Prior work addresses regression modeling, ensemble forecasting, LSTM time-series prediction, or anomaly detection in isolation, and almost never packages them into an affordable decision-support tool for resource-constrained enterprises. The stated gaps are: (1) no SME-targeted integrated energy digital twin, (2) single-method papers with no end-to-end pipeline, and (3) scarcity of interactive what-if dashboards converting models into operator decisions. Key Idea: The core move is integration, not algorithmic invention: bundle interpretable regression, benchmarked ML baselines, anomaly detection, scenario simulation, and KPI tracking into one vendor-neutral digital twin, then use the small-data cross-validation result to select the simplest deployable model (quadratic/linear regression plus a naive forecaster) rather than the highest-capacity one. The authors themselves state "The uniqueness of this study is not in its algorithms but in the way that it brings all together." Methodology: The pipeline has five layers: (1) industrial data ingestion from a live manufacturing plant (daily production units, grid kWh, diesel-generator kWh; 59 valid records after removing missing/non-physical rows), (2) preprocessing and KPI derivation (total energy, efficiency, EPU, cost, CO₂ via Eqs. 2–8 with grid factor γ = 0.7117 kg CO₂/kWh from India's CEA v21.0 database), (3) modeling — OLS linear and quadratic production→energy regression scored by R²/RMSE, an RF regressor and an RF generator-activation classifier (100 trees each, 5-fold CV), and an LSTM (50 units, dense 25→1, Adam, MSE, 10 epochs, batch size 1) for next-day forecasting, (4) a digital-twin core exposing REST services for KPIs, forecasts, five scenario modes (energy prediction, generator reduction ρ, production increase, base-load reduction via regression intercept, peak-load analysis on the top-20% production days), and anomaly detection (7-day rolling window, 2σ rule, Eq. 14), and (5) a web dashboard. The dispatch rule is deterministic: if forecast < E_lim = 9,740 kWh (observed max 10,255 kWh minus 5% safety factor), recommend grid-only; else flag the excess for off-peak shifting. Critical design decisions: cross-validation instead of holdout for small data (justified); treating the RF classifier as an unvalidated alert because only 6/59 days were generator-active (justified and honest); deriving the grid threshold from observed history rather than sanctioned capacity (acknowledged as an approximation). The scenario savings objective is a deterministic tariff-difference calculation, not an optimization. Key Results: On the case-study dataset (59 days, 245,956.6 units produced, 526,625 kWh total energy, DG share 1.48%): quadratic regression fits better than linear in-sample (R² 0.6597 vs. 0.6137; RMSE 540.4 vs. 578.8 kWh). Under 5-fold CV, linear regression wins (R² 0.49 ± 0.26; 0.51 ± 0.17 with demand lags), RF 0.17 ± 0.37, gradient boosting −0.03 ± 0.78, XGBoost −0.23 ± 0.66 — higher-capacity models overfit. On a chronological holdout (47 train / 12 test), the 3-day moving average is the best forecaster (RMSE 417 / MAE 334 kWh), beating damped Holt (425/388), ARIMA(1,1,1) (443/337), persistence (451/428), AR(1) (483/395), and the LSTM (546/457). Scenario estimates: 50% DG reduction saves 35,190 MU (~1.1% of period cost) and 345.3 kg net CO₂; peak-day load shifting of 515 kWh saves 4,635 MU (~7.0% of peak-day cost) and 45.5 kg CO₂. Counter-intuitive finding: EPU is lower during peak-production days (scale efficiency), yet generator share is higher then, indicating a supply constraint. A learning-curve check (RF train/validation R² gap of ~0.62–0.82 across n = 12–47) supports the overfitting interpretation. Scale: a single facility, ~60 daily records — toy-to-small by any ML standard, though appropriate to the stated use case. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the integrated, SME-targeted, vendor-neutral platform combining seven capabilities in one dashboard (per the authors' own capability-comparison Table 1, no single prior work covers more than two), plus the documented small-data result that complex models underperform interpretable regression and naive forecasters. All constituent algorithms — OLS, RF, XGBoost, LSTM, rolling 2σ detection, persistence/MA baselines — are standard techniques applied unchanged; the dispatch rule is a simple threshold heuristic. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually strong for an integration paper: 5-fold cross-validation with error bars (mean ± SD) for all regressors, a chronological holdout with six forecasting baselines including naive and statistical ones, 2,000-resample bootstrap CIs on R² (linear 0.445–0.759; quadratic 0.464–0.817), Shapiro-Wilk, Breusch-Pagan, Durbin-Watson, and VIF diagnostics (revealing non-normality, heteroscedasticity, and serial dependence, which the authors explicitly downplay by framing regressions as descriptive), a learning-curve overfitting check, an Isolation Forest sensitivity comparison for anomaly detection, and section-level traceability for the literature-comparison table. The LSTM configuration is fixed and declared "a reproducible proof-of-concept rather than an optimally tuned model." Concerns: no code or model release is mentioned; data is only available "on reasonable request" because it came from a company; the anomaly detectors disagree materially (10 flags vs. 3, 2 overlapping) with no ground-truth labels to adjudicate; and all economic/CO₂ results are scenario estimates, not measured outcomes. No Goodhart-style benchmark gaming is apparent — the paper does not optimize on its evaluation metric. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built platform with a REST backend and dashboard, evaluated via a case-study dataset rather than live deployment). - Practical: Yes — the components run in a standard numerical environment on spreadsheet data with no IoT hardware required, deliberately matching SME constraints. - Efficient: Extremely low compute cost by design — the deployable models are 2-parameter regressions and a 3-day moving average; the LSTM is the most expensive component and is explicitly not recommended for deployment. - Effective: Partially — model accuracy is validated (modestly: CV R² ≈ 0.49), but the decision value (savings, CO₂ avoidance) is demonstrated only through scenario arithmetic assuming one-for-one energy substitution and sufficient off-peak grid capacity, never through realized measurements. - Scalable: Untested beyond one facility and 59 days; the paper claims (not shows) that multi-tenant cloud deployment and IoT streaming are future work, and the small-data regime is precisely what limits generalization. The work ships as a paper with a described dashboard artifact; no public repository, dataset, or trained model is released. Strengths: - The negative-result benchmarking is the paper's real contribution: it quantifies, with cross-validated error bars and six forecasting baselines, when ensemble and recurrent models fail at SME data scales — a finding many authors would have buried. - Methodological candor throughout: the RF classifier is explicitly downgraded to an "exploratory alert" (6/59 positives), the base-load scenario is labeled "directional only" because the intercept is a statistical extrapolation, and regression diagnostics are reported even though they undermine causal interpretation. - Complete pipeline thinking — from raw plant data through KPIs, models, scenario engine, to an operator-facing dashboard — closes the model-to-decision gap the literature review correctly identifies as rare. - Careful, region-portable parameterization (currency-agnostic MU, replaceable grid emission factor) with cited sources (CEA v21.0, IPCC stationary combustion). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive): single facility, limited time span, no generalization claim; small-data regime makes high-capacity models impractical and the DG classifier unvalidatable (6/59 positives); Scope 1/2-only carbon accounting with a static grid factor; batch (not IoT) data collection; LSTM using energy history only; threshold derived from observed maximum rather than sanctioned capacity; no power-quality (voltage/current/power factor) analysis; fixed 7-day anomaly window; no dashboard usability study; scenario savings are estimates with no implementation cost or payback analysis; LSTM underperforming naive baselines with a recommendation to use locally validated forecasters instead. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No measured outcome: the paper never records whether operators acted on any recommendation or whether any predicted saving materialized; the "digital twin" is never closed-loop against the physical plant during the study. - No code, configuration files, or dataset release, so reproducibility rests entirely on the (fairly detailed) text; fixed seeds (42) are mentioned only for the sensitivity reruns. - The headline integration claim rests on a capability table the authors themselves qualify as "a literature-level capability summary rather than a claim that every unmarked capability was experimentally disproved" — the comparison against prior work is checkbox-level, not head-to-head. - The anomaly-detector disagreement (10 vs. 3 flags, no labels) means the dashboard's anomaly view may be largely arbitrary; the authors note calibration needs but still ship the 2σ rule as default. - With only 6 generator-active days, the entire generator-alerting and load-shifting value proposition is exercised on essentially one peak day; the 4,635 MU / 45.5 kg CO₂ headline rests on a single 515 kWh shift assuming unconstrained off-peak grid capacity. - Author-contribution block inconsistencies ("M.R." and "S.P." appear in the contributions text but are not listed authors) suggest loose manuscript hygiene, though this does not affect the technical content. Bottom Line: A practitioner building energy tooling for small manufacturers gains a genuinely useful, honest reference architecture and a memorable small-data lesson (simple, interpretable models plus naive forecasters beat ML complexity at this scale), but anyone expecting a validated, deployable, or algorithmically novel system should look elsewhere.

Problem & Motivation: Teams running long-horizon agentic RL — where one rollout is a multi-turn SWE interaction capped at 131,072 tokens and a training batch holds ~1,024 rollouts (~39M tokens) — need both fast rollout generation and training over very long sequences. Existing open-source RL stacks (DeepSpeed-Chat, OpenRLHF, HybridFlow, AReaL) fail on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next for three concrete reasons the paper quantifies: activation checkpointing of the 48-layer 10,240-wide residual stream needs ~129 GB/GPU before weights and gradients; CPU-offloaded AdamW state for ~129B parameters needs ~1,922 GiB of host memory, exceeding the ~1,937 GiB node once the 95.4 GiB frozen n-gram table is added; and no efficient backward kernels exist for QSA sparse attention, MoE with intermediate size 640 at expert parallelism 8, or the 4-branch gated residual. The paper's goal is explicitly not model accuracy but identifying the model-specific optimizations that make this training practical. Key Idea: The central insight is that for architecturally unusual models (hybrid GDN/QSA attention, multi-stream gated residual, huge frozen lookup tables, fine-grained MoE), the binding RL-training constraints are host-memory traffic and missing backward kernels — not FLOPs — so the optimization order matters: fix the offload path and gradient accumulation first (a 7.4× combined gain on 8 layers), after which custom kernels (MoE megakernel, token-level sparse attention, fused residual glue) yield their full value. A secondary non-obvious trick is router replay: because BF16 routing flips explain ~96% of offline trainer–inference mismatch, inference engines return the routed experts of every token (960 bytes/token) and the trainer replays them instead of recomputing routing. Methodology: The system spans four 8×B200 nodes (one trainer, three inference) connected by 8×400 Gb/s EFA. Inference: vLLM 0.31, 2 engines per node at TP4+EP (chosen by replaying real SWE rollouts against TP2/TP4/TP8 candidates; TP4 reaches 1,091 output tokens/s/GPU at 26 sessions/GPU), MTP3 speculative decoding via the model's own 4B MTP head (acceptance 2.55 tokens/pass live), BF16 weights/KV cache, prefix caching, a per-node shared tmpfs mapping of the n-gram table, and KV-usage-based session admission (throttle above 65%, resume below 55%). Training: FSDP2 with CPU offload, StreamingMuon (Newton–Schulz orthogonalization streamed one parameter at a time from a cudaHostRegister'd exact-size PinnedArena), expert parallelism 8 with static longest-processing-time-first expert placement, Ulysses context parallelism 4 with headwise GDN/QSA adaptations, full activation checkpointing reusing forward routing decisions, and the first two layers frozen. Individual optimizations are isolated (PinnedArena cuts Muon step 75→12.4 s; GPU-resident expert gradients give 2.4–2.7×; MoK at native size-640 with 52/52 comm SMs is 1.56–2.24× faster than DeepEP per layer; a CuTe-DSL dK/dV kernel reaches 46.7 ms at 64K, within ~13% of its gather and MMA floors; UVA n-gram gather gives +8.1% on the full model). End-to-end loop: layerwise NCCL weight broadcast (~260 GB in 15–18 s), DCP checkpoints to local NVMe with per-tensor arena storage (940 GiB saved per save), and HF export overlapped with the broadcast (checkpoint-step overhead 307→102 s). The RL objective and advantage estimator are not specified in this paper — it is a systems study riding on prime-rl/verifiers. Key Results: Full-model trainer throughput went from ~395 REAL tokens/s/GPU (initial 32K-bin configuration) to 4,438 at 131K bins, with hardware matmul throughput 20→213 TFLOPs/GPU — though the authors correctly flag this is a development progression, not a controlled same-configuration speedup (batch size and bin size change). The controlled 8-layer ladder runs 2,391→17,678 tokens/s/GPU (7.4×, noise ±0.3%), and leave-one-out removal confirms MoK (−22.4%), fused gated residual/glue (−19.6%), and GQA-native QSA (−14.9%) as the largest kernel contributors. The live SWE run (steps 5–15, 11 steps, 1,393 rollouts collected/1,026 trained per step on average) achieves 22.4-minute mean iterations (1,344 s), 4,737 packed tokens/s/GPU over forward/backward, 17.1K output tokens/s generation, 18.6 s mean weight broadcast, entropy bounded at 0.66–0.76 nats/token, and trainer–sampler mismatch KL of 3.6–4.0×10⁻³ with router replay. Generation binds the loop: the trainer waits 331 s per iteration on average. The capacity estimate that 8–11 training nodes of an unoptimized trainer would be needed to match the optimized service time is explicitly labeled an unmeasured extrapolation. Novelty Classification: ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel elements are the integrated memory plan (exact-size pinned arenas avoiding PyTorch's power-of-two caching allocator and registration failures), GPU-resident expert-gradient accumulation for size-1 FSDP units, the sm100 CuTe-DSL sparse-attention dK/dV kernel, and the router-replay mechanism — each a non-trivial but incremental advance over known techniques (ZeRO offload, ThunderKittens-style megakernels, Ulysses CP, existing router-alignment work [23]). The paper is candid that it is a tailored-optimization study, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually strong for a systems paper: a 15-rung cumulative ladder on 8 layers with mean-of-7-steps measurements, run-to-run noise (±0.3%), and a complementary leave-one-out table. The authors transparently flag that full-model endpoints are not a controlled comparison, that TFLOP rates are accounting estimates rather than hardware-counter measurements, and that the ladder baseline already includes mandatory correctness fixes (so it is not a stock implementation). Weaknesses: throughput is measured by replaying recorded rollouts rather than live co-measured generation+training in Section 3; the live run is a single run of 11 post-warmup steps with no error bars possible; only one hardware configuration (B200/sm100) and one model are tested; no code release URL for FlashNext-RL is stated in the paper; and no comparison of end-to-end RL iteration time against an alternative framework (e.g., OpenRLHF, AReaL) at any scale — the claim that general-purpose infrastructure fails is supported only by the authors' own encountered limitations, not by benchmarked baselines. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, deployed RL training system evaluated by a live run). Practical: No — the demonstrated configuration requires 32 B200 GPUs across four nodes plus ~2 TB host RAM on the trainer, beyond most academic and many industrial budgets, and depends on sm100-specific CuTe kernels and vLLM 0.31 behavior. Efficient: Relative to the unoptimized alternative it is highly efficient (7.4× on the controlled ladder), and the loop is now generation-bound rather than trainer-bound, which is the correct end state. Effective: For the stated goal (make this training configuration run), yes — the live run demonstrates 22.4-minute iterations with bounded entropy and KL; but effectiveness at RL's actual goal (capability improvement) is unmeasured. Scalable: Only extrapolated — multi-node training scaling is a back-of-envelope estimate assuming linear scaling, explicitly not measured, and 10× scale would need the stated 8–11 training nodes under optimistic assumptions. Deliverable: the paper documents the system in detail but states no public code, weights, or artifact release; it stops at paper form as far as the text indicates. Strengths: (1) Attribution discipline: the cumulative ladder plus leave-one-out ablation lets a reader know exactly which optimization buys what (e.g., offload-path fixes precede and dominate kernel gains — a transferable lesson, since torch.compile actually costs 20% on the unoptimized baseline). (2) Unusual candor: the paper labels its own headline 10.4× full-model ratio as not a controlled comparison, calls its TFLOP numbers accounting estimates, and marks its capacity estimate as an extrapolation — this is a credibility positive. (3) Several concrete, reusable engineering findings: router flips cause ~96% of trainer–inference mismatch in BF16 MoE; cudaHostRegister's failure mode on freed-and-reused regions; PSS vs RSS accounting (43% overstatement) for shared tmpfs mappings; KV-cache prefix-hit collapse above ~70% usage in hybrid attention. (4) The end-to-end integration work (memory-safe batch path, layerwise weight broadcast, checkpoint-from-broadcast) addresses the unglamorous loop-level constraints that most RL papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly that the evaluation is limited to one hardware configuration and a short training run; that it does not establish long-run convergence, final task accuracy, or multi-node training scalability; that the full-model speedup endpoints are not controlled; that the capacity estimate is illustrative; and that MTP acceptance may decay since the draft head is not updated (they monitor it). They also note the generation-side wait includes sandbox command-execution time that they did not isolate from GPU limits. This is direct confrontation of limitations, not minimization. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Zero task-quality metrics — no reward curves, no SWE-bench-style resolution rates, not even per-step mean reward; a reader cannot tell if the RL run was learning anything, only that it was numerically stable. (2) No benchmarked comparison against any alternative RL framework; the motivating failure of open-source stacks is asserted from the authors' experience, not measured. (3) The RL algorithm (objective, advantage estimation, reward design, KL regularization toward a reference policy) is entirely unspecified, making the stability numbers uninterpretable in algorithmic terms and the system hard to evaluate against prime-rl defaults. (4) Only 11 evaluable steps from one run — entropy and KL bounded over 11 steps is weak evidence for anything about long-horizon RL dynamics. (5) Router replay trades 960 bytes/token of extra communication and trainer memory for mismatch control, but the paper does not report the mismatch KL without replay in the live run, so the live-run benefit of the mechanism is inferred from offline measurement. (6) No public artifact release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of a paper whose value is largely in engineering details. Bottom Line: For engineers building RL post-training infrastructure for large MoE or hybrid-attention models, this is a high-value, candidly reported playbook whose offload-path and router-replay lessons generalize; for anyone seeking RL algorithm insights, SWE-agent capability results, or a deployable open artifact, there is currently nothing here beyond the described techniques.

DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration (189 ▲ )

Ruhao Liu, Qi Li, Shizun Wang, Xinchao Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DynaFlow, a framework that makes free-form executable workflow synthesis (JavaScript programs coordinating frozen sub-agents) a native action of the task-solving main agent, trained via two-stage SFT on orchestration-quality-filtered distilled trajectories. - Why it's important: Multi-agent LLM systems typically bolt on fixed collaboration topologies that waste computation on easy queries and under-serve hard ones; if one 27B model can learn when and how to orchestrate, practitioners can reuse existing models as executors without retraining them. - How it does it: The main agent's policy chooses among direct answers, tool calls, or synthesizing a workflow program; training uses teacher-distilled first-turn demonstrations (Stage 1) followed by a subset curated by an LLM judge that rejects demonstrations with premise injection, biased verification, or information-flow defects (Stage 2), while all sub-agents stay frozen. - The good: The staged ablation is convincing — an untrained main agent forced to use workflows loses accuracy on five of six benchmarks (65–77% overall), while the trained agent reaches 88.08% overall and 100% on 90 pooled AIME questions, cleanly showing orchestration skill, not workflow access, drives the gains. - The missing: The paper states an equal-size random-subset continuation control is "required" to separate curation effects from extra training, but never reports it, so the Stage 2 gain (+2.6 points overall) may be an artifact of more SFT; skip it if you only need another benchmark number.

Resilience (52) falls with it, since the headline 100% AIME result and the curation claim would not survive adversarial questioning. Problem & Motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems typically fix collaboration structures (agent roles, communication patterns, topologies) at design time, which mismatches heterogeneous task difficulty: simple queries get unnecessary communication overhead, and dependent stages may lose intermediate results. Prior adaptive approaches (DyFlow, MAS-Orchestra, MAS-GPT, FlowReasoner) still constrain workflow construction to operator templates, single-shot topology generation, or designs made without observing execution. The authors argue scalable multi-agent systems need "Free Orchestration": one agent deciding when collaboration helps and constructing task-specific workflows during solving. This matters to anyone deploying agent systems where per-query compute and reliability both count. Key Idea: Treat a workflow program as just another action in the solver's own policy — alongside tool calls and direct answers — so the same model learns when to collaborate, writes the coordinating JavaScript (sub-agent roles, parallel/sequential dependencies, explicit passing of upstream outputs), and revises based on returned outputs and execution traces. The second half of the idea is supervising orchestration quality directly: rather than filtering demonstrations by answer correctness alone, an LLM judge screens for three named coordination defects (premise injection, biased verification, information-flow defects), making reliable information transfer an explicit training criterion. Methodology: The main agent samples actions a_k ~ π_θ(·|I, q, h_{k−1}) from an action space A = A_tool ∪ {A_ans, (P, W(P))}, where P is a synthesized JavaScript program executed by a budget-constrained runtime exposing `agent`, `parallel`, `pipeline`, and `phase` primitives; the returned observation (program output plus per-call execution trace) is appended to history until the agent emits a final answer. Training updates only the main agent with a masked-token SFT loss (Eq. 2) supervising first-turn reasoning and workflow action. Stage 1 uses 2,257 teacher-distilled first-turn demonstrations from GLM-5.3 Max on HotpotQA/BrowseComp tasks; Stage 2 continues on 712 examples retained after LLM-judge screening of the three defect types with excerpt-verified evidence. Critical design decisions: (1) freezing all sub-agents (same Qwen3.5-27B base checkpoint) — well justified, it isolates orchestration learning and is validated by the Base/Stage1/DynaFlow × Direct/Dynamic/Forced grid (Table 2); (2) defect-based data curation — motivated by Stage 1 error analysis, but the promised random-subset control is not reported; (3) first-turn-only supervision rather than multi-turn trajectories — acknowledged as a limitation. Training is 4-bit NF4 QLoRA (116.7M trainable parameters, ~69 GPU-hours on 2×H100). Key Results: On 688 questions across AIME 2024/2025/2026 (30 each), PolyMATH (200), GPQA-Diamond (198), and HotpotQA (200), all with a Qwen3.5-27B backbone, DynaFlow reaches 88.08% micro-averaged accuracy in Forced mode and 87.94% in Dynamic mode, versus 77.18% for the strongest evaluated baseline (Self-Refine) and 76.45% for AFlow — a 10.90-point margin. It solves 100% of the 90 pooled AIME questions in Forced mode. In Dynamic mode it answers 47.1% of questions directly and uses 2.44 sub-agents per question versus 4.16 under Forced (~41% fewer). Untrained Forced-mode execution hurts on five of six benchmarks (Base, Forced 75.87% vs Base, Direct 71.51%, but with HotpotQA driving the average; AIME24 drops from 93.33 to 76.67). After training, hybrid parallel/sequential workflows rise from 3.4% to 85.6%, and output-reuse ("Consumed") from 12.6% to 97.7%. Baselines are reasonably current single-agent methods but weak on the multi-agent side: AFlow is run with transferred, un-searched workflows, and no head-to-head against MAS-GPT, MAS-Zero, DyFlow, FlowReasoner, or MAS-Orchestra despite these being the closest related systems. Scale is modest (688 questions, 30-question AIME sets, single seed). Notably, Self-Refine (88.38%) and AFlow (87.37%) still beat DynaFlow Forced (84.85%) on GPQA-Diamond — honestly reported. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an ELEMENT of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel combination is (a) free-form executable workflow synthesis embedded as a native action of the solving agent with multi-turn feedback, and (b) demonstration selection keyed to a taxonomy of orchestration defects rather than answer correctness. Individual ingredients are known: CodeAct-style executable code actions, MAS-GPT-style SFT on query-specific system generation, MAS-Zero/DyFlow-style feedback-driven revision, and LLM-judge data filtering. The finding that forced workflow use degrades accuracy before training and helps after it is a useful, non-obvious empirical result. Rigor & Reproducibility: A partial ablation grid exists (Base/Stage 1/Stage 2 × Direct/Dynamic/Forced, per-benchmark in Table 6), and the training-vs-execution-mode factorial is the paper's strongest experimental element. However: the random-subset continuation control that the authors themselves call "required" for attributing Stage 2 gains to curation is not reported anywhere in the visible text; all results appear to be single runs (seed 42, temperature 1.0) with no error bars or significance tests, on 30-question AIME subsets where 100% vs 96.67% is one question; and the workflow-quality analyses (Figures 4–6) are scored by an LLM judge (deepseek-flash) rather than humans beyond a rubric-agreement check described only in an appendix. Hyperparameters, prompts, judging rubric, and decoding settings are documented in appendices, and header links to code and a project page are indicated, but no URL or weights release appears in the provided text. Methodological concerns: Stage 1/2 training data come from HotpotQA and BrowseComp while HotpotQA is also an evaluation benchmark (200 sampled questions) with no stated de-duplication against training; the AFlow baseline was not given the workflow-search step that defines the method; and the main comparison set omits the closest competing learned-orchestration systems. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained policy evaluated on benchmarks; the workflow runtime is a supporting system, not the artifact under deployment evaluation). Practical: Yes — a 27B backbone fine-tuned with 4-bit QLoRA on 2×H100 (~69 GPU-hours) is within reach of most labs, and inference is standard model serving plus a JS execution sandbox. Efficient: Mixed — Dynamic mode cuts sub-agent usage ~41% versus Forced (2.44 vs 4.16 agents/question), but no wall-clock, token, or dollar cost is reported against the single-agent baselines, which matters since workflow paths invoke multiple 27B calls with thinking enabled. Effective: Strong evidence on 688 benchmark questions that orchestration training solves the stated problem, though effectiveness rests on a single unverified run per cell and unreported controls. Scalable: Not tested — nothing beyond 688 questions, no long-horizon tasks, and the cost of multi-agent fan-out at 10× task complexity is unexamined. The paper stops at paper form plus indicated code/project-page links; no trained weights are stated as released. Strengths: - The factorial design (three checkpoints × three execution modes with frozen sub-agents) is the right experiment for the claim: it isolates orchestration learning from executor capability and produces the memorable result that workflows are harmful before training on five of six benchmarks. - The three-defect taxonomy (premise injection, biased verification, information-flow defects) is a concrete, transferable contribution to data curation for agent training, with excerpt-verified judging rather than free-form LLM scores. - The structural analysis of learned workflows (six dimensions including output reuse and aggregation strategy) goes beyond accuracy and substantiates the mechanistic story — e.g., correction/refinement stages rising from 28.1% to 35.9% between Stages 1 and 2. - Honest negative reporting: the paper shows DynaFlow losing to Self-Refine and AFlow on GPQA-Diamond and analyzes the failure mode (correct intermediate evidence overridden during verification/synthesis). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that only first-turn supervision is used and that extending to multi-turn trajectories containing disagreements and erroneous results is future work; they acknowledge GPQA failures where correct intermediate conclusions are lost or overridden during final synthesis; they note tool-free baselines lack the retrieval access given to workflow settings (interpreting HotpotQA comparisons separately); and they flag that their Stage 2 comparison requires a random-subset control to attribute gains to curation. This is a credibility positive — the limitations section confronts real issues rather than minimizing them, though the unreported control undercuts how directly they followed through on their own caveat. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The random-subset Stage 2 control is promised but never reported, leaving the headline Stage 2 contribution (curation beats more training) unsupported by the shown evidence. - Possible train/test contamination: Stage 1 and Stage 2 data include HotpotQA demonstrations, and HotpotQA is an evaluation benchmark; no de-duplication or held-out check is stated. - Missing head-to-head baselines against the closest methods (MAS-GPT, MAS-Zero, DyFlow, MAS-Orchestra, FlowReasoner), and AFlow is handicapped by running transferred workflows without its defining search step. - Single run, single seed, no variance estimates, and 30-question AIME subsets make the 100% AIME claims statistically fragile. - All workflow-quality and behavioral analyses are scored by LLM judges (deepseek-flash for both data selection and evaluation), with only appendix-level human-agreement validation; judge circularity and rubric-sensitivity are unexamined. - No cost/latency comparison against baselines, so the accuracy gains' compute price is unknown. - Training data come only from retrieval/QA-style tasks (HotpotQA, BrowseComp), yet the biggest gains are on math; the paper does not explain why cross-domain transfer is so strong, which deserves investigation before assuming generality. Bottom Line: A practitioner building trainable multi-agent orchestration should read this for its defect-taxonomy data curation and its clean demonstration that orchestration skill — not workflow access — is what makes collaboration pay, but should not treat the headline numbers as settled given the unreported control, thin baselines, and single-seed evaluation; the workflow-synthesis-as-action idea is promising but likely will be superseded by RL-trained and more thoroughly benchmarked follow-ups.

Adaptive Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Multi-Image Understanding in Large Visual Language Models

R Zhang, C Lu, C Li, H Gu, T Shen, X Zhi, Q Wang… · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AVTP, a training-free visual token pruning framework for large vision-language models (LVLMs) that selects pruning layers per architecture, scores token importance from hidden-state variation (attention-free, FlashAttention-compatible), and allocates keep ratios across images in multi-image inputs. - Why it's important: Multi-image inputs generate 8k+ visual tokens, causing memory blowups and slow inference; existing attention-based pruning methods run out of memory under FlashAttention-incompatible settings and do not transfer across LVLM architectures, so deployment cost is the binding constraint on multi-image applications. - How it does it: The core trick is scoring each visual token by 1 − cosine-like similarity between its embedding at the current pruning layer and its embedding at the previous pruning layer, so importance needs only forward passes—no attention weights—plus an offline sampling pass that ranks LLM layers by visual-token attention to pick per-model pruning layers. - The good: The empirical observation that visual-attention concentration depth differs systematically across LVLM families (shallow for LLaVA, mid/late for Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5), with a layer-selection ablation (Figure 3) showing pruning high-attention layers beats pruning layer 1 only or low-attention layers, is the most credible and transferable insight. - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests on any result, and the abstract's headline '2× inference speedup' is not supported by the reported latency table, which shows roughly 1.4–1.5× wall-clock reduction on Qwen3VL-8B (e.g., 2086.79→1454.00 ms on MuirBench). - Read it or not: Worth reading for engineers deploying LVLMs on multi-image or video workloads who need a FlashAttention-compatible pruning recipe and for researchers studying cross-architecture attention behavior; skip it if you want a fundamentally new pruning algorithm or statistically rigorous evaluation.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Rigor (55) is pulled down by the absence of any seeds, error bars, or significance tests while many claimed wins over V2DROP are sub-point, the unsupported '2× speedup' abstract claim, and partial benchmark contamination in layer selection. Novelty (55) is limited: the authors themselves concede this is an evolutionary advance on V2DROP, with the cross-architecture attention-layer finding as the one reusable insight. Resilience (50) suffers from strawmanned baseline configurations and claims that would not survive scrutiny of the discrepancy between abstract and tables. Completeness (65) is aided by honest, direct limitation acknowledgment; Impact (65) reflects a genuinely deployable FlashAttention-compatible recipe. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying LVLMs on multi-image tasks (documents, comparisons, GUI agents, video) face quadratic attention cost from thousands of visual tokens. Existing token pruning methods have three concrete shortcomings the authors demonstrate: (1) attention-score-based pruning (FAST-V, VisionZip) requires materializing attention values, conflicting with FlashAttention and causing frequent OOM—Table 1 reports 1,070 OOM cases for FAST-V on MuirBench and 1,632 for VisionZip on InternVL3.5-8B with a single A100 80GB; (2) shallow-layer pruning, derived from LLaVA attention patterns, does not transfer to other architectures, since Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 concentrate visual attention in middle-to-late layers; (3) uniform pruning across all images in a multi-image prompt discards information from task-relevant images disproportionately. Key Idea: Replace attention-based token importance with embedding-drift importance: a token is important if its hidden state changes substantially between successive pruning layers (I_vi = 1 − Sim(h^l_vi, h^prior_vi)). This requires only forward-pass hidden states, so it composes with FlashAttention, and the prior embedding anchor (the state after the most recent pruning op) accumulates a token's sustained relevance across layers. The second supporting idea is that the correct pruning layers are an architectural property, discoverable offline by ranking layers by cumulative attention to visual tokens over ~100 sampled cases. Methodology: Three components. (1) Offline architecture-aware layer selection: sample N instances, prefill, compute per-layer total attention to visual tokens A^(i)_l = Σ_j Attention(l, v_j), average ranks across samples, select top-k layers; this yields layer 1 for LLaVA-OneVision, layers 1/19/25 for InternVL3.5-8B, layers 1/14/19 for Qwen3VL-8B. (2) Online token importance from hidden-state drift between the current layer and the last pruning layer. (3) Image-aware adaptive pruning: per-image average importance I_i yields keep ratio r_i = r_base + α·(I_i − I_avg), with α=1.0 and rates clamped to [5%, 95%]; pruning is applied progressively at the selected layers. All methods retain 50% of visual tokens in main experiments. Design decisions: the attention-free importance proxy is justified by the FlashAttention OOM evidence; the per-architecture layer selection is justified by the Figure 2 attention distributions and Figure 3 ablation; the linear adaptive keep-ratio is only weakly justified—α ablations (Table 6) show gains of at most ~0.7 accuracy points and are benchmark-dependent, so this component is the least supported. Key Results: Three 8B-class LVLMs (InternVL3.5-8B, LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Qwen3VL-8B) on five multi-image benchmarks (MuirBench 2,600 cases, MIRB 1,013, BLINK 1,901, QBench2 1,000, NLVR2 6,967) versus FAST-V, VisionZip, DivPrune, and V2DROP, all at 50% keep ratio, single A100, with FlashAttention-2 base. Representative numbers: Qwen3VL-8B AVTP 65.54 on MuirBench (base 64.81) at 1454 ms vs 2087 ms; on NLVR2 86.15 vs base 87.99 (97.9% retention) at 2794 vs 4267 ms; InternVL3.5-8B AVTP 50.38 MuirBench vs base 52.31 and V2DROP 49.31. LLaVA-OneVision-7B with AVTP exceeds its unpruned base on MuirBench (36.50 vs 31.92) and QBench2 (52.20 vs 45.20), attributed to pruning returning sequences to the model's trained context length. Baselines are current (2024–2025 methods), but several are partially strawmanned in this setting: FAST-V and VisionZip produce OOM on most multi-image benchmarks, so their latency is unmeasurable; FAST-V fails outright on LLaVA-OneVision and VisionZip is incompatible with Qwen3-VL. Ablations confirm each component adds 0.3–1.3 accuracy points over a V2DROP-style fixed-layer configuration. Appendix extends to keep ratios of 20% and 5% (5% degrades MIRB from 45.21 to 33.17) and to single-image/video benchmarks (MMBench, MMStar, POPE, MME, MVBench), where AVTP is competitive but adaptive pruning contributes nothing by construction. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (cross-architecture visual-attention layer distributions) + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION with a modest NEW METHOD component. The hidden-state-variation importance score is an increment on V2DROP's variation-based dropping—the authors say so explicitly in Limitations—and image-aware keep-ratio allocation is a straightforward extension; the genuinely novel, reusable contribution is the demonstration that pruning-layer placement is an architectural property and the attention-free, FlashAttention-compatible importance proxy. Rigor & Reproducibility: Component ablations exist and are informative (Table 3, Figure 3, Table 5 pruning ratios, Table 6 α sweep), which is a strength. However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; many headline differences over V2DROP are 0.2–1.9 accuracy points, within plausible run-to-run noise. A Goodhart concern: layer selection samples 100 cases each from MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA, and MMStar, and MMBench, MMStar, and POPE also serve as appendix evaluation benchmarks (Table 7), so layer selection is tuned partly on evaluation data for those results. Code is stated to be available 'at this link' but no concrete URL/repository appears in the text. The abstract's '2× inference speedup' for Qwen3VL-8B is not reconciled with the reported latencies (~1.43–1.53× in Table 2); the 96.1% accuracy-retention figure also cannot be directly reconstructed from Table 2. All experiments run on a single A100 80GB at 50% keep ratio—reasonable, standard scale, not stress-scale. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (inference-time method, empirically evaluated; no formal proofs despite the conclusion's gesture at 'theoretical analysis'). - Practical: Yes—training-free, runs on a single A100 80GB, fully FlashAttention-2 compatible by construction. - Efficient: ~1.4–1.5× latency reduction at 50% keep ratio with no extra memory for attention storage, the concrete advantage over FAST-V/VisionZip which OOM in multi-image settings. - Effective: Evidence shows accuracy retention (94–96%+ on most benchmarks, above-baseline on LLaVA-OV) on multi-image benchmarks—real task metrics, not just proxy perplexity—though the adaptive component's marginal effect (≤0.7 points in Table 6) suggests most benefit comes from layer selection plus the drift score. - Scalable: Not tested beyond ~8k visual tokens on one 80GB GPU; the paper claims large-scale deployability but provides no throughput experiments at higher concurrency, longer contexts, or larger models. Delivers a described method with code claimed (URL not shown); no trained model or dataset artifact. Strengths: - The cross-architecture attention-distribution analysis (Figure 2) is a genuinely useful empirical finding: it explains why LLaVA-tuned shallow pruning underperforms on Qwen3-VL/InternVL3.5 and gives a cheap, reproducible offline procedure (rank layers by visual-token attention over ~100 samples) to fix it. - The FlashAttention-compatibility framing is well-grounded: Table 1's OOM counts (1,070 for FAST-V, 1,632 for VisionZip on InternVL3.5-8B) turn an abstract architectural objection into concrete, deployment-relevant evidence that attention-based pruning can be strictly worse than uncompressed FlashAttention inference. - Honest self-assessment: the Limitations section explicitly concedes the method is an evolutionary advance over V2DROP and that key hyperparameters lack theoretical grounding—credibility-positive. - Ablation coverage is above average for this subfield: component ablations, keep-ratio sweep (50/20/5%), α sweep, layer-choice comparison, and image-count-stratified results (Table 4). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) top-k, α, and the embedding-variation-to-importance correlation are empirically set without formal substantiation; (2) no comparison against orthogonal acceleration techniques (quantization, distillation), which they argue are complementary rather than competing; (3) the method is an incremental advance on V2DROP rather than a new algorithmic paradigm. These are confronted directly and are consistent with the evidence. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor: single runs, no seeds, no error bars, while several claimed wins over V2DROP are under 1 accuracy point (e.g., Qwen3VL MIRB 41.88 vs V2DROP 36.23 is safe, but MuirBench 65.54 vs 63.69 with a 0.5-point α-effect suggests noise-level margins elsewhere). - The '2× speedup' abstract claim is not substantiated by any table in the paper (max observed ~1.53× on Qwen3VL NLVR2); abstract and evidence are inconsistent. - Partial benchmark contamination: layer-selection sampling uses MMBench, MMStar, and POPE, which are also reported as evaluation benchmarks in Appendix B. - Baseline configuration risk: FAST-V pinned to layer 2 and V2DROP to layers 3/17/22 across all models exaggerates their cross-architecture failure; a stronger evaluation would retune baseline pruning layers per model to isolate the importance-score contribution from the layer-placement contribution. - The claimed 'theoretical analysis' in the conclusion is absent from the paper; the drift-importance heuristic is motivated only verbally. - Scaling evidence is thin: no experiments above 50% keep ratio on the multi-image benchmarks in the main text beyond Qwen3VL, no throughput/concurrency measurements, and no >8B models, so architecture-agnosticism is established over exactly three families. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying multi-image LVLM inference gains real, actionable value—especially the layer-selection procedure and the FlashAttention-compatible drift-based importance score—but should treat the 2× speedup claim skeptically, and a researcher seeking a novel algorithm will find V2DROP and follow-ups already cover most of this ground.

The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents (312 ▲ )

Weidong Tang, Ruiheng Wang, Jingxuan Zhang, Hexin Wang, Haoyuan Chen, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Yixing Ma, Zichen Jiang, Ziyu Guo, Haodong Li, Zhengbo Jiao, Zhiqing Cui, Xinxiang Yin, Shuo Liang, Zhenglin Wan, Hongzhan Lin, Wangbo Zhao Kaipeng Zhang, Pengfei Zhou, Odin Zhang, Yang You · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework that reorganizes 28 heterogeneous multimodal benchmarks into a hierarchical capability tree, generates simplified verifiable simulated worlds per capability node, and evolves a tree of module-based agent Harnesses with a frozen Claude Opus 5 backbone, raising mean Train performance from 39.06 to 73.16 and mean Unseen performance from 37.45 to 63.61 over 4 RSI iterations. - Why it's important: Manual Harness iteration and hand-built training environments cannot keep pace with growing task diversity, and existing task-specific Harness RSI overfits to narrow domains — this work targets cross-domain, cross-modality generalization without touching model weights. - How it does it: The core move is replacing task-driven organization with capability-driven organization: tasks sharing underlying capability requirements (induced from verified trajectories into a Trie over 6 capabilities) become one learning objective, trained in Creator-generated simulated worlds, with selective module inheritance down the tree and a retrieval-augmented Capability-Aware Router selecting Harness branches at test time. - The good: The breadth and protocol discipline of the evaluation is the strongest asset — 18 held-out benchmarks improve 26 points, the evolved system beats Codex (47.49) and DeepSeek (46.18) Harness references on 16 unseen non-robot benchmarks (64.06), and capability-evolved Harnesses transfer to two real robots (SOON 0%→60%, CaP-X 0%→60%). - The missing: Statistical rigor — most benchmarks are evaluated on as few as 3 instances (~9–45 episodes) with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, and evaluation-time skills are prepared via 5 trials on the very instances being scored, an adaptation the Codex/DeepSeek baselines do not appear to receive. - Read it or not: Researchers working on agent Harness RSI, automated environment design, or agent routing should read it for the capability-tree formulation and unusually careful anti-leakage protocol design; readers needing statistically defensible empirical claims should treat the headline numbers as directional.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) is the strongest dimension — the capability-tree formulation with trajectory-induced Trie organization and the Real2Sim2Real training loop are a real conceptual contribution, and the anti-leakage protocol discipline is above average. But Rigor (45) and Resilience (48) pull the composite down sharply: most benchmark cells rest on ~3 instances (9–45 episodes) with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, 9 of 28 training benchmarks are the authors' own re-implementations, the skill-preparation asymmetry (5 evaluation-instance trials the Codex/DeepSeek baselines do not receive) plausibly inflates the headline 17-point unseen gap, and the fixed capability ordering that determines the entire tree has no sensitivity analysis. Completeness (56) is reduced because the authors do not confront the small-instance issue or the baseline asymmetry. Problem & Motivation: Teams building multimodal agents face two scaling bottlenecks: constructing large-scale, heterogeneous, verifiable training environments is expensive, and manually iterating on the agent "Harness" (the scaffolding coordinating a frozen model) cannot keep up with task diversity. Existing Harness RSI methods (Darwin Gödel Machine, JIT-Agent, HSI, ModularRSI) evolve task-specific or single-global Harnesses on text-only tasks; the former overfits across heterogeneous tasks, the latter cannot accommodate conflicting demands (e.g., performance–efficiency trade-offs in embodied tasks). The paper targets practitioners who need one agent stack to generalize across games, GUI control, embodied interaction, video understanding, and multi-agent strategy without per-task manual engineering. Key Idea: Tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements (e.g., ARC-AGI-3 and Micromouse both need perception and state tracking), so grouping tasks by these shared requirements — rather than by task domain — yields a common learning objective per capability node, enabling transfer. Concretely: sort each task's capability set under a fixed order, build a Trie (the capability tree, 11 non-root nodes), train each node's modules in a Creator-built simplified simulated world that preserves the decision process but excludes target-task layouts and solutions, and let nodes selectively inherit parent modules only when strictly improving verified performance. Methodology: A frozen backbone (Claude Opus 5) is coordinated by a Harness of six control-flow protocols (Perception, Memory, Inference, Planning, Orchestration, Loop), where modules are pure functions behind typed interfaces, validated by a host for evidence, ownership, interface, and version lineage. The pipeline has three stages: (1) Task Tree — Evolver normalizes 28 public benchmarks (9 of them agent-rebuilt from published rules via web search) into goal/observation/action/feedback specifications with a common interface; Explorer collects verified trajectories with the Base Harness; (2) Capability Tree — independent LLM agents propose capability categories, a judge consolidates, reviewers verify; the result is 6 capabilities and 30 defect types; the fixed order (c, d, a, b, e, f) defines Trie paths (Eq. 3); Creator implements Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real, building simplified worlds per node screened into a predefined intermediate-performance band by a frozen Harness, with host-executed verifier pools checking binding, execution, state transitions, and completion; (3) Harness Tree — Explorer evolves node-local modules from success/failure trajectory contrasts (Eq. 5) with right-biased-union selective inheritance (Eq. 4), retained only under strictly higher verified task completions; Creator evolves only on verifier-detected world failures and consolidates validated proposals into a deduplicated Base Harness per iteration (Eq. 7). At deployment, a Capability-Aware Router selects one Harness branch from public task information, retrieved execution experience (cosine similarity ≥ 0.5, ≤10 records, 20k-record FIFO memory), and performance–cost summaries (Eq. 8–9). Critical design decisions: (a) fixing the capability order before construction — justified as preventing causal claims, but no sensitivity analysis over alternative orderings; (b) training in simulation rather than on real tasks — justified by the Real-vs-Sim ablation (56.95/47.26 vs 53.44/42.31); (c) strict-improvement admission for inheritance — a conservative, well-specified guard against regression. Key Results: Across 4 RSI iterations on a fixed tree: Train mean (28 benchmarks) 39.06→63.80→67.75→70.85→73.16; Unseen mean (18 benchmarks) 37.45→53.53→55.17→59.56→63.61; iterations 2–4 add 9.4 Train and 6.4 Unseen points beyond iteration 1. On the 16 unseen non-robot benchmarks, the system scores 64.06 versus 47.49 (Codex Harness) and 46.18 (DeepSeek Harness) with the same backbone, though Crafter (60 vs 82.7) and DiG-bench (36.8 vs 54.4) remain below both. Organization ablation (module-only, iteration 1): Global 53.04/42.92, Task-Domain (15 Harnesses) 51.17/40.82, flat Capability-Domain 49.25/39.43, Capability Tree Real 53.44/42.31, Capability Tree Sim 56.95/47.26 with the lowest inference cost (514.42M/549.07M tokens). Routing: full self-routing 71.27 Train / 60.96 Unseen vs Oracle 73.16/63.61; random 52.74/46.23. Module interventions: adding one relevant module to H0 gains +19.39 vs +1.02 for an irrelevant module; removing one relevant module from H(4) costs −2.74 and ~20M tokens. Embodied transfer (Unitree G1 on SOON; AlohaMini2 on CaP-X): SOON 0→80% sim / 0→60% real; CaP-X 10→60% sim / 0→60% real across iterations, with only 1 route (SOON) and 10 layouts (CaP-X). Benchmark counts per cell are tiny — e.g., AdaPlanBench: 3 queries/27 episodes; Memory Maze: 3 mazes/9 episodes — so per-benchmark swings carry high variance. Baselines are current (Codex, DeepSeek Harnesses, 2026) but only run on unseen splits. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD, with components of NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel element is the capability tree — inducing a Trie over shared capability requirements from verified trajectories as the organizing principle for Harness RSI, replacing both task-specific and global Harness evolution — plus the coupling of per-node Real2Sim2Real world generation to node-level module evolution. Selective inheritance, trajectory-contrast module evolution, world-generation-from-failures, and agentic routing are each competent assemblies of existing ideas (Darwin Gödel Machine, SPADE, Voyager-style curricula, Agent-as-a-Router); the closest prior work the authors cite (Harness Continual Learning's flat capability map, Adaptive Auto-Harness's regime-branched tree) lacks trajectory-induced hierarchical capability induction and simulated-world training. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: organization comparison (5 variants), skills-vs-modules factorial (Table 2), routing ablation (4 self-routing configurations vs random and oracle), module add/remove interventions, and per-iteration cost breakdowns. Protocol hygiene is above average: train/unseen split fixed before capability induction, instance selectors and initial-state hashes pre-fixed, hash-chain verification of execution records, unseen capability assignments locked until after prediction-ledger hash-locking, invalid router selections scored zero with no fallback. However: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; many benchmark cells rest on 3 instances, making the benchmark-equal means statistically fragile; 9 of 28 training environments were built by the authors' own agents from web-searched rules (self-constructed evaluation substrate); the Codex/DeepSeek baselines receive no evaluation-time skill preparation, while the proposed system does (5 preparation trials per benchmark–Harness pair on the evaluated instances) — an asymmetry that inflates the headline gap; and the capability taxonomy is proposed by LLM agents from the same model family that later benefits from it. A project page and GitHub are referenced in the header but no URL, repository, or release statement appears in the provided text; reproducibility therefore cannot be confirmed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a framework run at scale with ablations; the deliverable is evolved Harness configurations plus a set of generated worlds, not infrastructure others install). - Practical: Yes — everything runs through a commercially available frozen backbone API plus host-side verifier code; no training hardware required. - Efficient: Competitive — evolved Harnesses cut inference tokens (497.89M vs 582.54M for Base on Train routing; H(4) at 496.70M), but first-iteration Sim training costs 405.70M evolution tokens plus Creator's world-construction overhead, amortized only via world reuse in later iterations. - Effective: The evidence supports improvement on the tested splits, but the effect sizes rest on 3-instance benchmark cells for many Train benchmarks, and the skill-preparation mechanism partially conflates Harness evolution gains with per-benchmark adaptation. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 44 benchmarks, 11 capability nodes, and 29+25 modules; the fixed tree topology and per-node iteration loops are claimed to extend (dynamic tree expansion is future work), but behavior at 10× the node count or on continuously arriving tasks is unverified. Deliverable form: a paper with evolved Harness trees, module libraries, and generated worlds; no confirmed public code or model artifact. Strengths: - The capability-tree formulation is a real conceptual contribution: the ablation showing flat capability grouping (49.25/39.43) underperforming hierarchical capability organization with simulation (56.95/47.26) directly tests the paper's central claim rather than assuming it. - The Real2Sim2Real loop is a substantive mechanism, not just synthetic-data generation: worlds exclude target-task layouts and solution traces, are adversarially verifier-checked, and are screened into an intermediate difficulty band — and Sim beats Real-task training at both accuracy and inference cost. - Anti-leakage protocol discipline (pre-fixed splits and hashes, hash-locked prediction ledgers, oracle-vs-router gap of only ~2 points) is unusually careful for an RSI paper, where self-evaluation circularity is the dominant failure mode. - Evidence breadth across the modality spectrum — from ARC-AGI-3 and Hanabi to video benchmarks and two physical robots — is far beyond typical Harness-RSI evaluations, which are mostly text-only. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two: web-search-based benchmark discovery has variable retrieval coverage and result quality, and the study addresses only Harness-level self-improvement (not parameter training). They also candidly flag, in the embodied section, that recorded deployments differ in interfaces and acceptance rules, so those comparisons evaluate complete Harness–skill configurations and do not isolate module evolution from skill preparation — a credibility-positive admission. They do not, however, confront the small-instance-count issue or the skill-preparation asymmetry with baselines. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: with 3 instances and 9–45 episodes for most Train benchmarks and single-run evaluations (e.g., SOON: 1 route, 10 episodes), several headline movements (±5 points on a benchmark mean) are within plausible noise; benchmark-equal means aggregate this noise without any uncertainty quantification. - Evaluation-time skill preparation runs 5 trials per benchmark–Harness pair on the evaluated instances themselves — effectively task-specific adaptation at test time — while the Codex/DeepSeek comparison baselines apparently receive no equivalent budget; part of the 17-point unseen gap may come from this asymmetry, not from capability evolution. - The capability order (c, d, a, b, e, f) that determines the entire Trie topology is fixed by "breadth of domains spanned" with no sensitivity analysis; a different order yields a different tree, different inheritance paths, and plausibly different results. - The capability taxonomy is induced by LLM agents from the same backbone family that consumes it, and six capabilities/30 defect types are derived from 26 training benchmarks — a small base for a taxonomy claimed to generalize. - The Train curve includes the 9 author-rebuilt environments scored on the authors' own re-implementations, mixing self-built evaluation into the headline 34-point gain; the native-benchmark-only Train mean (64.4→68.8) shows much smaller gains on third-party evaluations. - No empirical head-to-head with the closest prior systems (ModularRSI, HSI, SPADE, Adaptive Auto-Harness); the only external baselines are Codex and DeepSeek Harnesses, run only on unseen splits. Bottom Line: For researchers building self-improving agent systems, this is worth reading for the capability-tree formulation and the Real2Sim2Real training loop — the clearest current articulation of capability-driven (as opposed to task-driven) Harness evolution — but the headline numbers should be discounted substantially for tiny evaluation cells and a skill-preparation asymmetry, so it complements rather than replaces careful per-domain evaluation of any specific claim.

MedACE: A Time-Aware Asynchronous Clinical Environment for Long - Horizon Medical Treatment Decision-Making

Z Fan, R Chen, H Wang, R Peng, Z Meng, W Ma, J Wu… · aclanthology.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MedACE, a time-aware asynchronous clinical simulation environment built on MedWorld-JEPA, a JEPA-style latent world model trained on timestamped MIMIC-IV trajectories that predicts future patient states conditioned on elapsed time, treatment history, clinical context, and disease knowledge. - Why it's important: Existing medical agent environments are turn-based—patient states change only after physician actions—so agents cannot learn intervention timing, delayed treatment effects, or when not to act, which are core skills in real clinical care. - How it does it: The core move is formulating patient evolution as an elapsed-time-conditioned latent dynamics process (s_{t+Δt} = f_θ(s≤t, a≤t, Δt, c, d)) and training a dual-branch JEPA predictor in latent space rather than generating noisy observations directly, wrapped in an environment with a global clinical clock and sparse, outcome-grounded rewards tied to real clinical endpoints. - The good: The simulator achieves the best ICU performance of all tested models (RMSE 16.87 vs. 30.50 for the best LLM baseline; 98.51% Range Agree; 94.16% outcome accuracy), and ablations cleanly show that removing timestamp modeling degrades Hosp RMSE from 55.41 to 593.20. - The missing: No evidence that simulated patient rollouts match real disease progression over long multi-step horizons (evaluation is single-window forecasting), no code or environment release is mentioned, and no variance/significance reporting for any numbers. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building medical agent environments or RL-based treatment policies—it defines a genuinely different interaction paradigm—but practitioners seeking a ready-to-use benchmark should note no artifact release is stated.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is pulled down by Rigor (55) — no error bars, no code release, single-dataset (MIMIC-IV) training and evaluation with Goodhart risk, and closed-loop rollout fidelity (the property the environment depends on) never quantitatively measured — and by Impact (40), since the paper ships no artifact. Novelty (72) is the strength: the elapsed-time-conditioned asynchronous environment is a genuine new formulation with clean supporting ablations, but Completeness (58) and Resilience (55) suffer because the central architectural claim (latent vs. observation-space prediction) is asserted rather than ablated.
