empirical Novelty 72 Rigor 55 Non-Obv 65 Completeness 58 Resilience 55 Impact 40
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Medical LLMs are evaluated mostly on static QA, while real treatment decision-making is a long-horizon interactive process. Existing clinical agent environments (AgentClinic, Agent Hospital, virtual EHR platforms) are turn-based: patient state transitions are triggered by discrete physician actions, ignoring natural disease progression and delayed drug effects. This makes it impossible to train or evaluate an agent's sense of timing—when to wait, when a treatment's effect will materialize, when to discharge. The gap is acute because clinical interaction data is costly, patient safety forbids naive experimentation, and repeated large-scale trials in real settings are infeasible, motivating a simulator that evolves asynchronously like a real patient. Key Idea: Reformulate the clinical environment as a continuous-time dynamical system: the patient state advances on a global clock by an action-dependent Δt even without interventions, and the transition function is conditioned on elapsed time, full treatment history, textual context, and disease-level knowledge. Predicting in latent space (JEPA) rather than token/observation space sidesteps the noise and irregularity of raw clinical measurements. This is a clear, identifiable key idea that drives both the simulator and the environment design. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Data construction: timestamped trajectories from MIMIC-IV in two scenarios—Hospital (223,452 patients, 546,028 stays, H=48h history, Δ=4h horizon) and ICU (65,366 patients, 94,458 stays, H=4h, Δ=0.5h)—with irregular observations stored as (value, timestamp, mask) triples and patient-level splits to prevent leakage. (2) Simulator training (MedWorld-JEPA): a frozen MIRA time-series encoder and a frozen LLM text encoder feed a trainable cross-modal fusion module; a predictor outputs the future latent state conditioned on the fused context, an elapsed-time embedding, and action-history embeddings; a target branch (EMA-updated) encodes the real future window, and training minimizes a symmetric contrastive loss plus a uniformity regularizer to avoid collapse; only fusion, predictor, projections, adapters, and decoder are trained (parameter-efficient). A lightweight decoder maps latent states back to labs, vitals, and event text for environment feedback. (3) Environment (MedACE): closed loop of observe → reason → act → simulate → observe with a global clock advanced by action-dependent Δt; the action space spans diagnostic, monitoring, therapeutic, waiting, and terminal actions; rewards are sparse and grounded in real endpoints (correct terminal action within temporal tolerance ε of the true terminal time), explicitly to prevent reward hacking on simulated intermediate states. Critical design decisions: latent-space prediction (justified by arguing direct observation generation amplifies noise over rollouts, though not directly ablated against an observation-generating variant), elapsed-time conditioning (well justified by ablation—removing timestamps is catastrophic in Hosp), and sparse outcome-grounded rewards (well motivated, but the authors themselves show it causes RL instability). Key Results: Physiological forecasting on patient-level-split MIMIC-IV test sets: in ICU, MedWorld-JEPA reaches RMSE 16.87, MAE 9.52, Range Agree 98.51%, outcome accuracy 94.16%, versus the best LLM baseline (GPT-5.2: RMSE 30.50, MAE 9.53, 94.82%, 83.62%) and time-series baselines (MIRA: RMSE 90.51; Time-MoE-200M: RMSE 57.63). In Hosp, it achieves RMSE 55.41 and outcome accuracy 91.72%, but Gemini-3.1-Pro (RMSE 29.96, Range Agree 81.01%) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (RMSE 30.22, 80.17%) beat it on raw forecasting accuracy—so the simulator wins decisively in ICU but is competitive, not dominant, in Hosp. Baselines are current frontier models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Kimi-K2.6, Qwen3-235B) plus medical time-series models (MIRA, Time-MoE-200M)—a strong, current baseline set. Ablations on environment modeling strategies (action-based, time-based, no-timestamp, full) confirm all three components matter: dropping timestamps inflates Hosp RMSE from 55.41 to 593.20. Doctor-agent evaluation shows frontier LLMs overwhelmingly discharge prematurely (Claude Sonnet 4.5: 26.00% Hosp success, 64.67% early discharge; DeepSeek-V4-Pro: 90.00% early discharge in Hosp, 98.68% in ICU); GRPO-based RL on Qwen3-8B raises success to 35.68% (Hosp) and 15.79% (ICU) but increases Failure/Dead rate from 18.54%→23.65% (Hosp) and 19.74%→36.18% (ICU). Scale is a standard large EHR corpus, not a stress test. The counter-intuitive finding is that more interaction steps under RL can hurt (longer, riskier interventions raise mortality), which the authors report candidly. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel element is the elapsed-time-conditioned asynchronous environment formulation with natural progression decoupled from actions—prior treatment-oriented simulators are turn-based—and the application of a JEPA latent world model to clinical state dynamics. The components themselves (contrastive JEPA training, EMA targets, frozen encoders with adapters, MIMIC-IV processing, GRPO) are standard; the novelty lies in their composition for asynchronous treatment simulation, not in any single technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: modality ablations (Qwen3-0.6B base, +SFT, MIRA-only, full model) and environment-modeling ablations (time-aware / natural progression / action-conditioned flags) both isolate the claimed components. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; no code, data pipeline, or environment release URL is mentioned, so reproducibility depends on appendix descriptions alone; the simulator is developed and evaluated on MIMIC-IV only (single-dataset evaluation, no external cohort such as eICU or HiRID); and evaluation of the simulator is largely single-window forecasting—multi-step closed-loop rollout fidelity (the property the environment actually depends on) is shown only qualitatively in Figure 4. The outcome-prediction metric mixes calibration-sensitive binary definitions (death/hospice-within-6-months = failure) that are stated but not validated against clinical plausibility. Range Agree in ICU relies on prompting generative models for binary warnings, a loosely specified protocol. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component—the environment is built and used for agent training).\n- Practical: Yes—training is parameter-efficient (frozen MIRA + frozen LLM encoder, trainable adapters/fusion/predictor), and RL uses Qwen3-8B, all feasible on commodity GPU hardware.\n- Efficient: Latent-space prediction avoids autoregressive generation of observations per step, so environment stepping should be cheap relative to LLM-simulated patients; exact inference cost/throughput is not reported.\n- Effective: Evidence supports the forecasting proxy (ICU results are convincing), but effectiveness of the environment as a faithful treatment simulator is only partially shown—RL agents exploit it in ways (rising mortality) that suggest reward/simulator mismatch.\n- Scalable: Not tested beyond single MIMIC-IV admissions; behavior at 10× horizon length or multi-window rollouts is claimed implicitly but not measured.\nThe paper stops at paper form: no released library, CLI, dataset, or trained weights are stated. Strengths: - The asynchronous, time-conditioned environment formulation is a real conceptual contribution: it converts intervention timing from an unmodeled confound into a first-class element of the action space and reward, which no prior turn-based medical environment does. - The component ablations are unusually clean for this genre—showing that removing timestamps inflates Hosp RMSE by ~10× (55.41 → 593.20) directly substantiates the central thesis rather than merely the architecture. - Honest negative results: the paper reports that RL-trained agents achieve higher success but higher Failure/Dead rates, and that frontier LLMs (GPT-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) early-discharge 88–98% of the time—findings that meaningfully characterize the environment's difficulty. - Strong and current baseline selection: six frontier LLMs plus two specialized time-series foundation models, evaluated under identical metrics. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that RL training uses only GRPO with sparse outcome-based rewards, which cannot capture fine-grained requirements like intervention timing and risk control; that RL induces instability and increased Failure/Dead rates; and that future work needs safety-aware reward modeling, denser clinical feedback, and more stable optimization. They also confine the work's scope to research simulation, explicitly disclaiming clinical use. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of the training-side limitations—a credibility positive—though they do not acknowledge evaluation-side limitations (single dataset, no rollout-fidelity metrics, no release). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Closed-loop fidelity is unmeasured: the environment's entire value rests on multi-step simulated rollouts resembling real progression, but evaluation is per-window forecasting plus one qualitative trajectory figure; there is no quantitative rollout-drift metric over episodes of 20–30 steps. - No ablation of JEPA latent prediction against a direct observation-generation baseline (e.g., the same architecture trained with regression/token loss), so the central architectural claim is asserted, not tested. - Hosp results show the simulator is not the best forecaster in that scenario (Gemini-3.1-Pro beats it on RMSE and Range Agree), which the narrative of "competitive forecasting" softens. - The outcome-prediction metric and the terminal reward are defined from real endpoints, but the reward's temporal tolerance ε and its sensitivity are never specified or swept in the main text. - No public artifact: without released code/environment, the community cannot verify the headline difficulty results (e.g., 98.68% early-discharge for DeepSeek-V4-Pro) or build on the benchmark. - Possible Goodhart risk: the simulator is trained and evaluated on the same MIMIC-IV distribution, and agent rewards derive from real endpoints of the same cohort—generalization to other hospitals or care settings is untested. Bottom Line: A practitioner building medical treatment agents should read this for its genuinely new asynchronous-environment formulation and its candid evidence that frontier LLMs fail at long-horizon treatment timing, but the lack of a released artifact and of closed-loop fidelity evaluation means it is a promising research direction rather than yet a usable community benchmark.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TGR-EvoDAG, a multi-agent LLM framework that autonomously evolves the complete three-stage training pipeline (tokenizer, pre-training, alignment) of a generative recommender as a Code DAG with stage-aware GPU-hour budgeting and downstream co-adaptation. - Why it's important: Generative recommendation (GR) pipelines have asymmetric retraining costs across stages and tightly coupled stages where upstream edits temporarily regress metrics, so existing greedy or linear code-evolution frameworks waste compute budgets and discard promising innovations that only pay off after downstream re-adaptation. - How it does it: It represents evolution history as a DAG of self-contained experimental nodes expanded by EXPLORE/MUTATE/MERGE operators through a five-stage agent pipeline (Operator Selector, Architect-Critic, Coder-Reviewer, Distiller, Pruner), where a stage-aware cost plan weighs expected gain against measured GPU-hours and a Pruner tags regressed upstream edits as [Needs-Downstream-Adaptation] instead of pruning them. - The good: The evaluation is unusually well-controlled for an industrial paper: all baselines run on an identical seed codebase and budget, two naive-integration baselines (CORAL+Diag., Arbor+Diag.) cleanly disentangle diagnostic feedback from search topology, and results include a statistically rigorous 14-day online A/B test (+0.40% CTR, p=0.019, CUPED + Benjamini-Hochberg correction). - The missing: All evolution and offline evaluation happens on a single tiny dataset (Amazon Office: 4,905 users, 53,258 interactions) with what appears to be a single evolution run per framework — no seeds, error bars, or second public dataset — so run-to-run variance of LLM-driven search and dataset generalization are unquantified. - Read it or not: Read it if you build LLM-driven algorithm-discovery or auto-ML systems for multi-stage training pipelines (the cost-planning and co-adaptation mechanisms generalize beyond recommendation); skip it if you want a new recommendation model itself, since the discovered architecture is dataset- and baseline-specific.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building generative recommenders face a two-sided gap. General-purpose LLM code-evolution frameworks (AlphaEvolve, CORAL, Arbor) have multi-branch search and merging but only consume scalar offline metrics, while recommender-specific evolution frameworks (SERS, EvoRec, Self-EvolveRec) have rich feedback (user simulators, diagnostic probes) but use greedy or linear search. Neither works on GR's cascaded pipeline (RQ-VAE-style tokenization → autoregressive pre-training → preference alignment) because of two structural mismatches the paper formalizes: (1) cost blindness — search policies evaluate all edits uniformly, but a tokenizer edit forces full-pipeline retraining while an alignment edit re-runs only the last stage; (2) short-sighted evaluation — greedy frameworks prune candidates that regress metrics, yet upstream edits almost always regress before downstream adaptation recovers the gain. The beneficiaries are recommendation engineers spending GPU budgets on manual architecture iteration, and, by the authors' extension, anyone training multi-stage LLM pipelines. Key Idea: Treat the evolution search space as a Code DAG whose nodes record which pipeline stages an edit touches and its measured per-stage GPU cost, and add two mechanisms exploiting this structure: stage-aware cost planning (the Operator Selector weighs expected gain against estimated GPU-hours, deferring expensive upstream edits until downstream architectures mature) and active downstream co-adaptation (the Pruner tags regressed upstream edits and forces child nodes to adapt the downstream stage rather than discarding them). This is the single insight a reader needs: make the cascade's cost asymmetry and stage coupling explicit in the search state. Methodology: Each DAG node stores provenance (parents, operator, hypothesis, branch status), artifacts (code delta, snapshot, checkpoints), and empirical records (feedback, distilled lessons, measured cost). Node expansion runs a five-stage pipeline of seven LLM agents communicating via strict JSON schemas: (1) the Operator Selector picks an operator (EXPLORE, MUTATE, MERGE with r≥2 parents) and parents conditioned on the serialized graph and remaining GPU-hour budget, using recorded stage-wise costs to estimate expected cost; (2) an Architect-Critic pair iterates on a structured hypothesis blueprint until it passes consistency/measurability checks; (3) a Coder-Reviewer pair implements in an isolated workspace with a repair loop checking for data leakage and cross-stage compatibility (MERGE nodes serialize parents as unified diffs against the lowest common ancestor to fit context windows); (4) a standardized environment evaluates the candidate and a Distiller writes mechanism-level lessons; (5) the Pruner assigns [Pruned] or [Needs-Downstream-Adaptation] states. Budget accounting charges measured GPU-hours (with a τ_fail penalty for failed rounds), not estimates. The framework is a competent composition of known ideas — FunSearch/AlphaEvolve-style LLM code evolution, FunMap/tree-search DAG topologies, Self-EvolveRec-style diagnostic feedback — with the cost-planning and co-adaptation mechanisms as the genuinely new algorithmic pieces. The Agent workflow is specified precisely enough in Algorithm 1 to reconstruct. Key Results: On Amazon Office with a 24 GPU-hour budget evolving from an identical TIGER/APAO seed, TGR-EvoDAG reaches Hit@10 0.0869 / NDCG@10 0.0478 versus 0.0697/0.0348 for the strongest non-evolutionary baseline (APAO) — +24.7% Hit@10 and +37.4% NDCG@10 — and beats the best naive integration (Arbor+Diag., 0.0814 Hit@10) by +6.8% and the strongest recommender-specific baseline (Self-EvolveRec, 0.0718) by +21.0%. Agent4Rec simulated-user metrics move in the same direction (satisfaction 7.72 vs 6.45 for APAO, +19.7%). Ablations with restricted variants (A: greedy; B: multi-elite no merge; C: full search without cost planning) show monotonically increasing performance from A to full, with C failing to afford the upstream tokenizer retrain. The trajectory analysis is a highlight: a PSRQ tokenizer edit collapsed Hit@10 to 0.0599, distribution probes localized a 65.7% semantic-ID collision from k-means scale imbalance, an RMS-normalization repair dropped collisions to 1.0%, and post-merge co-adaptation of the fine-margin loss recovered the trunk to the final 0.0869. Industrial transfer on Tencent's platform (>10M DAU): trained from scratch on 10 days of logs, the evolved model beats APAO by +12.16% offline Hit@1, and as an additional retrieval channel in a 14-day A/B test on 5% of traffic (>1M users) delivers +0.40% system CTR (p=0.019) with >10% unique exposures and ~13% higher channel CTR than system average. Baselines are current (2025–2026) and reasonably strong; scale is standard for public benchmarks (deliberately tiny) and stress-scale for deployment. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The formulation — casting cascaded-pipeline code evolution as stage-cost-aware, co-adaptation-aware DAG search — is genuinely new, and the two mechanisms (stage-aware cost planning, active downstream co-adaptation) are novel. The rest is a competent combination of existing components: DAG/tree search topologies existed (Arbor, CORAL), diagnostic feedback existed (Self-EvolveRec), and the agent pipeline pattern is standard; the paper's own naive-integration baselines honestly demonstrate that the value lies in the integration, not the parts. Rigor & Reproducibility: The experimental design is above average for this genre: identical seed codebase, agent (Claude CLI with GLM-5.2), budget, and platform for all frameworks; a held-out Agent4Rec evaluation on a disjoint 100-user population (temperature 0, never exposed during evolution, used only post hoc); model selection on validation only with a single post-hoc test-set touch; and a proper online experiment with CUPED and tiered Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q≤0.05). Weaknesses: no multiple seeds or error bars for the offline evolution experiments — LLM-driven search is highly stochastic, so single-run gaps like +6.8% over Arbor+Diag. carry unquantified uncertainty; ablations are also single runs; no significance testing on offline metrics; code, platform, or evolved weights are not released (Uppimo is "future"); and the diagnostic-feedback channels are given to TGR-EvoDAG and recommender baselines but not general baselines — partially mitigated by the CORAL+Diag./Arbor+Diag. controls. The chosen Office dataset is extremely small (53K interactions), acknowledged by the authors as a deliberate compute-budget choice, but it raises external-validity questions for the offline claims; the industrial transfer partially answers this. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built evolution framework evaluated by deployment, with an embedded empirical study). Practical: The offline evolution loop needs modest hardware by design (sub-1-GPU-hour cycles, 24 GPU-hour budget), but depends on proprietary LLMs (GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-v4-flash) with unreported token costs. Efficient: Cost-awareness is the point — the framework demonstrably allocates its 24 GPU-hours better than cost-blind variants, though total cost including LLM inference across 39 rounds is not reported. Effective: Evidence spans offline metrics, held-out simulation, and a statistically significant online CTR lift, which is as close to solving the stated problem as this field gets; the offline gains remain confined to one small dataset. Scalable: Not tested for the search itself — a 10× budget or a larger catalog could change operator-selection dynamics and context-window pressure on MERGE diffing; the authors claim extension to LLM training pipelines without experiments. Deliverable: an internal platform (Tencent Uppimo) with promised future public trial; no public artifact at publication time. Strengths: - The problem formulation is the real contribution: identifying why naive integration of good search + good feedback fails on cascaded pipelines (cost asymmetry, deferred gains) is an insight the field has not articulated, and it is plausibly transferable to any multi-stage ML pipeline. - The CORAL+Diag. and Arbor+Diag. controls are exactly the right experiment — they isolate search topology from feedback richness and show feedback alone recovers only part of the gain (+6.8–8.1% Hit@10 gap remaining). - The trajectory analysis (Figure 3, five phases with per-round operator counts and probe-driven repairs, e.g., the 65.7%→1.0% SID collision fix) gives mechanistic evidence for how each mechanism contributed, not just that the final number is higher. - Full industrial validation path — scratch retraining on 10M+ interactions and a rigorously corrected A/B test — is rare in agentic-search papers and substantially de-risks the offline claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly justify choosing the small Office dataset (keeping one train/validate cycle under one GPU-hour so the fixed budget admits many evolution rounds) and note that absolute user/item counts and CTR values are withheld for confidentiality. They state the platform will open for public trial in the future (i.e., not currently available). There is no dedicated limitations section; the framing is confident, and issues like single-run variance or dependence on specific frontier LLMs are not confronted directly — a moderate credibility deduction. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run, single-dataset offline evaluation: LLM agent search variance across seeds/runs is never measured; the +6.8% margin over Arbor+Diag. could be within run-to-run noise. - The evolved champion's specific components (recency bias γ=0.5, within-coarse hard negatives, PSRQ+RMS tokenizer, margin 0.7) are conflated with the framework's value; a human-expert baseline or a simple hyperparameter sweep on the same budget would calibrate how much autonomy actually bought. - The Agent4Rec "user satisfaction" gains are LLM-simulator self-consistency, not human evidence — the simulator's own biases (persona construction, DeepSeek-v4-flash judgment) are unvalidated against real user data. - Token/inference cost of ~39 rounds × 7 agents per node is logged but never reported, so end-to-end cost-effectiveness versus a human engineer or a cheaper search cannot be assessed. - The Pruner's [Needs-Downstream-Adaptation] routing depends on correctly attributing a regression to an upstream cause — the paper shows one success case but no measurement of the tag's precision/recall; systematic misrouting could silently waste budget. - No public artifact exists, so none of the central claims are independently reproducible today. Bottom Line: Practitioners building automated ML-discovery or RSI systems — especially over multi-stage training pipelines — should read this for the cost-planning and co-adaptation formulation, which no prior framework offers, while treating the headline percentages as single-run results on a tiny benchmark that happen to be corroborated by an unusually credible industrial deployment.

Work Agents : Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization

Z Xu, E Du, M Gao, C Yang, J Shen, Z Chen, Z Yao… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a unified, work-centric survey framework for "work agents" — systems combining a foundation model and a runtime harness that execute delegated digital tasks in stateful workspaces — organized around six system elements, two working-condition dimensions (work persistence and work openness), five work forms, five capability families, and a taxonomy of optimization and evaluation methods. - Why it's important: Agents are being delegated real productivity work (software engineering, office operations, enterprise services), but the research landscape is fragmented across long-horizon, computer-use, and office-agent paradigms with no shared vocabulary for why systems succeed or fail on delegated, verifiable work. - How it does it: The core move is re-focusing the unit of analysis from model outputs and tool calls to the complete delegated-work process — task, model, harness, workspace, outcome, and verification — and characterizing work by when responsibility may close (persistence) and how much the agent must discover during execution (openness). - The good: The persistence/openness distinction is genuinely clarifying — it separates when work may stop and how much must be found out, and the paper shows all four combinations exist in prior benchmarks (SQuAD, GAIA, τ-bench, OSWorld 2.0), demonstrating the axes are independent rather than one continuum. - The missing: As a survey, it runs no primary experiments; its taxonomy is validated only through example coverage and citation of other papers' numbers (e.g., Nemotron's SWE-bench Verified 60.7%→64.5% mid-training gain), with no quantitative meta-analysis or empirical test of whether the proposed capability families predict real system performance. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers and engineers building or evaluating agentic systems who need a structured map of 2023–2026 agent work, benchmarks, training-environment construction, and model/harness optimization — skippable for experts seeking new methods, since it proposes none.

Problem & Motivation: Foundation-model-based agents are increasingly handed complex digital work — software engineering (SWE-bench), office tasks (OfficeBench), enterprise operations (τ-bench, CRMArena-Pro), and research (PaperBench) — where success depends on evidence in related files, records, applications, and states established by earlier actions. Practitioners and researchers lack a unified account of how such systems reliably complete delegated work: existing research is siloed into long-horizon agents (execution length), computer-use agents (action interface), and office agents (artifact type), each tracking one facet of the same problem. The paper targets the gap that prior perspectives analyze isolated model outputs or tool calls rather than the full chain from task requirements through execution in a stateful workspace to verified outcomes. Key Idea: The central insight is that a work agent should be analyzed as a six-element system — task (T), model (M), harness (H), workspace (E), work outcome (O), and verification (V) — executing a closed loop formalized as (T, E0) →(M,H) (τ0:t, Et, Ot) with assessment St = V(T, E0, τ0:t, Et, Ot), and that working conditions decompose into two conceptually distinct dimensions: work persistence (whether responsibility closes at delivery or remains open across stages, confirmations, and later events) and work openness (whether the task world is predefined or must be discovered during execution). These two axes, combined with five work forms (Conversation, Atomic Action, Multi-step, Workflow, Workspace levels), determine the demands on five capability families (perception/understanding, reasoning/decision-making, planning/coordination, execution/state management, verification/recovery/replanning). Methodology: This is a survey/position paper; its "method" is taxonomy construction and literature synthesis rather than an algorithmic pipeline. The framework is built in layers: (1) a formal system definition with the execution/verification loop above; (2) the two working-condition dimensions, each traced through existing benchmarks; (3) a classification of ~90 representative works from 2023–2026 into five work forms by task scope and organization; (4) an optimization taxonomy covering training-environment construction, corpus/trajectory curation, and feedback design (Table 4), model optimization across pre-training, mid-training, and post-training with the standard NTP objective and RL/post-training signals (Table 5), harness optimization over interfaces, workflows, and memory/skills (Table 6), and joint model–harness adaptation including recursive self-improvement (Table 7); and (5) an outcome-oriented analysis of evaluation benchmarks, judging methods, and metrics. Critical design decisions include separating persistence from task difficulty and execution length (well-argued with concrete counterexamples), distinguishing delegated workflow stages from the agent system's own internal stages (a sharp and useful distinction, e.g., Anthropic's research/citation stages vs. requester-defined stages), and distinguishing attempted → accepted → committed → verified effect states in execution records (well-motivated for non-idempotent operations). The PDF text provided is truncated mid-Section 4.4.2, so later sections (evaluation detail, frontiers) are summarized from the table of contents and introduction only. Key Results: The paper reports no primary experimental results. It synthesizes quantitative findings from cited works: CompoWorld's composed multi-service environments raise AutomationBench success from 12.83% to 33.33% over single-service environments under matched 1K-trajectory SFT; WorkForge scaling training data from 1K to 16K trajectories improves ALE by 13.0 points and WildClaw by 8.4 points, and its combined programmatic+semantic task selection reaches ALE 22.11 vs. 15.62 (semantic-only) and 14.89 (programmatic-only); Nemotron's mid-training stage raises SWE-bench Verified Pass@1 from 60.7% to 64.5%, and masking tool responses during training raises it from 27.5% to 37.8% in a 100B-token ablation; Mercor/SkyRL's 397B model improves held-out APEX-Agents Pass@1 from 16.11% to 27.29%; Kimi K2's knowledge-rephrasing experiment yields 28.94% vs. 23.76% SimpleQA accuracy; CoworkEnv teacher SFT improves Claw-Eval from 46.6 to 64.1; VERSE reports controlled self-evolution gains (39.20% baseline → 41.05% with verification plus self-evolution, while self-evolution alone degrades to 31.79%). Baselines in these cited comparisons are the original papers' own contemporary controls, generally strong. The synthesis itself delivers qualitative findings, e.g., that broader artifact coverage beats deeper transitions at 1K–5K trajectory budgets but parity emerges at 8K, and that dataset-size reports across papers are incomparable without specifying generation-attempt vs. accepted-task vs. usable-trajectory counts. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and a survey synthesis; the genuinely novel elements are the persistence/openness working-condition dimensions, the six-element system formalization with the verification loop, and the delegated-workflow-vs-internal-stage distinction. Everything else — the capability families, the pre/mid/post-training and harness-optimization taxonomy, and the evaluation catalog — is a competent organization of existing ideas into a new frame; the paper proposes no new method, dataset, or empirical finding of its own. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a survey, there are no author-run ablations, seeds, or significance tests to assess; internal rigor rests on the consistency of the taxonomy, the independence argument for the two dimensions (backed by four real benchmark combinations), and disciplined use of cited ablations with matched budgets (e.g., WorkForge's 1K-trajectory ablation, TrajLong's fixed 40B-token budget). The paper references an "Awesome Work Agents" list and project homepage, but no concrete repository URL appears in the provided text. Concerns: the paper re-reports other works' numbers without independent verification; the 2023–2026 timeline figure classifies benchmark settings by author judgment without stated inter-rater reliability; the framework is validated by example coverage rather than by any predictive or falsifiable test; and the survey's own evaluation-analysis section (Section 5) is not covered in the provided text, limiting assessment of that contribution. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL (a survey/formulation paper with no primary experiments). Sound: The framework's assumptions are explicit (digital knowledge work scope; delegated, verifiable tasks) and the taxonomy is internally consistent, though the formal equations are definitional rather than derived results. General: The formulation applies broadly across office, software, enterprise, and research settings, with the deliberate exclusion of physical/embodied work stated upfront. Tight: Not applicable — there are no bounds; the closest analogue is whether the five capability families are jointly exhaustive, which is argued by example, not proven. Implementable: The framework suggests actionable engineering practices (e.g., reporting generation-attempt/accepted-task/trajectory counts; separating requirement specification from verifier roles; dependency-based re-verification), several of which are already operationalized in the cited systems. The work delivers a paper plus a curated resource collection (Awesome Work Agents list and project homepage); no software artifact, dataset, or trained model is produced. Strengths: - The persistence/openness decomposition is a real conceptual contribution: it cleanly separates "when may the agent stop" from "what must the agent discover," and the paper proves their independence by exhibiting real benchmarks in all four quadrants rather than asserting it. - The distinction between requester-delegated workflow stages and the agent system's internal orchestration stages (Section 3.4) resolves a genuine source of confusion in multi-agent literature with a crisp criterion (could an alternative arrangement complete the request equally well?). - The attempted/accepted/committed/verified effect-state hierarchy for execution records (Section 2.3.4) is practically valuable and directly addresses non-idempotency failures that plague real agent deployments. - The optimization sections synthesize ablation-backed findings from industrial training efforts (Nemotron, Kimi K2/K2.5, DeepSeek-V4, Step 3.5 Flash, Mercor/SkyRL) that are otherwise scattered across technical reports, with unusually honest methodological commentary (e.g., that dataset-size metrics are incomparable across papers, and that intermediate model metrics do not predict downstream agent performance). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper scopes itself explicitly to digital knowledge work (office productivity, professional services, enterprise operations, software engineering, scientific research), excluding other domains. It acknowledges that reported dataset sizes across environment-construction works are incomparable without standardized reporting, that verification can become a bottleneck as execution parallelizes, and (via the VERSE study it cites) that unconstrained self-evolution without verification degrades performance (31.79% vs. 39.20% baseline). The text provided is truncated, so any limitations discussion in Sections 5–7 (e.g., on evaluation unreliability or safety) cannot be assessed. Within the covered sections the authors confront measurement and validation problems directly, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The five capability families and five work forms are asserted and illustrated, but never tested: no analysis shows the taxonomy predicts system failure modes, transfer behavior, or benchmark performance better than alternatives (e.g., a simple task-length × interface-type grid). - The survey's quantitative evidence is drawn disproportionately from industrial technical reports (Nemotron, Kimi, DeepSeek, Step, Mercor/SkyRL) that are vendor self-reports without peer review, and the paper does not flag the resulting confidence asymmetry. - The "90 representative works" timeline (Figure 4) and benchmark catalog cover English-centric, commercially salient settings almost exclusively; the survey does not discuss multilingual, low-resource, or non-corporate work contexts. - Safety, security, and adversarial considerations for agents holding permissions over live workspaces (prompt injection, unauthorized state changes, audit) are absent from the covered sections despite the framework's emphasis on permissions and authority. - The formalization (Equations 1–2) is notation, not theory: no properties are proven about the loop (e.g., convergence, verification soundness under model-based judges), and the paper does not connect to the formal planning or POMDP literature that treats similar structures. - The provided text truncates mid-Section 4.4.2, so the treatment of joint optimization conclusions, evaluation (Section 5), and frontiers (Section 6) could not be fully verified against the summary above. Bottom Line: For researchers and engineers entering the agentic-systems space, this is currently one of the most useful maps of the work-agent landscape and worth reading for its persistence/openness formulation alone; specialists already immersed in the 2024–2026 agent literature will find the synthesis competent but unlikely to change how they build or evaluate systems.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ImageRSI, a verification-driven agentic framework that wraps a frozen text-to-image generator with five-dimensional verification, requirement-locked prompt repair, an A/B-validated cross-task experience library, and an offline SFT+GRPO-post-trained judge, plus a new 961-request benchmark (ImageReq-Bench) with per-request checklists. - Why it's important: Complex multi-constraint text-to-image requests (exact text, counts, spatial relations, world knowledge) fail reliably even in frontier generators, and prior agentic systems retain memory without validating when retained strategies are actually useful. - How it does it: The core trick is treating repair trajectories as evidence under an admission protocol: a repair strategy is promoted to the reusable library only after paired same-seed A/B generation with a blinded evaluator, and the verification judge itself is retrained offline on accumulated image-judgment records with a GRPO reward that places false accepts in an unforgivable low band. - The good: The matched-budget ablation is convincing: with the same first image and at most two images per request, localized repair with requirement locking reaches 65.7% CSA versus 55.0% for best-of-2 resampling and 57.8% without requirement locking, isolating that the gain comes from targeted repair, not extra sampling. - The missing: The full recursive loop is never closed — only one round of judge update is evaluated, the authors state that repeated collection–training cycles "remain a proposed extension," there are no error bars or multiple seeds, and training requests are constructed along the same category taxonomies as the evaluated benchmarks (MindBench, WISE), raising contamination concerns. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agentic image-generation or experience-reuse systems — the admission protocol and judge-reward design are directly reusable — but general readers can skip it, as it combines known agentic ingredients (ReAct-style repair, GRPO, memory libraries) in a new domain.

Problem & Motivation: Text-to-image models still fail on requests combining multiple interacting constraints: factual knowledge, exact text rendering, object counts, attribute binding, and spatial relations — and requests often leave constraints implicit (a solar-eclipse diagram implicitly requires the Moon between Sun and Earth with legible labels). Existing agentic systems either verify-and-repair a single request or reuse cross-task memory without a protocol for deciding when a stored strategy actually applies; meanwhile, fixed-prompt benchmarks measure final output quality but cannot show whether an agent improves as it accumulates experience. The paper targets practitioners building reliable image-generation pipelines who need repair strategies that provably transfer and a judge that improves with use. Key Idea: The key idea is verification-driven recursive self-improvement with three loops sharing one judge signal: (1) within-task, localized repair rewrites the prompt against defect-specific feedback while the parsed requirement set is locked, so satisfied requirements cannot be silently dropped; (2) across tasks, candidate repair strategies (with explicit Trigger, Negative Trigger, Action, Effect, Side Effects fields) are admitted to the experience library only after paired A/B validation — identical request, seed, and inputs, with and without the strategy's action, scored by a blinded evaluator — rather than trusting a single lucky repair; (3) the judge is updated offline via SFT then GRPO on versioned image–judgment records, with a reward band that penalizes false accepts and critical fabrications regardless of other dimensions. The generator stays frozen throughout. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Online generation and verification: a requirement parser extracts a fixed constraint set C_t; bounded ReAct-style retrieval assembles factual/visual evidence; experience retrieval (three most similar entries by character-bigram TF-IDF) injects procedural advice; the frozen generator produces one image per round (up to two repair rounds); the judge scores five dimensions (Alignment, Faithfulness, Quality, Aesthetic, Physics, base weights 0.40/0.20/0.25/0.20/0.15) with confidence-adjusted weighted aggregation, acceptance requires weighted score ≥ 4.5 and no hard veto (Quality ≤ 3 or Alignment ≤ 3 vetoes). (2) Cross-task experience: an extractor distills candidate strategies from trajectories; admission requires ≥2 source trajectories, a calibration phase (≥3 trials, ≥2 positive Δe(q), no negative, mean ≥0.05) and a holdout phase (≥2 trials, ≥1 positive, no negative), where Δe(q) = u(x_q+e, q) − u(x_q−e, q) from a blinded paired evaluator. (3) Judger self-evolution: ~2,000 requests (530 from the ImageReq-Bench experience split plus ~1,500 built along WISE and MindBench taxonomies) are paired with model-generated five-dimensional score-and-reason targets; Qwen3.8-27B is SFT'd (loss on response tokens only) then GRPO-trained on disjoint requests with a reward combining pointwise score/rationale accuracy and within-group ranking, plus a lower reward band for false accepts and critical omissions. Design decisions: requirement locking is well-justified by a 7.9 pp ablation gap; the A/B admission protocol is justified as guarding against stochastic luck, though its calibration thresholds appear hand-set without sensitivity analysis; constant-confidence adapters for trained judges are acknowledged as a simplification. Key Results: On MindBench (500 requests, 10 categories), ImageRSI reaches 48.2% CSA with Qwen-Image-2.0 and 52.6% with Nano Banana Pro (263/500), versus 42.4% for the strongest agent baseline GEMS and 42.0% for direct Nano Banana Pro generation; on Math it leads 80% vs 46% for Nano Banana Pro. On ImageReq-Bench (431-request held-out test set, 8,165 checklist items), ImageRSI achieves 65.66% CSA vs 56.38% for Nano Banana, 55.68% for GEMS, 47.56% for MemoGen R2, and 38.28% for direct Wan2.7-Image — leads of 9.28 pp over the best generative model and 9.98 pp over the best agent baseline. Matched-budget ablation (431 requests): first-round only 53.4%; best-of-2 resampling 55.0%; generic-feedback repair 56.6%; localized repair without locking 57.8%; full localized repair 65.7%. Experience library scaling is monotonic: 55.7%, 56.8%, 61.3%, 65.7% CSA at 0, 131, 266, 527 entries. Judge training: base Qwen3.8-27B judge yields 38.6% CSA, SFT100% 44.8%, GRPO100% 48.2% (MAE vs teacher scores falls 0.598 → 0.453 → 0.403); GRPO-trained 27B judge beats off-the-shelf GPT-6-Astra (44.2%) by 4.0 pp. Baselines span current frontier generators and recent agent systems; on MindBench the authors report the higher of their reproduction and the original paper's number, which is fair. Testing is at standard benchmark scale, not stress scale. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any headline comparison. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (ImageReq-Bench, 961 checklist-annotated requests) and, to a lesser degree, NEW FORMULATION (a validated admission protocol for agentic experience plus offline judge self-evolution applied to image generation). The components are individually standard: ReAct-style repair, requirement decomposition, memory libraries, SFT+GRPO judge training all exist in text/image agentic work (Qwen-Image-Agent, GEMS, T2I-Copilot). What is genuinely new is the discipline applied to experience: paired same-seed A/B admission with explicit trigger/negative-trigger conditions and revision/retirement, plus a judge-reward structure that makes false accepts unrecoverable. Calling the system "recursive self-improvement" overstates it, since only a single update round is evaluated. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: second-round strategy comparison (Table 5), requirement-locking removal, experience-library size sweep (Figure 3b), judge training stages (Table 3), and an offline score-aggregation ablation (Figure 5) showing removing Alignment raises false-accept rate from 24.8% to 37.1%. However, no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests appear anywhere, and with ~431 test requests a 9–10 pp margin is likely robust but unverified. Evaluation uses a single external judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro) with an all-items-must-pass CSA metric — strict, with failures counted in the denominator, but LLM-as-judge variance is unquantified. Methodological concerns: (a) the judge training pool is constructed "along MindBench's task categories" and WISE's taxonomy, i.e., the same distributions the system is evaluated on, a partial Goodhart risk despite the claim that no MindBench examples are reused; (b) ImageReq-Bench is the authors' own benchmark, and although experience is distilled only from the disjoint experience split, checklist authors and system designers are the same team; (c) some agent baselines are the authors' local reproductions (GEMS, GenSearcher-style, with image retrieval unavailable), and MemoGen R2's configuration is not described. No code, data, or model weights release is mentioned in the paper. The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.32120), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system run on public benchmarks, no formal claims). - Practical: Yes — the pipeline runs on commercially available generators (Qwen-Image-2.0, Wan2.7-Image, Nano Banana Pro) and API-accessible judges (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.8-27B); no exotic hardware beyond standard MLLM inference. - Efficient: Costs are 1–3 image generations plus judge calls per request (vs one for direct generation), plus an offline 27B SFT+GRPO stage; the paper never reports latency, dollar cost, or compute, so efficiency relative to baselines is unevaluated. - Effective: The evidence supports the claim on checklist-based joint-satisfaction metrics on two benchmarks, with the matched-budget ablation ruling out extra-sampling as the source of gains; but effectiveness is measured only through LLM-judge verdicts, a proxy for human satisfaction — no human evaluation is reported. - Scalable: Not tested — the library tops out at 527 entries with monotonic but unexamined growth (no saturation, no retrieval-quality degradation analysis), and only one judge-update cycle is run, so behavior of the claimed repeated self-improvement loop is unknown. Deliverable form: the paper alone; no library, CLI, dataset download, or model weights are mentioned. Strengths: - The paired A/B experience-admission protocol is the paper's most original element: requiring ≥2 source trajectories, calibration + holdout phases with no negative difference, and structured Trigger/Negative-Trigger fields directly addresses why naive agent-memory reuse fails (stochastic luck, non-transferable repairs), which prior image-agent memory work ignores. - The matched-budget repair ablation is a well-designed experiment that cleanly decomposes the gain into targeted repair (+12.3 pp), requirement locking (+7.9 pp of that), and defect localization, rather than the +1.6 pp from resampling. - The judge-training result is substantive: a 27B open judge post-trained on system-accumulated records (48.2% CSA) beats all evaluated off-the-shelf closed judges including GPT-6-Astra (44.2%), and the GRPO reward band for false accepts is a sensible design for a verification model where false acceptance is the costly error. - The CSA metric counts missing images, evaluator errors, and malformed verdicts as failures in the denominator, a conservative choice many benchmark papers skip. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section is thin: it notes only that cross-generator experience transfer (reusing library entries when the base generator is swapped) is unexplored and left as an optional extension. In the conclusion and Section 3.4 the authors more candidly concede that repeated collection–training cycles — the very mechanism implied by "recursive self-improvement" — "remain to be evaluated" and are a "proposed extension." The honesty about the unrun recursive loop is a credibility positive, but the one-paragraph Limitations section substantially under-reports the paper's evaluation boundaries. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Training/evaluation contamination: the ~1,500 additional judge-training requests are built using WISE's taxonomy and MindBench's task categories as guidance; while the authors assert no evaluation examples are reused, the judge is trained on the same task distributions it is later evaluated on, and no decontamination audit or ablation removing these requests is provided. - Single evaluation judge: all headline results depend on Gemini 3.1 Pro verdicts under an all-items-must-pass metric; no second external judge, no human study, and no inter-rater agreement are reported, so CSA numbers across all systems share a common measurement bias. - Baseline configuration opacity: MemoGen R2 and SCOPE configurations on ImageReq-Bench are not described; GEMS and GenSearcher-style are local reproductions (one with a disabled retrieval component), and baselines appear to lack experience libraries equivalent in size, so part of the ImageRSI advantage may reflect memory rather than the framework. - No cost accounting: the system uses up to 3 generations plus multiple judge/retrieval calls per request versus 1 for direct generation; the CSA gain per unit of extra compute is never stated. - Calibration thresholds for experience admission (mean Δe ≥ 0.05, trial minimums) are fixed without sensitivity analysis, and the confidence mechanism is replaced with constants for trained judges — an unexamined mismatch between the scoring equation and the deployed judges. - Library scaling is shown only to 527 entries on a single random ordering; no variance over orderings, and no analysis of which experience types drive gains. Bottom Line: This is a competently executed and honestly ablated agentic image-generation system whose A/B-validated experience admission and false-accept-penalized judge training are worth borrowing, but its recursive-self-improvement headline is a single evaluated update round on partly self-built benchmarks with no code release — read it for the admission protocol and ablation design, not as demonstrated self-improvement.

Intrinsic Distribution Matching (238 ▲ )

Deyuan Liu, Yansen Han, Kaiwen Zheng, Jun Xie, Jiacheng Liu, Zhenglin Cheng, Peng Sun, Jintao Zhang, Jianguo Li, Tao Lin · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), a few-step text-to-image distillation objective that augments internal distribution-matching distillation (DMD) with an explicit loss on the means and per-coordinate standard deviations of the generator's own EMA features, evaluated on 6B and 20B backbones. - Why it's important: One- and two-step generators must render dense prompt details (especially long Chinese/English text) in one or two forward passes, where errors cannot be refined away; the paper targets this cost-quality trade-off for deployable fast generation. - How it does it: The core move is decomposing the reverse-KL score-difference field into a Gaussian moment component (determined by means/covariances) and a non-Gaussian residual, then adding a pooled feature-moment loss (a diagonal 2-Wasserstein term) in the generator's EMA feature space on top of the full DMD correction. - The good: Controlled ablations under a shared training setting isolate each loss: adding the moment loss improves all five aggregate metrics (e.g., GenEval 77.46→77.81, LongText-CN 93.87→94.25), and EMA features match DINOv2-encoder features (77.81 vs 77.75 GenEval) without an external encoder. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, the headline gains are 0.3–3.9 percentage points on benchmarks the authors also tune against, and the closest baseline (APEX) is trained on a smaller, different dataset, so the method-vs-data attribution for the headline LongText result is not clean. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on few-step diffusion/flow distillation and want a concrete recipe plus ablations for adding distributional moment supervision without an external encoder; skip it if you want a validated theoretical advance or statistically robust empirical claims, since the theory is motivational and the empirical margins are small.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is pulled down chiefly by Rigor (46): no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; ablations and model selection run on the same benchmarks reported as headline results (a Goodhart risk); the APEX comparison is data-confounded with no data-matched control; and the code link is referenced but absent, so reproducibility cannot be verified. Novelty (60) is incremental — the moment loss is a diagonal 2-Wasserstein regularizer layered on existing internal-DMD machinery, with the decomposition explicitly motivational rather than a validated mechanism — limiting Non-Obviousness (50). Completeness (65) is a credibility positive (direct disclosure of the DPG-Bench loss to APEX, the pooling simplification, and the density-assumption failure), but Resilience (55) drops because the 0.05–0.35-point ablation margins would plausibly flip under seeding scrutiny. Impact (65) reflects a deployable low-NFE recipe at 6B/20B scale with strong latency, though artifacts are only implied. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*46 + 0.15*50 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*65 = 55.5 ≈ 56.

Problem & Motivation: Diffusion and flow-matching text-to-image models need many network evaluations, and one-/few-step distillation methods (DMD and its variants) compress them at the cost of fine detail fidelity — concretely, rendering long, dense text in prompts at 1–2 NFE. DMD-style training uses the score difference between a reference (teacher) and the generated distribution, estimated either by a separate fake-score network or, in recent work (TwinFlow, APEX), by internally separated velocity branches of the generator itself. The authors ask whether the learned score supervision from these internal constructions leaves statistical discrepancies that an explicit constraint on distribution statistics can reduce, and who has this problem: practitioners deploying large text-to-image models (Z-Image-Turbo 6B, Qwen-Image 20B) at low sampling budgets. Key Idea: Decompose the reverse-KL distribution gradient g_KL = s_θ − s_r into a Gaussian moment component (depending only on means and covariances of the two distributions) plus a non-Gaussian score residual; since matching moments provably cannot capture the residual, the method retains the full DMD correction and additionally constrains feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations — computed in the generator's own EMA feature space rather than via an external encoder like DINOv2. The theory is motivational rather than constructive: the moment loss is explicitly described as a pooled feature-space regularizer "motivated by" the Gaussian component, not an estimate of it. Methodology: The training objective is L_IDM = L_base (RCGM recursive consistent velocity regression) + λ_score·L_score + λ_pop·L̂pop with λ_score = 1, λ_pop = 0.5 fixed. L_score follows APEX's internal DMD: the reference and model velocity branches are separated by negating the conditioning vector (F_θ(x_t,t,c) vs F_θ(x_t,t,−c)); the predicted clean sample is re-noised at t′, the internal velocity difference is evaluated there, detached, weighted, and normalized to form velocity and endpoint regression targets (combined squared loss, Eq. 12). L̂pop mean-pools the last-layer hidden activations of the generator's EMA copy (EMA rate 0.99) for generated and reference samples at high noise levels, matches pooled means and per-coordinate standard deviations using detached queues of K = 16384 features (the empirical loss equals the squared 2-Wasserstein distance between diagonal Gaussians in feature space), with gradients flowing through the fixed EMA network to current samples. Critical design decisions: (1) keeping the full DMD correction rather than replacing it with moment matching — well justified by the paper's own decomposition showing moments alone are insufficient; (2) EMA self-features instead of an external DINOv2 encoder — justified empirically (near-identical ablation scores) but the theoretical motivation for feature-space rather than sample-space moments is loose; (3) pooling moments across conditions rather than matching conditional distributions — a pragmatic simplification that is acknowledged but only weakly justified. Key Results: Tested on Z-Image-Turbo 6B (15K steps, 32×H100) and Qwen-Image 20B (10K steps, 8×A100), full-parameter and LoRA (r=32, 64; 0.4B trainable), batch size 64. At 2 NFE, IDM (Z-Image) scores 94.25% LongText-CN and 90.20% LongText-EN — the highest among compared 2-NFE methods — beating Z-Image-Turbo++ by 2.63/0.32 points and APEX by 3.87/1.44 points. GenEval: 0.91 (Qwen-Image full, 2 NFE) vs APEX's 0.90; FID 6.34 vs 6.44; WISE 0.56 vs 0.54. Latency 0.44 s (Qwen) and 0.30 s (Z-Image) per sample on a single A100; the same checkpoint serves 1 and 2 NFE. Ablations (all on Z-Image full tuning, 2 NFE): removing Lpop costs 0.35 GenEval points; removing Lscore costs 0.91; removing both costs 1.57. EMA features (77.81 GenEval) edge out DINOv2 (77.75), teacher features (77.36), and live self-features (77.51). Counterpoint the paper reports honestly: APEX leads on DPG-Bench (88.64 vs 86.82), and the APEX comparison is confounded by its smaller (200K poster-prompt vs 5M text-rendering) training set. Baselines include recent strong systems (APEX, TwinFlow, Z-Image-Turbo++, Qwen-Image-Lightning, Sana-Sprint), so comparisons are against current methods, though published baselines retain their own training configurations. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (incremental) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the explicit feature-moment loss in the generator's EMA space layered on internal DMD, and the systematic ablation isolating moment matching from score supervision. The supporting decomposition is an application of the existing Gaussian-plus-residual score representation (Wang & Vastola 2023/2024) plus Stein-identity algebra; the internal score estimation is adopted from APEX/TwinFlow; moment-matching losses date to GMMN/MMD-GAN and FD-Loss. The paper itself is careful to state the moment loss is a regularizer motivated by the decomposition, not a new estimator of the Gaussian component. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a genuine strength: a single shared training setting (data, backbone, budget) with loss-removal, regression-weighting (v-only/x-only/mixed), and feature-map (DINOv2/teacher/live-self/EMA) controls, plus per-category breakdowns. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and the headline ablation deltas (0.29–0.35 GenEval points on a 6-category mean; 0.19 OneIG points) are within plausible run-to-run noise. Code is said to be available ("Code is available here") but no URL appears in the extracted text; no dataset release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) system-level comparisons mix published baselines trained on different data with the authors' own setting; (2) ablations and model selection use the same benchmarks reported as headline results (LongText-Bench, GenEval), a Goodhart risk; (3) the theory assumes smooth strictly positive densities, which the authors themselves note fails for deterministic generator maps (singular laws) — they carry this assumption explicitly and confine it to the clean-field interpretation, which is credible but means the clean-score theory does not strictly apply to their own generator; (4) some baselines marked as noncanonical operating points or secondary sources. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained generative models with benchmark and latency evaluation, plus a released training recipe). - Practical: Yes — training on 8×A100 80GB (Qwen LoRA) to 32×H100 (Z-Image full) and inference on a single A100 in BF16; LoRA variants train only 0.2–0.4B parameters. - Efficient: Inference is the point of the method — 0.30–0.44 s latency at 2 NFE, 5.18 samples/s (Z-Image) — comparable to or faster than same-size baselines; training adds EMA feature extraction and queue maintenance but the paper does not quantify training-time overhead. - Effective: Evidence supports improved long-text rendering at 1–2 NFE over the strongest internal-DMD baselines, but the effect on DPG-Bench is negative relative to APEX, and gains are small on several metrics, so the improvement is real but narrow. - Scalable: Not stated beyond the two backbones tested (6B and 20B); no experiment or claim addresses 10× scale, and queue-based moment estimation at 16K features is untested for higher feature diversity. Deliverable: trained checkpoints (implied), code (link referenced but not printed), and a recipe; no standalone library or dataset artifact is described. Strengths: - The loss-removal ablation cleanly separates the contributions of score supervision and moment matching under an identical training setting, which most distillation papers omit; the ordering (DMD > moment > neither) is consistent across all five aggregate metrics. - The EMA self-feature result is a useful practical finding: matching DINOv2-encoder moment matching (77.75 vs 77.81 GenEval) without any external encoder removes a whole dependency class from the training pipeline. - The theory appendix is unusually honest: it states the density assumption can fail for deterministic generators, proves the residual is orthogonal only under its own measure, and explicitly disclaims that the moment loss estimates the Gaussian component — claims and evidence are well separated. - Same-checkpoint 1- and 2-NFE evaluation with documented per-NFE results is operationally useful for deployment decisions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that (1) matching moments cannot capture non-Gaussian score structure, hence the retained full DMD correction; (2) the APEX comparison reflects the complete training settings (different, larger data), not just the objective — they state this directly in the ablation section; (3) APEX leads on DPG-Bench (88.64 vs 86.82); (4) the moment loss is a pooled (not conditional) feature-space regularizer, not an estimate of the sample-space Gaussian component; (5) the clean-density assumption fails for degenerate generator maps (Appendix B.1); (6) queue staleness can bias empirical moments; (7) the mixed-regression ablation results "do not establish independent distributional information in the two regression terms." This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: with 6-category GenEval means, a 0.35-point ablation delta and the 0.05-point EMA-vs-DINOv2 gap could plausibly flip across seeds; the paper's strongest claims (moment loss helps, EMA matches DINOv2) rest on single-run point estimates. - The headline LongText gains (+2.63 CN over Z-Image-Turbo++) come from a model also trained with 5M text-rendering samples and 600K reasoning prompts versus APEX's 200K poster prompts — no data-matched control for APEX is run, so the objective's contribution to the headline number is not isolated at system level. - The negative DPG-Bench result relative to APEX (−1.82 points) is reported but not analyzed; no failure-mode study of what moment matching costs. - The condition-negation trick (F_θ(x_t,t,−c) as the model branch) assumes conditioning is odd-symmetric in a specific way; nothing validates that −c reliably selects the model branch on these backbones beyond inherited APEX practice. - Moments are pooled across conditions and averaged over feature-extraction noise; the paper does not test conditional moment matching, which the decomposition argument would arguably motivate more strongly. - Code URL is referenced but absent from the provided text, so reproducibility cannot be confirmed from the document alone. Bottom Line: A practitioner building few-step text-to-image generators gains a concrete, ablated recipe — add a pooled EMA-feature moment loss on top of internal DMD, skip the external encoder — but should treat the headline margins as unreplicated point estimates on partially data-confounded comparisons, and the theory as motivation rather than a validated mechanism; reading the APEX/TwinFlow papers first is a prerequisite rather than an alternative.

Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery? (101 ▲ )

Yepeng Liu, Shengmai Chen, Xuandong Zhao, Chengzhi Liu, Dawn Song, Xin Eric Wang, Yuheng Bu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Test-Time Memory Evolution (TTME), a plug-and-play method that distills search experience into two external memory modules (operational guidelines and reusable algorithmic strategies) that guide a fixed-weight LLM during iterative scientific discovery, replacing test-time RL weight updates. - Why it's important: Test-time training (TTT) makes open-weight LLMs competitive with frontier-model systems on discovery tasks but requires expensive online weight updates (tens of EFLOPs, ~12 h/task), which blocks scaling to larger models; a cheaper adaptation mechanism removes that bottleneck. - How it does it: Every K=2 search steps, the same frozen base model distills execution failures into up to 24 capacity-limited "Guidelines" (with Jaccard-based dedup, recency expiry) and extracts experience notes from score-improving parent-child program pairs into consolidated "Strategy" families, which are then selected and adapted into per-parent modification instructions for half of each generation budget. - The good: The evaluation is unusually clean for this space — TTME is swapped into two published TTT frameworks (TTT-Discover, ThetaEvolve) with all other settings (archives, verifiers, candidate budgets of 25,600–33,280 primary attempts) held fixed, and it beats the reported TTT numbers on all five tasks while cutting FLOPs by 82.8–84.6%. - The missing: All headline comparisons rest on single runs with best-found scores that differ from TTT by as little as 5×10⁻⁶ (Erdős: 0.380927 vs 0.380932), with no error bars or seed variance reported, so the claim of universal superiority is not statistically supported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building LLM-based program-search or discovery systems who is deciding between test-time RL and context/memory adaptation — the head-to-head cost analysis is the most direct evidence available — but skip if you need the result replicated with variance estimates first.

Completeness (60) and the clean head-to-head design, plus the interesting TTT+TTME negative result, keep this a solid contribution.
