Problem & Motivation: DPSGD (Abadi et al., 2016) clips every per-sample gradient to a fixed L2 radius before adding Gaussian noise. This isotropic clipping introduces a systematic bias — the expected clipped gradient no longer points along the true gradient — and existing remedies either reduce DP noise variance (temporal filtering, subspace projection) or reduce clipping bias temporally (error feedback, momentum), often at the cost of extra memory, complex hyperparameter tuning, or specialized architectures. The authors target the unaddressed geometric dimension of clipping bias: Euclidean balls ignore the anisotropic structure of gradient distributions, so directions with large gradient second moments get clipped unnecessarily. The audience is anyone training deep models under (ε,δ)-DP constraints. Key Idea: Generalize the clipping operation from an L2 ball to a G-norm ball (clip in √(gᵀGg)), derive the bias upper bound ‖b_G(C)‖_G ≤ Tr(GF_t)/C where F_t is the gradient second-moment (Fisher) matrix, and solve min Tr(GF_t)/C subject to Tr(G^{-1})=d — the trace constraint pins total injected noise variance to match isotropic DPSGD. The closed-form solution is G_t = λ_t F_t^{-1/2} with λ_t = Tr(F_t^{1/2})/d, i.e., loosen clipping in high-curvature directions, tighten it in low-curvature ones. The diagonal approximation is built purely from previously privatized* batch gradients, so adapting the geometry is post-processing and costs no additional privacy budget. Methodology: The pipeline per iteration is: (1) clip each per-sample gradient in the current G_t-norm to radius C; (2) average and inject anisotropic Gaussian noise with covariance σ²G_t^{-1} (equivalently, isotropic noise in the transformed space); (3) update an EMA of squared privatized gradients Ṽ_{t+1} = βṼ_t + (1−β)ĝ_t²; (4) apply the noise-correction — solving ṽ_{t+1} = v_{t+1} + (σ²/λ_t)√v_{t+1} for its positive root — to strip the known DP-noise contribution; (5) set λ_{t+1} = Mean(√v_{t+1}) and G_{t+1} = λ_{t+1}diag(v_{t+1}^{-1/2}), which enforces Tr(G^{-1})=d. The framework is constrained optimization for the geometry derivation, exponential-moving-average estimation with a quadratic-root denoising step, and moments-accountant privacy analysis. Critical design decisions: (a) using privatized batch gradients instead of per-sample statistics — well justified, since it avoids extra privacy spend; (b) the temporal approximation ṽ_t ≈ ṽ_{t+1} needed for the closed-form correction — supported by a Lemma 7 bound of O((1−β)(C²+dσ²/µ)), though the bound itself scales with dσ², which is loose in high dimension; (c) a diagonal geometry for scalability — acknowledged as sacrificing cross-parameter correlations, and the ablation on adaptive λ vs. fixed λ is reasonably convincing. Key Results: Across nine benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 with SimCLRv2, ImageNette and CelebA with ResNet9; MNLI, QQP, QNLI, SST-2 with RoBERTa-base) at ε ∈ {2,3,8}, CA-DPSGD posts the highest mean accuracy among {vanilla DPSGD, Auto-S, DP-PSAC} on all nine, e.g., 62.21±0.47% on ImageNette (ε=8) vs 60.91±0.71% for DPSGD (+1.30), 86.29±0.65% on QNLI vs 85.79±0.42 (+0.50), and 92.82±0.09% on CIFAR-10 (ε=2) vs 92.62±0.03. On MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CelebA/QQP/SST-2 the margins are ≤0.23 points and frequently within one standard deviation of a baseline. Composition experiments show CA-DPSGD stacked on IOM, KFSGD, and DP-AdamBC improves ImageNette accuracy by ~2.0 and ~1.8 points for KFSGD and DP-AdamBC respectively, though CA-IOM slightly hurts IOM on Fashion-MNIST. Ablations (noise correction, adaptive λ, β sweep) are in appendices, restricted to three image datasets. The baselines (Auto-S NeurIPS 2023, DP-PSAC AAAI 2023) are recent clipping-focused methods but not the strongest overall DPSGD variants (e.g., no comparison against DiceSGD or the noise-reduction methods the paper itself cites), and GeoClip — the closest geometric method — is omitted. Testing is at standard academic scale (largest model: RoBERTa-base; largest dataset: MNLI); no large-scale or high-dimensional stress test. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with a theoretical component. The genuinely novel elements are (i) formulating clipping-geometry selection as a trace-minimization under a noise-variance-matching constraint, yielding the closed-form F^{-1/2} geometry, and (ii) the closed-form noise-correction of the privatized second moment that makes the geometry estimable for free. The ingredients — Adam-style diagonal second moments, EMA statistics, anisotropic preconditioning (Shampoo/AdaHessian lineage), and privatized-statistic-based adaptation (GeoClip) — are established; the novelty lies in the specific bias-minimizing objective, the constraint tying noise variance to isotropic DPSGD, and the correction step, applied to the clipping operator rather than the optimizer update. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for the noise-correction module, the adaptive λ mechanism, and β, covering MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 — though the noise-correction ablation shows a negligible gap on CIFAR-10, which weakens the claim that this module matters generally. Results are mean±std over five seeds; no significance tests are reported, and several headline margins are within noise. Proofs for the bias bound, optimal geometry, privacy, and convergence are given in appendices and appear correct, though the convergence bound's clipping term (4/(µC²T)·Σ Tr(G_tF_t)²) is not shown to vanish, and Assumption 3 (G_t ⪰ µI) is assumed rather than proven for the actual update rule. No code, data, or artifact release is mentioned — a reproducibility gap given the number of hyperparameter-sensitive choices (β, correction formula). The GeoClip exclusion is a methodological concern: the closest related method is dropped from comparison for the very scalability reason the diagonal design claims to fix, without even a small-scale head-to-head. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with supporting theory). Practical: Runs on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) with standard frameworks; the diagonal geometry adds only O(d) state, so it is deployable on commodity hardware. Efficient: Cheaper than full-rank geometric alternatives (GeoClip) and error-feedback methods since it reuses privatized gradients with no per-sample second-moment computation, but it does add an EMA and a per-coordinate root-finding step per iteration — cost relative to vanilla DPSGD is not explicitly quantified. Effective: The evidence shows consistent but small accuracy gains over clipping-focused baselines on standard benchmarks; it does not demonstrate gains over the strongest overall DPSGD pipelines, so it solves the clipping-bias proxy rather than proving end-to-end DP-training improvement against the field. Scalable: Only claimed via the diagonal design; the largest model tested is RoBERTa-base (~125M params), and no experiment approaches 10× that scale, so high-dimensional behavior of the noise correction at large dσ² is untested. The work stops at paper form — no library, CLI, or trained-model artifact is released or mentioned. Strengths: (1) The bias-bound-then-constrained-minimization derivation is clean and yields a closed-form optimal geometry — a genuinely new lens on clipping design, distinct from prior temporal (IOM, DiceSGD) and noise-reduction approaches. (2) The observation that adapting the geometry from previously privatized gradients is free under post-processing is an elegant and correct privacy-economic argument. (3) The closed-form noise correction (solving out the DP-noise contribution to the second moment) is a concrete, reusable trick for any method estimating statistics from noisy gradients. (4) Orthogonality is demonstrated empirically by stacking the method on three independent DPSGD variants with measured gains (up to ~2.0 points on ImageNette for KFSGD+CA). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states the diagonal geometry cannot capture cross-parameter correlations and motivates more expressive geometries as future work. Appendix J admits CA-IOM degrades IOM on Fashion-MNIST and offers a mechanistic explanation (momentum smoothing amplifies low-curvature dimensions that CA-DPSGD deliberately suppresses). Appendix K candidly notes the noise-correction module is nearly inert on CIFAR-10 due to low noise variance in fine-tuning settings. The authors confront these limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge the within-noise margins on several benchmarks or the absence of GeoClip from the comparison as limitations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The convergence bound's clipping-bias term Tr(G_tF_t)² is never related back to the minimized objective in a way that shows the bound actually improves over isotropic DPSGD — the theory is structural, not a comparative guarantee. (2) Lemma 7's stability bound scales as dσ²/µ, so the temporal approximation underlying the noise correction may degrade precisely in the high-dimensional, high-noise regimes where the method is motivated; this is untested beyond ≤ResNet9/RoBERTa-base scale. (3) Assumption 3 (uniform lower eigenvalue µ on G_t) is assumed, but the actual update G_t = λ_t diag(v^{-1/2}) has no mechanism forcing a lower bound — the paper never shows µ > 0 holds in practice. (4) Missing baselines beyond the clipping subfamily: DiceSGD [37] and DISK/KFSGD-style noise reduction are cited, analyzed qualitatively, and one is used in composition, but the main table lacks any non-clipping-based strong baseline. (5) The GeoClip exclusion would be more persuasive with even a small-model head-to-head. (6) No code release despite the method's hyperparameter (β) sensitivity, limiting independent verification. Bottom Line: A theoretically tidy and privacy-economical contribution to the clipping-geometry literature that a DP-ML researcher should read for the F^{-1/2} formulation and noise-correction trick, but whose sub-point gains on half its benchmarks, missing strongest baselines, and absent code release mean practitioners get more value from DiceSGD or Auto-S today.

#198 — Moderately Innovative (54)

DEPPO: Dual Experience Pool Policy Optimization for Long - Horizon Reinforcement Learning

H Dong, J Guo, M Yan, Y Yuan, M Jia, H Sun · aclanthology.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DEPPO, a critic-free policy optimization framework that converts historical successful and failed trajectories into task-conditioned success–failure statistics used to adaptively reweight step-level advantages in long-horizon RL for LLM agents. - Why it's important: Outcome-level RL broadcasts a single terminal reward to every step, so redundant actions in successes get reinforced and useful actions in failures get penalized—a core credit-assignment mismatch that limits training stability and final performance for long-horizon agents without requiring extra critics, process reward models, or human annotations. - How it does it: It maintains two count-based experience pools (success and failure) indexed by task–state–action keys, computes a smoothed log-ratio preference score for the current action under both pools, gates reweighting on sufficient statistical support, and multiplies the base GiGPO advantage by a clipped exponential of this preference, with asymmetric (freshness-aware success / risk-weighted failure) insertion plus decay and pruning. - The good: The evaluation includes very recent 2025–2026 credit-assignment baselines (GiGPO, HCAPO, RewardFlow, EMPG) under a matched rollout/optimization protocol, and DEPPO wins broadly—e.g., ALFWorld average 92.2 vs. 84.5/85.1 (GiGPO/HCAPO) at 1.5B and 95.7 vs. 86.2/85.1 at 7B, with measured overhead of only ~85 ms/step (0.04–0.07% over GiGPO) and 3–8 MB CPU memory. - The missing: No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported, no code release is stated, and the state–action keys come from normalized environment observations—so generalization to settings without discrete, repeatable states (or larger backbones beyond 8B) is untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building step-level credit assignment for LLM agent RL, since it offers a lightweight, critic-free alternative to process reward models with detailed ablations and dynamics analysis; skip it if you need general-purpose RL theory or work in continuous/high-dimensional state spaces where count-based experience matching will not apply.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (50) is the primary drag: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere, no code release stated, and an unexplained baseline-ordering inversion on Sokoban — this despite current, well-matched baselines. Resilience (52) suffers because the discrete-state-key requirement is never stress-tested and the method's behavior in open-ended state spaces is unexamined, while Impact (40) is low given no artifact is released. Novelty (62) and Non-Obviousness (60) are moderate — the dual-pool log-ratio credit signal is a clean idea rooted in count-based replay. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*50 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*52 + 0.10*40 = 54.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents and multi-step reasoning models are typically trained with outcome-level rewards, creating a mismatch between trajectory-level supervision and step-level decisions. Uniformly broadcasting terminal rewards over-reinforces incidental actions in successful trajectories and penalizes useful actions in failed ones, producing noisy gradients and unstable optimization. Practitioners training interactive agents (embodied, web, planning) face this directly. Prior fixes—critic-based value estimation, process reward models, rollout-tree methods—require extra models, annotations, or task-specific designs, and most methods derive learning signals only from the current batch without exploiting accumulated training history. The paper's framing question is whether historical trajectories can be repurposed as state-conditioned contrastive signals for step-level credit assignment. Key Idea: Treat accumulated past trajectories as two count-based distributions (success-conditioned and failure-conditioned action statistics keyed by task–state pairs) and use the log-ratio of an action's smoothed probability under these two distributions—rather than any learned value model—as a direct step-level credit signal that multiplicatively rescales the trajectory-level advantage. Methodology: DEPPO is built on GiGPO's state-aware group-based advantage computation, wrapped in a PPO-style clipped objective (KL coefficient 0.01, lr 1e-6, 8 rollouts per prompt, 150 epochs, 8 GPUs). Pipeline: (1) roll out trajectories and label outcomes y ∈ {+1, −1}; (2) query dual pools D+/D− (hierarchical task → state → action histograms over normalized environment observations, not token IDs) for the current (u, s, a); (3) compute additive-smoothed probabilities P±(a|u,s) and the preference score Δt = log[(P+ + ε)/(P− + ε)]; (4) apply a support-aware gate requiring minimum total and per-pool support (Smin = 8) and a preference margin (τΔ = 0.03), falling back to the base advantage otherwise; (5) reweight the advantage as Â = clip(exp(β·y·Δt), 0.2, 1.8)·g·A. Pool updates are asymmetric: success insertions get a freshness boost for underrepresented actions, failure insertions get late-stage, repeat, and invalid-action multipliers; both pools undergo exponential decay (λ = 0.995), action/state pruning, and per-task state budgets. Pools are queried before the current batch is written to prevent self-leakage. Critical design decisions: (a) the support gate—well justified, and Appendix E.1 shows filtering outperforms unfiltered reweighting in final success rate; (b) count-based state keys from environment observations rather than token-level traces—pragmatic but limits applicability to natural-language-state settings, and this trade-off is not empirically probed; (c) asymmetric pool updates—the ablation (Table 3) shows dynamic updates add consistent gains over static pools, justifying the mechanism. Key Results: On ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, DEPPO reaches a 92.2 average across six subtasks versus 84.5 (GiGPO), 85.1 (HCAPO), 83.1/65.0 WebShop score/success, and 73.1 WebShop success; with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct it reaches 95.7 ALFWorld average (+7.1 over GiGPO) and 90.1/84.3 WebShop score/success (+9.1 success over GiGPO). On Sokoban (visual), it reaches 86.4% (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) and 89.8% (Qwen3-VL-8B) versus GRPO's 67.1%/82.9%, though GiGPO beats GRPO but loses to DEPPO only at 8B (78.1 vs 89.8; at 3B GiGPO's 80.8 trails DEPPO's 86.4). Against skill-based mechanisms (using o3-generated skills), DEPPO wins ALFWorld (95.7 vs SkillRL 89.1) and WebShop (84.3 vs 82.8). Measured overhead is 85.12 ms/step amortized (0.04–0.07% of GiGPO training time), 1.02 MB serialized pools. Ablations attribute gains progressively: positive pool lifts 1.5B ALFWorld from 84.5→90.4, negative pool →91.3, dynamic update →92.2. Baselines are current (2024–2026 methods) and strong; the main analysis is confined to 1.5B/7B backbones on two text benchmarks plus one visual benchmark—standard scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (and arguably a NEW FORMULATION of historical experience as contrastive success–failure credit). The genuinely novel element is the dual-pool, state-conditioned log-ratio preference signal used to rescale advantages without any learned critic or PRM. The surrounding machinery—PPO clipping, GiGPO group advantages, exponential decay of counts, top-K pruning—is a standard combination of known ideas; the freshness/risk-aware asymmetric insertion rules are engineering refinements on a count-based memory, a concept with roots in prioritized replay and hindsight methods. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (Table 3 isolates positive pool, negative pool, and dynamic updates; Appendix E.1 isolates support-aware filtering; Table 5 sweeps α, Smin, clipping range; Figure 5 sweeps β). Pool-dynamics figures (6–8, 13) give mechanistic insight into when reweighting activates. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; results are single-run point estimates. No code, data, or model release is mentioned. A methodological concern: the method and its hyperparameters (β, α, Smin, τΔ) are tuned and analyzed primarily on ALFWorld with the 1.5B model, and headline numbers come from the same benchmarks used for that tuning (mild Goodhart risk, mitigated by the WebShop and Sokoban cross-task results). The rollout/evaluation protocol is stated to match GiGPO exactly, which strengthens baseline fairness. Baselines are current and strong, so the comparison is credible on those terms. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training method run and measured by the authors). - Practical: Yes—runs on 8 GPUs with open Qwen 1.5B–8B backbones, and the experience pools live in CPU dictionaries requiring no extra GPU memory. - Efficient: Extremely cheap relative to alternatives—85 ms/step amortized CPU overhead (0.04–0.07% of training time), 3–8 MB RAM, versus a critic network or PRM which adds parameters and GPU compute. - Effective: Evidence supports the claim on discrete-state sparse-reward agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, Sokoban), but these are simulation proxies; no real-world or open-ended-state evaluation is provided. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested—the authors concede that broader settings and larger foundation models are future work, and count-based state matching may degrade with state-space growth beyond a few hundred thousand entries (the pools here hold ~10⁴–10⁵ state entries). The work delivers a method description and algorithms (Algorithms 1–2) but, per the paper text, no public software artifact. Strengths: (1) A genuinely critic-free, annotation-free mechanism for step-level credit assignment—the log-ratio of success/failure counts is a simple, interpretable signal with a measured cost under 0.1% of training time. (2) Baseline selection is unusually current for an agent-RL paper: comparisons against HCAPO, RewardFlow, EMPG, and GiGPO under an identical protocol, plus a skill-based comparison, make the gains meaningful. (3) The support-aware gate is validated empirically (Appendix E.1), showing that conservative, filtered reweighting beats aggressive reweighting—a non-obvious finding. (4) The stage-wise dynamics analysis (negative pool dominating early, positive pool later) provides insight into why the method works, not just that it works. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that DEPPO depends on the diversity and coverage of the experience pools, especially in open-ended environments with sparse successes, and that evaluation is limited to long-horizon agent/reasoning benchmarks—broader real-world settings and larger foundation models are needed to assess scalability and generalization. This is a direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment, a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single-run results with no variance reporting anywhere, so differences like 92.2 vs. 91.3 (ablation rows) cannot be judged for significance. (2) The method requires discrete, repeatable task–state keys; the paper never tests or discusses what happens in environments with continuously varying or natural-language states where exact state matching yields near-zero support—the gated ratio would collapse to ~0 and DEPPO would reduce to GiGPO, a degenerate case left unexamined. (3) The skill-based comparison (Figure 4) uses o3-generated external skills, introducing a third-party model dependency whose quality is uncontrolled. (4) Sokoban results show GiGPO exceeding GRPO at 8B (82.9 vs 78.1... wait, GRPO 82.9 vs GiGPO 78.1 at 8B—an inversion where GRPO beats GiGPO) but the paper does not comment on this baseline ordering inconsistency. (5) Hyperparameter count is high (α, β, τΔ, Smin, Seach_min, wmin/wmax, λ, δa, δs, Ka, Ks, plus four γ coefficients in the failure insertion), and sensitivity is reported only for a subset; transfer of defaults to new environments is unverified. (6) No code release is stated, which given the fine-grained implementation details (query-before-write ordering, normalization of keys) materially affects reproducibility. Bottom Line: A practitioner training LLM agents on discrete, repeatable-state environments gains a cheap and well-evaluated credit-assignment upgrade over GiGPO by reading this paper, but those working in open-ended or continuous state spaces should look elsewhere, and everyone should wait for a code release and multi-seed confirmation before treating the exact numbers as solid.

#199 — Moderately Innovative (54)

Beyond Attack Success Rate: Cost-Aware Metric for Evaluating Iterative LLM Jailbreaks

R Menon, CH Cheng · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ASR_STEP, a cost-aware extension of attack success rate (ASR) that discounts jailbreak success by the number of additional queries a successful attack makes to the victim LLM, using a quadratic step penalty. - Why it's important: Conventional ASR gives equal credit to a one-query success and one obtained after hundreds of victim-model calls, even though every extra call gives a deployed system's monitoring another chance to detect and block the attack — so ASR alone can misrank attacks by operational threat. - How it does it: Each successful trial's score is max(0, S_i − c·(K_i/N)²), where K_i counts additional victim calls, N is a pre-specified step bound, and c = 0.2; single-step attacks recover standard ASR exactly, and the metric is reported alongside ASR so the discount is explicit. - The good: The evaluation isolates the metric's behavior cleanly: on 100 JailBreakBench prompts across three 7B model families, GCG loses 7.0–8.7 percentage points, PAIR loses 3.4–12 points, and the single-step PAP baseline is provably unchanged, confirming the metric behaves as designed and discriminates iterative from single-step attacks. - The missing: The penalty shape and hyperparameter (c = 0.2, quadratic) are arbitrary and unvalidated against any real detection/intervention mechanism, and the experiments are small (100 prompts, one run, no seeds or error bars). - Read it or not: Worth a quick read for red-teaming and safety-benchmark researchers thinking about evaluation methodology; practitioners running attacks or deploying defenses will find the metric easy to adopt but the empirical evidence too thin to change conclusions.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (55) is modest — a new metric formulation, but a thin and incremental methodological proposal — and Rigor (45) is the primary weakness: no ablation over the arbitrary penalty constant or functional form, single executions with no seeds or error bars on a 100-prompt benchmark, and an uncalibrated LLM judge with a possible judge–attacker correlation. Non-Obviousness (55) is middling: the victim-call-count framing is useful but the core detection-motivation premise is asserted, never measured. Completeness (65) and Resilience (60) benefit from a candid, direct limitations section, while Impact (45) reflects only evaluation code and a metric definition. Weighted composite: 0.20*55 + 0.25*45 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*45 = 54.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Jailbreak evaluation currently relies on attack success rate (ASR): the fraction of forbidden requests for which an attack elicits an unsafe response. ASR treats an immediate success and one obtained after hundreds of victim-model queries identically, even though iterative attacks (GCG, PAIR) interact with the protected system repeatedly, and each interaction is an additional opportunity for deployment-side monitoring — intrusion detection, rate anomaly analysis — to detect and intervene. The gap: no standard jailbreak metric accounts for the number of victim-model calls spent per successful attack. The authors argue victim-call count is operationally relevant, not merely a proxy for compute (distinguishing their view from FLOPs-based cost accounting such as Ehghaghi et al.'s risk–compute curves). Key Idea: Discount a successful attack's binary score by a quadratic function of the number of additional victim-model calls, Z_i = max(0, S_i − c·(K_i/N)²), and average over requests. The trick is that this leaves single-step attacks (K_i = 0) unchanged — recovering conventional ASR — so reporting ASR and ASR_STEP together exposes the step-cost discount as a gap between the two numbers. A secondary, more interesting design decision: for gradient attacks like GCG, the step count is back-dated to the iteration that produced the lowest-loss suffix (which may be well before the final iteration), rather than counting the full optimization budget. Methodology: The paper formalizes an attack A that, per forbidden request q_i, issues queries q_i^(0) … q_i^(K_i) to the victim f, stopping on success or at budget B; success is judged by a binary evaluator (LLM-as-a-Judge). Standard ASR averages success indicators S_i (Eq. 2). ASR_STEP averages the discounted scores Z_i (Eq. 3–4) with c = 0.2 and N the step bound, so successful attacks score in [0.8, 1]. Intermediate computations that do not call the victim (e.g., attacker-side optimization) are not counted as steps. Evaluation: three attacks — GCG (nanoGCG, probe sampling, n_iter = 250), PAIR (Gemma 4 12B attacker, n_iter = 20), and single-step PAP Misrepresentation (n_iter = 1) — on 100 JailBreakBench prompts against Vicuna-7b-v1.5, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Zephyr-7b-beta, judged by Gemma 4 26B A4B-it without calibration, on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPU. Critical design decisions: (1) the quadratic penalty form and c = 0.2 are chosen without justification or sensitivity analysis; (2) counting GCG's steps from the lowest-loss iteration rather than the budget endpoint is sensible but specific to loss-based attacks; (3) excluding PAP requests whose transformation stayed empty (marked with asterisks) slightly weakens the PAP row's comparability. Key Results: On 100 JailBreakBench prompts: GCG scores ASR 54.00%/46.00%/53.00% on Vicuna/Mistral/Zephyr, dropping to ASR_STEP 45.33%/39.00%/45.07% (−7.0 to −8.7 pp). PAIR scores ASR 17.00%/31.00%/60.00%, dropping to 13.6%/24.8%/48.00% (−3.4 to −12 pp, the widest discount, attributed to PAIR's judge-in-the-loop steps costing more per iteration). PAP is unchanged at 16.16%/25.00%/60.82% (ASR = ASR_STEP since it is single-step). PAIR is highest on both metrics on Zephyr; GCG is most effective on Vicuna; PAP outperforms GCG on Zephyr. Baselines are the standard, current representatives of the three attack categories (GCG, PAIR, PAP). Scale is small and standard — 100 prompts, three 7B models, one execution per request — not stress-scale. No surprising counter-intuitive findings beyond the expected ordering; the per-strategy difference in what constitutes a "step" (GCG's best suffix often found early vs. PAIR's judge-gated iterations) is the most informative observation. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION / NEW METRIC — the genuinely novel piece is the victim-call-count discount applied to binary jailbreak success, with the explicit design constraint that single-step attacks are unchanged. Everything else (the attacks, the benchmark, the LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation) is a competent, standard combination of existing tools applied to instantiate the metric. It is a short, incremental methodological proposal, not a new attack or system. Rigor & Reproducibility: There is no ablation over the penalty constant c or the functional form (quadratic vs. linear vs. logarithmic), so the reader cannot tell whether the reported 3–12 pp discounts are artifacts of the chosen c = 0.2. Each attack is executed exactly once per request — no seeds, repetitions, error bars, or significance tests are reported, which matters because the authors themselves note victim-response stochasticity (they list repeated-evaluation uncertainty as future work). The judge (Gemma 4 26B) is used without calibration and is acknowledged as a potential bias source; no human agreement check is reported. Code is stated to be available ("Code is available here" — no explicit URL in the text). Methodological concerns: evaluation confined to the authors' own run of one benchmark (JailBreakBench only, 100 prompts); PAP rows exclude failed transformations (asterisked), a small asymmetry; and the central operational claim — that extra victim calls translate into detection probability — is asserted, not measured. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a metric plus experiments; the artifact is a scoring procedure and evaluation code, not a deployed system). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPU with off-the-shelf 7B models and public attack packages; the metric itself costs nothing beyond logging step counts already available. - Efficient: The evaluation adds essentially no overhead over a standard ASR run; no compute comparison is reported, but GCG at n_iter = 250 is by far the most expensive component. - Effective: The evidence shows the metric measures what it claims (a step-discounted success score) on a proxy setting; whether it predicts real-world attack detectability — its stated motivation — is not evaluated. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested; at 100 prompts × 3 models the discounts are estimated from a single run, and stability at larger scale or across attack retries is explicitly deferred to future work. The work delivers evaluation code and a metric definition; no trained models or datasets are released. Strengths: - The metric is deliberately minimal and backward-compatible: single-step attacks recover ASR exactly, and reporting the ASR/ASR_STEP gap isolates the step-cost effect without breaking comparability with prior results. - The distinction between victim-model calls and attacker-side compute is a genuinely useful framing — it separates this from FLOPs-based cost accounting (Ehghaghi et al.) and ties the metric to defense-side detection opportunities. - The back-dating of GCG's step count to the lowest-loss suffix iteration (rather than the budget endpoint) is a thoughtful detail that avoids unfairly penalizing gradient attacks that find good suffixes early. - The related-work positioning against StrongREJECT, AttackEval, Expected Harm, Security Cube, and distributional-ASR proposals (Maple et al.) is precise about which axis each alternative covers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that evidence is limited to JailBreakBench, three model families, and selected attack configurations; that scores rely on a single uncalibrated LLM-as-a-Judge and may be biased by its classification errors; and that this limits generalizability of the numbers. They also defer uncertainty estimation, repeated evaluation, and non-binary harm scores to future work, and candidly note in ethics that findings could reveal which attacks elicit harmful content most effectively. This is a direct, non-defensive limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The penalty's functional form and constant c = 0.2 are unmotivated; a sensitivity analysis or a principled derivation (e.g., tied to detection probability per call) is absent, so all reported discounts are conditional on an arbitrary choice. - The core premise — each additional victim call yields a meaningful chance of detection and intervention — is never connected to an actual detection mechanism or measured detection rate, so "operationally relevant" remains an assertion. - One execution per request with no seeds means the 1–12 pp discounts (e.g., 45.33% vs. 45.07% vs. 46.00% on similar ASRs) may be within noise; no variance quantification is offered. - Cross-attack comparisons are confounded by very different iteration budgets (GCG 250 vs. PAIR 20) and by the exclusion of empty-transformation PAP prompts, so the GCG-vs-PAIR discount gap (their headline qualitative finding) is explained only by hypothesis, not isolated experimentally. - The judge is a Gemma model while PAIR's attacker is also a Gemma model — a potential correlation in judge–attacker behavior that is not discussed. - Only three 7B open models from 2023–24 are tested; no modern frontier or heavily aligned model is included, limiting relevance to current deployment. Bottom Line: A competent, honest, but thin metric proposal that is worth adopting as a cheap secondary statistic in red-teaming reports; its impact will hinge on follow-up work justifying the penalty against real detection mechanisms, and readers seeking a fully developed cost-aware evaluation framework should look to the risk–compute line of work (Ehghaghi et al.) it cites rather than expecting this paper to settle the question.

CodeCap-Bench: Can Code Serve as a Good Video Caption? (49 ▲ )

Jiafu Tang, Yifan Xu, Eric Tang, Junjie Zhao, Shipeng Luo, Te Sun, Haoxuan Hu, Yiyan Ji, Xinlong Chen, Zihao Wang, Yang Shi, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Jiaheng Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CodeCap-Bench, a 323-video benchmark with fine-grained spatio-temporal annotations for evaluating how faithfully multimodal LLMs can caption videos as executable HTML/CSS/JS code, plus empirical evidence that code captions preserve more video information than natural-language captions. - Why it's important: Fine-grained spatial structure and temporal dynamics in video are ambiguous and lossy when expressed in natural language, and a reliable programmatic representation could improve video understanding, editing, and reconstruction pipelines that depend on faithful captioning. - How it does it: Generated code is rendered into a video and scored against the reference along three levels — V-JEPA 2.1 feature cosine similarity, object-level spatio-temporal IoU via SAM 3.1 segmentation, and MLLM-judged retention of human-annotated static/dynamic focal points — with QA and video-reconstruction comparisons against natural-language captions. - The good: The MLLM-judge metric correlates strongly with human scores (Pearson r=0.942 on 50 videos, 4 models), and the head-to-head comparisons are concrete: code-rendered videos reach 83.02% QA accuracy (Opus-5 captions) vs. 72.64% for natural-language captions, nearly matching 83.96% on original videos. - The missing: All headline metrics are LLM- or feature-extractor-mediated rather than directly measured, the human validation covers only 50 videos and 4 models, and the core claim that code beats natural language is tested only on structured 2D content the benchmark itself pre-selects as code-representable. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on video captioning evaluation, video-to-code generation, or benchmarking MLLM perception; skip it if you need captioning for general or photorealistic video, which this benchmark explicitly excludes.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (52) and Resilience (48) pull the composite down most: the retention judge (GPT-6-sol) is also an evaluated caption model with human validation covering only 50 of 323 videos and 4 of 7 models, IoU evaluation inserts a second unvalidated model in the loop, no significance testing appears anywhere, and the headline 'code beats natural language' claim is circular by construction — the benchmark pre-selects code-representable content and the NL branch rests on a single text-to-video generator with an uncharacterized ceiling. Novelty (60) is anchored by the three-level render-and-compare benchmark and the crisp dynamic-vs-static retention gap (Non-Obviousness 58), a genuinely useful failure localization, but the vision-to-code lineage (Design2Code, Animation2Code, BVB) makes this a scope extension more than a new idea. Completeness (58) is mixed — scope limits are confronted directly, but judge circularity and annotation agreement are never addressed. Impact (48) is limited by an unclear code/data release status. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*52 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*48 + 0.10*48 = 54.
empirical Novelty 60 Rigor 52 Non-Obv 58 Completeness 58 Resilience 48 Impact 48

Problem & Motivation: Video captioning today uses natural language, which requires lengthy, ambiguous descriptions to express fine-grained spatial layouts, motion trajectories, and multi-object temporal coordination. The authors propose "Code as Video Caption" — executable programs encoding graphical primitives, layout rules, and temporal logic — and identify two open problems: (1) whether code captions actually preserve and convey video information better than text, and (2) whether current MLLMs can generate faithful code captions at all. Prior vision-to-code work covers narrower domains: Design2Code (webpages), ChartMimic (charts), Image2Struct (static images), Animation2Code (short ~5.1 s CodePen animations), VCode (SVG for images), and BVB (Blender reconstruction of indoor video). None systematically evaluates code captioning across diverse structured 2D video with fine-grained spatio-temporal annotations. Key Idea: Render the generated code and score the rendered video against the reference — turning caption fidelity from a text-matching problem into a verifiable, executable visual specification check. The core insight enabling the benchmark is that for structured 2D content, a code caption has a ground-truth executable interpretation, so fidelity can be measured at three granularities (global features, per-object boxes over time, and human-annotated focal points) rather than by caption-text similarity. Methodology: The task is formulated as: given reference video V of duration T, generate a single-file HTML/CSS/JS program C whose rendering R(C) = V̂ must match V across the shared timeline (pure-code setting; no reference frames, embedded imagery, or external assets allowed; a `seek(seconds)` API must be exposed). Evaluation has three components: (1) Visual similarity — cosine similarity of V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-G/384 features with identical temporal sampling; (2) Object-level spatio-temporal IoU — GPT-6-sol locates each annotated object in V̂, prompts SAM 3.1 for segmentation, and per-frame IoU is averaged over the visible interval (zero if absent); (3) Fine-grained visual information retention — GPT-6-sol scores 0–5 per annotated focal point (static: appearance/layout; dynamic: state changes, pacing, coordination). Data construction is a three-stage pipeline: collection from Bilibili/YouTube/Behance/Vimeo, filtering to 2D layouts with explicit object trajectories (excluding complex 3D viewpoints, textures, dense particle dynamics), and annotation of focal points plus object bounding boxes/visible intervals with human review. Generation is tested in agentic (Pi Agent, Codex CLI, or Claude Code harnesses with frame inspection and render-feedback iteration) and non-agentic (single pass from 2 fps sampled frames) settings across 7 MLLMs and three thinking-effort levels. Design decisions worth noting: the GPT-6-sol judge (validated against humans at r=0.942 and cross-checked with a Gemini judge), the zero-score-for-missing-object IoU convention (penalizes omission), and the prompt's explicit anti-cheating constraints against embedding reference imagery. The anti-embedding rules are well-justified; the choice of the captioning models themselves as judges is a convenience choice validated only on a 50-video subset. Key Results: The benchmark spans 323 videos (mean 19.0 s, median 17 s), five categories (desktop/apps, 2D games, design/media, data/science, icons/motion), with mean 16.8 objects and 8.6 focal points per video. Best model: GPT-6-astra with Codex achieves 73.24 overall retention, 75.37 spatio-temporal IoU, and 0.9735 visual similarity, beating second-best Opus-5 (Pi Agent) by 14.40 retention points; open-source models (Qwen3.8-max at 48.83, DeepSeek-v4.1-flash at 44.29) lag by ~25–30 points. Dynamic retention is consistently below static retention for every configuration (e.g., GPT-6-astra/Codex: 68.61 vs. 80.72; GPT-6-sol/Codex: 43.92 vs. 64.04). Agentic generation reliably raises video production success (Qwen3.8-max: 82.0%→93.2%) but reduces retention for GPT-6-sol and GPT-5.6-sol relative to non-agentic generation. Higher thinking effort helps but at cost (GPT-6-sol medium→xhigh: IoU 50.42→67.13, cost $0.315→$1.409/video). Cost does not predict fidelity (GPT-6-astra scores 72.87 cheaper than Opus-5's 58.84), and more tool calls do not predict fidelity (GPT-6-astra: 47.4 calls/72.87 vs. Gemini-3.8-flash: 99.6 calls/47.73). In the head-to-head against natural language: code-rendered video QA reaches 76.42–83.02% vs. 72.64–78.30% for text captions across three caption models (original video: 83.96%, 100 videos from DVBench/VideoMathQA/GUI-World); reconstruction via code rendering beats Seedance-2.5 caption-to-video on DreamSim appearance similarity (gains of 0.20–0.23), keyframe SSIM (+0.18–0.22), and CoTracker3 motion similarity (smaller gains). Baselines compared are current flagship proprietary and open models (per the paper's 2026 citations), so the model comparison is against contemporaneous systems, though the code-vs-text comparison relies on a single text-to-video generator (Seedance-2.5) for the natural-language branch. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the benchmark's scope (structured 2D video across five categories at ~19 s mean duration, ~4× longer than Animation2Code), its focal-point + object-level spatio-temporal annotations with human review, and the three-level render-and-compare evaluation. The representation idea (vision→code) and the agentic generate-render-refine loop are standard combinations of existing ideas (Design2Code/Image2Struct lineage, Animation2Code/BVB for video) applied to a broader video setting; the code-beats-text caption finding is the new empirical claim, established only within this benchmark's scope. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: the judge metric is validated against human scoring (Pearson r=0.942, 50 videos × 4 models) and cross-checked with a second judge (Gemini-3.1-pro), with consistent relative rankings; failure-mode analysis decomposes the 2.96% overall production failures by model and cause; ablations cover thinking effort, agentic vs. non-agentic harness, per-category breakdowns, and cost/token/time decomposition. Concerns: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any headline number; the fine-grained retention metric is judged by GPT-6-sol, which is also an evaluated caption model (self-judging risk, partially mitigated but only checked on two models); the human correlation study is small (50 of 323 videos) and covers only 4 of 7 models; IoU annotation itself is model-derived (SAM 3.1) with human review but no reported annotation agreement statistics; the code-vs-text QA comparison uses 100 questions from external benchmarks with Gemini-3.8-flash as sole answerer. The project page (codecap-bench.github.io) is listed, but no explicit code/data release URL or license is stated in the text. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus evaluation study; no new trained model or system is built). Practical: Runs on commodity cloud — browser rendering, ffmpeg, and commercial MLLM APIs; no special hardware. Efficient: Generation costs range from ~$0.32 to ~$1.41 per video at medium effort, but wall-clock is heavy — open-weight models need 42–50 minutes and up to ~7,000k input tokens per video vs. 12.5 minutes for GPT-6-astra. Effective: The evidence shows code captions beat text on QA and reconstruction within the benchmark's structured-2D scope; no evidence is offered for natural or photorealistic video. Scalable: Not tested — longer videos, more objects, or 3D/texture-rich content are untested by construction, and dynamic retention already degrades sharply, so scaling claims would be extrapolation. Deliverable form: a benchmark dataset with annotations, prompts, and a multi-metric evaluation harness (release status stated only via project page), not a library or trained model. Strengths: - The render-and-score paradigm converts caption fidelity into a directly checkable executable specification, sidestepping text-similarity evaluation problems that plague natural-language caption metrics. - The dynamic-vs-static retention gap is a crisp, reproducible empirical finding (present in every configuration) that localizes exactly where current MLLMs fail — temporal dynamics — rather than a blanket capability claim. - The cost/efficiency analysis separates monetary cost, token consumption, and wall-clock time, exposing non-obvious inversions (cheap API but slow runtime for Qwen3.8-max/DeepSeek) rarely reported in benchmark papers. - Anti-gaming prompt constraints (no base64 imagery, no pixel dumps, no traced shapes, mandatory `seek()` timeline API) are carefully engineered to keep the task genuinely programmatic. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the benchmark covers only structured 2D content amenable to programmatic representation (excluding complex 3D viewpoints, textures, and dense pixel-level dynamics), that leading models still struggle with complex temporal dynamics, and that open-source models lag substantially. They acknowledge agentic workflows do not always improve fidelity. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility. Not stated: any discussion of judge-model circularity, annotation inter-annotator agreement, or the limited human validation sample size. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The retention judge (GPT-6-sol) is also an evaluated caption model; the human correlation study covers only 50 videos and 4 models, leaving open whether judge bias inflates GPT-family scores on the full benchmark. - The headline "code beats natural language" result is circular by construction: the benchmark selects videos that are code-representable, and the NL branch depends on a single text-to-video model (Seedance-2.5) whose own reconstruction ceiling is never characterized; on non-representable content the comparison could reverse. - No significance testing or variance reporting for any table, and IoU evaluation depends on GPT-6-sol locating objects in rendered videos — a second unvalidated model-in-the-loop step. - The QA comparison (100 questions, one answerer model) is small and confounds question style across three different source benchmarks. - No code/data release URL or license is explicitly stated beyond the project page, limiting reproducibility of the annotation pipeline, which involves model-assisted labeling with human review but no reported agreement metrics. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on video captioning evaluation or video-to-code generation should read this — it is the broadest benchmark yet for code-based video captioning with a well-validated (if model-mediated) metric and a genuinely useful dynamic-vs-static failure finding — but its headline code-beats-text conclusion should be trusted only within its deliberately code-friendly structured-2D scope, and it likely overlaps substantially with Animation2Code/BVB for readers already in that literature.

EMBODIEDSMITH: SCALING EMBODIED DATA THROUGH RECURSIVE SELF - IMPROVEMENT FLYWHEEL IN SIMULATION

TR SELF · openreview.net · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EmbodiedSmith, a simulation data-generation system that unifies asset, scene, and robot task generation in an agentic recursive self-improvement loop where scene and task generation iteratively refine each other to produce validated robot demonstrations. - Why it's important: Robotic foundation models are bottlenecked by the diversity-versus-hardware-alignment trade-off of real-world data, and simulation can break this only if generated environments actually support executable, physically valid tasks — which prior pipelines fail at, especially for long-horizon tasks and complex embodiments. - How it does it: The core mechanism is a coupled refinement loop: task planning grounds a Skill DAG against a generated scene, execution failures return targeted feedback that triggers schema-constrained scene edits or plan repairs, and the two generation stages converge on a feasible, validated task configuration. - The good: The demonstration-generation results are large and mechanistically supported by ablations — 67% average acceptance success rate versus 21% for both SceneSmith and EmbodiedGen V2 across 16 tasks, with the ablation showing that removing execution feedback collapses success to ~0%. - The missing: The perceptual evaluation relies on GPT-5.5 as the judge while the system itself is built on GPT-family agents, there is no real-robot transfer experiment, and the policy-training study uses only 20 hours of data on 10 tasks in 2 scenes despite motivating large-scale pretraining. - Read it or not: Read it if you build simulation data engines, embodied agent harnesses, or robot demo-generation pipelines and want the current design template for scene–task co-refinement; skip it if you want evidence that synthetic sim data actually improves real-world robot generalization, because that link is asserted rather than tested.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. The composite is pulled down by Completeness (50) and Resilience (50): the scaling and human-level-dexterity framing in the title is unsupported — humanoid and dexterous-hand results are showcase-only, the policy study covers 2 scenes and 20 hours with single seeds, there is no real-robot experiment of any kind, and the limitations are stated tersely without confronting LLM-judge circularity. Rigor (55) suffers from GPT-5.5 as judge for a GPT-family system and no code-release commitment. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Teams training robotic foundation models need training data that is simultaneously diverse, hardware-aligned, and scalable. Real teleoperation matches hardware but scales poorly; egocentric video is diverse but lacks action labels at the right embodiment; existing simulation generation pipelines generate scenes decoupled from task feasibility, rely on predefined assets and skills, and offer limited physics (no deformables/fluids) or embodiment coverage (no humanoids, dexterous hands, mobile manipulators). The consequence is that generated sim scenes often cannot support executable demonstrations — feasibility is discovered only at execution time and never fed back into scene design. The paper targets researchers building data engines and evaluation environments for generalist robot policies. Key Idea: The single core insight is to make scene generation and task generation bidirectional consumers of each other's failures: scenes are constructed with anticipation of downstream task requirements (reachability-validated placement, interaction constraints), and task-generation failures trigger targeted scene edits (repositioning, rescaling, asset replacement) rather than plan-only retries. This closed loop — plan, execute in simulation, diagnose, edit scene or plan, revalidate — is what the authors call the RSI flywheel, and it is what lets acceptance rates stay high even on long-horizon recall-style tasks. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Environment construction: an asset pool of validated open-source plus generated assets (retrieval, else SAM3D image-to-3D with adaptive convex decomposition, VLM-assigned physics parameters, resting/contact/perturbation tests); specialized generation for articulated (LLM-written construction programs revised on physics-validation feedback), deformable, and fluid assets. Scene generation parses a language specification plus task context and robot embodiment into a typed relational scene graph, instantiates nodes with assets, and solves layout hierarchically (Beam-DFS joint optimization over fixture compositions) enforcing collision, clearance, connectivity, and CuRobo-verified reachability, yielding an initial scene S0 = (G, O, X, Q). A schema-constrained Scene Edit module applies traceable, previewable edits. (2) Trajectory generation: a Task Plan Agent grounds the instruction to scene entities and atomic skills into a Skill DAG with checkable success conditions; a Harness orchestrates five tools (build, run, inspect, finish, revise) and drives compile checks, programmatic acceptance, independent VLM review, and repair-revalidation cycles. (3) Embodiment adapters: a 50 Hz adapter merges locomotion and arm commands into 29-DoF actions for the Unitree G1 humanoid; a contact solver with fail-closed contact contracts drives Sharpa Wave dexterous hands on Split ALOHA. The framework is an agentic LLM/VLM system (gpt-5.6-sol for the task agent) built on Isaac Sim 6.0.1 at 30 Hz, with CuRobo motion planning. Critical design decisions: freezing task-success criteria during refinement (prevents goal softening — well justified); decoupling open-ended semantic structuring (VLM) from deterministic geometric solving (layout solver — well justified by the COL/OOB results); confining embodiment specifics to adapters beneath the shared skill DAG (asserted for reusability, not ablated). Key Results: (1) Scene generation (20 indoor specs, 3 generations each, 5 baselines: Holodeck, LayoutVLM, SAGE, EmbodiedGen V2, SceneSmith): highest scores on Content/Function 7.13±1.48 (vs 5.57 best baseline, +28% relative), Spatial Layout 7.27, Physical Plausibility 7.68, Visual Quality 7.32; lowest collisions (0.29±0.35), zero out-of-bounds objects, NAV 0.9984, highest openness 0.9875. SceneSmith leads on Text Fidelity (8.92 vs 8.33). (2) Demonstration generation (16 tasks — 10 fixed-base, 6 mobile; 10 agent sessions/task, 10 held-out seeds): average ASR 67% (Top-5 76%) versus 21% for both SceneSmith and EmbodiedGen V2 with "+Planner"; mean VLM tokens 40,204 versus 137,062 and 91,061 — i.e., roughly 3× the success at ~⅓ the token cost of SceneSmith. Baselines fail outright on memory/recall long-horizon tasks (0–15%) where EmbodiedSmith reaches 51–93%. EmbodiedGen V2 cannot generate required articulated assets for several tasks (marked ✗). (3) Ablations: removing execution feedback collapses ASR to 4.0%/0.0%/0.0%/0.0% across fixed-short, fixed-long, mobile-short, mobile-long; removing placement validation drops fixed-long ASR from 71.6% to 13.2%. (4) Policy training: π0.5 and FastWAM fine-tuned on clean (20 h fixed layout) vs mixed (10 h clean + 10 h randomized) data; mixed training raises π0.5 average success from 34.2% to 45.5% and random-setting success from 7.2% to 40.2%; FastWAM averages remain low (15.3% vs 13.3%) with mixed better only marginally. Baselines in the scene comparison are current (2024–2026 systems including SceneSmith from ICML 2026 and EmbodiedGen V2), making this a reasonably strong comparison set. Notably, the humanoid and dexterous-hand results are showcase-only (Figure 6), not part of the quantitative benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW METHOD component. The genuinely novel element is the bidirectional scene–task co-refinement loop (task execution feedback driving schema-constrained scene edits, and scene constraints informing task grounding), which measurably improves acceptance rates. The individual components — VLM scene-graph parsing, Beam-DFS layout optimization, CuRobo planning, image-to-3D asset generation, agent-with-tools harnesses — are standard or existing ideas (several from the baselines themselves, e.g., SceneSmith's agentic refinement); the contribution is their integration and the coupling, not the parts. The RSI framing largely repackages agentic generate-validate-repair loops under a trendy name. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are informative (feedback and placement validation are shown to matter, and where). Error reporting is mean ± sample standard deviation across generations; no significance tests and no multiple-seed variance over the evaluation protocol itself are reported for the headline ASR numbers beyond the 10-seed evaluation design, which is reasonable. The held-out seed protocol (frozen candidate evaluated on 10 seeds excluded from refinement) is a good design against benchmark gaming. Two methodological concerns stand out: (a) the perceptual scene metrics are scored by GPT-5.5, a single LLM judge, while the system's own agents are GPT-family models — potential judge–system circularity and no human evaluation; (b) token-cost comparisons between systems with different capabilities are reported but wall-clock/compute cost is not. No public code, data, or weights URL is given; the reproducibility statement points to appendices and supplementary material only. The 20-scene and 16-task evaluation scales are modest. The downstream policy experiment (2 scenes, 10 tasks, 20 hours) is well-controlled within its scope (equal-duration clean vs mixed) but small. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built data-generation framework evaluated by generation quality, cost, and downstream policy training; the empirical policy experiments serve as validation of the artifact). Practical: Runs on Isaac Sim with GPT-family API models and standard GPU planning (CuRobo), so it is usable on commercially available hardware, though it depends on proprietary frontier LLM/VLM APIs. Efficient: Token cost is ~⅓ of SceneSmith per successful session (40,204 vs 137,062 mean VLM tokens) with higher yield, but the w/o-feedback ablation shows the efficiency comes precisely from the feedback machinery — the cost profile is not characterized beyond tokens (no GPU-hours, no per-demo wall-clock). Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem of generating executable, validated sim demonstrations (67% vs 21% ASR), but only a proxy for the ultimate goal of improving real-world robot generalization — all policy evaluation is in simulation. Scalable: Not tested; "scaling" is the title's claim, yet the largest experiment is 20 hours of data across 2 scenes, and 10×–100× data generation throughput, asset-pool growth, and failure-mode drift at scale are unexamined. The work delivers a system framework and validated datasets but no released artifact URL is stated in the provided text. Strengths: - The scene–task coupling is a real, non-obvious design move with direct evidence: the targeted-edit pathway converts environment-induced execution failures into scene fixes, which is why long-horizon recall tasks (e.g., Block Order Nav at 93% ASR) succeed where baselines score 0%. - The ablation design is unusually clean for a systems paper: removing feedback (→~0% ASR) and removing placement validation (→13.2% on fixed-long) isolates which parts of the loop carry the performance, and the token accounting includes failed sessions. - The evaluation protocol guards against Goodharting: success criteria are frozen during refinement, and final candidates are re-executed on 10 held-out seeds excluded from generation. - Breadth of physical and embodiment coverage (articulated, deformable, fluid assets; mobile manipulation; humanoid and dexterous-hand adapters) in a single generation loop exceeds what the compared baselines support, and per-task tables honestly report unsupported tasks (✗) and mobile-vs-fixed failure asymmetries (Open Drawer degrading from fixed to mobile). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that mobile tasks show a different success profile than fixed-base (navigation can compensate for placement but not for joint-constrained motions like drawer opening), that baselines vary in asset support, and in the ethics statement that generated demonstrations "should not be assumed to be safe for direct deployment on physical robots without additional hardware-specific validation." The limitations are stated tersely; the paper does not contain a dedicated limitations section confronting, e.g., LLM-judge circularity, the sim-only policy evaluation, or the small data scale. The reproducibility statement is detailed about what is documented but does not commit to a code release. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - LLM-judge circularity and subjectivity: GPT-5.5 assigns the perceptual scene scores (the largest claimed margins, e.g., +28% CF), with no human raters, no inter-rater check, and a judge plausibly correlated with the models used inside the system. - No real-robot experiment of any kind: the entire value proposition — better generalist policies — is evaluated only in simulation, and the sim-to-real gap that the deformable/fluid and high-fidelity rendering features are meant to narrow is never measured (the authors even cite a physical-fidelity benchmark, GAUGE, without using it). - The policy study confounds data diversity with data content: the "mixed" dataset differs from "clean" in randomization only, which is the right control, but it covers 2 scenes and 10 tasks with a single training seed per condition and no confidence intervals, and FastWAM results (15.3% vs 13.3% average) show the effect is model-dependent. - The humanoid and dexterous-hand capabilities — heavily advertised in the title-adjacent framing as "human-level dexterity" — contribute zero quantitative results; they appear only as showcase figures, so their reliability relative to the fixed-base benchmark is unknown. - Token cost is the only efficiency metric; frontier-model API dependence, retry depth (up to 30 refinement rounds), and the fraction of sessions that hit budget are not reported, leaving the true cost per accepted demonstration unclear. - Deformable and fluid assets are described in the method but are absent from every quantitative table; no task or metric exercises them. Bottom Line: This is the strongest currently documented design for scene–task co-generative demonstration pipelines and worth reading closely if you are building one, but its headline claims about scaling and human-level dexterity outrun the evidence, which remains confined to 16 sim tasks, an LLM judge, and 20 hours of synthetic data with no real-robot validation.

R-IDEAL: Reinforcing Insight-Driven Experience for Agent Learning

W Hong, X Zhou, Y Xu, J Yu, S Yang, S Gao, W Xu · aclanthology.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces R-IDEAL, a framework that trains a lightweight 8B "Insight Model" to generate structured guidance (Plans + negative Lessons) for LLM agents via SFT on contrastively synthesized insights and GRPO reinforcement learning against real environment feedback. - Why it's important: Agents fail at long-horizon interactive tasks through repeated trial-and-error and hallucinated guidance; existing experience-learning methods either lock knowledge into weights (untransferable, inapplicable to closed-source models) or retrieve static rules that are not grounded in execution. - How it does it: Contrast successful vs. failed trajectories from the target agent's own environment to synthesize Plan/Lesson pairs, SFT a generator on them, then optimize with GRPO using a hybrid reward (format gating, utility summed over heterogeneous 7–8B agents, path-efficiency bonus, length penalty) so insights transfer across models. - The good: The GPT-5 control (Table 2) is the most convincing evidence: directly prompted GPT-5 insights lift Llama-3.1-8B only to 38.8% average success on AlfWorld, while the environment-grounded 8B Insight Model reaches 93.8%, cleanly isolating the value of trajectory grounding and RL. - The missing: Evaluation is confined to two text-based simulation environments whose training tasks overlap the evaluation distribution; there are no error bars or significance tests, no public code release mentioned, and the headline gains (~60-point jumps over strong baselines) are large enough to warrant independent replication. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building explicit-experience or agent-guidance systems — the heterogeneous-feedback reward and Plan/Lesson ablations are directly reusable — but practitioners seeking deployable web/SWE agents should note the authors' own admission that the method is unvalidated outside text-based discrete environments.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (46) and Practical Impact (35) pull the composite down: the RL reward optimizes exactly the reported metric on the same two environments (severe Goodhart exposure), no significance tests accompany the 1–3 point ablation deltas carrying the component story, and no code, data, or checkpoint release is mentioned. The headline 50–60 point jumps over baselines are large enough to demand external replication. Novelty (62) is moderate — RL-tuning an insight generator against heterogeneous-agent execution feedback is a genuine recombination — and the GPT-5 control (Non-Obviousness 60) is a well-designed experiment answering the obvious objection. Completeness (64) is aided by candid scope limitations. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*46 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*64 + 0.15*52 + 0.10*35 = 54.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks (household, scientific simulation) must convert interaction experience into reusable guidance. Two prior paradigms fall short: (1) implicit methods (AgentTuning, ETO, DPO-style training) couple experience to model weights, blocking transfer across architectures and excluding closed-source models that cannot be fine-tuned; (2) explicit methods (ExpeL, AutoManual, AutoGuide) extract guidance from successful trajectories only, ignore failures, and retrieve from external experience pools without environmental grounding, producing "guidance hallucinations" — plausible suggestions that are not executable. The paper targets researchers building transferable, interpretable agent-improvement modules that work without fine-tuning large or proprietary agents. Key Idea: Convert raw agent trajectories into a structured insight format — a positive Plan (shortest successful trajectory abstracted into steps) plus negative Lessons (rules extracted by contrasting the optimal trajectory against each failure) — and then, crucially, treat the insight generator as a policy to be RL-tuned: the reward for an insight is its measured utility when executed by a set of heterogeneous small agents in the real environment, which suppresses insights that only sound plausible and filters model-specific "shortcuts." Methodology: Three stages. (1) Data Construction: for each task instruction, sample N trajectories with the target agent (Llama-3.1-8B, temperature 0.8, 4 samples); select the fewest-step successful trajectory as optimal; a teacher (Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507) induces a general Plan from it, and generates one Lesson per (success, failure) pair, followed by prompt-based semantic deduplication (Eq. 2). (2) SFT: full fine-tuning of the Insight Model on (instruction → [P; L]) pairs with standard autoregressive loss (Eq. 3), constraining generation from the instruction alone. (3) RL with GRPO (DeepSeekMath-style, group size 8, KL-regularized against the SFT policy): the hybrid reward R = R_utility − β_len·r_len applies a −1.0 format gate (XML <workflow>/<lessons> tags), sums per heterogeneous model (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) of environment reward plus a 0.25-weighted step-efficiency bonus (only on success), and a piecewise length penalty (soft 512, hard 2048 tokens, β_len = 0.25). At inference, the Insight Model emits insights from the task instruction and they are text-concatenated onto any agent's prompt — no retrieval database, no agent fine-tuning. Critical design decisions: heterogeneous-model reward (well justified by a dedicated +1.6-point ablation), efficiency reward (justified by +2.9 points and step-count reduction), and instruction-only insight generation (justified by the trajectory-contrast ablation showing direct generation collapses to 20.9% on unseen tasks vs. 62.9% with contrast). Key Results: On AlfWorld (140 seen / 134 unseen tasks) and SciWorld (194 seen / 211 unseen), reporting average reward over three runs: Llama-3.1-8B agent improves from 35.3 (ReAct baseline) to 86.2 with R-IDEAL, beating the strongest prior baseline MPO (53.6) by 32.6 points; GPT-4o rises 69.6 → 89.3; Llama-3.1-70B rises 73.8 → 90.9, reaching 99.5 on AlfWorld Unseen (+25.6 over MPO). On trained agents, ETO+R-IDEAL reaches 91.5 average vs. 82.1 for ETO+MPO. The GPT-5 insight-generation control scores 38.8 vs. R-IDEAL's 93.8 with the same 8B executor. Ablations: removing Plan at inference drops AlfWorld to 70.3 vs. 91.0 for removing Lessons (Plans matter more); RL ablations give 92.8 (single model, binary reward) → 94.4 (add Qwen) → 97.3 (add efficiency reward); trajectory contrast is essential post-SFT (58.3 vs. 24.8 without). Invalid-action rates on AlfWorld drop from 49.56 (baseline) to 14.03 with full R-IDEAL, and successful-episode step counts drop by roughly 2–5 steps versus the MPO baseline. Baselines (MPO 2025, ETO 2024, KnowAgent, WKM, AgentTuning) are recent and relevant, though results come from the authors' own runs under their evaluation harness. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component. Genuinely novel: optimizing an explicit textual-guidance generator with RL against heterogeneous-agent execution feedback, plus the Plan/Lesson structure with training-time vs. inference-time ablation of each. Standard components: GRPO, SFT-then-RL pipeline, trajectory contrast for data synthesis, and the general idea of learning from failures all exist; the combination applied to insight generation is the contribution, not any single ingredient. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for this venue segment — Plan/Lesson removal at both training and inference time, each reward component, and a teacher-controlled trajectory-contrast ablation — and results are averaged over three runs with temperature-0 decoding. However, no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported; the ±1–3 point component gains in Table 4 are not shown to be significant. No public code, data, or model release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (a) the Insight Model is trained and RL-tuned on tasks from the same environments it is evaluated on — the seen/unseen split varies task instances but not environment dynamics, so Goodhart-style overfitting to AlfWorld/SciWorld specifics cannot be ruled out; (b) the RL reward optimizes exactly the metric reported (task success via heterogeneous agents), so near-ceiling scores may partly reflect reward optimization on the benchmark rather than transferable insight quality; (c) headline deltas of 50–60 points over baselines are exceptional and deserve external replication; (d) the efficiency-reward condition conflates a reward change with an added reward signal, and the claim that one extra model call is offset by fewer steps is asserted from step counts without wall-clock or token-cost measurement. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored plug-and-play module). - Practical: Yes — the Insight Model is an 8B model on commodity hardware, and inference adds one text-generation call per task; no exotic infrastructure. - Efficient: RL training requires rolling out two 7–8B agents per insight sample (group size 8, batch 64), a non-trivial but moderate cost; at inference, the paper claims step reductions offset the extra call, but no measured runtime or token-cost comparison is given. - Effective: Strong proxy evidence — success rate, step counts, and invalid-action rates all improve on the tested benchmarks — but only on two text-game simulators, so real-world effectiveness is unproven. - Scalable: Not tested — the authors acknowledge insights become static after training and may go stale in stochastic novel environments; behavior on larger action spaces (web, SWE) is explicitly flagged as open. The work delivers a method and trained-model recipe but ships no software artifact, dataset release, or checkpoint (none is mentioned). Strengths: (1) The GPT-5 insight-generation control directly answers the obvious "why not just prompt a frontier model?" objection with data (38.8 vs. 93.8), a comparison most experience-learning papers omit. (2) The heterogeneous-utility reward is a clean, mechanistically plausible mechanism for cross-model generalization, and its contribution is isolated by ablation (+1.6 points). (3) The Plan/Lesson decomposition with matched training-time and inference-time ablations establishes which part of the structured insight carries which benefit (Plan drives success, Lessons drive OOD robustness). (4) Demonstrated small-to-large transfer — an 8B generator improving a 70B agent and GPT-4o without fine-tuning them — is a practically meaningful deployment property. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (a) validation is restricted to text-based discrete-decision environments, with larger-action-space domains like SWE-bench and open-ended web research left as open problems; and (b) insights are fixed after training, so in stochastic novel environments they may become invalid, with dynamic insight updating left to future work. This is a candid, direct confrontation of the two most obvious scope limits — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The RL reward optimizes exactly the evaluation metric on the same environments, so the near-perfect seen-task scores may reflect benchmark-specific reward hacking rather than generalizable insight quality; no held-out environment (a third simulator) is used to test transfer. (2) No significance testing or variance reporting accompanies the 1–3 point ablation deltas that carry the component-analysis story. (3) The efficiency analysis counts steps but never measures latency or token cost, so the "cost-effective" claim is unevaluated. (4) The trajectory-contrast ablation uses a different teacher (Qwen3-235B) than the main pipeline implies, and the contribution of teacher strength vs. contrastive construction is not fully disentangled. (5) No release of code or the trained Insight Model is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of a system whose value lies in replication across environments. (6) Insight generation is zero-shot per task; whether the 8B generator degrades on task types far from the training distribution is untested beyond two related simulators. Bottom Line: For researchers in explicit agent-experience learning, this is a worthwhile read for its heterogeneous-execution-feedback reward design and unusually well-isolated ablations, but the evidence base — two text simulators, no significance tests, no artifact release, and reward optimized on the evaluation metric — means the spectacular headline numbers should be treated as promising rather than established.

Exploring Recurrent-Depth Language Models for Multitask Clinical Text Processing

X Yang, G Liu, C Peng, K Smith, Y Zhang, X He, Y Guo… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents the first systematic evaluation of pretrained recurrent-depth language models (Ouro looped models, HRM-Text hierarchical recurrent model) against standard Qwen3 transformers after joint multitask fine-tuning on 9 clinical NLP datasets, tested on 13 benchmarks total. - Why it's important: Clinical NLP teams deploy many task-specific models over sensitive EHR text; a small unified model that matches larger ones reduces maintenance cost and latency, and latent reasoning avoids chain-of-thought prompts that a cited systematic study found hurt 86.3% of 95 LLMs on clinical text tasks. - How it does it: All tasks are cast as text-to-text JSON generation, one unified model per checkpoint is fine-tuned on merged data, and recurrent-depth models add inference-time computation by re-applying shared layers (Ouro: 4 fixed steps; HRM-Text: 2 high-level cycles of low-level updates) instead of emitting reasoning text. - The good: Ouro-1.4B-Thinking beat Qwen3-1.7B on 11 of 13 dataset-level comparisons and Ouro-2.6B-Thinking matched or beat Qwen3-8B (e.g., MedQA 0.6127 vs 0.5734, MMLU-Pro Health 0.5456 vs 0.5067) despite 3× fewer parameters and 5× fewer pretraining tokens. - The missing: Each configuration was trained exactly once with no seeds, no significance tests, and no control for pretraining data, so single-run score differences of 0.01–0.07 across architecture families with 5× different pretraining corpora cannot be attributed to recurrence. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or deploy small models for clinical NLP and want the first benchmark-style evidence on looped/recurrent architectures in this domain; skip it if you want a controlled architectural study — the authors themselves say that remains future work.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (52) and Rigor (48) jointly pull the composite down: this is a competent application-evaluation of externally released architectures to a new domain, with each configuration trained exactly once, no seeds or significance tests, no recurrent-depth ablation (the paper's central variable is never isolated), and massive pretraining-corpus confounds (36T vs 40B tokens) that the authors acknowledge but cannot remove. Completeness (70) is a genuine positive — the limitation section is among the most candid at this tier, including the pipeline round-trip calibration — and Resilience (60) is moderate because claims are framed as descriptive rather than causal. Impact (45) is low: no released weights, no latency or cost measurements for the very efficiency claims motivating the work, and code only promised. Weighted composite: 0.20*52 + 0.25*48 + 0.15*50 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*45 = 54.
