Problem & Motivation: Manufacturers, infrastructure providers, and service organizations face a tension between emissions targets and constrained resources, and are increasingly positioning AI/IoT/analytics as core sustainability tools. However, the evidence base is fragmented across separate research tracks (AI-for-sustainability, IoT-monitoring, operations analytics), and prior reviews are criticized for treating these technologies as uniformly beneficial without addressing boundary conditions, baseline variability, life-cycle costs of the digital infrastructure itself, or the traceability of quantitative claims. Practitioners and researchers need to know not just whether digital technologies help sustainability (already established, per the authors) but under what conditions, with what measured magnitude, and with what unmeasured trade-offs — a question this review addresses as an evidence map rather than an effect-size estimate. Key Idea: The core move is methodological discipline over synthesis ambition: rather than pooling heterogeneous percentage savings into a (statistically meaningless) headline number, every quantitative claim is traced to a named primary study with its own baseline and system boundary, and the review's conceptual output (the DOS framework) is framed explicitly as falsifiable propositions (P1–P5) rather than validated relationships. The one substantive theoretical differentiator claimed versus the TOE framework is treating sustainability outcomes as a domain with its own feedback loop into technology selection and governance (P2, P4), rather than as an external contingency. Methodology: The review follows PRISMA 2020: (1) identification — 420 records from Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ScienceDirect, and IEEE Xplore (search executed 15 March 2026; peer-reviewed English journal articles, January 2023–March 2026); (2) deduplication — 110 removed; (3) title/abstract screening — 310 screened, 215 excluded; (4) full-text eligibility — 95 assessed, 53 excluded; 42 studies retained for narrative synthesis. A structured extraction template captured sector, technology, research design, implementation scale, exact metrics with baseline and system boundary, and stated limitations. Quality appraisal used a custom four-dimension rubric (0–2 per dimension, 0–8 total, informed by but not identical to MMAT); low-scoring studies were retained but flagged. Meta-analysis was deliberately rejected because studies lack a common estimand, baseline, or variance structure — so no I²/τ², no pooled estimate, and no cross-study range is reported. Critical design decisions: (a) single-reviewer execution with a documented second full-text pass as partial mitigation — acknowledged as the most important limitation and not substituted for dual review; (b) strict segregation of the 42-study core evidence base from contextual citations (industry reports, preprints, IEA statistics) used in the trade-off sections (9.4–9.8) — well-justified and explicitly disclosed; (c) a custom quality rubric instead of a standard instrument — reasonable given the heterogeneous designs, but unvalidated. Key Results: Because the design precludes pooling, results are study-level observations: a physics-guided neural network with gradient aggregation reduced energy consumption 4.21% across two industrial case studies (Bardeeniz et al.); digital-twin-based AGV scheduling in a plant factory reduced AGV energy 7.62% under energy constraints (Dai et al.); IIoT energy/compressed-air monitoring on a single turret punch press at Mitsubishi Electric (Scotland) recorded a 51.5% energy reduction (6,783→3,293 kWh) and 83.34% compressed-air reduction over three months, with the authors of that study noting an unusually high April baseline and operator shutdown instructions as contributors, and no variance reported; an XGBoost model on ~1,100 pelleting-press batches with 67 features predicted (not measured) 6.0% energy-consumption and 5.3% energy-cost reductions and 21.0% fewer overutilization events. Section 7.3 reports sector-specific ranges attributed to secondary sources (raw-material reductions ~5–20%, structural material ~10–30%, recycling-rate improvements ~15–25%), which is inconsistent with the review's own no-untraceable-ranges discipline. Firm-level econometric evidence (Chinese manufacturers) shows AI's effect on energy intensity varies by region, sector, and firm characteristics. Scale of the evidence base: mostly pilots, simulations, and single-site case studies; virtually no longitudinal full-scale deployments. There is no conventional baseline comparison here — the comparison class is prior reviews, against which this one distinguishes itself by source traceability and explicit refusal to generalize. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (an evidence-reporting discipline: per-claim source tracing with explicit non-poolability) plus a conceptual framework proposal; no new method, dataset, or empirical finding of the paper's own. What is genuinely novel is the deliberate refusal to report cross-study percentages and the transparent labeling of each figure's evidentiary status; the technology taxonomy (IoT sensing → AI/analytics → decision loop), the adoption-barrier discussion, and the trade-off catalog (rebound, e-waste, data-center water/energy, digital divide, critical minerals) are standard combinations of existing literature applied to a 2023–2026 corpus. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations apply (this is a review). No inter-rater reliability exists by construction; no second reviewer; protocol not registered in PROSPERO/OSF. The PRISMA counts are internally consistent and reconciled across three places in the manuscript, but per-database counts and reason-level exclusion counts were not preserved — the paper says so explicitly rather than fabricating them, which is honest but leaves the screening audit trail weak. Boolean strings are reported verbatim in Appendix A, and a quality-appraisal rubric in Appendix C; however, the completed 42-study extraction record is stated to be missing from the manuscript and 'should be provided as supplementary material' — it is not included, so Section 7 claims cannot currently be traced to a systematic extraction artifact. Methodological red flags a reviewer would note: development of a custom quality rubric applied by its own designer; the paper reads like a revised manuscript responding to prior referee comments (phrases like 'to be confirmed by the authors against the eligibility record'), leaving unresolved internal inconsistencies (e.g., Section 7.3's untraceable ranges, the unresolved status of two Table 1 studies). No code/data release is applicable; the data-availability statement says no datasets were generated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS-adjacent EMPIRICAL — it is a literature-synthesis artifact rather than a deployed tool, so the check is applied to the review as an artifact. - Practical: Yes — a review requires no hardware and is openly accessible under CC BY-NC-ND. - Efficient: Not applicable in a compute sense; the relevant cost is the missing dual-reviewer labor, which is precisely the corner cut. - Effective: It solves the stated narrow problem (a source-traced, boundary-aware evidence map) but explicitly fails to deliver generalizable effect sizes, by design and by necessity. - Scalable: Not tested — the single-reviewer process would be the bottleneck for a larger corpus, and the paper itself calls for a dual-reviewer, prospectively registered replication rather than claiming scalability. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or reusable tool; its outputs are the paper, Table 1's traceable claims, and the DOS framework's five propositions. Strengths: - Exceptional evidentiary candor: the paper states its own most damaging limitation (single-reviewer design, no kappa, no registration) in the abstract, Section 2.1, Section 7's preamble, and a dedicated Section 11.7 'stated here without qualification' — this level of self-scrutiny is rare and materially aids correct citation. - The source-tracing discipline (Table 1) is a real methodological contribution to a literature plagued by recycled, untraceable percentages; the paper even reports it removed earlier-draft ranges that could not be traced to primary sources. - The refusal to pool heterogeneous percentages (Section 2.7) is statistically correct and explicitly reasoned, not an omission. - Trade-offs (rebound, e-waste, data-center water/energy, labor, digital divide, critical minerals) are treated as first-class content with careful distinction between core-evidence findings and adjacent context, and the DOS propositions P1–P5 are operationalizable and falsifiable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensively acknowledged, arguably to a fault: single-reviewer screening/extraction/appraisal with no inter-rater statistic; no prospective protocol registration; restriction to four databases, English-language journal articles only (under-representing SMEs and developing economies); geographic/organizational skew of quantitative evidence toward well-resourced settings; heterogeneity precluding meta-analysis; Sections 9.4–9.8 resting on non-peer-reviewed and preprint sources outside the core evidence base; the DOS framework being unvalidated conceptual mapping. The authors confront limitations directly and repeatedly — the strongest credibility feature of the paper. They do not minimize; if anything they over-flag. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The manuscript carries visible scars of a prior review cycle (instructions to the authors to 'confirm' inclusion status and supply the extraction record remain unresolved in the text), meaning the published artifact is internally incomplete: the 42-study extraction record and reason-level exclusion counts are absent, so the PRISMA process cannot be audited. - Section 7.3 violates the paper's own traceability rule by citing 5–20%, 10–30%, and 15–25% ranges attributed to secondary sources — the exact practice the paper criticizes. - Two of the four quantitative anchors in the abstract (Hanifi et al.; Ekwaro-Osire et al.) have explicitly unresolved inclusion status against the 42-study set, so the headline numbers partially rest on studies outside the verified corpus. - The DOS framework's five propositions are plausible but thin: P1–P5 largely restate socio-technical and adoption-theory commonplaces, and the claimed point of difference from TOE (feedback loop from outcomes to technology selection) is asserted, not derived. - No grey literature, conference papers, or industry deployment reports were searched despite the review's practitioner-facing framing — the most relevant real-deployment evidence may live exactly where the search excludes it. - The quality rubric's scoring distribution across the 42 studies is never reported, so the reader cannot tell how much of the evidence base is low-confidence. Bottom Line: This is a methodologically self-aware but structurally hobbled evidence map — read it as a candid first-pass synthesis and a source of verifiable per-study data points and testable propositions, but anyone needing a defensible quantitative synthesis of digital technologies for sustainable operations should wait for, or conduct, the dual-reviewer registered replication the authors themselves call for.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Logic Tree, a DAG-based agentic framework for deep research tasks that decomposes queries into parallel execution branches and recovers from failures via two-level self-correction: local backtracking to a faulty node's state and global replanning with knowledge sanitation of failed trajectories. - Why it's important: Sequential ReAct-style agents accumulate errors over long-horizon information-seeking tasks, producing hallucination cascades and irreversible dead ends; a recoverable execution structure targets robustness where it matters most for deployed research agents. - How it does it: A Planner builds a dependency-annotated DAG of search/process nodes, an Orchestrator schedules ready (in-degree-zero) nodes in parallel, and a Judge arbitrates backtrack/replan/answer signals, with a Sanitation Agent distilling verified facts from failed trajectories into the next planning round. - The good: The framework comparison with a fixed backbone (GLM-4.6) is the most convincing evidence: Logic Tree reaches 53.94 on GAIA versus 49.70 (ReAct), 45.45 (Plan-and-Solve), and 32.73 (Flash-Searcher), showing that DAG parallelism alone (Flash-Searcher) is worse than parallelism plus recovery. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported on stochastic web benchmarks, no code release is stated, and BrowseComp-EN uses only a 300-instance sample, so the headline gains carry wide unknown uncertainty. - Read it or not: Worth reading for agent-architecture researchers and builders of deep-research systems, since the Judge-mediated rollback/sanitation design and the negative result that prompt-only orchestration hurts small models are directly transferable lessons; skip it if you only want a new algorithm with theoretical guarantees.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building LLM agents for open-ended, multi-step information-seeking ("deep research") face error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning: a single early wrong step in a sequential ReAct trajectory cascades, and fixed plan-and-execute methods cannot revise intermediate failures. Prior structural approaches are either linear (ReAct), static plans (Plan-and-Solve), or DAG-parallel without recovery (Flash-Searcher), so none can prune invalid branches or restructure the execution graph mid-run. The paper targets the gap of a dynamically evolving, recoverable execution topology for tool-using research agents. Key Idea: Reformulate agent execution as a dynamically evolving DAG in which failure recovery is a graph operation: a backtrack signal triggers a cascade reset of the faulty node and all its topological descendants (states reverted to PENDING with failure reasons injected as retry history), while global replanning preserves only evidence-verified facts from the failed trajectory ("knowledge sanitation") into the new plan context. The Judge node that validates or blocks worker-issued control signals is the mechanism that keeps this self-correction from degenerating into thrashing. Methodology: The framework is a prompt-separated multi-role system over one model backbone: a RollbackPlanner generates an initial DAG G_init (choosing multi-entity decoupling vs. single-entity feature-cross strategies), a Plan Critic rejects shallow topologies (e.g., no edges or no process nodes), an Orchestrator schedules ready nodes V_ready = {v pending with all predecessors COMPLETED} onto a ThreadPoolExecutor, Workers execute search/process nodes and emit control signals, and a Judge maps each signal to {ANSWER, VALID_BACKTRACK, INVALID_BACKTRACK, REPLAN} against the execution log. Recovery is budgeted: four local backtracks per rollout, the fifth request converts to a global replan; at most five global replans and 100 controller steps, after which final-attempt mode forces an answer. Context assembly per node concatenates sanitized prior knowledge K_prior, the query, direct parents' outputs, and targeted feedback (Eq. 4). Key design decisions: (1) the Judge's strict node-ID matching for backtracks — justified by loop prevention but shown in the paper's own case study III to be brittle; (2) budgeted recovery limits — reasonable but essentially hand-tuned; (3) knowledge sanitation before replanning — intuitively motivated and illustrated, but the filtering is LLM-based and unquantified. Key Results: Zero-shot, Logic Tree lifts DeepSeek-V3.2 from 35.67 to 50.00 on BrowseComp-EN (+14.33), with +9.23 on BrowseComp-ZH and +3.84 on GAIA; GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 gain +3.8 to +6.3 points on BrowseComp subsets. With GLM-4.6 fixed across frameworks, Logic Tree scores 61.00/40.00/53.94 on XBench-2505/XBench-2510/GAIA versus ReAct (57.0/37.0/49.7), Plan-and-Solve (55.0/39.0/45.5), and Flash-Searcher (47.0/34.0/32.7) — notably, Flash-Searcher underperforms even ReAct on GAIA. Ablations (GLM-4.6): removing dynamic backtracking costs 9.09 points on GAIA (53.94→44.85), removing DAG planning costs 7.00 on XBench-2505 (61.00→54.00). SFT on Logic Tree trajectories raises Qwen3-4B macro-average from 9.14 (base) to 23.09 and Qwen3-30B from 11.98 to 28.94, while prompt-only orchestration hurts both models (5.84 and 10.85). A matched 495-query efficiency study shows accuracy 54.5% vs. 48.5% for ReAct with a shorter median latency (179s vs. 195s) and comparable median tokens (869 vs. 820), but a heavier tail (mean 629s vs. 518s; P95 3,122s vs. 1,828s). Baselines are recent and reasonably chosen, though BrowseComp-EN is only a 300-instance subsample and baselines were re-run by the authors rather than compared against published leaderboard numbers. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely new element is the integration of graph-structural recovery operators (descendant-set cascade reset, evidence-filtered knowledge sanitation, Judge-arbitrated control signals) into a DAG executor; DAG planning itself and LLM self-correction are each established ideas, and the primary novelty claim relative to Flash-Searcher is the dynamic-recovery layer rather than parallel execution. The SFT trajectory-synthesis angle is a competent but standard reuse of an agent framework as a data generator. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and cleanly isolate the two structural components (DAG planning vs. backtracking), and the matched query-run cost analysis (990 trajectories, full latency/token distributions in the appendix) is above the norm for agent papers. However: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported despite acknowledged non-determinism (web environment drift, model API updates, temperature 0.6); BrowseComp-EN is a 300-instance subsample; GAIA and XBench item counts are not stated; no code, prompts are included (fully in Appendix A.2) but no repository or artifact release is mentioned. The framework comparison on XBench/GAIA uses only one backbone (GLM-4.6), and the cross-model results in Figure 3 lack per-benchmark tables in the main text, making exact numbers hard to audit. No Goodhart-style train/eval contamination exists (no training on the eval benchmarks; SFT data synthesis is separate), but the sanitation agent's precision/recall is never measured. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built orchestration system evaluated by benchmark runs). Practical: Runs on a standard OpenAI-compatible API plus ThreadPoolExecutor, so any commercial LLM endpoint suffices. Efficient: Median latency and token cost are comparable to ReAct (179s vs. 195s; 869 vs. 820 tokens), but P95 latency grows ~71% (3,122s vs. 1,828s) and 4.3% of runs exceed one hour. Effective: The evidence (framework-controlled comparison, ablations) supports solving the stated robustness problem on web benchmarks, though gains on stochastic web evals carry unquantified variance. Scalable: Not tested beyond standard benchmark scale; long-tail latency and the authors' own replanning-loop failure case suggest costs grow super-linearly on hard instances. Deliverable: paper with complete system prompts; no code or model release is stated. Strengths: (1) The controlled framework comparison isolating execution paradigm with one fixed backbone, showing Flash-Searcher's DAG parallelism without recovery degrades to 32.73 on GAIA, is a genuinely informative negative result about aggressive parallelism. (2) The Judge mechanism addressing worker-hallucinated backtracks is a non-obvious control-flow design point, backed by execution-log evidence. (3) The finding that prompt-only orchestration transfers negatively to 4B/30B models while trajectory SFT yields large gains (9.14→23.09 macro on Qwen3-4B) is a useful, actionable insight. (4) Unusually candid failure analysis: Case Study III dissects a full failure trace with token exhaustion and brittle backtrack rejection. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state higher token consumption and inference latency versus single-pass paradigms, and that in hostile environments (paywalls, unresponsive endpoints) self-correction can over-trigger into redundant replanning loops rather than aborting gracefully. They also acknowledge evaluation variance from dynamic web environments and silent model updates. They confront limitations directly, including a dedicated failure case study (A.3.3) and a dual-use/termination discussion — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No statistical treatment of results on inherently noisy web benchmarks — the claimed consistency across models could partly reflect run-to-run variance; multiple runs per configuration are not reported. (2) The Judge, Critic, and Sanitation Agent are all same-backbone LLM calls, so framework gains may conflate with the backbone's own arbitration ability; no weaker-backbone Judge ablation exists. (3) Knowledge sanitation quality (retained-fact correctness) is never quantified; a sanitizer that keeps a wrong "verified" fact could be worse than clean replanning. (4) Budget constants (4 local backtracks, 5 replans, 100 steps) are hand-set with no sensitivity analysis. (5) Cross-model results are reported in a figure without per-item tables, hindering verification, and the published leaderboard context for the baselines is not established. (6) The 67.2% under-five-minutes / long-tail statistics come from a single deployment profile; no analysis of how budgets interact with benchmark difficulty. Bottom Line: A practitioner building long-horizon research agents should read this for its recoverable-DAG design and the sharp evidence that parallelism without rollback is worse than sequential execution, but should treat the headline numbers as directionally (not precisely) supportive given absent uncertainty quantification and no released code.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds and releases an open-source tool, PMU Foundation Model Bridge, that connects live C37.118 synchrophasor streams (PMU/PDC) to four public time series foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, TimesFM-3, Timestral) for online forecasting with file and streaming outputs. - Why it's important: Power systems researchers who want to apply zero-shot foundation-model forecasting to grid measurements currently have to hand-build the glue code for out-of-order samples, data-quality gating, latency management, and C37.118 output framing; this tool removes that barrier. - How it does it: A persistent worker runtime buffers measurements sorted by measurement time, applies quality checks and optional user-defined Python preprocessing, calls a fixed TSFM on each eligible history window, and republishes selected forecast leads as analog channels in a C37.118 output stream with explicit reference/target timestamping. - The good: The timing validation is concrete and honest: on a live 10 samples/s laboratory FDR stream, computation finished 0.39–0.69 s after reference (median 0.60 s) and local TCP send 0.41–0.76 s (median 0.64 s), leaving 0.24–0.59 s of margin before the 1 s forecast target in every send. - The missing: There is no quantitative forecast accuracy evaluation at all — no RMSE/MAE, no baseline comparison, and only TimesFM 2.5 (of the four supported models) is exercised in the validation runs. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on synchrophasor analytics or grid streaming infrastructure and want to adopt or extend this tool; skip it if you want evidence that TSFMs forecast power-system signals well, because that question is not evaluated here.

Problem & Motivation: Forecasting fast grid dynamics from PMU measurements (e.g., predicting system state when communication delays leave gaps, or post-disturbance dynamics) has traditionally used task-specific statistical or deep-learning models that require per-task training. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) offer zero-shot forecasting without task-specific fitting, but integrating them with online synchrophasor pipelines is nontrivial: measurements arrive out of order, contain missing/invalid/unsynchronized data, inference latency is variable, and downstream C37.118-based applications need unambiguous timestamp and channel semantics for forecast outputs. The stated audience is the power systems research community, which currently lacks a reusable connector between PMU/PDC streams and TSFMs. Key Idea: The core move is treating a forecast as a first-class timed record in a streaming pipeline: each forecast carries an explicit reference time (last input sample), per-lead target times (tr + k∆), and completion/send times, so that timeliness can be checked (remaining lead ℓ > 0) and forecasts can be republished as fixed-lead analog channels in a standard C37.118 stream with a mapping record for downstream interpretation. This timing formalism, plus a latest-window-wins policy (a newer eligible window replaces a still-waiting one when inference is slower than the call interval), is the paper's main intellectual content; the rest is competent systems integration. Methodology: The system is a shared runtime with: (1) a receiver/decoder that stores selected channels with measurement times, reception times, and quality flags in a fixed-capacity buffer, sorting by measurement time and discarding duplicates/late samples; (2) window assembly with a short out-of-order wait, rounded-timestamp matching against expected times (bounded tolerance, unique matches required), and quality gating that skips windows with missing/nonfinite/invalid/unsynchronized data (with optional user-enabled repair); (3) an optional user Python preprocessing function that derives custom channels (with an optional inverse transform to restore scale/units); (4) a persistent single-job worker process that loads one of four TSFMs once and produces per-channel independent H-step point forecasts (median); and (5) file (CSV + metadata + events) and network outputs that emit C37.118 frames with forecast leads in floating-point analog channels, FREQ/DFREQ passthrough, and a status flag for modified data. Supervision includes monotonic-clock timeouts, memory limits with worker restart (bounded retries), history clearing on reconnection, and bounded per-client queues with disconnect on overflow. Design decisions: per-channel univariate forecasting (justified as simplification; covariates/joint multivariate deferred), latest-window-wins scheduling (reasonable for recency-critical streaming, but silently drops older windows), and C37.118 analog-channel repurposing for forecast leads (clever reuse of an existing standard, though it modifies data flagged only by a status bit). Key Results: Validation is functional, not comparative. Test 1 (virtual PMU, same workstation, TimesFM 2.5): forecast stream was correctly parsed by PMU Connection Tester, confirming end-to-end frame generation; plots show predictions following the main frequency oscillation qualitatively, and computation/send completed before the 1 s target for the three shown forecasts. Test 2 (live laboratory FDR stream at 10 samples/s, TimesFM 2.5, 4 s history → 1 s forecast, one call/s, predicting frequency, ROCOF, voltage magnitude, and angle): computation finished 0.39–0.69 s after reference (median 0.60 s); local TCP send finished 0.41–0.76 s (median 0.64 s); all local sends met the 1 s target with 0.24–0.59 s remaining. No accuracy metrics (RMSE, MAE, etc.), no baseline methods, no comparison among the four supported models, and no stress-scale test beyond a single-lab 10 Hz stream. Note the two timing panels (Fig. 3/4) come from separate runs on the same day, and Fig. 4(a) uses saved input windows from a different run than the timing data. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component (latest-window-wins scheduling, bounded-tolerance timestamp matching, timeout/memory supervision). Nothing here is a new forecasting method: the TSFMs are off-the-shelf with frozen weights, and the genuine novelty is the timing-aware bridge between the C37.118 synchrophasor ecosystem and the TSFM ecosystem, which to the authors' implied claim did not previously exist as a reusable open-source artifact. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations (each pipeline stage is described but not independently evaluated), no error bars or multiple seeds, no significance testing, and no accuracy quantification. Code is publicly released on GitHub (https://github.com/wanghaozong88/pmu-fm), which is the main reproducibility asset — the tool can be rerun, but the paper's claims cannot be statistically checked from the reported numbers. Methodological concerns: (1) the tool is validated only on the authors' own virtual PMU and laboratory FDR, not on any public dataset or benchmark; (2) only 1 of 4 supported backends is actually exercised; (3) Fig. 4 mixes runs (accuracy from a saved-input run, timing from a network run), so accuracy and latency are never measured on the same execution; (4) the acknowledgment that the code was developed by OpenAI Codex is transparent but means the system has no human-audited implementation lineage stated. The timing measurements themselves are straightforward and credible for what they cover. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, released tool validated by running it on live streams). Practical: Yes — runs on a single workstation with locally hosted open-weight models (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5/3, Timestral), no special hardware claimed. Efficient: A 1 s-ahead forecast with one call per second on four channels at 10 Hz completes in a median 0.60 s on unspecified hardware, leaving ~40% headroom; cost relative to lightweight baselines (e.g., AR) is not measured. Effective: The evidence shows the pipeline works mechanically and meets its own timing budget; it does not show the forecasts are accurate or useful, so effectiveness against the motivating forecasting problem is demonstrated only at the proxy level. Scalable: Untested — a single worker processes one forecast at a time, higher-rate streams, more channels, larger models, or joint multivariate forecasting would consume the latency margin; the paper claims no scalability beyond the lab setting. Deliverable: a real software artifact (open-source tool with CLI and desktop UI), not just a paper. Strengths: - The timestamp formalism (reference/target/completion/send times with remaining lead) is a genuinely useful abstraction that makes forecast timeliness checkable and lets downstream C37.118 applications unambiguously interpret predicted channels — most ad hoc streaming-forecast setups get this wrong. - Real systems-engineering attention to failure modes practitioners actually hit: out-of-order and rounded timestamps, quality gating with recorded skip reasons, worker timeout/memory kill with bounded restart, per-client bounded queues, and history clearing on reconnection. - Reusing the C37.118 standard's analog channels plus a channel-to-lead mapping record is a low-friction integration path that lets existing synchrophasor consumers ingest forecasts without new protocols. - Full open-source release with both GUI and CLI lowers adoption cost for the target research community. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that all four backends currently forecast channels independently (no covariates, no joint multivariate forecasting), that positive remaining lead is necessary but not sufficient for timely downstream delivery (local send does not confirm receipt), and that validation should extend to "a wider range of power system data" in future work. These are stated directly rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. They do not acknowledge the absence of any accuracy evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central implicit claim — that TSFMs produce useful forecasts of synchrophasor quantities — is never tested: no error metrics, no comparison against even trivial baselines (persistence, AR), and only qualitative visual agreement in Fig. 3/4. - Three of the four supported models (Chronos-2, TimesFM-3, Timestral) are advertised but never run in any reported test, so model-selection claims within the tool are unsupported. - Both validation streams are local, single-source, and near-stationary; no disturbance events, no multi-PMU/PDC aggregation, no network latency between tool and clients — the motivation cites disturbance prediction and communication delays, but neither is exercised. - No memory footprint, model size, or hardware specification is reported, so the 0.60 s median latency cannot be contextualized or predicted on other machines. - Quality-gated window skipping could silently reduce forecast availability under realistic dirty data; skip rates are recorded by the tool but never reported in the paper. - Publishing synthetic forecasts as modified C37.118 frames raises interoperability/safety questions for any consumer that does not check the status flag; the paper flags the data but does not discuss this risk. Bottom Line: For a synchrophasor-tooling researcher, this is a useful, honestly-documented piece of infrastructure worth adopting and extending; as a research contribution on TSFM forecasting for power grids it is a functional demo only, and readers seeking evidence of forecast quality should look elsewhere.

Problem & Motivation: Teams using LLMs to generate tests face a gap between generation and trustworthy quality evidence: current pipelines treat execution as a mere filter, so tests pass with weak oracles, duplicate scenarios, hallucinated interfaces, or repairs that adjust tests until they turn green. The cited ULT benchmark shows LLM-generated tests achieve only 41.32% accuracy, 45.10% statement coverage, and 40.21% mutation score on real-world Python functions, versus much higher numbers on simpler, possibly contaminated benchmarks — so headline results do not transfer to realistic software. The paper further positions this gap inside AWS's AI-DLC lifecycle framework, arguing that greenfield projects risk tests derived from generated code (confirming what the code does, not what it should) and brownfield projects risk the 'characterization trap' of tests pinning current, possibly defective behavior. The intended audience is practitioners and researchers building AI-assisted testing infrastructure. Key Idea: The core insight is that the unit of evaluation should be the governed pipeline, not the generated test: probabilistic LLM reasoning is separated from deterministic execution by canonical artifacts (Test Intent, Test Specification, API Contract, Execution Package, Evidence) that must cross a policy gate, so that a test only becomes 'evidence' after execution against the intended system, and a repair is only accepted when an assertion checker confirms original intent survives re-execution. A second, methodological key idea is treating the architecture claim itself as a falsifiable hypothesis set with pre-registered ablations, mirroring registered-report practice. Methodology: The paper specifies (but does not run) a four-condition paired experiment: (A) traditional human-authored automation as reference, (B) LLM-only generation (weak baseline), (C) LLM + execution feedback (intermediate baseline), and (D) full QUALTAN — all sharing tasks, environments, and an identical per-task token budget ceiling to prevent attributing gains to extra model calls. The architecture has four layers: a quality-intelligence layer producing structured test strategy, an agentic orchestration layer (eight specialized agents: specification, planner, generator, validator, executor coordinator, failure analyzer, repair, selector), a governed artifact layer of six canonical schemas, and a deterministic execution layer (Playwright plus API/GraphQL adapters). The execution-grounded loop routes failing tests to controlled repair that re-enters at specification and requires policy validation plus re-execution. Evaluation uses open-source applications, synthetic enterprise workflows, REST/GraphQL services, and browser workflows with seeded defects spanning functional, validation, boundary, authorization, and integration categories; ≥5 runs per task-condition; a power analysis targeting 80% power at α=0.05 for d_z=0.5; blinded two-reviewer oracle classification with Cohen's kappa; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Vargha–Delaney A12 effect sizes, Holm correction, and 10,000-resample bootstrap CIs clustered on tasks; and hard falsification criteria (adjusted p<0.05, predicted direction, A12≥0.64, CI excluding zero; for the non-inferiority H5, ≤70% execution volume with defect-detection ratio lower bound ≥0.95). Well-justified decisions include the budget ceiling, the assertion checker to prevent repair bias, and equivalent-mutant review; less justified is the single pinned model configuration, acknowledged only as a threat. Key Results: Not stated. The paper contains no results — all quantitative content is either motivating evidence from prior work (e.g., ULT's 40.21% mutation score for LLM-generated tests) or protocol parameters (80% power, d_z=0.5, A12≥0.64, five-run minimum, H5 thresholds of 70% volume and 0.95 detection ratio). No condition was executed, no baseline was compared, and no benchmark task was run. The authors explicitly state: 'the importance claimed here is therefore a claim about where the protocol's hypotheses apply, not a result.' Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (framing test-generation evaluation as a pre-registered, falsifiable architectural claim with ablation isolation) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (proposed, unbuilt). The genuinely novel element is the governance-boundary formulation — canonical artifacts as the sole interface between reasoning and execution, with intent-preserving repair gated by an assertion checker — applied with registered-report-style rigor to agentic testing. The individual mechanisms (specification-driven generation, execution feedback, mutation analysis, risk-based selection, LLM repair) are standard; TestGen-LLM already used execution filters, and CodaMosa combined LLM and search-based generation. The abstract calls itself a 'protocol,' which is an accurate self-description. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a protocol, its rigor is in design, not execution — and the design is unusually careful: ablations isolating all six mechanisms, paired designs, nonparametric statistics with effect sizes and multiple-comparison correction, bootstrap CIs respecting task clustering, variance decomposition via coefficient of variation and intraclass correlation, stratified reporting for greenfield/brownfield, contamination checks against model training cutoffs, and pre-committed falsification criteria with a promise to report deviations. No seeds, error bars, or significance tests can exist yet since no experiment ran. No code, data, or artifact is publicly available; Section 12 promises future release (benchmark definitions, schemas, evaluation scripts, archived DOI) with the identifier 'to be inserted at submission.' Methodological concerns: the benchmark is self-constructed and not yet released, so evaluability depends entirely on a future artifact; there is no strong external baseline condition (no CodaMosa-style or commercial agentic-testing comparison — condition C, LLM + execution feedback, is the strongest comparator); and the paper appears in IJSREM, a low-visibility venue with an 8.659 SJIF rating rather than a recognized software engineering conference, which weakens external review guarantees. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL — but at protocol stage; every property is a projection, not a measurement. Practical: Presumably yes — Playwright, containerized environments, and commercial LLM APIs are all commodity components, though nothing has been run. Efficient: Cost per validated test is a specified metric, and token budget ceilings equalize spend across conditions, but actual costs are unknown. Effective: Not evaluated — effectiveness is the very hypothesis set the protocol exists to test. Scalable: Unknown; no scale is defined even at the planned level (task counts await the power analysis), and risk-aware selection's claimed volume reduction (H5) is untested. The paper delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model — only a specification and an appendix example artifact — so it stops at paper form. Strengths: - Pre-registration discipline rare in agentic-systems research: directional hypotheses, hard falsification thresholds fixed before data collection, a commitment to publish negative results, and a stated policy of reporting any protocol deviation. - The assertion-checker-gated repair mechanism directly targets the most insidious failure mode of self-healing test agents (silent weakening of test intent), with repair success measured separately from mutation score so the two cannot mask each other. - The ablation design cleanly isolates the marginal contribution of each governance mechanism, pre-empting the 'agentic system works because it has more parts' critique. - Honest epistemic framing throughout — the paper repeatedly distinguishes claims from results, including the explicit admission that QUALTAN cannot detect wrong requirements and treats specification quality as an assumed input. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that tests derived from the same specification as the code inherit specification errors and cannot detect wrong requirements; that mutation score can be inflated by easy-to-kill mutants and passing tests can have weak oracles (mitigated by oracle review and equivalent-mutant checks); that generalization beyond the selected applications is open; that results are model-dependent with a single pinned configuration; that benchmark contamination, environment dependence, and agent nondeterminism are risks with specified mitigations; and that repair mechanisms can appear effective by weakening assertions. They confront limitations directly and systematically — Section 10 is substantive rather than boilerplate, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No strong external baseline: the conditions omit any comparison to existing published systems (CodaMosa, TestGen-LLM-style filtering, or commercial agentic testing tools), so even a successful study would only show D beats stripped-down LLM prompting, not that it beats the best known alternative. - The benchmark does not yet exist, and all contamination, licensing, and buildability claims are promises; the entire protocol's value hinges on a future release that is not yet verifiable. - The AI-DLC positioning (Section 3.1, Table 1) is a framing device tied to one vendor's methodology blog; it is asserted as relevance but no hypothesis tests whether integration with AI-DLC matters. - The 'reproduction rate' metric (H6) is defined but the procedure for independent re-execution of a pipeline from recorded artifacts is underspecified, and reproducibility of agentic traces across model API changes is likely harder than the protocol suggests. - Oracle review blinding to condition may be fragile: agent-produced tests often have stylistic signatures, risking unblinding. - Publication venue: the paper is a single-author protocol in IJSREM (dated October 2026) with no peer review evidence or external pre-registration registry (e.g., no OSF registration), so the pre-registration claim currently rests on the paper's own timestamp alone. Bottom Line: The protocol design is genuinely instructive — arguably a better contribution than many under-controlled agentic-testing evaluations — but until the experiment runs, the benchmark and code are released, and the hypotheses are tested, a practitioner gets a reusable evaluation template here and should look elsewhere for evidence about whether governed agentic testing actually works.

Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models (16 ▲ )

Zhefan Rao, Meng Chu, Xuan Billy Zhang, Jingfan Chen, Guohao Cai, Runyi Li, Shiyi Du, Xu Huang, Ning Lu, Trusure Chen, Feng Nie, Zhenhao Liang, Haodong Chen, Hanwen Wang, Wenjie Shu, Yajing Bai, Xianfeng Wu, Xuanhua He, An Wang, Shuhan Guo, Ziyue Ma, Ruichuan An, Long Bai, Miaosen Chai, Wenhao Chai, Jingye Chen, Qi Chen, Xuhang Chen, Wei Chow, Minghao Fu, Shenyuan Gao, Yunhao Gou, Haokun Gui, Dong Huang, Wei Huang, Zi Cheng Huang, Ziyan Jiang, Haibo Jin, Lingdong Kong, Leung Chun Ho, Tianqin Li, Yanheng Li, Jiayuan Liu, Jiyang Liu, Mingyu Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Xiaocheng Lu, Yawen Luo, Zeyu Qin, Tiancheng Shen, Yueqi Song, Zhaolong Su, Hengkai Tan, Tianhao Tang, Yiran Tao, Juncheng Wang, Qinghe Wang, Shangshang Wang, Yingying Wang, Fang Wu, Tiange Xiang, Qiushi Yang, Weicai Ye, Weichen Yu, Jiarui Zhang, Jize Zhang, Liuzhou Zhang, Renrui Zhang, Sheng Zhang, Wenhu Zhang, Junru Zhao, Lingting Zhu, Xi Zhu, Yuxin Zuo, Yutong Bai, Qifeng Chen, Long Chen, Yang Deng, Ziqi Huang, Yeying Jin, Weijia Li, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Quande Liu, Dimitris Metaxas, See-Kiong Ng, Hongliang Ren, Hongru Wang, Gerbrand Ceder, Shujun Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Alan Yuille, Haoxuan Che · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Dual Exam, a dual-track benchmark that separately evaluates Multimodal Agents under a fixed environment response mechanism (1,088 items, 15 categories, 10 configurations) and World Models under fixed action interventions (400 cases, 8 scenarios, 16 configurations), across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. - Why it's important: Coupled Agent–World Model systems fail opaquely — when a joint rollout fails, neither decision errors nor simulation errors can be attributed — so component-isolated evidence is a prerequisite for diagnosing and pairing these systems. - How it does it: The core move is component isolation: hold the environment's response mechanism fixed while testing the Agent's action selection, and hold the action sequence fixed while testing the World Model's state evolution, with evidence-checked rubrics for goals, invariants, and state preservation. - The good: The paper is unusually candid about its own limits — it reports that equal-domain reweighting moves DeepSeek V4.1 Flash from 6th to 2nd, that a raw EdgeBench score of 100.493 was clipped with the reason unresolved, and that six ToolChoice prompts omitted a required task_id, which is exactly the transparency most leaderboards lack. - The missing: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated runs anywhere; the tracks' component scores are never validated as predictors of coupled success (the only coupled test, a 150-case pilot, yielded 0% task success and no attribution), and ~90% of the Scientific inventory is repurposed from existing benchmarks (ALE, SWE-bench, EdgeBench). - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate Agent–World Model systems and need a component-level diagnostic template and a sobering picture of current state preservation failures; skip it if you want a leaderboard with statistical rigor — it explicitly does not provide one.

Problem & Motivation: World Models (WMs) can supply simulated experience and action-conditioned predictions to Multimodal Agents (MAs), and Agent trajectories can in turn refine WMs. Both components remain unreliable over extended interaction — Agents fail at grounding, sequencing, and completion; WMs fail at memory and action control. Because each component consumes the other's outputs, a failed coupled run cannot distinguish Agent errors from World Model errors or their interaction. The authors demonstrate this ambiguity concretely: a 150-case coupled pilot (GPT-5.6 Sol acting, Seedance 2.5 generating observations) across ten scenarios produced 0% task success, with mean World State Consistency of 26.6% and Agent Corrective Response of only 9.2%, but no way to assign blame per failure. Existing benchmarks (per their Table 2) cover either Agent or WM evaluation, and none combine component isolation, persistent-state testing, and four-domain coverage. Key Idea: Component isolation via dual tracks: evaluate the Agent against a fixed reference environment response mechanism (so failures reflect the Agent's action selection), and evaluate the World Model against predefined fixed action interventions (so failures reflect state evolution, not the Agent). Each track verifies recorded evidence against explicit task requirements — initial state, permitted actions, required changes, protected state, and evidence rules — with the two tracks deliberately not required to use matched episodes. Methodology: The Agent track (1,088 items: 524 Physical, 255 Digital, 200 Social, 109 Scientific; 15 reporting categories) runs long-horizon rollouts under fixed budgets against reference environments, scoring task-specific 0–100 values (strict completion or graded), aggregated as a case-count-weighted Index (Physical 48.16%, Digital 23.44%, Social 18.38%, Scientific 10.02%). The Scientific inventory combines 63 Agents' Last Exam tasks, 30 SWE-bench repair tasks, 10 derived ToolChoice decision checkpoints, and 6 EdgeBench optimization tasks. The World Model track (400 cases, 50 per scenario across Embodiment, Driving, Daily Life, Web, Game, Human Interaction, Natural Science, Expert Science) seeds cases from behavior traces, expands them into 3–5 step intervention sequences with rubrics, screens automatically plus expert review, then scores fixed-intervention rollouts on action effects, entity/identity preservation, shared-state consistency, and rule adherence; WM Overall is the equal-weight mean of eight scenario scores. Critical design decisions: (1) unequal domain weighting by inventory count — acknowledged as arbitrary, with a sensitivity analysis showing rank churn; (2) merging heterogeneous scientific evaluation units (binary SWE passes at 100, graded Edge scores, published ALE means at one-decimal precision) into single category scores — flagged by the authors as not a uniform success rate, and arguably the weakest methodological choice; (3) a Borden/DABIC clipping convention for EdgeBench scores that is explicitly non-official and left partially unexplained. Key Results: Agent track: GPT 6 Astra leads the Index at 31.3, followed by GPT 5.6 Sol (20.7), Gemini 3.6 Flash (20.1), Qwen 3.8 Max (20.0), Kimi K3 (19.8); Astra leads 9 of 15 categories. Performance is highly uneven: Manipulation tops out at 9.5 and Desktop Application Interaction at 5.6, versus 47.1 for Game Environment Interaction and 42.9 for Mobile. On the 40 added SWE/ToolChoice items, Astra achieves 14/30 SWE passes and 2/10 ToolChoice; Kimi K3 and Seed 2.1 Pro score 0/30 SWE. World Model track: GPT-Image-2 leads full-coverage Overall at 21.7 (Qwen-Image-3.0 21.1, Nano Banana 2 19.5 on 0–100 scales); Seedance 2.5 covers only six scenarios (18.7, excluded from full-coverage ranking). Digital scenarios are uniformly hard: no configuration exceeds 16.5 on Web or 13.3 on Game. Scenario profiles invert rankings — MiniMax H3 scores 53.8 on Embodiment but 3.7 on Web, versus GPT-Image-2's 20.9 and 16.5. Under equal-domain weighting, DeepSeek moves from 6th to 2nd among Agents, and >22.9% weight on Embodiment flips the WM leader. The coupled pilot: 0% task success on 150 cases, 26.6% state consistency, 9.2% corrective response. Baselines are the models themselves (contemporary frontier systems); benchmark baselines are scope comparisons (Table 2), not performance comparisons. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (dual-track component-isolated evaluation) plus a modest NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the systematic dissociation between realizing requested changes and preserving task-relevant state in WMs, and between local progress and verified completion in Agents). The isolation principle itself — fix the other side of the interaction to attribute failures — is a sensible but not conceptually deep move; the Scientific inventory is largely a re-aggregation of ALE, SWE-bench, and EdgeBench, and the Social track's 200 cases come from only 40 templates, limiting genuinely new test content. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are limited to a domain-weighting sensitivity analysis for both tracks — useful and honest, but not component ablations of the benchmark design itself. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; the authors state plainly that rankings do not establish statistical superiority and that shared Social templates and SWE/ToolChoice parent links violate independence assumptions. Provenance is a persistent weakness: many case studies are retrospective replays of historical archives with partially unknown harnesses and model identities, original API responses are unavailable for the Navigation examples, per-model budgets/histories/retries/dates are not consolidated, the pilot's excluded-failure count is unavailable, and the single automated trajectory audit was not independently adjudicated. Six ToolChoice checkpoints had a specification defect (missing task_id) yet their scores remain in the leaderboard. No code, data, or leaderboard artifact release is mentioned beyond a blog URL (xgenlabs.ai/research/dual-exam/). The methodology is developed and evaluated on the same inventory it reports — there is no held-out validation of the rubrics or of scorer agreement (expert review during construction is explicitly not independent scoring-agreement testing). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark with executed evaluations; no primary system or theory). - Practical: Runs on commercially available models and APIs by construction, though the reference environments and verifiers for the bespoke Physical/Social/WM cases are not described as publicly available. - Efficient: Not evaluated in cost terms; the paper notes per-model generation durations and budgets are not consolidated, so compute overhead of running the benchmark is unknown. - Effective: The benchmark reliably detects the failure modes it targets (state corruption, unverified completion claims), but the evidence that component scores predict anything about coupled performance is absent — the only coupled test failed 100%. - Scalable: Not tested beyond the fixed inventory; scaling claims are not made, and the authors correctly warn against extrapolating rankings across task mixtures. The work delivers a paper and a blog page; no reusable library, dataset release, or trained model is stated. Strengths: - The dual-track isolation design directly addresses a real, well-articulated diagnostic ambiguity (attribution of coupled failures) that no surveyed prior benchmark (Table 2, 16 entries) covers simultaneously. - Exceptional epistemic hygiene for a leaderboard paper: it repeatedly and specifically undermines its own rankings — weighting sensitivity (DeepSeek 6th→2nd), non-comparability of the two Indices, one-decimal precision limits, unresolved score anomalies (100.493 Borden), and harness non-matching — which makes the reported numbers more trustworthy, not less. - The case analyses draw genuinely useful distinctions with concrete evidence: a completion claim at 183/255 brightness against the verifier, correct navigation feasibility with nonexistent route edges, correct clip membership with wrong ordering, and WM outputs that realize an instruction while adding cups or replacing trays — each illustrating a failure mode aggregate scores hide. - The World Model finding that models preserve required object counts while altering unrelated scene attributes (or vice versa) is a crisp, reusable diagnostic framing (requested effect vs. protected state vs. observation modality, Table 13). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and extensively: no statistical uncertainty or significance testing; unequal and arbitrary domain weights; scientific scores mixing binary, graded, and published-mean units under non-matched harnesses; non-independent items (shared templates, parent-task links); incomplete provenance for historical runs and truncated archives; missing task_id in six ToolChoice prompts; single un-adjudicated automated audit; no unified independent error audit or WM scoring-agreement study; and explicit statements that component scores do not predict coupled success and that no reciprocal learning is tested. This level of self-critique is a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central promise — that Dual Exam helps diagnose coupled failures — is never cashed out: the tracks use different tasks, episodes, and metrics, so the paper provides no demonstrated instance of a coupled failure being attributed to a component via these tools. The 0%-success pilot remains undiagnosed by construction. - Nearly the entire Scientific track (99 of 109 items) is inherited from ALE, SWE-bench, and EdgeBench, meaning the four-domain claim rests heavily on repurposed content, and the aggregation of these heterogeneous sources into single category numbers (e.g., Astra's Scientific 50.6) is the least defensible scoring in the paper. - The 0% coupled task success across all ten scenarios, with no retries and excluded-failure counts unavailable, is so extreme that protocol or harness pathology cannot be ruled out; the paper offers no sanity check that the pairing protocol is achievable by any configuration. - WM evaluation compares image-generation and video-generation models descriptively but cannot support cross-modality conclusions, and several case panels come from batches and versions that need not match leaderboard settings — weakening the link between case evidence and rankings. - No inter-annotator or scorer agreement statistics for the rubric-based WM checks, which involve subjective judgments of identity, gaze, and state persistence. Bottom Line: Practitioners building Agent–World Model pipelines gain a genuinely useful diagnostic template and the clearest available evidence that current frontier models fail at state preservation and verified completion, but they should treat every ranking in this paper as a descriptive point estimate on an idiosyncratic task mixture — and the field still lacks the validated coupled-evaluation methodology this paper only sets up.

#218 — Moderately Innovative (51)

Assertionista: Teaching LLMs to Generate Provably Correct Code

S Bansal, C Gao, A Gawde, E Shen · atharvagawde.com · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Assertionista, a dual-model (writer + annotator) GRPO-style RLVR post-training pipeline on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct that uses the Dafny verifier as the reward signal to generate provably correct Dafny code, and reports a negative/proof-of-concept result: 4.4 epochs of annotator training produced no measurable verification-rate improvement. - Why it's important: LLM-generated code that compiles but is semantically wrong is a blocker for safety-critical use, and formal verification offers a binary, human-free reward signal — but sparse verifier rewards make RL post-training in this domain genuinely hard, and this paper documents that difficulty empirically. - How it does it: It decomposes the task into a writer (implements a specification) and an annotator (inserts proof annotations via a compact JSON-patch action space), rewards the annotator with a stage-gated reward (format → no-assume → compile → verify) computed by running Dafny on the patched program, and optimizes both with group-relative REINFORCE (GRPO without a KL term). - The good: The staged reward demonstrably shaped intermediate behavior — format compliance stayed near 100% and post-refinement compilation success reached 94.5% — while the JSON-patch action space cut generation length from 411 to ~120 tokens (71%), and the authors honestly report the flat verification curve (mean 29.0%, σ=0.313, regression slope ≈10⁻⁶, p=0.88). - The missing: There is no supervised fine-tuning warm start (which the authors themselves identify as likely necessary), the writer model was never trained, and no external baseline or comparison system (e.g., DafnyBench's own hinted-solving approaches) is evaluated — so the central claim of RLVR viability for formal verification remains untested, not merely unproven. - Read it or not: Read it only if you are specifically designing verifier-in-the-loop RL pipelines on limited compute and want a candid engineering post-mortem (memory bottlenecks, ~2 min/sample verifier latency, reward-inflation pitfalls); skip it if you want demonstrated method performance on Dafny-style proof generation.

Novelty (50) is modest — the JSON-patch action space and DafnyBench extension are real but small contributions — and Completeness (70) is the one strong dimension thanks to unusually candid negative-result reporting with actual statistics. Resilience (50) is undermined by the Conclusion's claim that the pipeline 'proves the viability' of verifier-based RL, which the paper's own evidence contradicts. Problem & Motivation: LLMs routinely emit syntactically valid but logically incorrect code, which precludes deployment in safety-critical settings where correctness must be guaranteed rather than suggested. RLHF is subjective and expensive; SFT cannot guarantee provable correctness. RLVR (per DeepSeek-R1/DeepSeekMath) replaces human judgment with programmatic checks, and formal verification with Dafny provides an exact ground-truth judge — but existing RLVR results do not transfer trivially because verifier rewards are extremely sparse, verifier feedback is slow (subprocess + SMT solver per sample), and naive generation can produce syntactically valid but logically vacuous proofs. The authors target the DafnyBench setting: given a Hoare-triple specification, produce an implementation plus proof annotations that the Dafny verifier accepts. The intended audience is anyone post-training LLMs for formal methods. Key Idea: Decompose the hard task A: (P,Q) → S into two independently rewardable stages — a Writer that synthesizes an implementation from a specification, and an Annotator that repairs it with localized proof annotations — and make the annotator's action space a minimal JSON patch (line number + single-line annotation) rather than full code regeneration. The patch interface is the load-bearing trick: it slashes output tokens (~71%), makes output-to-artifact application deterministic (insertions applied in descending line order), and lets the verifier-in-the-loop reward concentrate learning pressure on the proof-annotation subtask. The writer is rewarded only through the downstream annotator+verifier outcome (Rwrite = 1{Verify(P̂)} + λcmp·1{Compiles}), forcing it to emit implementations 'close in proof space' to verifiable programs. This dual-model split is a reasonable formulation, but it is a design, not a proven mechanism — the writer half was never trained, so only the annotator half of the idea is exercised. Methodology: The pipeline is: spec → Writer → Pwrite → Annotator → JSON patch J → ApplyEdits → P̂ → Dafny compile_no_verify → Dafny verify → stage-gated reward. The annotator reward is Rann = rfmt (0.3 for valid JSON patch) + rassume (−1.0 if any annotation begins with `assume`, an anti-vacuity cheat penalty) + rcmp (1.0 for compile) + rver (3.0 for verification), with short-circuiting at the first failing stage. Optimization is group-relative REINFORCE: M completions per prompt, rewards z-scored within each group (εᵢ = (Rᵢ−μx)/(σx+ε)), gradient on generated-token log-probs scaled by εᵢ, no explicit KL penalty to a reference policy (acknowledged deviation from standard GRPO, justified by memory limits). Training data comes from DafnyBench (620+ samples/epoch), extended with a new `unimplemented_body` field (specification-only skeletons) enabling triples (skeleton, hints-removed body, ground-truth annotated body) — a genuine dataset contribution for a writer curriculum. Three critical design decisions: (1) JSON-patch action space — well-justified by the token-reduction measurement and determinism guarantee; (2) dropping the KL term — plausible under memory constraints but risks policy collapse, and the observed entropy drop (0.37→0.24) suggests premature exploitation; (3) skipping SFT before RL — explicitly identified post-hoc as a mistake, making the cold-start RL setup the paper's own acknowledged weak point. Writer training never ran. Key Results: All experiments ran on a single AWS g6e.2xlarge (A40, 48 GB VRAM). The annotator trained ~4.4 epochs / 2,735 steps on DafnyBench. Headline outcome is negative: training verification rate fluctuated between 0.05 and 0.45 with mean 29.0% (σ=0.313), and linear regression on the trajectory gives slope ≈10⁻⁶, R² < 0.001, p = 0.88 — no statistically significant improvement; test verification rate was flat at ~29%, matching the training mean. After a mid-training reward re-weighting (step ~1,200, down-weighting compilation), mean reward fell from 2.93±1.14 to 2.09±0.99 while verification stayed at 29% — evidence that compilation reward was inflating returns without improving proofs. Intermediate objectives did improve: compilation success reached 94.5% post-refinement and JSON format compliance held near 100% throughout. Policy entropy fell from 0.37 to 0.24, which the authors read as possible premature exploitation. Token output dropped from 411 to ~120 per sample with the JSON-patch interface. Baselines: only the untrained initial policy (effectively) — no comparison against SFT-only, PPO, DafnyBench leaderboard systems, or hint-recovery baselines, so baselines are minimal rather than weak or strong. Scale is toy-to-standard: 620+ samples, 3B model, single GPU. The honest interpretation — sparse binary rewards cannot drive discovery without an SFT warm start — is the paper's most credible empirical claim. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (weak) + NEW DATASET extension + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (negative result). Genuinely novel pieces: the JSON-patch annotation action space with the anti-`assume` penalty and stage-gated verifier reward is a concrete, measured interface design (the 71% token reduction is a real, if small, finding), and the `unimplemented_body` extension of DafnyBench is a reusable dataset artifact. The rest — GRPO-style group-relative REINFORCE, verifier-as-reward, writer/annotator decomposition — is a competent combination of existing ideas (DeepSeek-R1's RLVR, DafnyBench's task) applied to a constrained setting; the paper itself positions this way ('Rather than emphasizing large-scale performance gains...'). It is not a NEW METHOD with demonstrated efficacy, since the method did not outperform its own initialization. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the mid-training reward re-weighting functions as a natural experiment showing compilation reward caused reward inflation without verification gains — this is the paper's best-controlled finding. Component-wise logging (format, compile, verify, assume violations) enables genuine failure attribution. However: no error bars across seeds (single training run), no significance testing beyond one regression on the reward curve, no comparison against any external baseline, and the writer model — half the architecture — was never trained, so the end-to-end pipeline was evaluated only as writer-abstained annotation recovery. Code is released via a Google Drive link (Appendix C); no model weights are mentioned. A methodological concern: the verification rate is measured on the same DafnyBench distribution used for training, and the ~29% test rate matching the training mean may partly reflect limited data (620+ samples) rather than generalization. The negative result is reported with unusual candor (flat-trend statistics, explicit 'no definitive results' statement), which raises confidence in what is claimed but does not strengthen the paper's central positive claim, which remains unsupported. This reads as a student/course-scale preprint-style report, not peer-reviewed work. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training pipeline actually run, with negative headline results). Practical: Yes in principle — Qwen2.5-3B and Dafny run on a single 48 GB consumer-adjacent GPU, though the authors hit memory walls that forced sequential reward computation. Efficient: Poor — ~2 minutes per sample for environment+reward, ~20 hours per epoch plus 4 hours evaluation on 620+ samples, driven by subprocess-spawned Dafny compilation and SMT solving; the JSON-patch action space mitigates generation cost but not verifier latency. Effective: Not demonstrated — format and compilation objectives were met (≈100%, 94.5%), but the stated problem (provably correct code) showed zero measured improvement over the base policy. Scalable: Untested and doubtful as-is — the authors only claim (conjecture, not experiment) that multi-GPU rollout collection plus SFT warm-starting would scale; at 10× data or 100× steps the sequential verifier loop becomes the binding bottleneck. Deliverable: code artifact via Google Drive and a dataset extension; no trained model of value (the policy is not better than its initialization); the reusable contribution is the pipeline design and the documented failure mode. Strengths: - Honest negative-result reporting with actual statistics: the flat-trend regression (slope ≈10⁻⁶, p=0.88) and the before/after reward-reweighting analysis (2.93→2.09 mean reward at constant 29% verification) are clean, quantified demonstrations of reward inflation in sparse-reward RLVR — many papers would have buried this. - The JSON-patch annotation interface is a concrete, measurable contribution: deterministic edit application, a 71% generation-token reduction (411→120), a near-100% format-compliance outcome traceable to the format reward, and an anti-cheating `assume` penalty guarding against logically vacuous proofs. - The `unimplemented_body` DafnyBench extension creates specification-only training triples enabling a staged (implementation synthesis → annotation recovery) curriculum that others can reuse. - The dual-model decomposition (implementation vs. proof-hint synthesis as separable reward surfaces) is a sensible formulation of the (P,Q)→S problem, even though only half of it was exercised. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are direct and non-defensive: they state upfront they 'were unable to generate definitive results due to hardware and time constraints'; they enumerate computational bottlenecks (sequential rollouts, 2 min/sample, 20 h/epoch), the absence of SFT warm-starting ('RLVR cannot succeed from a cold start' under these conditions), writer training being infeasible, environment complexity (subprocess latency, SMT timeouts producing ambiguous rewards), and explicitly frame results as 'proof-of-concept validation... rather than a demonstration of converged model performance.' They also flag entropy collapse as possible premature exploitation. This level of self-criticism is a credibility positive. They additionally propose a two-phase SFT→RL pipeline and scaled infrastructure as next steps. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No external baseline whatsoever: no comparison to DafnyBench's published results, to few-shot prompting of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct without any RL, or to an SFT-only model — so even the 'base policy at 29%' number has no context (is 29% good, bad, or trivially the verifier accepting near-identical ground-truth-style patches?). - The claim that the pipeline 'proves the viability of formal verification-based systems' (Conclusion) is not supported by any positive result; the paper's evidence actually supports the opposite conclusion for cold-start RL, and the conclusion overreaches its own data. - The writer's downstream-verification reward (Rwrite) is defined but never implemented or tested, so the architectural claim that writer and annotator 'behave differently under verifiable reward signals' is entirely unvalidated. - The KL-free GRPO variant introduces unmanaged drift risk (visible in entropy collapse), and no reference-model regularization ablation was run — the paper cannot distinguish 'sparse rewards' from 'no KL anchoring' as the cause of failure. - Single seed, single run, small dataset (620+ samples), and evaluation on the training distribution limit all statistical claims; the flat regression on a noisy curve with σ=0.313 across 2,735 steps is suggestive, not conclusive. - Anti-cheating analysis is incomplete: only the `assume` keyword is penalized; logically vacuous but assumption-free annotations (e.g., tautological invariants, `assert true`) that satisfy Dafny are not discussed. Bottom Line: A practitioner building verifier-in-the-loop RL systems gains a useful, honestly-documented post-mortem (verifier latency, reward inflation, cold-start sparsity) and a reusable JSON-patch action-space design, but the paper demonstrates no working method — SFT-then-RL papers and the DafnyBench literature cover the same ground with actual results, so this is worth reading mainly as a cautionary engineering report, not as a technique to adopt.

Puzzles to Paradigms: A Survey of Human–Agent Collaboration in Scientific Innovation

Z Liang, H Zhang, H Chen, T Xiao, J Ding, Y Zhang · aclanthology.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CSCW×Kuhn, a coordination-aware analytical framework that connects three CSCW coordination dimensions (articulation work, common ground, awareness) with three Kuhnian epistemic modes of scientific work (puzzle-solving in normal science, anomaly evaluation, paradigm-shift exploration), and applies it to code 54 papers / 59 human–agent scientific systems. - Why it's important: Current evaluations of scientific agents emphasize bounded task accuracy while ignoring workflow integrity, evidential grounding, disagreement preservation, and provenance — failures that can produce seemingly correct outputs that are scientifically unreliable, a stake that grows as agents enter peer review and discovery pipelines. - How it does it: The core move is a two-axis coding scheme: each system is assigned a dominant epistemic context and scored 0–3 on three ordinal CSCW dimensions, then failure risks are inferred where the system's coordination support misaligns with its task's epistemic demands, yielding five named failure modes (procedural drift, grounding substitution, evaluative flattening, proxy optimization, epistemic black-boxing). - The good: The five failure modes are crisply defined, grounded in classical CSCW theory (Schmidt & Bannon, Clark & Brennan, Dourish & Bellotti), mapped to concrete evaluation targets, and illustrated with worked examples (AAAR-1.0, SchNovel, Si et al. 2025) that genuinely show where task-centric metrics under-measure coordination quality. - The missing: The framework is never empirically validated — coding was done by the authors with no inter-annotator agreement, no independent annotators, and no test that researchers can reliably apply the rubric to real workflows (the authors acknowledge this). - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building or evaluating scientific agents and LLM-as-reviewer systems who need an argument for coordination-aware evaluation beyond benchmark scores; skippable for those seeking a new method, dataset, or experimental results, since this is a conceptual survey.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The score is pulled down primarily by Rigor (48) — single-team coding with no inter-annotator agreement or reliability statistics leaves the framework's central operationality claim resting on two worked examples, and Table 5's coverage-gap judgments lack decision rules — and by Practical Impact (35), since the deliverable is an unvalidated coding rubric and bibliographic artifact rather than a usable method. Novelty (55) is genuine but modest: the CSCW×Kuhn coupling and five failure modes are a new lens, while the underlying observations are drawn from prior work. Completeness (58) benefits from unusually direct limitation acknowledgment, but Resilience (52) suffers from the stretched inclusion of fully autonomous systems under 'human–agent collaboration' and decorative formalism.
