Problem & Motivation: The paper targets the enterprise practice of using LLMs to synthesize candidate populations for testing and training hiring systems, under the assumption that synthetic generation yields a demographically neutral baseline. The authors argue this is dangerous because the generator, not the screener, now decides who gets an Ivy League degree, a STEM career, an executive title, and a multi-million-dollar budget — and those decisions may encode historical bias. The intended audience is CISOs, general counsel, HR technologists, and auditors concerned with EEOC liability. The gap addressed is real: prior algorithmic-fairness auditing (including the authors' own prior report, "AI Agents and the Meritocracy Delusion") focused on evaluation bias against provided resumes; bias in generation of synthetic humans is less studied. The framing, however, is written for a corporate/buyer audience rather than a research community, and the vendor (Trinitite) has a direct commercial interest in the conclusion that out-of-the-box models are uninsurable without its governance product. Key Idea: The core move is a shift from auditing evaluation to auditing generation: constrain an LLM's output with a deterministic JSON schema ("generate_resume") so demographic bias in the model's latent priors surfaces as measurable structured quantities (universities, budgets, tenures, verb ratios), rather than being hidden in free-form text. The second, genuinely interesting observation is the "vendor lottery": bias magnitude and even direction (e.g., GPT 5.4 penalizing women's budgets vs. Claude Sonnet 4.6 inflating women's agentic language; aligned models over-assigning HBCUs at ~100% while open-weight models generate larger maternal-wall gaps) are model-specific artifacts of safety alignment rather than universal properties of LLMs. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Cohort construction: 100 demographic personas (from the authors' prior audit), generated via "Gemini 3.0 Pro Deep Research" from US Census distributions across ages 22–60, equal sex split, five racial categories, with census-clustered surnames, SSA-generation-matched first names, and 28% assigned Schedule A disabilities stratified epidemiologically. (2) Generation: six models (listed as OpenAI GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, "Moonthot Kimi 2.5," Zai GLM 5.0, DeepSeek 3.2) each generated 10 resumes per persona under a fixed system directive and enforced JSON schema with institution names, tenures, titles, and budget-bearing bullet points — 6,000 events total. (3) Feature engineering: RapidFuzz token-set matching (≥85% threshold) of hallucinated universities against ranking/HBCU/Ivy datasets; PCA "Prestige Index" over expenditure, selectivity, graduation, and top-10% class metrics; regex-based Agentic Ratio (agentic vs. communal verbs); Flesch-Kincaid grade; career-gap computation (expected years = age − 22 minus generated employment); Overeducation Index (degree weight minus leadership score); generation-latency tracking. (4) Inference: OLS with HC3 robust errors for continuous outcomes, logistic regression for binary outcomes, interaction terms for intersectionality, Tukey HSD all-to-all pairwise comparisons, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR across the whole test battery. Critical design decisions: schema-forcing to eliminate qualitative noise (well-justified); persona reuse from a prior audit (justified for control but creates dependency on an unaudited Gemini-generated cohort); age-squared terms to detect non-linear ageism (well-executed). Notably, the study conflates model identity with alignment strategy and does not report prompt variants, temperature settings, seeds, or any robustness checks on the extraction pipeline itself. Key Results: Headline numbers: Black personas assigned to HBCUs in 74.79% of 714 evaluations (p < 1e-100 claimed), vs. ~10% real-world baseline; per-model HBCU rates: Claude Sonnet 4.6 100.0%, Claude Opus 4.6 97.5%, GPT 5.4 94.16%, DeepSeek 3.2 21.93%. Per-student university expenditure regressions: Hispanic −$5,590 and Black −$2,753 against a $10,290 intercept; Ivy League log-odds +2.026 for males (7.58× odds); disability penalties of −1.314 (Ivy), −1.223 (advanced degree), −0.523 (board seats). STEM assignment: males 5.31× more likely (+1.670 log-odds); Black −85.9% and Hispanic −74.5% odds reductions; STEM exclusion against women significant for all six models (penalties 1.39–2.945). Budgets: White males vs. White females differ by 0.9278 log-10 (≈8.46×); disabled personas −0.907 log (≈88% reduction); Asian females receive ~24× the budgets of White females yet Asian males face a 24.94-month first-promotion delay. Semantic/temporal effects: disabled resumes 12.87 words shorter (+0.541 Flesch-Kincaid grade); male resumes generated 3.46 seconds faster; 60-year-olds take ~8 extra seconds to generate; Kimi 2.5 injects 0.740 years of unexplained career gap onto female resumes. Scale is modest but non-trivial: 6,000 generations across six models. Baselines are weak — the only comparison to external reality is the HBCU attendance rate; there is no comparison of generated outcome distributions against actual labor statistics (CPS, EEOC data) or against debiased/guardrailed generation baselines. Several findings (e.g., identical-deduction effects) are plausible but the report's rhetorical severity (“astronomical,” “catastrophic”) is not matched by effect-size contextualization against real-world disparities. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus an untested NEW SYSTEM/TOOL proposal. The genuinely novel element is the systematic demonstration that safety alignment amplifies certain generation-time stereotypes (near-100% HBCU assignment by aligned models) while open-weight models exhibit raw stereotype-driven gaps — a direction that contradicts the naive expectation that alignment reduces bias. The methodology itself (persona prompting, JSON schema forcing, regression auditing) is a competent combination of established bias-auditing techniques applied to the generation setting, and the proposed AGRC governance framework (deterministic sidecar governor, negative unit tests, cryptographic output ledger) is described but entirely unvalidated — it is product marketing rather than a research contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Statistical hygiene is above average for this genre: HC3 robust standard errors, BH-FDR correction across all tests, Tukey HSD pairwise structure, and exact binomial tests against real-world baselines where available. However: (1) no code, data, prompts, or raw JSON corpus are released — no URL or repository is mentioned, making the audit unreplicable as published; (2) no multiple-seed runs of the study itself (10 generations per persona is reported, but no variance decomposition across prompt instantiations); (3) the persona cohort was itself LLM-generated (Gemini 3.0 Pro) and carried over from the authors' prior report, so persona construction bias is unquantified; (4) model names are non-standard and unverifiable ("GPT 5.4," "Claude Opus 4.6," "Moonthot Kimi 2.5"), and no versions, dates, or API settings are given — this is a serious provenance defect; (5) the audit is entirely self-reported by a vendor whose product thesis is the paper's conclusion; (6) the text contains duplicated sentences and duplicated p-value placeholders (apparently formatting corruption), undermining confidence in editorial rigor; (7) no ablation isolates which schema fields drive which regressions. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (an audit study with a bolt-on product pitch). - Practical: The audit method runs on commercial APIs plus standard Python tooling (RapidFuzz, scikit-learn-style regression), so any enterprise could replicate it cheaply — though they'd have to rebuild everything from the paper. - Efficient: 6,000 generations is a few hundred dollars of API spend at most; the statistical stack is trivial to compute. - Effective: The evidence shows the models produce biased synthetic corpora — the stated problem — but the downstream-contagion claim (that this data poisons trained screeners) is asserted, never experimentally demonstrated by training a screener on the corpus. - Scalable: Untested beyond 6,000 events and 6 models; whether the vendor-specific bias directions persist across prompt templates, temperature settings, or model updates is unknown and unclaimed with evidence. The paper's proposed artifact (AGRC governor, Teleological Generation Engine, State Tuple Ledger) delivers no software, benchmarks, or evaluation; the research component stops at paper form. Strengths: - The generation-vs-evaluation framing is a real conceptual contribution to bias auditing: measuring what a model imagines rather than how it judges, using schema-forced output to make latent priors measurable. - The HBCU/safety-alignment paradox is the paper's most credible and non-obvious finding: the direction of the effect (aligned proprietary models at 94–100% vs. open-weight at ~22%) is internally coherent and directly challenges the assumption that RLHF-style safety training reduces stereotype expression. - Breadth of measured dimensions — institution economics, PCA prestige, budget log-transforms, agentic verb ratios, Flesch-Kincaid, career-gap years, generation latency — goes well beyond binary pass/fail audits and captures mechanisms (word-count suppression, latency differences) rarely examined elsewhere. - Consistent use of FDR correction and robust errors across a large test battery avoids the multiple-comparisons failure common in this literature. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that heavily aligned models produce "clumsy diversity overcorrections" (i.e., their own safety training induces stereotyping) and that open-weight models hallucinate raw prejudice — effectively conceding that no tested model class is safe. They note the study is a second phase building on their prior audit and that bias is vendor-specific rather than universal. They do not, however, confront methodological limitations: no discussion of persona-construction validity, prompt sensitivity, lack of released artifacts, or the fact that their proposed governance framework is untested. Limitations are framed rhetorically as evidence for the product rather than as scope boundaries of the study. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Unverifiable model identity: the model names (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus/Sonnet 4.6, "Moonthot" Kimi 2.5, Zai GLM 5.0, DeepSeek 3.2) do not match any publicly documented releases and no API details, dates, or versions are given; the entire empirical section rests on unauditable provenance. - The downstream-contagion thesis — the paper's central claim for enterprise harm — is never tested: no experiment trains a screener on the generated corpus and measures disparate impact on real candidates. - Confounding of persona design and model bias: personas were generated by another LLM using census marginals; joint distributions (e.g., disability-by-age-by-race correlations, name-university base rates) may inject structure the regressions attribute to the audited models. - No comparison to real labor-market outcome distributions (education attainment, budget/compensation, promotion timing by demographics), so "8.46× budget gap" cannot be interpreted as model-induced distortion vs. reflection of real-world statistics the models merely represent. - Prompt sensitivity is unexamined: one system directive, one schema; the vendor-lottery conclusions could be prompt-template artifacts. - Extraction-pipeline error is unquantified: the 85% RapidFuzz threshold for university matching, dollar-amount extraction via regex, and gap computation (age − 22) each embed assumptions with no reported precision or manual validation sample. - The AGRC remedy (geometric policy manifolds, semantic rectification, cryptographic ledgers) is technologically underspecified and never evaluated — even a toy demonstration of the governor intercepting one biased output is absent. - Generation-latency differences (3.46 s) are offered as evidence of "demographic friction" without controlling for output length, schema-fill order, or provider-side load. Bottom Line: A practitioner in AI fairness or HR-tech risk gains a genuinely useful hypothesis set — especially that safety alignment amplifies generation-time stereotyping and that bias direction is vendor-specific — but this self-published, unverifiable, artifact-free vendor report should be treated as a signal to run your own audit, not as evidence; peer-reviewed audits of synthetic-data bias and the authors' cited academic literature (Bender et al., Benjamin) provide more reliable ground to stand on.

Framework for increased Interpretability within Aligned Process Models

R Brinkman · pure.tue.nl · business process mining or process mining - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This master's thesis introduces a prototype framework of six visualization features (distinguishable gateway shapes, gateway-partner highlighting, sub-process selective highlighting, sub-process collapsing, LLM-generated sub-process names, and semi-permanent edge highlighting) that improves the interpretability of aligned process models in UiPath's process mining product. - Why it's important: Process mining vendors must convey complex, gateway-rich models to non-expert business users; no prior work had studied interpretability of aligned process models (models augmented with event-log/conformance data), leaving product design guided only by intuition. - How it does it: A three-round Delphi-style user study (12 UiPath employees) elicits and ranks 15 interpretability issues, which are converted into six requirements and implemented as known visualization techniques—selective highlighting, modularization, semantic abstraction—applied to aligned process models, with sub-process names generated by feeding a natural-language rendering of the process tree to an LLM. - The good: The issue inventory (IS1–IS15 with user-report counts and Delphi priorities, e.g., gateway distinguishability ranked #1 with 11/12 reports) is a genuinely useful, reusable empirical artifact for the process-model-visualization community. - The missing: Evaluation is purely qualitative with 3 of the original 12 participants (all UiPath staff, single coder for all data), with no quantitative task-performance, error-rate, or timing metrics, and no external validation of LLM-generated sub-process names. - Read it or not: Worth reading for HCI-in-process-mining researchers and process-mining product designers who want a catalog of concrete usability issues and mitigation patterns; rigorous visualization researchers can skip it due to the small, single-company, unquantified evaluation.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Impact (45) is the top dimension — the six-feature prototype is integrated into UiPath's production stack, and the 15-issue ranked catalog is a genuinely reusable artifact for the visualization community. However, Rigor (30) is weak: evaluation involved only 3 of 12 participants drawn from the same group that shaped the requirements (circularity), no task-performance, error, or timing metrics exist, no external baseline system was compared, and the thesis is not peer-reviewed. Problem & Motivation: UiPath's process mining product visualizes processes as "aligned process models"—process graphs with BPMN-like gateway semantics (XOR, parallel, loop) augmented with event-log data and conformance information—rather than the industry-standard directly-follows graphs (DFGs). While DFG and BPMN readability have been studied (e.g., La Rosa et al.'s 12 abstraction patterns, density-reduction work by Conforti, Tax, and Chapela-Campa), no prior research addresses interpretability of these richer aligned models. The problem was posed by UiPath: users struggle with excessive gateway nodes, unclear process structure at overview zoom levels, unclear sub-process boundaries, and edge density ("spaghetti"). The affected population is process analysts and business stakeholders of varying process-mining expertise who must read these models to optimize business processes. Key Idea: The core move is user-driven requirement elicitation mapped onto known visualization techniques: gateways are made distinguishable via shape differentiation (not just icons), gateway pairs and sub-process memberships are made visible through on-hover selective highlighting (partner highlighting plus de-emphasizing everything outside the sub-process), and models are made abstractable by collapsing gateway-rooted sub-processes whose names are generated by an LLM from a depth-first, indentation-encoded natural-language rendering of the process tree (e.g., "Clandestine Cake Consumption with Possible Repercussions" for a cake-stealing loop). There is no single deep algorithmic insight; the contribution is the systematic combination. Methodology: The work follows Design Science Research (Hevner-style) with a Delphi method (Okoli & Pawlowski) user study in three rounds. Round 1: 12 semi-structured think-aloud interviews (5 experts, 4 experienced, 3 novices, all UiPath employees) over three models of increasing complexity (a laundry toy model, a cake-acquisition model, and a BPI2017 loan-application model), using 8 tasks (UST1–UST8) derived from 8 task types (filtering, lookup, pathfinding, etc.) and 5 use cases; screen recordings were re-coded into 15 generalized issues. Round 2: private issue ranking (converged without a second iteration), yielding a prioritized list. Design & development: requirements REQ1–REQ6 were derived from the top issues, prototyped through internal UiPath feedback iterations, and implemented in production code (C# back-end for sub-process discovery and natural-language tree generation; TypeScript front-end/visualization library). Round 3: evaluation with 3 participants (2 experts, 1 experienced) performing the same tasks, with per-requirement discussion. The LLM pipeline pre-computes names once per model, bottom-up through the tree. Notable design decisions: rejecting permanent gateway colorization (colorblind-safety, clutter), rejecting Reichert-style minimized closing gateways (users backtrack), and deferring edge filtering (REQ6) as future work—each justified from user-study evidence. Key Results: Results are qualitative. The Delphi study produced a ranked issue table (IS1 gateway distinguishability: 11 reports, priority 1; IS2 gateway-pair pairing: 8 reports, priority 2; IS3 trace filtering: 5 reports, priority 3, down to IS12–IS15 with 2–3 reports). Evaluation with 3 experts reported all implemented requirements as improving interpretability: new gateways were distinguishable even zoomed out, partner highlighting plus selective highlighting made sub-processes easy to isolate, and LLM sub-process naming was called the single highest-impact feature—though naming on BPI2017 was sometimes incorrect or non-descriptive, and participants warned LLM names could be mistaken for ground truth. REQ6 (edge filtering) was not implemented; users still wanted it but ranked it lower after abstraction. Anecdotal but unmeasured observation: participants completed tasks faster in round 3, which the author correctly declines to treat as a metric (no timings recorded, possible familiarity effects). No accuracy, error-rate, time-on-task, or statistical measures are reported anywhere; baselines are the pre-prototype UiPath product only. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first catalog and ranking of interpretability issues for aligned process models) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the integrated prototype in a commercial product); the individual techniques—selective highlighting from Emens et al., modularization/collapsing from La Rosa et al. and Deurloo, hover-based partner emphasis, semi-permanent highlighting—are standard ideas applied to a new model type, and the LLM-based sub-process naming is the only freshly combined element (and even that is a straightforward prompt over a rendered tree). Rigor & Reproducibility: There are no ablations in the quantitative sense; per-requirement evaluation discussions approximate component-level assessment but rely on 3 participants' opinions. No error bars, significance tests, or timings exist because the design is qualitative interview-based, which is defensible for exploratory DSR but limits evidential strength. The author honestly flags single-coder bias, the 12-participant single-company sample, and the 25% evaluation coverage. No code, dataset, or artifact release is mentioned; everything lives inside UiPath's proprietary codebase. Methodological concerns: evaluation participants are drawn from the same pool that shaped the requirements (circularity), the evaluation compares against only the authors' own prior product with no external system (e.g., Celonis BPMN views) as a baseline, and LLM naming correctness is never validated against any ground truth. As a student thesis, this is not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a prototype built into UiPath's commercial product and evaluated through guided user sessions) with a strong EMPIRICAL user-study component. - Practical: Yes—implemented in UiPath's existing product stack (C# back-end, TypeScript front-end) on standard hardware; the LLM step was even executed via copy-paste into an LLM rather than an API to control cost. - Efficient: Sub-process discovery and naming are pre-computed once per model, so interactive cost is comparable to the base viewer; no measurements are given, but nothing suggests added runtime burden. - Effective: Evidence is user-reported satisfaction from 3 insiders, not task-performance improvement—so it solves the problem only by proxy (perceived interpretability), and layout instability when expanding sub-processes actively degraded clarity. - Scalable: Not tested; the largest model is BPI2017, and the author notes the layout engine degrades with dynamic model changes, so behavior on models an order of magnitude larger is unknown and unclaimed beyond hope. The work delivers a production-integrated prototype inside UiPath, not a publicly released library, dataset, or trained model; its durable artifact is the paper-form issue catalog and requirements. Strengths: - The 15-issue ranked catalog of aligned-process-model interpretability problems, with per-issue report counts, is a concrete empirical contribution no prior work provides for this model class, and it generalizes to BPMN-style viewers. - The LLM-generated sub-process naming from a natural-language process-tree rendering is a timely, well-motivated idea (users called it the highest-impact feature), and the author proactively surfaces its correctness and trust risks rather than overselling it. - Design decisions are consistently grounded in user evidence and existing literature (e.g., rejecting colorization on colorblind-accessibility grounds, rejecting minimized closing gateways because users backtrack), not just designer preference. - Honest critical self-assessment: single-coder bias, single-company sample, unmeasured timing observations, and unsolved layout-engine issues are all openly stated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author explicitly states: all issue extraction was done by one person, introducing unavoidable bias; all 12 participants came from one company (UiPath), limiting generalizability; only 3 of 12 participants (25%) evaluated the prototype; layout instability under dynamic collapsing/expansion hurts interpretability and was out of scope; edge filtering (REQ6) remains unimplemented; LLM-generated names can be wrong and may be treated by users as ground truth; individual (per-edge) semi-permanent highlighting was requested but not delivered; and IS8 (gateway-pair vertical alignment) was deferred to the layout algorithm. This is a direct, non-defensive treatment of limitations—a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits, a reviewer would flag: (1) evaluation circularity—round-3 participants came from the same group whose feedback shaped the requirements, guaranteeing favorable reception; (2) no objective outcome measure of interpretability (task success rate, time, or errors) even though task completion speed was casually observed, so "interpretability improved" is claim, not measurement; (3) no comparison against any alternative approach (e.g., Celonis-style views, plain DFG with filtering, or a legend—which the author argues away without testing); (4) LLM naming was validated on only two toy domains and one real dataset, with no systematic accuracy assessment or failure-mode analysis despite naming being the headline feature; (5) the claimed generalization to "general process models" and conformance-checking use is asserted, not evaluated; and (6) no discussion of LLM cost or latency at scale for per-model, per-sub-process naming in customer deployments. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or designing process-model visualizations gains a genuinely useful, field-derived checklist of interpretability pitfalls and pragmatic fixes—especially the LLM sub-process naming pattern—but anyone seeking rigorous evidence of effectiveness should look to stronger controlled studies of process-model comprehension rather than this thesis's insider qualitative evaluation.

J Davison, K Liu, X Liu, Y Shao, C Pan, J Wyrzykowski · ieomsociety.org · digital twins for enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SupplyAssistAI, an LLM-powered multi-agent assistant deployed at Ford Motor Company that unifies structured supplier performance data and unstructured incident records into a conversational interface for delivery risk analytics and case management. - Why it's important: Automotive supply chain practitioners currently must manually synthesize fragmented dashboards, incident artifacts, and policy documents before acting on supplier disruptions, slowing decisions in a domain where disruptions cascade through multi-tier networks. - How it does it: The core mechanism is a distributed Model Context Protocol (MCP) toolset—each SCOR-aligned business domain (reliability, cost, agility, inventory exposure, risk, case resolution) is encapsulated in its own MCP server exposing retrieval, prompt templates, and insight generation—coordinated by an LLM orchestration layer. - The good: The system is described as actively deployed and production-integrated at Ford, grounded in a real digital twin and a SHAP-based predictive disruption model, which gives the architectural pattern more credibility than a pure lab prototype. - The missing: There is no quantitative evaluation of any kind—no accuracy, latency, cost, adoption, or user-study numbers—so the paper cannot substantiate that the system improves decision speed or quality over the fragmented workflows it critiques. - Read it or not: Read it if you are an enterprise architect or supply chain analytics lead designing multi-agent LLM systems over federated industrial data; skip it if you want rigorous evidence of agentic AI effectiveness, since the paper offers architecture and claims, not measurements.

Problem & Motivation: Business users in automotive supply chain operations face fragmented analytics workflows: when a supplier disruption occurs, they must navigate multiple dashboards, incident-resolution artifacts, performance metrics, and policy documents to assess risk and choose a response. The authors argue that even well-developed supply chain digital twin and risk analytics research (Ivanov and Dolgui 2021; Simchi-Levi et al. 2015; Do et al. 2024) remains fragmented across disconnected tools and teams, with limited integration into real-time decision workflows. The gap addressed is the absence of a unified, user-facing system that translates digital twin data and predictive risk signals into interactive, context-aware decision support for non-technical stakeholders. Key Idea: The core insight is that enterprise business logic can be modularized into a "knowledge broadcast layer" of independent MCP servers—one per SCOR-aligned data domain—each encapsulating data retrieval, curated prompts, and interpretation instructions, so that a generic LLM orchestrator can dynamically compose domain expertise on demand rather than baking it into a monolithic system. This decouples domain knowledge from orchestration, enabling independent development, reuse across applications, and additive scalability (new domains are new servers, not core-system changes). Methodology: This is a design/architecture paper for a production system, explicitly stated as a "functional proof-of-concept" rather than a model evaluation study. The pipeline has three components: (1) a web UI accepting natural language queries; (2) an LLM orchestration layer using function-calling to interpret intent and route requests; (3) a distributed MCP toolset organized by SCOR domains (RL.2.6 delivery reliability, CO.1.1 cost, AG.1.1/AG.2.2 agility, AM.2.2 inventory exposure, AG.1.4 risk exposure, supplier information, and two Enable-domain servers for knowledge and case resolution), each exposing structured retrieval, prompt generation, and LLM-based insight generation. A single-pass analysis follows: intent routing → tool deployment → data-driven reasoning under pre-defined domain instructions → response with follow-up suggestions, with conversation history maintained for context. Structured data comes from a supplier operations digital twin; unstructured data (policies, ICA/PCA corrective-action artifacts) is indexed via search-based semantic retrieval. A weekly-granularity XAI disruption-risk model (SHAP-based, automated ML pipeline, building on Do et al. 2024) supplies forward-looking risk signals that the assistant translates into natural-language explanations. A reporting pipeline generates analyst-level reports first, then derives management and executive summaries from them (to avoid duplication and reduce compute). Two design decisions deserve scrutiny: deriving higher-level reports from analyst reports rather than regenerating them is justified by consistency and cost arguments but is asserted, not measured; and embedding per-domain interpretation instructions in MCP server prompts is justified only by "business feedback," with no ablation of what this contributes to output quality. Key Results: Not stated. The paper reports no quantitative outcomes—no accuracy, precision/recall, latency, cost, adoption, or user-satisfaction figures for SupplyAssistAI itself. The "Results and Discussion" section presents functional capabilities (supplier performance/risk analysis, case management support, multi-level reporting, Custom Assistant for no-code persona creation, Scenario Planning Assistant for what-if simulation) illustrated via synthetic, generic walkthroughs (e.g., a hypothetical query about steering-column component risk). The underlying predictive risk model cites no performance metrics here; the reader is referred to prior work (Do et al. 2024). The claims of improved accessibility, faster decision-making, and emergent cross-domain insights are explicitly aspirational ("aims to," "potential for"), not measured. Baselines: none. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component; the genuinely novel element is the concrete enterprise instantiation of MCP servers as a decentralized, SCOR-aligned knowledge-broadcast layer for supply chain analytics—the constituent techniques (ReAct-style orchestration, function calling, RAG over unstructured documents, federated data access, SHAP explainability) are all standard, and their combination is a competent application to a new domain setting rather than a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak. There are no ablations, no error bars, no seeds, no significance tests, and no user evaluation—arguably forgivable for a proof-of-concept systems paper, but the absence of even basic operational telemetry (queries handled, time saved, report generation time) undercuts the "actively deployed" claim's evidentiary value. No code, data, or model weights are released, and the system is proprietary (figures are annotated as illustrating "interaction pattern, not proprietary logic"). The synthetic use-case is authored by the same team demonstrating the system on their own architecture, with no independent assessment. The predictive model component is trained and evaluated outside this paper, so its quality cannot be verified from this document. Methodological concern: the paper claims scalability and reusability as architectural advantages but presents no experiment at any scale beyond the single Ford deployment. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, deployed tool evaluated—if at all—by deployment, not by benchmarks). - Practical: Yes—it runs within Ford's secure enterprise cloud boundary with RBAC, on commercially available cloud infrastructure, and is described as in production use. - Efficient: Not stated—no cost, latency, or token-throughput figures are given, though the reporting pipeline's pre-stored analyst reports are claimed to reduce compute for higher-level summaries. - Effective: Unproven—the paper shows the system can synthesize cross-domain data into conversational answers, but offers no evidence it solves the decision-speed or decision-quality problem better than the dashboard workflows it replaces. - Scalable: Claimed architecturally (add MCP servers additively) but untested at any expanded scale; 10×–100× behavior in cost, orchestration complexity, or routing accuracy is unexamined. The work delivers a deployed internal enterprise tool plus a reusable architectural pattern; no software artifact or dataset is publicly released. Strengths: - The MCP-server-as-knowledge-broadcast-layer pattern is a genuinely useful architectural abstraction for enterprises with federated, domain-owned data: it cleanly separates domain logic (data access, curated prompts, interpretation instructions) from orchestration, and the per-domain "broadcast" of both data slices and interpretation guidance to the LLM is a concrete, transferable design. - The grounding in a real, standardized ontology (SCOR Digital Standard, with specific metric codes like RL.2.6 and AG.1.4) gives the domain decomposition a principled, industry-legible structure rather than ad-hoc bucketing. - The tiered reporting pipeline (analyst report generated once from all MCP domains, then derived upward for management and executives) is a sensible cost/consistency tradeoff for multi-audience reporting that most agentic-system papers ignore. - The integration of a SHAP-based XAI pipeline with LLM natural-language translation connects quantitative risk modeling to business-readable explanations—a concrete answer to the known gap between predictive analytics and actionable insight. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge hallucination risk, mitigated via a human-in-the-loop paradigm where all final operational actions and case resolutions require human validation, and note governance constraints (RBAC, secure cloud boundary). They implicitly acknowledge the proof-of-concept nature of the work ("Rather than evaluating a single predictive model, this study defines the architecture..."). They do not, however, confront the absence of any effectiveness measurement, and the "business impact" section is framed in potential terms—this is partial acknowledgment, with the severity of the evidentiary gap minimized rather than addressed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Zero quantitative evaluation: no adoption metrics, no time-to-decision comparisons, no error analysis of routed queries, no measurement of answer accuracy against ground truth—a critical omission for a system whose value proposition is faster, better decisions. - No LLM failure-mode analysis: routing errors, incorrect tool selection, and cross-domain synthesis mistakes are not studied, even though the orchestration layer's correctness is the system's linchpin. - The predictive risk model's performance is unreported here, so the "forward-looking risk" capability the system relies on cannot be assessed from this paper. - Figures 2–4 use synthetic, generic scenarios; no real production interaction (even anonymized) is shown, weakening the deployment claim. - Security/prompt-injection risks—agentic systems with tool access over unstructured enterprise documents—receive no treatment beyond RBAC. - The claimed advantage over simpler alternatives (a single well-prompted LLM with a unified RAG index over the same data) is never tested; the multi-server decomposition's benefit over a monolithic assistant is asserted, not demonstrated. - No external or independent validation; all authors are Ford employees reporting on their own system (vendor-style self-report). Bottom Line: Practitioners designing federated multi-agent LLM architectures for industrial analytics will find a useful, transferable architectural pattern here, but anyone seeking evidence that such systems actually improve supply chain decision-making will need to look elsewhere—this paper sells the blueprint, not the proof.

Problem & Motivation: Universities — as institutions with teaching, research, and civic-engagement missions — are undergoing digitalization that reshapes authority, professional autonomy, and organizational culture, yet prior approaches treat digital transformation as discrete technology adoption within an otherwise stable institution. International bodies (OECD, UNESCO, European University Association) have flagged AI, data infrastructures, and digitally enhanced learning as system-level forces, raising unresolved questions about fairness, academic honesty, and institutional accountability. The book targets the gap between descriptive accounts of technology uptake and explanatory accounts of institutional change, deliberately focusing on the post-pandemic phase as a period of strategic consolidation distinct from crisis-driven emergency remote teaching. Key Idea: The single core insight is the "new academic wave" framing: digitalization is an institutional recomposition — it restructures authority, redistributes professional autonomy, and redefines missions — rather than a tooling problem. Once this is accepted, every chapter's content follows: governance becomes data-informed and contested (Ch. 4), power simultaneously centralizes (enterprise systems, executive data control) and decentralizes (information access, participation) depending on how institutions manage the tension (Ch. 9), and culture, not technology, becomes the binding constraint on transformation (Ch. 8). This is a lens, not a mechanism with testable predictions. Methodology: The book is organized in five parts and sixteen chapters moving from academic missions (research ecosystems, teaching, third mission), through governance/leadership/administration, organizational dynamics (strategy, culture, power), and management functions (HR, marketing, finance), to a synthetic articulation of the framework and a dedicated empirical case-study chapter (Ch. 16). The stated empirical design uses methodological triangulation across three evidence types: documentary sources (strategy documents, transformation reports, governance communications), semi-structured interviews with leaders, faculty, administrators, and IT staff, and direct/participant observation of digitally mediated environments. Case studies are positioned as analytically selective illustrations anchored to specific conceptual strands, explicitly not as institutional portraits or comparative evaluations; institutions span North America, Europe, and Asia, including research universities, born-digital institutions, and universities of applied sciences. Critical design decisions: (1) restricting fieldwork to the post-pandemic window to separate strategic digitalization from crisis response — well-motivated and clearly argued; (2) using cases as interpretive lenses rather than evaluation units — defensible for a theory-driven monograph but it forecloses falsification; (3) separating methodology from the introduction — transparency-positive, though the excerpt does not contain the methodology itself. Key Results: Not stated in the conventional sense — this is a qualitative conceptual monograph with no quantitative outcomes, benchmarks, or baselines. The reported findings are conceptual claims: digitalization both centralizes and decentralizes authority, with outcomes contingent on governance design; commercial publishers have vertically integrated the research lifecycle (repositories, CRIS, analytics), creating a "closed loop of algorithmic surveillance" sold back to universities; global-South institutions face infrastructure, labor-division, and data-sovereignty inequalities constituting "data colonialism"; AI detectors and remote proctoring are unreliable and inequitable integrity responses; and post-pandemic digitalization exposed layered digital divides (material, literacy, cognitive-load, accessibility). Chapter 1 explicitly disclaims a generalizable empirical model, positioning itself as theoretical foundation-setting. Scale of empirical testing: Not stated in the excerpt (case details reside in Chapter 16, not included in the provided text). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the "new academic wave" integrative framework) plus a synthesis/position contribution. The genuinely novel element is the packaging: a single framework unifying missions, governance, culture, power, and management functions under one institutional-recomposition lens. The underlying content — FAIR principles, open science tensions, learning-analytics ethics, actor-network theory, surveillance capitalism critiques, digital divides, micro-credentials — is a standard assembly of well-established ideas from higher education studies and STS applied to the post-pandemic moment; readers familiar with that literature will find little conceptually new per topic. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests are applicable or reported; this is interpretive qualitative scholarship, where rigor would instead mean a transparent protocol, case-selection logic, coding strategy, and inter-coder handling — the authors promise a dedicated methodological section and Chapter 16, neither of which is in the provided excerpt, so the actual evidentiary chain cannot be verified here. The book is gold open access under CC BY-NC-ND (DOI: 10.4324/9781042001422), published by Routledge; no code, dataset, or instrument release is mentioned. Two flags: (1) several chapters, including all of Chapter 1 in the excerpt, are admittedly built on "conceptual and literature-based examples" rather than the authors' fieldwork, which risks the framework being evaluated against illustrations chosen to fit it (circularity); (2) the authors disclose substantial LLM-assisted drafting (ChatGPT/GPT-4o and Claude) with human revision — disclosed transparently and scoped away from data analysis and theory development, which is credibility-positive but places the burden of verification entirely on the authors' self-report. The 2027 imprint date indicates a forthcoming publication. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (qualitative fieldwork and case studies, though much of the excerpt is conceptual synthesis rather than primary empirical reporting). - Practical: As a scholarly monograph, its "deployment" is readership — it is freely and legally reusable (with No-Derivatives restrictions) by administrators and researchers, requiring no specialized resources. - Efficient: Not applicable to compute; the framework is lightweight to adopt as a diagnostic vocabulary, though the authors themselves warn that cultural change, not tooling, is the expensive part. - Effective: The evidence that the framework explains institutional change (rather than merely describes it) rests on case illustrations promised for Chapter 16 and is not demonstrated in the provided material — effectiveness is claimed, not yet shown. - Scalable: The framework is stated to apply across institution types and continents, but no systematic cross-case analysis appears in the excerpt; generalization is asserted by design intent, not tested at breadth. The deliverable is a book (conceptual framework plus practical guidance); no software artifact, dataset, or reusable instrument is produced. Strengths: - Genuine integrative ambition: most accounts of digital higher education address one slice (pedagogy, or governance, or open science); this framework explicitly binds missions, management functions, culture, and power into one analytical structure, which is a real contribution to the field's vocabulary. - Exceptional transparency practices: the detailed author's note on LLM assistance (specifying tools, tasks, and exclusions) and the explicit repositioning of case studies as non-generalizable illustrations model disclosure standards the field itself lacks — a performatively apt choice for a book about academic integrity in the AI era. - The critical chapters are substantively sharp, not decorative: the analysis of publisher vertical integration of research infrastructure (platform gatekeeping, proprietary metrics sold back to universities) and of data colonialism in global research labor divisions are concrete, well-sourced critiques rather than generic anxieties. - The post-pandemic phase demarcation is a useful analytical discipline that distinguishes strategic digital maturation from emergency remote teaching, a distinction most practitioner literature still blurs. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that case studies are not comprehensive institutional portraits, do not claim generalizable models, and are not comparative or evaluative; Chapter 1 additionally disclaims any generalizable empirical model of digital research transformation. They acknowledge that the framework will need adjustment where evidence proves "more complex or contested than initially anticipated" (Ch. 13's stated function) and that digitalization's contradictions — ethical dilemmas, structural inequality, resistance — are unresolved (Ch. 14). They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility. They also candidly surface the irony of their own LLM use as part of the phenomenon under study. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central weakness a reviewer would flag: the framework appears unfalsifiable as presented — cases are selected as "analytically selective illustrations" of mechanisms the framework posits, which cannot confirm or disconfirm it; no disconfirming case, negative instance, or competing-framework comparison is described in the excerpt. - The provided material shows Chapters 1–2 built substantially on literature synthesis and generic vignettes ("a medium-sized university used an AI-based personalised learning platform") rather than the authors' own fieldwork, blurring the boundary between the book's claimed original empirical contribution and a well-organized literature review. - No competing frameworks (e.g., established digital-transformation maturity models, institutional theory variants) are engaged or outperformed; the reader cannot tell what the new academic wave explains that existing frameworks do not. - Heavy citation of a small set of anchor works per section, with some empirical assertions stated in unconditional language ("algorithms prioritise corporate profitability over scientific validity") that outrun the cited evidence. - The book critiques proprietary metrics and algorithmic evaluation of academia while being an LLM-drafted monograph — the authors address this irony, but a skeptical reader may want stronger procedural safeguards (e.g., independent verification of AI-drafted passages) than self-attestation. Bottom Line: A higher-education researcher, leader, or policymaker gains a useful, honestly constructed synthetic vocabulary for institutional digital change, but anyone seeking tested theory, quantitative evidence, or a framework superior to existing alternatives should wait to see whether Chapter 16's case studies deliver the evidentiary weight the framing promises.

Problem & Motivation: Manufacturing organizations face unplanned downtime, inefficient resource use, quality deviations, and mounting sustainability pressures. The paper argues the core gap is an "isolation gap": digital twins are mostly deployed as monitoring/visualization layers, while AI/ML initiatives are trained on historical data with no live, synchronized representation of the plant — so twins describe what is happening but cannot predict what will happen, and AI models operate on stale context. A second gap is that DT/AI projects are evaluated on technical metrics (accuracy, precision) rather than operational, financial, resilience, or sustainability outcomes, weakening investment justification. A third is that governance concerns (data quality, model drift, cybersecurity of converged IT/OT, human oversight) are treated as afterthoughts rather than cross-cutting requirements. The intended audience is manufacturers (including SMEs with varying digital maturity), technology providers, and researchers. Key Idea: The core move is architectural consolidation plus value tracing: compose the recurring components found independently across ten fragmented literatures into one six-layer, closed-loop socio-technical architecture, and require every technical layer to be traceable to at least one measurable business or sustainability outcome via a value-mapping table and KPI framework, with a governance layer spanning all layers rather than appended at the end. There is no new algorithm or mathematical insight — the paper itself states its contribution "lies not in proposing a single technology or algorithm." Methodology: The paper follows design-science research methodology with a structured (not fully systematic) literature synthesis: (1) problem identification from prior studies; (2) a Boolean-keyword search across engineering, CS, manufacturing, and operations-management sources (2015–2025, peer-reviewed, English); (3) title/abstract screening then full-text review; (4) extraction of publication year, focus, benefits, limitations, and governance/sustainability findings; (5) thematic coding into ten categories (DT architecture; predictive maintenance/ML; prescriptive analytics; DT-AI integration; smart factory/Industry 4.0; resilience; sustainability; explainable AI; cybersecurity/governance; IIoT/edge infrastructure); (6) framework synthesis in which components recurring across several independent studies became core layers and single-study components became optional. Conceptual validation comprises three checks: literature traceability of each layer, coverage of six research objectives (Table 3), and structural comparison with RAMI 4.0, ISO 23247, the 5C architecture, and Tao's five-dimension model (Table 4). Critical design decisions: treating sustainability as an embedded value metric rather than a separate stream, separating human decision support from analytics as distinct layers, and staging automation via a six-phase roadmap — all argued from the literature but none justified experimentally. Key Results: There are no quantitative results; the paper explicitly states results are "the framework, mappings, and validation checks produced by that synthesis rather than statistical findings." The reported outcomes are: (1) identification of the isolation gap as the most consistent cross-literature finding from the 150 coded sources; (2) convergence of independently reported components from ten themes onto a stable six-layer structure plus cross-cutting governance layer; (3) a business-value mapping (Table 1) linking seven capabilities (predictive maintenance alerts, prescriptive scheduling, quality forecasting, energy analytics, twin simulation, explainable AI, resilience forecasting) to operational and financial/sustainability outcomes; (4) a KPI taxonomy (Table 2) spanning operational/detection, quality, financial, sustainability, resilience, and governance/trust categories; and (5) conceptual validation showing each layer traces to multiple sources, all six objectives are covered, and no element of the four reference architectures is omitted. No baseline comparisons, benchmarks, or measured effects exist. The reference architectures compared are appropriate and current for this domain, but the comparison is a self-assessed qualitative table, not an independent evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (a consolidated reference architecture + value-mapping/KPI structure) and, marginally, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL in blueprint form only. The genuinely new element is the explicit, table-level linkage of every technical layer to business and sustainability KPIs and governance domains — an integration prior reference models (RAMI 4.0, ISO 23247, 5C, Tao) leave implicit. Everything else is a competent combination of well-established ideas: layered DT architectures, predictive maintenance, human-in-the-loop AI, phased maturity roadmaps, and standard governance domains, all applied to a setting where each ingredient already exists. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations, error bars, seeds, and significance tests are inapplicable — no experiments were run. The literature synthesis is reproducible only in outline: search keywords and inclusion/exclusion criteria are described, but no PRISMA-style flow, source list of the 150 included works (the visible reference list appears truncated), coding scheme, or inter-rater procedure is provided, and the authors admit the review was single-reviewer with no inter-rater reliability testing. No code, data, or artifact is released. The conceptual validation is self-referential: the same author who constructed the framework judges its traceability, coverage, and consistency, which limits independence. The KPI framework (e.g., model drift frequency, operator override rate) is well-conceived but has never been operationalized, so the framework risks being unfalsifiable as written. Deployability: Profile: none of the three cleanly fits — this is a conceptual design-science paper with no experiments and no proofs; applying the closest SYSTEMS-style check to the proposed (unbuilt) architecture: Practical: the architecture targets commercially available industrial hardware (PLCs, IIoT sensors, edge/cloud), so nothing is inherently impractical; Efficient: no compute, latency, bandwidth, or cost figures are given for any layer — the edge-processing rationale is asserted, not quantified; Effective: no evidence shows it solves the stated problem; the authors themselves state all benefit claims "should be considered conceptual rather than conclusively demonstrated"; Scalable: multi-site expansion is discussed qualitatively (federated DTs, transfer learning) but nothing has been tested beyond the paper's own hypothetical. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model — it stops at paper form (tables, roadmap, KPI list). Strengths: - Honest, front-loaded acknowledgment that the framework is conceptual and unvalidated — the limitations section and conclusion repeatedly bar readers from treating expected benefits as established, which is rarer and more credible than typical framework papers. - The business-value mapping (Table 1) and KPI taxonomy (Table 2) are the most actionable artifacts: they convert a vague "integrate DT and AI" ambition into a checkable list of capabilities → outcomes → indicators, which practitioners could adopt directly as an investment-justification template. - The structural comparison against RAMI 4.0, ISO 23247, the 5C architecture, and Tao's model is done precisely and positions the contribution honestly as an extension (explicit value/KPI mapping) rather than a replacement. - Broad, current synthesis (150 sources, 2015–2025) across ten themes, correctly surfacing cross-cutting requirements — governance, data quality, explainability, IT/OT cybersecurity — that most single-technology papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly: (1) the framework has never been tested with operational data, so expected benefits are not empirically proven; (2) the literature search was not a fully systematic review (no multiple independent reviewers, no inter-rater reliability); (3) the 2015–2025 window may miss very recent developments; (4) legacy-equipment interoperability, scarce historical failure data, poor model generalization across assets, explainability/trust barriers, IT/OT cybersecurity risk, and workforce readiness all complicate adoption. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No minimal worked example: even a synthetic or single-asset toy case exercising the six layers (e.g., a simulated vibration-to-alert-to-maintenance-window loop) would have tested internal coherence; none is provided. - The conceptual validation is self-assessed by the framework's designer; no independent reviewer or external expert panel checked traceability or architecture coverage, weakening the "validation" label. - The value mapping is qualitative; no illustrative quantification (e.g., published downtime-reduction percentages from the predictive-maintenance literature it cites) is attached to any capability-to-outcome link, so the mapping's practical bite is untested. - The visible reference list contains entries that appear unrelated to the paper's topic (photovoltaic quantum-dot sensitization, triboelectric nanogenerators, CRM analytics, fraud detection) from a small cluster of authors and DOI prefixes; whatever the explanation, this undermines confidence in the screening rigor of a synthesis whose entire contribution rests on literature quality. - Trade-offs the framework claims to handle (throughput vs. energy, prediction accuracy vs. explanation latency, automation vs. oversight cost) are named but never formalized — no multi-objective structure or decision procedure is specified for how a plant would actually resolve them. - The 150-source corpus is not retrievable from the paper, so the central synthesis cannot be independently audited. Bottom Line: A practitioner designing a DT-AI adoption program could steal the value-mapping table, KPI taxonomy, and six-phase roadmap as useful checklists, but anyone wanting evidence that this integration actually works — or a technical advance beyond existing reference architectures — should look to the empirical DT-AI pilot literature and established standards (ISO 23247, RAMI 4.0) that this paper merely extends on paper.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations cannot rely on signature-based IDS to catch zero-day exploits, modified malware, or never-seen behaviors; ML-based anomaly and open-set methods are the leading alternative, but the research is fragmented across subfields and prior reviews do not connect the limitations reported in individual studies to the design of a small, deployable detection system. The authors (undergraduate students and a faculty guide) target that gap with a structured literature review intended for readers deciding which detection paradigm and dataset to adopt, and which evaluation protocols actually predict real-world zero-day performance. Key Idea: There is no single new technical insight. The organizing idea is an eight-theme taxonomy plus a three-part empirical pattern extracted from the surveyed work: (1) headline scores above 99.9% come almost exclusively from binary or in-distribution tests, (2) performance drops 13–17 points when the task changes to naming unseen attacks or crossing datasets, and (3) deployment evidence (real-vehicle tests, latency measurements) is rare. This pattern motivates the paper's prescriptive recommendation: a layered design combining a supervised known-attack classifier with a one-class unknown-behavior detector, evaluated with withheld attack families and cross-dataset splits. Methodology: The review follows Kitchenham's planning–conducting–reporting structure. The corpus is twenty peer-reviewed studies (2024–2026) in venues such as IEEE Access, Scientific Reports, Computers & Security, Computer Networks, and PLOS ONE, supplemented by foundational method papers (Isolation Forest, OC-SVM, OpenMax, MAML, VAE), dataset papers (NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, CIC-DDoS2019, AWID, ToN-IoT, CICIoT2023, Kitsune, NetFlow feature sets), and NIST guidance. Inclusion required relevance to at least one taxonomy theme, reported evaluation, and a verifiable source. The paper explicitly positions itself as integrative, not a quantitative meta-analysis, because quoted results were produced on incomparable datasets, splits, and definitions of "unknown." The reference prototype uses a Decision Tree (max depth 5, 80/20 split) for known attacks and an Isolation Forest (contamination 0.1) for unknown behavior, served through a Flask web API with four hand-entered flow features (duration, source bytes, destination bytes, connection count); the authors correctly identify that a combination rule for the two models is still needed and that the fixed contamination assumption is a weakness. Key Results: The paper reports no new experimental results beyond the prototype's single measured figure: ~66.67% accuracy for the Decision Tree through the Flask interface on a small, unnamed sample dataset — with no confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, or dataset description. The substantive quantitative content is secondhand: Dai et al. report 99.99% F1 with autoencoder+RF/XGBoost; Krishnan et al. report 99.9966% binary but only 71.09% accuracy / 74.41% F1 on zero-day multiclass; Zhang et al. drop from 97.28% (CICIDS2017) to 85.47% (UNSW-NB15); MAML falls ~13 points across CICIDS2017 → CICIoT2023 → CIC-UNSW-NB15; Li et al. measured a 13% false-positive rate in a real-vehicle deployment; Hossain et al. report 93.94% zero-day detection at 0.50 ms latency with Siamese+PPO. All baselines and numbers are the original authors' self-reports on heterogeneous protocols, which the review acknowledges are not directly comparable. Novelty Classification: At most NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (weak) and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (weak) — the taxonomy, the synthesis of the binary-vs-multiclass and cross-dataset degradation patterns, and the Flask prototype are all standard combinations of existing ideas; the survey's differentiator is its explicit linkage of per-study limitations to deployment guidance, which earlier surveys (Por et al. 2024; Al Siam et al. 2026) already partially cover. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a review, its rigor rests on corpus selection and synthesis; the selection process is described but not systematic in the PRISMA sense (no search strings, no exclusion counts, no duplicate screening), and the corpus of twenty hand-picked studies risks selection bias. No ablations, seeds, or significance tests apply, and no code, data, or model artifacts are released (no repository URL is given). The prototype is irreproducible as described: the "small sample dataset" is not named or sized, and only one accuracy figure is reported. A credibility positive: the authors repeatedly and explicitly refuse to generalize the 66.67% figure and call their own results a "starting point." Methodological concern: the review quotes vendor-style self-reported numbers (e.g., 99.99% accuracy claims) without independent verification, though it does flag known dataset problems via Engelen et al.'s CIC-IDS2017 critique and Arp et al.'s pitfalls list. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built Flask prototype) wrapped in a survey; the check applies to the prototype. Practical: Yes — it runs on commodity hardware with Python, Scikit-learn, and Flask, using a depth-5 Decision Tree and Isolation Forest. Efficient: Trivially cheap relative to deep alternatives, though efficiency was not measured. Effective: Not established — the only evidence is 66.67% accuracy on an unnamed small dataset, far below every surveyed system, and the unknown-attack combination rule is still unspecified. Scalable: Not tested or claimed beyond the toy sample; real traffic ingestion, retraining, and latency under load are unaddressed. The deliverable is a paper only; no library, dataset, or trained model artifact is released. Strengths: - Honest calibration of evidence: the paper distinguishes self-reported claims from measured reality and explicitly refuses to compare incomparable numbers — rare discipline for a survey at this level. - The synthesis of degradation patterns (99.9%+ binary vs. 71.09% zero-day multiclass; 13–17 point cross-dataset drops; one 13% real-world false-positive rate) is a useful, quotable takeaway for anyone evaluating detection papers. - Strong engagement with evaluation-methodology literature (Arp et al.'s dos-and-don'ts, Engelen et al.'s CIC-IDS2017 audit, time-based and withheld-family protocols), which correctly identifies random train–test splits as invalid for zero-day claims. - The prototype critique of its own design (fixed contamination = assuming 10% anomaly rate; need to fit Isolation Forest on benign-only traffic and calibrate thresholds) is technically sound. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that quoted results are not directly comparable; that the prototype's 66.67% is not a general claim and lacks confusion matrix/precision/recall/F1; that the Isolation Forest's fixed 0.1 contamination assumes an unsupported anomaly rate; that a rule for combining the two models is missing; that the system has not been tested on modern datasets, across datasets, or with withheld attack families; and that all intended outcomes (real-time monitoring, fewer false alarms) "must be established by controlled evaluation." This is unusually direct limitation disclosure and a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The corpus of twenty studies is selected without documented search strategy, keyword lists, or exclusion accounting, so coverage claims ("eight themes," "twenty recent studies") cannot be assessed for completeness; the 2024–2026 window excludes the foundational deep-learning IDS work the field actually builds on (only Kitsune 2018 and Hindy 2020 appear). - The reference system ingests four manually entered flow features through a web form — this is a demo, not a network detector; the gap between "web form with four numbers" and "real-time traffic monitoring" is not confronted as bluntly as it should be. - The review does not evaluate the surveyed studies against the pitfalls criteria it endorses (e.g., which of the twenty actually used withheld-family or time-based splits), so the taxonomy is descriptive rather than a quality assessment. - No comparison of the prototype against even the weakest surveyed baseline, and no discussion of why a depth-5 Decision Tree was chosen over the stronger surveyed methods it reviews. - Several cited works carry 2026 publication dates in a journal issue dated October 2026, and the SJIF self-rating of the venue (8.659) is not a recognized quality signal; peer-review rigor of the surveyed claims should be treated cautiously. Bottom Line: A student cannot do better than to read the primary surveys this paper cites (Por et al. 2024, Al Siam et al. 2026, Arp et al. 2022) — this review adds only a modest reading list and a candid but untested toy prototype, and a practitioner will find stronger, deeper coverage elsewhere.

Problem & Motivation: Construction knowledge is distributed across temporary, multidisciplinary teams, firms, and lifecycle stages (design, construction, facility management). Practical judgment is often tacit and held by experienced participants who may be reassigned before their reasoning is documented, while written records may omit the conditions, alternatives, and outcome measures needed for a later team to judge a lesson's applicability. Prior literature (e.g., Wang & Meng's review of 115 IT-based and 73 BIM-supported knowledge-management publications through 2018) reports barriers such as delayed reporting, staff movement, unread reports, terminology mismatch in keyword retrieval, siloed working, and late stakeholder involvement — yet those reviews lack empirical support and cover only pre-2019 material. The paper targets the gap that no one has verified whether these reported gaps persisted through 2022–2026, and that existing accounts conflate the existence of a recording practice with evidence that its contents are retrieved, interpreted, and reused on another project. Key Idea: The single core insight is that knowledge transfer must be evaluated as a chain of analytically separable events — capture, sharing, storage, retrieval, interpretation, and application — and that a record's availability is never itself evidence of reuse. Concretely: a repository entry, a search hit, or a BIM object attachment does not establish that a later user understood or applied a lesson; a contextually justified decision not to repeat a recorded practice (because operating conditions differ) is not failed learning. This yields an extraction/appraisal framework coding each study by setting, lifecycle stage, knowledge activity, method, intended users, and evidence of application, while tagging relationships as observed, proposed, or uncertain. Methodology: The planned method is a qualitative evidence synthesis restricted to published, peer-reviewed research dated 2022–2026, modeled on Wang and Meng's procedure (explicit search and screening criteria, extraction by project phase and knowledge-management activity, independent second-author checks, documented disagreement resolution). The delivered portion of the paper is a narrative conceptual synthesis of a set of supplied sources — the BAN knowledge-management model (built on SECI: socialization, externalization, combination, internalization), Duryan & Smyth's client/supply-chain interview study, Wang & Meng's reviews, Murguia et al.'s facility-management taxonomy and preliminary tool, technical case material (Bijleveld's asphalt compaction monitoring), and several proposed tools (BIM-based sharing systems, knowledge maps, scheduling search tools). Critical design decisions: (1) treating capture/transfer/reuse as distinct rather than a single documentation act — well argued; (2) using SECI only as a lens and explicitly rejecting a fixed four-step conversion sequence — justified, including flagging an internal inconsistency in Yalçın & Yavuz Pelvan's definition of socialization; (3) including technical case studies (asphalt: roller strategies varying across comparable mixtures, 2–9 minute paving-to-roller intervals implying ~25 °C differences, fracture energy up to ~20–30% lower outside the 135–155 °C compaction window) as illustrations of why lessons need conditions attached — defensible but tangential to knowledge-management evaluation. Key Results: No quantitative or completed-synthesis results are reported — the paper states plainly that "no completed search, screening record, or eligible study set for the target period is available." The qualitative outcomes are: (a) a catalog of situated barriers from Duryan & Smyth's interview study (detail lost between learning and reporting, staff movement, unread reports, platforms unavailable across a programme, low compliance with required lessons-learned processes, hierarchical/defensive sharing); (b) a catalog of candidate mechanisms (post-project reviews, knowledge maps, the BAN model's review/categorization/consultation provisions, BIM-based visual sharing systems, communities of practice) none of which, the paper stresses, has demonstrated cross-project reuse; and (c) the observation from prior reviews that lessons have "not been implemented in later projects as extensively as expected" despite widespread recording practices. Baseline comparisons are not applicable; the evidence scale is a handful of narrative sources rather than a systematic corpus. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (partially) — the genuine contribution is an evidential-status and transfer-chain appraisal scheme that separates proposed mechanisms from observed outcomes in construction knowledge-management literature; everything else (SECI, the capture–storage–retrieval–reuse decomposition, the barrier catalog, the BAN model, BIM-based tools) is a competent combination of existing ideas. No new method, dataset, system, or empirical finding is delivered in this document. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations, error bars, seeds, and significance tests are not applicable to a qualitative synthesis. Reproducibility is the central weakness: the paper itself concedes there is no search strategy, no screening record, no exclusion log, and no eligible study set — so another researcher cannot reproduce or verify any claim about 2022–2026 literature. No code, data, or artifact is released. Methodological concerns: the corpus is the authors' own supplied chunks (including a dissertation, an accepted-but-dated review, and preliminary tool proposals) rather than a systematically assembled body of evidence; the framework is developed on the same informal material it would later appraise; and citations include items dated "n.d." and forthcoming (2026). The paper does follow review-methodology precedent explicitly and cites it (Wang & Meng's screening/extraction protocol), which is a rigor positive for the planned protocol even though none of it has been executed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (qualitative literature synthesis / conceptual analysis), though closer to a protocol than a completed study. - Practical: Yes — it requires no hardware or software, only database access for the planned search. - Efficient: Cost is low (single-author narrative synthesis), but the completed protocol (search, dual screening, appraisal) would require substantially more effort not yet budgeted or demonstrated. - Effective: Not yet demonstrated — the framework solves a proxy (organizing how to appraise studies) but has not been shown to yield valid conclusions when applied to a real corpus. - Scalable: Not evaluated — whether the extraction framework remains tractable over a full 2022–2026 publication corpus is untested. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model; it stops at paper (protocol/framework) form. Strengths: - Exceptional epistemic discipline: the paper consistently refuses to convert proposed mechanisms (BAN model features, BIM systems, taxonomies) into claims of demonstrated reuse, and explicitly bounds its conclusions until eligible studies are appraised — a level of claim-evidence hygiene rarely seen in this literature. - A genuinely useful analytical decomposition (availability vs. interpretation vs. application; reported barrier vs. proposed response vs. observed reuse) that directly addresses a real flaw in prior reviews, including Wang & Meng's own acknowledged lack of empirical support. - Sharp identification of conceptual inconsistencies in the source literature, e.g., the contradictory definitions of SECI socialization across two cited accounts, and the caution that keyword retrieval fails across disciplinary terminology boundaries. - The asphalt-compaction material, while tangential, is deployed to make a non-obvious point: a lesson needs its operating conditions and outcome measures (e.g., density achieved but fracture energy ~20–30% lower outside the optimum temperature window) to be appraisable — a concrete grounding for an otherwise abstract argument. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensively and directly acknowledged — this is the paper's most distinctive feature. The authors state that: no completed search, screening record, or eligible study set exists for 2022–2026; the supplied chunks include non-eligible material (an older review, a dissertation, preliminary tool structures); barriers reported in the Duryan & Smyth study are situated findings, not prevalence estimates; proposed models and theoretical-stage frameworks are not validated interventions; the published-only restriction limits claims about practice; and the eventual framework would be an "evidence-informed synthesis, not an empirically validated intervention." The authors confront limitations head-on rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central deliverable (the qualitative evidence synthesis of 2022–2026 literature) is absent, making the paper a protocol/prelude rather than a contribution that can be assessed on outcomes; a reviewer must judge a framework that has never been applied. - No comparison to existing evidence-synthesis frameworks in construction management (e.g., prior systematic reviews or meta-aggregation approaches beyond Wang & Meng), so the claim that the framework improves appraisal is unbenchmarked. - The corpus is self-supplied and possibly curated by the author or an external pipeline (the text references "supplied chunks" repeatedly), which raises selection-bias concerns the paper does not address. - The asphalt-compaction case material consumes substantial space but does not evaluate any knowledge-management mechanism, and the paper does not justify its proportionate weight in the argument. - No timeline, criteria, or feasibility evidence for actually completing the promised synthesis; nothing prevents the framework from remaining permanently unvalidated. - Single author with no reported inter-rater reliability for the extraction/appraisal scheme, despite recommending independent extraction in the protocol. Bottom Line: A rigorously hedged but ultimately incomplete protocol-plus-framework that a construction knowledge-management researcher designing a systematic review may find useful as an appraisal template, but which offers no findings, no validation, and no deliverable beyond promises — stronger, completed syntheses of construction lessons-learned literature are available elsewhere.
